[Page 1]
SPECIAL ISSUE ARTICLE
What is the glamor of black-and-white? The effect of color
design on evaluations of luxury brand ads
Yu Wang1 | Tao Wang 1,2 | Wenlong Mu 1 | Yifan Sun 1
1School of Economics and Management,
Wuhan University, Wuhan, China
2Research Center for Organizational
Marketing, Wuhan University, Wuhan, China
Correspondence
Wenlong Mu, School of Economics and
Management, Wuhan University, Bayi Road,
Wuchang District, Wuhan, Hubei, China.
Email: mu.w@whu.edu.cn
Funding information
National Natural Science Foundation of China,
Grant/Award Number: 72172107
Abstract
Visual esthetic stimuli are believed to be an important factor in increasing luxury
brands attitudes. However, less attention has been given by existing research to how
the presence or absence of color (i.e., color vs. black-and-white) influences con-
sumers' perceptions of products and evaluations toward luxury ads. Drawing on the
perspective of esthetic meaning and the theory of psychological distance, this study
provides key evidence for addressing this gap. Three studies have found that black-
and-white (BW) (vs. color) is associated with the luxuriousness of products and evalu-
ations of luxury brand ads. Specifically, Study 1 shows that BW (vs. color) design can
enhance consumers' evaluations of luxury brand ads by enhancing the perceived lux-
uriousness of products. In addition, Study 2 indicates that ad appeal plays a moderat-
ing role in the link between color design (BW vs. color) and ad evaluations such that
the effect of BW designs (vs. color design) will be higher for consumers when ads
focus on hedonic (vs. utilitarian) appeals. Study 3 further shows that BW is more
effective for luxury brand ads than both iconic and noniconic colors. In sum, our
results extend the existing literature and provide valuable management strategies for
luxury brand marketing management in visual esthetic design.
1 | INTRODUCTION
Global luxury marketing has seen major growth in the last 30 years
and is expected to grow exponentially in the future as Millennials and
Generation Z take the lead in luxury consumption (de Kerviler &
Rodriguez, 2019; Shin et al., 2017). Notably, this great attractive-
ness cannot be separated from the marketing principles that luxury
brands have always adhered to, namely, creating and maintaining
the rarity and uniqueness of brands so that customers dream of
owning them (Amatulli et al., 2020; Wiedmann et al., 2009). How-
ever, the prevalence of digital business and social media, while pro-
viding customers with greater access to luxury brands (Schivinski &
Dabrowski, 2016), has significantly diluted the perception of the
core values of luxury (Park et al., 2020). Thus, a particularly key
question for practitioners and academics is how to deliver a genu-
inely unique impression of luxury to the new generation of con-
sumers who are accustomed to overwhelming marketing blurbs
(Kusumasondjaja, 2020).
A subtle way for marketers in the luxury industry to address this
challenge is allowing customers to enter a visually esthetic world
where they experience the brand's uniqueness, heritage and superior-
ity (de Kerviler & Rodriguez, 2019). Existing studies have explored the
role of specific visual elements (e.g., visual art, visual temperature, and
luxury image type) in luxury perceived values and luxury brand atti-
tudes (Jin & Ryu, 2020; Kusumasondjaja, 2020; Park & Hadi, 2020).
However, considerably less research has discussed the effect of color
elements on luxury brand attitudes.
To our knowledge, only a few studies have investigated the
effects of specific color hues (warm vs. cool; Baek et al., 2018) and
the intensity of background color lightness and saturation (high
vs. low; Kim et al., 2020) on luxury brand attitudes based on embodied
cognition theory and the stimulus-organism-response (SOR) model,
respectively. What is still unclear to scholars is how an advertisement
being fully achromatic or chromatic (i.e., black-and-white versus color)
affects consumers' perceptions and evaluations of luxury brand ads.
Intriguingly, black and white (BW) advertising is favored by major
Received: 18 May 2021 Revised: 12 December 2021 Accepted: 12 January 2022
DOI: 10.1002/cb.2030
J Consumer Behav. 2022;1–14. wileyonlinelibrary.com/journal/cb © 2022 John Wiley & Sons Ltd. 1


[Page 2]
luxury goods such as Dior, Prada, Givenchy and Chanel that launch an
annual sequence of BW photographs or videos to capture the atten-
tion of consumers. For example, in 2020, Chanel announced a set of
BW ads for the 20th anniversary of the J12 watch, not only conveying
the “refined, irreproachable simplicity ” of the J12 but also highlighting
Chanel's iconic attitude of “freedom and ease ” (Malaysia, 2020). A
dataset extracted from AdForum.com —a global digital advertising
archive that includes many production companies and advertising
agencies—shows that 17% of luxury print ads were designed with BW
between 2001 and 2018.
A number of early works on psychology, photography and mar-
keting have examined the effect of BW on perceptions and consid-
ered that BW might convey timelessness and endurance (Zettl, 2014),
enhance the sense of creativity and artistry (Baetens, 2011), and pre-
sent a special atmosphere (e.g., nostalgia; Grainge, 2000). This findings
appear to explain why BW is favored by luxury goods that typical
strive for uniqueness and authenticity. Regrettably, there is still a lack
of strong theoretical research that systematically supports anecdotal
mentions of BW in textbooks, and even fewer studies investigate the
links between BW and luxury brand attitudes.
Drawing on the perspective of esthetic meaning (Labrecque &
Milne, 2012) and the theory of psychological distance (Lee
et al., 2014, 2017), our paper argues that BW (vs. color) images are
tied to luxuriousness. Second, based on image consistency theory, we
posit that BW (vs. color) can lead to a higher positive evaluation
toward luxury brand ads through increasing luxuriousness. Third, the
current paper illustrates a moderating role of ad appeal on the link
between color design (BW vs. color) and ad evaluations. Evaluations
of BW-design (vs. color design) ads will be higher for consumers when
ads focus on hedonic (vs. utilitarian) appeals. Finally, the current study
further investigated whether special color (i.e., iconic color) has an
effect on ad evaluations similar to the effect of BW. Our findings add
key evidence to the perceptions of BW and visual-relevant literature
in the luxury-marketing domain. Next, we review the luxury- and
color-related literature to establish our theoretical hypotheses,
followed by three studies to test the hypotheses. In addition, this
paper discusses the theoretical and practical implications and suggests
potential future research directions.
2 | LITERATURE AND HYPOTHESIS
DEVELOPMENT
2.1 | Luxury brands and luxury marketing
Luxury brands are defined as “high quality, expensive, and nonessen-
tial products and services that appear to be rare, exclusive, presti-
gious, and authentic ” (Terence & Andrews, 2013, p. 1158).

utilitarian) appeals. Finally, the current study
further investigated whether special color (i.e., iconic color) has an
effect on ad evaluations similar to the effect of BW. Our findings add
key evidence to the perceptions of BW and visual-relevant literature
in the luxury-marketing domain. Next, we review the luxury- and
color-related literature to establish our theoretical hypotheses,
followed by three studies to test the hypotheses. In addition, this
paper discusses the theoretical and practical implications and suggests
potential future research directions.
2 | LITERATURE AND HYPOTHESIS
DEVELOPMENT
2.1 | Luxury brands and luxury marketing
Luxury brands are defined as “high quality, expensive, and nonessen-
tial products and services that appear to be rare, exclusive, presti-
gious, and authentic ” (Terence & Andrews, 2013, p. 1158). Thus, one
of the major goals of luxury marketing is distancing the luxury brand
from the mass market (Hagtvedt & Patrick, 2009; Kapferer &
Bastien, 2017; Kapferer & Valette-Florence, 2018). To achieve this
“dream formula ”, luxury brands often adopt some “anti-law market-
ing” approaches (Bastien & Kapferer, 2013), such as targeting narrow
(vs. broad) markets, having relatively limited (vs. boundless) attainabil-
ity and being less (vs. more) frequently purchased (Amatulli
et al., 2020; Baek et al., 2018; Kapferer & Bastien, 2012).
These exceptional marketing approaches lead the research of
which factors drive luxury consumption to be an interesting topic
(Husic & Cicic, 2009). According to previous studies, social status,
uniqueness, and quality perception have been established as three
key factors to generate positive luxury brand attitudes (Kapferer &
Bastien, 2012; Wiedmann et al., 2009). Indeed, luxury products are
high price and sold to upper socioeconomic classes (Kapferer, 1997;
Young et al., 2010); for consumers, owning such items typically signals
one's wealth and high social status (Park & Hadi, 2020). In addition,
what makes luxury brands valuable and desirable lies in the fact that
they can enhance one's self-image by making customers feel they are
unique and belong to special niche groups (Tian et al., 2001;
Vigneron & Johnson, 2004). Finally, as high prices indicate outstand-
ing quality (Dodds et al., 1991; Kirmani & Rao, 2000), customers sub-
jectively perceive higher quality in luxury goods (Park et al., 2020).
Visual esthetics are regard as an important element in increasing
luxury brands attitudes (Amatulli et al., 2020). Currently, emerging
studies have investigated the role of color in value perceptions and
evaluations of luxury brand ads. For instance, Baek et al. (2018)
suggested that the positive effect of warm visual colors on the
approach intention toward stores is not significant for luxury brands.
In addition, Kim et al. (2020) found that low saturation and a high
brightness background could promote positive advertising attitudes
and purchasing intentions toward luxury products. Although these
studies have explored the impact of specific color attributes of spe-
cific stimuli, they still set the picture in a polychromatic pattern and
ignore how the presence or absence of color saturations (i.e., BW
vs. color) of the whole picture affects the perceived value of luxury
products and ad evaluations. In the next section, we will review the
impact of BW on individual psychology and hypothesize the relation-
ship between BW and luxury ad evaluations.
2.2 | The color and its psychological function
Color is a multidimensional construct that consists of three attribu-
tions: hue, brightness and saturation (Singh, 2006). Hue reflects the
appearance parameters and wavelength of light of color (Elliot &
Maier, 2014). Brightness is characteristically white-to-black of the
color in essence (Hsieh et al., 2018). Saturation refers to the property
of intensity or vividness of color (Hagtvedt & Brasel, 2017). Typically,
BW images are made up of achromatic black, white and gray and only
have variations in brightness but not in hue or saturation (Hagtvedt &
Brasel, 2017; Lee et al., 2014).
Color as an esthetic stimulus can potentially affect people's psy-
chology by embodied and referential meaning (Labrecque &
Milne, 2012). Embodied meaning is a biological predisposition that
reflects people's responses to specific colors in physiology (e.g., red
leads to a higher level of arousal), and referential meaning refers to
learned associations related to corresponding concepts, meanings or
2 WANG ET AL .

[Page 3]
experiences that a particular color brings to mind (e.g., red signals dan-
ger; Elliot & Maier, 2007; Kim et al., 2020; Zeltner, 1975). The embod-
ied meaning of color is a result of collative and structural properties of
color, while the referential meaning depends on the repeated pairings
of colors with specific information in a specific context (Elliot &
Maier, 2007, 2014). Many studies on consumer behavior have used
this two-dimensional framework to discuss how color elements
affects consumer perception and behavior (Puccinelli et al., 2013;
Sokolik et al., 2014).
Building upon this framework, our paper has reviewed the impact
of BW on people's psychology. In terms of embodied meaning, a par-
ticularly notable claim about BW images is that they are psychologi-
cally perceived as more distant than color (Lee et al., 2017; Stillman
et al., 2020). Indeed, the real world around us is colored rather than
uncolored (Freeman, 2009; Zettl, 2014). Anything that cannot be
directly felt is psychologically distant (Stephan et al., 2011), as per-
ceiving the object that transcends the “me” in the “here and now ”
requires the mind to connect with a more distal time, place or person
(Liberman & Förster, 2009; Page & Last, 2009). As a result, experienc-
ing BW generates a sense of detachment from reality (Lee
et al., 2014). This is achieved by the systematic desaturation of all
components of the image, rather than the single effect of black, white
or gray or the mere combined effect of these three colors
(Baetens, 2011; Davis & Davis, 2017).
Thus, a significant effect of BW (vs. color) socially distances con-
sumers from objectives since a society entity without color may be
alien to the majority of people. Increasing social distance is often
accompanied by a change in an individual's perception of the stimulus
(Henderson et al., 2006; Liberman et al., 2007; Trope &
Liberman, 2010). For instance, prior studies have indicated that social
distance is central to social status and uniqueness (Lammers
et al., 2012; Magee, 2020; Won et al., 2018), such that individuals
tend to associate people or products that are socially distant and emo-
tionally distant from themselves with a higher sense of exclusion and
social status (Park & Hadi, 2020). Furthermore, shortening consumers'
social distance from luxury brands would undermine the perception of
exclusivity, social status and quality toward the brands (Park
et al., 2020). Thus, BW (vs.

metadata.core_insight_ko: 이 연구는 색상 디자인이 고급 광고에 미치는 영향을 탐구합니다.

text:
Increasing social distance is often
accompanied by a change in an individual's perception of the stimulus
(Henderson et al., 2006; Liberman et al., 2007; Trope &
Liberman, 2010). For instance, prior studies have indicated that social
distance is central to social status and uniqueness (Lammers
et al., 2012; Magee, 2020; Won et al., 2018), such that individuals
tend to associate people or products that are socially distant and emo-
tionally distant from themselves with a higher sense of exclusion and
social status (Park & Hadi, 2020). Furthermore, shortening consumers'
social distance from luxury brands would undermine the perception of
exclusivity, social status and quality toward the brands (Park
et al., 2020). Thus, BW (vs. color) is likely to enhance consumers' per-
ception of brand status, exclusivity and scarcity by distancing the con-
sumers from the brand in the social dimension. In addition, this
relationship is also influenced by esthetic philosophies in visual art.
Most of the modern BW works that audiences are exposed to are the
product of the creators' esthetic and artistic considerations (Davis &
Davis, 2017). Indeed, the infinite processing power of digital image
technology gives every color an equal chance of being selected, and
what makes BW stand out above color is its unique ability to express
art (Hoffmann, 2012). As Freeman (2009) suggested, the strong asso-
ciation between BW (vs. color) and art is rooted in the fact that BW
confers on us a different way of seeing the world. Thus, BW in the
contemporary region is often associated with unique and creative fac-
tors and has become a common way for people to fulfill their artistic
pursuits and creative expression. Studies have shown that art is dis-
tinct from everyday experience (Winston & Cupchik, 1992), and
closely tied to the concepts of exclusivity and creativeness
(Hagtvedt & Patrick, 2008). Given that BW is a classic form of artistic
expression, advertising images with this color scheme can significantly
enhance the uniqueness or exclusivity of a product.
In addition, as BW is perceived to be associated with a more
remote past relative to color (Lee et al., 2014), it can enhance the per-
ception of temporal distance between the viewer's present time and
the time of the story taking place in the advertisement. That is, BW
has a time travel effect, allowing consumers to perceive that the brand
or product in the past has seemingly traveled to the now. The tempo-
ral component plays a crucial role in shaping consumers' brand per-
ceptions, especially in brand heritage and quality perception
(Balmer, 2017; Pecot et al., 2019). For example, Zhang et al. (2019)
found that marketing cues linking existing brands to the distant past
(e.g., “since....” or “established…”) could lead consumers to perceive
the brand as high quality and credible because such cues imply that
brands are competitive and consistent. Baumert and de Obesso (2021)
indicated that a brand's property of antiquity is strongly associated
with brand heritage. Notably, these brand perceptions are conceptual
similarities with brand authenticity, as quality commitment and heri-
tage are important sources of brand authenticity (Napoli et al., 2014).
Thus, it is possible that BW increases consumers' perception of brand
authenticity.
As mentioned above, by distancing consumers psychologically
from brands or products, BW increases two important referential
meanings: exclusivity-related perceptions (e.g., social status and
uniqueness) and authenticity-related perceptions (e.g., brand heritage
and quality commitment). Furthermore, these two perceptions are
considered to be the essential elements of luxuriousness (Gurzki &
Woisetschläger, 2017). As Septianto et al. (2020, p. 1307) suggested,
luxury brands can be understood as “either exclusive or authentic or
both exclusive and authentic at the same time ”. Accordingly, this
paper posits that:
H1. BW (vs. color) design increases consumers' percep-
tion of luxuriousness in a product.
2.3 | The effect of color designs on luxury brand
ad evaluations
Park et al. (2020) indicated that social value perception (i.e., social sta-
tus), uniqueness perception, and quality value perception are three
core values offered by luxury brands. More importantly, these attri-
butes correspond to the two components of luxuriousness: social sta-
tus and uniqueness parallel exclusivity (Tsai et al., 2013; Wiedmann
et al., 2009), and quality perception responds to authenticity (Morhart
et al., 2013; Napoli et al., 2014). The perceptions (i.e., luxuriousness)
evoked by BW (vs. color) precisely coincide with the value expecta-
tions of luxury products. According to congruence theory, consumers
will have a positive attitude toward an ad when the ad information
(e.g., message, celebrities) fits with the overall evaluation of the brand
image in their minds (Chien et al., 2011; Goh et al., 2013). Indeed,
WANG ET AL . 3

[Page 4]
congruence contributes to identifying and understanding the brand
concepts and meanings, increasing brand attitudes and ad evaluations
(Batra & Homer, 2004; Zhang, 2010). Thus, this paper proposes that:
H2. BW (vs. color) design leads consumers to a greater
positive evaluation of luxury brand ads.
H3. Luxuriousness mediates the relationship between
BW (vs. color) design and luxury brand ads.
2.4 | The interactive effect of color design and ad
appeals on luxury brand ad evaluations
Although BW can increase the perception of luxuriousness, which
leads to higher consumer attitudes toward luxury brand ads (Childs &
Jin, 2016), its benefits may not always be generated (Huettl &
Gierl, 2012; Rucker & Galinsky, 2009). In particular, we suggest that
whether an ad appeal concerned with hedonics or utility may influ-
ence the effect of BW (vs. color) on luxury brand ad evaluations.
As an important tool in luxury brand marketing communication
(Kulkarni et al., 2020), ad appeal can change consumers' attention and
subsequent brand attitudes by stressing different message contents
(Kazakova et al., 2016; Yoo & MacInnis, 2005). In the literature on lux-
ury brands, hedonic and utilitarian brands are two ad appeals that
have been widely discussed (Amatulli et al., 2020; Kwon et al., 2016).
Specifically, hedonic appeals are often associated with promotion
goals (e.g., aspiration, achievement and enhancement), inducing the
feeling of delight, pleasure and excitement to satisfy consumers'
sensory-social needs (Chitturi et al., 2008; Wiedmann et al., 2009). In
contrast, utilitarian appeals are often related to prevention goals
(e.g., physiology, information and security) by highlighting superior
material and sophisticated design to meet consumers' practical needs
(Chitturi et al., 2007; Dhar & Wertenbroch, 2000).
According to previous studies, when advertising resorts to
hedonic messaging, consumers are more concerned about whether
the product or brand satisfies their pleasure-seeking and identity-
expressing needs (Bottomley & Doyle, 2006; Huang et al., 2020). At
this moment, social cues related to intuitive feelings and heuristics
dominate viewers' ad evaluation (Schulze et al., 2014).

metadata.core_insight_en: Increasing social distance can enhance luxury brand perception by conveying exclusivity, social status, and uniqueness, leveraging the associations of black and white with art and a remote past.

text:
In
contrast, utilitarian appeals are often related to prevention goals
(e.g., physiology, information and security) by highlighting superior
material and sophisticated design to meet consumers' practical needs
(Chitturi et al., 2007; Dhar & Wertenbroch, 2000).
According to previous studies, when advertising resorts to
hedonic messaging, consumers are more concerned about whether
the product or brand satisfies their pleasure-seeking and identity-
expressing needs (Bottomley & Doyle, 2006; Huang et al., 2020). At
this moment, social cues related to intuitive feelings and heuristics
dominate viewers' ad evaluation (Schulze et al., 2014). Compared to
color, BW triggers a sense of rarity, exclusivity and authenticity, offer-
ing esthetic pleasure and status symbols to consumers. Such
perceptions are consistent with the benefits that consumers seek in
hedonic ad appeals of luxury brands and, thus, may lead to a greater
positive ad evaluation. However, when advertising focuses on the util-
ity of products, consumers pay more attention to informational cues,
as they need adequate fact-based attributes about products to judge
whether their decision is wise and correct (Terence & Andrews, 2013;
Zhang et al., 2014). Here, consumers are more likely to rely on practi-
cal reasons rather than feelings to process various marketing cues
(Gong & Cummins, 2020). As such, BW-design fails to meet the inter-
ests of consumers seeking utilitarian ad appeals because its meaning
expression and esthetic function are weakened. Accordingly, we
posit that:
H4. Ad evaluations of BW (vs. color) design ads will be
higher for consumers when ads focus on hedonic
(vs. utilitarian) appeals.
2.5 | The current research
The current paper tests the hypotheses through three studies. Specifi-
cally, Study 1 examines BW's (vs. color) effect on perceived luxurious-
ness and its two components (i.e., uniqueness and authenticity). In
addition, Study 1 preliminarily investigates the relationship between
color design and luxury ad evaluation and the mediating role of per-
ceived luxuriousness. Study 2 further identifies the mediating role of
perceived luxuriousness and examines the moderating effect of the ad
appeal on the relationship between color design and ad evaluation.
Finally, by introducing iconic color conditions, Study 3 provides more
detailed evidence for understanding the color effects of luxury ads.
The framework is shown in Figure 1.
3 | STUDY 1
3.1 | Design and participants
Study 1 aims to preliminarily examine how color design (BW vs. color)
influences consumers' evaluation of luxury brand ads and whether
luxuriousness mediates this process. In this study, we employed a
two-level one-factor between-subjects design (color design: BW
vs. color). Two hundred and sixty-six China-based college students
FIGURE 1 The conceptual framework
4 WANG ET AL .

[Page 5]
recruited from two universities located in Wuhan took part in this
study for cash rewards (CNY 25). Chinese participants were suitable
for this research on luxury consumption because China's luxury mar-
ket has grown rapidly in the last 10 years and may continue to grow
in the future (Deloitte, 2020). Many major luxury products are popular
with Chinese consumers. Forty participants were removed from the
final sample because they did not pass the attention test, and 17 par-
ticipants were eliminated from the analysis because they did not
understand the questionnaire properly. Ultimately, we collected
209 valid data points (78.6% valid return rate). The results of the
demographic description demonstrated that 43.5% were male, the
average age was 23.35, undergraduates accounted for 93.3%, and the
majority of students had monthly expenditures less than CNY 5000,
accounting for 79.9%. G*Power was 0.99 (>0.80), after setting group
number of the one-way ANOVA as 2, sample size as 209, and the
effect size ( f ) as 0.4 within 95% confidence interval.
3.2 | Stimuli and procedures
Participants were randomly recruited through an electronic bulletin
board on the university's on-campus website. When participants
arrived individually at the laboratory, they were presented with infor-
mation about the procedure and purpose of the study on an electronic
display in the laboratory. Then, they were asked to sign a statement
of willingness to participate in the study.
The study was carried out under the guise of a luxury goods com-
pany preparing to test different advertisements before the official
launch. After agreeing to the survey, each participant was notified
that Hermès was planning to launch its fall/winter 2021 clothing for
men and women in the Asian market, and he or she was invited as a
guest to assess one of Hermès' possible advertisements (see detail in
AppendixA). Next, all participants were randomly assigned to one of
the two color design groups (BW vs. color). In the BW condition, the
whole picture is designed as black and white, including background
patterns and fonts. Under color conditions, all these components of
the ads are colored. The difference between the two groups was only
the absence or presence of saturation, and other factors did not
change. In addition, the ads include both male and female versions to
match the gender of the participants. To check whether the color
design met expectations, we conducted a pretest with another inde-
pendent sample of 30 undergraduates (56.7% male; average age
22.57, 76.7% monthly expenditure less CNY 5000) recruited from the
same universities. Participants first took turns viewing color and BW
images of the same product and then estimated the colors using a
7-point scale (1 = definitely colored, 7 = definitely colored black and
white). As expected, the results suggested that the mean score of per-
ceived color in BW condition is significantly higher than color condi-
tion ( M
BW = 5.10; SD = 1.58; MColor = 2.80; SD = 1.56;
t [29] = /C06.35; p < .001).
After that, all participants were required to rate the luxuriousness,
uniqueness and authenticity of products. Specifically, luxuriousness
was a 7-point, four-item scale (high class/attractive/prestigious/
luxurious; α = .84) used by Hagtvedt and Patrick (2008). Uniqueness
was measured on three 7-point items (uniqueness/exclusiveness/
expensiveness; α = .80) based on Park et al. (2020). Authenticity was
measured with eight 7-point items (heritage, quality commitment, and
sincerity) adapted from Napoli et al. (2014)'s Consumer-Based Brand
Authenticity scale (CBBA; α = .90). After that, consumers reported ad
evaluation with four 7-point items (favorable –unfavorable, positive –
negative, like –dislike, good –bad; α = .94) adapted from Park and
Hadi (2020).
Then, participants answered the perceived color of the ads on
7-point items ( “whether you thought the ad was in color or in BW ”;
1 = definitely colored, 7 = definitely black-and-white; Wang
et al., 2020) as a manipulation check of color. In addition, the partici-
pants were asked to indicate their brand likeability (to what extent do
you like this brand; 1 = “dislike extremely,” and 7 = “like very much ”)
and brand familiarity (to what extent do you were familiar with this
brand; 1 = “extremely unfamiliar, ” and 7 = “extremely familiar ”).

evaluation with four 7-point items (favorable –unfavorable, positive –

Then, participants answered the perceived color of the ads on

and brand familiarity (to what extent do you were familiar with this

Finally, participants reported their gender, monthly expenditures and
level of education.
3.3 | Results
Manipulation check. ANOVA results showed that the mean score in
the BW conditions was significantly higher than that in the color con-
ditions ( M
BW = 6.61, SD = 2.15; Mcolor = 3.68, SD = 0.79; F
(1, 207) = 182.16, p < .001, η2
p = 0.47), confirming that the manipula-
tion of the color design was successful.
Luxuriousness, uniqueness and authenticity. ANOVA indicates
that compared to color, BW lead to a higher perception of luxurious-
ness ( MBW = 5.64, SD = 1.12; Mcolor = 4.61, SD = 1.10; F
(1, 207) = 44.86, p < .001, η2
p = 0.17), uniqueness ( MBW = 5.36,
SD = 1.06; Mcolor = 4.60, SD = 1.29; F(1, 207) = 21.55, p < .001,
η2
p = 0.09) and authenticity ( MBW = 5.45, SD = 1.07; M color = 4.63,
SD = 1.13; F(1, 207) =28.53, p < .001, η2
p = 0.12). Furthermore, given
that luxuriousness is, in theory, associated with authenticity and
uniqueness, it is not surprising that luxuriousness was significantly
correlated with both uniqueness ( r = 0.72, p < .01) and authenticity
(r = 0.72, p < .01). In addition, factor analysis was conducted using the
maximum variance method with eigenvalues greater than 1. The
results showed that 15 items from the three scales loaded onto the
two factors and accounted for 61.17% of the cumulative variance,
indicating that uniqueness and authenticity are two important compo-
nents of luxuriousness. As such, this paper combined all 15 items into
one aggregated scale to measure luxuriousness ( α = .93). Consistent
with H1, BW designed ads are associated with a higher perception of
luxuriousness than those designed as color ( M
BW = 5.48, SD = 1.00;
Mcolor = 4.62, SD = 0.98; F(1, 207) =39.39, p < .001, η2
p = 0.16).
Ad evaluations. ANOVA results revealed that manipulating the
color design of ads affected participants' evaluations of the ads.
Supporting H2, BW (vs. color) led consumers to a greater positive
evaluation of luxury brand ads ( M
BW = 5.62, SD = 1.17; Mcolor = 4.72,
SD = 1.21; F(1, 207) = 30.02, p < .001, η2
p = 0.13; see detail in
WANG ET AL . 5

[Page 6]
Figure 2). Furthermore, after controlling for brand likeability and brand
familiarity, BW still had a greater impact on ad evaluation than color
(F(1, 205) = 34.96, p < .001, η
2
p = 0.14).
Mediation analysis. To test whether color design indirectly
affected luxury brand ad evaluation through perceptions of luxurious-
ness (H3), we used the bootstrap method developed by Preacher and
Hayes (2004) to conduct a mediation analysis (Model 4, bootstrap
sample size of 5000 and 95% bias-corrected confidence intervals).
The results indicate that the indirect effect of perceived luxuriousness
was significant (indirect effect = 0.65; 95% CI = 0.4477, 0.9094),
while the direct effect of color design on ad evaluation was no longer
significant (direct effect = 0.25; 95% CI = /C00.0241, 0.5294),
suggesting that luxuriousness completely mediated the effect of color
design on consumer evaluations of luxury brand ads.
3.4 | Discussion
In this study, we investigated the effect of color designs (color
vs. BW) on the luxuriousness of products and ad evaluations. As
expected, the results showed that BW (vs. color) increased consumers'
perception of the luxuriousness of products (H1) and evaluations of
luxury brand ads (H2). Moreover, perceived luxuriousness mediated
the relationship between color design and ad evaluations (H3). Study
1 still had some limitations. As such, Study 2 was conducted to
explore the robustness of the findings of Study 1 and to verify the
interactive effects of ad appeal and color design on ad evalua-
tion (H4).
4 | STUDY 2
4.1 | Design and participants
Study 1 provides preliminary evidence for the relationship between
color design (BW vs. color) and ad evaluations. However, the sample
in Study 1 involved undergraduates with relatively low levels of con-
sumption, which would limit the validity of the study's findings. In
addition, the stimulus of Study 1 may be limited (i.e., women and men
wear). To improve the robustness of the results, we designed a new
manipulation scenario, selected another sample, and only measured
luxuriousness in Study 2. In addition, another goal of Study 2 was to
investigate the moderating role of advertising appeals on the relation-
ship between color design and ad evaluations.
This study employed a two-way between-group design with
2 color designs (BW vs. color) /C22 ad appeals (hedonic vs. utilitarian).
Ad appeals and color designs were the two independent variables, ad
evaluation was the dependent variable, and perceived luxuriousness
was the mediating variable. Two hundred and twenty-three adult par-
ticipants across mainland China were recruited from Sojump, a profes-
sional online survey company (https://www.sojump.com) in exchange
for a random monetary compensation (Liu et al., 2021). Only female
consumers born after the 1990s were recruited to participate in this
study to ensure a proper match between the target consumers and
luxury goods. After checking the completion of the experiment and
the attention test, 20 participants were removed from the final sam-
ple. In addition, six were excluded since duplicate IP addresses. Finally,
we obtained 197 valid samples (88% valid return rate). Demographic
description indicated that the average age was 26.25; those with col-
lege degrees accounted for 92.5%, and those with a CNY 3000 –8000
monthly income accounted for 73.3%.

Two hundred and twenty-three adult par-
ticipants across mainland China were recruited from Sojump, a profes-
sional online survey company (https://www.sojump.com) in exchange
for a random monetary compensation (Liu et al., 2021). Only female
consumers born after the 1990s were recruited to participate in this
study to ensure a proper match between the target consumers and
luxury goods. After checking the completion of the experiment and
the attention test, 20 participants were removed from the final sam-
ple. In addition, six were excluded since duplicate IP addresses. Finally,
we obtained 197 valid samples (88% valid return rate). Demographic
description indicated that the average age was 26.25; those with col-
lege degrees accounted for 92.5%, and those with a CNY 3000 –8000
monthly income accounted for 73.3%. G*Power was 0.98 (>0.80)
when the group number of the ANCOVA was set as 4, sample size as
197, and the effect size ( f ) as 0.4 within the 95% confidence interval.
4.2 | Stimuli and procedures
At the beginning of the study, participants were asked to imagine that
they were planning to purchase a bag as a reward for their upcoming
birthday and were browsing an online magazine for the new Prada bags
soon to be available. Each ad was designed as either BW or color, similar
to Study 1. In addition, we manipulated the ad appeals using wording
from Amatulli et al. (2020). Specifically, hedonic appeals focused on the
products' sensory-social benefits (i.e., a prestigious bag with classical
style makes you feel luxurious and sophisticated), while utilitarian
appeals focused on the functional benefits (i.e., a functional bag with
superior leather makes you feel comfortable and durable; see detail in
AppendixB). The content of each of the two ad appeals had similar word
counts. In addition, we conducted a one-way within-subject design pre-
test with an independent sample of 33 adults (48.5% male, average age
21.88, and 69.7% monthly income less than CNY 8,000) recruited from
one community located in Wuhan city to verify whether the ad appeal
has been correctly understood. In the pretest, all participants in turn
read stimulus material about both utilitarian (material A) and hedonic
appeals (material B) and their definitions; then they were asked to
answer the “What did you think the material A/B highlight? (1= utilitar-
ian; 7 = hedonic)” As predicted, stimulus material A scored significantly
lower than material B ( M
A = 3.09, SD = 1.68; MB = 5.18, SD = 1.31,
t [32] = /C05.61, p <. 0 0 1 ) .
All participants were randomly assigned to one of four group's
ads. After that, participants answered four 7-point items about
FIGURE 2 The main effect of color design on ad evaluation
(Study 1)
6 WANG ET AL .

[Page 7]
product luxuriousness, that is, “to what extent this product is luxuri-
ous/prestigious/attractive/high class ” (α = .86; Hagtvedt &
Patrick, 2008). Then, participants reported their evaluation of the ad
with three 7-point scales (negative/positive, bad/good, unfavorable/
favorable; α = .83; Lee & Aaker, 2004). In addition, participants were
asked to rate “whether you thought the ad was in color or in BW ”
(1 = definitely colored, 7 = definitely black-and-white; Wang
et al., 2020) as a manipulation of color. To verify the success of our
manipulation regarding advertising appeals, consumers were asked to
rate “this ad message appealed to my pleasure-seeking and identity-
expressing needs ” (r = 0.74) and “this ad message contained much
rational information ” (1 = strongly disagree; 7 = strongly agree;
r = 0.70; Zhang et al., 2014). Finally, participants were asked to indi-
cate their brand likeability and brand familiarity and to report demo-
graphic variables.
4.3 | Results
Manipulation check. As expected, the mean score of perceived color
in the BW conditions was significantly higher than that in the color
conditions ( M
BW = 6.68, SD = 1.08; Mcolor = 1.99, SD = 1.36; F
(1, 195) = 720.89, p < .001, η2
p =0.79), which confirmed that the
manipulation of the color design was successful. Regarding the manip-
ulation of ad appeals, the results showed that the mean hedonic rating
in the hedonic appeal condition was significantly higher than that in
the utilitarian appeal condition ( M
hedonic appeal = 6.01, SD = 0.81;
Mutilitarian appeal = 2.86, SD = 1.79; F(1, 195) = 257.52, p < .001,
η2
p = 0.57), while the mean utilitarian rating in the hedonic appeal con-
dition was significantly lower than that in the utilitarian appeal condi-
tion ( Mhedonic appeal = 2.61, SD = 1.62; Mutilitarian appeal = 5.03,
SD = 1.50; F(1, 195) = 118.05, p < .001, η2
p = 0.37). Thus, the color
design and ad appeal manipulations for this study were successful.
Main effect. A two-way ANCOVA shows that the interaction
between advertising appeals and color designs on ad evaluation
(F(1, 191) = 14.51, p < .01, η
2
p = 0.08) was significant while controlling
for brand likeability and brand familiarity. Neither the main effect of
color design ( p > .05, η2
p = 0.01) nor ad appeals ( p > .05, η2
p = 0.01) on
ad evaluation were significant. Furthermore, simple effects analysis
showed that the use of BW images was more conducive to positive
consumer ad evaluations when the ad was a hedonic appeal
(M
BW = 5.55, SD = 1.14; Mcolor = 4.49, SD = 1.09; F(1, 98) = 22.18,
p < .001, η2
p = 0.17). However, when the advertisement was a utilitar-
ian appeal, the use of color images lead to a higher ad evaluation but
statistically insignificant ( M
BW = 4.45, SD = 1.08; Mcolor = 4.80,
SD = 1.28; F(1, 95) = 2.17, p > .05, η2
p = 0.02; see detail in Figure 3).
Mediation analysis. This paper uses the Preacher and
Hayes' (2004) Bootstrap method to test for moderated mediation
effects. We set a bootstrap sample size of 5000 and selected 95%
confidence intervals using model 8 (color = 0, BW = 1; utilitarian
appeal = 0, hedonic appeal = 1). The results indicated that the moder-
ated mediation effect was statistically significant (index = 0.51, 95%
CI = 0.2076, 0.9202; see detail in Figure 4).

Thereafter, the authors related the scores on 
field dependen ce and sensation -seeking with each of these dimensions. It was 
hypothesized that participants scoring high on field dependence would show 
greater preference for the representational categories (landscape, portrait, and 
hunting) –those with greater structur e- and less preference for the abstract 
categories than participants scoring low on field dependence. It was also 
hypothesized that participants with high scores on sensation -seeking would prefer 
abstract categories and the representational paintings rende ring aggressive themes 
than participants low in sensation -seeking. Results showed support for some of 
these expectations. Specifically, highly field -dependent participants showed greater 
preference for representational landscape, portrait, and hunting pain tings, but did 
not show less preference for paintings in the abstract categories. Additionally, 
participants with high scores on sensation -seeking awarded higher ratings to 
aggressive, abstract futurist, and abstract impressionist pictures, than participan ts 
low in sensation -seeking, but there were no significant differences for the other 
painting categories. Although these results support the influence of cognitive styles 
and personality traits on aesthetic preference, we feel there are two aspects of the 
present study that suggest caution. First, given that stimuli were deliberately 
chosen by the experimenter to create meaningful differences between participants 
scoring high and low in both measures of individual differences, there is a chance 
that their results might not generalize to a broader range of artistic stimuli. Second, 
the largest amount of variance accounted for by either measure on any category 
was only 9% (Tobacyk, Myers, & Bailey, 1981). 

[Page 118]
108 
 Heinrichs and Cupchik (1985)  carried out a study to clarify the relation 
between personality and aesthetic preference. Three aspects distinguish this effort 
from the ones we have just de scribed. First, the authors wished to contrast 
responses to realist vs. abstract art, to representations of specific content 
(sexuality, aggression) created in different styles: idealized (emphasis on form and 
conveying proportion and perfection) vs. expre ssionist (emphasis on the 
subjective and conveying emotions), and linear (emphasis on outline) vs. painterly 
(emphasis on mass). Second, participants’ responses were recorded on two 
preference dimensions: interest and pleasure. Third, they did not rely on standard 
personality inventories, but used a combination of questionnaires, as well as a 
series of measures of background in art. Materials were constituted by 48 
paintings, 32 of which had been rated by judges as to emphasis on sexuality or 
aggression, an d idealization vs. expressionism. There were 8 stimulus in each 
category resulting from crossing these two dimensions. An additional 16 stimuli 
were included. These were 4 linear, 4 painterly, 4 representational, and 4 abstract 
artworks. The 24 male and female participants were asked to view the whole set of 
materials, presented in pairs, and rate the pleasingness and interest of each 
stimulus on an 8 -point scale: “The subjective set consisted of instructions to view 
the pairs of paintings in a ‘very emotio nal manner’. Subjects were asked to use 
their emotional reactions as a guide in indicating on bipolar 8 -point scales which 
painting in a pair was more pleasing and which painting they would like to see 
again. Under the objective set subjects were encourage d to ‘analyse the paintings 
in terms of composition, style, etc.’ in an objective manner.” (Heinrichs & 
Cupchik, 1985, p. 508).  
 The results of this study revealed significant relations within the sexual and 
aggression subject dimensions, as well as withi n the linear -painterly and abstract -
representational dimensions. Given the conceptual weakness of some of the 
independent variables, and the amount of interactions that are difficult to 
interpret, we will concentrate on the most significant and straightfor ward results. 
Participants’ ratings of paintings with sexual and aggressive content in the 

[Page 119]
 
109 
subjective set were predicted by two variables: memories of emotionally 
inexpressive mothers and emotional lability (intense experiences elicited by 
affectively charged imagery). Objective ratings were predicted by sex, memories of 
unaffective fathers, and trait -anxiety. Turning to results concerning the linear -
painterly dimension, it was found that participants who showed a great subjective 
preference for the painter ly style, also scored higher on trait -anxiety, felt closer to 
their mothers than fathers, and reported feeling comfortable in social situations. 
There were no significant relations for the objective preference ratings. Finally, 
preference for abstract art was governed by emotional lability, in that people who 
awarded higher subjective preference ratings to abstract art also tended to report 
stronger reactions to affectively charged imagery. No significant relations were 
found for objective preference on the  abstract -representational dimension 
(Heinrichs & Cupchik, 1985). 
 Furnham and Walker's (2001)  study attempted to clarify the relation 
between aesthetic preference and measures of sensation seeking, conservatism, 
and the Big Five personali ty traits. Specifically, the authors set out to show that 
aesthetic preference for artworks is influenced by conservatism, sensation seeking, 
neuroticism, openness, agreeableness, conscientiousness, and exposure to art. In 
order to do so, the authors asked  71 female and 30 male psychology students to 
express their preferences for 40 paintings, which included traditional 
representational artworks, abstract paintings, pop art pictures, and 18 th and 19 th 
century Japanese paintings. There were five rating scale s: how much would they 
like the painting in an art gallery, how much would they like it in their living room, 
talent of the artist, how much would they pay for the painting, and their familiarity 
with it. Additionally, participants were administered a test  of art knowledge, a 
sensation seeking scale, the five factor inventory, and an attitude inventory. 
 Correlational analyses revealed that scores on Extraversion and 
Agreeableness were unrelated to preference ratings for the four stimuli categories. 
On the other hand, participants with high scores on Disinhibition considered pop 

[Page 120]
110 
art and Japanese artists as more talented than low scorers on this scale. 
Participants who scored high on Thrill and Adventure Seeking considered abstract 
artists to be more talented , and showed a greater preference for abstract art, than 
did participants that scored low. Openness to experience was also positively 
related with preference for pop art and abstract paintings. Conscientiousness was 
negatively correlated with preference fo r pop art, but, contrary to original 
hypotheses, high scorers on this scale rated the talent of representational artists 
lower than participants with low scores. Finally, Conservatism was negatively 
related to preference for abstract, Japanese, and pop art . In fact, the negative 
relation between Conservatism and preference for art which is not traditional or 
representational, turned out to be the most consistent finding of the study.

metadata.core_insight_en: This dissertation, 'Complexity and Aesthetic Preference for Diverse Visual Stimuli,' explores the relationship between visual stimulus complexity and aesthetic preference. Researchers have long sought to understand this relationship, but the field is plagued by conceptual confusion. The study relies on McWhinnie's criterion, defining aesthetic preference as the degree to which people like or dislike a particular visual stimulus. The research focuses on the divergence of results obtained by studies attempting to verify Daniel Berlyne's framework, which predicts a relation between complexity and aesthetic preference.
metadata.core_insight_ko: 이 논문 '다양한 시각 자극에 대한 복잡성과 미적 선호도'는 시각 자극의 복잡성과 미적 선호도 간의 관계를 탐구한다. 오랫동안 이 관계를 이해하려는 노력이 있었으나, 개념적 혼란이 존재했다. 본 연구는 맥휘니의 기준을 바탕으로 미적 선호도를 특정 시각 자극에 대한 호감도나 반감도로 정의하며, 다니엘 베르린의 복잡성과 미적 선호도 간의 연관성 예측 모델 검증 연구 결과의 차이에 초점을 맞춘다.

On the other hand, participants with high scores on Disinhibition considered pop 

[Page 120]
110 
art and Japanese artists as more talented than low scorers on this scale. 
Participants who scored high on Thrill and Adventure Seeking considered abstract 
artists to be more talented , and showed a greater preference for abstract art, than 
did participants that scored low. Openness to experience was also positively 
related with preference for pop art and abstract paintings. Conscientiousness was 
negatively correlated with preference fo r pop art, but, contrary to original 
hypotheses, high scorers on this scale rated the talent of representational artists 
lower than participants with low scores. Finally, Conservatism was negatively 
related to preference for abstract, Japanese, and pop art . In fact, the negative 
relation between Conservatism and preference for art which is not traditional or 
representational, turned out to be the most consistent finding of the study. 
However, several combinations of Conservatism, sex, familiarity and measur es of 
experience with art explain only between 16 and 32% of the overall variation in 
preference scores (Furnham & Walker, 2001). 
 Feist and Brady's (2004)  experiment was carried out to study how 
personality and non -conformist attitudes are related with aesthetic preference for 
abstract and representational artworks. Based on different theoretical approaches, 
as well as on prior emp irical results, Feist and Brady (2004)  expected that, in 
general, their participants would pr efer representational art over abstract art. They 
predicted, however, that abstract art would be especially preferred by participants 
with high scores on measures of openness, liberal attitudes, and tolerance for drug 
use. The selection of participants wit h high and low scores on openness produced 
a sample including 55 highly open participants, 36 of which were women and 19 
were men, and 49 participants scoring low in openness, 32 women and 16 men. In 
this case, openness was computed by combining scores on an experience-seeking 
scale (part of a sensation -seeking test) and an openness scale. Attitudinal 
information was retrieved by means of an especially designed questionnaire. 
Participants were asked to rate how much they liked each of the 45 artworks that 
constituted this experiment’s material on a 9 -point Likert scale. Stimuli had 

[Page 121]
 
111 
previously been classified into three categories: abstract, representational, and 
ambiguous. 
 Results of this experiment showed that, overall, representational artworks 
were prefe rred more than abstract and ambiguous ones. In regards to the 
magnitude of this effect, the authors report that the degree of abstraction 
explained 29% of the variance in art preference. Concerning the individual 
differences studied in this experiment, res ults also showed that participants with 
high scores on openness preferred all kinds of art more than participants with low 
openness scores. This difference was especially marked for the abstract artworks. 
However, the magnitude of the interaction effect be tween openness and 
abstraction explained less than 5% of the variance of preference scores. Finally, 
liberal attitudes were also associated with a greater preference for abstract art. 
Demographic variables such as age or sex did not show any significant ef fects on 
preference ratings for abstract art (Feist & Brady, 2004) . The authors took their 
results as supporting the notion that people who approach novel events with an 
open attitude are more appreciative of art in general, and of abstract art in 
particular. 
 
1.3.3.1. Summary 
 
  Some of the studies we have just gone over suggest there might be a 
relation between certain personality traits or cognitive styles and aesthetic 
preference. However, these personality traits vary from study to study, especially 
in the early ones. For instance, whereas Knapp and Wulff's (1963) study suggested 
the relevant traits were intuitiveness vs. sensation and holding strong religious vs. 
aesthetic values, Wilson, Ausman and Mathews' (1973)  results show conservatism 
to have a significant impact on aesthetic preference. Subsequent studies have 
supported the notion that conservatism determines, at least  to a certain extent, the 

[Page 122]
112 
responses participants give in aesthetic preference tasks (Feist & Brady, 2004; 
Furnham & Walker, 2001) , though they have also added other s ignificant traits, 
such as openness (Feist & Brady, 2004) , and sensation -seeking (Furnham & 
Walker, 2001; Tobacyk, Myers, & Bailey, 1981) . Some cognitive styles have also 
been shown to influence aesthetic preference, such as analytic vs. synthetic 
(Savarese & Miller, 1979), or field dependence (Tobacyk, Myers, & Bailey, 1981). 
 However, not all the studies have found significant effects of personality 
on aesthetic preference. Kloss and Dreger (1971)  found no relation between 
personality and aesthetic preference, and Furnham and Chamorro -Premuzic's 
(2004) model predicting aesthetic preference by a combination of the Big 5 
personality traits and intelligence did not reach significance levels. Even in those 
cases that have found a significant relation between both variables, it seems to be a 
rather weak one. Furnham and Walker's (2001)  study accounte d for between 16 
and 32% of the variance in aesthetic preference scores, whereas Tobacyk and 
colleagues' (1981) study did so just for 9%, and Feist and Brady (2004)  only for 
5%. This has also been noted in previous reviews  of studies on the relation 
between personality measures  and aesthetic preference (Hekkert & Wieringen, 
1996a). Heinrichs and Cupchik (1985) wrote that “One notable limitation of these 
and similar studies is the finding that personality measures rarely account for more 
than a small amount of variability in preferences for different kinds of paintings.” 
(Heinrichs & Cupchik, 1985, p. 503). Hardiman & Zernich (1977) reviewed several 
early studies attempting to draw relations between aesthetic preference and 
personality. They noted that their results range from no evidence of such relation 
to a significant correlation between preference scores and certain pe rsonality traits. 
However, the majority of the studies have produced only small correlations 
between these two measures. Hardiman & Zernich (1977)  concluded that “These 
studies bring little clarity to the hypothesized relationships between preference and 
personality. Although several studies used personality assessment instruments that 
are reliable and valid, there was no generalizability of the stimulus dimensions used 
to elicit these preference judgments.” (Hardiman & Zernich, 1977, p. 469). 

[Page 123]
 
113 
 Heinrichs and Cupchik (1985)  noted that cultural background and general 
educational level have shown to influence aesthetic appreciation, and that these 
factors might better explain aesthetic preferences.

text:
They noted that their results range from no evidence of such relation 
to a significant correlation between preference scores and certain pe rsonality traits. 
However, the majority of the studies have produced only small correlations 
between these two measures. Hardiman & Zernich (1977)  concluded that “These 
studies bring little clarity to the hypothesized relationships between preference and 
personality. Although several studies used personality assessment instruments that 
are reliable and valid, there was no generalizability of the stimulus dimensions used 
to elicit these preference judgments.” (Hardiman & Zernich, 1977, p. 469). 

[Page 123]
 
113 
 Heinrichs and Cupchik (1985)  noted that cultural background and general 
educational level have shown to influence aesthetic appreciation, and that these 
factors might better explain aesthetic preferences. For instan ce, Knapp, Brimner 
and  White (1959)  found that social class predicted aesthetic preference for 
Scottish tartan designs. Whereas middle class adolescents s howed strong 
preferences for complex designs without saturated colours or striking contrasts, 
lower class adolescents preferred simple designs with saturated colours and strong 
contrasts. Francès (1976) recorded the aesthetic preferences of participants with 
high and low general edu cational background for stimuli varying on six kinds of 
complexity. Results showed that, overall, participants with a high educational 
background preferred complex stimuli over simple ones, whereas participants with 
little general education showed the oppo site preference trend. Whereas number 
and variety of elements produced no significant differences between the 
preferences of both groups, regularity and incongruity produced very significant 
differences (Francès, 1976). 
 However, effects of class and educational level on aesthetic p reference are 
not as strong as the influence of art -specific education. It has been suggested that 
the observed effects of general background are actually due to differences in the 
amount of specific art education  (Hekkert & Wieringen, 1996a). It is interesting to 
recall that some of the studies we have reviewed above suggest that personality 
might have a greater impact on artistic interests and activ ities than on aesthetic 
judgment and preference per se (Furnham & Chamorro -Premuzic, 2004). Thus, 
certain personality traits, such as Openness to experience and Conservatism, might 
attract people towards and away from artistic interests and experience. It is this 
experience with art, be it formal or informal, which seems to have a greater impact 
on aesthetic preferences, especially for those styles which are more  unfamiliar, 
such as abstract painting. Let us review some of the studies that have examined 
this influence of art education on aesthetic preference. 

[Page 124]
114 
1.3.4. The influence of art training  
 
 
 
 In this section we will review studies that have searched for di fferences in 
aesthetic preference for visual stimuli between groups of people with and without 
artistic education. Given the objectives of the present work, we will emphasize 
studies that have taken into account the complexity of stimuli in the determinati on 
of aesthetic preference. 
 The main objective of Eysenck and Castle's (1970b)  study was to assess 
whether participants with and without artistic trai ning would agree in their 
preference for Birkhoff's (1932) 90 polygons. They asked a very large number of 
participants to ra te the aesthetic pleasingness of each figure on a 7 -point scale. 
Their groups were composed by 369 male and 408 female artists, and 176 male 
and 180 female controls. The group of artists included people who were attending 
or had attended courses in graphic , typographic, textile, industrial, interior, stained 
glass or fashion design, fine arts (painting and sculpture), architectural studies, 
photography, cinematography, and so on, as well as some professional artists. The 
group of controls included students enrolled in law, accounting, electrical 
engineering, catering, hairdressing, surveying, retailing, among other careers. The 
main finding of this study was that participants with artistic training prefer forms 
which are characterized by simplicity and order, while the control group seemed to 
give higher preference ratings to figures which were more complex. Similar results 
were obtained later Eysenck and Castle (1971)  with similar groups of participants 
but using a different set of stimuli, namely the Maitland Graves Design Judgment Test . 
There are two possible explanations for th ese results, but these studies were not 
designed to decide between them. First, training in arts might lead people to 
develop an appreciation for simplicity and order. Second, people who appreciate 

[Page 125]
 
115 
simplicity and order are especially proficient in artistic  activities. Although only a 
longitudinal study could actually settle this question, the fact that the scores of 
artistically trained participants on three different measures of aesthetic sensitivity 
showed low correlations, led Eysenck (1971b)  to tentatively favour the first 
option. 
 Bezrucsko and Schroeder (1994) were able to carry out a similar study with 
even a larger sample of art-trained and untrained participants. They recruited 1,578 
people, approximately the same number of men and women, with li ttle or no art 
training or experience, 107 participants, also almost even numbers of men and 
women, with some art training and experience, and 62 professional artists whose 
main activity was the design and production of visual artworks at the time of the 
study. The latter groups included slightly more women than men, but the main 
occupation of all of them was painting, sculpting, architecture, or stage and film 
production. They were all asked to complete a series of artistic judgment scales as 
well as a bat tery of cognitive aptitude tests. The former set included the Design 
Judgment Test, the Visual Designs Test, and the Proportion Appraisal task. The first one, 
which we have already mentioned, is composed of ninety items, each of which 
presents the examinee s with three visual designs, two of which violate such basic 
aesthetic principles as balance, symmetry, proportion, unity, and so on. The viewer 
is asked to indicate which one of the three designs he or she prefers or likes the 
most. The final score reflec ts the number of choices that match the one 
considered by the test’s authors to be artistically superior. The second test also 
requires participants to indicate which stimuli they like most. In this case, they 
have to choose among stimuli varying in comple xity, defined as the number of 
elements, and order, defined as the degree of repetition of the pattern. The last 
tests measures preferences for 50 sets of 3 visual designs that differ in their 
proportions, such as the ratio of width to length of parabolic curves. The set of 
aptitude tests participants were asked to complete included the assessment of 
colour perception, several modes of reasoning, numerical abilities, visualization of 
three-dimensional forms, rotation of two -dimensional shapes, several forms  of 

[Page 126]
116 
memory and motor ability, among others.

metadata.core_insight_ko: 이 논문 '다양한 시각 자극에 대한 복잡성과 미적 선호도'는 시각 자극의 복잡성과 미적 선호도 간의 관계를 탐구한다. 오랫동안 이 관계를 이해하려는 노력이 있었으나 개념적 혼란이 존재했으며, 본 연구는 맥휘니의 기준을 바탕으로 미적 선호도를 특정 시각 자극에 대한 호감도나 반감도로 정의한다. 특히 다니엘 베르린의 프레임워크 검증을 시도한 연구들 간의 결과 불일치에 초점을 맞춘다.

text:
The final score reflec ts the number of choices that match the one 
considered by the test’s authors to be artistically superior. The second test also 
requires participants to indicate which stimuli they like most. In this case, they 
have to choose among stimuli varying in comple xity, defined as the number of 
elements, and order, defined as the degree of repetition of the pattern. The last 
tests measures preferences for 50 sets of 3 visual designs that differ in their 
proportions, such as the ratio of width to length of parabolic curves. The set of 
aptitude tests participants were asked to complete included the assessment of 
colour perception, several modes of reasoning, numerical abilities, visualization of 
three-dimensional forms, rotation of two -dimensional shapes, several forms  of 

[Page 126]
116 
memory and motor ability, among others. The results of this study showed 
significant differences between the preferences of professional artists and non -
artists on the following dimensions: symmetry, complexity, order, and shape. The 
most relevant resu lts for our study include: (i) the finding that whereas artists 
tended to prefer the asymmetrical designs, non -artists preferred the more 
symmetrical ones; (ii) artists preferred less complex designs than non -artists; (iii) 
artists preference for unordered  designs was higher than that of non -artists; and 
finally, (iv) the scores of artists on inductive reasoning, spatial ability, visual 
memory and dexterity were higher than those of non-artists. 
 However, Eysenck's (1971b; Eysenck & Castle, 1970b)  and Bezrucsko and 
Schroeder's (1994)  results are in sharp contrast with studies that have suggested 
that artistically trained participants tend to prefer more complex stimuli than 
untrained participants. This trend appeared in the study performed by Barron and 
Welsh (1952), which had a twofold obje ctive: to discover systematic differences 
between artists and non -artists in preferences for figures and to construct a scale 
of artistic discrimination. They asked a group of 37 artists and art students and a 
group of 150 people without artistic training,  who varied in educational and 
occupational background, to sort 400 figures according to their preference for 
them. Thereafter, the authors selected 40 items which were consistently disliked by 
artists more often than non -artists and 25 which were preferre d by artists but not 
by laypeople, making sure that the differences were statistically significant. The 
study of these figures revealed that all 40 figures disliked by the artist group were 
simple and symmetrical, while all the figures they preferred, but non-artists 
rejected, were complex and asymmetrical. The set of 65 figures were used to 
construct a scale, such that agreement with preferences expressed by the art group 
awarded examinees a high score. This scale effectively separated the original 
participating groups, with scores of 16.9 and 40.25 for non -artists and artists 
respectively. Its application to two different groups also separated artists from 
non-artists, with scores of 18.37 and 39.07, a highly significant difference. Thus, it 
is suggested t hat people with art training or professional artists have a higher 

[Page 127]
 
117 
preference for complexity than those who do not have art education or carry out 
artistic activities. 
 Munsinger and Kessen (1964)  designed a series of experiments to study 
preference for random polygons varying in complexity, determined by the number 
of turns, which ranged from 3 to 40. They compared the preferences of art 
students, who had extensive experience with painting and graphic design, with 
those of inexperienced participants. Results showed that whereas the latter group’s 
preferences increased with the complexity of the polygons to a certain point –
around ten turns -, and  then decreased for more complex polygons, art students 
gave very low preference ratings for simple polygons and very high ratings for the 
most complex polygons. The authors concluded that  
The almost linear relation between preference and number of turns suggests 
that the art students’ past experience with patterns and shapes has changed their 
preference for variability from that of the unsophisticated observer. This 
difference can be taken as evidence that experience increases one’s ability to 
group indep endent characteristics of stimuli and thereby reduce cognitive 
uncertainty (Munsinger & Kessen, 1964 , p. 16).  
 The study carried out by Taylor and Eisenman (1964)  lead to similar 
conclusions. In this case, however, only art students were included in the 
experiment, but they varied in creativity (as rated by a member of an ar t faculty) 
and experience with arts. Participants were asked to indicate which three polygons 
he or she preferred most and least out of a set of twelve varying from 4 to 24 
vertices. Overall, participants tended to prefer the more complex polygons. 
However, significant differences were observed between participants rated as 
highly creative and with greater experience and those rated as less creative and 
lacking experience in arts. Creative participants showed a tendency to choose more 
complex figures than t he less creative participants. Eisenman and Cofee (1964)  
attempted to verify whether there were differences between the preference for 
polygons of art students and mathematics students, who were also familiar wit h 
geometrical forms, although from quite a different perspective. They asked 10 art 
students and 10 mathematics students to express their aesthetic preference for 5 

[Page 128]
118 
symmetrical and 5 asymmetrical polygons, each of which had six points. Their 
results showed  that the first choice of all art students was an asymmetrical 
polygon, whereas the first choice of each mathematics student was a symmetrical 
polygon. The authors concluded that, given that asymmetrical polygons are more 
complex than their symmetrical cou nterparts, artists prefer more complex forms 
than non-artists. 
 Hare (1974) framed his study of the influence of expertise in the arts on 
the relation between complexity and aesthetic preference within Berlyne’s 
conceptual structure. As an explanation for the fact that stimu li preferred by 
artistically experienced participants tend to be more complex than those preferred 
by laypeople, as revealed by the studies we have just commented (Barron & Welsh, 
1952; Eisenman & Cofee, 196 4; Taylor & Eisenman, 1964) , he suggested that 
experience with a variety of artistic stimuli might improve the ability to process 
more complex stimuli, which may increase the amount of complexity required to 
produce an optimal hedonic tone. Hare's (1974)  aim was to verify w hether the 
preference for complexity was limited to the most familiar stimuli class, or 
whether it would extend to other classes. First he studied the differences between 
the ratings of complexity, pleasingness and interest for 12 sound sequences 
varying in uncertainty made by a group of 24 fine art students (enrolled in painting 
and sculpture courses) and 24 psychology students with not art background. His 
results showed that the complexity and interest ratings of both groups of 
participants grew linearly with the uncertainty of the sound sequences.

metadata.core_insight_ko: 본 논문 '다양한 시각 자극에 대한 복잡성과 미적 선호도'는 시각 자극의 복잡성과 미적 선호도 간의 관계를 탐구한다. 연구자들은 오랜 기간 이 관계를 이해하려 했으나 개념적 혼란이 존재했다. 본 연구는 맥휘니의 기준을 바탕으로 미적 선호도를 특정 시각 자극에 대한 호감도나 반감도로 정의하며, 다니엘 베르라인의 프레임워크 검증을 시도한 연구들 간의 결과 차이에 초점을 맞춘다.

text:
Hare's (1974)  aim was to verify w hether the 
preference for complexity was limited to the most familiar stimuli class, or 
whether it would extend to other classes. First he studied the differences between 
the ratings of complexity, pleasingness and interest for 12 sound sequences 
varying in uncertainty made by a group of 24 fine art students (enrolled in painting 
and sculpture courses) and 24 psychology students with not art background. His 
results showed that the complexity and interest ratings of both groups of 
participants grew linearly with the uncertainty of the sound sequences. Importantly 
for our purposes, there were no significant differences between complexity ratings 
made by participants with and without artistic education. However, preference 
scores awarded by art students to stim uli with high uncertainty were significantly 
higher than those awarded by psychology students. A second experiment 
paralleled this one, but assessed the ratings of random polygons varying in number 
of sides from 3 to 146 by music and psychology students. A gain, participants were 
asked to rate the stimuli on pleasingness, complexity and interest. Although in this 
case scores in the three scales increased with the number of sides, there were no 

[Page 129]
 
119 
significant differences between music and psychology students. Al though this 
study suggests a certain cross -modal transfer of complexity preference, the choice 
of materials might be masking interesting relations, and the reader is left 
wondering why the first experiment did not include a group of music students and 
the second one a group of fine art students, which would have provided an 
interesting reference point. 
 More recently, Hekkert, Peper and Van Wieringen (1994)  designed an 
experiment to clarify the influence of the instructions given by the experimenter 
on differences between artistically trained and untrained participants’ ratings of 
rectangles varying in pro portions. They created two counterbalanced conditions. 
In one of them, twelve participants with art education and twelve with no art -
related experience, were asked to express their (subjective) aesthetic preference for 
a series of rectangles presented in a  paired comparison procedure. Specifically, 
they had to choose the one they found more pleasing or attractive. In the other 
condition, participants were asked to make an (objective) aesthetic judgment by 
choosing the one they believed was better proportion ed or more balanced. The 
analysis of the participants’ responses indicated that in the subjective condition 
both groups showed a preference peak for proportions close to the golden 
section, with trained participants exhibiting an additional peak for propor tions 
close to the square. Under the objective condition both groups of participants 
showed a maximum preference for rectangle proportions close to the square. 
Thus, it seems that differences between groups of participants varying in 
experience with art ar e especially large when they are asked to rate their 
preferences. These differences tend to disappear when they are asked to conform 
to some external objective criterion (Hekkert, Peper, & Van Wieringen, 1994). 
 Neperud (1986) asked seventeen art students, 4 of which were male, and 31 
non-art students, including 7 males, to rate representational and abstract pictures, 
collages, and patterns on a series of bipolar adjective scales designed to measure 
pleasingness, hedonic tone, arousal, and uncertainty. Evaluative ratings (which 

[Page 130]
120 
were taken to  represent hedonic tone) of art students were higher than non -art 
students. The ratings on pleasingness given by art students to abstract stimuli were 
also significantly higher than those given by non -art students. There were no 
significant differences between these two groups of participants on the arousal and 
uncertainty scores, nor on the pleasingness scores given to representational 
pictures. These results were interpreted by the author as evidence that artistic 
education provides information about art styles, the structure and organization of 
compositions, that results in differences in the way art is viewed and valued 
(Neperud, 1986). 
 Winston and Cupchik's (1992)  work represents one of the best -designed 
studies of the effects of art education on aesthetic preference, and stimulated 
further research in this are a with more ecologically valid stimuli. They recruited 17 
male and 14 female Psychology students, who had never undergone any art -related 
courses, and 10 male and 15 female art students, who had taken at least five art 
history or studio art courses. All pa rticipants were asked to rate 50 stimuli on four 
7-point scales: pleasant -unpleasant, simple -complex, warm -cold, and like -dislike. 
Half of the stimuli used in this study belonged to the popular art category, and the 
other were exemplars of high art. The fo rmer included sentimental, anecdotal 
paintings and wildlife prints, country scenes and children, while the latter included 
works exhibited in great museums and collections of the world, and are valued by 
art critics and curators. Whereas popular pictures emphasize the pleasing effects of 
the represented subject, providing soothing emotions for the viewer, high art 
pictures achieve a balance between subject matter and style, and explore a greater 
variety of emotional effects (Winston & Cupchik, 1992). 
 Results showed significant differences between art -trained and untrained 
participants on some of the measurements. Whereas untraine d participants 
expressed a greater liking for popular art than for high art, experienced 
participants expressed the opposite preference. Furthermore, untrained 
participants found popular art to be warm and pleasant and high art to be more 

[Page 131]
 
121 
unpleasant and colder, while there were no significant differences between ratings 
of art -trained participants on warmth and pleasantness for high art and popular 
art. The last significant difference on the scales refers to the ratings of complexity. 
Untrained participants  did not rate high art and popular art differently, but 
experienced participants rated the complexity of high art stimuli higher than that 
of popular art (Winston & Cupchik, 1992). 
 Hekkert and Wieringen (1996b)  compared the ratings of a group of non -
experts (university students lacking experience or interest in art), a group of 
relative experts (senior industrial design students), and a group of exper ts (senior 
art school students with at least two years of education and experience related with 
visual arts) on a series of scales. These included three referring to colour, as well as 
like-dislike, abstract -figurative, balanced -unbalanced, and complex -simple. The 
materials used in this study consisted of 12 postimpressionist paintings, 12 black 
and white versions of the same paintings, 12 distorted versions of the same 
paintings which appeared abstract, and 12 black and white versions of the 
distorted pictures. The analysis of these ratings led to several interesting results. 
First, the liking scores given by non -experts and relative experts to 
representational stimuli were significantly greater than those given to abstract 
stimuli. However, this difference  was not significant for the group of art experts, 
which suggests that as expertise increases, the preference of the representational 
over the abstract versions decreases.
