4. PILOT STUDY USING "PALETTES"
With Palettes set up, a study on website coloration can be conducted. The
initial objectives for this study was to clear up some questions designers struggle
with when designing for specific cultures and industries:
1. What are the most common colors on the web?
2. Do industries prefer certain colors?
3. Do cultures prefer certain colors?
4. Where are colors usually placed on a site?
5. What colors are generally found together?
Using empirical data collected using Palettes, this study aims to answers the
aforementioned questions and be able to make generalized color palette selections
for cultures and industries.
4.1 SCOPE OF STUDY
The scope of this pilot study was carefully determined. There are hundreds of
millions of active websites in the world, and over sixteen million colors that are
capable of being rendered on the web [lo]. Choosing which sites to include in the
study required a method for filtering and/or categorizing all the websites in the
world. This would reduce the data points to a manageable scope.
Alexa Internet, Inc. [3], a California-based subsidiary company of
Amazon.com, provides comprehensive commercial web traffic data. It collects data
on browsing behavior, and publishes rankings and other information on over 30
million websites [2]. Among the public data Alexa.com releases each year are
rankings of the top 500 most visited websites broken down by country and by
"(category." Due to its credibility as a web traffic and tanking website, these rankings
28


[Page 29]
from Alexa.com were used to analyze colors in websites. Because running all 500
websites for each country/category using Palettes proved to be too time-intensive,
only the top 100 websites were used in the pilot study.
Alexa.com provides website rankings for over 120 countries and 17 categories.
This pilot study chooses to focus on a subset of that data. 24 countries and 12
categories were chosen. The 24 countries are the countries with the highest number
of internet users, listed by the International Telecommunications Union [9]. Internet
users are persons using the Internet in the last 12 months from any device, including
mobile phones [6]. The 10 categories were chosen by eliminating non-industry
related categories, such as "World" and "Regional."
The scope of the pilot study is thus defined by the following data:
1. Top 100 websites (ranked by total visits per year) for 24 countries
2. Top 100 websites (ranked by total visits per year) for 12 industries
The full lists of the websites included in this study can be found in Apendex A.
4.2 RESULTS
The study aims to generalize website colors across a single country and a
single industry. This is done by first collecting the top 10 colors of each website in a
country/industry. Then, the top 30 colors of a country/industry is graphed and
analyzed. Over 2000 websites were analyzed using Palettes, and results ranged from
expected to astonishing. The initial questions of interest were:
1. What are the most common colors on the web?
2. Do industries prefer certain colors?
3. Do cultures prefer certain colors?
4. Where are colors usually placed on a site?

[Page 30]

formulate.
First, it can be seen from the results that the most common colors on the web
are blues, grays, and oranges/yellows.

5. CONCLUSIONS AND FURTHER RESEARCH
In spite of the wealth of information currently available for designing
websites, it is not easy for web designers to create cultural and industry appropriate
color selections and determine the best usage for color on a webpage. This thesis
project addresses these concerns in two parts. In the first part, a color analysis tool
("Palettes") is created to collect data on how colors are being used in existing
websites. The abilities of Palettes include finding 1) the full spectrum of colors used
on a website, 2) the percentage of each color on the page, 3) the CSS properties of
each color, and 4) the HTML classes or ID associated with each color. In the second
part, a semi-automated empirical study of approximately 2,000 websites across 24
countries and 12 different industry-related categories was conducted using this tool.
From the pilot study, it can be seen that the primary usage of a website's main
colors are in highlighting "action" features, such as buttons and links. Results also
show that certain colors can be identified as universally used in website design for all
countries and categories studied, but culture-specific and industry-specific palettes
can also be identified. Universally used colors include shades of blues, grays and
oranges/yellows. Select industry-specific color palettes include:
- Reference: Low saturation, earthy tones, browns, oranges and forrest green
- Heath: High saturation, crisp tones, blues, light grays and white
" Kids: High saturation, high range of hues, blue, purple, yellow
- Social Media: High saturation, high range of hues, oranges, yellows, blues
- University: Low saturation, dark blues, dark purples, browns
" Music: Low saturation, blacks and whites
Select culture-specific color palettes include:
- China: Blues and Reds
40


[Page 41]
- Russia: Blues
- Brazil: Grays with pops of greens and yellow
- France: Blacks and whites
- US: Blacks and whites and some blue
These are a selection of results from the pilot study. As an initial study, these results
open the door to further research into color in website design. Some suggestions for
future research in this area are listed below:
For further development of the color analysis tool - Palettes
1. Be able to not only capture the colors on the main page of a URL, but also the
children pages (i.e. not just facebook.com but also the profile pages)
2. Faster runtime (currently takes up to 3 seconds to convert a page into an
image)
3. Be able to separate images from DOM elements
4. Be able to collect data of a website's history (i.e. not just the colors on the site
currently, but also the colors of the site a year ago, two years ago, etc.)
For further development in researching colors in website design
1. Compare colors of a website over time - how do colors change?
2. Compare colors of a website to color trends in fashion, technology, etc - are
there correlations?
3. Research the use of textures and gradients with colors

[Page 1]
Measuring Processing Fluency: One versus Five Items
Laura K. M. Graf , Stefan Mayer , and Jan R. Landwehr
Goethe University Frankfurt
Accepted by Amna Kirmani, Editor; Associate Editor, Joann Peck
While there is an ample amount of consumer behavior research that recruits processing ﬂuency as an explana-
tory construct, the question how to best measure the ﬂuency experience has received little attention. Therefore,
there is a lack of consistency in measuring the construct, particularly with regard to the use of single-item ver-
sus multi-item measures. The current research, thus, aims to investigate how processing ﬂuency can be consis-
tently measured across different experimental ﬂuency manipulations and which type of measure has the
highest validity. Based on classic scale development procedures, we propose a reliable and valid multi-item
measure and compare this measure against a single-item measure in terms of predictive validity. We show
that both measures mediate the effect of ﬁve established ﬂuency manipulations and that the single-item mea-
sure is suf ﬁcient. In addition to providing a measure for future research that can be adapted to different
empirical settings, we provide empirical evidence on the replicability of ﬂuency effects and on the theoretical
conjecture that people have a uniform ﬂuency experience across different manipulations of ﬂuency.
Keywords Processing ﬂuency; Scale development; Replication; (Aesthetic) liking; Truth; Risk
perception
In 2004, Journal of Consumer Psychology published a
seminal article by Norbert Schwarz that laid the
groundwork for most of the current theoretical
understanding of the processing ﬂuency construct
in consumer behavior research. In this article, Sch-
warz (2004) summarized the theoretical and empiri-
cal work on metacognitive experiences, that is, the
ease or dif ﬁculty with which information can be
processed, or the ease or dif ﬁculty with which con-
tent can be brought to mind. Furthermore, he pro-
posed that these metacognitive experiences, which
have been summarized under the term “processing
ﬂuency” (Alter & Oppenheimer, 2009), are of great
importance in consumer behavior research for two
reasons: ﬁrst because they in ﬂuence a broad range
of consumer judgments, ranging from judgments of
liking (King & Janiszewski, 2011; Labroo, Dhar, &
Schwarz, 2008; Lee & Labroo, 2004) to judgments
of truth (Hansen, Dech ^ene, & W €anke, 2008) and
risk (Song & Schwarz, 2009), and second because
they can be triggered by many different, easy-to-
manipulate variables, such as color contrast
(Thompson & Ince, 2013), typicality (Landwehr,
Labroo, & Herrmann, 2011; Landwehr, Wentzel, &
Herrmann, 2013), exposure (Ferraro, Bettman, &
Chartrand, 2009; Landwehr, Golla, & Reber, 2017),
or pronounceability (Alter & Oppenheimer, 2008;
Song & Schwarz, 2009). Not surprisingly, the article
by Schwarz (2004) stipulated an ample amount of
consumer behavior research that draws on the ﬂu-
ency construct to explain a large variety of effects.
While these studies strikingly demonstrate the
broad applicability of the ﬂuency construct,
research on how the subjective ﬂuency experience
can be empirically operationalized by a consistent
measure has received little attention. More speci ﬁ-
cally, there exists no psychometrically validated
and canonical scale for the somewhat “wooly” ﬂu-
ency construct; that is, a construct that has both
versatile sources and consequences. Thus, the relia-
bility and validity of existing measures used to cap-
ture processing ﬂuency cannot be taken for
granted. In addition, the lack of an established mea-
sure prevents a rigorous comparison of ﬂuency

effects across different manipulations because it
would require measures of ﬂuency that share a
common metric (Lynch, Nettemeyer, Spiller, &
Zammit, 2009). Hence, the present research aims to
develop a psychometrically sound measure of pro-
cessing ﬂuency that can capture the broad range of
ﬂuency effects. That is, we aim to provide a generic
measure that is context-independent and can thus
be used across different manipulations of ﬂuency.
In this way, we intend to make three substantial
contributions to the literature. First, we add to the
theoretical understanding of processing ﬂuency by
providing systematic empirical evidence for the the-
oretical notion that different ﬂuency effects bear on
the same subjective experience and that this uni-
form experience mediates the effect of highly
diverse phenomena. That is, while previous
researchers have made this claim based on retro-
spectively classifying existing studies as ﬂuency
effects (Alter & Oppenheimer, 2009; Reber, Sch-
warz, & Winkielman, 2004), we provide empirical
evidence on this conjecture and thus emphasize the
theoretical potency of the construct. Second, we
show that a single item re ﬂecting the difﬁcult-easy
dimension of mental processing is suf ﬁcient to cap-
ture the ﬂuency experience. More precisely, our lit-
erature review suggests that the two items difﬁcult
and easy are often used in published research on
ﬂuency effects, thereby suggesting that a single
item that re ﬂects this bipolar dimension may be an
adequate measure. However, the suf ﬁciency and
validity of this item has not been tested, and one
may also argue that the broadness of the construct
can be captured only using multiple items. Hence,
we compare a multi-item scale that we develop
based on psychometric procedures with the single-
item measure in terms of predictive validity and
show that both measures are equally effective.
Therefore, we recommend the more parsimonious
single-item measure for future research. Finally, we
show that subjective ﬂuency mediates ﬁve standard
ﬂuency effects, thus contributing to the increased
awareness on the replicability of psychological
research (Lindsay, 2015) and attesting to the impor-
tance and robustness of the ﬂuency construct.

validity of this item has not been tested, and one
may also argue that the broadness of the construct
can be captured only using multiple items. Hence,
we compare a multi-item scale that we develop
based on psychometric procedures with the single-
item measure in terms of predictive validity and
show that both measures are equally effective.
Therefore, we recommend the more parsimonious
single-item measure for future research. Finally, we
show that subjective ﬂuency mediates ﬁve standard
ﬂuency effects, thus contributing to the increased
awareness on the replicability of psychological
research (Lindsay, 2015) and attesting to the impor-
tance and robustness of the ﬂuency construct.
We organize the remainder of the paper as fol-
lows. First, we explain how we theoretically de ﬁne
processing ﬂuency in this research. Then, we per-
form an in-depth literature review of existing ﬂu-
ency measures, generating a comprehensive list of
items that have been used in previous literature to
measure the subjective ﬂuency experience (Item
Generation Step). Subsequently, we reduce the item
pool based on an expert study that assessed the
content validity of the items (Pilot Study). Follow-
ing this step, the remaining items are puri ﬁed
(Study 1), and the resulting multi-item measure is
tested against a single-item measure in terms of
predictive validity (Study 2). Finally, the results are
discussed, and implications for future research are
provided.
Conceptual Background
Theoretical De ﬁnition and Foundation
Because this research aims to develop a measure
of processing ﬂuency that is applicable to various
domains, we de ﬁne processing ﬂuency as “
a subjec-
tive feeling of ease or dif ﬁculty associated with any
type of mental processing. ” Notably, although
researchers often differentiate only between dis ﬂu-
ent (i.e., dif ﬁcult) and ﬂuent (i.e., easy) processing,
the experience encompasses the full continuum
from dif ﬁcult to easy, that is, from dis ﬂuency to ﬂu-
ency (Greifeneder & Unkelbach, 2013).
Our de ﬁnition assumes that every mental opera-
tion, ranging from perceiving to processing to
retrieving information, can trigger an experience or
feeling of ﬂuency that re ﬂects how dif ﬁcult or easy
the mental operation feels (Unkelbach & Greifene-
der, 2013a). This experience has fundamental conse-
quences for (consumer) judgments (Alter &
Oppenheimer, 2009; Reber, Schwarz, & Winkiel-
man, 2004; Schwarz, 2004). For instance, ﬂuently
processed products are liked more (King & Janis-
zewski, 2011; Labroo et al., 2008; Lee & Labroo,
2004), ﬂuently processed product designs are
judged as more beautiful (Landwehr et al., 2011,
2013), and ﬂuently perceived product claims are
perceived as truer (Hansen et al., 2008).
In addition to in ﬂuencing many diverse judg-
ments, the ﬂuency experience itself has been shown
to have a large variety of causes, which are
assumed to affect various types of ﬂuency. In this
regard, researchers usually distinguish between per-
ceptual and conceptual ﬂuency. Perceptual ﬂuency
refers to the ease of identifying the perceptual fea-
tures of a stimulus (e.g., a product design or an
advertisement), such as its form, size, or visual
details (Reber, Schwarz, & Winkielman, 2004; Sch-
warz, 2004), and has been shown to be in ﬂuenced
by variables such as repeated exposure (Bornstein
&D ’Agostino, 1994; Fang, Singh, & Ahluwalia,
2007; Landwehr et al., 2017), the font in which
information is presented (Cabooter, Millet, Weijters,
& Pandelaere, 2016; DeMotta, Chao, & Kramer,
2016), visual clarity (Whittlesea, Jacoby, & Girard,

[Page 3]
1990), complexity (Landwehr et al., 2011), or ﬁgure-
ground contrast (Reber, Winkielman, & Schwarz,
1998; Thompson & Ince, 2013). Conceptual ﬂuency,
by contrast, refers to the ease of mental operations
concerned with assigning meaning to a stimulus
(e.g., to a product; Lee & Labroo, 2004; Reber, Sch-
warz, & Winkielman, 2004; Reber, Wurtz, & Zim-
mermann, 2004), and empirical evidence suggests
that this ﬂuency can arise when a product is pre-
sented in a predictive context or when it is primed
by a related construct (Lee & Labroo, 2004). A fur-
ther type of ﬂuency, which has received less atten-
tion in the consumer behavior literature, is retrieval
ﬂuency (Alter & Oppenheimer, 2009; Schwarz,
2004). Retrieval ﬂuency is the subjective ease or dif-
ﬁculty with which people can bring to mind certain
information, such as arguments in favor of a particu-
lar brand (W €anke, Bohner, & Jurkowitsch, 1997).
Importantly, even though researchers have come to
distinguish between these different ﬂuency types,
available research suggests that the different ﬂuency
types are experientially the same (Schwarz, 2004).
That is, they all seem to result in a general feeling of
ﬂuency and have similar effects on judgments
(Winkielman, Schwarz, Fazendeiro, & Reber, 2003).
Based on the ﬁnding that the subjective experience
of ﬂuency in ﬂuences judgments to a greater extent
than objective ﬂuency (Forster, Leder, & Ansorge,
2013), our view of processing ﬂuency emphasizes
that ﬂuency is a subjective experience that can be dis-
entangled from its objective basis (Reber, Wurtz, &
Zimmermann, 2004). Objective ﬂuency refers to “ob-
jective” facilitators of processing (Forster et al.,
2013), such as repeated exposure, symmetry, or pre-
sentation duration (Reber et al., 1998), or objectively
measurable indicators of ef ﬁcient processing, such as
response time or judgment accuracy (Reber, Wurtz,
& Zimmermann, 2004). How this objective ﬂuency
translates into an experience of ease or dif ﬁculty on
an individual level, however, is highly subjective,
which is why objective ﬂuency and the subjective
experience of ﬂuency are not the same thing. In fact,
what is easy for one person may be dif ﬁcult for
another; what is easy in one context may be dif ﬁcult
in another context; and what is easy at one point in
time may be dif ﬁcult at another point in time. As a
consequence of this subjectivity, predicting whether
an individual will experience processing ﬂuency is
difﬁcult (Unkelbach & Greifeneder, 2013b). For
instance, whether reading this article is dif ﬁcult or
easy may depend on the reader ’s background on the-
ories on metacognitive experiences and on his or her
degree of distraction when reading this article.
Another reason why predicting whether an
individual will experience ﬂuency is dif ﬁcult is the
location of the experience at the “fringe of conscious-
ness,” which implies that humans are not necessarily
aware of the ﬂuency of their mental processing
(Reber, Wurtz, & Zimmermann, 2004, p. 48). Instead,
people experience ﬂuency only when it deviates
from the ﬂuency of the surrounding context or from
their expected level of ﬂuency (Hansen & W €anke,
2013). Applied to the example of reading this article,
the ﬂuency experience should be more salient when
reading is easier than expected based on prior expe-
rience with scienti ﬁc articles or easier than reading
the previous article.
Measures of the Subjective Fluency Experience
Although researchers agree that the processing
ﬂuency construct is important and interesting, a
comprehensive literature review
1 of all empirical
articles using the ﬂuency construct in psychology
and marketing research demonstrates that the mea-
surement of the construct has been rather neglected
(date of access of the literature review: 04/10/
2017). Speci ﬁcally, of the 604 empirical ﬂuency arti-
cles that we analyzed, only 120 articles employed a
direct measure of the subjective ﬂuency experience,
and to date, there exists no psychometrical investi-
gation of the ﬂuency experience. Rather, measures
are usually chosen ad hoc and are highly speci ﬁct o
the empirical context.
An important caveat of many existing scales is
that they include items that do not correspond to
our—and the most common —deﬁnition of process-
ing ﬂuency. That is, many scales do not measure
the subjective experience as such but (additionally)
include items that refer to an assessment or evalua-
tion of the stimulus, thereby referring either to the
sources or to the consequences of ﬂuency. For
instance, items such as organized or complex, which
reﬂect sources of ﬂuency, or items such as attractive
or eye-catching, which re ﬂect consequences of ﬂu-
ency, are often used.
A considerable inconsistency in the design of
existing scales refers to the variability in the num-
ber of items employed. That is, of the 120 articles
that used a direct measure of the subjective ﬂuency
experience, roughly one half (i.e., 45%) used multi-
ple items to measure ﬂuency, whereas the other
half (i.e., 51.67%) used only a single item to mea-
sure ﬂuency (3.33% used both a multi-item measure
and a single-item measure). Notably, most single-
item measures employ some variation of the items
easy and/or difﬁcult (e.g., Cabooter et al., 2016; Fang
et al., 2007; Lembregts & Pandelaere, 2012; Shen,

text:
[Page 4]
Jiang, & Adaval, 2010). In fact, the two items difﬁ-
cult and easy, which are also often used within the
reviewed multi-item measures (e.g., DeMotta et al.,
2016; Labroo & Lee, 2006; Landwehr et al., 2011;
Lee, Keller, & Sternthal, 2010), closely re ﬂect the
theoretical de ﬁnition of processing ﬂuency. How-
ever, even if these items seem to be reasonable from
a theoretical perspective, they have not been empir-
ically tested in a systematic way in order to assess
whether they validly and suf ﬁciently measure the
subjective ﬂuency experience.
Hence, the question remains whether a single-
item measure with the semantic differential difﬁcult
to easy is suf ﬁcient to capture the ﬂuency experi-
ence or whether a multi-item measure is required.
In fact, this inquiry is interesting in light of the gen-
eral discussion on whether to measure a construct
with a single-item scale or a multi-item scale
(Bergkvist & Rossiter, 2007; Rossiter, 2016). Interest-
ingly, we ﬁnd that the large majority of articles that
used multiple items to measure ﬂuency are from
the ﬁeld of marketing or consumer behavior. More
speciﬁcally, of the articles in our database that used
a multi-item measure, 74.14% are from the ﬁeld of
marketing, whereas only 22.41% are from the ﬁeld
of psychology (the remaining 3.45% are from mar-
keting-related ﬁelds such as ﬁnance or information
systems). Thus, it seems that marketing and con-
sumer behavior researchers in the ﬁeld of process-
ing ﬂuency have followed the recommendation
advocated by Churchill (1979) and Peter (1979) that
multi-item measures are generally superior to sin-
gle-item measures. According to this perspective,
multi-item measures are inherently more reliable
and valid (Churchill, 1979; Peter, 1979; Wanous &
Reichers, 1996), given their ability to compute item
correlations and thus to demonstrate “internal con-
sistency.” In addition, because the measurement
error tends to decrease as the number of items
increases, multi-item measures are assumed to have
a lower measurement error than single-item mea-
sures. With respect to validity concerns, multiple
items are assumed to possess a higher construct
validity; a larger set of items can capture more
information than a single item and should thus be
more likely to cover all facets of the focal construct
(Baumgartner & Homburg, 1996).
In contrast, we ﬁnd the opposite pattern for the
articles that used only a single item; only 24.24%
are from the ﬁeld of marketing, whereas 69.70% are
from psychology and 6.06% are from marketing-
related ﬁelds such as accounting or management.
Compared with multi-item measures, single-item
measures have clear practical advantages (Bergkvist
& Rossiter, 2007) because they minimize respondent
refusal and the costs of data collection. In his
C-OAR-SE procedure for scale development, how-
ever, Rossiter (2002) argued that there is also a the-
oretical argument in favor of a single-item measure,
which applies when the construct is such that in
the minds of the raters, “(a) the object of the con-
struct (i.e., what exactly is being evaluated) is “con-
crete singular, ” meaning that it consists of one
object that is easily and uniformly imagined, and
(b) the attribute of the construct (i.e., the dimension
on which the object is judged) is “concrete,” again
meaning that it is easily and uniformly imagined ”
(Bergkvist & Rossiter, 2007, p. 176). Hence, accord-
ing to Bergkvist and Rossiter (2007) and Rossiter
(2002), whether to use a single-item or a multi-item
measure depends on the de ﬁnition of the construct,
particularly on whether its object and attributes are
concrete.
From our perspective, a precise construct de ﬁni-
tion of the ﬂuency experience is dif ﬁcult, particu-
larly with regard to the attributes of the construct
(i.e., the object of the construct represents the focal
mental process, such as reading, which should be a
concrete object). Following our theoretical de ﬁnition
of the ﬂuency experience (i.e., a subjective feeling of
ease or dif ﬁculty associated with any type of men-
tal processing), the attribute (i.e., judgment dimen-
sion) of the construct is difﬁcult … easy, but the
question is whether this attribute is concrete singu-
lar or not. On one hand, one may argue that there
is “unanimous agreement ” by respondents in terms
of what difﬁcult and easy mean. On the other hand,
one may argue that these two items are not suf ﬁ-
cient to fully capture the manifoldness of the ﬂu-
ency experience with its heterogeneous sources.
Additionally, as an assessment of peoples ’ mental
processes, it is a construct that cannot be directly
and objectively observed and may thus better be
assessed by a set of items (Rossiter, 2002). Hence, in
addition to developing a universally applicable
measure of processing ﬂuency, a further aim of the
following investigation is, therefore, to assess on
empirical grounds whether the ﬂuency experience
is better captured by a multi-item measure or
whether a single-item measure with the endpoints
difﬁcult and easy is suf ﬁcient.
Overview of Multi-Item Scale Development and
Validation Procedures
Following classic psychometric procedures, we
began with a literature review that generated a

text:
[Page 5]
comprehensive and exhaustive pool of items that
previous literature used to measure the subjective
ﬂuency experience (Churchill, 1979). Subsequently,
this list was carefully edited by the three authors to
obtain a nonredundant list of items. In doing so,
the least possible adjustment of the existing items
was performed. The resulting list of 46 items was
then evaluated for content validity by eight ﬂuency
experts (Pilot Study). This resulted in a further
reduction to ﬁve items. We then conducted an
online study to assess the dimensionality and relia-
bility of the ﬁve items (Study 1). Because our aim is
to develop a generic measure of subjective ﬂuency,
we tested the dimensionality and reliability of the
ﬁve items across various types of ﬂuency: percep-
tual ﬂuency, conceptual ﬂuency, ﬁt ﬂuency, and
retrieval ﬂuency. The results of this study reveal a
one-factor structure of the ﬁve items. Hence, the
ﬁve items form our multi-item scale. Finally, we
compare this 5-item scale with a 1-item scale in
terms of predictive validity across ﬁve different
ﬂuency manipulations (Study 2).
Item Generation
We began the item generation process by review-
ing in detail the 120 articles (identi ﬁed in the litera-
ture review) that used a direct measure of subjective
ﬂuency. For each measure, we extracted the adjec-
tive/adverb used to describe the ﬂuency construct
to compile an exhaustive list of items. For the mea-
sures that use a semantic differential, we recorded
both endpoints, and for the measures that use a Lik-
ert-type format, we recorded the adjective/adverb
describing the ﬂuency construct in the Likert ques-
tion. This ﬁrst step of item generation, in which we
deleted only completely identical items/item pairs
and retained all different variations and wording
nuances (e.g., we retained difﬁcult … not at all dif ﬁ-
cult as well as extremely dif ﬁcult … not at all dif ﬁcult)
produced an initial list of 95 items/item pairs. For
the items without a counterpart (i.e., the items gen-
erated from Likert-type measures), we then added
the opposite pole by either adding not at all (e.g., the
item complex received the counter pole not at all com-
plex) or by deleting the negation (e.g., the item not
easy received the counter pole easy).
In the next step, we iteratively reduced and care-
fully edited the list of 95 item pairs to achieve a
nonredundant set of semantic differentials. We
began by eliminating all items with essentially iden-
tical meanings that had only slight variations in the
wording. Items with slightly different shades of
meaning were retained (Churchill, 1979), yielding a
reduced list of 55 item pairs. This list was then fur-
ther discussed by the three authors and adjusted in
accordance with the following rules: (a) when an
item was used both in a Likert-type format and as
part of a semantic differential, only the semantic
differential was included; (b) we created semantic
differentials from items that form natural endpoints
of a bipolar dimension but were used only sepa-
rately as part of Likert-type measures; and (c) we
used only the plain item without any additional
speciﬁcations such as very or extremely. This proce-
dure resulted in a revised pool of 46 different
semantic differentials (see Appendix S1 for an
overview of the 46 items). Notably, no additional
item pairs were added because the authors agreed
on the comprehensiveness and completeness of the
list.
Pilot Study: Item Reduction Based on Content Validity
Following the item generation step, we con-
ducted a study in which ﬂuency experts judged the
content validity of the items. This study and the fol-
lowing two studies were all approved by our uni-
versity’s ethics committee.
Researchers were classi ﬁed as ﬂuency experts
based on their research output. Speci ﬁcally, using
the same criteria as at the ﬁrst time, we conducted
the literature review once again (date 05/22/2017)
and analyzed the results according to “record
counts by author. ” Twelve researchers made up the
top 10 record counts and were thus quali ﬁed as ﬂu-
ency experts (the number of ﬂuency-related publica-
tions ranged from 10 to 19).
On June 1, 2017, we contacted the ﬂuency
experts via e-mail and invited them to participate
in our study designed to receive their expert input
on the list of 46-item pairs. At the beginning of the
study, expert judges were given our de ﬁnition of
ﬂuency and were instructed to rate to what extent
each of the 46 word pairs is representative of the
ﬂuency construct (1 = not at all representative to
5 = clearly representative ). The order in which the 46-
item pairs were presented varied randomly for each
ﬂuency expert. Next to each item, an open text ﬁeld
allowed the experts to comment on each item pair.
By July 16, eight experts participated in our study.

text:
[Page 6]
ﬂuent, hard to easy, difﬁcult to comes naturally to me ,
complicated to simple, and not at all comprehensible to
comprehensible (see Appendix S1, for an overview
for the representativeness evaluations of the 46
items). These eight items were then extensively dis-
cussed by the authors, and a native English speaker
was consulted to check the wording of the items.
Because three item pairs were in fact variations of
the other items, we dropped these items. Addition-
ally, we replaced the item pair not at all compre-
hensible to comprehensible by incomprehensible to
comprehensible to ensure consistent usage of oppo-
site poles. Thus, the ﬁnal ﬁve semantic differentials
that were then used as input for the next step
aimed at item puri ﬁcation (Churchill, 1979) were
the following: difﬁcult to easy, unclear to clear, disﬂu-
ent to ﬂuent, effortful to effortless, incomprehensible to
comprehensible.
Study 1: Multi-Item Scale Dimensionality and
Reliability
The aim of Study 1 is to assess the reliability and
the dimensionality of the 5-item scale. Because we
aim to develop a scale of subjective ﬂuency that is
valid in different empirical domains, we tested the
scale for four different types of ﬂuency: (a) percep-
tual ﬂuency, (b) conceptual ﬂuency, (c) a speci ﬁc
form of conceptual ﬂuency that we call “ﬁt ﬂu-
ency,” and (d) retrieval ﬂuency. A second aim is to
compare the 5-item scale against an objective mea-
sure of ﬂuency, that is, reaction times. Notably, we
pre-registered this study, as well as the following
study (Study 2) on the “Open Science Framework
”
platform, where we also provide all data and data
analysis scripts for full transparency and repro-
ducibility (see: https://osf.io/wyvrx/).
Participants were recruited using Amazon
MTurk in July 2017; they provided informed con-
sent, were debriefed at the end of the study, and
had the opportunity to contact the principal investi-
gator at the end of the study. In total, 201 subjects
(47.3% females, M
age = 34.14) completed the four
parts (a –d) of our experimental study in a random
order. For each part of the study, participants were
randomly assigned to one of two ﬂuency conditions
(ﬂuency high vs. ﬂuency low), and we varied the
order of the ﬁve ﬂuency items in each task. In all
four parts of the study, there was a self-paced pre-
exposure to the stimulus prior to the ﬂuency evalu-
ation in order to record participants ’ processing
times as an objective ﬂuency measure. In all the
studies reported in the current paper, the ﬂuency
item(s) were evaluated on a visual analog scale
with an internal resolution of 100 increments.
Study 1a: Perceptual Fluency
Perceptual ﬂuency was manipulated by objective
picture complexity. For a set of 620 abstract, digi-
tally created art pictures, we calculated objective
picture complexity based on the size of the image
ﬁle after compression (Landwehr et al., 2011). One
picture very high in complexity and one picture
very low in complexity were used as stimuli for
this task. Participants were ﬁrst exposed to either of
the two pictures and instructed to study the picture
for as long as they wanted and then to click on the
“continue” button. On the next page, we asked
them to evaluate how they perceived the process of
studying the picture using the ﬁve ﬂuency items.
Speciﬁcally, they were asked the following ques-
tion: “The process of studying the picture was …,”
anchored at difﬁcult to easy, unclear to clear, disﬂuent
to ﬂuent, effortful to effortless, incomprehensible to com-
prehensible.
Study 1b: Conceptual Fluency
The operationalization of conceptual ﬂuency was
adapted from Lee and Labroo (2004) and followed
the idea that consumers can process a product in a
conceptually more ﬂuent fashion when it is pre-
sented in a predictive, compared with a nonpredic-
tive, advertising context. In the style of the stimulus
material used by Lee and Labroo (2004), we created
two advertisements for “HEINZ Tomato Ketchup ”
that consisted of four consecutively shown picture
slides. In the high conceptual ﬂuency condition, the
ﬁrst three slides depicted friends at a barbecue, ham-
burger patties on a grill, and a hamburger on a plate.
In the low conceptual ﬂuency condition, a woman in
a supermarket was shown, followed by a detergent
and then by a package of cereal. In both conditions,
the last slide depicted the target product, “HEINZ
Tomato Ketchup. ” Participants were told that we
were interested in their feedback on the sketch of a
new TV commercial for “HEINZ Tomato Ketchup ”
and that we would present them with four slides that
made up the storyline of the ad. In a ﬁrst pre-expo-
sure phase, we asked them to study each slide for as
long as they wanted and to immediately proceed to
the next slide when ﬁnished. Afterward, we showed
them the target product a second time and asked
them to respond to the question: “The process of
studying the advertised product was …” by provid-
ing ratings on the ﬁve ﬂuency items.

text:
[Page 7]
Study 1c: Fit Fluency
Our literature analysis of the 120 articles that
employed a subjective measure of processing ﬂu-
ency revealed that the most common ﬂuency
manipulation within the marketing and consumer
behavior articles is varying the ﬁt or congruency
between two factors (e.g., Chae & Hoegg, 2013;
Labroo & Lee, 2006; Lee et al., 2010; White,
MacDonnel, & Dahl, 2011). We propose subsuming
these manipulations under the term “ﬁt ﬂuency”
and tested our measure for this type of ﬂuency. To
operationalize ﬁt ﬂuency, we drew on the ﬁnding
by Chae and Hoegg (2013) who showed that the
congruency or ﬁt between a product ’s horizontal
presentation in an advertisement and consumers ’
expected spatial representation of time (i.e.,
past = left & future = right) increases the ﬂuency
with which the advertisement can be processed and
thus consumers ’ attitude toward the advertised
product. We used the same stimulus material as
Chae and Hoegg (2013; Study 1), who showed a
weight loss advertisement that displayed a before-
and-after image. In the time-space representation
congruent condition, the before picture was placed
on the left side of the advertisement and the after
picture was presented on the right side. In the time-
space incongruent condition, this presentation was
reversed. Again, participants were ﬁrst instructed
to study the advertisement for as long as they
wanted. Then, we asked them to evaluate how they
perceived the process of studying the pictures. In
particular, we asked: “The process of studying the
advertisement was …,” followed by the ﬁve ﬂuency
items.
Study 1d: Retrieval Fluency
In this study, we investigated the ease of self-
generating product-related information. Drawing
on the study by W €anke et al. (1997), we created
two different advertisements for the car brand
“Tesla.” Ease of retrieval was varied by using a slo-
gan stating “There are many reasons to drive a
Tesla. Could you name one? ” in the high- ﬂuency
condition and “There are many reasons to drive a
Tesla. Could you name 10? ” in the low- ﬂuency con-
dition. In the pre-exposure phase, we recorded par-
ticipants’ response time after asking them to study
the advertisement and to think about it for as long
as they wanted. Next, participants reported their
ﬂuency experience by providing ratings on the ﬁve
items in response to the question: “The process of
coming up with reasons/a reason was …”
Results
We conducted both the dimensionality and the reli-
ability analyses in two steps. First, we analyzed
each experimental manipulation separately. Second,
we analyzed the data aggregated across the four
experimental studies. To assess the factor structure
of the ﬁve items, we conducted a principal compo-
nents analysis (PCA) of the ﬁve items. For all exper-
imental manipulations and for the aggregated data,
only the ﬁrst factor had an eigenvalue greater than
the Kaiser ’s criterion of 1; for all models, the ﬁrst
factor explained at least 78% of the variance, which
shows a highly unidimensional factor structure,
and only one component was retained in the fur-
ther analyses. The factor loadings of the one-factor
model can be found in Table 1.
Next, we assessed the reliability of the scale. For
all experimental studies and for the aggregate data,
Cronbach’s alpha for the overall scale is .93 or
above. The item-to-total correlations are also very
high ( r ≥ .87), and none of the ﬁve items increase
Cronbach’s alpha when deleted. The results of all
reliability analyses can be found in the two right
columns of Table 1.
Next, as an initial test of the validity of the scale,
we investigated whether the averages of the ﬁve
items produced ﬂuency responses in line with the
experimental conditions. Table 2 reports the mean
averaged ﬂuency score separately for each ﬂuency
condition and for each of the four tasks. All mean
differences were in the intended direction, and for
all tasks, this difference was signi ﬁcant on at least a
10% level. To evaluate the performance of the scale
across all experimental manipulations, we con-
ducted a single paper meta-analysis (SPM) accord-
ing to McShane and B €ockenholt (2017). SPM
analyzes multiple studies of a common phe-
nomenon conjointly and thus has the bene ﬁto f
yielding an estimate of the effect that is more accu-
rate than the estimate of any individual study on
average (McShane & B €ockenholt, 2017). In addition,
decreasing the uncertainty of the estimate increases
its statistical power relative to individual studies. A
SPM of our four studies estimates the effect of ﬂu-
ency at 9.629, 95% CI [5.512, 13.746], indicating that
participants reported a higher level of ﬂuency on
our 5-item measure in the high- ﬂuency condition
than in the low- ﬂuency condition (for a presenta-
tion of the four individual study estimates and the
SPM estimate see Appendix S2).
To support the results of the SPM, we addition-
ally estimated a regression model using a linear
mixed model approach (LMM; Fitzmaurice, Laird,

ingly strong results, considering that ﬂuency effects
tend to be limited to within-subjects designs (Hansen
&W €anke, 2013), which suggests that the examined
ﬂuency phenomena produce a particularly strong
processing experience and can be considered as
remarkably robust.
Since we also recorded reaction times, which have
been proposed as an objective measure of ﬂuency
(Reber, Wurtz, & Zimmermann, 2004), we investi-
gated the extent to which the subjective 5-item mea-
sure converges with an objective reaction time
measure. However, correlational analyses show that
for all experimental studies, the 5-item measure and
the log-transformed objective reaction time measure
are not signi ﬁcantly correlated ( /C0 .093 ≤ r ≤ .086;
p ≥ .189) except for ﬁt ﬂuency, for which the log-
transformed reaction time is positively correlated to
the 5-item measure ( r = .177; p = .012). That is, con-
trary our expectations, this result suggests that a
higher experienced ﬁt ﬂuency is associated with
longer reaction times. To obtain a better understand-
ing of the performance of the reaction time measure
as a function of the ﬂuency manipulations, we also
estimated a regression model using the same linear
mixed model approach (LMM; Fitzmaurice et al.,
2004) speci ﬁed earlier. That is, we tested the effect of
the ﬂuency manipulation on log-transformed reac-
tion time, and we included a random intercept for
each participant and ﬂuency task. The results show
that the ﬂuency manipulation has no signi ﬁcant
effect on reaction times ( p = .297). Thus, reaction
times do not capture processing ﬂuency in the cur-
rent set of studies, which is in line with prior research
showing that objective measures are only marginally
related to the subjective experience of ﬂuency (Reber,
Wurtz, & Zimmermann, 2004).
In sum, a 5-item scale emerges from the dimen-
sionality and reliability phases of our scale develop-
ment. Because of our aim to develop a scale of
subjective ﬂuency that can be adapted to different
types of ﬂuency and ﬂuency manipulations, we
tested these ﬁve items across the four most impor-
tant ﬂuency types (i.e., perceptual ﬂuency, concep-
tual ﬂuency, ﬁt ﬂuency, and retrieval
ﬂuency) and
found consistent results in favor of the 5-item scale.
Notably, the item pair difﬁcult to easy, which forms
our single-item scale, was also included in the ﬁnal
multi-item scale.
Study 2: Predictive Validity Comparison between
the Multi-Item and Single-Item Scales
Study 2 had ﬁve parts (a –e) and two major aims.
The ﬁrst was to validate the newly developed 5-
item scale by testing its predictive validity. The sec-
ond was to compare its performance against the
most frequently used single item in published
research, that is, a semantic differential with the
endpoints difﬁcult to easy. To these ends, ﬁve experi-
mental tasks that cover ﬁve established ﬂuency
effects were used, and the measures ’ predictive
validity was assessed by testing their ability to
mediate these ﬁve effects. Figure 1 provides an
overview of the composition of Study 2a –e.
Participants were recruited using Amazon
MTurk in July 2017; they provided informed con-
sent, were debriefed at the end of the study and
afterward had the opportunity to contact the princi-
pal investigator. A sample of 502 subjects (52.6%
females, M
age = 36.86) participated in our study;
the order of the ﬁve parts 2a –2e varied randomly.
Sample size was determined based on a priori
power analyses; because of its lowest effect size, the
sample size was chosen based on the truth effect.
In each study (a –e), the ﬂuency source was
manipulated on two levels and within subjects. We
further varied between subjects whether partici-
pants evaluated their subjective ﬂuency experience

on the 1-item measure ( n = 254) or on the 5-item
measure ( n = 248). As in Study 1, we used a visual
analog scale with an internal resolution of 100
increments to measure ﬂuency. In the following sec-
tion, we brie ﬂy delineate Studies 2a –2e.
Study 2a: Perceived Truth of Geographic Statements
with Varying Color Contrast
Study 2a tested the effect of statement readability
on truth judgments of geographic statements.
Research suggests that people tend to associate ﬂu-
ency with truth and dis ﬂuency with untruth (Sch-
warz, 2004). This tendency presumably exists
because people often draw on social consensus
information in the absence of objective knowledge;
they assume that if many people believe something,
there must be truth to it (Festinger, 1954). Because
familiarity is often a valid indicator of social con-
sensus, people may assess the apparent familiarity
of the information by drawing on the ﬂuency with
which they can process the relevant input (Schwarz,
Sanna, Skurnik, & Yoon, 2007). According to one of
the most prominent naive theories, previously seen
material is easier to process and ﬂuency is used as
a cue for familiarity (Schwarz, 2004). Thus, people
(erroneously) infer familiarity from processing ease
even when ﬂuent processing is due to the in ﬂuence
of other variables.
In the present study, ﬂuency was manipulated
according to the original study by Reber and Sch-
warz (1999), which uses colors to vary statement
readability. We used two operationalizations per
readability level; dif ﬁcult-to-read statements were
shown in green (RGB = 0, 255, 0) or yellow
(RGB = 255, 255, 0), and easy-to-read statements
were shown in blue (RGB = 0, 0, 255) or red
(RGB = 255, 0, 0). Participants evaluated 16 state-
ments, and readability was manipulated within
subjects. That is, each of the 16 statements was ran-
domly shown either in a dif ﬁcult-to-read color (i.e.,
green or yellow) or in an easy-to-read color (i.e.,
blue or red). Of the 16 statements, half were actu-
ally true and the other half were actually untrue. In
contrast to previous studies on the truth effect, we
adapted the measurement of truth. In particular, to
increase the statistical power of the task, we used a
continuous scale instead of a binary response. The
following question: “How likely do you consider
the following statement to be true? ” was answered
on a scale ranging from 1 ( not at all )t o6( very
likely). Hence, by omitting a midpoint, participants
were required to indicate a tendency but could
adjust their level of certainty.
Study 2b: Liking of Car Designs Varying in Visual
Typicality
Previous research has shown that people prefer
stimuli that are more typical to those that are less
typical, and one of the most common explanations
for this effect is that typical stimuli are processed
more ﬂuently, thus leading to higher liking judg-
ments (Landwehr et al., 2013; Mayer & Landwehr,
in press; Reber, Schwarz, & Winkielman, 2004).
Therefore, this study is designed to test how ﬂu-
ency mediates the effect of car design typicality on
aesthetic liking (Landwehr et al., 2013; Mayer &
Landwehr, in press). The stimulus material was
drawn from Landwehr et al. (2013) and consisted
of four stimuli: a compact car and a premium car
that were each designed to feature either high or
low visual typicality. The procedure was such that
there was one pre-exposure phase in which partici-
pants saw all four stimuli on a single page (i.e., a
typical compact car, an atypical compact car, a typi-
cal premium car, and an atypical premium car) and
in which participants were told that they would
have to evaluate each design relative to the other
three designs. Afterward, they saw each of the four
stimuli on a single page in a random order and had
to indicate how much they liked the design (on a
visual analog scale with the following internal cod-
ing: 1 = not at all and 101 = very much ). Finally,
they evaluated one of our two ﬂuency measures
regarding the
ﬂuency experience they had when
they studied each car design.
Study 2c: Liking of Art Pictures Varying in Symmetry
Prior research has shown that symmetrical stim-
uli are liked more than less symmetrical stimuli,
which can be ascribed to the higher processing ﬂu-
ency associated with the former (Reber, Schwarz, &
Winkielman, 2004; Wurtz, Reber, & Zimmermann,
2008). Thus, this study seeks to analyze whether
our ﬂuency measures mediate the effect of art pic-
tures’ visual symmetry (Wurtz et al., 2008) on lik-
ing. The stimuli were drawn from the set of 620
abstract art pictures that we also used in Study 1a.
The objective visual symmetry of each picture was
computed in accordance with Mayer and Landwehr
(2014), and we selected three pictures with a high
level of symmetry (high ﬂuency) and three pictures
with a low level of symmetry (low ﬂuency) as stim-
uli for this study. Participants ﬁrst saw all six pic-
tures in a random order and rated how much they
liked each picture on a visual analog scale (internal
coding: 1 = not at all and 101 = very much ).

Afterward, participants were re-exposed to the pic-
tures in a random order and were asked to evaluate
the ﬂuency that they experienced when they
studied each picture on one of the two ﬂuency
measures.
Study 2d: Liking of Kanji Characters after Mere
Exposure
A very well known “ﬂuency effect ” is the
mere-exposure effect, according to which repeated
exposure to an initially neutral stimulus leads to a
gradual increased liking for that stimulus (Zajonc,
1968). Because exposure induces an increase in
ﬂuency, the mere-exposure effect can be explained
based on a ﬂuency account (Bornstein &
D’Agostino, 1994). To provide empirical evidence
on ﬂuency in the mere-exposure paradigm, Study
2d manipulates within subjects the number of expo-
sures to Kanji characters (i.e., adopted Chinese
characters that are used in the modern Japanese
writing system; Dech ^ene, Stahl, Hansen, & W €anke,
2009). More precisely, we used a set of ten Kanji
characters (all with ﬁve strokes); of these, ﬁve were
randomly selected to be repeatedly (eight times)
presented to participants for evaluation on different
dimensions (e.g., round versus angular, balanced
versus unbalanced). The other ﬁve characters were
not shown during the exposure phase. Afterward,
all 10 characters were presented in a random order
and participants rated their liking of the characters
(visual analog scale with the following internal cod-
ing: 1 = not at all and 101 = very much ), followed by
an additional round in which participants rated the
ﬂuency that they experienced when they studied
each character.
Study 2e: Perceived Risk of Food Additive Names
Varying in Pronounceability
As with liking and truth judgments, ﬂuency has
been suggested to have important implications for
risk perception: people perceive dis ﬂuently pro-
cessed stimuli as riskier than ﬂuently processed
stimuli (Song & Schwarz, 2009). Again, such per-
ceptions may be explained by the naive theory that
links ﬂuent processing to familiarity; low ﬂuency
fosters the impression that a stimulus is unfamiliar,
thereby leading to perceptions of higher risk irre-
spective of whether the risk is desirable (e.g.,
amusement park rides) or undesirable (e.g., food
additives). In Study 2e, we, thus manipulated the
ease of pronunciation of ostensible food additives
in line with Song and Schwarz (2009) and assessed
how this manipulation affected risk perceptions. As
with the art pictures in Study 2c, we used three
operationalizations per pronunciation level. Thus,
we used three dif ﬁcult-to-pronounce food additives
as dis ﬂuent stimuli (Nxungzictrop, Hnegripitrom,
Cytrigmcmium) and three easy-to-pronounce food
additives as ﬂuent stimuli (Fastinorbe, Mangalrox-
ante, Allotoneline). Again, participants ﬁrst rated
how potentially harmful they thought each sub-
stance was (1 = very harmful to 7 = very safe ) and
then indicated their subjective ﬂuency experience
when reading the name of each substance.
Results
Averaged across all experimental Studies (2a –e),
Cronbach’s alpha for the 5-item scale is a = .975;
for the individual studies Cronbach ’s alpha for the
5-item scale ranges between .956 ≤ a ≤ .982. Prior
to assessing the predictive validity of the ﬂuency
measures, we z-transformed the ﬂuency measures
and the respective dependent variables to allow for
comparable estimates. Again, we used linear mixed
models (LMMs; Fitzmaurice et al., 2004) and the
“lmer”-function of the “lmerTest” library of the
software R (Kuznetsova et al., 2016) to account for
the repeated measures structure of our data. In par-
ticular, because our experimental designs required
repeated evaluations of the geographic statements,
the car designs, the art pictures, the Kanji charac-
ters, and the food additive names, the error terms
of the individual observations are not independent
from one another.
To investigate whether the respective measure
of subjective ﬂuency mediates the effects of the
manipulated ﬂuency source on the respective
dependent variable, we followed the procedure by
Hayes and Rockwood (2017) and tested the signi ﬁ-
cance of the indirect effect using bootstrapping
procedures. To assess the total effect, we ﬁrst esti-
mated a model in which we regressed the depen-
dent variable on the ﬂuency source (Equation 1).
Second, we regressed subjective ﬂuency on the ﬂu-
ency source (Equation 2) to obtain the effect of the
manipulation on the mediator. Finally, we esti-
mated a model in which we regressed the depen-
dent variable on the ﬂuency source and subjective
ﬂuency (Equation 3). The models to predict the
rating of stimulus i nested within the jth partici-
pant on the dependent variable (DV
ij) and on the
subjective ﬂuency experience (SF ij), respectively,
had the following forms, where FS i refers to the
experimental level of the ﬂuency source of

text:
[Page 15]
General Discussion
In the last decade, numerous articles in the areas of
consumer, social, and general psychology have been
published that recruit processing ﬂuency as an
explanatory construct. In doing so, researchers have
focused on accumulating increasingly new and
intriguing effects, while processing ﬂuency has only
been treated as a subsidiary variable to explain the
phenomenon of interest. As a consequence, empirical
research into the construct as such —and particularly
its measurement —has received little attention. The
present research intends to ﬁll this gap by conducting
a systematic investigation of how the experience of
processing ﬂuency should be empirically measured
and in doing so provides a psychometrically validated
measure of the subjective ﬂuency experience that can
be applied in various empirical settings.
Following classic scale development procedures,
we began the search for items with a comprehen-
sive literature review, which demonstrates that
existing research uses almost equally frequent sin-
gle-item and multi-item measures. In addition, we
ﬁnd that in accordance with the theoretical de ﬁni-
tion of ﬂuency, the items difﬁcult and easy are used
very often in existing studies. Hence, we decided to
develop a new multi-item measure of the ﬂuency
experience according to best practices in psycho-
metrics and to compare this measure against a sin-
gle-item measure consisting of the semantic
differential difﬁcult to easy.
We found that processing ﬂuency can be reliably
and validly measured with a 5-item scale consisting
of the following items: difﬁcult to easy, unclear to
clear, disﬂuent to ﬂuent, effortful to effortless, incompre-
hensible to comprehensible. Notably, we tested these
items for four different types of ﬂuency—perceptual
ﬂuency, conceptual ﬂuency, ﬁt ﬂuency, and retrie-
val ﬂuency—thereby assuring that the scale can be
applied to different types of ﬂuency. Across ﬁ
ve
experimental ﬂuency manipulations, we then com-
pared this 5-item scale to the 1-item scale in terms
of predictive validity. That is, we tested the extent
to which the two measures mediate the effect of
color contrast on truth judgments, the effect of typi-
cality on the liking of car designs, the effect of sym-
metry on the liking of art pictures, the effect of
exposure on the liking of Kanji characters, and the
effect of pronounceability on risk judgments. The
results show that both measures mediate all ﬁve
ﬂuency effects, thereby demonstrating predictive
validity for both measures. With regard to future
research, we recommend using the 1-item measure
because participants preferred answering this mea-
sure and single-item scales have the advantage of
minimizing respondent refusal and data collection
and processing costs (Bergkvist & Rossiter, 2007).
Notably, the ﬁnding that the single-item scale is
as valid as the multi-item measure may be due to
the very high reliability of the multi-item scale.
That is, the very high internal consistency (i.e.,

metadata.core_insight_ko: 본 연구는 신뢰성과 타당성을 갖춘 다중 항목 처리 유창성 측정 도구를 제공하고, 이를 단일 항목 측정 도구와 비교 분석합니다. 연구는 다섯 가지 확립된 유창성 조작 방법의 효과를 조사하여 유창성 효과의 재현성을 실증적으로 입증합니다.

text:
[Page 16]
Cronbach’s alpha) may indicate an unnecessary
duplication of content across items and thus points
to redundancy rather than homogeneity (Streiner,
2003). Hence, the items of our carefully developed
multi-item scale may all measure the very same
thing and therefore do not show higher predictive
validity than the 1-item scale. Put differently, our
results suggest that the attribute of the subjective
ﬂuency experience is concrete such that respondents
can “easily and uniformly ” imagine the construct ’s
attributes (Rossiter, 2002).
Apart from providing an easy-to-use measure for
future empirical research, this research provides
further theoretical insights. Speci ﬁcally, we con-
tribute to a better understanding of the ﬂuency con-
struct by providing systematic empirical evidence
for the theoretical notion that different ﬂuency
effects bear on the same subjective experience and
that this uniform experience mediates the effect of
highly diverse phenomena. While the theoretical
notion per se is not new (Alter & Oppenheimer,
2009; Reber, Schwarz, et al., 2004), this is the ﬁrst
study to empirically show that the ﬂuency experi-
ence is indeed remarkably uniform across various
phenomena. Our research can, therefore, counteract
the criticism that ﬂuency is a construct so malleable
that it can be used as a post hoc explanation for
almost any effect (Unkelbach & Greifeneder, 2013a).
We also add to the existing literature on process-
ing ﬂuency by pointing to a new ﬂuency type that
is of particular importance in consumer behavior
research. In particular, most existing research distin-
guishes only between perceptual, conceptual
(Reber, Schwarz, & Winkielman, 2004; Schwarz,
2004), and retrieval ﬂuency (Schwarz, 2004; W €anke
et al., 1997). Our literature review suggests that the
most frequently used means to manipulate ﬂuency
in consumer behavior research is the ﬁt versus non-
ﬁt between two factors, such as the ﬁt between an
individual’s regulatory focus and the construal at
which information is presented (Lee et al., 2010).
We call this “ﬁt ﬂuency,” and even though it is a
form of conceptual ﬂuency (Labroo & Pocheptsova,
2016), we believe it is useful to use a separate term
to categorize this very popular way of manipulat-
ing ﬂuency.
Moreover, our research supports the notion that
despite the introspective and preconscious nature of
the cognitive processes that precede greater or lesser
ﬂuency, people can report their subjective ﬂuency
experience (Forster, Fabi, & Leder, 2015; Forster
et al., 2013). That is, our respondents felt differences
in processing ﬂuency as a result of “objective” ﬂu-
ency manipulations (Studies 1 and 2). Importantly,
we also show that asking people to report their ﬂu-
ency experience was more valid than using objective
measures such as processing speed, given that objec-
tive processing speed did not re ﬂect objective manip-
ulations of
ﬂuency in our study (Study 1). Although
this result may have occurred because we conducted
the study online and thus had limited control over
the experimental procedure, it may also indicate that
objective and subjective indicators of processing ﬂu-
ency are indeed not the same thing (Forster et al.,
2013; Reber, Wurtz, et al., 2004).
An avenue for future research on ﬂuency and its
measurement may grow out of a dual-process dis-
tinction of the information processing that underlies
processing ﬂuency (Graf & Landwehr, 2015). In
particular, we restricted our empirical analysis to
rather simple and quickly accomplished mental
tasks. Because of the tasks ’ simplicity, people likely
invested few cognitive resources so that processing
the stimuli occurred rather automatically (Graf &
Landwehr, 2015). For this type of processing, it
seems reasonable to expect that people have only
one, static subjective ﬂuency experience and that
this experience in ﬂuences subsequent judgments.
However, when people process stimuli in a more
elaborate and controlled manner, they may also
experience a more cognitively driven, presumably
dynamic ﬂuency experience (Graf & Landwehr,
2015). Therefore, future research may investigate
how to measure ﬂuency experiences in more cogni-
tively demanding contexts.
Finally, future research should further investigate
the ﬂuency construct as such, particularly the link
between the experience and the meaning of that
experience. As we have empirically shown, ﬂuency
is a uniform experience, but the various outcomes
of ﬂuency imply that the meaning of the ﬂuency
experience varies considerably (Schwarz, 2004). In
this regard, future research is needed to better
understand what drives the meaning and interpre-
tation of the ﬂuency experience. Aiding these
endeavors and all other ﬂuency-related investiga-
tions, we have provided a scale that can be used to
validly and consistently measure the ﬂuency experi-
ence. We hope that our single-item measure of the
subjective ﬂuency experience is a ﬁrst and impor-
tant step toward more comparable and more rigor-
ous ﬂuency research.

Active White Space (AWS) in Logo Designs: Effects on Logo Evaluations and Brand 
Communication 
In this paper, we explore Active White Space (AWS) (space between individual logo design 
elements) as a stylistic modification that revamps a logo design, yet preserves its extant 
associations. Across three studies, we find AWS to be an effective stylistic logo tool. In Study 1, 
we find that adding AWS to pictorial logos improves their visual evaluation. In Study 2, we find 
this positive evaluation to spill-over to verbal brand aspects such that logo designs with AWS are 
perceived to communicate brand descriptions more clearly. In Study 3, we find that logo designs 
with AWS benefit sophisticated brand personalities the most followed by sincere, exciting, and 
competent brand personalities, with no effect on rugged brand personalities.

 Logos are high-value firm assets that impact a firm’s performance (Henderson and Cote 
1998; Park et al. 2013). A logo as “a graphic design that is used as a continuing symbol for a 
company, organization, or brand” (AMA 2017) fosters brand identity through recognition and 
by differentiating it from its competitors (Henderson and Cote 1998; Keller 2008). Advertising 
research shows that even stylistic changes (where the core design elements remain the same - 
Peracchio and Meyers-Levy 2005) can impact consumer perceptions (Sharma 2016). Similarly, 
in logo research, stylistic manipulations such as tilting a logo has been found to add perceptions 
of movement, thereby increasing consumer visual engagement (Cian, Krishna, and Elder 2014). 
In this research, we examine adding Active White Space (AWS) to a logo (see Figure 1) as 
another stylistic manipulation. 
INSERT FIGURE 1 HERE 
 AWS is forwarded by design practitioners as the space between design elements, in 
contrast to Passive White Space (PWS), i.e., the space around a design (see Figure 1) (Boulton 
2007; Turnbull 2011). Prior advertising research shows that adding Passive White Space, PWS 
(i.e., ‘structural space around the ad elements such as between the margins or borders’) 
improves perceptions of product quality and brand prestige (Pracejus, Olsen, and O’Guinn 
2006). In addition to improving design aesthetics, PWS is believed to invoke perceptions of 
extravagance by signaling higher advertising spends and effort (Ambler and Hollier 2004; 
Kirmani 1990). While prior research has looked at PWS, the merits of Active White Space 
(AWS) have not been examined. 
 A qualitative assessment of brand logos shows a progressive trend towards adding AWS 
to pictorial logo designs, for example, Starbucks, Google Chrome, NBC, Microsoft, and Adidas.

investigate some of these claims made by practitioners in how adding AWS to logos improves 
the visual evaluations of these logo designs (including aspects such as visual clarity, aesthetics, 
and attractiveness). In addition we explore how well logos with AWS are perceived to 
communicate a brand’s verbal descriptions, as well as their fit with different brand personalities 
(Aaker 1997). The logos that we focus on are pictorial (non-textual) or stand-alone graphic logo 
designs, consistent with the broader definition of a logos as symbolic brand representations 
(AMA 2017; McQuarrie and Phillips 2016). 
 Prior research suggests that perceptual fluency  (i.e., the ease of processing of physical 
attributes of a stimulus including its surface features and presentation context – (Lee and Labroo 
2004)) can be increased by enhancing physical aspects such as stimulus clarity through figure-
ground contrast, which in turn improves judgments of stimulus aesthetics, attractiveness, and 
affect (Reber, Winkielman, and Schwarz 1998; Reber, Schwarz, and Winkielman 2004). In the 
studies presented here, we examine the perceptual fluency effects of AWS given that AWS 
manipulates the physical aspects of the logo design by adding white space between the individual 
design elements.
1,3  
In Study 1, we examine whether a stylistic change such as AWS can impact the visual 
evaluations of a logo design (Lee and Labroo 2004; Reber, Winkielman, and Schwarz 1998).3 In 
Study 2, we determine whether the perceptual benefits of adding AWS to a logo also improve 
brand communication clarity, i.e., the perceived clarity with which a logo design communicates 
the verbal description of the brand (Keller 2008; Shapiro 1999). In Study 3, we examine which 
brand personalities identified under the Aaker (1997) framework benefit the most from

AWS IN LOGO DESIGNS AND PERCEPTUAL FLUENCY 
 Considerable research has been done on Passive White Space (PWS), i.e., the undefined 
white space around a design. For example, PWS has been found to add minimalism characterized 
by cleanliness and visual balance (Olsen, Pracejus, and O'Guinn 2012; Pracejus, Olsen, and 
O’Guinn 2006). Presence of PWS draws attention to a design and enhances its noticeability 
further in cluttered advertising scenarios (Olsen, Pracejus, and O’Guinn 2012). Overall, 
advertising research suggests that PWS isolates a design, making it cleaner, more aesthetic, 
sophisticated, and tasteful (Kwan, Dai, and Wyer Jr. 2017; Olsen, Pracejus, and O’Guinn 2012).  
 In contrast, AWS defines each specific logo element by adding white space between the 
individual logo design elements (Mauloni 2013). In this context, Hagtvedt’s (2011) work can be 
seen as an example of AWS. Hagtvedt (2011) shows that incompleteness in logo designs (where 
parts of the characters are left intentionally blank, e.g., versus CONSUL) improves 
perceptions of a firm’s innovativeness and lowers perceptions of its trustworthiness. The spaces 
within the brand names used by Hagtvedt (e.g., ) can be considered as AWS. 
 However, our work differs from Hagtvedt in that his work is limited to typeface logos 
whereas we investigate the effect of AWS on pictorial logo designs, which are more common 
and consistent with the typical definition of logos as symbolic brand representations (AMA 
2017; Henderson and Cote 1998; McQuarrie and Phillips 2016). Additionally, we examine the 
effects of adding AWS to logo designs on visual evaluations of the logo designs, brand 
communication clarity (i.e., the clarity with which logo designs with AWS convey verbal brand 
descriptions), as well as its differential effect on different brand personalities (Aaker 1997).

and Mittal 2010). Adding AWS to a logo outlines, isolates, and delimits each individual logo 
element, visually leading the observer from one logo element to another, thus providing a cleaner 
hierarchy or structure to the overall logo design (Ciripitca 2011). Similar to the established 
positive effects of adding PWS in making a design cleaner, aesthetic, and more tasteful, adding 
AWS to a logo will make the logo design visually clearer and more aesthetic by separating and 
surrounding each individual logo element with some white space. Therefore, adding AWS to a 
logo will improve the visual evaluations of the logo design.
 
In addition to enhancing a logo’s visual assessment, AWS will prompt consumers to seek 
logo design-closure, thereby increasing the overall positive affect derived in the process (Zhao 
and Meyer 2007). Prior advertising research shows that moderate amounts of omissions from 
visuals enhances consumer evaluation and processing fluency (Peracchio and Meyers-Levy 
1994; Sengupta and Gorn 2002). In providing the missing visual portions themselves, consumers 
feel accomplished in resolving the slight visual ambiguity, which enhances their overall affect 
(Peracchio and Meyers-Levy 1994). Similarly, by slightly separating the individual design 
elements in the visual space and prompting visual closure, we expect AWS to have a further 
positive impact on the logo’s overall visual evaluations.  
 Literature under the processing fluency model identifies two specific kinds of fluency 
mechanisms: perceptual and conceptual (Lee 2002; Lee and Labroo 2004).
1 Perceptual fluency 
pertains to the ease of visual processing of a design’s physical features, and conceptual fluency 
reflects the ease of semantic processing of a stimulus (Lee 2002; Lee and Labroo 2004; Shapiro 
1999). Perceptual fluency is influenced by the physical attributes of a stimulus including its 
surface features and presentation context (Lee and Labroo 2004).

visual clarity, visual aesthetics, and visual attractiveness. Accordingly, we propose that:

improve the logo’s visual evaluations.

logo designs on their visual evaluations using measures such as visual clarity, attractiveness, and 
aesthetics (Reber, Schwarz, and Winkielman 2004; Shapiro 1999).

to access and share files” on its website. In this section, we examine whether the positive effect

conveys the brand intended associations to consumers (Henderson and Cote 1998). Therefore, a 
logo design that enhances the clarity of a brand’s given associations (as stated in its verbal 
description) becomes critical to a firm attempting to foster a coherent brand-image in the minds

Research on feelings-as-information model shows that affective feelings induced by 
unrelated factors such as background music (Schwarz 1990; Winkielman et al. 2003) or ambient 
scents (Spangenberg, Crowley, and Henderson 1996) can be (mis)attributed towards the focal 
stimulus. Consumers have been shown to rely on their current, momentary affect as an 
informational source towards decision making (Avnet, Pham, and Stephan 2012). Wadhwa and 
Zhang (2014) show that rounded price figures lead to experiences of ‘feeling right’, i.e., 
affectively positive and perceptually fluent. In all such cases, consumer perceptions are driven by 
a bottom-up process i.e., perceptual fluency aspects of the stimuli (Lee 2002; Shapiro 1999).

correspondingly generated affect can spillover to other brand aspects such as the brand 
descriptions.

CONGRUENCY BETWEEN AWS IN LOGO DESIGN AND BRAND PERSONALITY 
 Labroo, Dhar, and Schwarz (2008) show that visual stimuli with perceptual features that 
closely match or are congruent with the given word-primes are evaluated more positively. For 
example, participants primed with dog-related words evaluated a product package with a dog’s 
image on its label more positively than those primed with cat-related words due to a greater ease 
in processing of the product’s perceptual features (Labroo, Dhar, and Schwarz 2008). Reber, 
Schwarz, and Winkielman (2004) also posit that matches between visual images and related 
words can increase aesthetic affect. In this section, we examine whether AWS will have 
differential positive effects depending upon the underlying brand personality being 
communicated (Aaker 1997). 
 A brand’s personality is defined as “ the set of human characteristics associated with a 
brand” (Aaker 1997, p. 347). Aaker’s framework identifies five specific brand personality 
dimensions: Sincerity, Excitement, Competence, Sophistication, and Ruggedness (Aaker 1997). 
A sincere brand is honest and real, an exciting brand is aspirational, imaginative, and creative, a 
competent brand is intelligent and reliable, a sophisticated brand is good looking, charming, and 
glamorous, and a rugged brand is outdoorsy and tough (Aaker 1997).

 Given the perceptual, aesthetic benefits of adding AWS to logos, we expect logo designs 
with added AWS to be most consistent with sophisticated brand personalities (Aaker 1997, 
1999). Sophisticated brands help fulfil consumer symbolic needs such as social status, 
exclusivity, and fashion (Keller 2008; Park, Jaworski, and MacInnis 1986). For instance, 
sophisticated brands such as Gucci and Burberry are associated with self-expression of upper-
class status and aesthetics (Kim and Sung 2013). Similarly, Mercedes-Benz and Rolex symbolize 
one’s wealth, and keenness for luxury and fashion (Park, Milberg, and Lawson 1991). Therefore, 
AWS in logo designs will be most appropriate for such brand personalities. 
 Following sophisticated brands, we propose that the presence of AWS in logo designs 
will also positively complement exciting, sincere, and competent brand personalities. Since 
incorporating AWS to a logo defines and isolates each individual logo element, the added white 
space between the logo elements provides dynamism and activeness to the overall logo design 
(Cian, Krishna, and Elder 2014). This complements the independent, imaginative, creative, and 
spirited aspects of exciting brands (Aaker 1997). 
 In prior research, creative directors have mentioned that beyond the aesthetic motives, 
other reasons for incorporating PWS include communication of brand trust, integrity, reliability, 
and leadership (Olsen, Pracejus, and O’Guinn 2012). Therefore, logo designs with AWS should 
match competent brand aspects such as intelligence, reliability, and successfulness, as well as 
sincere brand aspects of honesty and genuineness (Aaker 1997). Finally, given that rugged 
brands have the least in common in terms of their toughness and outdoorsy appeal with the 
perceptual effects of adding AWS to a logo design, we do not foresee AWS to impact rugged 
brands. Accordingly, we hypothesize that:

STUDY 1: PERCEPTUAL FLUENCY EFFECTS OF AWS 
 The main objective of Study 1 is to test H1, i.e., the effect of adding AWS to a logo 
design on the logo’s visual evaluations. Study 1 manipulates AWS for two different logo designs 
under a repeated-measures paradigm, and captures the effect of AWS on measures such as visual 
clarity, attractiveness, and aesthetics. Additionally, we assess changes in perceptual fluency 
based upon adding AWS in logo designs via the changes in consumer perceived design 
familiarity with the unknown logos employed in this study.
3  
Research on processing fluency model and mere exposure effects evidences that stimulus 
repetitions increase consumer evaluations by generating feelings of stimulus familiarity 
(Janiszewski 1993; Lee and Labroo 2004; Zajonc 1968). The relative ease of stimulus 
recognition on subsequent exposures and enhanced familiarity is attributed to perceptual fluency, 
i.e., the processing of the stimulus’s physical features (Lee and Labroo 2004; Whittlesea, Jacoby, 
and Girard 1990). Whittlesea (1993) shows that feelings of familiarity can be induced even in the 
absence of a prior exposure, when the processing of the stimulus is perceptually fluent. 
Therefore, we use changes in perceived familiarity of unknown logo designs when presented 
with (versus without) AWS as a manipulation check in this study.

2 (AWS: absent followed by present) mixed-design, with brand personality manipulated 
between-subjects through verbal brand descriptions (five-levels), and each of the five groups 
exposed to logo designs first with and then without AWS (two-levels), within-subjects. 
Study 3: Method 
Pretest. Prior to the main study, we conducted a pretest to ensure that the brand 
descriptions were indeed conveying the respective brand personalities (Aaker 1997). Participants 
recruited from Amazon’s MTurk (N = 53, 57% males, 43% females, M
age = 36 years, 
compensation = $.35) were told that Claro is a consulting company (Mfamiliarity = 2.64 on a 7-
point scale) attempting to understand how certain brand descriptions fit the given brand 
personality classifications (of Aaker 1997), and requested them to help the company match each 
brand script to its most appropriate brand personality type. Participants were requested to match 
each of the listed brand descriptions (see Appendix 4) to one of the five brand personality 
categories shown to them (Sincere, Exciting, Competent, Sophisticated, or Rugged). 
Given a 20% chance of matching a given description to one of the five brand personality 
types, participants matched each brand description correctly at a rate much greater than 20%. For 
the sincere brand, 32 out of 53 respondents matched the script to the sincere brand personality 
(Chi
2 = 62.00, p < .001). Thirty-eight out of 53 participants categorized the exciting script to the 
same brand personality category (Chi2 = 89.36, p < .001). Thirty-five respondents categorized the

Study 3: Findings 
Except for rugged brand personality type, there was a significant positive impact of 
adding AWS to the logo design for each brand personality, as revealed by the one-sample t-test 
values (p < .05) (see Table 3). As predicted, presence (versus absence) of AWS in a logo design 
was found to be most consistent with sophisticated brand personality type (M = 2.11, t (1, 29) = 
7.69, p < .001). This was followed by a positive effect of AWS in logo designs for sincere (M = 
1.20, t (1, 27) = 3.08, p < .01), exciting (M = .96, t (1, 31) = 2.10, p < .05), and competent brands 
(M = .81, t (1, 29) = 2.50, p < .05). There was no effect of adding AWS to rugged brand logo (p 
> .10). Overall, these findings support H3.
