emotional cognition, and driv ing purchases. Notably, Nielsen[1] reported that approximately 64% of 
fast-moving consumer goods purchases are unplanned, with packaging as one of the most direct 
factors influencing such decisions. Among them, color, as the core visual element (which can form  a 
preliminary impression of the product within 90 seconds), plays a decisive role in the extremely short 
terminal decision -making window. Specifically, in the context of fruit juice beverages, current 
packaging design still faces significant challenges: d esign homogenization leads to insufficient brand 
recognition (especially in functional beverages, sparkling water, fruit flavored drinks, and other 
categories); The application of color mostly stays at the decorative level, lacking precise matching 
with the psychological expectations and cultural background of the target group ; Insufficient attention 
has been paid to intergenerational differences, usage scenario demands, and consumers ’ growing 
expectations for interaction/socialization . These factors collec tively underscore the urgency of a 
systematic transformation in packaging design from "functional carrying" to "value conveying". Of 
particular note is that although there has been extensive research on the role of packaging in brand 
awareness and perceived value, there is still a lack of systematic empirical research on how packaging 
color perception (especially differences in temperature and color tones) affects explicitly consumers’ 
emotional states, satisfaction, and final purchasing behavior in the spe cific category of fruit juice 
beverages, which focuses on "health," "pleasure," and "instant satisfaction." Existing understanding is 
mainly at the macro level and lacks refined comparative analysis. 
Therefore, this study focuses on the core dimension of p ackaging color for fruit juice beverages - 
cool and warm color tones . Theoretical basis suggests that warm tones (such as red, orange, yellow) 
may have potential advantages in eliciting emotional resonance and behavioral motivation among 
consumers due to t heir strong association with high arousal emotions (excitement, vitality, pleasure), 
higher psychological affinity, and close association with positive imagery such as "sunshine," 
"warmth," and "natural vitality ; And cool tones (such as blue and green) ten d to convey low arousal 
feelings such as freshness and calmness . Based on this, this study expects that both cool and warm 
color packaging can have a positive impact on consumers ’ positive emotions, satisfaction, and 
purchase intention . Specifically, it ex plores whether warm colors, due to their inherent emotional 
attributes, can more effectively enhance consumers ’ subjective experience and behavioral tendencies 
in the category of juice drinks that emphasize immediate pleasure and sensory experience . Through a 
questionnaire survey targeting the main consumer group aged 18 -40, this study aims to empirically 
compare and analyze the differences in psychological reactions (positive emotions, satisfaction,  and 
purchase intention) of consumers towards cool and warm-toned juice packaging, and explore the 
relationships between  these variables. This study fills the gap by empirically comparing cool and 
warm tones in the juice category, focusing on their impact on positive emotions and behavioral 
responses. Its finding s will provide empirical evidence and refined design suggestions based on 
consumer psychological reactions for  selecting a  color strategy in juice beverage packaging, 
particularly for verifying the potential effectiveness of warm tone applications. 
2. Theoretical Background 
2.1 Color Perception 
The visual perception of color is determined by its three -dimensional attributes - hue, brightness, 
and purity [Fig. 1]. The combination of these attributes creates subtle visual differences and triggers 
different emotional experiences. Among them, the combination of brightness and purity forms hue, 
and hue and hue together shape the visual image of color . Hue (such as red, yellow, blue, green) is the 
fundamental attribute that distinguishes colors . The warmth and coo lness caused by colors mainly 
stem from associations with natural experiences: red, orange, and yellow are often associated with the 

[Page 3]
Research on the Influence of Color Perception on Emotional Response, Satisfaction, and Behavioral Intent in Fruit Juice 
Beverage Packaging Design 
 
Copyright ⓒ 2025 KCTRS  117 
sun and flames, bringing warmth and comfort; Blue and green are easily associated with the ocean and 
sky, and are considered cool and calm colors. On the hue circle [Fig. 2], the line connecting light green 
and purple can serve as the boundary axis for temperature . The red, orange, and yellow above the axis 
represent warm colors, presenting a lively and active image  that is easy to stimulate emotions ; The 
blue, blue, and green below represent cool colors, with more rational and calm characteristics, 
conveying a sense of calmness[2].

text:
The warmth and coo lness caused by colors mainly 
stem from associations with natural experiences: red, orange, and yellow are often associated with the

Beverage Packaging Design 
 
Copyright ⓒ 2025 KCTRS  117 
sun and flames, bringing warmth and comfort; Blue and green are easily associated with the ocean and 
sky, and are considered cool and calm colors. On the hue circle [Fig. 2], the line connecting light green 
and purple can serve as the boundary axis for temperature . The red, orange, and yellow above the axis 
represent warm colors, presenting a lively and active image  that is easy to stimulate emotions ; The 
blue, blue, and green below represent cool colors, with more rational and calm characteristics, 
conveying a sense of calmness[2]. 
In the study of visual communication and consumer psychology, color serves not only as a means of 
recognition and aesthetic appeal but also plays a crucial role in evoking emotions and shaping 
perception. Numerous studies have shown that the warm and cool properties of colors are important 
factors influencing individual emotional responses [3]. Specifically, warm tones such as red, orange, 
and yellow typically have high arousal and can evoke emotions such as pleasure, excitement, and 
tension; Cool tones (such as blue, green, and cyan) have a more calming effect and can evoke low 
arousal emotions such as calmness, refreshment, and peace[4]. Therefore, warm and cool tones not 
only affect consumers’ attention at the visual level but also stimulate emotional reactions at the 
subconscious level, thereby subtly influencing their attitudes and behavioral decisions[5]. 
The research object of fruit juice beverage packaging design is primarily based on the emotional 
guidance and value -conveying function of packaging color during the product consumption process. 
As a product with "health," "freshness," a nd "pleasant taste" as its core consumer demands, fruit juice 
beverages have packaging colors that convey emotional signals to consumers, influencing their 
expectations of product attributes, emotional reactions, and ultimately, purchasing intentions. 
Therefore, exploring the influence of cool and warm color tones on emotions can help reveal how 
packaging colors affect consumers’ satisfaction and consumption behavior towards beverages through 
emotional reactions, which has important theoretical value and practical significance. 
This study focuses on two types of color tones, cool and warm, mainly considering the following 
two aspects: firstly, cool and warm tones have a relatively stable emotional connection in human 
natural experience, such as red and yello w often being associated with vitality and enthusiasm, while 
blue and green represent coolness and rationality. This connection is not only easy to perceive but also 
has good cross -cultural explanatory power. Secondly, compared to other color attributes, t he division 
of cool and warm tones is clear and has good experimental controllability, which helps to control 
variable interference and improve the reliability and validity of the study. Therefore, this article 
chooses cool and warm colors as key elements in juice beverage packaging design, systematically 
analyzes their impact on consumer emotional reactions, and further explores the influence of emotions 
on satisfaction and purchase intention.

2.2 Emotional Response 
Although research on the relationship between color and emotion at the theoretical level is relatively 
limited in China, international research provides a valuable foundation. The core of understanding this 
association lies in the fundamental emotion theory (such as happiness, sadness, fear, anger, surprise, 
disgust), which provides a structured framework for studying color associations [6]. Research using 
such frameworks, including the use of visual stimuli such as emojis, has shown that specific colors can 
selectively correspond to specific underlying emotions (e.g., yellow is often associated with happiness, 
and red is associated with anger)[7]. 
This association is not universally consistent but exhibits signific ant cultural differences.  Cross-
cultural research reveals the coexistence of commonalities and differences . For example, although 
happiness may be associated with bright red in cultures such as India and the United States, the 
association between sadness a nd blue appears stronger in specific contexts such as the United 
States[8]. Similarly, the association between anger (often associated with black/red) and fear (black) 
shows some consistency, while other emotions, such as jealousy, exhibit considerable cultural diversity 
(e.g., associated with purple in Poland and Russia, and yellow in Germany)[9]. These studies highlight 
the interplay between universality and cultural specificity in color-emotion associations. 
The above research establishes a fundamental cross-cultural pattern of how colors universally evoke 
emotions. However, in the specific field of consumer packaging design, research has shifted its focus 
to understanding how color triggers immediate emotional states related to product pe rception and 
decision-making. 
In this study, we focus on the emotional state evoked by consumers when perceiving the color of 
juice beverage packaging . These states represent instantaneous positive emotional responses and 
psychological feelings (such as pl easure, excitement, satisfaction), distinct from conscious cognitive 
processing of product information . To  systematically study the relationship between color tones 
(especially warm and cool tones) and these positive states in packaging contexts, we drew o n the 
results of  a meta-analysis, which identified core positive emotion types associated with evaluative 
responses[10]. This enables us to examine how warm and cool tones in juice packaging influence 
consumers’ positive emotional states.

2.3 Satisfaction  
Consumer satisfaction in the context of consumer behavior refers to the consumer ’s post-purchase 
evaluative judgment regarding the extent to which a product ’s performance aligns with their initial 
expectations and consumption goals. A post -purchase evalu ation is the broader assessment process, 
while satisfaction is the outcome of this evaluation that reflects the consumer ’s overall cognitive -
affective response [11][12]. Unlike broad , service-focused definitions, satisfaction in consumer 
behavior is specifically viewed as a cognitive -affective state resulting from a comparison between  the 
expected and actual product performance. It is a psychological response that arises after consumption , 
reflecting the consumer ’s perceived value assessment based on prior e xpectations, perceived 
performance, and disconfirmation of beliefs. 
Satisfaction is a key post-consumption construct that functions as a critical determinant of consumer 
retention, repurchase behavior, and brand loyalty. In the consumer decision -making process, it acts as 
a mediating variable between product experience and subsequent behavioral intentions, including 
positive word-of-mouth and long-term brand commitment[13][14]. Therefore, a precise understanding 
of how satisfaction is formed,  through cognitive evaluations and emotional responses , is essential for 
exploring the full trajectory of consumer decision-making and loyalty development. 
 
2.4 Purchasing Behavior 
Purchasing behavior refers to  the physical and mental activities involved in acquiring, us ing, and 
disposing of goods or services to satisfy human needs and desires. In other words, as a follow -up of 
purchase intention, it refers to the behavior of purchasing in the order of purchase and evaluation after 
exploring products, services, and other information that meet personal expectations[15]. Consumer 
purchasing behavior can be divided into multiple stages, including problem identification, information 
collection, substitute evaluation, purchase decision formation, purchase execution, and post -purchase 
behavior. This process involves not only the external behavior of consumers but also their internal 
psychological and cognitive changes. 
It reflects consumers’ reactions to the contact, purchase, and use of products or services in the 
process of meeting their needs[16].

2.4 Purchasing Behavior 
Purchasing behavior refers to  the physical and mental activities involved in acquiring, us ing, and 
disposing of goods or services to satisfy human needs and desires. In other words, as a follow -up of 
purchase intention, it refers to the behavior of purchasing in the order of purchase and evaluation after 
exploring products, services, and other information that meet personal expectations[15]. Consumer 
purchasing behavior can be divided into multiple stages, including problem identification, information 
collection, substitute evaluation, purchase decision formation, purchase execution, and post -purchase 
behavior. This process involves not only the external behavior of consumers but also their internal 
psychological and cognitive changes. 
It reflects consumers’ reactions to the contact, purchase, and use of products or services in the 
process of meeting their needs[16]. 
Therefore, based on the above background, this study focuses on the following research questions: 
firstly, what are the differences between co ol and warm color tones in beverage packaging design in 
terms of consumers’ positive emotional reactions, satisfaction, and purchasing behavior? The second is 
the impact of cool and warm tones in beverage packaging design on consumer emotional reactions, 
satisfaction, and purchasing behavior. Thirdly, what impact does the positive emotional respo nse of 
consumers in the design of co ol and warm color beverage packaging have on satisfaction and 
purchasing behavior? The fourth question is whether satisfaction further affects consumers’ intention 
to make a purchase. 
3. Research Methodology 
3.1 Research Object 
According to Mintel (2023)[17]’ s "China Juice and Juice Drinks Market Report", young consumers 
aged 18 to 40 are the primary consumer group in the Chinese juice beverage market. Therefore, this 
study focuses on consumers aged 18 –40 in Main land China to ensure both representativeness and 
market applicability [Table 1]. To ensure data quality, questionnaires with a response time of less than 
3 minutes will be considered invalid and excluded.

Beverage Packaging Design

The questionnaire employs a structured design and i s distributed and collected  randomly through 
the online research platform "Wenjuanxing". Participants must read the informed consent form before 
completing the questionnaire. Only with consent can they continue , and they may terminate the 
questionnaire at any time. The formal survey will be conducted from April 9 to April 18, 2025, over a 
period of 10 days. A pilot test was conducted prior to distribution to eliminate issues such as logical 
repetition and vague expressions, ensuring the reliability and clarity of the formal questionnaire. 
This questionnaire design revolves around three core variables -positive emotional response, 
satisfaction, and purchase behavior intention-with a total of 11 measurement items, all rated using a 5-
point Likert scale (1=completely disagree, 5=completely agree). 
The interviewee first reads the instructions, then sequentially views two sets of fruit juice beverage 
packaging sample images, and completes the relevant evaluation based on the image display. 
The picture material description is as follows: 
To control color perception variables and enhance the realism of the experiment, the research team 
selected two sets of real product packaging images from existing juice beverage brands in the Korean 
market as visual stimuli, representing the cool color packaging group (mainly blue and green) and the 
warm color packaging group (mainly red and yellow). All image backgrounds are maintained with a 
uniform gray white background, and the color tone is controlled within the range of medium -high 
brightness and medium purity to minimize visual interference factors other than "hue". 
During the process of filling out the questionnaire, respondents will randomly present two sets of 
packaging images and evaluate their emotional reactions, satisfac tion, and purchasing tendencies 
based on their personal feelings, ensuring the subjectivity and continuity of the measurement. 
A total of 446 questionnaires were collected this time. After data screening, 22 invalid samples with 
careless filling (such as a bnormal consistency of options) and 16 invalid samples without beverage 
purchasing experience were excluded. Finally, 408 valid questionnaires were retained, with an 
effective response rate of 91.5%. 
The sample has a relatively balanced distribution in demographic variables, such as gender, age, and 
occupation, and provides a good representativeness and analytical foundation.

3.2 Measuring Variables and Items (Data) 
The survey tool used in this study was a questionnaire. Based on previous research, three 
constituent concepts were designed for the research model, including a total of 11 measurement items, 
as shown in [Table 2]: the positive emotional response was measured using the scales developed by  
Cowen &  Keltner (2017)[10], totaling 3 items; Satisfaction was measured using four single scales 
used by Ning (2024)[18] and Yang & Tan (2022)[19]; The purchasing behavior was measured using 
four single-item measures used by Shin (2020)[20]  and Yang & Tan (2022)[ 19]. All items used a 5 -
point Likert scale (1=Strongly disagree, 5=Strongly agree).

3.3 Data Processing and Analysis Methods 
After data encoding, in  order to investigate the differences in positive emotional reactions, 
satisfaction, and purchasing behavior of consumers regarding the design of co ol and warm-colored 
beverage packaging, SPSS 26.0 was first used for reliability analysis to verify the effe ctiveness of 
Cronbach’s alpha. The Cronbach ’s alpha values of the questionnaire ranged from 0.775 to 0.834, 
indicating that the survey tool has good reliability . Using the AMOS 26.0 program for confirmatory 
factor analysis for validity analysis, the standa rdized coefficients of the survey questionnaire were all 
greater than 0.5, with CR greater than 0.7 and A VE greater than 0.5, indicating that the survey tool has 
good performance. Then, SPSS was used for correlation analysis and multiple regression analysis, and 
independent sample t -tests were conducted to explore the impact of consumers ’ positive emotional 
response to cool and warm colored beverage packaging on satisfaction and purchasing behavior.

4.2 Discussion 
Firstly, this study confirms that positive emotional responses significantly enhance both consumer 
satisfaction and purchase intention  in the context of beverage packaging. More importantly, positive 
emotions serve as a dual-path driver —both directly influencing purchase intention and indirectly 
doing so through satisfaction. Based on the emoti on-attitude-behavior model, emotional experiences 
such as pleasure and excitement create favorable evaluations that promote satisfaction and subsequent 
behavioral intentions[22]. Interestingly, warm-colored packaging induced significantly stronger 
positive emotional responses and higher satisfaction scores compared to cool -colored packaging , 
suggesting a clear effect size advantage  for warm tones. This aligns with prior findings on color -
emotion associations, where warm tones (e.g., red, orange) are consist ently tied to high -arousal 
emotions like enthusiasm, vitality, and joy[23][24]. In contrast, cool tones , though associated with 
calmness and clarity, generated weaker emotional arousal and lower behavioral intention scores. This 
contrast reflects the theoretical distinction between high -arousal (warm) and low -arousal (cool) 
emotional responses, supporting theories of emotional aesthetics and color psychology. 
In the current study, satisfaction was a significant predictor of purchase intention , and the model  
demonstrated high explanatory power (R²>0.67), reaffirming the expectancy-confirmation theory[25]. 
However, it is worth noting that while both warm and cool tones positively influenced satisfaction, the 
difference in satisfaction between the two was not statistically significant in all cases. This unexpected 
result may be due to the mediating role of emotion —that is, emotional response plays a stronger role 

[Page 12]
Research on the Influence of Color Perception on Emotional Response, Satisfaction, and Behavioral Intent in Fruit Juice 
Beverage Packaging Design 
 
126  Copyright ⓒ 2025 KCTRS 
in shaping satisfaction than the color itself. Future studies could explore interactive effects between 
color temperature and individual preferences or context to clarify this outcome further. From a design 
perspective, warm -toned packaging has superior visual dominance  due to its expansive and high -
brightness characteristics, making it more likely to ca pture attention (“foreground color effect”) and 
convey a sense of emotional warmth. This advantage fosters greater psychological proximity, quicker 
emotional engagement, and stronger behavioral activation in fast -moving consumer goods 
environments. Taken t ogether, this study extends prior theoretical frameworks by empirically 
confirming that warm-colored packaging has a stronger emotional and behavioral impact than cool -
colored alternatives, especially in hedonic product categories such as juice beverages. Compared with 
other FMCG categories (e.g., snacks or household products), beverages are highly sensory -driven and 
consumed in immediate contexts, which may explain why color -induced emotions play a more 
decisive role in shaping satisfaction and purchase in tention. Moreover, the use of Korean brand 
packaging as experimental stimuli and Chinese consumers as the evaluation sample highlights cross -
cultural implications, as the meaning of warm versus cool tones may differ across cultural settings.  
These findings validate theories from neuroaesthetics, color-emotion mapping , and emotion-driven 
brand association[26][27], while also broadening their application to culturally embedded packaging 
strategies. 
5. Conclusion 
5.1 Research Conclusion 
Firstly, warm-toned packaging significantly enhances positive emotions and purchasing intentions . 
Compared to cool-toned beverage packaging,  beverage packaging can significantly stimulate 
consumers’ positive emotional reactions and effectively enhance purchasing behavior intenti ons 
(p<0.01). 
Secondly, both cool and warm color tones can positively affect consumer emotions, satisfaction, and 
purchase intention . Both cool and warm color packaging can trigger positive feelings and have a 
positive correlation with consumer satisfaction and purchasing behavior tendencies (p<0.01). 
In addition, consumer satisfaction has a significant predictive power on purchasing behavior . 
Satisfaction has a significant impact on  purchase intention, and the model exhibits strong explanatory 
power ( R²>0.67), which is a key factor driving consumer purchasing decisions. Given the cross -
cultural research design (Korean packaging stimuli, Chinese consumers), these findings also provide 
theoretical contributions for international brand marketing and color-based differentiation strategies. 
 
5.2 Practical Suggestions 
Based on the empirical findings of this study, several practical and actionable recommendations are 
proposed for beverage brands and packaging designers. 
Firstly, the color strategy should align with the product’s market positioning and its intended 
emotional guidance goals. For juice drinks that emphasize a "healthy" and "fresh" image, it is 
recommended to prioritize using cool tones such as blue a nd green to convey a natural, pure, rational, 
and reassuring impression. In contrast, for products that emphasize "vitality," "emotional arousal," and 
"social attributes," warm tones such as red, orange, or yellow are more suitable to stimulate positive 
emotional responses from consumers, thereby enhancing brand appeal and purchasing impulse. The 
high consistency between this color and product positioning helps to improve the strategic value of 
packaging design and deepen consumers’ cognitive associations with product attributes. 
Secondly, more attention should be paid to the potential of color in stimulating emotional responses, 

[Page 13]
Research on the Influence of Color Perception on Emotional Response, Satisfaction, and Behavioral Intent in Fruit Juice 
Beverage Packaging Design 
 
Copyright ⓒ 2025 KCTRS  127 
fully leveraging its key role in shaping consumers’ first impressions. The use of high -brightness and 
high-saturation warm color elements in packaging design can not only attract consumers’ attention in a 
short period but also quickly evoke emotional resonance, enhancing the visual competitiveness of 
products on shelves. Considering that the purchasing behavior of most fast -moving consumer goods is 
significantly unplanned, the immediate impact of color on consumer emotions is directly related to the 
probability of impulsive purchasing behavior. Therefore, designers should prioritize the emotional 
arousal function of colors during the packaging design phase, using it as a key means to enhance 
consumer stimulation. 
Finally, packaging design should consider the preferences and cultural differences of different 
segmented markets, and make more refined color scheme adjustments. Consumers of various ages, 
genders, and cultural backgrounds have significant differences in color preferences. For example, 
young consumers usually prefer warm colors with high saturation, while middle -aged and elderly 
consumers tend to prefer natural and  calm cool tones. At the same time, when promoting cross -
regional brands, it is also necessary to fully respect the differences in understanding the symbolic 
meaning of colors in local culture and avoid weakening the brand communication effect due to cultural 
misunderstandings. By combining color strategy with market segmentation dimensions, not only can 
the brand’s cultural adaptability be enhanced, but a more precise user reach can also be achieved in 
diversified markets.

5.3 Research Limitations and Prospects 
First, the sample structure has certain limitations: First, the sample is concentrated on consumers in 
Chinese Mainland aged 18 -40, which is difficult to represent the group perception differences of 
different age groups and cultural backgrounds ; Secondly, the sample size is limited and balanced 
coverage of various groups has not been achieved, which poses a risk of sampling bias. In the future, 
the sample size and diversity should be expanded to enhance the universality and external validity of 
research conclusions. 
Secondly, this study used a subjective questionnaire survey method. Although it has strong practical 
perceptual value, the data is easily influenced by social expectations and individual subjective 
emotional states, which may cause certai n data biases. Moreover, the exposure time to packaging 
images was not standardized, which may act as a potential confounding factor, and should be 
explicitly considered in future studies. 
Additionally, the stimulating materials are limited to fruit juice beverage packaging and do not 
encompass various categories, such as tea drinks, carbonated drinks,  and functional drinks, etc. The 
product range is relatively single, making it difficult to fully reflect the role and performance of 
packaging colors in diff erent categories. Subsequent research may consider introducing more product 
types and constructing cross-category comparative models. Furthermore, this study has a limitation 
regarding data diagnostics. Although we noted satisfactory reliability and validi ty metrics, we did not 
report the diagnostic tests for regression assumptions, including multicollinearity, normality of 
residuals, and homoscedasticity. Future research should reinforce the robustness of statistical 
conclusions by incorporating these crit ical diagnostic checks. Moreover, other sensory design 
elements, such as brand awareness, packaging form, and material, have not been included in this study, 
which fails to fully reflect the synergistic mechanism between color and other packaging informati on. 
In the future, it may be worthwhile to further explore the linkage effect between color and design 
elements, such as graphics, text, and shape , within a multimodal perception framework, in order to 
construct a more comprehensive packaging perception model. In addition, the potential mediating role 
of emotional response in influencing satisfaction and purchase intention is conceptually important. 
While formal mediation testing is beyond the current scope, future studies are encouraged to employ

structural equation modeling or PROCESS macro analysis to verify these mediating mechanisms. 
In summary, future research can start from optimizing sample structure, diversifying methods and 
means, expanding categories, and integrating design variables to promote the in-depth development of 
color psychology and consumer behavior research, and expand its application breadth and depth in 
packaging design and marketing practice.

Designing for Naturalness: Insights from Processing 
Fluency and Visual Processing
Yeong Ji Hwang
1
, Taig Youn Cho
2*
1
Major in Spatial Design, Graduate School, Ph.D. candidate, Hongik University, Seoul, Korea
2
Department of Industrial Design, Professor, Ph.D., AIA, Hongik University, Seoul, Korea 
Abstract
Background Naturalness has long been defined in contrast to artificiality across philosophical, 
environmental-ethical, and Korean aesthetic traditions. Yet in contemporary digital environments, the 
notion of naturalness must be reconsidered in cognitive and perceptual terms. Despite their artificial 
origins, design artifacts are often experienced as natural, a phenomenon not fully explained by traditional 
perspectives.
Methods This study applies insights from processing fluency theory to design research. Processing 
fluency suggests that stimuli processed with ease are often judged as more pleasing, a response closely 
associated with the perception of naturalness. By translating this framework into the context of design, the 
study establishes a conceptual basis for understanding naturalness beyond its metaphysical or normative 
definitions.
Results Naturalness can be understood in two complementary forms: perceptual naturalness , 
arising from unfelt fluency in effortless sensory processing, and conceptual naturalness, emerging from 
relative fluency in coherent meaning integration. Accordingly, two corresponding design strategies are 
proposed: enhancing perceptual fluency by reducing visual disruption and reinforcing conceptual fluency 
by strengthening contextual coherence, each illustrated through examples from UX/UI, product, and 
spatial design.
Conclusions This paper reframes naturalness not as an abstract essence but as a cognitive and aesthetic 
response grounded in processing fluency theory. The study provides theoretical clarification for explaining 
experiences of naturalness in artificial contexts and proposes domain-sensitive strategies for design, 
thereby contributing to ongoing discussions in design research and practice.
Keywords Naturalness, Processing Fluency Theory, Design Strategy, Aesthetic Experience, 
Neuroaesthetics


[Page 2]
130    Archives of Design Research 2025. 11. vol 38. no 4 
1. Introduction
Design grounded in contemporary digital technology inherently produces artificial artifacts, 
which makes the design of natural experiences for users a critical concern. For example, in 
automobile design, radical changes to the “face” of a model, such as enlarging the front grille, 
have often been criticized by users as awkward or unnatural. Similarly, while some humanoid 
robots and works of science fiction evoke a sense of naturalness, others elicit the uncanny 
valley effect. These cases raise fundamental questions about what counts as natural and how 
consumers perceive naturalness in artifacts.
Traditionally, naturalness has been understood in opposition to artificiality. Philosophically, 
the notion is rooted in the Daoist concept of wu wei zi ran ( 無爲自然), referring to what 
emerges unselfconsciously, without coercion or deliberate manipulation (Laozi, 2018). 
In environmental discourse, naturalness denotes what originates in nature and remains 
untouched by human intervention, standing in contrast to the artificial or engineered (Siipi, 
2008). In addition, Korean aesthetics situates naturalness as a visual value, expressed 
through principles such as sobakmi (the beauty of simplicity) and mugigyo-ui gigyo (the art 
of concealing artistry), which emphasize subtle balance and restraint while avoiding visual 
intrusion (Cho, 2016).
However, understanding naturalness merely as the opposite of artificiality cannot fully 
capture the complexity of natural experiences in designed artifacts. To address this gap, 
the present study examines the cognitive basis of naturalness through the framework of 
processing fluency theory, which holds that the ease of information processing shapes 
aesthetic experience. This framework provides a basis for interpreting naturalness as 
grounded in both perceptual and conceptual fluency.
Accordingly, this study aims to clarify the cognitive foundations of naturalness experience 
and to propose design principles that evoke a sense of naturalness in digital and artificially 
constructed environments. Based on this aim, the following research questions are posed:
1.    What cognitive processes underlie the perception of naturalness?
2.     How can perceptual and conceptual naturalness be distinguished, and under what 
conditions is each form evoked?
3.     Based on these distinctions, what strategies can be proposed to guide the design of 
naturalness in digital environments?
2. Theoretical Framework
  2. 1. Multidisciplinary Perspectives on Naturalness
The concept of naturalness has been interpreted in diverse ways across disciplines, typically 
as an ideal state contrasted with artificiality, intervention, or manipulation. In Daoist 
philosophy, it is captured by wu wei zi ran ( 無爲自然), often translated as “effortless action 
in accordance with nature” (Slingerland, 2007). Wu wei refers to non-coercive action that 
follows the inherent flow of things, while zi ran signifies a state in which nothing is imposed, 
forced, or restrained. From this perspective, what is considered natural emerges without 

[Page 3]
    www.aodr.org    131
cognitive resistance, embodying a state free from imposed control or effortful adjustment 
(Laozi, 2018).
In environmental ethics, naturalness has also been defined concerning human intervention 
(Ridder, 2007), but Siipi (2008) offers a more nuanced account. Their tripartite model 
distinguishes history-based, property-based, and relation-based perspectives. The first 
emphasizes origin, whether something emerged without human involvement, while the 
second evaluates conformity to natural characteristics, such as ecological or chemical 
properties. Crucially, the relation-based account highlights contextual appropriateness: hay 
is natural for horses but not for humans. In line with this relational view, the author further 
observes that both excessive and insufficient satisfaction of needs may be judged unnatural, 
underscoring that naturalness involves an optimal cognitive fit where stimuli are neither 
overwhelming nor deficient (Siipi, 2008). Thus, even in environmental discourse, naturalness 
is not only about origin or substance but also about the absence of cognitive strain in human 
perception.
Korean aesthetics similarly frames naturalness in terms of perceptual ease. It is often 
expressed through sobakmi (the aesthetics of modesty) and mugigyo-ui gigyo (the art of 
concealing artistry) (Kwon, 2005; Cho, 2016). These principles value balance, restraint, and 
visual modesty. For example, this is achieved by preserving the raw texture of materials 
(Hong, 2016), using balanced proportions, and integrating built forms with the surrounding 
landscape (Yeon & Lee, 2003). Such sensibilities minimize visual intrusion and support a 
sense of effortless perception. Contemporary culture reflects this same logic. The popularity 
of “no-makeup makeup” in South Korea illustrates how naturalness remains associated 
with enhancing appearance without drawing conscious attention to the act of enhancement 
(Russon, 2018).
Despite its significance in Korean aesthetics, naturalness has rarely been treated as an 
independent object of study. Within digital media, the concept has only been explored 
sporadically, with Lee (2021) offering one of the few dedicated analyses in the context of 
animation and the uncanny valley. The study contrasts unnaturalness, marked by expectancy 
violation, uncertainty, and heightened attentional focus, with naturalness, characterized 
by plausibility and the absence of conscious awareness.

Such sensibilities minimize visual intrusion and support a 
sense of effortless perception. Contemporary culture reflects this same logic. The popularity 
of “no-makeup makeup” in South Korea illustrates how naturalness remains associated 
with enhancing appearance without drawing conscious attention to the act of enhancement 
(Russon, 2018).
Despite its significance in Korean aesthetics, naturalness has rarely been treated as an 
independent object of study. Within digital media, the concept has only been explored 
sporadically, with Lee (2021) offering one of the few dedicated analyses in the context of 
animation and the uncanny valley. The study contrasts unnaturalness, marked by expectancy 
violation, uncertainty, and heightened attentional focus, with naturalness, characterized 
by plausibility and the absence of conscious awareness. From this perspective, naturalness 
is not a metaphysical essence but a perceptual state in which characters or phenomena are 
accepted “as they are,” without disrupting cognitive flow.
In sum, philosophy conceives naturalness as a state aligned with the flow of things without 
coercion, environmental thought frames it as the opposite of artificial intervention, Korean 
aesthetics views it as a state free from intrusive visual attention, and digital media treats it as 
a state without cognitive disruption, as summarized in Table 1. Together, these perspectives 
converge on naturalness as an experiential condition grounded in cognitive ease.

132    Archives of Design Research 2025. 11. vol 38. no 4 
  2. 2. Naturalness and Processing Fluency
Naturalness has often been regarded as a positively valenced quality, contrasted with 
artificiality or manipulation (Ridder, 2007; Siipi, 2008). Unnatural experiences, by contrast, 
disrupt perceptual or cognitive processing and draw undue attention, eliciting unease (Lee, 
2021). In this sense, naturalness can be understood as the positive experience that arises 
when stimuli are processed without disruption or effortful attention. This account positions 
naturalness as an experiential state that emerges from fluent processing.
This conceptualization aligns closely with processing fluency theory, which posits that 
stimuli that are easier to process elicit more favorable responses (Reber et al., 2004). For 
example, people are generally drawn to symmetrical shapes and landscapes (Bertamini et al., 
2019) and tend to prefer prototypical features in faces and consumer products (Rhodes et al., 
2007; Winkielman et al., 2006). Repeated exposure to objects such as brands, artworks, or 
faces also increases familiarity and likability over time (Baker,1999; Cutting, 2003; Zajonc, 
1968). These features illustrate how easily processed stimuli tend to elicit positive affect, 
exemplifying the hedonic effect of fluency.
More recently, researchers have extended the fluency framework by integrating predictive 
processing models to explain how fluent processing elicits hedonic effects. Yoo and 
colleagues (2023) emphasize the role of prediction in generating hedonic responses to fluent 
experiences. In predictive processing models, the brain constructs internal representations 
of the external world and compares predicted input with sensory input to detect errors. The 
central function of this comparison is the minimization of prediction error, regarded as a 
core goal of cognition because it supports adaptive and energy-efficient functioning (Friston, 
2010). When sensory information matches expectations, cognitive load is reduced, and the 
experience is more likely to be positively evaluated (Brielmann & Dayan, 2022).
More importantly, Brouillet and Friston (2023) argue that it is not fluency itself, but rather 
relative fluency, that evokes affective responses. Ordinarily, fluent processing operates 
beneath conscious awareness (unfelt fluency), whereas relative fluency becomes salient when 
a stimulus is processed more easily than expected. For instance, when an initially unfamiliar 
stimulus suddenly becomes comprehensible through contextual cues. Such moments elicit 
surprise and draw attention, prompting the brain to update predictive models by assimilating 
unfamiliar stimuli into familiar categories (Yoo et al., 2024). Empirical findings further 
support this account: people sometimes misattribute fluently processed but unfamiliar 
stimuli as familiar (Whittlesea & Williams, 1998). From a computational perspective, 
prediction-error minimization not only refines internal models but also produces a reward 
signal, such that the refinement itself is experienced as intrinsically pleasurable (Brielmann 
& Dayan, 2022). Together, these processes show how relative fluency informs cognitive 
updating and shapes affective experience. Figure 1 presents a schema of these processes.
Beyond theoretical accounts, recent empirical work has begun to examine the relationship 
between fluency and naturalness (Hwang & Cho, 2025). This study investigated AI-generated 
spatial imagery, measuring fluency via response times and naturalness via subjective ratings. 
Its findings showed that familiarity was the strongest predictor of perceived naturalness, 
while naturalness in turn predicted aesthetic pleasure. Importantly, this effect was amplified 
when responses were faster, suggesting that processing fluency indirectly contributes to the 
aesthetic impact of naturalness.

4. Discussion
  4. 1. Perceptual and Conceptual Naturalness
The account of visual processing outlined above suggests two primary routes to processing 
fluency. First, perceptual fluency arises when a stimulus contains perceptual cues that 
the visual system can readily process. Second, conceptual fluency occurs when a stimulus 
is conceptually easy to interpret, allowing recognition to bypass or guide detailed visual 
analysis. In this study, experiences based on perceptual fluency are defined as perceptual 
naturalness, whereas those grounded in conceptual fluency are defined as conceptual 
naturalness. Table 3 provides a schematic overview of how these two forms of fluency 
contribute to the experience of naturalness through distinct processing routes.
Table 3 Perceptual and conceptual routes to naturalness in design
Naturalness Type Cognitive Basis Stimulus Type Subjective Experience
Perceptual 
Naturalness

fluency; unconscious processing)

Perceptual naturalness often arises from stimuli grounded in salient perceptual cues. 
Prototypical features that signal categorical familiarity (e.g., feathers, wings, and a beak for 
a bird) are processed efficiently in the ventral pathway (Kravitz et al., 2013), while global 
attributes such as motion and coarse structural patterns are rapidly registered in the dorsal 
pathway (Freud et al., 2015; Ayzenberg et al., 2023). Together, these cues enhance fluency and 
support efficient object identification. The perceptual cues are often experienced directly, 
without conscious awareness of the category, and can evoke what feels like an ontological 
sense of necessity that things must appear in this way. Conversely, deviations from such 
expectations frequently lead to awkwardness or negative aesthetic judgments. (Halberstadt & 
Winkielman, 2014).
By contrast, conceptual naturalness arises from stimuli that maintain contextual coherence.

a bird) are processed efficiently in the ventral pathway (Kravitz et al., 2013), while global 
attributes such as motion and coarse structural patterns are rapidly registered in the dorsal 
pathway (Freud et al., 2015; Ayzenberg et al., 2023). Together, these cues enhance fluency and

sense of necessity that things must appear in this way. Conversely, deviations from such

Winkielman, 2014).
By contrast, conceptual naturalness arises from stimuli that maintain contextual coherence. 
Visual artworks, digital environments, or science fiction films, though unrealistic, can still 

[Page 11]
    www.aodr.org    139
or normative value (e.g., Daoism, environmental ethics) or as a sensory aesthetic in Korean 
thought, this study extends the concept into artificial contexts such as digital environment 
design.
Across traditions and practices, what is perceived as “natural” often coincides with what is 
processed fluently, whether perceptually or conceptually. Drawing on predictive processing 
and fluency theory, we argue that naturalness emerges when sensory input or meaning aligns 
efficiently with internal expectations, thereby reducing cognitive effort and heightening 
affective salience.
More specifically, we distinguish perceptual fluency, arising from unconscious processing 
that makes stimuli feel effortless, from conceptual fluency, arising from consciously 
recognized ease of meaning integration. Accordingly, two design strategies follow: (1) 
enhancing perceptual fluency by emphasizing easily processed cues, and (2) reinforcing 
conceptual fluency by strengthening semantic coherence over physical realism.
By reframing naturalness as a cognitive construct, this study clarifies its underlying 
mechanisms and offers practical design strategies. It suggests that perceptual and conceptual 
fluency should be prioritized in creating experiences that feel both natural and aesthetically 
engaging in contemporary digital and technological contexts.

Impact of Cultural and Regional Preferences on Product Color
Variations Using AI-Enhanced Market Analysis
Date: January 21, 2025
Author: Lawrence Emma
Abstract
In the rapidly evolving landscape of consumer markets, businesses face the challenge of aligning
their product offerings with dynamic market trends. This paper explores the concept of Adaptive
Color Variation Management (ACVM) as a strategic approach to enhance product appeal and
market relevance through the manipulation of color variations. Leveraging AI-driven predictive
analytics, ACVM enables organizations to anticipate consumer preferences and optimize color
choices in real-time.
The proposed framework integrates data from various sources, including social media trends,
sales data, and consumer feedback, to build predictive models that identify emerging color trends.
These models employ machine learning algorithms to analyze historical data and identify
patterns, facilitating swift decision-making in product design and marketing strategies.
By implementing ACVM, companies can achieve a more responsive supply chain, reduce excess
inventory, and increase consumer engagement. The adaptive nature of this approach allows for
continuous feedback loops, where real-time data informs design iterations, ultimately leading to
a more personalized consumer experience.
Furthermore, this study highlights case studies demonstrating successful implementation of
ACVM in various industries, illustrating the tangible benefits of incorporating AI-driven insights
into color management strategies. The findings suggest that ACVM not only enhances market
adaptability but also drives competitive advantage in an increasingly color-conscious consumer
landscape.
In conclusion, this paper advocates for the integration of AI-driven predictive analytics into color
variation management, presenting ACVM as a vital tool for businesses aiming to thrive amid
changing market dynamics. Future research will explore the scalability of this approach across
different sectors and its potential implications for sustainability in product design.

II. Literature Review
A. Overview of Color Theory in Marketing
Color theory explores how colors influence human perception and behavior. In marketing, this
knowledge is applied to design logos, packaging, and advertisements to evoke specific emotional
responses. For example:
 Warm colors (e.g., red, orange) are often associated with energy and excitement.
 Cool colors (e.g., blue, green) convey calmness and trust. The section would review
seminal theories and studies, highlighting how color impacts brand recognition, product
appeal, and purchase decisions.
B. Current Practices in Color Management
Traditional color management practices involve periodic trend analysis, consumer surveys, and
expert consultations. However, these methods are often time-consuming and reactive. Industries
like fashion and consumer electronics have started adopting technology-driven approaches such
as digital color forecasting tools, but the gap in predictive capabilities remains.
C. Role of Predictive Analytics in Business
Predictive analytics leverages historical and real-time data to forecast future trends and behaviors.
In the context of color management, predictive analytics can identify patterns in consumer
preferences, anticipate seasonal trends, and detect cultural shifts that might influence color
choices. Techniques such as clustering, sentiment analysis, and trend extrapolation are crucial for
tailoring color strategies to specific market segments.
D. Existing Frameworks for Market Trend Analysis
Market trend analysis frameworks often incorporate:
 Quantitative models (e.g., statistical trend analysis).
 Qualitative insights (e.g., focus groups, expert interviews).
 Hybrid approaches combining historical data with machine learning algorithms. This
section would critically analyze existing frameworks, identifying gaps and opportunities
for incorporating dynamic, color-specific adaptive methods.
III. Methodology
A. Data Collection
1. Sources of Data
Data for ACVM can be gathered from diverse sources, including:

[Page 5]
o Social media: Platforms like Instagram and Pinterest to track visual content and
emerging trends.
o Sales data: Retail sales and online shopping data to correlate color choices with
consumer purchasing behavior.
o Consumer feedback: Surveys, reviews, and focus group discussions to
understand color preferences directly from consumers.
2. Tools and Technologies Used for Data Gathering
o Web scraping tools for collecting data from social media and e-commerce
websites.
o Sentiment analysis software to extract consumer opinions.
o CRM systems to analyze historical sales data.
B. Predictive Modeling
1. Machine Learning Algorithms Employed
o Clustering algorithms (e.g., K-Means, DBSCAN) for grouping consumers based
on color preferences.
o Time-series analysis models (e.g., ARIMA, LSTM) for forecasting seasonal
color trends.
o Sentiment analysis algorithms for evaluating consumer attitudes towards
specific colors.
2. Model Training and Validation Processes
o Training datasets would include historical sales data, social media trends, and
consumer feedback.
o Validation involves splitting data into training and testing subsets, using metrics
like accuracy, precision, and recall to measure model performance.
C. Framework Development
1. Components of the ACVM Framework
o Data input module: Collects and preprocesses data.
o Predictive engine: Uses machine learning models to forecast trends.
o Decision support system: Provides actionable insights for product design and
marketing.
o Visualization tools: Displays trend predictions in user-friendly dashboards.
2. Integration of Real-Time Data Analysis
The ACVM framework incorporates APIs and IoT devices for real-time data collection,
ensuring decisions reflect the latest market dynamics. For example, incorporating live
social media trend analysis can help brands identify viral color trends and respond
promptly.
IV. Implementation of ACVM
A. Case Studies
1. Industry-Specific Examples

[Page 6]
o Fashion:
In the fashion industry, ACVM is employed to predict trending colors, optimize
fabric dyeing processes, and personalize product recommendations. AI tools
analyze data from social media, runway trends, and historical sales to create
palettes that resonate with target audiences.
Example: A global fashion brand uses ACVM to identify trending colors, leading
to a 20% increase in seasonal sales by aligning their collection with consumer
preferences.
o Home Decor:
Home decor companies leverage ACVM to simulate room designs, recommend
paint colors, and customize furniture finishes. AI algorithms process user
preferences and spatial data to deliver tailored suggestions, enhancing customer
satisfaction.
Example: A paint company uses a virtual assistant powered by ACVM to help
customers visualize color combinations, reducing product returns by 15%.
o Automotive:
Automotive manufacturers use ACVM to develop appealing car colors and
finishes, integrating consumer preferences and regional trends. AI also aids in
quality control during production by detecting inconsistencies in paint application.
Example: An automotive firm introduces a new color series, optimized using
ACVM insights, resulting in a 10% increase in customer inquiries.
2. Strategies Employed and Outcomes Achieved
o Data Integration: Combining consumer preference data, market trends, and
production capabilities to create accurate predictions.
o AI-Driven Testing: Virtual simulations of products with various color schemes to
gauge potential customer responses.
o Feedback Loops: Implementing systems to gather post-purchase feedback,
refining color management strategies over time.
Outcomes include reduced time-to-market, increased product desirability, and
enhanced brand loyalty.
B. Benefits of ACVM
1. Enhanced Market Responsiveness:
AI tools analyze real-time data, enabling businesses to adapt swiftly to changing
consumer trends, thereby staying competitive.

1. Enhanced Market Responsiveness:

2. Reduction in Excess Inventory:
By accurately predicting demand for specific colors and designs, ACVM minimizes
overproduction, cutting costs and reducing environmental impact.
3. Improved Consumer Engagement:
Personalized recommendations and visualization tools enhance the shopping experience,
fostering stronger customer relationships and higher conversion rates.
V. Challenges and Limitations

[Page 7]
A. Data Privacy and Ethical Considerations
 Collecting and processing consumer data raises concerns about privacy, requiring
compliance with regulations like GDPR.
 Transparency in AI algorithms is essential to avoid biases in color recommendations and
ensure fairness.
B. Technical Challenges in Implementation
 Integrating AI systems with existing workflows and legacy technologies can be complex
and resource-intensive.
 Ensuring the accuracy of predictive models requires high-quality, diverse datasets and
significant computational power.
C. Limitations of Predictive Models
 AI models may struggle with highly subjective factors in color preferences influenced by
cultural nuances or individual tastes.
 Over-reliance on AI could limit creative experimentation, potentially stifling innovation.
VI. Future Directions
A. Expansion of ACVM Across Different Sectors
 Exploring applications in healthcare (e.g., therapeutic environments), food and beverage
(packaging aesthetics), and education (color-enhanced learning tools).
B. Exploration of Sustainable Practices in Color Management
 Developing eco-friendly dyes and finishes guided by AI insights.
 Utilizing ACVM to optimize material use, reduce waste, and lower environmental
footprints in production processes.
C. Potential for Further Research and Development
 Enhancing AI models to include emotional and psychological responses to color.
 Integrating ACVM with augmented reality (AR) for immersive consumer experiences.
VII. Conclusion
A. Summary of Key Findings
ACVM drives innovation across industries by enhancing market responsiveness, reducing waste,
and improving customer experiences.

[Page 8]
B. Implications for Businesses
Adopting ACVM enables companies to remain agile in competitive markets, offering
personalized solutions and fostering sustainable practices.
C. Final Thoughts on the Importance of AI-Driven Approaches in Color Management
As industries increasingly embrace AI, ACVM stands out as a transformative tool, enabling data-
driven decision-making, fostering creativity, and aligning with global sustainability goals.

REVIEW
The multidimensional impact of packaging design
on purchase intention: a systematic hybrid review
Chang Liu 1 ✉, Mat Redhuan Samsudin 2 ✉ & Yuwen Zou 3
Despite the widely recognised importance of packaging design ’si n ﬂuence on purchase
intention in both academic and industrial spheres, there remains a dearth of comprehensive
research at the intersection of these two concepts, particularly as no evaluation in the current
ﬁeld has been conducted through systematic bibliometric analysis. Based on this, this study
aims to explore the current state and trends in the research domain of packaging design and
purchase intention relationships through a mixed-methods systematic review. A total of 221
academic articles were selected from high-quality journals indexed in the Web of Science
(WoS) database. The study employs a hybrid methodology combining bibliometric analysis
techniques (including performance analysis and science mapping) with the Scienti ﬁc Pro-
cedures and Rationales for Systematic Literature Reviews (SPAR-4-SLR) protocol for sys-
tematic literature reviews, whilst utilising bibliometric visualisation analysis tools CiteSpace
and VOSviewer to analyse annual publications, scienti ﬁc collaboration networks, disciplinary
distribution, research hotspots and trends, and key variables. The ﬁndings indicate that the
ﬁve core research themes in this ﬁeld are: The Role of Packaging in Consumer Decision
Process, Visual and Structural Elements of Packaging Design, Product Expectations and
Evaluation Induced by Packaging, Packaging Information Communication and Processing, and
Environmental Impact and Sustainability of Packaging. Furthermore, this study proposes
future research directions using the Theory, Method, Context (TMC) framework. This
research not only provides researchers with important research trends in the ﬁeld but also
offers valuable references and guidance for marketers and designers.
Introduction
A
ccording to a global consumer survey by Ipsos, 72% of consumers stated that product
packaging design plays an important role in their purchasing decisions (Gil, 2018), and
packaging, as one of the key touchpoints of a product or brand, not only communicates
directly to potential customers, but also plays a fundamental role in marketing decisions
(Dopico-Parada et al. 2021). The global consumer packaging market continues to grow and is
expected to increase from $655 billion in 2024 to $950 billion in 2034, at a CAGR of 3.8%
(Future Market Insights, 2024). However, in today ’ s increasingly competitive marketplace, it is

[Page 2]
more dif ﬁcult than ever to capture consumers ’ attention (Charif
Hamdar, 2018), and continually improving product packaging is
considered one of the most viable ways to capture consumer
attention (Hassan et al. 2012; Khuong and Tran, 2018). The
importance and research potential of packaging design have also
been increasingly highlighted due to the escalating consumption
and changes in marketing budgets (Harahsheh et al. 2007; Silayoi
and Speece, 2007). Questions such as which elements of package
design in ﬂuence consumer decision-making and how package
design elements can stand out from the crowd are important
issues for designers, researchers and marketers to consider.
In addition, willingness to buy refers to the likelihood that a
consumer will purchase a particular product or service, and its
importance as an important predictive attribute (Fishbein and
Ajzen, 1975) has been widely recognised by scholars when dis-
cussing consumer purchasing decisions (Suci et al. 2022). In other
words, consumers ’ purchasing decisions can be predicted by
measuring willingness to buy. A large number of current studies
have revealed the importance of packaging design in in ﬂuencing
consumer preferences, purchase decisions, and purchase beha-
viour (Ampuero and Vila, 2006; Ahani et al. 2013; Bahrainizad
and Rajabi, 2018; Charif Hamdar, 2018; Kova č et al. 2019;
Margariti, 2021; Ck et al. 2022). For example, Kova č et al. ( 2019)
veriﬁed the impact of visual elements of packaging design on
consumer preferences, Charif Hamdar ( 2018) identi ﬁed the key
role of packaging design in the purchase decision process, and
Margariti ( 2021) found that ‘ white space ’ in organic food
packaging can enhance purchase intention by improving per-
ceived quality.
With the rapidly changing times, the ﬁeld of packaging design
is also evolving. Digital technology is reshaping the packaging
industry (Sadeghi et al. 2022), and the global packaging industry
is facing the trend of digitisation, personalisation, intelligence,
and the integration of new connotations such as social interac-
tion, data tracking, and so on, in addition to the traditional
functions (Panagiotakopoulos et al. 2021). Along with the rapid
changes of the times, the ﬁeld of packaging design is also evolving
rapidly, constantly being given new connotations, and the ﬁeld is
becoming more complex and diverse (Orth and Malkewitz, 2008;
De La Fuente et al. 2019). Despite the fact that packaging as a
powerful marketing tool has become more and more important in
terms of its impact on consumer purchasing decisions and has
received extensive attention from researchers, there is still a lack
of comprehensive research at the intersection of these two con-
cepts, and research trends in the ﬁeld are unclear. That is,
although there is a large body of research on packaging design
and purchase intention in the ﬁeld, these studies are usually
product- or application-speci ﬁc (Silayoi and Speece, 2007;
Wulansari, 2019; Ck et al. 2022; Suci et al. 2022; Kongprasert and
Wangphanich, 2023), an integrated global perspective is lacking.
In addition, the lack of a framework-based ﬁeld review means
that academic attention is urgently needed to address this
research gap. Meanwhile, due to the complexity of packaging
elements and the variability of consumer behaviour, it remains
difﬁcult for companies to grasp the key and achieve signi ﬁcant
sales growth (Gil, 2018; Çad ırcı, 2022; Vidal-Ayuso et al. 2023).
Through a systematic analysis of the review publications rela-
ted to packaging design listed in Table 1, we found that these
review studies focus on different areas, including packaging
technology, sustainability, and consumer behaviour (Azzi et al.
2012; Ketelsen et al. 2020;A ﬁf et al. 2022; Silva and Pålsson, 2022;
Z. Zhu et al. 2022; Palazzo et al. 2023; Branca et al. 2024).
However, there are no mixed review analyses that speci ﬁcally
explore the relationship between package design and purchase
intention.

Through a systematic analysis of the review publications rela-

review studies focus on different areas, including packaging
technology, sustainability, and consumer behaviour (Azzi et al.
2012; Ketelsen et al. 2020;A ﬁf et al. 2022; Silva and Pålsson, 2022;
Z. Zhu et al. 2022; Palazzo et al. 2023; Branca et al. 2024).
However, there are no mixed review analyses that speci ﬁcally
explore the relationship between package design and purchase
intention. In terms of methodology, most of the existing studies
used a systematic review approach, with only Vila-Lopez and
Küster-Boluda ( 2020a) employing a bibliometric analysis, which
highlights the potential value of adopting a mixed-method
approach that combines bibliometrics with a systematic litera-
ture review. This approach is particularly effective when dealing
with interdisciplinary research areas and large volumes of lit-
erature, providing both macro-knowledge structures and micro-
thematic insights (Donthu et al. 2021; Paul et al. 2021).
Given that packaging design research spans multiple dis-
ciplines such as marketing, design, and psychology, a mixed-
method approach combining bibliometric analysis and systematic
literature review was used in this study, which drew on a com-
bination of review protocols, ﬂowcharts, bibliometric analysis
procedures, and content analysis frameworks, respectively,
namely Scienti ﬁc Procedures and Rationales for Systematic Lit-
erature Reviews (SPAR-4-SLR) protocol (Paul et al. 2021), Pre-
ferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-
Analyses (PRISMA) four-stage ﬂowchart (Moher et al. 2010;
Page et al. 2021; Parums, 2021), bibliometric analysis procedure
(Donthu et al. 2021), and Theory, Method, Context (TMC) fra-
mework (Paul et al. 2017). This study explored the following
research questions:
RQ1. How can the performance of research in the ﬁeld of
packaging design and purchase intention be analysed (including
core contributing countries, institutions, authors, and journals)?
RQ2. What are the primary research themes, evolutionary
trends, and key packaging design in ﬂuencing factors within the
relationship between packaging design and purchase intention?
RQ3. What advancements are needed in theoretical, metho-
dological, and contextual aspects to further deepen our under-
standing of the domain of packaging design and purchase
intention?
literature review
The literature review serves as a key stage in the research process
to examine the substantive contributions of previous studies,
deepen the understanding of the problem, and provide direction
for future research (Yudiatmaja et al. 2023). This section outlines
the concepts of package design and purchase intention and their
interactions.
Packaging design . Packaging design protects products as well as
being an important marketing tool in consumer markets (Vyas
and V. 2015; He, 2018; Klimchuk and Krasovec, 2021). It com-
bines aesthetics and functionality to enhance consumer appeal
and facilitate purchase decisions (Ck et al. 2022). Through various
elements such as colour, typography and structural design,
packaging design greatly in ﬂuences consumer purchasing beha-
viour (Underwood, 2003).
As packaging design expands from basic functionality to
strategic communication, scholars are adopting increasingly
sophisticated methods to assess its impact (Margariti, 2021;S .
Liang et al. 2022; Xia et al. 2023; Xu et al. 2023; Zhao et al. 2024).
In recent years, research methods have continued to innovate,
with Riswanto et al. ( 2025) applying eye-tracking technology to
packaging research to accurately measure consumer attention
allocation, and arti ﬁcial intelligence and machine learning being
widely used to optimise packaging design (Gao and Li, 2025;G u
and Lee, 2025). However, despite continuous methodological
innovations, current research lacks a systematic overview of the
historical evolution of the relationship between packaging design
and purchase intention, making it dif ﬁcult to capture the
developmental stages that characterise the ﬁeld.
The importance of packaging design in in ﬂuencing consumer
purchasing decisions has been well documented. Silayoi and
Speece ( 2007) found that packaging aesthetics have a signi ﬁcant

impact on product evaluation, with visual elements making a
strong ﬁrst impression and directly increasing the likelihood of
purchase. F Wang et al. ( 2022) and Wulansari ( 2019) emphasised
that packaging design in ﬂuences consumer behaviour by chan-
ging perceptions of quality, safety, and value. Effective packaging
communicates product bene ﬁts and brand promise through the
strategic use of visual and informational cues (Wells et al. 2007;
Cortina-Mercado, 2017; Heide and Olsen, 2017; Benachenhou
et al. 2018; Bou-Mitri et al. 2021). Theoretical and methodological
innovations continue to drive the ﬁeld, with Dadras ( 2015)
applying Kano Attractiveness Quality Theory to categorise
packaging features based on consumer satisfaction, and Djatna
and Kurniati ( 2015) utilising perceptual engineering to combine
product attributes with consumers ’ emotional responses.
With the development of e-commerce, the mechanism of
packaging design ’ s role in online environments has received
attention. Al ‐Samarraie et al. ( 2019) pointed out that the lack of
direct access to products by consumers in online shopping
environments makes packaging design more critical in visual
communication, which directly affects consumers ’ purchase
intentions. However, relevant analyses of the in ﬂuence mechan-
isms of packaging design in different purchasing contexts are still
insufﬁcient (Pan et al. 2021). Although packaging design research
has made signi ﬁcant progress, existing research still faces
important challenges: the correlation between different research
topics is not suf ﬁciently explored, which makes it dif ﬁcult to form
a holistic understanding of the in ﬂuence of packaging design on
purchase intention; and the lack of systematic summarisation and
analysis of the core research topics hinders the grasping of the
hotspots and trends of research in this ﬁeld. There is still a
knowledge gap between companies in understanding and utilising
packaging information to guide consumers ’ purchasing decisions
(Hanbing Li et al. 2024). This discrepancy highlights the
disconnect between academic research and industry needs, and
there is an urgent need for systematic literature analysis to
integrate existing knowledge.
In summary, packaging design has a key in ﬂuence on
consumer purchasing decisions in the current competitive market
environment. Packaging design has evolved into an interdisci-
plinary ﬁeld, encompassing a variety of disciplines such as
psychology, marketing, and materials science (Velasco and
Spence,
2019). Recent studies have incorporated behavioural
economics principles and sustainability concepts (Augustin and
Cole, 2022; Corona et al. 2024), showing that the ﬁeld is moving
towards the integration of multiple perspectives. However, the
existing literature lacks a systematic categorisation of research
perspectives, making it dif ﬁcult to fully capture the multi-
dimensional nature of the ﬁeld and highlighting the need for
bibliometric analysis.

In summary, packaging design has a key in ﬂuence on
consumer purchasing decisions in the current competitive market
environment. Packaging design has evolved into an interdisci-
plinary ﬁeld, encompassing a variety of disciplines such as
psychology, marketing, and materials science (Velasco and
Spence,
2019). Recent studies have incorporated behavioural
economics principles and sustainability concepts (Augustin and
Cole, 2022; Corona et al. 2024), showing that the ﬁeld is moving
towards the integration of multiple perspectives. However, the
existing literature lacks a systematic categorisation of research
perspectives, making it dif ﬁcult to fully capture the multi-
dimensional nature of the ﬁeld and highlighting the need for
bibliometric analysis.
Purchase intention . Willingness to buy represents a consumer ’ s
propensity to purchase a product and serves as a predictor of
purchase behaviour (Ajzen, 1991). This study focuses on will-
ingness to buy rather than purchase decision in the key difference
between the two: purchase decision re ﬂects actual consumer
behaviour at the point of sale, while willingness to buy measures
potential future behaviour based on current attitudes (Fishbein
and Ajzen, 1975). Kytö et al. ( 2019) state that willingness to buy is
the key link that connects the product attributes, the consumer ’ s
psychological response, and the actual purchase behaviour. Pur-
chase decisions are more limited by practical factors such as
product price, promotional activities and economic conditions
(Van Heerde and Neslin, 2017).
Packaging design signi ﬁcantly in ﬂuences consumers ’ purchase
intentions by integrating functional and emotional cues
(Underwood, 2003). Studies have been conducted to explore the
mechanisms by which various attributes of package design
inﬂuence: Kotler and Keller ( 2016) found that vibrant colours

and innovative designs increase purchase intention; Suci et al.
(2022) con ﬁrmed that extrinsic package design cues increase
consumers’ willingness to pay for traditional food products; and
Kongprasert and Wangphanich ( 2023) emphasised that the
positive impact of eco-friendly packaging on purchase intention.
However, there are several obvious limitations in the existing
studies: the lack of systematic sorting of major research themes
makes it dif ﬁcult to grasp the research hotspots and trends; the
focus on individual packaging elements or speci ﬁc contexts lacks
a comprehensive analysis of the overall impact mechanisms; and
the lack of correlation analysis with other research themes despite
the attention paid to sustainable packaging design.
What is more noteworthy is that the ﬁeld spans multiple
disciplines such as behaviour, cultural sociology, marketing,
neuroscience, psychology, sustainability and visual design, but the
lack of systematic generalisation and comparison of these
research perspectives makes it dif ﬁcult for researchers to fully
grasp the complexity of the ﬁeld. Meanwhile, there is a relative
lack of research on the in ﬂuence mechanism of packaging design
in the e-commerce environment, which makes it dif ﬁcult to adapt
to the rapidly developing online consumption trend.
Therefore, bibliometric analysis serves as an important tool to
map the development pulse of the ﬁeld and synthesise research
ﬁndings. By systematically analysing the annual publications,
scientiﬁc cooperation networks, disciplinary distributions,
research hotspots and variables of the research on the relationship
between packaging design and purchase intention, we can not
only reveal the historical evolution and development stage of the
ﬁeld, but also identify the core research themes and diversi ﬁed
research perspectives, which will provide theoretical guidance for
future research. There is a lack of systematic bibliometric analysis
in the ﬁeld, and this study aims to provide precise insights into
the potential gap between academic research and practical
applications.
Research methodology
This study employed a comprehensive systematic literature
review methodology, combining the quantitative approach of
bibliometric analysis with the qualitative approach of the Sys-
tematic Literature Review protocol. The research design inte-
grated several established frameworks: the SPAR-4-SLR protocol
(Paul et al. 2021), the Preferred Reporting Items for PRISMA
four-stage ﬂowchart (Moher et al. 2010; Page et al. 2021; Parums,
2021), the bibliometric analysis procedure (Donthu et al. 2021),
and the TMC framework (Paul et al. 2017). The investigation
proceeded through three main stages: performance analysis, sci-
ence mapping, and content analysis (shown in Fig. 1). Through
this methodological integration, the study aims to present a
comprehensive research landscape of packaging design in relation
to purchase intention, identify research trends, trace the ﬁeld’ s
evolution and knowledge structure over the past two decades, and
suggest directions for future research.
Bibliometrics is a systematic approach that applies quantitative
analysis and statistics to publications such as journal articles
(Diodato, 1994; De Bellis, 2009; YiQin Chen et al. 2023). Com-
pared to traditional literature reviews, bibliometric literature
reviews have clear criteria for literature selection and statistically
analyse literature information in a quantitative way, which is
more scienti ﬁc and objective (M.-J. Li et al. 2022; Dincer and
Dincer, 2023).

Bibliometrics is a systematic approach that applies quantitative
analysis and statistics to publications such as journal articles
(Diodato, 1994; De Bellis, 2009; YiQin Chen et al. 2023). Com-
pared to traditional literature reviews, bibliometric literature
reviews have clear criteria for literature selection and statistically
analyse literature information in a quantitative way, which is
more scienti ﬁc and objective (M.-J. Li et al. 2022; Dincer and
Dincer, 2023). This study followed a systematic process of lit-
erature review, which not only increased the transparency of the
study, but also helped to achieve replicability of the review and its
ﬁndings, and to verify the reliability of the study (Higgins and
Green, 2008; Ali and Johl, 2022; Kraus et al. 2022).
Retrieval strategies and data sources . The science of any
knowledge mapping is rooted in the database (Chen et al. 2015).
The ﬁeld of packaging design and purchase intention research
spans a number of disciplines, including marketing, design and
psychology. Given the interdisciplinary nature of the ﬁeld, the
Web of Science Core Collection (WoSCC) was selected as the
primary data source for this study, which is widely used for sci-
entiﬁc research and evaluation due to its groundbreaking content,
high-quality data, and long history (K. Li et al. 2018; Odriozola-
Fernández et al. 2019; Yu and Sheng, 2020; Tan et al. 2021).
WoSCC was chosen over Scopus because (1) WoSCC provides
more complete citation network data, which is particularly
suitable for bibliometric analysis; (2) its compatibility with
CiteSpace and VOSviewer is better; and (3) its coverage in the
ﬁeld of packaging design research is more comprehensive. We
conducted an initial comparative test and found that WoSCC
provided more accurate search results on the topic of this study.
Although parallel searches were not performed using Scopus,
WoSCC’ s citation indexes cover a wide range of topics, including
Science Citation Index Expanded (SCI-EXPANDED), Social
Sciences Citation Index (SSCI), Arts & Humanities Citation
Index (AHCI), Book Citation Index-Science (BKCI-S), Book
Citation Index-Social Sciences & Humanities (BKCI-SSH) and
