In this study, a detailed search strategy was determined after
referring to previous reviews and academic experts ’ opinions. For
‘ packaging design ’ , the search was extended to include related
concepts and expression variants ‘ package design ’ , ‘ packaging’ ,
‘ design of package ’ ; for ‘ purchase intention ’ , the search was
extended to include ‘ willingness to buy ’ and ‘ willingness to
purchase’ . Variants such as ‘ purchase* intent*’ and ‘ buying
intention’ were considered, but initial testing showed that these
terms produced too many irrelevant results in the current
research topic. After expert consultation and pre-search testing, it
was determined that a more precise combination of terms would
be used to balance the comprehensiveness and accuracy of the
search.
A data search was conducted on 23 November 2023, using a
combination of Boolean logic ‘ AND’ and ‘ OR’ (Létourneau et al.
2022), and the ﬁnal search equation was [TS = ((‘ package design’
OR packaging OR ‘ packaging design ’ OR ‘ design of package ’ )
AND ( ‘ purchase Intention ’ OR ‘ willingness to buy ’ OR ‘ will-
ingness to purchase ’ ))], the initial search resulted in 408
documents.
Literature screening process . In this study, the earliest relevant
literature in the ﬁeld was found to have been published in 1995
through a search, so the publication time span was set from 1995
to 2023 to cover the complete development cycle. The screening
process was conducted in strict adherence to the PRISMA ﬂow-
chart, which has been shown to be effective in improving trans-
parency and reproducibility in systematic literature reviews (Page
et al. 2021).
Firstly, in the Identi ﬁcation stage, 408 publications were
obtained through the search strategy described above. Subse-
quently, in the Screening phase, the document type was limited to
article (367) and the language to English (354). In the Eligibility
phase, manual screening was performed to ensure that the
selected documents were highly relevant to the study of the
relationship between package design and purchase intention.
The screening criteria were: literature that included research on
the relationship between package design and purchase intention,
and literature that dealt with only one of them was excluded.
Three researchers conducted the screening independently and
disagreements were resolved through voting. The ﬁnal result was
221 pieces of literature.
Notably, most of the source journals for this literature are
included in the Australian Business Deans Council Journal
Quality List (ABDC-JQL) and the Chartered Association of
Business Schools-Academic Journal Guide (CABS-AJG). Speci ﬁ-
cally, 158 documents (71.5%) were from journals included in
ABDC-JQL, 115 documents (52.1%) were from journals included
in CABS-AJG, and 48 documents were included in both lists.
These two lists were chosen because they are recognised
indicators of journal quality in the ﬁeld of business and
management (Paul et al. 2021). Given the interdisciplinary nature
of the research ﬁeld, a small number of journals that are not
CABS-AJG or ABDC-JQL but are of signi ﬁcant value were also
included.
Finally, at the included stage, 221 eligible documents were
included in the bibliometric analysis after checking that there
were no duplicates. A ‘ txt’ ﬁle containing the ‘ full record and cited
references’ was downloaded from WoSCC to ensure that the data
contained all available metadata for each scienti ﬁc paper (R. Li
et al. 2022). It is worth noting that 32 documents were not
available in full text in the WoSCC database, and we attempted to
access them through Google Scholar, ResearchGate, and
institutional library resources, but some were still unavailable.
These 32 documents were still included in the bibliometric
analyses (due to their complete metadata availability), but were
not included in the subsequent TMC framework analyses that
required full text reading. Therefore, 189 full texts were ultimately
used for the TMC framework analysis. This discrepancy did not
affect the overall results of the bibliometric analysis, which relied
heavily on the metadata of the literature rather than the full-text
content.
Analysis methods . This study strictly follows the SPAR-4-SLR
protocol proposed by Paul et al. ( 2021), which provides a scien-
tiﬁc and rigorous methodological framework for systematic lit-
erature review. The SPAR-4-SLR protocol consists of three main
phases: Assembling, Arranging, and Assessing, as shown in Fig. 2.

Analysis methods . This study strictly follows the SPAR-4-SLR
protocol proposed by Paul et al. ( 2021), which provides a scien-
tiﬁc and rigorous methodological framework for systematic lit-
erature review. The SPAR-4-SLR protocol consists of three main
phases: Assembling, Arranging, and Assessing, as shown in Fig. 2.
Each phase has clear sub-steps and criteria to ensure a systematic
and reliable research process. Many recent studies have empha-
sised the importance and critical value of this protocol (Raman
et al. 2022; Achuthan et al. 2023; Mahajan et al.
2023; Prihantika
et al. 2023; Sauer and Seuring, 2023; Sinha and Sharma, 2024).
In the Assembling phase, we identi ﬁed the research area,
research questions, and selected appropriate databases and search
strategies. The Arranging phase systematically screened the
retrieved literature in conjunction with the PRISMA ﬂowchart
to ensure transparency and repeatability of the screening process.
The Assessing phase consisted of two sub-phases: evaluating and
reporting. In the evaluating sub-phase, we conducted a biblio-
metric analysis and proposed a research agenda, whilst in the
reporting sub-phase, we discussed the limitations of the study and
followed a standardised reporting format.
The bibliometric analyses used in this study fall into two
categories: performance analysis, which examines the contribu-
tion of research components, and science mapping, which focuses
on the relationships between research components (Noyons et al.
1999; Cobo et al. 2011a; Donthu et al. 2021). Performance
analysis covers the assessment of publication metrics, citation
analysis, and the assessment of research performance of authors,
countries, institutions, journals, and disciplines (Thelwall, 2008;
Cobo et al. 2011a). Science mapping includes the analysis of
scientiﬁc collaborative networks, the analysis of keyword co-
occurrences, the analysis of the evolution of research themes, and
the visualisation of research variable relationships (Cobo et al.
2011a; Gaviria-Marin et al. 2019; Donthu et al. 2021).
In this study, bibliometric visualisation was performed using
two software packages, CiteSpace (version 6.2.3) and VOSviewer
(version 1.6.19). CiteSpace focuses on knowledge structure and
evolutionary trends in the temporal dimension of the literature
(C. Chen, 2006; C. Chen and Leydesdorff, 2014; Y. Zhu and Hu,
2023), and VOSviewer has advantages in data visualisation and
ease of operation in showing literature relationships (Van Eck
and Waltman, 2010; Cobo et al. 2011b; Zhong and Lin, 2022;
Cândido et al. 2023). The two tools can be used in conjunction to
complement each other ’ s strengths and to fully reveal the
knowledge structure and dynamics of the research ﬁeld (Pessin
et al. 2022). In addition, Microsoft Excel was used for content
analysis and descriptive analysis.
Based on the ﬁndings of the bibliometric analysis, we planned and
organised future research paths under the TMC framework to
advance the theoretical development, methodological innovation, and
contextual expansion of the research ﬁeld of package design and
purchase intention, and to formulate future research questions. The
TMC framework serves as an effect ive method for systematically
constructing and analysing research models, enabling multidimen-
sional analyses of the current researchﬁeld. The framework makes it
more effective to identify and analyse current theories, research

In order to answer the research questions of this study, the
ﬁndings are divided into three parts: analysis of scienti ﬁc
collaboration networks, analysis of journals and disciplines, and
analysis of research hotspots and trends.
Analysis of scienti ﬁc cooperation networks
National and institutional co-operation networks . This study
included 221 articles published between 1995 and 2023, written

number of articles published. China published the largest number
of articles (45, or 20% of the total), followed by the United States

pattern is not coincidental, but re ﬂects structural changes in the
global consumer market. China ’ s leading position is directly

competitiveness of their products through innovative packaging

of quantitative results . The 221 papers of this study were pub-
lished in 107 journals. Table 5 demonstrates the top 8 journals in

of number of publications are Food Quality and Preference (20),
Sustainability (13), and Journal of Retailing and Consumer Ser-
vices (8). Food Quality and Preference has not only the highest
number of articles, but also the highest number of citations (744),
making it the most in ﬂuential journal in the ﬁeld. This dis-

reveals important research trends: ﬁrstly, ﬁve out of the top eight

is an important research object and its impact on consumers ’
purchasing intention has received high attention; secondly, Sus-
tainability journals are ranked second, which re ﬂects the
increasing attention of researchers to sustainable packaging
design. This is closely related to the improvement of global
environmental protection awareness and the promotion of related
policies. This change in the distribution of journals re ﬂects the
fact that packaging design research is moving in a direction that is
more in line with the UN ’ s Sustainable Development Goals

potential for integrating business, technology and sustainability
perspectives in particular.

keywords such as Impact, Cues, Attention, etc. This theme

environmental responsibility rather than purely design. This
theme focuses on the environmental impact of packaging and
consumer responses to sustainable packaging, and is approached
from an environmental responsibility rather than a purely design
perspective. For example, Magnier and Schoormans ( 2015) found
that consumers ’ environmental concerns in ﬂuence their
responses to packaging visual appearance and sustainability
claims. What distinguishes this theme from the others is the
introduction of a unique dimension of environmental values.
Evolution of trending topics . Figure 5 illustrates the temporal
evolution of the hot topics of research on the relationship
between package design and purchase intention during the period
1995–2023. Based on the keyword distribution status and node
information, the development of this research ﬁeld can be cate-
gorised into ﬁve main time periods, corresponding to the afore-
mentioned ﬁve major research topics with temporal overlap:
Packaging Information Communication and Processing Phase
(#4 & #7, 1995 onwards): this phase, which started around 1995
and peaked around 2021, is mainly based on a marketing
perspective, focusing on the impact of labelling and information
design on packaging on consumer purchasing decisions. The rise
of this phase is closely related to the implementation of the
Nutrition Labelling and Education Act (NLEA) in the United
States in the 1990s, which required the labelling of nutritional
content and standardised labelling formats for food packages
(Moorman et al. 2012), and the increased awareness of
consumers’ right to know and food safety has pushed forward
the direction of this research. In recent years, keywords such as
‘ Advertising Effectiveness ’ , ‘ Appeals’ , and ‘ Nutrition’ have
become the emerging focus of the topic, and these are likely to
be at the forefront of research in this area in the coming years.
The Role of Packaging in Consumer Decision Process Phase
(#0 & #1, 1995 onwards): this phase also began around 1995, with
keywords such as ‘ Perceived Value ’ , ‘ Planned Behaviour ’ and
‘ Behavioural Intentions ’ appearing frequently between 2012 and
2019, representing the widespread application of the theory of
planned behaviour in the ﬁeld. During this period, the focus of

Sustainable packaging research has attracted widespread
attention in academia, which is closely related to the growing
concern about global environmental issues (Olsson, 2017;R . - L .
Wang et al. 2021; Chirilli et al. 2022). According to the United
Nations SDGs report, global resource consumption is still on
the rise, although resource productivity increased by 33.3%
between 2000 and 2022 (United Nations, 2024). Given the
importance of sustainable packa ging research, managers should
increase research and development on environmentally friendly
packaging materials and adopt bi odegradable materials. Studies
have shown that consumers respond more positively to
packaging that uses biorecycled designs and have a higher
willingness to purchase (Steenis et al. 2018). In addition,
managers should communicate s ustainable attributes to con-
sumers through packaging signage and labelling to enhance
environmental awareness and trust (Boz et al. 2020). By
combining packaging strategies with sustainability trends,
companies can not only improve their market position, but
also better ful ﬁl consumer expectations.
Perceptual and emotional responses play a key role in
consumer decision-making. Although neuroscience techniques
represent a relatively small part of current research, they
represent an important direction for innovation. Researchers
have found that consumers ’ emotional responses provide insights
into product perceptions (Mehta et al. 2022). Therefore,
managers should design packaging elements that trigger positive
emotions and optimise packaging to enhance consumers ’ sensory,
affective, and cognitive experiences. Meanwhile, it is recom-
mended that managers consider applying neuromarketing
techniques such as eye tracking and heart rate monitoring to
evaluate packaging effectiveness (Rawnaque et al. 2020). Through
the application of neuromarketing techniques, companies can
gain deeper consumer insights and reduce marketing trial-and-
error costs.

Cultural factors have a signi ﬁcant impact on consumer
packaging perception (Ploom et al. 2020). Therefore, globalised
companies should have a deep understanding of the cultural
background of their target markets (Khan et al. 2022) and gain
insights into the preferences of different cultural groups (Madden
et al. 2000). Marketers should adapt design strategies for different
markets, such as focusing more on cultural and social factors in
China, sustainability and visual design in the US, and
neuromarketing techniques in Spain. At the same time,
companies should invest in cross-cultural consumer research to
ensure the cultural adaptation of packaging design elements by
applying semiotic analysis methods (Lemon, 2018; Celhay et al.
2020). By implementing these strategies, companies can better
address the challenges of cultural diversity in globalised markets
and enhance market competitiveness.
Directions for future research . This study adopts the TMC
framework proposed by Paul et al. ( 2017) to analyse the estab-
lished theories, research methodologies, and research contexts in
the ﬁeld of research on the relationship between packaging design
and purchase intention in order to provide structured paths for
future research.

text:
2000). Marketers should adapt design strategies for different
markets, such as focusing more on cultural and social factors in
China, sustainability and visual design in the US, and
neuromarketing techniques in Spain. At the same time,
companies should invest in cross-cultural consumer research to
ensure the cultural adaptation of packaging design elements by
applying semiotic analysis methods (Lemon, 2018; Celhay et al.
2020). By implementing these strategies, companies can better
address the challenges of cultural diversity in globalised markets
and enhance market competitiveness.
Directions for future research . This study adopts the TMC
framework proposed by Paul et al. ( 2017) to analyse the estab-
lished theories, research methodologies, and research contexts in
the ﬁeld of research on the relationship between packaging design
and purchase intention in order to provide structured paths for
future research. Through this systematic analysis, a speci ﬁc dis-
cussion of these three dimensions is developed below, and
research directions that can be explored are proposed.
Theory. Given the diversity of the research ﬁeld on the relation-
ship between package design and purchase intention, scholars
have utilised a number of theoretical frameworks to understand
the complex mechanisms involved. Supplementary Material Table
S1 lists the theoretical frameworks that have been widely adopted
in the ﬁeld of research on the effect of package design on pur-
chase intention. Among them, the Theory of Planned Behaviour
(TPB) is the most widely used (12.70%), followed by the Theory
of Reasoned Action (TRA) (4.23%) and Cue Exploitation Theory
(3.70%). The TPB, as a theoretical framework for understanding
and predicting consumer behavioural intentions, possesses strong
explanatory power and wide application (Ajzen, 2016; Tau ﬁque
and Vaithianathan, 2018; Conner, 2020). Researchers used TPB
as a theoretical framework to study the purchase intention of
sustainably packaged organic food and found that the set of
variables of attitudes, personal norms, and perceived behavioural
control were able to explain 70.3% of the variance (Santos et al.
2021). In particular, the TPB demonstrated strong explanatory
power in terms of explaining the effect of labelling information of
the package on consumer product attitudes and purchase inten-
tions (Grappe et al. 2022). Existing studies are still limited in
exploring how speci ﬁc elements of package design can explain
consumers’ purchase intentions through TPB. Packaging visual
attributes and design awareness may have different effects on the
three main elements of TPB. Therefore, this study proposes:
Research Direction 1: Explore the effects of packaging visual
attributes (e.g. Packaging Colours, Logo, and Packaging Graphics,
etc.) and design consciousness (e.g. Clarity, Continuity in Visual
Package Design, and Experiential Packaging, etc.) on the
mechanisms that differentially in ﬂuence attitudes, subjective
norms, and perceived behavioural control in TPB.
Many studies in this ﬁeld still lack clear theoretical support.
Considering that the in ﬂuence of package design on purchase
intention is a complex process, Stimulus-Organism-Response (S-
O-R) theory, as a widely used theoretical framework that
integrates individuals ’ perceptions and responses to external
stimuli (C.-C. Chen and Yao, 2018), is valuable in analysing how
package design elements affect consumers ’ perceptions and
emotions, which in turn in ﬂuence their purchase intention
(Harjadi and Gunardi, 2022). Therefore, this study proposes:
Research Direction 2: Integrate multiple theoretical frame-
works to develop a comprehensive model of packaging design
inﬂuence on purchase intention, especially combining S-O-R
theory with TPB or Expectation Discrepancy Theory (EDT) to
capture the dual cognitive and affective paths of packaging design
inﬂuence.
Method. A large number of empirical studies exist in the current
literature in this research area. Supplementary Material Table S2
lists the research methods used in the literature of the current
research area. The current research area is dominated by quan-
titative methods (84.13%), with relatively few mixed methods
(14.29%) and qualitative methods (1.59%). In terms of data
analysis techniques, traditional statistical methods and partial
least squares (PLS-SEM) techniques in structural equation mod-
elling (SEM) were widely used, the latter being suitable for small
samples and non-normally distributed data (Hair et al. 2022;
Kline and Little, 2023; Mohd Ghazali et al. 2023). Very few stu-
dies have used qualitative research methods, such as Zhang et al.
(2023) who found that certain design elements such as colour,
shape, and contrast can enhance the risk perception of labels, and
Acquah et al. ( 2023) who used a focus group discussion method
to gain insights into the factors that in ﬂuence the demand for
plant-based beverages. The use of mixed research methods can
combine the strengths of qualitative and quantitative (Schoon-
enboom and Johnson, 2017). Therefore, this study proposes:
Research Direction 3: Apply a sequential explanatory mixed
research design to quantitatively measure the effect of package
design on purchase intention, and then explain the psychological
mechanisms behind the quantitative results through in-depth
interviews or focus group discussions.
The use of more advanced statistical analysis techniques such
as multilevel structural equation modelling (MSEM) (Meuleman,
2019), dynamic structural equation modelling (DSEM) (Aspar-
ouhov and Muthén, 2020; Geiser, 2021), and machine learning
(ML) techniques (Sarker, 2021) is lacking in existing research.
Researchers have suggested that consideration be given to
evaluating consumer behaviour in more realistic environments,
including measuring willingness to pay, applying choice-based
conjoint analysis, and using virtual supermarket environment
techniques (Nuojua et al. 2022). Therefore, this study proposes:
Research Direction 4: improve the prediction accuracy of the
impact of package design on willingness to buy using advanced
analytical techniques such as deep learning models, conjoint
analysis and virtual shopping environments.
Context. The current research contexts in this ﬁeld of study can
be assessed in terms of cultural and industry contexts, respec-
tively. Supplementary Material Table S3 lists the cultural contexts
used in the current literature in the research area, as well as each
of the main industry contexts. In terms of cultural contexts, the
existing research focuses on mono-cultural contexts (97.88%),
with very few cross-cultural studies (2.12%). In terms of industry
context, food packaging (48.15%), beverage packaging (10.05%),
and Fast Moving Consumer Goods (FMCG) packaging (8.99%)
dominated, while the online retail context was less studied
(1.59%). A few studies have made cross-country comparisons
(Claudia et al. 2023
), but there is a need for more extensive cross-
cultural research, especially in comparing differences in consumer
responses between developed and developing countries (Lavuri,
2022). Considering the cross-cultural differences in consumer
perceptions of food packaging risk, future research should con-
sider cross-cultural ﬁndings (Guo et al. 2023). The in ﬂuence of
cultural factors on consumer behaviour is increasingly complex in
the context of globalisation (Velasco and Spence, 2019).

Research Direction 5: To conduct systematic cross-cultural
comparative research, with special attention to the differentiated
consumer responses to packaging design in the context of
collectivist and individualist cultures, and the role of cultural
values as moderating variables.
Existing studies have mainly focused on the food and beverage
category (Binninger, 2017; Rebollar et al. 2019; Di Cicco et al.
2021; Nascimento et al. 2022). The rapid growth of online
retailing has brought many opportunities and challenges to
companies (Phan Tan and Le, 2023), and it is even more
important to study the impact of packaging design on consumer
purchase intention in online purchasing situations (W. Liang
et al. 2023). Since the United Nations proposed the SDGs in 2015,
packaging sustainability research has received extensive attention
from scholars (Olsson, 2017; De Sousa, 2021), but research on the
impact of sustainable packaging is still limited (Magnier and Crié,
2015; Nguyen et al. 2020; Bandara et al. 2022). Therefore, this
study proposes:
Research Direction 6: Expanding the research contexts to
include high-involvement products, online purchasing scenarios,
and sustainable packaging, and comparing the differences in the
mechanisms that inﬂuence packaging design in different contexts.
Conclusion and limitations . In this study, a review of the lit-
erature within the ﬁeld of research on the relationship between
packaging design and purchase intention was conducted,
addressing three research questions through a systematic proce-
dure. Performance analysis and scienti ﬁc mapping were con-
ducted to analyse the scienti ﬁc collaborative networks within the
ﬁeld, which included an examination of national and institutional
collaborative networks, and author collaborative networks. The
distribution and number of journals and disciplines were also
analysed to provide insight into the organisation of the knowl-
edge system. In addition, a cluster analysis of keywords within the
ﬁeld was conducted, revealing the research themes that have
attracted the most attention in the study of the relationship
between packaging design and purchase intention, and providing
valuable insights by analysing their evolutionary paths to capture
their development. It is worth noting that this study further
combed through studies from the top 3 countries in the research
ﬁeld to summarise the in ﬂuences of packaging design found in
consumer purchase decisions. And by adopting the perspective of
the TMC framework, this study provides an in-depth analysis of
the performance and knowledge structure of the research ﬁeld of
packaging design and purchase intention, which not only
advances the theoretical construction, methodological innovation,
and contextual expansion of the current research ﬁeld, but also
provides valuable insights into the direction of future research by
posing the form of future research questions. This study has
achieved signiﬁcant results in the relationship between packaging
design and purchase intention, showing the evolution of research
in this area over time and context. Not only does it provide
academics and practitioners with a systematic understanding of
the progress of research in this area, but it also provides valuable
references and guidance for subsequent research.
To avoid misdirection of future research, it is important to
recognise several key limitations of this study. Firstly, this study
selected literature based on the WoSCC database only and did not
cover relevant articles from other sources such as Scopus or JSTOR.
We only considered peer-reviewed journal articles in English,
which ensured the quality of the literature but may have excluded
relevant studies from other sources. Second, this study did not fully
explore the differences in the effectiveness of packaging design in
different brand strength contexts. Although the analyses showed
that packaging design cannot be considered in isolation from the
brand context, it failed to systematically compare the differences in
packaging design effectiveness between established and emerging
brands. Similarly, a systematic comparison of packaging impact
mechanisms between high and low involvement products across
product categories was not provided. In addition, this study used
bibliometric methods to conduct a quantitative review, but did not
analyse in depth the speci ﬁc differences between the different
research methods. Future research could consider using multi-
database integrated analyses, incorporating non-English literature,
applying meta-analysis to test the effect sizes of speci ﬁcv a r i a b l e s ,
and exploring the moderating effect of brand strength in more
depth with differences across product categories.
Data availability
No datasets were generated or analysed during the current study.

[Page 1]
Journal of Business and Economic Research (JBER) ISSN 3058-9576 Vol.1 No.8 2025
The Commercial Role of Visual Design in Brand Value
Construction
Zhiqing Yin
Macau University of Science and Technology, Macau 999078
Abstract: In today's business landscape dominated by digitalization and the experience economy, brand value
construction has shifted from competing on product functionality to competing on consumer perception and emotional
connection. Visual design, as the most direct and efficient communication medium between brands and consumers, has
gained increasing strategic importance. This paper systematically explores how visual design plays a central role in brand
value construction by shaping brand identity, conveying brand value, enhancing user experience, and driving business
performance. Integrating theories from brand management, visual communication, and consumer behavior, the study
constructs a theoretical framework linking “visual design—brand perception—value recognition—business performance.”
This framework is analyzed through case studies of Apple, Nike, and Coca-Cola. Findings reveal that successful visual
design transcends aesthetic expression; it extends corporate strategy, significantly enhancing brand awareness, loyalty,
and premium pricing power. With technological advancements like artificial intelligence and the metaverse, visual design
is evolving toward dynamism and interactivity. Enterprises must elevate visual design to a strategic level and
systematically manage visual assets to achieve sustainable brand competitive advantages. This paper provides theoretical
support and practical guidance for brand managers and design practitioners.
Keywords: Visual design; Brand value; Brand identity
DOI:10.63887/jber.2025.1.8.8
Introduction
In the 21st century, business competition has
gradually shifted from traditional battles over product
features and pricing to a comprehensive contest of brand
value. A brand is no longer merely a trademark or name,
but a complex value system integrating products, services,
culture, emotions, and commitments. According to
Interbrand's 2024 Best Global Brands ranking, the most
valuable companies like Apple, Microsoft, and Amazon
derive the vast majority of their market capitalization
from brand equity rather than tangible assets. This
phenomenon demonstrates that brands have become
enterprises' most valuable intangible assets, with their
value-building process directly impacting long-term
survival and development. Within the brand value chain,
visual design plays an irreplaceable role. From the very
first moment consumers encounter a brand, visual
elements—including logos, colors, typography, graphics,
layouts, packaging, and advertising visuals—form the
brand's first impression. Research indicates that
consumers form preliminary judgments about a brand
within 7 seconds, with 90% of this information derived
from visual cues. Thus, visual design serves not only as
the brand's outward “face” but also as a ‘translator’ and
“amplifier” of its intrinsic value.
However, despite its widespread practical
application, visual design remains academically confined
to the realms of “aesthetics” or “communication tools,”
lacking systematic exploration of its deeper commercial
value. Many enterprises still view design departments as

[Page 2]
Journal of Business and Economic Research (JBER) ISSN 3058-9576 Vol.1 No.8 2025
support functions rather than core components of strategic
decision-making. This cognitive bias leads to insufficient
investment in visual design resources, inconsistent brand
visual systems, and ultimately weakens the cumulative
effect of brand value. This paper aims to fill this research
gap by deeply analyzing the commercial role of visual
design in brand value construction. The research
questions focus on: How does visual design
systematically enhance brand value by influencing
consumer perception and behavior? What similarities and
differences exist in the strategic functions of visual design
across different industries and market environments?
How will future technological transformations reshape
the role of visual design? By addressing these questions,
this paper seeks to establish an integrated theoretical
framework that reveals the logic behind visual design's
evolution from “decoration” to “strategy,” providing
brand managers with actionable practical guidance.
1 Theoretical Foundation
1.1 Theoretical Framework of Brand Value
1.1.1 Brand Equity Model
The concept of brand value is rooted in brand equity
theory. In Managing Brand Equity, brand equity is
defined as “a set of assets and liabilities associated with a
brand name and symbol that can add or subtract value
from products or services.” The book proposes a
five-dimensional model encompassing brand loyalty,
brand awareness, perceived quality, brand associations,
and proprietary assets. This framework systematically
elevated brands from marketing tools to manageable
strategic assets for the first time, providing a theoretical
foundation for enterprises to measure and invest in brands.
Aaker emphasized that brand equity is the result of
long-term accumulation, with its core residing in
consumer preference for the brand and willingness to pay
a premium. This provides an entry point for
understanding the long-term value of visual design in
brand building.
1.1.2 Customer-Based Brand Equity Model
From the consumer perspective, the
“Customer-Based Brand Equity” (CBBE) model was
proposed. He posits that brand value originates from
brand knowledge in consumers' minds, comprising brand
identity and brand image. His CBBE pyramid model
(2001) clarifies the brand-building pathway: from
enhancing brand salience to establishing brand meaning,
then eliciting brand response, ultimately achieving brand
resonance. This model emphasizes the depth of the
brand-consumer relationship, stressing that brands must
deepen value recognition through consistent and
meaningful interactions. Keller's theory provides a clear
framework for analyzing how visual design influences
consumer cognition and emotion, highlighting the
structural role of visual design within brand strategy.
1.2 Theoretical Foundations of Visual Design
1.2.1 Gestalt Psychology and Visual Perception
One of the theoretical foundations of visual design is
Gestalt psychology, which reveals the principles of
wholeness and organization in human visual perception.
People tend to perceive visual elements as wholes rather
than isolated parts. Its core principles include Proximity,
Similarity, Continuity, Closure, and Figure-Ground
relationships. These principles explain why a clean,
symmetrical logo is more readily recognized and
remembered by the brain. For example, IBM's “stripe”
logo leverages proximity and continuity principles to
maintain high recognizability even at small sizes or from
a distance. Gestalt principles provide cognitive science
foundations for effective visual design, guiding designers
to create brand symbols that are easy to understand and
remember.
1.2.2 Semiotics and Meaning Construction
Semiotics provides a critical framework for
understanding how meaning is generated in visual
symbols. Peirce's tripartite model of signs breaks them
down into the “signifier,” the “signified,” and the

[Page 3]
Journal of Business and Economic Research (JBER) ISSN 3058-9576 Vol.1 No.8 2025
“interpretant.” In a brand context, visual elements like
logos, colors, and typography serve as signifiers, pointing
to the brand's core values or personality (the signified).
Meaning emerges through consumers' cognitive processes
and cultural backgrounds (the interpretant). For instance,
green symbolizes nature and sustainability for
eco-friendly brands, while it may represent wealth and
stability for financial brands. The goal of brand design is
to “ensure consistency and recognizability across all
touchpoints,” which is fundamentally a strategic
management issue. Collectively, these theories
demonstrate that visual design is a process of meaning
construction, not mere aesthetic decoration.
2 The Mechanism of Visual Design in Brand
Value Construction
2.1 Shaping Brand Identity and Recognition
2.1.1 Enhancing Brand Salience
Brand salience—the consumer's ability to quickly
recognize and recall a brand in specific contexts—serves
as the foundation for brand value construction. Visual
design plays a pivotal role as a “cognitive anchor” in this
process, reducing cognitive load through highly
recognizable symbolic systems. A concise, distinctive,
and memorable brand logo swiftly establishes a position
in consumers' minds. For instance, Apple's “bite-marked
apple” logo, despite multiple iterations, consistently
maintains minimalist aesthetics. The graphic itself carries
philosophical metaphors of knowledge, innovation, and
imperfection, enabling global recognition even without
accompanying text.

text:
2 The Mechanism of Visual Design in Brand
Value Construction
2.1 Shaping Brand Identity and Recognition
2.1.1 Enhancing Brand Salience
Brand salience—the consumer's ability to quickly
recognize and recall a brand in specific contexts—serves
as the foundation for brand value construction. Visual
design plays a pivotal role as a “cognitive anchor” in this
process, reducing cognitive load through highly
recognizable symbolic systems. A concise, distinctive,
and memorable brand logo swiftly establishes a position
in consumers' minds. For instance, Apple's “bite-marked
apple” logo, despite multiple iterations, consistently
maintains minimalist aesthetics. The graphic itself carries
philosophical metaphors of knowledge, innovation, and
imperfection, enabling global recognition even without
accompanying text. This highly condensed visual
language not only enhances brand recognition but also
strengthens its cross-cultural communication capabilities.
Furthermore, color—as the fastest-acting visual
element to trigger perception—plays an irreplaceable role
in enhancing brand distinctiveness. Research indicates
color can boost brand recognition by up to 80% and
exerts a primacy effect in consumer decision-making.
Coca-Cola's longstanding commitment to “Coca-Cola
Red” as its primary hue has elevated this color beyond
functional attributes, transforming it into a core vessel for
brand emotion and cultural symbolism. Whether in
advertising, packaging, or retail environments,
“Coca-Cola Red” instantly captures attention and evokes
brand associations. Through decades of unwavering
visual consistency, Coca-Cola has successfully converted
color into brand equity, maintaining high visibility and
psychological presence amid fierce competition.
2.1.2 Building Brand Associations
Brand associations refer to the set of attributes,
benefits, personalities, and values consumers link to a
brand, forming a crucial foundation for differentiation.
Visual design proactively implants positive, deep-seated
brand associations through symbolic metaphors, visual
storytelling, and contextual immersion. Nike's “Swoosh”
logo, though composed of a single fluid curve, draws
inspiration from the wings of Nike, the Greek goddess of
victory. It embodies the core spirit of speed, dynamism,
and triumph, perfectly aligning with the brand's “Just Do
It” ethos. This logo, widely applied across athletic gear,
advertising campaigns, and digital platforms,
continuously strengthens its emotional connection to
perseverance, achievement, and self-transcendence. This
elevates the brand beyond product functionality,
transforming it into a symbol of a lifestyle attitude.
MUJI, conversely, constructs entirely distinct brand
associations through an ultra-minimalist visual language.
Its packaging eschews ornate decoration, employing kraft
paper, neutral tones, and standardized typography to
convey an anti-consumerist philosophy of “no brand,
good products.” This de-commercialized design approach
not only reduces environmental impact but also shapes a
brand image rooted in naturalness, authenticity, and
simplicity. When consumers encounter its visual system,
they naturally associate it with environmentalism,
restraint, and the essence of life, fostering deep value
alignment. Thus, visual design transcends mere

[Page 4]
Journal of Business and Economic Research (JBER) ISSN 3058-9576 Vol.1 No.8 2025
information conveyance—it embodies brand values,
subtly shaping consumers' cognitive frameworks and
emotional preferences.
2.2 Deepening Brand Experience and Emotional
Connection
2.2.1 Conveying Perceived Quality
Perceived quality represents consumers' overall
assessment of a product or service's quality, directly
influencing their purchase intent and price acceptance.
Visual design leverages the “design equals quality”
cognitive shortcut to establish high-quality expectations
before actual product use. Premium cosmetics brands like
Lancôme and Estée Lauder master this approach. Their
bottle designs often feature frosted glass, metallic finishes,
and precision-engineered closures, complemented by
elegant typography and intricate patterns. This creates a
visual impression blending luxury, professionalism, and
technological sophistication. Such details not only elevate
the product's aesthetic value but also convince consumers
of its exceptional intrinsic quality, making them willing to
pay a premium.
In the digital realm, user interface (UI) design
similarly conveys perceived quality. Google's Material
Design language builds an efficient, modern, and reliable
brand image through clear information hierarchy,
consistent icon standards, subtle shadow effects, and fluid
motion transitions. When users experience intuitive
operational logic and harmonious visual rhythms in
Android systems or applications like Gmail, they
naturally form the perception that “Google equals
technological leadership and stable reliability.”
Conversely, chaotic layouts, low-resolution images, or
inconsistent interactive feedback rapidly erode user trust
in product quality. Therefore, whether for physical goods
or digital services, visual design remains a critical lever
for shaping perceptions of high quality.
2.2.2 Evoking Emotional Resonance
Emotion serves as the core driver of brand loyalty,
and visual design is an effective means to evoke
emotional resonance. Starbucks creates a comfortable
“third space” atmosphere through its unified green logo,
warm-toned lighting, wooden furniture, hand-drawn style
menus, and the pervasive aroma of coffee within its stores.
This multisensory design strategy grants consumers a
sense of belonging and relaxation within the physical
space, thereby tightly linking the brand to emotional
needs beyond home and work. Here, visual elements
transcend mere decoration to become shapers of
emotional ambiance, elevating the brand from functional
consumption to emotional consumption.
The three-tier theory of emotional design further
reveals the emotional mechanisms of visual design: at the
instinctive level, aesthetics capture attention; at the
behavioral level, usability enhances satisfaction; at the
reflective level, meaning fosters deep identification.
Patagonia's eco-themed advertisements exemplify this
logic—their visuals often feature majestic natural
landscapes and close-ups of endangered animals, paired
with minimalist copy that powerfully evokes viewers'
awareness and responsibility toward ecological crises.
This visual narrative not only showcases the brand's
mission but invites consumers to participate in a
collective value-building journey. When users are moved
by the principles championed by the brand, loyalty shifts
from the product itself to a resonance of shared values,
forming an irreplaceable emotional bond.
2.3 Driving Business Performance and Brand
Equity
2.3.1 Building Brand Trust and Loyalty
Brand trust forms the foundation of long-term
customer relationships, and visual design effectively
establishes and reinforces trust through two key pathways:
consistency and transparency. A comprehensive Visual
Identity System ensures the brand maintains unified color,
typography, and graphic styles across all touch
points—including official websites, social media,

[Page 5]
Journal of Business and Economic Research (JBER) ISSN 3058-9576 Vol.1 No.8 2025
packaging, retail stores, and even employee uniforms.
Since establishing blue as its primary color in the
mid-20th century, IBM has steadfastly adhered to this
visual standard, even during its digital transformation.
This consistency communicates a stable, professional,
and trustworthy brand image to the market. Such
long-term visual coherence has solidified consumer
confidence in its positioning as a “technology leader.”
Simultaneously, transparent visual design is
emerging as a crucial trust-building tactic in the modern
era. Apparel brand Everlane implements its “Radical
Transparency” strategy, using clear infographics,
authentic photos, and itemized cost breakdowns on its
website to transparently display production costs and
factory information for each product. This open, honest
visual approach breaks down traditional information
barriers in the fashion industry, earning strong recognition
from ethically conscious younger consumers. In loyalty
building, Starbucks enhances member belonging through
exclusive visual elements in its Rewards app (like gold
badges and personalized recommendation interfaces).
Nike, via its Nike+ Run Club app, encourages users to
generate branded running route maps and share them on
social networks, weaving the brand into users' daily
narratives and transforming passive consumption into
active advocacy.
2.3.2 Translating into Commercial Outcomes
The ultimate manifestation of brand value lies in
quantifiable business performance, where strategic
investments in visual design directly translate into market
share, premium pricing power, and brand equity
appreciation.

This open, honest
visual approach breaks down traditional information
barriers in the fashion industry, earning strong recognition
from ethically conscious younger consumers. In loyalty
building, Starbucks enhances member belonging through
exclusive visual elements in its Rewards app (like gold
badges and personalized recommendation interfaces).
Nike, via its Nike+ Run Club app, encourages users to
generate branded running route maps and share them on
social networks, weaving the brand into users' daily
narratives and transforming passive consumption into
active advocacy.
2.3.2 Translating into Commercial Outcomes
The ultimate manifestation of brand value lies in
quantifiable business performance, where strategic
investments in visual design directly translate into market
share, premium pricing power, and brand equity
appreciation. Research indicates that brands with
consistently executed visual identity systems achieve
average market growth rates 33% higher than industry
benchmarks. Strong brand recognition not only reduces
marketing costs but also accelerates market penetration
for new product launches by leveraging existing brand
awareness. For instance, Apple consistently captures
global consumer attention and drives sales with minimal
explanation—merely through its signature minimalist
design language and the “Apple” logo—demonstrating
the compounding effect of sustained visual investment.
Moreover, exceptional visual design significantly
enhances a brand's premium pricing power. Despite
iPhone hardware costs being comparable to other flagship
models, its distinctive industrial design, iOS interface
aesthetics, and retail store experience collectively build a
holistic perception of “premium, innovative, and
user-centric”—convincing consumers to pay prices far
exceeding market averages. According to Interbrand's
valuation, over 70% of Coca-Cola's brand value stems
from its visual assets—including the logo, signature red
color, and iconic curved bottle—which have become the
company's most valuable intangible assets. In mergers
and acquisitions, licensing, and international expansion, a
robust visual system accelerates market acceptance and
lowers entry barriers. Therefore, visual design should not
be viewed as an expense but as a strategic investment that
continuously builds brand equity and drives sustainable
growth.
3 Case Study Analysis
3.1 Apple Inc.: Minimalism and
Innovation-driven
Apple exemplifies how visual design propels brand
value, with its success rooted in embedding “design as
strategy” deep within its corporate DNA. Since Steve
Jobs introduced “Think Different,” this philosophy has
permeated all visual expressions. The brand logo evolved
from the early rainbow-colored apple to today's
monochromatic metallic icon, symbolizing the brand's
maturation from emphasizing individuality and rebellion
to pursuing purity, simplicity, and a premium
technological aesthetic. Product designs like the iPhone
and Mac Book consistently uphold seamless, integrated
industrial aesthetics. By eliminating redundant buttons
and ports, they convey mastery over detail through

[Page 6]
Journal of Business and Economic Research (JBER) ISSN 3058-9576 Vol.1 No.8 2025
minimalist forms. This highly unified visual language not
only enhances product recognition but also shapes an
image of “innovation, precision, and user-friendliness,”
establishing high-quality expectations among consumers
even before they experience the functionality.
On the user experience front, Apple builds a
cohesive ecosystem perception through systematic visual
design. The iOS interface follows the “less is more”
principle, featuring flat icons, soft color palettes, and fluid
animations that minimize learning curves and enhance
interaction pleasure. Apple Stores extend this minimalist
ethos with open layouts, wooden tables, and barrier-free
spaces, creating an atmosphere where technology and
humanity converge. Campaigns like “Shot on iPhone”
showcase real-world user photography to demonstrate
product capabilities, reinforcing the brand association that
“everyone can create.” Consequently, Apple has held the
top spot in global brand value for a decade, with its
product premium pricing and user loyalty far surpassing
competitors. This fully demonstrates the pivotal role of
visual design in commercial success.
3.2 Nike: Dynamic Symbolism and Community
Building
Nike's visual design consistently revolves around the
core values of “dynamic energy, inspiration, and victory,”
successfully elevating the brand into a spiritual symbol.
Its iconic “Swoosh” logo—a sleek, powerful curve
inspired by the wings of Nike, the Greek goddess of
victory—embodies metaphors of speed and flight,
becoming one of the world's most recognizable brand
symbols. This emblem is extensively applied across
athletic footwear, apparel, advertising, and digital
platforms. Whether on the field or in urban settings, it
instantly evokes consumers' emotional resonance with
perseverance and achievement. Campaigns like the “Just
Do It” series employ high-speed photography, dynamic
compositions, and authentic athlete narratives. Combined
with striking visual contrasts and rhythmic pacing, they
powerfully convey the brand's spirit of pushing
boundaries. This transcends functional sports gear,
elevating Nike into a cultural symbol of
self-transcendence.
In the digital era, Nike deepens user connections
through platforms like the Nike App and Nike Training
Club. These applications feature personalized visual
interfaces that recommend content based on user
preferences, while enhancing engagement through badges,
progress bars, and social sharing mechanisms. Nike Run
Club generates branded visual route maps from recorded
runs, encouraging users to share them on social media
and creating a viral effect for brand dissemination. This
community strategy, anchored by visual connections, not
only boosts user retention but also weaves the brand into
consumers' daily narratives. Through its “design-driven
innovation” strategy, Nike's brand value has surpassed
$10 billion, maintaining long-term leadership in the
athletic apparel and footwear market. This demonstrates
the powerful driving force of visual design in building
brand loyalty and fueling commercial growth.
3.3 Coca-cola: Timeless Heritage and Local
Innovation
Coca-Cola's visual design has evolved over a
century while steadfastly preserving the stability of its
core elements, forming an exceptionally recognizable
brand asset system. Its classic Spencerian script logo,
iconic “Coke Red” primary color, and distinctive curved
glass bottle collectively constitute the brand's “three
treasures,” establishing powerful psychological
associations and emotional memories worldwide. This
highly consistent visual identity transcends cultures and
regions, enabling consumers to recognize the brand by
color or silhouette alone, significantly enhancing brand
distinctiveness. Red symbolizes vitality and joy, while the
ergonomic curved bottle design ensures comfortable grip.
These design details not only serve functional purposes
but also convey the brand's century-old culture of

[Page 7]
Journal of Business and Economic Research (JBER) ISSN 3058-9576 Vol.1 No.8 2025
celebration and social connection, becoming an emotional
anchor for consumers during festive gatherings and social
occasions.
Simultaneously, Coca-Cola adeptly infuses
innovation into its heritage, adapting visual design to
reflect changing times and local needs. Its “Share a Coke”
campaign personalized bottle labels with common names
or nicknames, sparking consumer desire to collect and
share bottles and igniting a global social media
phenomenon. In recent years, the brand introduced plant
-based eco -bottles, with packaging highlighting visuals
like “Made from Plants” and “Recyclable” to resonate
with younger consumers' sustainability concerns. These
innovations have not disrupted the brand's core visual
identity but rather flexibly expanded upon its stable
foundation. This approach maintains brand credibility
while enhancing modernity and approachability.
Consequently, Coca-Cola has been consistently ranked as
the world's most valuable beverage brand for multiple
years, with its visual assets becoming a core pillar of the
company's intangible value.
4 New Trends in Visual Design Amid
Technological Transformation
4.1 Dynamic Visuals and Interactive Design
Dynamic visuals are gradually replacing static
images as the core means for brands to engage with users.
Traditional brand logos, advertisements, and interface
designs are evolving toward dynamic and real-time
formats. Motion logos, micro-interactions, and immersive
animations are widely adopted across digital platforms.
For instance, Google's Doodles frequently celebrate
holidays or commemorate figures through dynamic
designs, enhancing brand affinity while increasing user
dwell time and engagement.

4 New Trends in Visual Design Amid
Technological Transformation
4.1 Dynamic Visuals and Interactive Design
Dynamic visuals are gradually replacing static
images as the core means for brands to engage with users.
Traditional brand logos, advertisements, and interface
designs are evolving toward dynamic and real-time
formats. Motion logos, micro-interactions, and immersive
animations are widely adopted across digital platforms.
For instance, Google's Doodles frequently celebrate
holidays or commemorate figures through dynamic
designs, enhancing brand affinity while increasing user
dwell time and engagement. Snap chat enables real-time
brand-user interaction through AR filters, allowing users
to “try on” virtual clothing or take photos with brand
characters, significantly boosting the fun and social
nature of communication. These dynamic visual elements
break the one-way communication model, shifting brands
from passive display to active dialogue, and significantly
strengthening users' emotional connection and memory
retention.
At the user experience level, micro-interaction
design is emerging as a critical detail for elevating
perceived brand quality. Haptic feedback upon button
clicks, fluid page transitions, and creative loading
animations silently convey a brand's professionalism and
human-centered care. For instance, Apple's iOS motion
design precisely controls duration and easing curves to
create natural, elegant operational rhythms, making users
feel “design with warmth.” In web and app design,
meticulously crafted interactive animations not only
guide user behavior but also reduce cognitive load and
boost operational efficiency. With the widespread
adoption of 5G and high-refresh-rate screens, the fluidity
and expressiveness of dynamic visuals will further
enhance. Moving forward, brands must establish dynamic
visual standards to ensure consistent interaction quality
across devices and scenarios, thereby building smarter,
more emotionally resonant digital brand identities.
4.2 Artificial Intelligence and Generative Design
Artificial intelligence (AI) is profoundly
transforming the creative workflow and decision -making
processes in visual design. Generative AI technologies
like DALL·E, Mid Journey, and Adobe Firefly can
rapidly generate vast quantities of high-quality visual
solutions based on textual prompts, significantly boosting
design efficiency. Brands can leverage AI for logo draft
generation, advertising concept exploration, color scheme
recommendations, and even personalized content
customization. For instance, Adobe Firefly, now
integrated into Creative Cloud, allows designers to
instantly generate textures, icons, or background images
aligned with brand aesthetics, shortening the journey
from concept to execution. AI can also automatically
optimize ad visuals—including composition, color

[Page 8]
Journal of Business and Economic Research (JBER) ISSN 3058-9576 Vol.1 No.8 2025
schemes, and copy combinations—through A/B testing
data analysis, boosting conversion rates. This
“human-machine collaboration” model enables brands to
achieve higher-frequency creative iterations at lower
costs.
However, the widespread adoption of AI also carries
the potential risk of “design homogenization.” Since AI
models are trained on existing data, their outputs often
fall into stylistic sameness, lacking originality and
cultural depth. Over reliance on algorithmic outputs may
lead to mediocre visual expressions, weakening a brand's
competitive differentiation. Therefore, human designers
should transition from “executors” to ‘curators’ and
“strategic guides,” responsible for setting creative
direction, selecting high-quality solutions, and infusing
brand values. Successful brands of the future will
establish a dual-track mechanism of “AI + human
creativity”: AI handles efficiency and scalability, while
humans manage emotional resonance, cultural relevance,
and strategic judgment. Only through this approach can
brands maintain their uniqueness and human warmth
amid the technological wave, achieving a design future
empowered by technology rather than dominated by it.
4.3 The Metaverse and Virtual Brand
Experiences
The rise of the metaverse is reshaping the spatial
dynamics of brand-consumer interactions, with visual
design emerging as the critical bridge connecting the
physical and digital worlds. Within virtual environments,
brands transcend limitations of two-dimensional planes or
physical products, instead requiring the construction of
comprehensive virtual visual assets—including 3D logos,
digital apparel, virtual spaces, and interactive avatars.
Nike acquired RTFKT Studios to launch limited-edition
virtual sneaker NFTs, allowing users to wear and display
them on platforms like Decent raland, thereby digitally
extending brand value. Though lacking physical
functionality, these virtual products derive real economic
value from their scarcity, artistic appeal, and social
attributes, becoming new identity carriers for the next
generation of consumers. Visual design in this process
transcends mere aesthetics, serving as a vessel for digital
ownership and brand narratives.
Luxury brands are also actively exploring visual
experience innovations within the met averse. Gucci
opened a virtual store on the Roblox platform where users
can purchase virtual handbags and clothing for avatar
styling. Its visual design meticulously replicates the
material textures and craftsmanship details of real-world
products, ensuring brand consistency. BMW constructed
a virtual showroom in the metaverse, enabling consumers
to immerse themselves in new car designs and driving
experiences through VR devices. These practices
demonstrate that future brand experiences will transcend
the boundaries between virtual and physical realms.
Visual design must possess cross-platform adaptability,
supporting multi modal expression from 2D to 3D and
from static to real-time rendering. Brands need to
proactively establish virtual asset libraries and formulate
meta verse visual standards to maintain recogniz ability
and authority within emerging digital ecosystems, thereby
capturing the minds of the next generation of users.
4.4 Sustainable Design
Sustainable design has become a vital pathway for
brands to fulfill social responsibilities and earn consumer
trust, with visual design serving as both an advocate and
witness in this process. Heightened environmental
awareness drives companies to reevaluate material
choices, production processes, and packaging structures.
Through material textures, color language, and
information communication, visual design intuitively
conveys a brand's commitment to sustainability. IKEA's
“Zero Packaging” experiment employs foldable structures
and natural hemp rope to bundle products. Its minimalist,
primal visual style not only reduces environmental impact
but also communicates a “less is more” eco-philosophy to

[Page 9]
Journal of Business and Economic Research (JBER) ISSN 3058-9576 Vol.1 No.8 2025
consumers. Lush, meanwhile, champions a “naked
packaging” strategy, eliminating plastic packaging and
relying solely on product color and form to attract
customers. This approach is reinforced by hand-drawn
in-store posters and eco-friendly slogans, strengthening
the brand's association with green consumption.
In the digital realm, “digital-first” design has
emerged as a new sustainability trend. Brands are
reducing printed materials, instead providing information
through QR codes, AR guides, and digital manuals to cut
paper and ink consumption. For example, Nike utilizes
digital fashion shows and virtual product previews for
new releases, minimizing physical sample production.
Visual design in digital interfaces employs green icons,
natural textures, and environmental data visualization
(like carbon footprint calculators) to heighten users' eco-
awareness. Furthermore, brands showcase sustainable
practices through visual storytelling. Patagonia's “Worn
Wear” campaign, for instance, highlights the enduring
beauty of mended garments while promoting a “buy less,
buy well” ethos. These designs not only minimize
environmental impact but also cultivate responsible brand
identities, attracting a growing ethical consumer base and
achieving dual enhancement of commercial and social
value.
Conclusion
This paper systematically demonstrates the core
commercial role of visual design in brand value
construction. Research reveals that visual design
transcends aesthetic expression to function as a strategic
tool. By shaping brand identity, deepening value
recognition, and driving business performance, it serves
as a key lever for accumulating brand equity.

Conclusion
This paper systematically demonstrates the core
commercial role of visual design in brand value
construction. Research reveals that visual design
transcends aesthetic expression to function as a strategic
tool. By shaping brand identity, deepening value
recognition, and driving business performance, it serves
as a key lever for accumulating brand equity. Successful
visual design effectively reduces consumer cognitive
costs, fosters emotional resonance, and creates
sustainable differentiation advantages in highly
competitive markets. Amid globalization and
digitalization, brands must integrate visual design into
their strategic core through systematic, forward-thinking,
and user-centered design thinking.
Companies should elevate visual design to a
strategic level by establishing a Chief Design Officer
(CDO) or design committee to ensure alignment with
brand strategy. Invest in establishing and rigorously
enforcing a brand visual identity system to guarantee
visual consistency across global, omni channel, and all
touch points. Simultaneously, develop a design ROI
assessment framework to quantify the impact of visual
design on brand perception, user engagement, and sales
conversion. Looking ahead, as technologies like AI, AR,
and the metaverse advance, brands must embrace
dynamic, interactive design trends and explore
sustainable design pathways to maintain long-term
competitive advantage.

Article
The Impact of Visual Elements of Packaging Design on Purchase
Intention: Brand Experience as a Mediator in the Tea Bag
Product Category
Chang Liu 1,*
 , Mat Redhuan Samsudin 2
 and Yuwen Zou 3
1 College of Creative Arts, Universiti Teknologi MARA (UiTM), Kelantan Branch, Kota Bharu 15050,
Kelantan, Malaysia
2 College of Creative Arts, Universiti Teknologi MARA (UiTM), Kelantan Branch, Machang 18500,
Kelantan, Malaysia; redhuansamsudin@uitm.edu.my
3 Faculty of Communication and Media Studies, Universiti Teknologi MARA (UiTM),
Shah Alam 40450, Selangor Darul Ehsan, Malaysia; 2024373967@student.uitm.edu.my
* Correspondence: 2021652984@student.uitm.edu.my; Tel.: +60-17-2699598
Abstract: While packaging design plays a vital role in experience-oriented markets,
how multiple visual elements influence purchase intention through brand experience
remains unclear. This study addresses this gap by employing innovative orthogonal
experiments to examine the complex relationship between the visual elements of packaging
design and purchase intention for low-involvement products, integrating both design
and marketing perspectives. Through orthogonal experimental design, we developed
14 packaging prototypes as stimuli by systematically manipulating five visual elements
(Colour, Graphics, Logo, Typography, and Layout). The framework and prototypes were
validated through expert evaluation. Data were collected via a cross-sectional survey
from 490 tea bag consumers and analysed using SPSS (version 29.0) for preliminary data
processing and Mplus (version 8.3) for structural equation modelling. Our results reveal
the direct effects of visual packaging elements on consumer purchase intention. Notably,
Colour, Graphics, Logo, and Layout significantly influence purchase intention through
brand experience mediation. Importantly, our multi-level analysis of visual elements
unveils distinct patterns in how different design levels (e.g., colour harmony, graphic
types) affect consumer responses. This study provides novel theoretical insights into how
consumers make purchase decisions based on packaging design visual elements, addressing
a significant gap in existing research. Unlike previous studies focusing on isolated design
elements, our systematic classification and multi-level analysis offer both theoretical
insights into packaging design mechanisms and practical guidelines for designers and
practitioners.
Keywords: packaging design; visual elements; brand experience; purchase intention;
orthogonal experiment
1. Introduction
In the global consumer goods market, packaging design has evolved from a simple
product protection function to a key strategic tool for brand competition. This evolution is
particularly evident in China’s fast-growing packaging market, which, according to the
China Packaging Market Size, Analysing Material Type, Innovations and Forecast to 2028 report
published by GlobalData (2024), reached 912.9 billion units in 2023 and is expected to grow
at a compound annual growth rate of more than one percent from 2023 to 2028. The strong
Behav. Sci. 2025, 15, 181 https://doi.org/10.3390/bs15020181

[Page 2]
Behav. Sci. 2025, 15, 181 2 of 37
growth in the output value of China’s packaging industry not only reflects high demand
but also fierce competition in the current market. A global consumer survey conducted by
Ipsos revealed that 72 percent of consumers believe that product packaging design plays a
key role in their purchasing decision-making process (Gil, 2018). Packaging has long been
used as an important contact point for communication between companies and consumers
throughout the life of the product, injecting vitality into the brand.
As the only brand medium that consumers experience fully 100 percent of the
time, packaging delivers a higher return on investment than any other branding strategy
(Wheeler, 2021). Packaging design, as an important tool for branding, has a significant
impact on consumer purchase intention (PI). Studies have shown that 73 to 85 percent of
consumer purchase decisions are made at the point of sale, and packaging design is often
the main differentiator between products (Klimchuk & Krasovec, 2021). This importance
is particularly evident in the increasingly competitive Chinese market, where packaging
design has become an important part of brand strategy.
Understanding how packaging design elements influence consumer behaviour is
becoming increasingly important for companies seeking a competitive advantage. Many
scholars have explored the impact of different attributes of package design on PI (e.g.,
Benachenhou et al., 2018; Ck et al., 2022; Cortina-Mercado, 2017; Kiygi Calli & Kilic, 2020;
Setiowati & Liem, 2018; Silayoi & Speece, 2007; Suci et al., 2022; Theben et al., 2020; F. Wang
et al., 2022; Wulansari, 2019). It is evident that the importance of packaging as a powerful
tool in brand marketing and its influence on consumer purchase decisions has been widely
recognised by academics, but there are still some important research gaps that have not yet
been addressed. These research gaps not only limit the theoretical understanding but also
the practical application of packaging design strategies.
Firstly , current research still suffers from methodological limitations. Many studies rely
primarily on questionnaires and lack the involvement of stimulus materials (Calderon-Monge
et al., 2024; Zafar et al., 2022). Although this type of research has validated consumers’
general tendencies towards the concept of design elements through quantitative research
methods, the limitation of most of these studies is the use of a single questionnaire without
stimulus materials, which makes it difficult to accurately assess consumers’ responses to
packaging design elements. More importantly, most studies on the visual design of product
packaging have dealt with individual visual elements at the expense of their combined
effects (Martinez et al., 2021; Pleyers, 2024; Spence & Van Doorn, 2022). Consequently, most
current studies have somewhat limited practical applicability in packaging design strategies
and cannot provide appropriate and specific guidance for packaging design strategies.
Secondly, existing research has specific limitations in testing the impact of visual
elements of packaging design (VEPD) at different levels. Research has generally explored
the impact of specific colours such as red or blue on consumer behaviour (Casales-Garcia
et al., 2024; J. Su & Wang, 2024; Van Esch et al., 2019), yet research on the application
of systemic colour systems remains limited. Similarly, research on graphics elements of
packaging is contradictory, with Thomas and Capelli (2023) demonstrating that repeated
figurative graphics can significantly influence both the intended and actual product
experience, thereby affecting PI, while some scholars maintain opposing views.

metadata.core_insight_en: This study examines the impact of visual packaging design elements on purchase intention through brand experience in the tea bag product category. The results show that color, graphics, logo, and layout significantly influence purchase intention through brand experience mediation. A systematic classification and multi-level analysis of visual elements reveal distinct patterns in how different design levels affect consumer responses.
