Autoplay. New video content on the feed is automatically played 
(or repeated) without any user interaction. Autoplay removes the 
need for autonomous decision-making [12] and reduces friction 
from the experience which can be useful [62]. However, Lukoff et 
al. [53] found that autoplay often makes users feel less in control 
by undermining their sense of agency. In TikTok, new content is 
played (or repeated) immediately without any pause. 
Infinite Scroll. Compulsive scrolling of social media feed is neg-
atively associated with users’ digital well-being [46, 92]. Infinite 
scrolling supports such behavior by automatically loading more 
content as user reaches the end of feed [60]. In TikTok, the scrolling 
is frictionless. Together with autoplay, such mechanisms automate 
the user experience to induce normative dissociative states, reduc-
ing self-awareness and intentional choice to keep users on the 
platform [63]. 
Social Investments. 
This pattern includes metrics such as the 
number of likes and comments [62]. Such social engagement cues 
affect users’ decision making by activating the bandwagon heuristic 
where users interpret popular content as inherently more valuable 
— something they should also like [41, 56, 80, 95]. Therefore, social 
investments may promote meaningless interaction rather than in-
tentional use. In TikTok, social investments, such as the number of 
likes and comments, are clearly visible with interaction buttons. 
2.2 Definitions of User Engagement 
User engagement is a guiding principle for evaluating product suc-
cess, providing measurable insights on user-product interactions 
[24, 47, 89]. Designers use engagement metrics such as daily inter-
actions or average time spent to optimize product success [24, 47] 
but these same measures are connected to problematic technology 
use [24, 63]. Exact definitions of engagement are highly domain-
and context-specific, which explains why human-computer interac-
tion (HCI) studies have used various definitions and measures for 
engagement [39], ranging from simple metrics like time spent [84] 
or likes, shares, and comments [17], to conceptual frameworks [5]. 
In order to provide clarity for our measurements of engagement 
in this study, we used categorization of Lehmann et al. [47]. They 
divided user engagement into three main groups: online behavioral 
engagement (usage or performance metrics), cognitive engagement 
(physiological data, e.g. eye-tracking), and self-reported engage-
ment (questionnaires). In this study, we measure the first two cate-
gories of engagement as they provide objective, quantitative data 
[47] on the effects of our ACDP interventions, something which 
current literature lacks. For simplicity, we define online behavior 
engagement as behavioral engagement (measured via high-fidelity 
TikTok prototype) and cognitive engagement as attentional engage-
ment (measured via eye-tracking device).

in this study, we used categorization of Lehmann et al. [47]. They 
divided user engagement into three main groups: online behavioral 
engagement (usage or performance metrics), cognitive engagement 
(physiological data, e.g. eye-tracking), and self-reported engage-
ment (questionnaires). In this study, we measure the first two cate-
gories of engagement as they provide objective, quantitative data 
[47] on the effects of our ACDP interventions, something which 
current literature lacks. For simplicity, we define online behavior 
engagement as behavioral engagement (measured via high-fidelity 
TikTok prototype) and cognitive engagement as attentional engage-
ment (measured via eye-tracking device).

2.3 Measuring ACDP Interventions 
2.3.1 Adding Friction to Design Patterns. Ruiz et al. [74] showed 
that switching from infinite scroll to reaction-based feed (requiring 
users to like posts before seeing the next one) improved content 
recall and reduced mindless scrolling. They utilized the concept of 
microboundaries that are small moments of friction designed to 
interrupt automatic interactions and provide reflection opportuni-
ties [23]. While this approach effectively modified internal ACDP 
mechanisms [53], their modification imposed fundamental changes 
to interaction patterns. Building on the notion of microboundaries, 
we apply targeted friction to selected ACDPs in TikTok without 
requiring users to learn entirely new interfaces. We investigate 
friction-based interventionson ACDPs in an established short-form 
video interface while preserving core interaction patterns. 
2.3.2 Quantitative ACDP Studies. Recent studies have attempted 
to mitigate the impact of ACDPs with modifications to internal 
attention-capture mechanisms and employed quantitative behav-
ioral metrics to measure the effects of their interventions. In the 
video-on-demand domain, Schaffner et al. [77] conducted a between-
subjects empirical study (N=76) of 10-17 days on the short-term 
effects of disabling autoplay ACDP in Netflix. The study tracked 
metrics such as daily watching time together with reflective ques-
tionnaires about user experiences. Similarly, Roffarello et al. [62] 
designed a browser extension to mitigate the effects of social in-
vestments on Facebook (N=7) in a 3-week within-subjects study. 
They measured behavioral data such as average daily time spent 
and number of mouse scrolls, together with psychological scales to 
measure indicators of passive versus active use. 
Both studies employed statistical analyses and results revealed 
nuanced outcomes: Schaffner et al. [77] found that while disabling 
autoplay reduced daily watching time and session durations and 
many participants appreciated increased control over their usage, 
most still preferred to keep autoplay for its convenience. Roffarello 
et al. [62] observed that hiding social metrics slightly reduced over-
all usage and shifting behavior from passive to more active engage-
ment patterns, while only two participants noticed any change. 
These mixed results demonstrate the value of holistic measure-
ments combining objective behavioral metrics with subjective as-
sessments. However, both above mentioned studies examined in-
dividual ACDP interventions without systematically measuring 
user experience quality or sense of agency using validated instru-
ments. Building on their quantitative approaches, we extend ACDP 
intervention research to mobile SNS context (TikTok), examining 
multiple interventions through controlled experiments. We use vali-
dated questionnaires to directly assess the impact of adding friction 
to ACDPs on user experience quality and sense of agency. 
2.3.3 High-Fidelity Prototyping. In user experience research, high-
fidelity prototyping has been found to identify nearly twice as many 
issues that emerge in real usage scenarios compared to low-fidelity 
prototypes [31]. Although low-fidelity prototypes are effective in 
identifying functional issues, high-fidelity prototypes are better at 
revealing contextual issues and more suitable for collecting effi-
ciency measures [8, 75], which is beneficial for our study, as we 
apply modifications to a platform-specific design mechanisms. Ad-
ditionally, high-fidelity prototypes are not as prone to idealization 
effects as low-fidelity prototypes. Christoforakos and Diefenbach 
[20] found that the lower the fidelity, the more people idealize a 
product idea. Moreover, with reduced fidelity prototypes, users 
compensate for limitations by overrating aesthetic qualities [76]. 
Academic studies in SNSs using high-fidelity prototypes are 
limited. Vraga et al. [94] simulated a realistic Facebook feed with 
custom content to study users’ attention patterns (via eye-tracking 
device) to different content types. Their approach enabled an ecolog-
ically valid study of Facebook with a modified experience. However, 
their prototype served only as a stimulus. It was not interactive, did 
not collect data from user interactions, and used artificial content 
suited for their research objectives. Our work builds on this by de-
veloping a fully interactive, high-fidelity prototype with real TikTok

content. It collects comprehensive behavioral data and integrates 
with eye-tracking hardware. 
2.3.4 Using Eye-Tracking Data. Humans usually look directly at 
the object of interest, and gaze reveals a lot about the internal locus 
of attention [22]. Eye-tracking devices provide continuous and 
objective gaze data about users’ focus of attention on visual displays 
without placing additional burden on users [1], offering multiple 
data points for assessment of attentional engagement [21]. Eye-
tracking has been extensively used in usability research, because 
some problems are directly related to users’ attentional engagement 
[78]. Since users are not fully aware of their attentional focus [29], 
eye-tracking data provides an additional level of objective detail 
beyond self-reported measures [78]. 
Eye-tracking is still largely underutilized methodology in decep-
tive design studies. In SNS context, we found a study by Hussain et 
al. [36] that configured an eye-tracking device to inspect how users’ 
attention distribution across different areas-of-interest (AOIs) in 
Facebook desktop interface were correlated with personality traits 
and mental well-being states. Users were instructed to use Facebook 
on desktop for three minutes, while their gaze in different AOIs, 
e.g. news feed area and notifications area, was tracked. Metrics like 
total inspection time per each AOI was analyzed. We adopt a simi-
lar AOI-based approach with time-restricted tasks to examine how 
interventions on ACDPs affect attentional engagement distribution 
across key interface elements in TikTok. 
2.3.5 Measuring User Experience and Agency. The AttrakDiff sur-
vey is a widely-used quantitative questionnaire to measure multiple 
pragmatic and hedonic qualities of a product [90]. In empirical de-
ceptive design studies, Purohit et al. [69] used AttrakDiff to evaluate 
the overall user experience of a browser extension that modified 
several addictive design patterns in social media sites. The exten-
sion received positive user experience scores. By contrast, we utilize 
AttrakDiff to measure how friction-based interventions on existing 
ACDPs affect the user experience quality of the TikTok feed.

2.3.5 Measuring User Experience and Agency. The AttrakDiff sur-
vey is a widely-used quantitative questionnaire to measure multiple 
pragmatic and hedonic qualities of a product [90]. In empirical de-
ceptive design studies, Purohit et al. [69] used AttrakDiff to evaluate 
the overall user experience of a browser extension that modified 
several addictive design patterns in social media sites. The exten-
sion received positive user experience scores. By contrast, we utilize 
AttrakDiff to measure how friction-based interventions on existing 
ACDPs affect the user experience quality of the TikTok feed. 
The Sense of Agency Scale (SoAS), developed by Tapal et al. 
[83], measures two sub-scales: sense of positive agency (SoPA) as 
feelings of control and sense of negative agency (SoNA) as feel-
ings that actions are not under one’s control. SoAS was originally 
designed to measure person’s context-free beliefs about having 
core agency [83], but user experience studies have utilized SoAS to 
assess context-specific agency [6, 50, 53]. Liu et al. [50] successfully 
used SoAS to quantify how technology-induced involuntary body 
movements significantly increased participants’ SoNA, confirming 
the utility of the scale for evaluating systems that impact user con-
trol. Following this approach, we use SoAS to evaluate whether 
our interventions on ACDPs affected users’ perceived control over 
their TikTok interface interactions. 
2.3.6 Summary. Research investigating the effects of deceptive 
designs has employed various methodologies [30] and suggests 
that with interventions on such patterns, users report feeling more 
in control and experience improved digital well-being [51, 62, 69, 
77, 98]. Overall, our study extends previous work in several key 
areas. 
1) Limited research has attempted to conduct quantitative user 
studies on deceptive designs in native, mobile SNS applica-
tions. Meinhardt et al. [58] developed an Android application 
that prompted users with pause-reminder overlays across 
various SNS apps’ infinite feeds, but did not modify or mea-
sure the platforms’ internal designs. Our work takes a sig-
nificant step forward by using a high-fidelity prototype that 
closely mimics the iOS TikTok application. It utilizes real 
user content and enabled us to apply direct friction to inter-
nal ACDP mechanisms and measure behavioral engagement 
metrics. 

[Page 6]

2) Few studies have employed eye-tracking technology to in-
vestigate how deceptive design patterns impact users’ visual 
attention distribution in the user interface [38, 49]. This work 
contributes a novel application of eye-tracking technology 
to mobile SNS research, examining how ACDP interven-
tions impact attentional engagement [78] and unconscious, 
automatic responses to the interface [94]. 
3 Methodology 
This section first explains the technical development of our high-
fidelity TikTok prototype to measure behavioral engagement and 
the integration of an eye-tracking device to collect attentional en-
gagement data. Second, it introduces and rationalizes the measured 
metrics across all dimensions of our study. Third, it describes the de-
sign and procedure of conducted user studies and, finally, concludes 
with the data analysis. 
3.1 Apparatus 
3.1.1 Development of High-Fidelity TikTok Prototype. In order to 
boost the ecological validity of our experiment and quantitatively 
measure our interventions on ACDPs in TikTok , we developed 
a high-fidelity prototype that closely resembled the real TikTok 
feed. The prototype was deployed as an iOS application, allowing 
us to conduct controlled user tests with a clone of the original 
"For You" feed and other conditions with targeted friction added 
to ACDPs. Instead of designing alternative solutions to ACDPs, 
this approach offered a straightforward way toward mitigating the 
effects of attention-capture mechanisms without overhauling the 
established interface architecture. For each condition, we could con-
duct timed usage sessions and log detailed engagement data. The 
prototype precisely replicated the TikTok feed, accurately repro-
ducing design tokens and scroll gesture physics. Core functionality 
included swiping between posts, liking, commenting and book-
marking, and saving soundtracks. Additionally, users could ’follow’ 
content creators and ’share’ content via mock interfaces. For the 
feed content, we scraped publicly available video-posts from the 
web application of TikTok with popular hashtags across content 
types for different user preferences (e.g., #pets, #motivation). We 
collected equal amounts of video-posts per hashtag, gathering full 
metadata and information about each posts, including comments. 
Each interface condition received different content with equiva-
lent duration distributions, popularity levels (likes), and ordering 
(shortest to longest). 
3.1.2 Friction-Based Interventions. We imposed friction on three 
attention-capture damaging patterns identified in TikTok: autoplay, 
infinite scrolling, and social investments. Our prototype included 
four conditions, visualized in Figure 1: 
A – Control. Direct TikTok clone with no ACDP interventions. 
B – Disabled Autoplay. This interface blocked autoplay by re-
quiring manual play button activation. 
C – Increased Scroll Friction. This interface modified infinite 
scrolling by increasing the required finger movement dis-
tance for scrolling between videos compared to minimal 
gesture in control. This condition required approximately 
50% of the vertical screen length to create noticeable scrolling 
friction in order to produce a difference in the scrolling ex-
perience. 
D – Obstructed Social Investments. This intervention con-
cealed social metrics (likes, comments, bookmarks, shares, 
music saves) and the instant follow button. Since social in-
vestments are core building blocks of modern SNS services 
[62], we made metrics visible only after user interaction 
rather than removing them entirely (e.g., liking a post re-
vealed its total like count and opening comments section 
revealed total comment count). 
3.1.3 Integration of Eye-Tracking Device. Attentional engagement 
was measured using a Tobii Pro Spark device mounted with an 
iPhone 12 having the prototype application installed. Windows 
laptop running Tobii Pro Studio software (version 24.21) was used 
to record usage sessions and eye-tracking data. We defined three 
AOIs as shown in Figure 4: Content (main video area), Caption 
(post description), and Social (interaction elements like likes and 
comments). We examined whether ACDP interventions affected 
users’ attention distribution across these AOIs, particularly whether 
changes indicated more active or passive engagement patterns. For 
instance, we expected that in Condition B (removal of autoplay), 
users would spend more attentional effort on Caption AOI, signaling 
a more informed decision by user on whether to play the video.

3.2.1 Behavioral Engagement. For behavioral engagement in our 
study, we implemented various usage-related measures into our 
prototype that allowed us to comprehensively analyze differences 
between control and experimental conditions. We used metrics

3.2.2 Attentional Engagement. Common metrics used from eye-
tracking data are saccades, fixations and visits. Fixations refer to 
relatively stable eye position during which the eye remains still for 
a brief period and represent a moment when visual information 
processing is occurring. Saccades refer to fast eye movements that 
we use to change our focus of attention. Visits present the time 
between the first fixation on AOI and then the first fixation outside 
that AOI, measuring a complete engagement period with a specific 
AOI [1, 21]. Visits are associated with general looking behavior 
and attention to AOIs [21]. Our defined AOIs together cover the 
whole area of the screen and we were not interested in attentional 
engagement patterns on smaller elements inside those areas, which 
is why we decided to analyze only visit metrics that capture users’ 
full attentional engagement in an AOI. Table 2 describes the visit 
metrics we measured. In addition to analyzing metrics, we provide 
a comparison of gaze heatmaps between interventions to visualize 
attention distribution in control and experimental interfaces.

3.3 Study Design 
3.3.1 Ethical Approval. The research plan, including a comprehen-
sive risk analysis from all stakeholders’ perspectives in accordance 
with ethical guidelines of our institution, was submitted to the 
ethics committee and approved before any research development 
and user studies took place. All data collection procedures adhered 
to the EU General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) requirements 
as demanded by the ethical approval. Pre-study questionnaire data 
was permanently deleted upon completion of the user studies, and 
all collected study data was anonymized through the assignment 
of unique numerical identifiers to each participant. 
3.3.2 Participant Screening. Participants were recruited via com-
munication channels of our institution and campus recruitment 
posters. Potential participants completed an online qualification 
questionnaire to assess study eligibility. Prerequisites included nor-
mal or corrected vision (contact lenses only, as eyeglasses could 
interfere with eye-tracking systems), no cognitive/neural impair-
ments, epilepsy tendencies, or motor control issues, age 18-30, reg-
ular TikTok usage (at least monthly), and sufficient English skills 
to use TikTok in English. After meeting prerequisites, participants 
could book a one hour user study session. 
3.3.3 Participant Demographics. A total of 48 participants took 
part in our study (29 male, 18 female, 1 other).

3.3.3 Participant Demographics. A total of 48 participants took 
part in our study (29 male, 18 female, 1 other). The age range was 
19 to 30 years old (median = 23, mean = 23.4, sd = 2.8). Majority of 
participants, 68.75% used iOS as their primary platform for TikTok 
usage, 29.17% Android and 2.08% other platforms. Most of the par-
ticipants reported active usage habits: 60.42% of participants used 
TikTok daily (41.67% for at least 1 hour, 18.75% for less than an hour) 
and 27.08% used TikTok on a weekly basis. Only 12.50% of partici-
pants reported using TikTok just a few times a month. Participants 
reported entertainment (83.33%) as the most popular purpose for 
using TikTok, followed by education and information (8.33%), trend 
discovery (4.17%), creativity (2.08%) and social connections (2.08%). 
3.3.4 Procedure. User studies were conducted individually in the 
usability laboratory of our institution. The environment lighting 
and device positioning were adjusted to optimize eye-tracking ac-
curacy per participant [86], with the mount placed on a height-
adjustable table allowing flexible adjustment for calibration. The 
study materials included information sheets, privacy notices, and 
consent forms for each participant. To maintain natural user behav-
ior, participants were not informed about the specific research focus 
(ACDPs) until after completing all tasks. This blind study design 
allowed us to assess ACDP intervention effects without influenc-
ing participant behavior through prior knowledge of the research 
objectives. 
Each session began with participants reviewing study documents 
and signing consent. They were introduced to the TikTok prototype 
and its limitations. Each participant completed four 3-minute tasks 
(conditions A, B, C, and D) in counterbalanced order to eliminate 
order bias. The within-subjects design minimized noise in the data 
as individual participants’ differences affect all conditions [71], en-
abling a robust statistical power at N=48 (meeting the recommenda-
tion of at least 40 data points per condition for quantitative usability 
studies [71, 72]). The 3-minute task duration avoided participant 
fatigue. The pilot studies with longer durations (e.g., 5 minutes) 
revealed difficulties of staying engaged due to non-personalized 
content and the mounted device. The 3-minute duration still al-
lowed participants to encounter and interact with tens of posts 
per session due to short-form nature of the content, providing sub-
stantial data per participant from repeated exposure to ACDPs and 
friction-based interventions to them. 
Before each task, participants adjusted their physical position 
and the eye-tracker was calibrated using a 5-point calibration pro-
cedure according to Tobii specifications [87]. Participants received 
identical instructions for each task: ’Imagine you have just created 
a new, personal TikTok account and want to interact with the ’For 
You’ feed for a few minutes’. This provided appropriate context

3.4 Data Analysis 
3.4.1 Data Pre-Processing. We performed data cleanup across all 
data categories (behavioral engagement, attentional engagement, 
AttrakDiff, and SoAS) based on issues identified during testing and 
data review. Two types of errors led to participant exclusion: (i) 
recording error where task recording was interrupted or failed due 
to system breakdown or human error; (ii) gaze error where Tobii 
eye-tracking gaze accuracy fell below 70%, indicating unreliable 
AOI data. Eye-tracking researchers recommend excluding partici-
pants with gaze samples, i.e., time spent looking at the screen [88], 
below 70% to ensure reliable data quality for screen-based tasks 
[18, 67]. Data from all conditions (A, B, C D) in a data category 
was discarded from a single participant if either error was found 
at least in one condition to preserve the comparability between 
conditions in statistical analysis. This resulted in final sample sizes 
of: behavioral engagement n=46 (2 participants excluded due to 
recording errors), attentional engagement n=38 (10 participants 
excluded due to gaze error), AttrakDiff n=48 (no exclusions), and 
SoAS n=48 (no exclusions). We then analyzed data distributions 
and normality across all metrics in different data categories using 
histograms and Shapiro-Wilk tests. Depending on whether normal-
ity was consistent across all metrics and conditions within a data 
category, we used either raw data or applied data transformations. 
3.4.2 Statistical Tests. All experimental conditions (B, C, D) were 
compared pairwise against the control condition (A) to evaluate 
effects of individual ACDP interventions in isolation. Attentional 
engagement data was normalized using winsorization (1.5 × IQR 
threshold) and Yeo-Johnson transformation, then analyzed using 
paired t-tests with effect sizes reported as Cohen’s d. Behavioral 
engagement, AttrakDiff, and SoAS data could not be normalized 
and therefore we used Wilcoxon signed-rank tests with effect sizes 
reported as r. All tests applied Holm-Bonferroni correction to ac-
count for multiple comparisons (to prevent finding false positives) 
with significance threshold of 𝛼 = 0.05. AttrakDiff was analyzed 
by dimension (ATT, HQ-I, HQ-S, PQ) and SoAS included both indi-
vidual items and sub-scale scores, while behavioral and attentional 
engagement were analyzed per individual metric. 
4 Results 
In this section, we present the most relevant results from our study. 
We analyze the quantitative effects of our friction-based interven-
tions on behavioral and attentional engagement, user experience 
quality, and sense of agency with comprehensive statistical com-
parisons. Additionally, we visualize the distributional differences 
underlying significant changes in Posts Per Session and Video Com-
pletion Rate using kernel density estimate curves that generate a 
smoothed representation of the frequency distribution [42], show-
ing where typical usage patterns are most densely distributed. 
4.1 Disabling Autoplay 
4.1.1 Decreased Automatic Content Repetition. Disabling autoplay 
(Condition B) had a significant impact on participants’ behavioral 
engagement as indicated in Table 5. Median Posts per Session sub-
stantially decreased from 36 (A) to 24 (B), with large effect size (p 
< 0.001***, r = 0.529) describing a consistent shift among partici-
pants as emphasized in distribution density curves between A and 
B (Figure 2). This reduction does indicate that removing autoplay 
promoted more deliberate behavior as scrolling is characterized by 
passive usage of social media [54].

Additionally, disabling autoplay led to more focused attention al-

and other static elements to inform their viewing decisions. 
4.1.2 Reduced User Experience. Disabling autoplay demonstrated 
a trade-off between more controlled engagement and user experi-
ence quality. While participants exhibited more deliberate engage-
ment patterns, as Table 7 shows, they perceived the interface as 
significantly less usable (PQ), attractive (ATT), expressive (HQ-I), 
and stimulating (HQ-S), demonstrating an overall reduced user 
experience consistent among participants with large effect sizes 
(r = 0.554-0.738). Median values for most scales (HQ-I, HQ-S, and 
ATT) fell below neutral (4.0), indicating a negative user experience, 
whereas the control condition showed positive medians across all 
dimensions. Since disabling autoplay significantly interferes with 
the established interaction flow and fundamentally disrupts users’ 
expectations of frictionless content engagement, this reduction in 
user experience measures is anticipated but significant. However, 
we had expected such reductions to manifest as improved agency. 
Contrary to these expectations, we see no significant differences in 
either SoPA or SoNA, and most differences in individual items were 
statistically non-significant as given in Tables 8 and 9. However, 
one specific SoNA item showed significant, consistent improve-
ment across participants: ’My movements are automatic – my body 
simply makes them’, with a decrease of median score from 5.0 (A) 
to 3.0 (B) with large effect size (p = 0.001**, r = 0.514). This suggests 
that while overall agency scores remained unchanged, participants 
did experience reduced automaticity in their interface interactions, 
aligning with our behavioral findings of more deliberate engage-
ment patterns. Figure 7 shows that participants unsurprisingly 
noticed that the autoplay was disabled, and 88% anticipated that 
such intervention would decrease their personal TikTok usage.

4.2.1 High Scroll Error Rates. Increasing scroll friction (Condition 
C) had a similar but more dramatic impact on behavioral engage-

supposed that it would reduce their TikTok usage (Figure 7). 
4.3 Obstructing Social Investments 
4.3.1 Minimal Engagement Changes. We expected to have signifi-
cant results in Interactions per Session and visit metrics in Social AOI, 
as obstructing social investments would make those interactions 
seem less interesting and attention-capturing. However, obstructing 
social investments did not result in significant differences in any of 
the behavioral engagement metrics we measured, as given in Table 
5. These results indicate that the lack of personalized content and 
artificial task setting likely impacted participants’ desire to interact 
with the posts. Moreover, we do not see significant differences in 
attentional engagement in Social AOI. In the Content AOI we do 
have a significant decrease in Number of Visits from 30.3 (A) to 25.7 
(D) with small effect size (p = 0.041*, d = 0.414) and an increase in 
A verage Duration of Visit from 6.34s (A) to 7.20s (D), with small 
effect size (p = 0.047*, d = -0.384), a similar trend that was observed 
in our other interventions as well. The significant changes in Con-
tent AOI attention patterns (fewer but longer visits) suggest that 
while obstructing social investments did not significantly reduce 
attentional engagement in Social AOI, it may have promoted more 
focused content consumption by eliminating visual distractions 
from social metrics. 
4.3.2 Less Attractive Interface. When it comes to AttrakDiff data, 
we do have a reduction in all AttrakDiff qualities, but a significant 
one only in attractiveness (ATT), a decrease from 5.0 (A) to 4.8 (D) 
with medium effect size (p = 0.003**, r = 0.436). Despite the fact that 
engagement data does not reveal differences compared to control, 
this demonstrates that social investments do play a part in making 
the feed engaging and appealing to users. Considering sense of 
agency, we have no major differences in Condition D compared to 
control in either SoPA or SoNA (Tables 8 and 9). Interestingly, as 
given in Table 7, 88% of participants did not notice the absence in-
stant follow button, while 71% noticed the obstructed social metrics. 
This does correlate with the findings of reduced attractiveness as 
social cues can make the content (that occupies most of the TikTok 
feed interface) perceived as more valuable [41, 80, 95]. Approxi-
mately two-thirds of the participants expected that obstructing 
social investments would have no effect on their TikTok usage. 
5 Discussion 
Prior to this study, paucity of quantitative studies have measured 
ACDP intervention effects in SNS applications, particularly in short-
form video interfaces such as TikTok. In this study, we have pro-
vided a holistic and quantitative measurement of friction-based 
interventions on ACDPs in TikTok, revealing multifaceted impacts 
on engagement metrics, user experience and agency. Additionally, 
we have provided a novel investigation on how ACDPs impact 
attentional distribution using eye-tracking device. This section

synthesizes our findings with previous research and connects the 
discussion to our research questions. We discuss how future work 
can build on our methodology and address its limitations. 
5.1 Strategies for ACDP Interventions 
Our findings reveal a crucial distinction between voluntary and 
forced control mechanisms. When we disabled autoplay, behav-
ioral engagement results reflected findings of the Netflix study 
by Schaffner et al. [77]. Despite significant methodological differ-
ences, both studies showed that removing autoplay reduced key 
engagement metrics associated with problematic usage (posts per 
session) while promoting more deliberate decision-making (higher 
video completion rate). However, increasing scroll friction revealed 
a fundamentally different mechanism. While producing similar re-
ductions in behavioral engagement metrics, the high scroll error 
rates imply that these results were caused by interface constraints 
rather than user choice. The results indicate that autoplay removal 
promoted conscious decision-making, as previous research has sug-
gested [53, 77], while scroll friction forced a behavioral change by 
working against users’ natural expectations of the scroll interaction 
rather than representing purely voluntary engagement changes. 
These findings point to two distinct strategies for ACDP inter-
ventions: agency-driven interventions that promote conscious user 
control (e.g., disabled autoplay) and effort-driven interventions that 
add barriers to interactions (e.g., increased scroll friction). Simi-
lar types of distinctions have been identified in digital well-being 
research: Lyngs et al. [55] reviewed digital self-control tools and 
identified mechanisms that, for example, add barriers to actions in 
order to prevent unwanted habits and self-monitoring features that 
support conscious decision making. We applied these strategies to 
the internal mechanisms of damaging patterns that scholars argue 
to be a more effective direction towards better digital well-being 
[53]. Our results demonstrate that internal, targeted interventions 
on specific ACDPs can effectively modify engagement patterns, but 
the strategy matters in user perceptions: mechanical constraints 
may be better tolerated than radical disruptions to familiar interac-
tion patterns, even at the expense of reduced sense of agency. 
Our study also explored a motivation-driven intervention through 
obstructing social investments, which removed the psychological 
rewards that may drive engagement by impacting how content 
is perceived [41, 80, 95], rather than changing the interaction me-
chanics. However, this intervention produced minimal behavioral 
changes with no impact on agency. Similarly, Sun et al. [79] found 
that the number of likes did not meaningfully impact perceptions 
of subjective norms on social media contrary to expectations. How-
ever, we did see a significant reduction in the attractiveness of 
the interface, indicating that social investments serve an aesthetic 
function. Overall, our findings suggest either that social metrics 
are less influential in driving short-term engagement as some, or 
that motivation-based interventions require longer usage periods 
to reveal effects. The latter is supported by Roffarello et al. [62] 
where hiding social investments measurably reduced engagement 
metrics on Facebook. 
Interestingly, this analysis aligns with Behavioral Model of Fogg 
[28] that identifies three intervention points: motivation, ability, and 
triggers.

changes with no impact on agency. Similarly, Sun et al. [79] found 
that the number of likes did not meaningfully impact perceptions 
of subjective norms on social media contrary to expectations. How-

the interface, indicating that social investments serve an aesthetic

are less influential in driving short-term engagement as some, or 
that motivation-based interventions require longer usage periods 
to reveal effects. The latter is supported by Roffarello et al. [62] 
where hiding social investments measurably reduced engagement 
metrics on Facebook. 
Interestingly, this analysis aligns with Behavioral Model of Fogg 
[28] that identifies three intervention points: motivation, ability, and 
triggers. Our interventions align well with this framework: Effort-
driven interventions reduce users’ ability to perform problematic 
behaviors by making actions more demanding (increased scroll 
friction), while agency-driven interventions modify triggers by re-
placing automatic actions with conscious decision points (disabled 
autoplay). Motivation-driven interventions target the psychological 
rewards that drive engagement (obstructed social investments). This 
suggests that our empirical results captured fundamental principles 
through which targeted ACDP or deceptive design interventions 
can operate, providing a foundation for more systematic develop-
ment of design modifications in future digital well-being research. 
5.2 Adaptive and Contextual Friction 
In this study, we utilized microboundaries [23] to apply friction to 
the internal mechanisms of ACDPs in order to investigate whether 
targeted interventions on ACDPs could support user experience, 
agency and more deliberate engagement within the existing inter-
face architecture. This intention was partially successful: the results 
indicate that targeting ACDPs with friction decreases problematic 
engagement patterns, yet we also observed reduced user experience 
quality and a marginal or negative impact on agency. These results 
do not demonstrate that ACDPs themselves are necessary for good 
user experience. Instead, our results suggest that the approach of

using Wilcoxon signed-rank tests (n=48). 
adding significant friction to existing mechanisms created usability 
challenges, which was anticipated since the interface of TikTok 
is fundamentally designed around these ACDPs. Comparably to 
our findings, Ruiz et al. [74] found that their reaction-based inter-
face caused similar user frustration, suggesting that simply adding 
interface friction to established interface architectures inherently 
creates usability issues. Therefore, future research could explore 
alternatives to ACDPs that comprehensively redesign the interface 
for sustainable attention and positive user experience. For instance, 
instead of infinite scrolling, TikTok’s short-form video content 
could be tested with an overhauled interface around alternative 
design patterns, such as pagination [85]. 
Nevertheless, microboundaries and friction-based interventions 
demonstrate potential for mitigating negative engagement patterns, 
providing a straightforward approach to test interventions on ex-
isting interface architectures and advance understanding of how 
attention-capture mechanisms work. As a solution to seemingly 
inherent usability issues of friction-based interventions, Ruiz et al. 
[74] discussed an intermittent approach in which friction would be 
applied at regular intervals (e.g., every 5–10 posts) rather than con-
tinuously in order to balance friction with the experience users’ are 
accustomed to. This balancing approach became evident already 
during our prototype development process, where we carefully 
examined the mechanics and physics of ACDPs in TikTok: they 
are meticulously optimized. As we emphasized in Section 3, the 
required finger movement distance to scroll between videos is neg-
ligible. Moreover, when a new video appears on screen from a 
successful scroll motion, it begins playing before even being fully 
visible. The TikTok feed design effectively exploits habitual move-
ments and limits moments for conscious decision-making. Since 
we explored extreme versions of friction on these mechanisms, this 
reveals a relevant design space where research could test gradu-
ated interventions that apply different intensity levels of the same 
microboundaries and maintain a positive user experience without 
exploiting attention-capturing mechanisms. 
For example, autoplay could introduce brief pauses between 
videos rather than requiring manual interaction, or scroll friction 
could add subtle resistance rather than dramatic movement changes. 
In the study by Roffarello et al. [62], this type of gradual interven-
tion was tested in the social investments of Facebook, where social 
metrics were first hidden, followed by complete removal of reac-
tion buttons. As friction strength increased, passive engagement 
patterns decreased, and users reported more active rather than 
passive usage habits. Moreover, increased scroll friction showed 
signs of fast user adaptation, as the core interaction mechanisms 
remained familiar despite added constraints. To maintain the effec-
tiveness of such friction, interventions could be implemented either 
at unpredictable moments to prevent habituation or triggered when 
the system detects problematic usage patterns, such as prolonged 
engagement sessions or excessive content repetition. 
Machine learning (ML) models could leverage these approaches. 
As Lu et al. [51] noted, ML models could potentially identify de-
ceptive designs and predict consequences of user behavior under 
their influence and generate interface modifications with targeted 
intervention strategies. Such adaptive systems could be integrated 
with user-defined digital well-being goals, allowing individuals to 
set their own usage objectives and customize friction intensity ac-
cordingly. This approach would align intervention strength with 
personal goals while preserving user autonomy over their digital 
experience. Goal-setting mechanisms in digital well-being studies 
have been shown to be effective in motivating users towards better 
habits [35, 68]. Additionally, users have shown different preferences 
for how to mitigate the effects of deceptive designs depending on 
their personal goals or context [51], strengthening the argument of 
exploring adaptive and context-dependent interventions to ACDPs. 
5.3 Implications of Eye-Tracking Findings 
The consistent pattern of deeper attentional engagement in Con-
tent AOI across our ACDP interventions suggests that different 
types of friction affect unconscious engagement in similar ways: 
they make users slow down and focus more on individual videos. 
Whether we changed how videos start (autoplay) or how users 
scroll between them, the end result was the same pattern of more 
concentrated viewing behavior. However, while our eye-tracking 
results revealed statistically significant changes, the reductions in 
visit frequency and increases in visit duration to the content were

The eye-tracking data from this study provided an important

especially as behavioral logging scales more easily to field studies 
than eye-tracking devices. However, given the small shift towards 
more focused attention in Content AOIs observed in our laboratory 
setting, ACDP interventions may require longitudinal study designs 
to show meaningful cumulative impacts on attention. There is evi-
dence that the front-facing camera systems in modern smartphones 
have potentially accurate eye-tracking capabilities [82, 91], reveal-
ing a future possibility of also exploring attentional engagement in 
cost-effective and large-scale long-term studies. 
In laboratory conditions, eye-tracking may be more valuable for 
task-based deceptive design research where specific attention distri-
bution in choice selection or sequential interactions matter, rather 
than for open-ended content consumption scenarios.

text:
The more pronounced effects on behavioral 
engagement indicate that usage metrics offer more practical mea-
sures for ACDP interventions than attentional engagement metrics, 
especially as behavioral logging scales more easily to field studies 
than eye-tracking devices. However, given the small shift towards 
more focused attention in Content AOIs observed in our laboratory 
setting, ACDP interventions may require longitudinal study designs 
to show meaningful cumulative impacts on attention. There is evi-
dence that the front-facing camera systems in modern smartphones 
have potentially accurate eye-tracking capabilities [82, 91], reveal-
ing a future possibility of also exploring attentional engagement in 
cost-effective and large-scale long-term studies. 
In laboratory conditions, eye-tracking may be more valuable for 
task-based deceptive design research where specific attention distri-
bution in choice selection or sequential interactions matter, rather 
than for open-ended content consumption scenarios. ACDPs manip-
ulate core system functionality, for example, by making expected 
system functionality excessively effortless compared to traditional 
deceptive designs that often manipulate choice architectures [62] 
to govern users’ decision making [61]. In TikTok, we also detected 
use of deceptive patterns, such as confirmshaming and decision 
uncertainty [61], during our auto-ethnography to identify ACDPs. 
Eye-tracking could be employed, for example, to assess attention 
order or allocation in deceptive strategies related to the registration 
privacy processes. 
Beyond evaluating intervention effectiveness, our findings of 
attentional shifts suggest the potential of utilizing eye-tracking as 
a direct measure of automatic focus in short-form video interfaces 
to identify problematic usage. More specifically, future research 
could explore whether eye-tracking metrics correlate with disso-
ciative states that are linked to compulsive social media usage [3]. 
Regarding ML-based intervention approaches discussed in Section 
5.2, attentional engagement metrics could be utilized as triggers of 
problematic engagement to deliver adaptive friction to ACDPs. For 
example, less frequent but sustained high-duration visits to content 
area combined with low visits to other areas of the interface could 
be an early signal of intense content absorption, triggering the 
system to introduce friction that prompts self-awareness. 
5.4 From Trade-Offs to Collaborative Solutions 
Our exploratory intervention approaches support the findings from 
previous work that prevalent ACDPs promote excessively engaging 
experiences by eliminating barriers and automating interactions 
[62, 63, 74], since adding friction to these mechanisms reduced 
compulsive engagement patterns. However, friction-based inter-
ventions on ACDPs predictably caused a substantial decrease in 
all AttrakDiff qualities. Directly modifying existing ACDPs illus-
trates a fundamental challenge: adding friction to harmful patterns 
may improve user well-being but this approach also degrades the 
engagement metrics and user experience that platforms strive to 

[Page 15]
Effects of Adding Friction to Attention-Capture Patterns in TikTok CHI ’26, April 13–17, 2026, Barcelona, Spain 
Figure 7: Participant awareness and anticipated usage effects for each ACDP intervention measured in the end questionnaire. 
For clarity, social investments (condition D) were assessed separately for the instant follow button and social metrics. 
optimize. Moreover, the consequences of friction-based interven-
tions for agency are not straightforward either. Despite causing 
more user errors, increased scroll friction produced a better user 
experience than autoplay removal, yet users felt less in control 
of the interface. This suggests that after the initial learning curve 
of increased friction, users prefer interactions that resemble their 
expectations over radical changes to interactions, such as disabling 
autoplay. However, users may quickly become habituated to the 
new movement and its effect may fade away, as Anderson et al. [2] 
noted to occur for efficiency of security warnings in their brain-
imaging study. 
These mixed outcomes demonstrate why quantitative evaluation 
is essential for understanding ACDPs. Subjective assessments and 
expert analysis alone cannot capture the complex trade-offs be-
tween user experience and well-being that emerge in practice. Our 
work addresses this gap and builds on the ideas of previous stud-
ies [62, 63], which argue that systematic design experiments and 
audits on ACDP effects that utilize both usage data and validated 
psychological measures should become fundamental components 
of technology design processes to assess negative influences on 
users. Yet, current research faces a key limitation: as shown by 
our need to build a high-fidelity TikTok iOS prototype to employ 
behavioral measures, scholars lack direct access especially to the 
mobile platforms where these patterns are most effective. Although 
many third-party digital well-being interventions exist [55], they 
generally do not target the internal design mechanisms, and the 
developers of these digital well-being tools and regulation lag be-
hind the rapid introduction of new features and technologies [53]. 
Moreover, users have shown preferences for non-intrusive solu-
tions to deceptive design interventions, which do not interrupt 
normal experiences [51]. While SNS platforms employ safety fea-
tures for users, for instance, to manage their content preferences, 
the features are usually limited in enabling users to customize key 
experiences and designs of a platform [14]. 
While our experimental results represent initial user responses 
to friction-based ACDP interventions and remain preliminary in 
scope, they strengthen the argument that ACDPs and internal plat-
form design mechanisms may have harmful implications for users 
and reveal that friction-based intervention approaches may have 
consequences to product quality. However, such short-term costs 
on engagement and business profits may increase user loyalty in 
the long term [62]. Taking breaks from online services such as so-
cial media for well-being purposes has recently gained popularity 
[81], but early research suggests that benefits and drawbacks of 
abstinence may cancel each other out [48]. Such implications do not 
benefit either users or business objectives of platforms. As social 
networks are deeply integrated into the modern society, our study 
highlights the need for further research into solutions that inter-
nally redesign these platforms to benefit the collective. The path 
forward requires direct collaboration between stakeholders (i.e., 
academia, legislation, companies and users) to deploy quantitative 
measures in the same manner to ours at scale in native platforms 
and transparent longitudinal study designs, as well as exploring 
various approaches to mitigate the effects of harmful interfaces. We 
have seen some reports of such internal A/B testing, with alleged 
experiments by Facebook removing ’Like’ buttons that reportedly 
caused anxiety among users [37]. However, the widespread impli-
cations of such tests on platform design are unclear to the public. 
Lu et al. [51] suggest that transparent design practices and infor-
mation sharing could also be mandated by policy makers, and we 
argue that a collaborative model is necessary in order to propose 
sustainable solutions that balance stakeholders’ interests through 
empirical, evidence-based design decisions. 
5.5 Summary of Findings 
RQ1: How does adding friction to ACDPs influence behav-
ioral engagement in TikTok? Both disabling autoplay and in-
creasing scroll friction reduced the number of posts participants 
viewed during sessions. Both interventions also increased video 

[Page 16]
CHI ’26, April 13–17, 2026, Barcelona, Spain Alin, Eck & Suoranta 
Figure 8: Perceived resemblance between experimental prototype (control condition A) and native TikTok application. 
completion rates. Furthermore, disabling autoplay prevented repet-
itive video watching, while increased scroll friction substantially in-
creased it. Disabling autoplay enforced conscious decision-making, 
while increased scroll friction forced behavioral changes. 
RQ2: How does adding friction to ACDPs influence atten-
tional engagement in TikTok? Overall, participants focused their 
attention more on the Content AOI, as all interventions reduced 
attentional shifts between key areas of the interface. 
RQ3: How does adding friction to ACDPs influence the user 
experience quality in TikTok? Disabling autoplay and increas-
ing scroll friction significantly reduced the user experience quality. 
Interestingly, scroll friction had better AttrakDiff scores despite 
high error rates in scroll gestures, indicating that participants pre-
ferred interventions that function according to original interaction 
patterns. Obstructing social investments reduced the overall appeal 
of the interface. 
RQ4: 
How does adding friction to ACDPs influence users’ 
sense of agency in TikTok? Although participants preferred 
increased scroll friction over disabled autoplay, it significantly re-
duced their sense of positive agency. Removing autoplay made 
participants feel that their interactions were less automatic.

RQ3: How does adding friction to ACDPs influence the user 
experience quality in TikTok? Disabling autoplay and increas-

Interestingly, scroll friction had better AttrakDiff scores despite 
high error rates in scroll gestures, indicating that participants pre-
ferred interventions that function according to original interaction 
patterns. Obstructing social investments reduced the overall appeal 
of the interface. 
RQ4: 
How does adding friction to ACDPs influence users’ 
sense of agency in TikTok? Although participants preferred 
increased scroll friction over disabled autoplay, it significantly re-
duced their sense of positive agency. Removing autoplay made 
participants feel that their interactions were less automatic. 
5.6 Limitations 
Our experimental design prioritized internal validity through con-
trolled, time-limited sessions using a high-fidelity prototype with 
standardized content across conditions. However, the controlled 
nature of our study, while essential for providing initial user re-
sponses to ACDP interventions to internal mechanisms in TikTok, 
introduces several limitations that constrain the generalization of 
our findings to real-world usage contexts. 
Our participant pool (N=48) consisted of young adults recruited 
from our institution’s premises and communication channels, with 
demographics limited to a specific age group and primarily active 
TikTok users. The lack of broader demographics and the relatively 
small participant pool restrict generalization to other populations 
and user groups. Moreover, while 68.75% of participants were iOS 
and 29.17% Android users, our prototype was developed only for 
iOS, which may limit transferability of findings across platforms, as 
they may have different interaction behaviors and optimizations. 
While our high-fidelity prototype closely replicated the user in-
terface of TikTok, several implementation differences may have 
affected the ecological validity. For example, some social network 
features required simplified alternatives. More significantly, our 
study used scraped content rather than participants’ personalized 
feeds and was conducted in controlled laboratory sessions rather 
than natural usage contexts. This limitation is reflected in our end 
questionnaire results: while the prototype was perceived to closely 
match real TikTok (control condition resemblance to TikTok was on 
average rated 6.13/7 on 7-point Likert scale, as shown in Figure 8), 
users found only 42.87% of the content hashtags interesting on av-
erage. The lack of personalized content and artificial task scenario 
(described in Section 3.3.4) might significantly affect their content 
watching behavior. Moreover, attentional engagement analysis re-
lied on a Tobii Pro Spark mounted to an iPhone 12, requiring fixed 
positioning and recalibration before each session. This setup con-
strained natural device handling, potentially influencing attentional 
patterns compared to typical handheld use. 
Some of our interventions, particularly disabling autoplay, were 
dramatic changes on the normal TikTok experience. These changes 
likely disrupted users’ mental models of how the interface should 
work, and research has shown that they can slow user behavior and 
increase errors [15, 34, 64]. Given our three-minute session length, 
the observed effects on behavioral and attentional engagement may 
be reflected both in the intended ACDP intervention and users’ 
initial struggles with unfamiliar interface behaviors, as the task 
duration may have been too short for users to adapt to the ACDP 
interventions. Adding friction to ACDPs within an architecture 
designed around seamless interaction of native ACDP mechanisms 
inherently risks UX degradation. Our findings therefore address 
friction-based interventions specifically and not whether ACDPs 
themselves impact user experience. Assessing that would require 
experimental conditions exploring alternative design patterns, not 
modifications to existing mechanisms. Moreover, the three-minute 
task exposure time and frequent interruptions for questionnaire 
completion may have somewhat limited users’ ability to achieve 
dissociative states that ACDPs can induce during normal use, po-
tentially influencing subjective measures (AttrakDiff, SoAS) across 
conditions. However, pilot studies on longer sessions reported fa-
tigue due to lack of personalized content in our prototype and 
unnatural device usage position. 
Future research should explore study settings that enable longer 
task durations without participant fatigue to better capture dis-
sociative states, enhancing user adaptation to interventions. Our 
study suggests this requires utilizing participants’ personalized con-
tent in experimental systems and conducting field studies beyond 
controlled laboratory environments. 
6 Conclusions 
We presented a novel, quantitative study measuring objective be-
havioral and eye-tracking data alongside AttrakDiff and SoAS ques-
tionnaires to examine the holistic effects of friction-based inter-
ventions on ACDPs in TikTok. Overall, we found that disabling 
autoplay and increasing scroll friction reduced engagement metrics 
associated with problematic usage and promoted more deliberate 
behavior. Disabling autoplay appeared to achieve these effects by 

[Page 17]
Effects of Adding Friction to Attention-Capture Patterns in TikTok CHI ’26, April 13–17, 2026, Barcelona, Spain 
enforcing conscious decision-making, while increasing scroll fric-
tion seemed to force behavioral change. These added frictions on 
existing ACDPs decreased the user experience quality although 
increasing scroll friction showed signs of better user adaptation. 
Neither intervention improved users’ sense of agency. Obstructing 
social investments significantly reduced the attractiveness of the 
interface, demonstrating that displaying social metrics does make 
the feed more appealing to users. Across all ACDP interventions, 
eye-tracking data revealed fewer but longer visits to the content 
area, suggesting more focused content engagement. 
This paper significantly enriches the discussion about the impact 
of interventions on attention-capture mechanisms in SNSs with 
quantitative behavioral and physiological evidence. More specifi-
cally, our results provide concrete support for claims that ACDPs 
have potentially negative consequences for users. Our findings also 
demonstrated the implications that friction-based interventions on 
existing ACDPs can have for user experience quality, reflecting the 
inherent usability issues caused by disrupting foundational designs 
of a prevalent interface architecture. This highlights the importance 
of objective data measures. Additionally, the high-fidelity proto-
type with behavioral data collection illustrates the current gap in 
analytical capabilities between platform designers and independent 
researchers. 
In pursuit of more ethical platform designs, we suggest future 
research explore gradual interventions to attention-capture pat-
terns as well interfaces that propose alternative design patterns to 
ACDPs in order to better balance the trade-offs between engage-
ment, user experience, and sense of agency. Moreover, exploring 
ML solutions for adaptive intervention based on behavioral and 
attentional metrics may enable more personalized interfaces that 
support digital well-being while accounting for individual user pref-
erences and goals. Ultimately, our holistic methodological approach 
calls for more transparent collaboration between stakeholders (i.e., 
researchers, companies, and users) to employ similar measures in 
larger-scale, longitudinal field studies within actual applications, 
extending beyond the limitations of short-duration laboratory ex-
periments.

REVIEW OPEN ACCESS
Color as A Narrative Device in Illustration: 
A Systematic Review
Lidia Jiménez-Duarte 1 |  María-José Terrón-López 2  |  Guillermo Castilla-Cebrián 3
1Faculty of Design and Creative Technologies, Universidad Europea de Madrid, Villaviciosa de Odón, Madrid, Spain | 2Polytechnic 
School, Universidad Europea de Andalucía, Málaga, Spain | 3School of Architecture, Engineering, Science and Computing – STEAM, 
Universidad Europea de Madrid, Villaviciosa de Odón, Madrid, Spain
Correspondence:  María- José Terrón- López (m_jose.terron@universidadeuropea.es )
Received:  4 April 2025 | Revised:  17 November 2025 | Accepted:  15 January 2026
Keywords: children's illustration | cognitive perception in illustration | color | color psychology | visual narrative
ABSTRACT
Picture books are a central medium through which children learn to interpret stories, emotions, and symbols, yet the role of 
color in these narratives remains underexplored and theoretically fragmented. This systematic review investigates how color 
in picture book illustrations has been reported to influence or appear to contribute to children's narrative comprehension and 
cognitive development, addressing persistent gaps in methodology and theory. Following PRISMA guidelines, four databases 
were systematically searched (2000–October 2024), identifying 78 eligible studies from an initial pool of 717 records. Studies 
were thematically categorized into four domains: the impact of color on emotional perception, cognitive processing and recog -
nition, narrative function in storytelling, and experimental applications. Across these domains, findings demonstrate that color 
functions simultaneously as a representational code, a cognitive scaffold, and an affective cue—shaping emotional engagement, 
guiding attention and memory, structuring narrative coherence, and enabling transfer of learning in experimental contexts. This 
review demonstrates that color in picture book illustration is not a decorative feature but a multimodal narrative device that mod-
ulates emotional tone, scaffolds cognitive processing, and structures story coherence, supporting theories such as Dual Coding 
and multimodal discourse. While evidence confirms systematic links between color choices, comprehension, and engagement, 
significant gaps remain, particularly the lack of longitudinal and cross-  cultural studies, the absence of a unified terminology, 
and limited integration across disciplines. The review concludes with a call for interdisciplinary, technologically informed, and 
developmentally sensitive research to advance a comprehensive theoretical model of color in visual storytelling.
1   |   Introduction
In the field of visual communication, picture books have be -
come a fundamental narrative tool for conveying meaning and 
emotions. Through the interaction between image and text, this 
literary format has evolved into a key medium for fostering vi -
sual literacy and cognitive development in children.
The origins of the picture book can be traced to early visual 
publications aimed at children. From the 17th century, with 
Comenius's [ 1]—considered the first visual encyclopedia for 
children—to 19th-  century works such as Heinrich Hoffmann's 
[2] and Beatrix Potter's The Tale of Peter Rabbit [ 3], images 
have played a crucial role in reinforcing learning and textual 
comprehension. However, in these early picture books, color 
was a secondary feature due to technological limitations in 
printing and the prioritization of the educational function of 
images. The Industrial Revolution and advancements in color 
printing techniques transformed picture books in children's 
literature. These developments allowed color to be strategically 
employed to enhance expressiveness and visual storytelling.

influenced picture book design in the late 19th and early 20th

metadata.core_insight_en: This systematic review, adhering to PRISMA guidelines, examines the impact of color usage in children's illustration on narrative comprehension and cognitive development, synthesizing findings from 78 studies published between 2000 and October 2024 to address theoretical gaps in color psychology within visual storytelling for young audiences.

conveying emotions and narrative atmospheres. By the mid-  
20th century, artists such as Maurice Sendak (Where the 
Wild Things Are, 1963) [ 4] and Eric Carle (The Very Hungry 
Caterpillar, 1969) [ 5] revolutionized children's illustration by 
integrating color intentionally into the narrative structure and 
employing chromatic contrasts to elicit specific emotional re -
sponses from readers.
Although color has long been recognized as a key expressive and 
symbolic component in picturebook illustration, its role as a nar-
rative mechanism remains insufficiently systematized in terms 
of its cognitive and emotional impact on readers [ 6–8]. Recent 
studies have explored how color guides perception and emotion; 
yet they also highlight the lack of a unified theoretical frame -
work integrating these dimensions [9, 10].
Therefore, it is essential to examine how color in illustration 
not only complements text but also may function as a visual 
language that contributes to structuring story sequences and 
influencing the reading experience [ 9] and potentially evoking 
an emotional response [10]. Color serves not only as an aesthetic 
element but also as a narrative device that appears to structure 
visual discourse, guide the reader's attention, and evoke specific 
emotional responses [ 7, 10, 11]. Empirical observations suggest 
that young readers intuitively respond to chromatic contrasts 
and palette shifts that signal mood and narrative transitions.
Existing analyses of color in illustration remain fragmented 
across visual narrative research, with limited attempts to con -
solidate its cognitive, emotional, and symbolic roles into an 
integrated framework [ 6, 8]. These studies underscore the im -
portance of color in meaning-  making while also pointing to the 
theoretical dispersion within the field.
Although research has explored color's influence on perception, 
emotion, and the structuring of visual narrative, recent analyses 
indicate that theoretical and methodological gaps persist, lim -
iting a comprehensive understanding of its narrative function 
[7, 11, 12 ]. These findings reinforce the need for a systematic 
synthesis of how color operates as a narrative mechanism in 
picturebooks.
This systematic review compiles and analyzes key studies on the 
topic, aiming to find a theoretical framework that deepens our 
understanding of the role of color in visual storytelling and its 
influence on the reading experience.
1.1   |   Rationale and Objectives
Numerous studies have examined the role of color in illustra -
tion from diverse perspectives. Simcock and DeLoache [ 13] an-
alyzed how the iconicity of images, including the presence of 
color, influences children's ability to imitate actions observed in 
picture books. Their findings indicate that children retain in -
formation more effectively from realistic and vibrantly colored 
illustrations than from monochromatic or schematic images. 
Similarly, Bergman Deitcher et al. [ 14] demonstrated that visual 
complexity, including color usage, affects parent–child interac -
tions during shared reading, influencing attention levels and 
narrative construction.
From a semiotic perspective, Lakizenko and Makarova [ 9] 
argue that color in illustration serves not only as an aesthetic 
element but also as a visual code that guides reader interpreta -
tion. Their analysis of early childhood picture books identified 
chromatic patterns associated with different emotions and nar -
rative structures, concluding that color palettes can modulate a 
story's reception and emotional impact. Additionally, Acer and 
Gözen [10] examined how preschoolers analyze and reinterpret 
colors in their own visual compositions, finding that children 
not only recognize the emotional function of color but also em -
ploy it strategically to enhance their graphic narratives.
Recent studies have expanded on these perspectives by linking 
color to childhood perception psychology. Sheibani Rezvani 
and Bakhtiarian [ 15] propose that the use of contrasting and 
saturated colors in picture books can facilitate young children's 
comprehension of abstract concepts, enhancing their ability to 
connect visual and narrative elements. Furthermore, research 
in cognitive neuroscience suggests that repeated exposure to 
specific color combinations in illustrations strengthens visual 
memory and semantic learning in early childhood [ 13].
Despite these contributions, the systematization of color as a 
narrative mechanism in children's illustration requires fur -
ther exploration. While studies have examined its impact on 
perception and emotion, the lack of clear categorization and 
longitudinal research presents challenges to develop a unified 
theoretical model.
To address this gap, a systematic review is proposed. This ap -
proach consolidates existing knowledge in a specific field of 
study and provides a rigorous basis for analyzing trends, ap -
proaches, and gaps in research. It should be noted that the scope 
of this review is not to establish causal relationships, but rather 
to synthesize and systematize the evidence available in the lit -
erature. By mapping methodological designs, populations stud -
ied, and reported outcomes, this work provides a comprehensive 
overview of how color has been examined in picture book re -
search and where future experimental studies may address 
causal questions more directly.
Accordingly, this study seeks to answer the following research 
question:
In what ways has color in picture book illustration 
been reported to shape children's narrative 
comprehension and cognitive development?
Through this analysis, the aim is to contribute to the develop -
ment of a theoretical framework that will allow us to understand 
the role of color in illustration and its narrative potential in chil-
dren's and young adults' literature.
2   |   Methodology
To ensure transparency and rigor in the collection, analysis, and 
synthesis of existing literature, this systematic review follows 
the PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews 
and Meta-  Analyses) protocol [ 16, 17 ]. This methodological 
framework comprises the following steps:

Despite growing research, a comprehensive theoretical framework integrating color's cognitive and emotional impacts remains lacking, underscoring the need for further systematic examination.

1. Defining the rationale for the review and explicitly formu -
lating the research question.
2. Establishing eligibility criteria and identifying relevant in -
formation sources
3. Defining the search strategy and outlining the study selec -
tion process.
4. Describing the methods for data collection, desired out -
comes and procedures for assessing risk of bias.
5. Reporting findings with a detailed description of the re -
view process.
Building on the objectives outlined above, this section details 
the methodological approach used to identify and analyze stud -
ies on color as a narrative mechanism in picture books.
2.1   |   Developing the Search Strategy
Our review was designed to answer our research question, which 
provided the search and inclusion criteria in the databases.
1. Studies analyzing the use of color in illustration within 
formats such as picture books, comics, animation, and 
graphic design will be included, excluding those that 
study color in photography or art in general, as these 
approaches do not focus on visual storytelling through 
illustration.
2. All studies must be framed within the context of color 
psychology and illustration, excluding those that ap -
proach color from perspectives unrelated to visual sto -
rytelling, such as skin color, ethnic, ideological, gender, 
or identity aspects, or their use for political, economic, 
scientific, or educational purposes unrelated to narrative 
construction.
3. Research studies that address color as a narrative element 
in the construction of stories within visual narrative will 
be selected. Studies that analyze color solely from a tech -
nical, psychological, or perceptual perspective unrelated to 
visual storytelling will be excluded.
4. Only research developed in the context of picture books or 
children's books will be considered, paying special atten -
tion to their role in visual storytelling, prioritizing research 
that examines color as an expressive, meaning-  bearing, 
or structural resource in the construction of narrative. 
Studies that do not include a specific analysis of color in its 
narrative function will be discarded.
5. Studies in English and Spanish will be prioritized. However, 
publications in other languages will be considered if they 
have abstracts translated into English or Spanish that 
allow for their analysis and inclusion in the review. Studies 
in other languages that do not have abstracts accessible in 
English or Spanish will be excluded.
No specific time period was established for the search, as the 
goal is to understand how the relationship between color and vi-
sual narrative has been worked on throughout history. However, 
the use of the picture book itself will situate the studies within 
a specific period. Still, in order to offer a review of the develop -
ment of this field throughout the 21st century, the search covers 
the period from 2000 to the present (October 2024), as studies 
prior to this period were limited to the color options available 
at each era, without a systematic analysis of color as a narra -
tive tool.
Table  1 summarizes the inclusion and exclusion criteria used in 
this review, which aim to ensure the homogeneity of the studies 
analyzed.
A scoping review was conducted to test preliminary sets of 
databases and search terms. This review also examined 
the breadth of literature on the use of color in picture book 
narratives.
During the review, to ensure the coverage and relevance 
of the  reviewed literature, the search terms and selected 
 databases were iteratively refined to eliminate sources that 
did  not meet  the inclusion criteria. Four databases were se -
lected for their relevance and international coverage in dis -
ciplines related to illustration, visual narrative, and graphic 
design, as well as for their ability to export data in CSV format 
to facilitate subsequent analysis: Web of Science, Academic 
Search Ultimate, PubMed, and SCOPUS. The search in -
cluded journal articles, book chapters, conference papers, and 
reviews.
The only language restriction applied at this point was that the 
title and abstract of the articles had to be in English, given the 
search terms used. However, no additional filter restrictions 
were applied in the filters. In addition, the possibility of using 
the snowball technique in the citation search was considered, 
reviewing references from key articles to expand the database 
of relevant studies. However, after evaluating the initial results 
obtained from the search, it was determined that the number of 
selected studies was sufficient to address the review objectives, 
so this strategy was not applied further.
2.2   |   Analysis and Filtering
Different searches were performed to define the final key -
words. Sets of Boolean operators were also determined to pro -
vide the most accurate and relevant results for analysis. The 
search was conducted from January 2000 to October 2024. 
The keywords, Boolean operators, and blocks related to the 
research question can be found in Appendix  A (Table  A1). 
An asterisk “*” was used to allow the search engine to in -
clude derivatives of the root word, such as “illustration” and 
“illustrated.”
The search strategy included the use of keywords in English, 
combining terms such as: [“color” OR “color” AND “narrative” 
AND “illustration”], [“color psychology” OR “color psychology” 
AND “illustration” NOT “skin”], [“illustration” AND “color OR 
colour” AND “picture books OR children's literature OR chil -
dren's books” AND “narrative”], among others. To refine the 
results, the exclusion filters were applied, eliminating studies 
outside the narrative context or with a purely technical focus 
without application in illustration.

The criteria strictly focus on color psychology within illustrative contexts to ensure relevance to narrative mechanisms in visual storytelling.
