This methodological process ensured that the selection of stud -
ies was rigorous and representative, providing a solid basis for 
analyzing the role of color in visual storytelling within illustra -
tion in picture books.
The initial search yielded 111 results in Web of Science, 225 in 
SCOPUS, 126 in Academic Search Ultimate, and 255 in PubMed, 
yielding a total of 717 articles. After merging the four sets and 
eliminating duplicates, the operational set included 307 studies, 
distributed as follows: 216 journal articles, 39 book chapters, 35 
conference papers, and 17 reviews.
The results were categorized and filtered according to the crite -
ria established in the research. Articles that did not focus on il -
lustration and its relationship to visual narrative were excluded. 
Studies that addressed color solely from a political, ideological, 
or economic perspective unrelated to narrative construction 
were also discarded.
Thirty-  seven studies were eliminated because their focus was 
linked to skin color, ethnic aspects, or ideological analyses with-
out a connection to the narrative function of color in illustration. 
Of the remaining 270 articles, 26 were discarded for focusing on 
the use of color for political, economic, scientific, or educational 
purposes without relation to the construction of stories in pic -
ture books.
In addition, 159 articles were eliminated because they described 
illustration in contexts not relevant to the study, such as photog-
raphy, visual arts, or film. Finally, seven reviews were excluded 
because their content did not explicitly consider the use of color 
as a narrative resource in illustration.
After this filtering process, the final number of selected studies 
was 78, distributed as follows: 55 journal articles, nine confer -
ence papers or presentations, 10 book chapters, and four reviews 
that analyzed the evolution of the use of color in illustrated 
narrative.
The analysis of the selected articles showed that the studies 
could be grouped into different thematic categories based on 
their focus on the role of color in illustration. Each reviewer 
independently assessed the studies, identifying recurring pat -
terns and research approaches. A final categorization was 
then established through a consensus process, ensuring that 
the classifications accurately represented the main objectives 
of each study.
The categorization process was carried out by three reviewers. 
During the consensus meeting, the three researchers deter -
mined the categories that best aligned with the research ques -
tion. One category dominated all others and was applied in the 
categorization. Therefore, the chosen categorization, agreed 
upon by the three reviewers involved in the process, was consid-
ered appropriate and relevant for a systematic understanding of 
the role of color in narrative illustration. The selected categories 
were as follows:
1. Impact of color on emotional perception within illustration.
2. Cognitive image processing and color recognition

Through meticulous categorization and exclusion criteria, the research ensured a focused analysis on how color functions specifically within the context of constructing visual narratives in children's illustrated literature.

3. Narrative function of color and its role in visual storytelling.
4. Experimental studies on color and its application in picture 
books.
This organization provided a structured approach for analyzing 
the different ways in which color contributes to storytelling, vi -
sual perception, and cognitive engagement in illustrated works. 
The results were divided into the following categories: 27 on the 
impact of color on emotional perception within illustration, 17 on 
the cognitive process of image analysis, 13 on narrative and its re-
lationship to color, and 22 experimental developments of studies 
involving color and picture books. The flowchart of the search and 
filtering process can be found in Appendix B, Figure  B1.
A detailed list of the 78 included studies, organized by the -
matic category and summarizing their methodological features 
and findings, is provided in Appendix  C (Tables  C1–C4). This 
Supporting Information allows readers to trace how specific study 
designs, participant characteristics, and approaches to color oper-
ationalization informed the synthesis of results. For transparency, 
we classified the risk of bias according to study type: theoretical 
and descriptive works were considered at moderate risk, as they 
provide conceptual insights without empirical validation; qualita-
tive observational studies were rated as moderate to high risk de-
pending on sampling and reporting practices; and experimental or 
quasi- experimental designs were generally rated as low risk when 
control groups and sufficient sample sizes were present. This stan-
dardized approach ensured consistency in assessing the reliability 
of evidence across heterogeneous study designs.
2.3   |   Publication Demographics
The publication year of included articles in relation to the type 
of article is shown in Figure  1. The distribution of publications 
over the years served to map the evolution of selected studies on 
color as a narrative mechanism in illustration. Six of the studies 
analyzed were published before 2010, reflecting an initial stage 
of research in this field. Between 2010 and 2015, five additional 
publications were added, indicating a moderate growth in the 
exploration of the topic.
Starting in 2016, the number of studies increased significantly, 
with five publications that year. This was followed by a progres -
sive rise: 7 in 2017, 3 in 2018, and 9 in 2019. The peak of academic 
production occurred in 2019, with a total of 9 publications, fol -
lowed by 8 in 2022. In recent years, the number of publications 
has shown a slight decrease, with 5 studies in 2024, reflecting a 
possible stabilization in research production on this topic. This 
distribution indicates that the study of color in illustration has 
gained relevance in recent years, with notable growth from 2016 
onward, peaking in 2022, and continuing to be a topic of active 
interest in academic research.
In terms of publication sources, the reviewed studies come from 
a combination of peer- reviewed journals.
In addition, studies published in conferences and symposia spe -
cializing in visual communication, early childhood education, 
and cognitive psychology were found, reflecting the interdisci -
plinary nature of the topic.
Most of the studies analyzed were published in English, which 
is consistent with the search criteria used. However, two arti -
cles were identified with titles and abstracts in English but 
with bodies in Spanish, as well as one with sections in Russian, 
demonstrating the global interest in the intersection of color, il -
lustration, and narrative in children's literature.
2.4   |   Thematic Coding and Validation Process
To contribute to the development of a theoretical framework for 
understanding the role of color in illustration and its narrative 
potential in children's and young adults' literature, the three 
researchers initiated discussions on the initial themes. Any 
discrepancies were addressed, and the eligibility criteria were 
clarified to guide the coding of the selected articles during the 
analysis process.
The validation process for the analysis was as follows: the se -
lected articles were read multiple times and individually coded 
by the three researchers, incorporating their independent

reflections. The articles were evaluated based on the eligibil -
ity criteria at three levels: title, abstract, and full text. During 
research group meetings, triangulation was used to establish 
an initial consensus on the coding. The initial themes and 
codes underwent two rounds of modification and refinement 
through group discussions. Four of the final 78 articles were 
reclassified into different categories. For example, one article 
was reclassified from impact to narrative, and another from 
impact to cognitive.
To enhance coder reliability, a researcher with qualitative re -
search experience but unfamiliar with this specific study was 
invited to independently code eight articles using the established 
codebook. Following this step, a subsequent discussion led to 
further refinement of the coding results. Any remaining dis -
crepancies between the researchers were thoroughly discussed 
until a common consensus was reached across all codes. Finally, 
an intentional sample of 78 articles was provided to a second re -
searcher experienced in qualitative research, along with the list 
of codes and their definitions, to refine the categorization within 
the established categories.
The reviewed studies employed a wide range of methodological 
approaches, from physiological recordings (e.g., EEG) to self- 
reported or interpretive assessments. Because the data reported 
by the original authors are heterogeneous, the present review 
limits itself to describing the type of analysis as provided in each 
source. Consequently, no assumptions have been made about 
sampling strategies or measurement procedures beyond what is 
explicitly stated in the reviewed publications.
3   |   Results
This section presents the analysis of the selected articles and 
their distribution across four main categories related to the use 
of color as a narrative mechanism in illustration. Given that 
the reviewed studies vary widely in methodology and scope, all 
references to color's “effects” are to be interpreted as reported 
associations or inferred relationships, rather than evidence of 
direct causality. The classification was conducted through a re -
view process in which each researcher independently evaluated 
the studies, identifying recurring patterns in their approaches 
and objectives. Subsequently, through reviewer consensus, 
four main groupings were defined to organize the findings: the 
impact of color on emotional perception within illustration (27 
studies), cognitive image processing and color recognition (17 
studies), the narrative function of color and its role in visual 
storytelling (13 studies), and experimental studies on color and 
its application in picture books (22 studies). The distribution of 
studies in each category is illustrated in Figure  2 and detailed 
tables with the total number of articles, their findings and their 
references can be found in Appendix  C.
3.1   |   Impact of Color on Emotional Perception in 
Illustration
This category includes studies that analyze how color influences 
the evocation of emotions and the affective interpretation of illus-
trations. Twenty- seven studies were identified within this classifi-
cation (Table  C1 in the Appendix  C), all of which highlight color 
as a visual and semantic code that shapes the reader's emotional 
engagement and interpretative processes. For example, Abacı 
[18] examined the use of illustration style and color harmony in 
Turkish picture books, finding that unbalanced palettes reduced 
educational suitability, while Albayrak [19] showed how legibility 
and contrast in book covers directly affected children's percep -
tion and accessibility. Historical analyses, such as Anderson [20] 
and Jackson [21], revealed how colorization practices in scientific 
and zoological illustrations expanded audiences and conveyed 
affective responses of curiosity and wonder, based on qualitative 
archival reviews of 18th–19th century colored plates and docu -
mentation of printing techniques.
Other contributions focused on the meaning- bearing dimension 
of color in narratives. Gubaidullina [ 22] demonstrated how cold 
blue hues and warm sepia tones structured the affective oppo -
sition between hostile and familiar spaces in The Snow Queen, 
through semiotic analysis of chromatic motifs across multiple 
illustrated editions. Hernández Contreras [ 23] and Hernández 
and Aya [24] argued for the transversal role of chromatic sym -
bolism in shaping both narrative meaning and socio-  political 
concepts such as freedom and discrimination. Similarly, Consejo 
[25] analyzed how peritexts such as endpapers guide children's 
expectations through color- coded atmospheres.

metadata.core_insight_en: This study rigorously validated its thematic coding framework across 78 color research articles through iterative refinement involving multiple coders, ensuring high reliability and consensus, despite initial heterogeneity in methodological approaches ranging from physiological recordings to self-reported assessments. The process highlighted the necessity for flexible reclassification based on content analysis to accurately categorize diverse research methodologies within established themes.

Several studies specifically addressed children's responses. Acer 
and Gözen [ 10] showed that preschoolers associated particular 
colors with moods and narrative situations, using color as the pri-
mary cue in their own storytelling. Cruz [26] found that carefully 
designed chromatic palettes in educational books enhanced atten-
tion and emotional comprehension of sensitive topics. Moreillon 
[27] emphasized Wildsmith's bold palettes and textures as foster-
ing imagination and emotional literacy, drawing on author inter-
views and classroom observations reported in the original study, 
which linked high-  saturation palettes to increased engagement 
and interpretive dialogue among children (in this study “bold 
palettes” refers to high saturation color palette). Marcus [28] dis-
cussed the expressive power of color across classic picture books.
Recent technological approaches have broadened this perspec -
tive. Liu et al. [29] applied deep learning and surveys to show that 
“healing” illustrations with rich colors and textures reduced neg-
ative emotions such as stress, while Hauff and Trieschnigg [ 30] 
demonstrated that color features significantly contributed to auto-
matic emotion annotation in images. Wang et al. [31] further used 
visual attribute transfer techniques to experimentally confirm that 
color transformations had the strongest impact on children's emo-
tional engagement compared to texture or material modifications.
In addition, although the initial categorization included 27 stud-
ies, we incorporated one further article [32] in the analysis and in 
Appendix  C (Table  C1). This decision was made because Wang 
et  al. [ 32] directly investigated children's emotional associations 
with color in picture books, showing that blue and yellow were 
linked to happiness, red to anger, and gray to sadness. Crucially, 
this study combined questionnaires with EEG measures in chil -
dren (n = 69 + n = 23), providing empirical evidence of attentional 
correlations associated with preferred colors. While methodolog-
ically it also belongs to Experimental Studies on Color and Its 
Applications (see Section 3.4), we considered it essential to include 
it here because of its explicit focus on emotional perception.
Taken together, these studies converge on the idea that color 
plays a dual role: it both facilitates semantic and narrative com -
prehension and modulates emotional responses, contributing to 
engagement, anticipation, and even emotional regulation.
3.2   |   Cognitive Processing of Images 
and Color Recognition
Within this category, 17 studies were identified that explore how 
color in illustrations styles are processed cognitively, shaping at-
tention, memory, imagination, and meaning-  making (Table  C2 
in the Appendix  C). These works span theoretical contributions, 
historical analyses, and empirical studies, together revealing 
how chromatic and visual codes interact with cognitive mecha -
nisms in both children and adults.
Several contributions emphasize the developmental role of pic -
turebooks. Lakizenko and Makarova [ 9] showed, through qual -
itative analysis of Russian picturebooks for children aged 3–11, 
that color palettes function as semiotic and motivational de -
vices, based on systematic coding of palette types and thematic 
associations, supporting engagement and comprehension while 
preferences evolve with age. Similarly, Rezvani and Bakhtiarian 
[15] examined Silverstein and Erlbruch's works, demonstrating 
how abstract forms and color symbolism foster philosophi -
cal reflection and questioning in children using interpretive 
visual- textual analysis of three picturebooks. Complementarily, 
Crawford et al. [ 33] highlighted the multimodal power of pic -
turebooks for literacy, empathy, and cultural understanding, 
underscoring color as a central meaning-  making cue.
Historical analyses show how color intersected with learning 
and imagination in different contexts. Korda [ 34] examined 
Victorian instructional books and demonstrated that hand- 
colored and chromolithographic illustrations mediated between 
rote memorization and curiosity-  driven learning. Likewise, 
Wierzbicki [ 35] studied color–music projections, examined 
Victorian instructional books and demonstrated that hand- 
colored and chromolithographic illustrations mediated between 
rote memorization and curiosity-  driven learning. Lazić et  al. 
[36] reviewed depictions of cerebral gyri in art, illustrating how 
visual representation bridged neuroscience and aesthetics.
From a conceptual and theoretical standpoint, several works 
stress that perception and cognition depend on context. Felin 
et al. [ 37] examined the assumption of an “all-  seeing eye” and 
argued that perception is situated and relational. Fuga [ 38] and 
Green and Sarkar [ 39] analyzed adult coloring books and ther -
apeutic illustration practices, highlighting color's role in cre -
ativity, wellness, and mental health recovery. Hodgkinson [ 40] 
explored symbolism in animation, while Castagnoli [41] focused 
on cultural codes in illustration, both emphasizing how color 
complicates translation and alternative realities.
Empirical and methodological studies further link color to vi -
sual adaptation and comprehension. Webster and Tregillus [ 42] 
provided experimental simulations showing how adaptation 
processes normalize perception across age, color deficiencies, 
and environments. Saletta et al. [ 43] found that adults with in -
tellectual or developmental disabilities improved reading com -
prehension and recall when texts included illustrations based on 
controlled comparisons of illustrated versus non- illustrated pas-
sages. O'Neil [ 44] similarly reported that color, line, and shape 
fostered visual literacy among elementary students through 
classroom- based interventions and qualitative observation.
Taken together, these studies converge on the idea that color 
functions not only as a perceptual stimulus but as a cognitive 
scaffold, mediating between visual input and higher-  level pro-
cesses such as comprehension, imagination, philosophical 
reflection, and cultural translation. While some works are the -
oretical or historical [ 34, 35, 37, 40, 45 ], others offer empirical 
evidence [ 9, 33, 42–44 ], demonstrating that the processing of 
color and imagery shapes both learning outcomes and semantic 
meaning- making across developmental stages.
3.3   |   Narrative Function of Color and Its Role in 
Visual Storytelling
Within this category, 13 studies were identified that address 
color as a structural and representational element resource 
within picture books (Table  C3 in the Appendix  C). These works 
examine how color choices contribute to shaping narrative

Recent technological studies further underscore the significant role of color in modulating children's emotional responses and facilitating emotional recognition in visual content.
metadata.core_insight_ko: 이 발췌문은 이야기나 교육 자료, 기술 응용 등 다양한 맥락에서 아이들의 색상에 대한 섬세한 반응을 종합하며, 특정 색상 팔레트가 감정적 참여, 이해, 상상력을 어떻게 향상시키는지 보여줍니다. 최근 기술 연구는 색상이 아이들의 감정 반응을 조절하고 시각 콘텐츠에서 감정 인식을 촉진하는 데 중요한 역할을 한다는 점을 더욱 강조합니다.

coherence, meaning-  making, and the semiotic layering of pic -
ture books, graphic novels, and other multimodal texts.
Several contributions focus on how color functions as a gram -
matical or structural code in illustration. Blair [ 45] analyzed 
the “ornament of grammar” through conceptual visual essays, 
coding color-  shape diagrams to illustrate syntactic patterns. 
This analysis shows how visual codes—including color, line, 
and ornamentation—act as syntactic devices that guide read -
ers' interpretation of complex texts. Similarly, Camasão et  al. 
[40] explored wordless picturebooks based on qualitative visual 
narrative analysis of multiple wordless albums. Their findings 
demonstrate that chromatic contrasts and recurring color motifs 
provide cohesion in the absence of verbal narration, acting as 
narrative signposts that help children reconstruct the storyline.
Hardman and Boavida [ 46] extended this argument by analyz -
ing The Three Little Pigs. They used geometric and chromatic 
patterns, where circular, triangular, and square motifs were 
matched with color palettes to differentiate characters and plot 
stages. The study included an educational design brief with first- 
year design students to examine how limited palettes and shapes 
influence narrative clarity. Their findings suggest that color, 
when systematically aligned with shape, may support children's 
recall of story structure.
Other works highlight the semantic and cultural dimensions 
of color. Laaniste [ 47] examined, through interpretive essay 
analysis of visual motifs and palette shifts, the Estonian comic 
Tagurpidi, where surrealist and postmodernist uses of color 
created narrative dissonance, challenging readers to question 
linearity and meaning. In a different cultural frame, Peres [ 48] 
studied, with a qualitative analysis of continuity sketches and 
color boards, Hayao Miyazaki's animated works. They showed 
that chromatic landscapes carry narrative weight, where recur -
ring palettes (such as red for vitality or blue for transcendence) 
help audiences navigate complex visual narratives.
Empirical and interpretive approaches converge in works like 
Roscoe [49], whose picturebook A Thing to Hold relies on muted 
colors to foreground themes of memory and loss, demonstrating 
how limited palettes can intensify narrative effect. Likewise, 
Serafini [50] argued that in wordless picturebooks, color acts as 
a substitute for text, demanding interpretive engagement and 
collaborative meaning- making from readers.
From an educational perspective, Smith and Pole [ 51] analyzed, 
via content analysis of panel structures and color-  emotion 
coding, how graphic novels such as El Deafo use multimodal 
features—panels, speech balloons, and color-  coded emotional 
cues—to foster comprehension. McTigue [ 52] further showed 
that teaching children to recognize imagery, including color 
choices, strengthens their ability to infer and extend narrative 
meaning through reflective classroom case studies.
Taken together, these studies support the view that color oper -
ates beyond mere decoration: it can function as a narrative device 
that structures, symbolizes, and amplifies storytelling. Whether 
through structural cohesion (as in wordless picturebooks [ 48]), 
cultural semiotics (Tagurpidi [ 47]), or instructional practice 
(teaching visual imagery [ 53]), color consistently emerges as a 
critical cue in narrative interpretation.
3.4   |   Experimental Studies on Color and Its 
Application in Picture Books
Within this category, 22 studies were reviewed that employed 
experimental or quasi- experimental designs to test how color in-
fluences children's learning, memory, and interaction with pic -
ture books. Unlike theoretical or descriptive contributions, these 
works directly manipulated chromatic variables and measured 
their effects on comprehension, transfer, or emotional engagement 
(Table  C4 in the Appendix  C). Several studies reported that color 
coding may facilitate comprehension and recall. Dwyer [54], in a 
controlled study with university students, found that colored cod-
ing in visually oriented tests improved performance compared to 
monochrome conditions, suggesting that chromatic cues facilitate 
attention and information retrieval. Similarly, Bergman Deitcher 
et al. [ 14] analyzed alphabet books and showed that simpler, less 
saturated palettes promoted metalinguistic engagement, as par -
ents and children produced more interpretive dialogue, indicating 
that reduced visual complexity redirects focus toward the sym -
bolic functions of illustration.
Experimental research with younger children highlights the 
role of color in transfer of learning. Ganea et al. [ 55] tested 104 
preschoolers (3–4 years) using picture books on animal camou -
flage and found that by age 4, children could transfer knowledge 
from illustrations to real animals, with color cues being criti -
cal for identifying camouflage and predicting predation risks. 
This aligns with Acer and Gözen's [10] qualitative- experimental 
work showing that preschoolers associated particular colors and 
shapes with moods and narrative situations, integrating them 
into their own drawings.
House and Rule [ 56] examined preschoolers' aesthetic prefer -
ences in 30 illustrations and found that bright colors and familiar 
objects were central criteria in judgments of beauty, indicating 
that color affects not only comprehension but also motivation 
and engagement with picture books.
Neurocognitive approaches provide further insight. Wang [ 36] 
combined questionnaires with EEG in Taiwanese children 
(N = 92, aged 9–12) and showed that specific colors (blue, yel -
low = happiness; red = anger; gray = sadness) elicited distinct 
neural and self-  reported responses. EEG results suggested in -
creased attention when illustrations included colors that chil -
dren identified as preferred. Self-  reports linked blue and yellow 
to happiness, red to anger, and gray to sadness. Importantly, 
this study was also considered under the “Impact of Color on 
Emotional Perception” category, but due to its robust experimen-
tal design, it is included here as well.
Transfer and retention effects have also been documented in lon-
gitudinal paradigms. Simcock and DeLoache [ 13] explored how 
repetition and narrative cues affected infants' imitation from 
books, showing that illustrations with consistent color schemes 
improved recall over time. Likewise, Simcock et al. [ 57] tested 
how narrative cues modulate learning from both television and

metadata.core_insight_en: This excerpt from "Color Research & Application" (2026) explores how color functions as a structural and grammatical element in multimodal texts like picture books and graphic novels, acting as syntactic devices that enhance meaning-making and narrative cohesion through visual codes such as chromatic contrasts and geometric patterns. Studies analyzed include Blair’s conceptual visual essays, Camasão et al.’s qualitative analysis of wordless picturebooks, and Hardman and Boavida’s examination of "The Three Little Pigs," all demonstrating color’s pivotal role in guiding reader interpretation and story recall.
metadata.core_insight_ko: 이 발췌문은 2026년 "색채 연구 및 응용"에서 그림책과 그래픽 노블 같은 다매체 텍스트에서 색이 구조적이고 문법적 요소로 작용하며, 색상 대비와 기하학적 패턴 같은 시각적 코드를 통해 의미 구성과 이야기의 일관성을 높이는 구문적 장치로 기능함을 탐구합니다. 분석된 연구로는 블레어의 개념적 시각 에세이, 카마소이 등 저자들의 단어 없는 그림책의 질적 분석, 그리고 하드먼과 보아비다의 "세 마리 새끼 돼지" 연구가 포함되어 있으며, 이들 모두 색이 독자의 해석 안내와 이야기 회상에 중요한 역할을 한다는 점을 보여줍니다.

picture books, with results indicating that congruent color and 
narrative scaffolds facilitated imitation.
Other experimental contributions extend these findings to sci -
entific or educational contexts. Ganea et  al. [ 55] (camouflage 
learning), Arribas [ 58] (analysis of award- winning albums with 
implicit pedagogical color functions), and Dos Santos [ 59] (Our 
Friend the Atom, integrating didactic illustration and chromatic 
symbolism) all emphasize that color supports conceptual trans -
fer beyond story comprehension, into domains such as science 
learning and cultural literacy.
Taken together, the studies in this category converge on three 
main tendencies:
– Color coding and simplification enhance memory and 
comprehension, especially in alphabet learning and vis -
ually demanding tasks.
– Color cues enable transfer of knowledge from picture 
books to real-  world referents, as in biological concepts of 
camouflage.
– Experimental and neurocognitive evidence links specific 
colors to emotional and attentional responses, showing 
how chromatic design mediates both narrative engagement 
and cognitive processing.
Thus, this body of work illustrates that experimental manipula -
tions of color in picture books are central for understanding the 
mechanisms through which illustrations contribute to children's 
narrative comprehension, abstract thinking, and cognitive- 
emotional development.
4   |   Discussion
In this systematic review, our objective was to analyze and cat -
egorize existing research on the use of color as a narrative de -
vice in picture book illustration, identifying its main functions 
and its impact on perception, cognition, and narrative structure. 
Through a structured approach, we consolidated the findings 
into four key categories: the impact of color on emotional per -
ception, cognitive image processing and color recognition, the 
narrative function of color, and experimental studies on color 
in illustration.
It should be noted that the reviewed studies use diverse meth -
odologies whose dependent measures vary from physiological 
to self-  reported indicators. As such, the relationships dis -
cussed in this review should be interpreted as associations 
reported by the original authors, rather than as direct causal 
effects. The aim of this synthesis is therefore descriptive and 
interpretive, reflecting the evidence as presented in the source 
studies.
The results support the relevance of color within visual narra -
tive, indicating its potential role in the construction of meaning 
and children's reading experience. Furthermore, it was evident 
that, while significant studies exist in each of these categories, 
there are still gaps in the systematization of color as a narrative 
tool. Below, the key findings in each of the established categories 
are discussed, and the limitations of the study are presented, as 
well as possible lines of future research.
These findings build on and extend prior research in the fields 
of visual literacy, developmental psychology, and illustration 
design. The emphasis children placed on color aligns with 
Paivio's [ 60] Dual Coding Theory, which suggests that visual 
and verbal stimuli are processed in separate but interconnected 
cognitive systems. Color, in this framework, serves as both a 
perceptual enhancer and a mnemonic device, a role confirmed 
by studies such as Acer and Gözen [ 10], who found that chil -
dren use color deliberately when narrating their own visual 
stories. Additionally, our results resonate with Lakizenko and 
Makarova's [ 9] analysis of chromatic evolution in illustrated 
books, which highlights how visual complexity must adjust 
across developmental stages to support cognitive and emotional 
comprehension. Furthermore, Liu et al.'s [ 29] AI-  based model-
ing of emotional responses to color strengthens the argument 
that specific palettes—particularly monochromatic schemes—
are not merely aesthetic choices but active narrative and af -
fective agents. These authors collectively indicate that color 
functions as a multimodal semiotic resource central to narrative 
construction [9, 10, 29]. Martínez et al. [ 6] analyzed color shifts 
in picturebooks and showed that palette transitions often signal 
changes in narrative tone, reinforcing color's semiotic role in 
storytelling. Sun et al. [ 7] conducted a systematic review on nat-
ural environment themes and found that color design in picture-
books influences children's cognitive development, particularly 
in ecological literacy. Schoppmann et  al. [ 12] tested the effect 
of picturebook reading on emotion regulation strategies, show -
ing that chromatic cues can support emotional self-  regulation 
during narrative engagement.
The implications of these findings are twofold, contributing 
meaningfully to both theory and practice. Theoretically, the 
study affirms the idea that color in illustrated narratives op -
erates not only as an aesthetic device but also as a carrier of 
meaning, emotion, and cognitive structure. This reinforces mul-
timodal theories of narrative posed by Kress and van Leeuwen 
[60], which posit that visual elements—especially color—work 
in tandem with text to shape narrative comprehension and affec-
tive response. Practically, the findings suggest that illustrators 
and picture book designers must consider the developmental 
sensitivities of their audience when choosing color palettes, sat -
uration, and compositional complexity. For early readers, high 
saturation and literal color schemes can scaffold early decod -
ing skills and emotional literacy, while for older children, more 
low- contrast and meaning-  based palettes may support abstract 
thinking and narrative inference. These perspectives can be 
complemented with Maule et al. [61] on the development of color 
perception and cognition, and with Jonauskaite et  al. [ 62, 63], 
whose cross-  cultural and systematic reviews demonstrate the 
consistency of color–emotion links across contexts.
4.1   |   Interpretation by Category
The categorization of studies into four thematic domains—emo -
tional perception, cognitive processing, narrative function, and 
experimental application—reveals the multifaceted role of color 
in children's illustrated narratives. Each category contributes

distinct insights into how color operates as a narrative device, 
while collectively they support a unified theoretical framework 
grounded in multimodal and cognitive theories.
Studies within the category “Impact of Color on Emotional 
Perception in Illustration” have shown that color is a crucial ele-
ment in evoking emotions and building a narrative atmosphere. 
The reviewed literature consistently highlights color as a key cue 
for eliciting affective responses in children's engagement with 
illustrations. Warm and saturated palettes were reported to be 
associated with joy and energy, whereas darker hues appeared 
to convey sadness or tension. These findings align with cross- 
cultural research on color–emotion correspondences. Such re -
search demonstrates systematic associations such as yellow with 
joy, blue with calmness, and black with sadness.
Importantly, picturebook studies contextualize these effects 
within narrative comprehension. Broader psychological litera -
ture suggests that such correspondences are robust across age 
groups and cultures. This indicates that children's responses 
to color in illustration may build on universal perceptual- 
emotional mappings, though modulated by cultural codes [ 57].
Specific hues—such as yellow and blue for happiness, red for 
anger, and gray for sadness—are repeatedly associated with 
distinct emotional states, suggesting a stable correspondence be-
tween chromatic stimuli and affective interpretation. These asso-
ciations are not merely perceptual but operate as communicative 
strategies embedded in the visual language of picture books.
Color, thus, can function as a mechanism for emotional modula-
tion, potentially enabling young readers to anticipate narrative 
developments, empathize with characters, and navigate affec -
tive landscapes.
In addition, research by Zentner [ 64] indicates that color pref -
erences and color–emotion associations vary significantly with 
age. For example, young children tend to favor warm colors such 
as red, whereas adults show a preference for cooler tones like 
blue. These differences suggest that the emotional impact of 
color is not static but evolves with development, reinforcing the 
need to adapt color palettes to the reader's developmental stage.
Moreover, certain palettes appear to support emotional regu -
lation, with balanced chromatic schemes fostering calmness, 
curiosity, or resilience. This dual function—expressive and reg -
ulatory—positions color as a key element in shaping emotional 
experiences and enhancing emotive communication within vi -
sual storytelling.
Recent psychological research further reinforces these insights 
by demonstrating that color–emotion correspondences are not 
only consistent across cultures but also structured along affec -
tive dimensions such as valence, arousal, and power.
For instance, light and saturated colors tend to be associated with 
positive, high- arousal emotions (e.g., joy, excitement), while dark 
and desaturated colors are linked to negative, low-  arousal states 
(e.g., sadness, boredom). Red stands out as emotionally ambiva -
lent, evoking both empowering and intense emotions—positive 
(love, passion) and negative (anger, rage).
These findings suggest that the emotional impact of color in 
illustration may be grounded in deeply rooted perceptual- 
emotional mappings that transcend specific contexts, making 
color a universally resonant tool for emotional storytelling [ 62].
Analysis of the category “Cognitive Processing of Images and 
Color Recognition” has revealed that color plays a fundamental 
role in information retention and concept association in chil -
dren's reading.
Research suggests that chromatic saturation and contrast may 
facilitate the recognition of visual patterns and the understand -
ing of abstract concepts, enhancing information retention and 
conceptual association during reading. Vibrant, distinct colors 
appear to support visual memory and may aid the development 
of inferential thinking. Maule et al. [ 61] made a comprehensive 
review of how color perception develops from infancy through 
adolescence. Trichromatic color vision emerges as early as 
2–3 months of age, but chromatic discrimination and color con -
stancy continue to mature over time.
This extended developmental trajectory suggests that color 
serves not only as a perceptual cue but also as a cognitive scaf -
fold that evolves with the learner [ 65]. Color perception pro -
gresses from basic hue discrimination to complex categorical 
and conceptual understanding. This developmental shift en -
ables children to use color to individuate objects. It also allows 
them to infer properties and organize narrative elements.
These findings align with Kress and van Leeuwen's [ 65] theory 
of multimodal discourse, which positions color as a semiotic 
mode essential to meaning-  making. In illustrated narratives, 
color supports visual literacy and inferential thinking, helping 
children anticipate plot developments and engage with story 
structure [ 66]. The acquisition of color terms—once considered 
uniquely difficult—is now understood as a gradual inductive 
process.
Wagner, Dobkins, and Barner [ 66] demonstrated that children's 
early use of color words is systematic rather than random. Before 
achieving adult- like understanding, children make overgeneral -
ized hypotheses about color meanings, indicating that the chal -
lenge lies in identifying the categorical boundaries defined by 
language [ 66]. Yurovsky et al. [ 67] expanded on this by show -
ing that the mechanisms underlying color word learning mirror 
those used in general category learning. Children's performance 
in color naming tasks is influenced by input frequency, category 
size, and perceptual salience, reinforcing the idea that color is 
cognitively meaningful and not merely perceptual.
Despite these insights, there remains a need for experimental 
studies that more accurately measure the impact of color on 
cognitive processing throughout child development, especially 
in educational contexts. Complementing these, research by 
Villarroel and Villanueva [ 68] and Villanueva et  al. [ 69] has 
shown that young children spontaneously use color in their 
drawings of natural elements, such as the sun and plants, re -
flecting emerging cognitive processes and conceptual under -
standing in educational contexts. Furthermore, Villarroel et al. 
[70] highlight that symmetry and chromatic choices often ap -
pear as intuitive strategies in children's representations of the

metadata.core_insight_en: This research synthesizes multimodal and cognitive theories to demonstrate how color functions as a pivotal narrative device in illustrations, significantly influencing emotional perception and engagement, particularly in children, through culturally consistent yet contextually modulated emotional associations. Specific colors like yellow and blue consistently evoke happiness and sadness respectively, highlighting universal yet culturally nuanced perceptual-emotional mappings in visual storytelling.

aesthetic function but also a conceptual role in early scientific 
thinking within educational contexts.
Studies within the category “Narrative Function of Color and 
Its Role in Visual Storytelling” show that color not only acts as 
an emotional and cognitive resource but also has a structural 
function within visual narratives.
Color guides the reader's attention, facilitates transitions be -
tween scenes and reinforces narrative coherence and temporal 
sequencing. Research such as that by Lakizenko and Makarova 
[9] shows that chromatic palettes in children's picture books 
function as semiotic and motivational tools, adapting to devel -
opmental stages to support comprehension and engagement.
Camasão et  al. [ 48] further illustrate that in wordless picture -
books, chromatic contrasts and recurring palettes act as narra -
tive signposts, enabling children to reconstruct storylines in the 
absence of text. This aligns with Kress and van Leeuwen's [ 71] 
multimodal theory, which positions color as a semiotic mode 
that contributes to compositional meaning alongside other visual 
elements. Moreover, cultural and cross-  cultural studies [ 53, 62] 
reveal that color- emotion associations are consistent across coun-
tries yet modulated by age and cultural context. For instance, 
older adults tend to associate fewer but more intense and positive 
emotions with colors, reflecting a positivity bias in aging.
These findings suggest that color choices in illustration are em -
bedded in culturally and developmentally specific storytelling 
conventions. Despite these insights, this category presents one 
of the most significant gaps in the literature.
There is still no consolidated theoretical framework that inte -
grates the narrative function of color with semiotic and psycho -
logical models in children's illustration. The reviewed studies 
highlight the need for interdisciplinary approaches that bridge 
visual semiotics, developmental psychology, and narrative the -
ory to fully understand how color structures meaning in illus -
trated texts.
Within the category “Experimental Studies on Color and Its 
Application in Picture Books” studies have been identified 
that provide empirical validation for the narrative role of color, 
demonstrating its impact on learning, emotional engagement, 
and knowledge transfer.
Within this category, researchers have employed innovative meth-
odologies—such as EEG, eye- tracking, and controlled visual mem-
ory tests—to analyze how chromatic design influences children's 
perception and comprehension of visual narratives. Simcock and 
DeLoache [8] showed that infants exposed to picture books with 
consistent color schemes exhibited improved recall and imitation, 
suggesting that perceptual consistency in color enhances narra -
tive comprehension and memory encoding. Similarly, Wang et al. 
[32] used wearable EEG headsets to measure children's atten -
tional responses to preferred colors, finding that hues like blue 
and yellow elicited higher engagement and emotional resonance.
These findings confirm the cognitive–emotional interplay 
of chromatic design and its role in sustaining attention and 
facilitating affective interpretation. Other studies have used 
eye- tracking to determine how color directs visual atten -
tion and supports story sequencing. For example, Bergman 
Deitcher et  al. [ 14] found that simplified, less saturated pal -
ettes in alphabet books prompted more metalinguistic en -
gagement between parents and children. In contrast, vibrant 
illustrations led to increased focus on visual elements. This 
suggests that chromatic complexity can modulate the balance 
between visual and verbal narrative processing. Jonauskaite 
et al. [ 63] further contribute to this understanding by demon -
strating that color–emotion associations are stable across age 
groups but vary in intensity and valence. Their cross-  cultural 
study revealed that older adults tend to associate fewer but 
more positive emotions with colors, reflecting a developmen -
tal positivity bias.
Although focused on adults, these findings underscore the im -
portance of considering age- related shifts in emotional interpre-
tation when designing color palettes for children's books.
Despite these advances, the review highlights a need to expand 
the use of cognitive neuroscience tools and mixed methodologies 
to analyze the relationship between color and narrative compre-
hension more comprehensively. While EEG and eye-  tracking 
offer valuable insights into attentional and emotional responses, 
few studies have integrated these approaches with longitudinal 
designs or multimodal analysis frameworks.
Future research should explore how color functions not only in 
isolated scenes but across entire narrative arcs, and how chil -
dren's responses evolve over time. In this regard, Epicoco et al. 
[72] have demonstrated that studies conducted in controlled en -
vironments, using gamma correction methods, allow for precise 
estimation of participants' color perception. This type of meth -
odological control is essential to ensure the validity of results in 
research on color and narrative, especially when comparing dif -
ferent devices or experimental conditions. Such methodological 
precision is particularly relevant for future studies aiming to com-
pare chromatic effects across different technological platforms.
In sum, experimental studies confirm that color in picture 
books is not merely decorative—it is a functional narrative el -
ement that shapes comprehension, emotional engagement, and 
cognitive development. These findings support the strategic in -
tegration of color in educational and storytelling contexts, re -
inforcing its role as a multimodal cue that bridges perception, 
emotion, and meaning- making.
4.2   |   Limitations of the Review and Future 
Research Directions
Despite the rigorous study selection and analysis process, this 
review has some limitations that should be considered when in -
terpreting its findings.
1. Accessibility of primary sources: Some potentially relevant 
articles were excluded due to access restrictions, which may 
have limited the scope of the review. Future research should 
promote open- access databases and collaborative projects to 
improve inclusivity and transparency in literature synthesis.

2. Lack of longitudinal studies: Much of the literature re -
viewed is based on short- term studies, making it difficult to 
assess the effects of color on visual storytelling over time. 
Longitudinal studies are needed to trace how children's 
use and interpretation of color evolves over time, and how 
early exposure to specific chromatic structures may shape 
later narrative comprehension and emotional literacy.
3. Focus on children's literature: While this review focused 
on picture books, excluding other visual storytelling for -
mats (such as comics, animation, and digital platforms) 
may have overlooked important comparative insights. 
Expanding future analyses to include these media could 
reveal how color functions differently depending on for -
mat, interactivity, and pacing.
4. Lack of consensus on terminology: The variability in termi-
nology used to describe the impact of color on storytelling 
complicates theoretical integration. The absence of a stand-
ardized lexicon across disciplines—such as psychology, se -
miotics, design, and education—hinders cross-  disciplinary 
synthesis and may obscure conceptual low-  contrast colors. 
Future work should aim to develop a shared vocabulary 
that facilitates comparative and integrative research.
Beyond these primary concerns, several underlying issues 
emerged that further illustrate the complexity of the field. One is 
the disciplinary fragmentation of color studies. Research on color 
in visual storytelling is spread across multiple fields (such as psy-
chology, education, semiotics, and art design), each with its own 
methodologies and epistemologies. This fragmentation can lead to 
conceptual silos and limit the depth of analysis. Interdisciplinary 
collaboration is essential to build a cohesive theoretical model that 
bridges cognitive, emotional, and semiotic dimensions of color.
Moreover, many studies rely heavily on subjective interpretation 
of illustrations or emotional tone, with minimal inter-  rater val-
idation or methodological transparency. This introduces poten -
tial bias in interpreting color's effects. Future research should 
incorporate mixed methods and ensure methodological rigor 
through triangulation and coder reliability checks.
Lastly, although several studies included diverse participants, few 
deeply examined sociocultural influences on color perception, 
emotional associations, or narrative interpretation. Cross- cultural 
and intersectional research is needed to understand how children 
from different contexts engage with chromatic storytelling and 
how cultural codes shape meaning- making.
Taken together, these limitations highlight the complexity of 
studying color as a narrative device and underscore the need for 
more robust, interdisciplinary, and culturally sensitive research 
designs. Addressing these gaps will be essential for advancing a 
comprehensive understanding of how color contributes to narra-
tive construction and cognitive-  emotional development in chil -
dren's visual media.
5   |   Conclusions and Implications
These outcomes directly address the objectives outlined at the 
start of this study—namely, to explore how color functions 
as a narrative device across different thematic domains in 
children's illustration. The thematic synthesis of studies has 
shown that color plays a central role in modulating emotional 
tone, supporting cognitive processing, and structuring nar -
rative flow. By categorizing and interpreting how color use 
varies across emotional, cognitive, narrative, and experimen -
tal contexts, the study provides a nuanced framework for un -
derstanding the semiotic and developmental significance of 
color. In doing so, it responds to the core research questions 
not only descriptively but analytically, offering a synthesized 
account of how color is not merely a stylistic choice, but a com -
municative strategy embedded in the narrative logic of illus -
trated texts.
The analysis provided an integrated view of how existing stud -
ies conceptualize color's role within picture book narratives. By 
categorizing the studies into the impact of color on emotional 
perception, cognitive processing, narrative function, and exper -
imental findings, this review systematically structures the exist -
ing literature, identifying both patterns and research gaps.
The implications are both theoretical and practical. Theoretically, 
the review supports Paivio's Dual Coding Theory and Kress and 
van Leeuwen's multimodal discourse framework, affirming 
that color operates in tandem with text and imagery to construct 
meaning. Practically, the findings suggest that illustrators, edu -
cators, and designers must consider developmental sensitivities 
when selecting color palettes, ensuring that color choices align 
with the cognitive and emotional needs of their audience. For 
instance, research indicates that for early readers, high-  contrast 
and saturated primary colors can enhance visual attention and 
decoding skills, whereas for older children, more desaturated, 
analogous, or contextually nuanced palettes may foster abstract 
thinking, emotional interpretation, and narrative comprehen -
sion. These examples illustrate how the intentional use of color 
can serve as a developmental bridge between perceptual engage-
ment and conceptual understanding within visual narratives.
Developmentally, the review shows that color perception evolves 
from basic hue discrimination in infancy to categorical labeling 
and meaning- based interpretation in later childhood [73]. These 
foundational abilities enable children to use color not only per -
ceptually but also semiotically, interpreting it as a cue for emo -
tion, character motivation, or narrative resolution. For example, 
children consistently associate red with danger or anger, blue 
with sadness or calm, and yellow with happiness, patterns that 
persist across cultures and age groups [ 74].
These emotional associations are not static. Jonauskaite et  al. 
[62] found that while younger individuals interpret a broader 
emotional range from colors, older adults exhibit a positivity 
bias, attributing stronger affective meaning to fewer, more emo -
tionally charged hues. This suggests that color functions as a 
developmentally adaptive narrative tool—one that evolves in its 
cognitive and emotional impact from early picturebook encoun-
ters to mature, affectively nuanced interpretation.
Experimental studies further validate these insights. Simcock 
and DeLoache [ 8] demonstrated that consistent color schemes 
in picture books enhance recall and imitation in infants, while

metadata.core_insight_en: This review highlights critical gaps in current research on color's impact on visual storytelling, particularly emphasizing the need for longitudinal studies and a standardized interdisciplinary vocabulary to better understand its evolving effects on children's narrative comprehension and emotional development across various media formats. Additionally, it underscores the challenge posed by fragmented disciplinary approaches that hinder comprehensive theoretical integration.

importance of chromatic design in shaping both emotional and 
cognitive responses to illustrated narratives.
In sum, color is not a passive element in children's illustration 
but an active agent of narrative construction: one that evolves 
with the reader, adapts to context, and communicates meaning 
across modalities.
This systematic review supports the view that color in children's 
illustration is not merely an aesthetic tool but a fundamental 
narrative element that appears to influence story comprehen -
sion, emotional perception, and cognitive processing. However, 
further research is needed to explore additional dimensions of 
this field.
Some future research directions include:
• Longitudinal studies analyzing how color perception in vi -
sual narratives evolves as children grow. Tracking the same 
cohort across multiple developmental stages would reveal 
how color moves from a perceptual feature to a represen -
tational and inferential tool—providing insight into the 
cognitive and emotional mechanisms that underpin this 
transition. Such research could also clarify whether early 
exposure to certain color-  narrative structures influences 
later reading strategies or emotional literacy.
• Interdisciplinary research combining semiotics, neurosci -
ence, and cognitive psychology to develop a more compre -
hensive theoretical model of the role of color in illustration.
• Use of advanced technologies such as artificial intelligence 
and eye tracking to more accurately analyze the impact of 
color on the reading experience. These technologies could 
also support dynamic interaction studies, particularly 
useful in evaluating color's role in interactive or adaptive 
narratives.
• Comparisons between different narrative formats, such as 
illustration in printed books versus interactive digital plat -
forms. Given the rise of digital storytelling platforms, it is 
especially important to investigate whether digital enhance-
ments (like animated color transitions or adaptive palette 
shifts) produce similar cognitive and emotional outcomes 
as static illustrations in print. Such research would clar -
ify whether findings from picturebooks generalize across 
media or whether color takes on different roles depending 
on interactivity, pacing, or user control.
Beyond early childhood, these insights may also inform strate -
gies for language acquisition in adulthood. For instance, color 
could serve as an additional semiotic resource to support com -
prehension and engagement in second-  language learning con -
texts, including programs for immigrants or adults learning a 
new language by necessity or interest. Integrating chromatic 
cues into instructional materials may enhance memory, facil -
itate conceptual associations, and provide affective support 
during the learning process.
In conclusion, this systematic review consolidates existing 
knowledge about color as a narrative mechanism in picture 
book illustration, providing a conceptual framework for future 
research and highlighting the importance of further exploring 
the impact of color on the construction of meaning within visual 
narrative.

metadata.core_insight_en: This collection of academic articles explores diverse aspects of children's literature and illustration, encompassing parental reading practices, illustration as a philosophical tool, guidelines for systematic review reporting, visual appropriateness in picture books, cover design analysis, and historical magazine illustration techniques. Collectively, they highlight the multifaceted roles of visual and textual elements in enhancing children's literacy and educational experiences across different contexts and eras.

metadata.core_insight_en: This collection of scholarly sources explores diverse facets of illustration, including its therapeutic applications in wellness contexts (Green & Sarkar, 2020), symbolic meanings in animation (Hodgkinson, 2020), cognitive benefits for diverse readers (Saletta et al., 2019), and the development of visual literacy across educational settings (O'Neil, 2011). These studies collectively underscore the multifaceted impact and evolving role of illustration in both artistic expression and educational enhancement.

metadata.core_insight_en: This collection of studies examines the multifaceted relationship between color perception, cognition, and emotion across diverse populations and developmental stages, highlighting both universal and culturally specific associations from early childhood to adulthood. Key research underscores the gradual development of color-emotion links and the cognitive processes involved in color learning and categorization.

metadata.core_insight_en: This excerpt from "Color Research & Application" (2026) reviews three studies focusing on color's role in visual storytelling across animated films and picturebooks, highlighting how color shapes narrative meaning, emotional responses, and character perception in diverse cultural contexts despite varying methodologies and biases. Notably, these analyses underscore the significant impact of color choices on thematic interpretation across Portugal, Poland, and Russia.

metadata.core_insight_en: This section of the text summarizes three studies exploring color's impact on various domains: an empirical study demonstrating that illustrations enhance reading comprehension in adults with intellectual or developmental disabilities, a simulation model illustrating color adaptation across different contexts and visual conditions, and a historical analysis examining the intersection of color and music through the work of Alexander B. Hector. Each study highlights distinct applications and findings related to color perception and utilization.

Article
The Application of Color in Modern Design: A
Visual Transformation from Emotional Expression
to Cultural Identity
Wu Jiawei1*
1 Qiqihar university, Qiqihar, china;
* Correspondence: 2025429864@qq.com
Received: 12 January 2026 / Accepted: 27 January 2026 / Published: 03 February 2026
Abstract: This study, through a combination of case analysis and literature review, examines the
contemporary application of color in the field of design from 2022 to 2025. The aim is to explore the
visual dynamic and internal mechanism of color in emotional expression, cultural identity construction,
and sustainable design practices. The research findings indicate that the application of contemporary
design colors is undergoing a paradigm shift from pursuing visual impact to emphasizing internal
connotations and from a single representation to multi-dimensional narration. Color not only changes
the external presentation of products but also deeply influences users' consumption experience and
behavioral decisions through emotional resonance, cultural decoding, and ethical transmission. This
study explores the core mechanism of color as a "cultural-emotional-technological" collaborative
medium, providing empirical evidence and analytical frameworks for the deepening of future design
theories.
Keywords: Color application; Emotional expression; Social and cultural identification
1. Introduction
Color is the most direct and most emotionally impactful form element in visual art, and has played
a significant role in the development of human material and spiritual civilizations since ancient times.
From prehistoric cave paintings and mineral pigments to the color schemes of feudal dynasties'
clothing, from the exploration of light and shadow by Impressionist painters to the rational color
composition of the Bauhaus school, color not only records the aesthetic changes of different eras but
also reflects human emotional patterns, cultural structures ， and technological levels. Under the
combined influence of multiple factors such as the aftermath of the global pandemic, the accelerated
iteration of digital technology, the popularization of sustainable development concepts ， and the
awakening of cultural identity consciousness, the connotation, extension and role of design color in
modern design are undergoing an unprecedented paradigm shift (Kong, 2025).
During this transformation process, color research urgently needs a solid theoretical foundation.
The semiotic theory provides crucial analytical tools for understanding the mechanism of the meaning
generation of colors as cultural carriers. Roland Barthes' semiotic system points out that a symbol
consists of the signifier and the signified, and their combination is arbitrary and culturally conventional.
In the fashion and design field, the specific color selection serves as the signifier, and its referent is

[Page 2]
often a complex social identity and cultural value. For example, the combination of light beige and navy
blue does not naturally point to "the upper class", but through historical construction and cultural
reproduction, it becomes a visual symbol of the aesthetic of inherited wealth. This article will apply
Barthes' theoretical framework to analyze how colors participate in the symbolic construction of social
identities as fashion symbols. At the same time, Pierre Bourdieu's practice theory provides a sociological
perspective for this research. Bourdieu's concept of "habitus" indicates that the aesthetic preferences of
a specific class are the product of a long-term socialization process, deeply rooted in the body and the
unconscious. The "distinction" mechanism reveals how the ruling class realizes the symbolic
reproduction of class boundaries through cultural tastes (including color preferences). The understated
and restrained color choices in the aesthetic of inherited wealth are an embodiment of class habitus,
serving to create a clear visual separation from the emerging class or the lower class. These two theories
together form the analytical basis of this research, enabling us to go beyond mere description of
phenomena and deeply reveal the operational logic of colors as a social technological system.
In the modern design context, the functionality of colors has been greatly expanded and redefined,
breaking away from the traditional aesthetic framework that merely serves as decoration and
beautification (Yuan, 2024). It actively participates in deeper mechanisms such as user psychological
experience, brand value transmission, and social group identity construction. From fashion catwalks to
product design, from UI interfaces to space creation, numerous representative color practice cases have
emerged. However, existing research mostly remains at the level of phenomenon description and lacks
systematic theoretical explanations of the color's action mechanism. This study adopts case comparison
analysis and inductive analysis methods, focusing on the typical applications of design colors during
the period from 2022 to 2025. The aim is to discuss the visual transfer path and internal mechanism of
colors shifting from an emotional expression medium to a cultural identity symbol, and to explore their
ethical carrying functions in sustainable design practices.
2. Color as a New Language for Expressing Emotions: Mechanism and
Path Analysis
In modern design, color has become the core medium for conveying emotions and
communicating moods. Based on color psychology theory and emotional design, the emotional
effect of color stems from its direct stimulation of the brain's limbic system, which can bypass
the cognitive defense mechanism and achieve rapid emotional arousal (Yu, 2022). The empirical
study by Elliot and Maier (2014) shows that warm colors can significantly enhance a sense of
closeness and security. This finding provides a neuroscientific basis for the emotional
application of design colors. This section compares typical cases to summarize the two core
mechanisms of emotional expression of contemporary design colors: the natural resonance
mechanism and the material synergy mechanism.
2.1Natural resonance mechanism: The emotional anchoring effect of earth tones
The "earth tones" trend that is popular in 2025 perfectly embodies the natural resonance
mechanism. These warm and simple tones derived from nature, through the ingenious blending
of intermediate colors, form a color system that is both familiar and emotionally compelling.
The authoritative color institution PANTONE and WGSN jointly pointed out in their 2025 color
trend report (WGSN & Coloro, 2024) that such color combinations that can help maintain the
stability of the emotional core are becoming a popular direction in the design field, It is worth
noting that the popularity of earth tones is not an accidental phenomenon; rather, it is a direct

[Page 3]
reflection of the collective psychological needs in the post-pandemic era. When society faces
uncertainty, humans tend to return to the color preferences determined by "biophilia" (the
human affinity for nature), which are those tones that are highly harmonious with the natural
environment. This psychological mechanism has been fully verified in evolutionary psychology.
Natural tones can lower cortisol levels and alleviate anxiety. Therefore, the emotional anchoring
effect of earth tones has universality across cultures and eras, and its application goes beyond
mere aesthetic choices, becoming a practical strategy for design therapy (Figure 1).
Figure 1. Analysis of Popular Colors
The 2025-2026 autumn/winter collection of ISSEY MIYAKE's "PUMPED-T" series and the
concurrent collection of Fendi both extensively utilized earth tones. However, the emotional
expression paths differed significantly. ISSEY MIYAKE created adjustable three-dimensional
contours by combining ultra-dense 46G elastic knitted fabric with lightweight filling layers,
making colors an important component in shaping the form, giving avant-garde designs a sense
of comfort and friendliness, and achieving the expression logic of "form innovation" to
"emotional buffering". While Fendi used silk, brocade, soft leather, and other fabrics with
natural luster, paired with amber luminous tones, to create a visual effect that combines retro
and fashionable elements, following the path of "material luxury" to "emotional evocation".
Together, both reveal the core mechanism of earth tones, which achieve emotional anchoring
by reducing visual aggression and enhancing tactile associations (Figure 2、Figure 3).
Figure 2. "PUMPED-T Series" Presentation

2.2 Material synergy mechanism: The emotional amplification effect of color and
texture
Contemporary color application has moved beyond the simple selection of hues and entered
a stage of systematic design involving color and materials (He et al., 2025). The luster, texture,
transparency, and thickness of the fabric have become integral components of color expression,
and this synergy follows the emotional amplification formula. Specifically, the material synergy
mechanism can be explained by the "Sensory Congruency Theory". This theory posits that when
visual input (color) and tactile input (material) are highly consistent, the brain activates a
broader neural network, resulting in a multiplied emotional effect. For instance, when rough
linen texture is combined with low-saturation grayish-brown, the sense of simplicity and
authenticity it conveys far exceeds the effect achievable by a single sensory stimulus. This
cross-modal enhancement effect has been supported by fMRI evidence in neuroaesthetics
research (Wang & Chen, 2025), showing that multi-sensory synergy can significantly activate the
orbitofrontal cortex, a region closely related to value judgment and emotional experience.
Therefore, contemporary designers must view material selection as an extension of the color
strategy rather than an independent design element.
When the amber luminescent tones are combined with high-gloss materials such as silk and
brocade, the nostalgic emotions they evoke are significantly stronger than those from ordinary
cotton fabrics. The overall color scheme and material selection of Donna Karan's 2025
autumn-winter collection fully align with the theme of amber luminescence. Through a
consistent material language, it reflects the beauty of luminous splendor. This mechanism
indicates that the emotional expression power of colors is not isolated but relies on the
synergistic amplification effect across sensory modalities (Figure 4).

[Page 5]
Figure 4. Donna Karan's autumn-winter fashion show presentation
3. The symbolic colors of social cultural identity: Construction logic and
class narrative
Colour, as a cultural symbol, is constructed in accordance with the dual encoding theory,
carrying both explicit aesthetic information and implicit social codes (Kan & Chen, 2025). In the
context of globalization and the awakening of cultural identity consciousness, specific colour
systems, through a three-stage process of "stylization - communityization - symbolization", have
become the visual boundaries of group identity. This part, through comparative analysis,
reveals the internal logic of how colours construct cultural identity. It is worth noting that the
social symbolic function of colours is not a modern product; rather, it has a profound historical
depth. In ancient Rome, "Emperor's Purple" (Tyrian Purple) was the exclusive colour of the
noble class. Its complex extraction process from the shellfish made it worth far more than gold,
becoming the ultimate symbol of power and status. In medieval Europe, the Sumptuary Laws
tied colours to classes through legal forms, stipulating that commoners were not allowed to
wear specific colours (such as deep red or golden yellow) of clothing. These historical cases
prove that colours, as a tool for social stratification, have universality across cultures. In the era
of social media, this symbolic mechanism presents new characteristics: the speed of
dissemination has grown exponentially, the boundaries of the meaning of symbols have become
increasingly blurred, and subcultural groups have significantly enhanced their ability to
"symbolic appropriation" through colour deconstruction. As Baldini & Hashmi (2024) pointed
out, the dissemination cycle of fashion symbols on platforms like Instagram and TikTok has
been shortened to within 72 hours, much faster than the six-month update cycle of traditional
fashion systems, which has made the construction and deconstruction of colour meanings
unprecedentedly rapid and fluid.

[Page 6]
3.1 The color grammar of class identity: The symbolic opposition between "old money
style" and "no-money style."
The symbolic opposition between the aesthetic of inherited wealth (often referred to as the
"old money style") and the aesthetic of deliberate frugality or resourcefulness (sometimes called
the "no money style") was chosen as the core analytical object. This was based on the following
academic considerations: These two cases represent two extreme and opposing visual
expressions of wealth, taste, and identity in the current social media context. Their color
systems have high typicality and contrastiveness, making them ideal analytical objects for this
study. More importantly, these two aesthetic styles have achieved viral dissemination on
platforms such as TikTok and Instagram, making them excellent samples for observing the
rapid evolution of symbolic meanings in the digital age. By the beginning of 2025, the
cumulative playback of the #OldMoneyAesthetic tag had reached 4.7 billion times, while the
related content of #NoMoneyStyle had generated over 1.2 billion interactions. This
unprecedented digital visibility has enabled them to transcend simple fashion trends and evolve
into an important signifier system of contemporary youth culture.
The so-called "No-Money Style" needs to be clearly defined here: It is not a literal "poverty
aesthetics", but rather an anti-consumerist design strategy originated from the digital natives of
Generation Z. The core features of this style include:
1. Deliberate mixing of highly saturated conflicting colors (such as fluorescent green and
bright orange combinations);
2. Extensive use of DIY renovation elements and second-hand materials;
3. Achieving "symbolic democratization" by deconstructing the color norms of traditional
luxury goods.
Its essence is to challenge the aesthetic hegemony of capitalism through visual
"imperfection" and "incoherence", expressing the pursuit of sustainability and individual
liberation.
The Ralph Lauren 2025 Burgundy Velvet Suit and the Brunello Cucinelli Foggy Blue Set,
through a balance of "apparent color but not ostentatious", follow Bourdieu's (2023) theory of
"segregation practice", transforming colors into symbols of cultural capital. Specifically, the
color system of the inherited wealth aesthetics can be decomposed into three core elements:
First, beige/ oatmeal (Beige/Oatmeal) forms the base color tone, and its psychological effect is to
convey "quiet certainty" - this color does not crave attention, but through the natural texture of
materials (such as cashmere, linen), it highlights value; Second, navy blue (Navy Blue) serves as
an auxiliary color, and its symbolic meaning stems from the tradition of the British Royal Navy
and the dress code of Ivy League schools, pointing to an inherited social network and
institutional power; Third, the logo-free design strategy and color selection form an intertextual
relationship, achieving the highest-level brand recognition through "de-branding" color
language, with examples such as Hermès' "windbreaker beige" and Chanel's "little black dress"
being typical. This color grammar, through habitual repetition (Bourdieu's "habitus"),
internalizes class taste as seemingly "natural" aesthetic preferences, thereby achieving symbolic
separation from other classes.
Meanwhile, the rise of "moneyless style" on social media reflects the strategy of young
people to achieve "reverse segregation" through color deconstruction, challenging the
traditional fashion power structure.
