RadViz represents data attributes in the form of annular bands and data samples as nodes, where 253 
the nodes are located inside the circle loop. At the time, the nodes reflect position values of the 254 
attribute keywords included in the annular band ac cording to the data attributes of the node [43]. 255 
These attribute keywords were called “dimensional  anchors”. The dimensional anchor refers to a 256 
point in the process where the applied strength of data instance nodes varies in accordance with their 257 
values [44,45]. Dimensional anchors are presented as points at equidistant intervals on a 258 
circumference. Figure 7a shows an example of a Ra dViz plot in which the color information of the 259

A parallel coordinates visualization plot shows a set of points in N-dimensional space. It is 264 
generally in a vertical form and consists of N equally spaced parallel lines. It enables one to 265 
understand the relationship between variables in the data easily. According to Inselberg [31], parallel 266 
coordinates can be interpreted to have a positive  correlation between two dimensions when most 267 
lines of each variable are parallel. When most li nes intersect, they can be interpreted to have a 268 
negative correlation. In Figure 7b, each data instance is represented by a line graph. The relationship 269 
between the variable MPG and the variable cylinders is negative, while the relationship between the 270 
variable horsepower and the variable weight is positive, in general.  271

Based on the pros and cons of the two aforementioned visualization methods, we concluded that
RadViz visualization requires an auxiliary means to support intuitively viewing the shape elements of
each logo trend model in detail. We also concluded that parallel coordinates fulﬁll this requirement.
Accordingly, we also concluded that using these two visualization methods simultaneously would
provide suitable results in displaying logo trend visualizations.
However, directly implementing the linear form of parallel coordinates without modiﬁcations
would cause gaze dispersion when the user switches between both visualizations. Furthermore, even
when applying a large number of variables, there exists a problem of poor readability because the axes
must be compactly placed in a linear space.
Thus, through assessments with the experts, we tried to devise a harmonious way to integrate both
visualization techniques. The combination of RadViz and circular parallel coordinates was selected
as the ﬁnal model system for visualization. This visualization is intended to secure readability in
understanding the data characteristics through presentation of the data variables by matching the
positions of the dimensional anchors of the RadViz and the axes of the parallel coordinates. The process
of implementing this visualization and its results are described in detail in the next section.
5. The Logo Trend Visualization System
This section introduces logo trend visualization based on design shape element data of logos that
have been quantiﬁed earlier. Our visualization system is in a circular form with parallel coordinates
around the ring where the dimensional anchors of RadViz are represented.
The reason for combining two visualization techniques (RadViz and the circular parallel coordinates)
in this study is that both serve different purposes. RadViz helps in representing the cluster of logo trend
model while the circular parallel coordinates allow us to analyze the details of logo design elements.

6.3. Case 3: Logo Trends Evolving within the Same Cluster
First, the patterns of evolution were observed when we analyzed the visualization of logo trends
present in a speciﬁc cluster. Figure 14 shows how the logo trend “Mosaic” in 2009 evolved over time
into a new trend. The trends that belong to the “Mosaic” trend evolution fall under Cluster 1 in RadViz
as these trends feature combinations of objects having diﬀerent colors. In the “Mosaic” trend, the shape
element characteristics are unions of surfaces having colorful concepts.
In 2010, the trend evolved to “Pixels”, which had similar color concepts and surfaces to the
previous trend. One diﬀerence of the “Pixels” trend is that it is composed of objects with square- and
rectangle-shaped surfaces to match the name “Pixels”.
Based on the “Pixels” trend, similar trends appeared in 2011 and 2012 after implementing diﬀerent
shape elements. The “Bucky” trend in 2011 featured triangular surfaces that were di ﬀerent from the
design patterns of the “Pixels” trend. Furthermore, in the “Bucky” trend, the characteristic of line
thickness was added to make each object seem separated from each other. For the “Tessellation” trend
in 2012, various types of surfaces were coordinated, and various elements related to natural objects
such as butterﬂies and ﬁsh were added to display the logo transformation.
The trends described above became integrated and evolved to the “Trixelate” trend in 2015.
Although this trend had similar surface characteristic to the “Bucky” trend, the existing colorful concept
was removed, acquiring a monochromatic and analogous color concept. Additionally, in contrast with
the “Tessellation” trend, the natural object element was removed and more artiﬁcial shape elements
(‘Artifact’ and ‘Geometry’) were incorporated in the “Trixelate” trend.
Figure 15 shows how the logo trend “Concentric”, created in 2011, evolved over time into a
new trend. The trends belonging to the evolution of “Concentric” fall under Cluster 5 in RadViz as
they share elements that commonly show rhythm. The “Concentric” trend has the characteristic of
conveying a feeling of rhythm in a process where numerous lines are arranged into a repetitive pattern.
After 2011, this trend received attention again in 2015 in relation with a trend called “Concentrak”,
with similar shape elements.

7. Conclusions
This study prepared the classiﬁcation criteria based on the Principles of Form and Design for logo
classiﬁcation and quantiﬁed the logo trend data accordingly. RadViz and circular parallel coordinates
visualization methods were used to implement the logo trend map based on the quantiﬁed data.
We were able to identify the frequently used shape elements through the visualization system that was
created. In addition, we were also able to understand how the concept of a shape element changes
when a logo trend leads to a new trend over time. In particular, eight cluster patterns featuring similar
shape elements were extracted after applying a large number of logo trend resources. In each cluster,
unique design shape elements were incorporated in addition to elements frequently used in the data of
this study. This can be considered as a successful result in contrast with our previous work, where
logo cluster trends could not be clearly identiﬁed and separated. Additionally, the evolutions of
logo trend patterns were observed in both cases, i.e., analysis of one cluster and analysis of multiple
clusters simultaneously.
Our research helps in comparing and judging trends that ﬁt the actual situation because it provides

In each cluster,
unique design shape elements were incorporated in addition to elements frequently used in the data of
this study. This can be considered as a successful result in contrast with our previous work, where
logo cluster trends could not be clearly identiﬁed and separated. Additionally, the evolutions of
logo trend patterns were observed in both cases, i.e., analysis of one cluster and analysis of multiple
clusters simultaneously.
Our research helps in comparing and judging trends that ﬁt the actual situation because it provides
a classiﬁcation system for aesthetic, geometric, and formative elements, while reﬂecting the latest

are able to use our analysis tools to understand the trend of logo trends requires further conﬁrmation
since the system in our study has been created targeting those who are engaged in logo design or those
evaluating design trends.
Therefore, in the future, we plan to verify the eﬀectiveness of this study after conducting usability
veriﬁcation experiments on general users in all ﬁelds who intend to make or analyze logos. In addition,

text:
[Page 1]
 
ATTENTION-DRIVEN DESIGN: HOW INSTRUCTIONAL DESIGNERS DESIGN 
TO CAPTURE THE LEARNER’S ATTENTION 
by 
Malik Stalbert 
 
WENDY ZENDER, PhD, Faculty Mentor and Chair 
CARLA LANE, EdD, Committee Member 
SUSETTE CZEROPSKI, PhD, Committee Member 
 
J. Heather Welzant, PhD, Dean 
School of Public Service and Education 
 
A Dissertation Presented in Partial Fulfillment 
Of the Requirements for the Degree 
Doctor of Philosophy 
 
 
Capella University 
May 2022 

[Page 2]
 
© Malik Stalbert, 2022 

[Page 3]
 
Abstract 
Capturing learners’ attention enables the human brain to learn and start the learning process. 
Instructional designers’ primary function is to adopt a learner-centered process of collaboration, 
solving challenges, and leveraging scientific research in neuroscience, psychology, and learning 
theories to create optimized instructional material that enables learners to transfer information to 
their long-term memory, which begins with capturing attention. Although instructional designers 
recognize the importance of capturing learners’ attention as a critical component of the learning 
process, they must currently rely on a definition of attention derived from other scientific 
domains that are incompatible with the systematic instructional design methods. Therefore, to 
continue advancing a learner-centered approach to instruction, there is a need to understand how 
instructional designers define and capture attention through their design. This study was essential 
to understand what procedures, decisions, successes, and failures practicing instructional 
designers experience when designing to capture learners’ attention. When capturing the 
experiences of a diverse group, a qualitative methodology was used in this research. The 
theoretical pillars for this study were the conditions of learning theory and cognitive load theory. 
The cognitive load and conditions of learning theories describe a learning and instructional 
theory, respectively. An essential focus of this study was to recruit participants who met 
predefined criteria through a purposeful sampling strategy. Thirteen eligible participants were 
interviewed for this study using audio-recorded virtual meeting technologies. The data analysis 
process identified expressions, codes, recurring words, themes, and categories throughout the 
interviews. This study’s analysis of the data produced seven themes grouped into the following 
three categories: defining attention, attentional design strategies, and knowing the learners. The 
findings reveal that instructional designers believe that capturing attention is critical to creating a 

[Page 4]
 
successful design and to transferring knowledge. According to the results of this study, 
instructional designers typically refer to attention as a conditional factor dependent on the 
specified objectives, goals, and context (i.e., the working environment). The participants 
described capturing attention as a cooperative effort from start to finish. Further research could 
investigate how instructional designers could maintain attention throughout each phase of their 
design processes in a collaborative work environment. 

[Page 12]
1 
CHAPTER 1. INTRODUCTION
An instructional designer’s function is to analyze and solve learning problems by 
effectively and efficiently developing material designed to transfer knowledge to learners’ long-
term memory (Antwi, 2017; Kirschner et al., 2018; Sanga, 2019). The instructional design 
process can either follow a list of prescribed procedures grounded in various relevant theories or 
be viewed as an open, dynamic, and nonlinear process guided by the situation (Z. Chen, 2018). 
Traditionally, the designer ensures that the principles of the design process are followed. In other 
words, the designer is expected to adhere to the rules of a specific model (Z. Chen, 2018). 
However, modern instructional design defines the designer as a human instrument in the design 
process and is expected to adapt to relevant contextual changes and situations (Z. Chen, 2018; 
Lim, 2016). Furthermore, Demiral-Uzan (2015) highlighted the inseparability of designers from 
the process judgments related to design. The inability to separate the two means that a designer’s 
practical experience, knowledge base, and opinions are directly connected to the success or 
failure of a design project (Demiral-Uzan, 2015; Newman, 2015). 
As there are variations within every process related to instructional design, the 
instructional designer must attempt to align the ideas of understanding learners, what it means to 
learn, and recognition of the science of how individuals obtain and understand new information 
(Lim, 2016). A designer must maintain a clear understanding of how learners learn to provide a 
clear path for the designer to develop effective instructional material. To accomplish a clearly 
defined path, the designer must adhere to instructional theories that represent a framework of 

[Page 13]
2 
procedures focused on explaining the phenomenon of how human performance is manifested. 
Gagné’s nine events of instruction provide such a framework. The nine events of instruction 
were developed as the second half of Gagné’s conditions of learning theory and provide a 
systematic approach that can assist in structuring training that is optimized for the learner 
(Newman, 2015). The first event Gagné identified was gaining attention. 
Gagné’s conditions of learning theory describe the conditions of learning that impact 
either the type of learning or the environment as internal and external conditions (Rose, 2019). 
Gagné described five distinct categories of learning along with nine events of instruction. The 
nine events of instruction were designed primarily to manage mental progression. Gagné’s nine 
events of instruction were designed to be systematically followed and focus on learning 
outcomes to achieve a successful design. Gaining attention is the first event that must be 
achieved to be successful through the remaining events. The remaining events include informing 
the learner of objectives, simulating recall prior to learning, presenting the content, providing 
learning guidance, eliciting performance, providing feedback, assessing performance, and 
improving transfer/preparation. 
While many researchers have studied the nine events of instruction, attention has not 
been thoroughly investigated in the context of instructional design. Much of the literature 
regarding attention concerning learning, instructional design, and practitioners in the field has 
revolved around a global definition stemming from neuroscientific, evolutional education 
psychology, human cognition, and behavioral science backgrounds (Anderson & Kim, 2019; 
Becker & Rohleder, 2020; Burnik et al., 2018; Kirschner et al., 2018; Theeuwes, 2018). 
However, the literature has mainly concentrated on physical reactions to stimuli, eye focus, and 
emotional responses (Risko & Kingstone, 2017). 

[Page 14]
3 
In essence, the research has looked at physical reactions and mental definitions. 
However, the research has not looked at attention in the way instructional designers must 
observe attention—as the entry point to working memory, a primary function of learning, 
affecting behavioral outcomes on micro and macro scales, and as a component that works 
together with the thinking process of the brain (Eyal et al., 2019; Güney, 2019; Kirschner et al., 
2018; Marchetti, 2014). Borrowing definitions of attention from resources that do not advocate 
for instructional design science may lead to an unclear definition of what attention truly means in 
instructional design (Merrill & Twitchell, 1994; Osler & Wright, 2015). Gathering attention and 
the subsequent strategies required to gather attention as a top-down cognitive process is at the 
core of what enables humans to learn (Bonicalzi & Gallotti, 2018). 
Bonicalzi and Gallotti (2018) revealed an interesting element about the effects of 
attention gathering; it can go in both directions by affecting the designer and all others involved. 
In other words, a planner unfamiliar with proper strategies for catching the learner’s attention 
runs the risk of unintentionally diverting the learner’s attention, causing split attention, and 
sabotaging the learning process (Sweller et al., 2019).

metadata.core_insight_en: This dissertation explores the concept of attention-driven design in instructional design. The study reveals that instructional designers consider capturing attention as a critical component of the learning process, which enables learners to transfer information to their long-term memory. However, there is a need to understand how designers define and capture attention through their design.
metadata.core_insight_ko: 이 논문은 교육 설계에서 주의 집중 기반 디자인 개념을 탐구하며, 학습자의 장기 기억으로 정보 전달을 가능하게 하는 주의 포착의 중요성을 강조한다. 그러나 디자이너들이 주의를 어떻게 정의하고 설계를 통해 포착하는지에 대한 이해는 아직 부족하다.

text:
Borrowing definitions of attention from resources that do not advocate 
for instructional design science may lead to an unclear definition of what attention truly means in 
instructional design (Merrill & Twitchell, 1994; Osler & Wright, 2015). Gathering attention and 
the subsequent strategies required to gather attention as a top-down cognitive process is at the 
core of what enables humans to learn (Bonicalzi & Gallotti, 2018). 
Bonicalzi and Gallotti (2018) revealed an interesting element about the effects of 
attention gathering; it can go in both directions by affecting the designer and all others involved. 
In other words, a planner unfamiliar with proper strategies for catching the learner’s attention 
runs the risk of unintentionally diverting the learner’s attention, causing split attention, and 
sabotaging the learning process (Sweller et al., 2019). 
Gathering attention is a potent element that, if misused, can morph well-designed 
contextually sound material into a systematic approach to instruction that leaves the learners and 
their environment out of the equation by using a vague definition of attention and thereby 
misdirecting or splitting their attention (Güney, 2019). From education to psychology to 
neuropsychology, instructional design draws from many disciplines to understand learners and 
their cognitive capacity to absorb information, as stated in John Sweller’s (2019) cognitive load 
theory. Cognitive load theory describes how the difficulty of a given task influences the 
resources available to the brain (Brachten et al., 2020). Regarding gathering attention, the 

[Page 15]
4 
literature consistently describes attention gathering as a critical concept to recognize when 
interfacing with humans and for humans to comprehend the outside world (Güney, 2019; Irons & 
Leber, 2018; Jeroen & Kirschner, 2020). 
Not only does the literature recognize attention as a critical element needed to understand 
how humans process information about the surrounding environment, but it is also essential to 
initiate the learning process (Jeroen & Kirschner, 2020; Kirschner et al., 2018). Cognitive load 
theory points out that all incoming information the learner receives is through sensory memory. 
However, if a learner’s attention is not adequately piqued, the sensory elements required to 
activate the working memory for encoding to long-term memory can never be reached 
(Kirschner et al., 2018). Accordingly, designers may jeopardize the success of a project by not 
familiarizing themselves with methods and ramifications of capturing attention and achieving the 
primary aim of transferring knowledge to long-term memory (Kirschner et al., 2018; Sweller, 
2019; Zhang & Goh, 2018). Furthermore, a lack of awareness concerning capturing attention can 
unintentionally divert the learner’s attention, causing a cognitive overload of redundant or 
distracting information (i.e., split attention) and sabotaging the initiation of the learning process 
(Shadiev et al., 2017; Sweller, 2019; Zhang & Goh, 2018). 
Although attention gathering exists in two domains (internal and external), it is 
fundamental to virtually all mental responsibilities and cascading cognitive effects (Plebanek & 
Sloutsky, 2019). Studies like Plebanek and Sloutsky’s have acknowledged the definition of 
selective attention as the ability to focus on essential data while sorting out unnecessary 
information. However, this process requires access to the working memory, which is not 
accessible without capturing attention (Bray, 2017; Connor, 2017; Likourezos & Kalyuga, 2017; 
Marchetti, 2014). 

[Page 16]
5 
Understanding how to gain attention at the design stage becomes even more critical 
because working memory decays over time, preventing even the capability of rehearsal from 
taking place (Peng, 2019; Plebanek & Sloutsky, 2019). Switching images, changing 
environmental objects, and introducing new concepts, if not filtered through attention-gaining 
strategies, can plague instructional material in a subtle but destructive way. Attention or lack 
thereof can affect cognitive alertness, memory, decision-making, behavior, and even muscular 
fatigue (Cruz-Montecinos et al., 2018). 
The practical knowledge of gaining attention highlights the issues: A clear understanding 
of what attention is to instructional designers, while important, is not widely understood or 
known (Demiral-Uzan, 2015). The literature maps out that gaining attention is at the heart of 
many industries, education, communication, learning, growth, perception, and personal 
development through society when interfacing with an audience of any type (Demiral-Uzan, 
2015; Kirschner et al., 2018). At the center of this are those who must harness this understanding 
of attention across domains (i.e., instructional designers) to be part of the dynamic solution while 
developing something that connects and guides learners and instructors to a successful outcome 
(Kirschner et al., 2018). 
This study examined instructional designers’ methods for addressing the critical function 
responsible for initiating learners’ thought processes, namely, capturing attention (Ali et al., 
2017; Jackson-Butler, 2016). Because instructional designers primarily learn from past 
experiences, other instructional designers, and case studies, this research is highly transferable to 
those who may need it in the field, as the need to gain the learner’s attention has become a 
priority throughout industries of all types (De Brito Neto, 2017). However, instructional 

[Page 17]
6 
designers may struggle to fully comprehend how to capture learners’ attention through design, 
resulting in adverse outcomes (Boukhechba & Bouhania, 2019; Varonis & Varonis, 2015). 
The literature consistently defines instructional designers as diverse and as working in 
many industries (Rabel, 2019). Therefore this research acknowledges the unpredictable number 
of factors that may arise during any given project by recruiting instructional designers of every 
level. The researcher recruited 13 self-described instructional designers of various professional 
working levels to answer the following research question: What design process do instructional 
designers use to gain attention identified as the first event of Gagné’s nine events of instruction? 
Background of the Study 
The idea of what instructional design would be and the tasks attributed to practitioners 
can be identified by the words of the American philosopher John Dewey. In 1899, during a 
presidential address to the American Psychological Association, Dewey (1900) articulated a need 
for what he called a “linking science” that would act as a middleman (Reigeluth, 1983). 
Reigeluth’s research on instructional design pointed out that the linking science is instructional 
design. 
Throughout the history of modern education and the many iterations of what we now call 
instructional design, there has been a push to find the synergy between technology, philosophy, 
learning processes, and a clear definition of what it means to be an instructional designer (Sharif 
& Cho, 2015; Sugar & Luterbach, 2016). While instructional design existed under other names 
before World War II (Schubert, 2019), its relevance was solidified as it was recognized for 
developing a successful composite of film and instructional material that is credited with the 
many successes of the war on the battlefield and in manufacturing (Sharif & Cho, 2015). The use 
of technology in the practice of instructional design sets in motion the desire for instructional 

[Page 18]
7 
designers to maintain a skill set that leverages ever-shifting modern technology in a culturally 
diverse environment (Bond et al., 2019; Valencic, 2019). 
Over time, the debate of what instructional designers are and what they do has shifted. 
However, the field of instructional design has not abandoned its scientific, philosophical, and 
technological principles designed to calculate precisely potential phenomena (Valencic, 2019).

metadata.core_insight_ko: 이 논문은 교육 설계에서 주의 집중 기반 설계 개념을 탐구하며, 교육 설계자들이 학습 과정에서 주의 집중을 핵심 요소로 인식하고 이를 통해 학습자의 장기 기억으로 정보 전달을 가능하게 한다는 점을 보여줍니다. 그러나 설계자들이 어떻게 주의를 정의하고 포착하는지에 대한 이해는 여전히 필요합니다.

text:
While instructional design existed under other names 
before World War II (Schubert, 2019), its relevance was solidified as it was recognized for 
developing a successful composite of film and instructional material that is credited with the 
many successes of the war on the battlefield and in manufacturing (Sharif & Cho, 2015). The use 
of technology in the practice of instructional design sets in motion the desire for instructional 

[Page 18]
7 
designers to maintain a skill set that leverages ever-shifting modern technology in a culturally 
diverse environment (Bond et al., 2019; Valencic, 2019). 
Over time, the debate of what instructional designers are and what they do has shifted. 
However, the field of instructional design has not abandoned its scientific, philosophical, and 
technological principles designed to calculate precisely potential phenomena (Valencic, 2019). 
The inclusive growth of the instructional design field, as described by Valencic, has made 
identifying a central procedure in instructional design more vague than precise to some 
instructional designers and stakeholders. However, as early designers were categorized simply as 
engaging in the design process (Valencic, 2019), today’s designers are considered a component 
in the process. In essence, the literature on instructional design points to the science of design 
(Osler & Wright, 2015). The science of design offers a path that directs designers from a 
scientific framework to a technological domain, finally ending up in a philosophical environment 
to translate their ideas as an art form (Boukhechba & Bouhania, 2019). 
As society has made giant leaps into the realm of high-tech gadgets and connected 
interfaces, the modern world is where instructional designers must contend with learners who 
have shorter attention spans and a necessity to adapt rapidly to global technological shifts 
(Ciampaglia et al., 2015). The base utility of instructional design was established during World 
War II for two reasons. The first was that pioneers like Gagné had the same technological 
knowledge of the tools utilized for training (training films) as the soldiers for whom they 
developed instruction (Sharif & Cho, 2015). Second, alongside instructional design progress on 
the front lines, it was also critical to train Ford Motor Company employees using rapid design 
and development to produce tanks, airplanes, firearms, and other materials needed for the war 
(Schubert, 2019). 

[Page 19]
8 
In essence, there was a common language, a joint attentional capturing threat on which 
stakeholders could focus, and an environment structured around communicating shared ideas. 
The second factor existed in that the adaptive nature of humans and the concept of war captured 
soldiers’ and industrial workers’ attention in what is referred to as preattention in this study 
(Leding, 2020; Schubert, 2019). The learners (soldiers and workers) understood that missing any 
information in their education could mean losing a life. Successfully integrating technology, 
capturing soldiers’ attention, and utilizing instructional design practices to transfer information 
all highlight what L. Chen (2019) referred to it as an environment that magnified the process of 
learning and interpretation of meaning. 
Over time, instructional design practitioners have found themselves constantly struggling 
to bridge a technological communication gap between their knowledge of emerging technologies 
and the cultural changes the disconnect brings (Bond et al., 2019). As a result of growing up in 
an interconnected society and rapid advancements in mobile technology, learners have shorter 
attention spans (Baghdasarin, 2020). This positions instructional designers between the 
frameworks that define a systematic approach to instructional design and learners who expect 
and require more information in a shorter amount of time. Many of the instructional design 
frameworks and theories used in practice today were developed before this shift in the attention 
span of learners occurred.  
The gap described created a shift from the instructional design practitioner incorporating 
new technologies to enhance the design’s overall effectiveness to the technology that complies 
with a more learner-centric environment that determines what technologies the designer would 
use (Bartlett & Vavrus, 2017; De Brito Neto, 2017; Richardson et al., 2019; Stanley, 2015). 
Although the combination of media technology and instructional design historically solidified 

[Page 20]
9 
the direction instructional design would take, the inability of the instructional design field to 
keep pace with technology and the culture surrounding it presents ambiguity regarding design 
decisions (Bond et al., 2019; Valencic, 2019). Misunderstandings of the instructional design 
process and how designers interact with stakeholders in various environments force instructional 
designers to mix and match various design methodologies to solve any number of real-world 
problems (Lachheb & Boling, 2018). 
In these environments, instructional designers are faced with solving problems using their 
repertoire or making an attempt to infer a solution when none is available (Kirschner et al., 2018; 
Zhu et al., 2020). The environment described highlights the issues in instructional design that 
leave designers to find a solution by observing other designers. The literature has indicated that 
many governments, agencies, and foundations worldwide are increasingly in need of 
professional instructional designers at various competency levels (i.e., novice, intermediate, or 
professional; Zhu et al., 2020). However, regardless of the instructional designer’s level of 
competency, judgment, environment, or content, the information may not be absorbed without a 
plan to capture learners’ attention successfully. As time passes, and with the rapid move to 
online education, capturing attention has become a vague idea in what Ciampaglia et al. (2015) 
called the attention economy (i.e., collective attention), defined as the vast amount of information 
traveling through a social information exchange network, all competing for attention or cognitive 
resources (see also Sha & Lu, 2015). 
Businesses have found a need to compete for the attention of a workforce surrounded by 
an abundance of attention-capturing stimuli (Suhasini & Suganthalakshmi, 2015). However, the 
proliferation of attention-capturing stimuli has a draining effect on the working population 
(Suhasini & Suganthalakshmi, 2015). Furthermore, the attentional drain effect could be the cause 

[Page 21]
10 
of many individuals not possessing sufficient attention capacity to fulfill the business needs of 
companies as they compete in the global market (Sha & Lu, 2015). Therefore industries are 
looking to instructional designers to develop efficient and practical material that captures 
learners’ attention to combat the effects of the attention economy (Sha & Lu, 2015). The 
literature concerned with attention is complex and, in some cases, contradictory (e.g., Nguyen et 
al., 2020). However, attention is the driving force for many, if not most, of known human 
experiences, motivations, and performances. 
Whether the attention is perceptual or intellectual, it is a critical component of how the 
human brain maps an unknown number of mental categories (Fortney, 2020; Valencic, 2019). 
Instructional designers must have a clear understanding or definition of something as crucial as 
gaining attention. A generic understanding of attention capturing would be analogous to medical 
doctors having a uniform understanding of pain, its cause, and the remedies to apply to every 
patient who complains of various aches and pains. In such a scenario, if a medical doctor treats 
all complaints of pain with the same solution, many patients will suffer. Unfortunately, the only 
option for the patients in this analogy would be to deal with the issue independently. This 
scenario would not be ethical, nor would it be effective on a grand scale. Similarly, instructional 
designers must avoid adopting a uniform understanding of attention. 
Instructional designers are charged with solving educational problems that begin with 
gathering the learner’s attention in a world where there is constant competition for attention and 
a thirst from every industry to harness it.

metadata.core_insight_ko: 이 논문은 교육 설계에서 주의 집중 기반 설계 개념을 탐구하며, 교육 설계자들이 학습 과정에서 주의 집중을 핵심 요소로 인식하고 이를 통해 학습자의 장기 기억으로의 정보 전달을 가능하게 한다는 점을 밝혔다. 그러나 설계자들이 어떻게 주의를 정의하고 포착하는지에 대한 이해가 더 필요함을 강조한다.

text:
Instructional designers must have a clear understanding or definition of something as crucial as 
gaining attention. A generic understanding of attention capturing would be analogous to medical 
doctors having a uniform understanding of pain, its cause, and the remedies to apply to every 
patient who complains of various aches and pains. In such a scenario, if a medical doctor treats 
all complaints of pain with the same solution, many patients will suffer. Unfortunately, the only 
option for the patients in this analogy would be to deal with the issue independently. This 
scenario would not be ethical, nor would it be effective on a grand scale. Similarly, instructional 
designers must avoid adopting a uniform understanding of attention. 
Instructional designers are charged with solving educational problems that begin with 
gathering the learner’s attention in a world where there is constant competition for attention and 
a thirst from every industry to harness it. When instructional designers focus on attention through 
design, they penetrate the fundamental purpose of education according to cognitive load theory: 
to transfer knowledge to long-term memory for later use (Sweller, 2019). The need to understand 
what attention means to working practitioners is an essential piece of the puzzle that gives them 

[Page 22]
11 
access to the learner’s cognitive, behavioral, and physical resources needed to comprehend, 
learn, and understand how to utilize what they have learned (Dong & Li, 2020; Fortney, 2020; 
Garlitch & Wahlheim, 2020; Y. Liu & Sun, 2018; Salzman et al., 2021; Tonelli et al., 2020). As 
learning has been the reason for human advancements (Ullah et al., 2015), instructional designers 
are the architects charged with paving the way through the micro, macro, and mega contexts of a 
given problem (Hoard et al., 2019; Sharif & Cho, 2015). 
This research views the instructional designer as a centerpiece to a more significant 
communication issue between the attention economy and the designer’s approach to compete for 
and capture the attention of the target audience through the design process. 
Need for the Study 
Most instructional design models contain some element of Gagné’s nine instructional 
events, and most instructional designers implement some form of Gagné’s theories because they 
can facilitate numerous learning styles (Das, 2017). Furthermore, Gagné’s theories are 
considered the cornerstones of instructional design practices (Das, 2017; Jaiswal, 2019; Wong, 
2018). Gagné’s theories are some of the most researched in instructional design (Jackson-Butler, 
2016) and are acknowledged as a necessary theoretical basis for current and future generations 
(Jackson-Butler, 2016). Although there are some disagreements among researchers about the 
effectiveness of some of the nine events of instruction, most instructional design theorists agree 
that gaining attention is a practical and critical stage of learning of any kind (Jackson-Butler, 
2016). 
However, it should be noted that much of the disagreement can be summed up by the fact 
that the nine events are applied differently by instructional designers and instructors as the events 
are utilized in teaching activities, learning, and design (Rose, 2019). Owing partially to a lack of 

[Page 23]
12 
job-specific professional development and a clear professional identity, many designers may 
have an internal understanding of concepts concerning how gaining attention works and how 
important it is to learning (Sharif & Cho, 2015; Valencic, 2019). However, few instructional 
designers have a detailed understanding of attention in various contexts, how to harness it, or the 
negative ramifications of misdirecting it (Varonis & Varonis, 2015). As shown in an attention-
driven game development study by Varonis and Varonis, designers would be better served with a 
fundamental understanding of capturing attention. 
This lack of a more in-depth understanding of attention is of great concern to the future of 
instructional design, education, technological advancements, and industries of all types due to a 
growing need for instructional designers in most fields (e.g., education, film, architecture, 
engineering; Basdogan et al., 2020; Clarke, 2020; Howard & Rose, 2020; Sharif & Cho, 2015). 
In addition, a need to move learners rapidly from the classroom to the working environment 
(virtual or real) and the idea that all learning has some connection to the learner’s attention 
highlight the need for instructional designers who understand capturing attention. Although only 
23% of instructional designers self-identify as primarily instructional designers, and 52% of the 
general public are not aware of what an instructional designer is, the core function of an 
instructional designer remains the same (Adnan & Ritzhaupt, 2018; Sharif & Cho, 2015). 
Instructional designers must work with stakeholders, solve problems (Antwi, 2017; 
Sanga, 2019), and harness scientific research in neuroscience, psychology, and learning theory to 
develop optimized instructional material to efficiently develop strategies that will allow learners 
to transfer information to their long-term memories (Eyal et al., 2019; Kirschner et al., 2018; 
Valencic, 2019). If instructional designers are not aware of strategies, frameworks, or 
consequences related to misdirecting or diverting attention, they run a significant risk of 

[Page 24]
13 
sabotaging an otherwise well-structured project and adding demands on learners’ working 
memory (Sweller, 2019). Throughout much of the literature, the demands placed on the working 
memory are referred to as cognitive load (Sweller, 2019). Cognitive load is defined as any 
demand on the working memory’s ability to store and process information (Sepp et al., 2019; 
Sweller, 2019). 
An instructional designer must understand that attention is key to the working memory 
(Güney, 2019); it can change a learner’s perception of an object’s perceived size or augment 
sound and color (Anderson & Kim, 2019; Güney, 2019; Symonds, 2018); it can alter a learner’s 
perception of the environment (Lai & Chang, 2020); it can prevent information absorption 
(Donald & Donald, 2015; Yang et al., 2020); it affects the learner’s muscle fatigue and blood 
flow to areas of the brain (Aleksandrov & Knyazeva, 2017; Salzman et al., 2021); and it is the 
main factor in a learner’s imagination and self-efficacy (Clark & Paunovic, 2018). 
Although the vast amount of research regarding attention swings dramatically between 
cognitive internal and external attention, much of the research has aimed to capture attention and 
understand what can distract from attention. Therefore, regardless of the instructional model, 
technology, or content of a particular design, instructional designers capturing learners’ attention 
is a critical element for learning to begin (Kuehn & Pleger, 2018; Nasrollahi & Daneshfar, 2018; 
Rasim et al., 2018; Szpiro & Carrasco, 2015; Wright, 2014). Unfortunately, however, the 
research revolving around instructional designers’ understanding of the scientific underpinnings 
of the cognitive process of attention and appropriate strategies for gathering learners’ attention in 
the design process is lacking (Khalil & Elkhider, 2016). Therefore, instructional designers must 
produce well-designed instruction that takes “capturing attention” as thoughtfully and as 
essential as the human brain does (Valencic, 2019). 

[Page 25]
14 
Purpose of the Study 
This study examined what procedures, decisions, successes, and failures practicing 
instructional designers experience when designing to capture learners’ attention. Designers, in 
many cases, exist as the centerpiece of developing content designed to activate learners’ 
cognitive processes in a given learning environment (Honebein, 2017).

However, there is a need to understand how designers define and capture attention through their design.

text:
Unfortunately, however, the 
research revolving around instructional designers’ understanding of the scientific underpinnings 
of the cognitive process of attention and appropriate strategies for gathering learners’ attention in 
the design process is lacking (Khalil & Elkhider, 2016). Therefore, instructional designers must 
produce well-designed instruction that takes “capturing attention” as thoughtfully and as 
essential as the human brain does (Valencic, 2019). 

[Page 25]
14 
Purpose of the Study 
This study examined what procedures, decisions, successes, and failures practicing 
instructional designers experience when designing to capture learners’ attention. Designers, in 
many cases, exist as the centerpiece of developing content designed to activate learners’ 
cognitive processes in a given learning environment (Honebein, 2017). Furthermore, depending 
on the work environment, instructional designers are expected to have specific production 
competencies (e.g., video editing, photo editing, web development, composition, and Microsoft 
technologies) in their repertoire for use at any given moment (Hoard et al., 2019; Schubert, 
2019), highlighting a need to understand how instructional designers operate and perform 
specific duties (i.e., capturing attention) continuously while maintaining a collaborative 
connection to an open exchange of ideas (Sharif & Cho, 2015). 
More specifically, all instructional designers must have a high level of comprehension 
regarding cognitive issues surrounding the science of learning (Morris, 2016) and develop 
interactive learning environments that motivate and stimulate the target audience by capturing 
attention and simplifying complex learning designs (Adnan & Ritzhaupt, 2018; Morris, 2016; 
Schubert, 2019). 
Significance of the Study 
The implication of this research exists in the significance of understanding what 
instructional designers comprehend as attention in the design process. This research adds to the 
scientific knowledge by concentrating on how instructional designers manage a vital component 
enabling a learner’s reception to incoming instruction and allowing learning to begin (i.e., 
gaining attention; Melina & Seufert, 2020). Professional development material for instructional 
designers is limited (McKenney, 2018), and this is compounded by the fact that details related to 

[Page 26]
15 
essential components of a designer’s decisions during the design process are even more limited 
(McKenney, 2018). This research produced needed context-driven data to add to the literature 
surrounding how instructional designers address capturing attention and avoiding the adverse 
effects of cognitive load. 
Much of the research on attention concerning learning, instructional design, and 
practitioners in the field has been centered on a broad definition derived from neuroscientific, 
cognitive, and behavioral scientific perspectives (Anderson & Kim, 2019; Becker & Rohleder, 
2020; Burnik et al., 2018; Theeuwes, 2018). The literature has not only recognized attention as a 
critical component to understanding how humans process information about their surroundings; 
attention is also required to initiate the learning process in the human brain (Melina & Seufert, 
2020). Examples of research regarding attention and the effect attention have on memory have 
been described in research conducted by Plebanek and Sloutsky (2019), who maintained that 
efficient allocation of attention is a critical element in many situations. Salzman et al.’s (2021) 
work concerning the effects of attention on behavior and motor skills is another example worth 
noting. It is also the case that the top-down process of imagination relies on attention (Plebanek 
& Sloutsky, 2019). Furthermore, managing muscle fatigue and visually understanding the world 
around one requires attention as the initiator and fuel of physical and cognitive events 
(Aleksandrov & Knyazeva, 2017; Cruz-Montecinos et al., 2018). 
Although attention is divided into two cognitive domains (i.e., voluntary and 
involuntary), attention in both domains is essential to almost all mental responsibilities. Most 
importantly, if attention in either domain is neglected, unexpected cascading cognitive effects 
may result (Aleksandrov & Knyazeva, 2017; Plebanek & Sloutsky, 2019). Therefore the data 
produced by this study are a critical piece of the puzzle for instructional designers who want to 

[Page 27]
16 
understand how other instructional designers deal with various types of attention in different 
environments, which includes the instructional designer’s attention. In essence, instructional 
designers must be responsible for collaborating with stakeholders and content experts; 
interfacing with new environments; managing interventions; leveraging their technological and 
interpersonal skills to the benefit of the project; produce a finished product that takes an 
unknown number of factors into considerations, while also compromising with project 
constraints; maintain high ethical and scientific standards; use both hemispheres of the brain; 
create interactive and creative learning environments; incorporate scientific design models; 
understand the learning process and the learner; and maintain their training to update their 
knowledge on all fronts (Adnan & Ritzhaupt, 2018; Antwi, 2017; Battle, 2019; Brill, 2016; 
Grincewicz, 2017; Jackson-Butler, 2016; Morris, 2016; Olson, 2018; Richardson et al., 2019; 
Schubert, 2019; Sharif & Cho, 2015; Tracey & Hutchinson, 2019). 
Although the preceding list of responsibilities may seem obtuse, it is not close to a 
complete list of duties and skills needed to manage large and small projects as an instructional 
designer (Basdogan et al., 2020). However, it should be noted that instructional designers mainly 
possess a plethora of skills by nature and are drawn to instructional design (Basdogan et al., 
2020; Sizemore, 2020; Stanley, 2015). With the multitude of tasks attributed to what an 
instructional designer must complete, each task (e.g., communicating with stakeholders, 
collaborating with subject matter experts, designing for the learner, working with instructors, or 
working as an instructional designer/educator) requires capturing the attention of all those 
involved. 
Each interaction requires instructional designers to adapt rapidly to unpredictable factors 
that stem from gathering the attention of those involved (Schubert, 2019). For example, failure of 

[Page 28]
17 
the design or the designer to capture stakeholder attention can jeopardize the future of a project. 
Furthermore, as the literature presented in this document suggests, if a design does not capture 
the learner’s attention, the core purpose of the design itself may become moot. 
From the attention requirements of the designer themselves to the attention they must 
capture in every stage of a project, the overall attention capture techniques used by instructional 
designers are the beginning of interfacing with others on cognitive and physical levels to garner 
interest in solving a problem and acting as an agent of change (Sugar & Luterbach, 2016; 
Theeuwes, 2018). In short, this research addressed the following research question, what design 
process do instructional designers use to gain attention identified as the first event of Gagné’s 
nine events of instruction? In addition, the research has added to the literature by clarifying the 
activities instructional designers of various levels of competency perform as they address 
capturing attention through their design processes. 
Research Question 
Instructional designers have many tools and resources at their disposal when addressing a 
problem. Although many of the tools and processes instructional designers may utilize can be 
mixed and matched to fit a particular situation, any solution that comes from such an effort is 
defined by the instructional designer’s understanding of the project and how to develop the 
project to capture the attention of the target audience and facilitate efficient knowledge transfer 
to learners. Little is known regarding instructional designers’ approach when integrating 
elements of attention capture into their design processes. This study addressed the following 
primary research question, what design process do instructional designers use to gain attention 
identified as the first event of Gagné’s nine events of instruction?

In addition, the research has added to the literature by clarifying the 
activities instructional designers of various levels of competency perform as they address 
capturing attention through their design processes. 
Research Question 
Instructional designers have many tools and resources at their disposal when addressing a 
problem. Although many of the tools and processes instructional designers may utilize can be 
mixed and matched to fit a particular situation, any solution that comes from such an effort is 
defined by the instructional designer’s understanding of the project and how to develop the 
project to capture the attention of the target audience and facilitate efficient knowledge transfer 
to learners. Little is known regarding instructional designers’ approach when integrating 
elements of attention capture into their design processes. This study addressed the following 
primary research question, what design process do instructional designers use to gain attention 
identified as the first event of Gagné’s nine events of instruction? 
This study also investigates the following subquestions: 

[Page 29]
18 
RQ1a: How do instructional designers describe their understanding of gathering attention 
related to the design process? 
RQ1b: How do instructional designers describe their decision-making processes when 
addressing Gagné’s first event of gathering attention? 
RQ1c: What approaches and resources do instructional designers use when addressing 
gathering attention? 
Definition of Terms 
This research uses the following definitions when discussing attention, instructional 
design, and the process of learning. 
Biologically primary skills. Biologically primary skills are those skills that are acquired 
through the evolutionary process (i.e., general problem solving, face recognition, listening and 
speaking a local language, imitation, socializing; Kirschner et al., 2018). 
 Biologically secondary skills. Biologically secondary skills are not acquired through the 
evolutionary process (i.e., computer skills, reading, mathematics, internet functionality; 
Kirschner et al., 2018). 
Cognitive load theory. Cognitive load theory is a theory that defines human cognition as 
limited. Cognitive load theory also puts forth that memory can only function when focused on 
short-term or long-term storage (Pouw et al., 2019). 
Component display theory. Component display theory was developed by M. David 
Merrill and puts forth that instructional outcomes may be classified according to content, content 
assets, and the learner’s performance (Antwi, 2017). 
Gagné’s conditions of learning theory. Gagné’s conditions of learning theory is a 
theory that defines five types of learning and their requirements for various instruction sets to 
promote learning (i.e., verbal data, intellectual skills, cognitive schemes, motor skills, and 
attitudes; Rose, 2019). 

[Page 30]
19 
Gagné’s nine events of instruction. Gagné’s nine events of instruction were developed 
as activities designed to align with Gagné’s conditions of learning theory. Gagné maintained that 
the nine events of instruction are required to complete the learning process (i.e., gaining 
attention, informing the learner of objectives, recall, presenting the content, providing learning 
guidance, eliciting performance, providing feedback, assessing performance, and improving 
transfer/preparation; Das, 2017). 
Selective attention. Selective attention is the learner’s ability to cognitively filter out 
unnecessary information and focus on important information (Plebanek & Sloutsky, 2019). 
Split attention. Split attention comprises principles that explain that there will be fewer 
cognitive problems in learners when information is integrated with mutually referring data. Split 
attention aims to mitigate the shift of learners’ focus from one category of information to another 
(Pouw et al., 2019). Mitigating this shift stimulates a less strenuous process of memorization 
(Pouw et al., 2019). 
Top-down attention. Top-down attention is the management of a critical cognitive 
process for interacting effectively with one’s environment. To bypass such signals and direct 
attention toward behavioral objectives, top-down control is needed (Muller Spaniol et al., 2018). 
Research Design 
This study utilized a basic qualitative research design to capture the participants’ 
experiences in their own words. A quantitative design was ruled out as it is designed to capture 
quantities or numerical data to explain a particular investigation (Coulter, 2005; Percy et al., 
2015). When conducting this research, the basic qualitative design was followed: how the 
participants view and articulate their experiences when capturing attention in the design process 
(Josilowski, 2019). According to Josilowski, qualitative research allows researchers to examine 

[Page 31]
20 
the interactions of individuals with a lived context and is thus positioned as the best way to 
answer the research question. It was important in this study that the participants were able to give 
their accounts of a particular strategy, solution, or event so that the researcher could acquire a 
deep understanding of the processes they deploy in a professional setting (Lemon & Hayes, 
2020; Neuman, 2014). 
Triangulation of data through interviews, descriptive notes, and artifacts was used in this 
research to optimize further the credibility of the data collected. NVivo 12 was used to establish 
credibility. NVivo 12 is a qualitative data management and data analysis application that data 
mines references, search for co-occurrences, and analyzes themes and relationships (Lemon & 
Hayes, 2020). This study collected data through semistructured interviews and work examples 
(artifacts). The interviews were audio-recorded and became more open-ended as the participants 
became more comfortable and provided more information. The recordings were transcribed and 
stored under randomly generated, unique alphanumeric identifiers that represent the participants. 
Instructional designers learn primarily from their and others’ experiences, which 
increases the transferability of the research findings (De Brito Neto, 2017). Therefore this study 
was conducted using a purposeful sampling strategy. Included in this study were 13 self-were 
analyzed inductively described instructional designers who had different backgrounds and 
professional career levels (N. Liu, 2018). This method increased the likelihood that the research 
would produce rich content and related material (Josilowski, 2019). The inclusion criteria were 
as follows: self-described instructional designers, those who have worked as a designer in the 
field, those who have worked as an instructional designer in any way in the development of 
educational materials, and those who are working in the field as a professional. 

[Page 32]
21 
Instructional designers are diverse and dynamic and work in various industries with a 
wide range of skills and experiences that must conform to real-world solutions, stakeholders, 
social environments, and community norms that present various constraints (Rabel, 2019). 
Therefore, this study revolved around the instructional designers’ definition of capturing 
attention and the theoretical underpinnings that support their efforts and experiences. As such, 
the researcher wrote all the research questions, filtered all transcribed themes, and organized all 
documents through the lens of three theoretical frameworks (i.e., cognitive load theory [Sweller, 
2019]; component display theory [Merrill, 2007]; and conditions of learning theory [Gagné, 
1985]) to maintain consistency in the categorization of events, techniques, discussion questions, 
technologies, and collected media. 
More precisely, the conditions of learning theory were used to categorize verbal 
information, intellectual skills, cognitive techniques, motor skills, and attitudes (Tough, 2012). 
Cognitive load theory was utilized to analyze cognitive concepts throughout the study to map 
each identified concept to a participant-described training system or method (Sepp et al., 2019). 
Finally, component display theory was used as a practical tool for classifying technological 
elements of the particular design methods participants described. Although each of the theories 
mentioned is uniquely qualified as a stand-alone basis of guidance, the work produced by 
instructional designers must fall under all or one of these theories (Wong, 2018).

Assumptions and Limitations 
Assumptions 
The following assumptions were made in this study: 
• Instructional design theory components are within every instructional designer’s 
successful project (Valencic, 2019). 

[Page 33]
22 
• Designers have an implicit or explicit working pattern that facilitates learners and 
captures their attention through proper design and analysis (Wong, 2018). 
Limitations 
Following are the limitations identified in this research: 
• The recorded interviews were audio-only, leaving descriptions of body language or 
mannerisms unobserved when participants responded. 
• A small sample size of 13 participants was a limitation of the study. However, 
empirical research has revealed that the first five to six interviews produce the newest 
data in research conducting interviews (Guest et al., 2020). Similarly, Guest et al. 
further described a West African study that discovered that approximately 92% of all 
the new information of a particular study relying on interviews was acquired with a 
cap of 12 participants (Guest et al., 2020). However, the small sample size limits the 
findings when placed in a broader context. 
Organization of the Remainder of the Study 
Chapter 1 addressed the study topic by providing an overview of the study’s need, 
purpose, significance, research question, definitions, research design, assumptions, and 
limitations. This chapter has identified attention as the focus of the study and one of the main 
components of learning used by the human brain (Fortney, 2020; Valencic, 2019). Chapter 1 also 
categorized instructional designers as the conductors of an induction design process that must 
balance an unknowable series of factors from stakeholders, project constraints, learners, social 
constraints/expectations, and technological constraints when navigating through a world that 
consumes the attention of the learner at every moment (Ciampaglia et al., 2015; Sha & Lu, 

[Page 34]
23 
2015). This chapter identified instructional designers as dynamic in their skill sets, with diverse 
backgrounds (Rabel, 2019). 
Chapter 1 introduced the idea that without a clear understanding of attention and how to 
gain it, the functions of the human brain required to induce learning may not be accessible. The 
ideas surrounding capturing attention lie at the foot of the primary function of what it means to 
be an instructional designer: to understand the target audience, stakeholders, technology, and 
science through engagement to solve problems (Antwi, 2017; Sanga, 2019). This chapter 
articulated that instructional designers must harness scientific research in neuroscience, 
psychology, and learning theory to develop optimized instructional material designed to enhance 
information transfer within the learner and deliver a project designed to capture attention and 
achieve the stated goal (Valencic, 2019). 
Instructional designers’ understanding of theoretical concepts around the human brain 
and how designers utilize this knowledge are part of the design’s anatomy. The implication of 
this research exists in the significance of understanding what instructional designers comprehend 
as attention in the design process, as it will also determine the functionality and ethics of a 
project designed to enhance information transfer within the learner in the most efficient manner 
(Antwi, 2017; Melina & Seufert, 2020; Sanga, 2019). 
Chapters 2–5 are remaining. Chapter 2 contains a review of the literature related to 
instructional designers and how they gather attention. Chapter 2 includes further discussion on 
the study’s theoretical basis while also summarizing relevant literature and frameworks. Chapter 
3 is a description of the methodology deployed in this study and an outline of the data collection 
instruments used in this research. Chapter 4 presents the data and includes an analysis of the 
data, a rationale of the methods used, and a description of the technologies deployed to support 

[Page 35]
24 
the research. Chapter 5 contains the discussion, implications, and recommendations. This chapter 
discusses the findings along with suggestions for future research. 

[Page 36]
25 
CHAPTER 2. LITERATURE REVIEW
This research examines instructional designers’ techniques for addressing the crucial 
component responsible for activating the learner’s mental process, namely, capturing attention 
(Ali et al., 2017; Jackson-Butler, 2016). Chapter 2 is a discussion on the following five specific 
points: source search methods, relevant theoretical orientations, a literature review of capturing 
attention, a synthesis of the review findings, and a critique of methods and procedures presented 
in the review. 
The method of searching section describes how the sources used in the literature review 
were found. A theoretical orientation section defines how the research components were 
developed. The literature review section provides an account of the foundational literature that 
supports this study. The synthesis of the research findings follows the literature review and 
discusses the more prominent themes surrounding capturing attention concerning instructional 
design. A critique of previous research methods provides a critique of the literature review. 
Chapter 2 concludes with a summary of conclusions derived from the literature. 
Methods of Searching 
An array of resources was used to compile the peer-reviewed literature used in this 
research. The technology used for the search is categorized as primary search, internal search, 
and verification search technologies. Primary search technologies represent technologies that are 
traditionally used to query online databases containing peer-reviewed research. These 

[Page 37]
26 
technologies are the following websites/database portals: ProQuest Central, SAGE, Academic 
Search Premier, ERIC, and Education Database. 
The preceding databases were accessible through the Capella University Library online 
portal by entering phrases or keywords. Primary keywords were as follows: instructional design, 
attention research, split attention, cognitive load theory, Gagné’s nine events of instruction, 
instructional designer’s methods, attention capturing techniques, defining attention, cognitive 
architecture, capturing attention, types of attention, learner’s attention, effects of attention, 
consequences of attention, attention capturing models, theories in attention, attention driven 
design, and attention defined. This list of phrases was used to refine the search and, in some 
cases, to categorize resources. The list was also used to filter out critical definitions of the search 
from the literature that may not apply to the research. For example, the databases allow the user 
to filter by date, document type, author, and more to confine the search criteria. 
Internal search represents the search between documents on a local level. In other words, 
after resources were identified, downloaded, and categorized, internal search technologies were 
used to search within each document. For example, the search method described above was done 
using Zotero, NVivo 12, and Microsoft Word search modules within each document. The 
software listed in the previous sentence helped to rapidly search through hundreds of documents 
in a short amount of time to find words, themes, cited references, and titles. In addition, using 
this method allowed the researcher to simultaneously highlight critical concepts in hundreds of 
documents while also exporting notes describing the nature of the highlighted literature. 
Verification search technologies are secondary databases used to verify documents with 
contradictory authors, dates, or missing information. Although these search methods were rarely 
used, they were helpful when a question arose regarding particular publishing data of a 

[Page 38]
27 
document. For this study, the primary verification databases/websites were Google Scholar and 
Summon.com.

Theoretical Orientation for the Study 
Two theoretical pillars supported this study: conditions of learning theory (Gagné, 1985) 
and cognitive load theory (Sweller, 2019). Cognitive load theory and conditions of learning 
theory represent learning and instructional theory, respectfully. Şanal et al. (2019) explained that 
a learning theory should guide all stages of the instructional design process to help identify 
learning principles. Similarly, Honebein (2017) pointed out that instructional theory may help 
designers be more precise in judging practical methods by isolating contextually effective 
methods over others. 
Both instructional and learning theories with accompanying guiding principles, according 
to Valencic (2019), are often blended with other learning theories as a practical, unique solution 
for instructional designers and educators. Historically speaking, advancements in learning 
theories have directly contributed to the development and growth of instructional design (An, 
2021). Valencic (2019) suggested that there is no one ideal learning theory; instead, there are 
applications of theory that are optimal for a specific task, learner, or learning environment. 
Şanal et al. (2019) further explicated that education cannot occur randomly but must be 
organized and primarily supported by learning theories that support the instructional design 
process. Likewise, the nature of attention capturing through the design process presented in this 
study aligns closely with constructivist and instructional learning theories. 
Learning Theories 
Şanal et al. (2019) explored the critical importance of learning theories concerning 
instruction practices by examining behaviorism, cognitivism, and constructivism learning 

[Page 39]
28 
theories. This study observed the complex nature of learning as existing within the three listed. 
Although the literature routinely groups educational learning theories as a list of six, that is, 
behaviorism, cognitivism, constructivism, experiential, humanistic, and social-situational 
learning theories (Boylan-Ashraf, 2020), this dissertation describes only the three theories listed 
herein to provide a brief contextual outline of the theoretical orientation used in this study. 
Behaviorism 
Behaviorism follows the premise that knowledge is self-contained and external to the 
learner and uses stimuli to elicit a change in a learner’s behavior (Drumm, 2019). Although 
behaviorism was the first primary theory to become popularized in modern education, many 
educators lament behaviorism’s failure to address issues surrounding teaching knowledge 
(Valencic, 2019). 
Cognitivism 
The failure of behaviorism to account for all types of learning gave rise to cognitivism 
(Boylan-Ashraf, 2020). While behaviorism views learning as a passive participant where the 
instructor transfers knowledge, cognitivism views the learning as an active participant in the 
learning process (Boylan-Ashraf, 2020; Drumm, 2019). Boylan-Ashraf (2020) described 
cognitivism as a theory that views knowledge as a symbolic mental construction where the mind 
orders and processes all information. In cognitivist learning techniques, internal cognitive 
processes, such as motivation, reflection, and prior knowledge, are considered (Drumm, 2019). 
Constructivism 
Constructivism shifts the role of the instructor from an architectural position to a 
facilitator that helps learners develop structures of knowledge on their own in a student-centered 
teaching environment (Drumm, 2019). Constructivism assumes a process of learning that 

[Page 40]
29 
resembles building blocks; in other words, the learner is in a constant mode of constructing 
knowledge rather than immediately acquiring it (Boylan-Ashraf, 2020). The constructivist 
learning theory describes how individuals form meaning based on their environment (Şanal et 
al., 2019). That is to say, constructivist theory explains how individuals know what they know 
(Igwe et al., 2020). To be more specific, constructivist theory helped this study explain what 
instructional designers know when designing to capture attention. 
Conditions of Learning Theory 
Modern instructional design can be directly attributed to Robert Gagné, who created the 
conditions of learning theory and was regarded as a pioneer in the field (Jaiswal, 2019; Ullah et 
al., 2015). Gagné’s conditions of learning theory was structured to define various levels of 
learning by outlining the mental conditions needed to maintain a practical path to the intended 
learning outcomes (Jaiswal, 2019). The various learning outcomes articulated by conditions of 
learning theory are coupled with the internal and external factors required to facilitate each. 
Conditions of learning theory define five categories of learning: intellectual skills, cognitive 
strategies, verbal information, motor skills, and attitudes (Ullah et al., 2015). When using 
conditions of learning theory, analysis and planning are needed to achieve appropriate instruction 
designed to produce a successful learning outcome (Wong, 2018). 
Nine Events of Instruction 
Gagné’s conditions of learning theory are split between learning and methods for 
determining if learning has occurred for two types of learning circumstances: internal and 
external conditions (Alam & Ahmad, 2017). Internal conditions are the learner’s prior skills that 
can be altered during the learning process; nevertheless, various external factors significantly 
impact the learner’s capacity to learn (Alam & Ahmad, 2017). Alam and Ahmad explained how 

[Page 41]
30 
some external conditions could include family, instructors, or environmental factors. Alam and 
Ahmad further explained how undesired external factors could cause issues within the learning 
process. 
The core structure of Gagné’s conditions of learning theory exists as four components: 
conditions of learning, association learning, five categories of learning outcomes, and the nine 
events of instruction (Alam & Ahmad, 2017). The nine events of instruction comprise the 
framework to achieve the desired learning outcomes (Woo, 2016). Each learning outcome 
requires a different method of instruction to promote learning. For example, Gagné’s nine events 
of instruction are capturing attention, informing the learner of objectives, stimulating recall prior 
to learning, presenting the stimulus, providing learning guidance, eliciting performance, 
providing feedback, assessing performance, and enhancing preparation and transfer. This 
research is centered around the first event, capturing attention. 
In other words, the five conditions of learning require the nine events of instruction. 
Furthermore, the nine events of instruction are designed to affect the internal processing of 
information in a strictly prescribed order to achieve successful results (Ullah et al., 2015). The 
first event (i.e., gaining attention) is the starting point that must be achieved to proceed to the 
remaining events of instruction. Therefore it is more likely that learning will not occur if the first 
event is not achieved and the learning conditions are not satisfied. 
Cognitive Load Theory 
With a focus on various training types (e.g., e-learning, in-class learning, hybrid), 
Sweller’s (2019) cognitive load theory focuses on specific domains and secondary information 
that refers to the stresses imposed by the brain’s cognitive processes on working memory. For 

[Page 42]
31 
example, cognitive processes like planning, development, automation, and problem-solving are a 
few categories that load the process (Ginns & Leppink, 2019).

first event (i.e., gaining attention) is the starting point that must be achieved to proceed to the 
remaining events of instruction. Therefore it is more likely that learning will not occur if the first 
event is not achieved and the learning conditions are not satisfied. 
Cognitive Load Theory 
With a focus on various training types (e.g., e-learning, in-class learning, hybrid), 
Sweller’s (2019) cognitive load theory focuses on specific domains and secondary information 
that refers to the stresses imposed by the brain’s cognitive processes on working memory. For 

[Page 42]
31 
example, cognitive processes like planning, development, automation, and problem-solving are a 
few categories that load the process (Ginns & Leppink, 2019). 
Cognitive load theory states that the primary focus of instruction of any kind is to assist 
in transferring information from the external environment (e.g., sensory information, 
environmental data, contextual information, biologically secondary skills) to the working 
memory. Biologically secondary skills are skills that must be taught in an educational and 
training situation (Kirschner et al., 2018). The working memory can augment the information, 
which can be imprinted/encoded into the long-term memory for processing (Güney, 2019). 
Güney, in a study on cognitive learning, pointed out that cognitive load theory defines the 
structure of cognition as being a platform held up by short-term memory and long-term memory 
consisting of limited and limitless capacity, respectfully. Figure 1 outlines the processes of 
incoming data as they pass through from working memory to long-term memory. Figure 1 
illustrates the importance of understanding cognitive load and how it may stress the input data to 
imprint the information. Acceptance of the incoming data is activated by capturing attention and 
later avoiding unnecessary distractions or stress. 
Cognitive load theory explains how information is visually translated, understood, and 
memorized and details the capacity of memory to absorb input information physically and 
visually through the cognitive process of learning (Güney, 2019). Thus, understanding and 
utilizing cognitive load theory is essential to many instructional ecosystems. From the human 
cognitive architecture, evolutional psychology, or the processes of instructional design from 
analysis through implementation, the importance of cognitive load is documented as it represents 
humans’ capacity to absorb, interact with, and ignore mental processes for learning (Güney, 
2019; Jeroen & Kirschner, 2020; Kirschner et al., 2018; Sweller, 2019). 

[Page 43]
32 
Figure 1 
Cognitive Load Theory 
 
Note. Information process model illustrating the process data takes through human memory and how long incoming 
data remain available for recall. Adapted from “Human Memory: A Proposed System and Its Control Process,” by
