Copyright 1968 by Academic Press. Adopted with permission. 
In addition, cognitive load theory recognizes knowledge as being separated between 
biologically primary and secondary knowledge (Jeroen & Kirschner, 2020). Biologically primary 
knowledge effortlessly follows the dotted line illustrated in Figure 1, entering the sensory 
memory through the working memory and stored in the long-term memory. However, 
biologically secondary knowledge may be forgotten without an intentionally designed learning 
environment (Jeroen & Kirschner, 2020). Biologically primary knowledge represents knowledge 
humans have evolved to acquire effortlessly without direct instruction. For example, skills such 
as supporting the community or troubleshooting problems are two biologically primary 
knowledges. Conversely, biologically secondary knowledge represents skills that generally take 
a reasonable amount of effort, are acquired consciously, and are determined by cultural 
determinations of what is essential (Jeroen & Kirschner, 2020; Kirschner et al., 2018; Sweller, 
2019). Writing a well-formatted document or research paper would be an example of 
biologically secondary knowledge. 


[Page 44]
33 
Types of Cognitive Load 
Cognitive load theory recognizes intrinsic, germane, and extraneous load as three types of 
strain brought on by learning tasks, instruction, and the design of the instruction (Sweller, 2019). 
However, germane load is historically recognized as indistinguishable from intrinsic load and is 
considered redundant when an intrinsic load is being addressed (Jeroen & Kirschner, 2020). 
Intrinsic Load. New information within a lesson or training presents inherent 
complexities and is defined in cognitive load theory as intrinsic load. Therefore intrinsic load 
occurs naturally when new or challenging information is presented to the learner (Sweller, 2019). 
Extraneous Load. The vast majority of the adverse effects of cognitive load theory 
derive from extraneous load and are mainly triggered by instructional design methods (Sweller, 
2019). For example, when tasks like discovery are performed, extraneous load is present in 
instructional material that does not inform the expected results. As a result, unproductive stress is 
placed on the learners and their working memory while increasing the effort required to analyze, 
process, and complete unexpected tasks or incorporate new data (Jeroen & Kirschner, 2020). For 
example, if a student was learning a new skill and was introduced to multiple ways to achieve the 
desired results too early, it could confuse the learner and cause an extraneous load. 
This research used cognitive load theory to formulate and guide questions related to 
human cognition. Cognitive load was used in this research to discover themes and acquire a 
deeper understanding of answers provided by the participants while also shedding some light on 
descriptions by participants that needed further exploration or clarity. 
Review of the Literature 
This literature review focuses on investigating how instructional designers capture 
attention through their design methods. It is crucial to explore how the field defined and 

[Page 45]
34 
harnessed attention over time to understand better the role of capturing attention in instructional 
design. Although recent literature explicitly acknowledges gaining attention as a priority for 
instructional designers to produce engaging content (De Brito Neto, 2017), historically, it was 
not always clearly defined how critical gaining attention is to the instructional design process 
(Logan, 2020; Sharif & Cho, 2015). For example, Logan (2020) observed, in a research article 
that summarizes 35 years of the Professors of Instructional Design and Technology conference 
meetings, that the focus of the historic conferences had been focused on program design, 
development, and new research. 
However, the initial participants of the Professors of the Instructional Design and 
Technology conference concluded that gaining the attention of groups outside of the instructional 
design field to address the day-to-day issues of learners was the path forward. The focus on 
addressing the global issues of instructional design by gaining learners’ attention and outside 
partnerships gave rise to many of the dynamic partnerships of technologically advanced 
companies. Companies like Google and Virtual Reality/3D partnered with instructional design 
and technology professors to further understand how to interface with the learners’ attention and 
facilitate their professional growth across industries (Logan, 2020). 
Instructional Design Guided by Attention 
The symbiotic relationship between the instructional design process and gaining attention 
is fundamental and begins at the inception of the learner’s cognitive process (Melina & Seufert, 
2020). Not only is the learners’ mental process greatly influenced by the state of attention, but 
the literature also shows a relationship between instructional design and gaining the attention of 
the target audience that closely connects advancements in instructional design with the 

[Page 46]
35 
technology used throughout its evolution (Acland, 2017; An, 2021; Bond et al., 2019; Logan, 
2020; Sharif & Cho, 2015). 
As a developing discipline, social environment and cognitive attention availability 
determined the instructional design field’s direction (Sharif & Cho, 2015).

text:
Instructional Design Guided by Attention 
The symbiotic relationship between the instructional design process and gaining attention 
is fundamental and begins at the inception of the learner’s cognitive process (Melina & Seufert, 
2020). Not only is the learners’ mental process greatly influenced by the state of attention, but 
the literature also shows a relationship between instructional design and gaining the attention of 
the target audience that closely connects advancements in instructional design with the 

[Page 46]
35 
technology used throughout its evolution (Acland, 2017; An, 2021; Bond et al., 2019; Logan, 
2020; Sharif & Cho, 2015). 
As a developing discipline, social environment and cognitive attention availability 
determined the instructional design field’s direction (Sharif & Cho, 2015). In particular, 
instructional designers became evenly concerned with behavior and cognitive attention capacity 
using constructivist and behaviorist methods as a response to the attention generated by new 
technologies, politics, and social mood (Logan, 2020; Sharif & Cho, 2015; Sizemore, 2020). For 
example, Reiser (2001) explained that during World War II, the advancements of film and audio 
in the schools had halted because the learners’ attention to the military was a priority. Therefore, 
Reiser explained that audiovisual instructions shifted to industries and military services to 
respond to the type of learners being targeted and the greater need of society. In essence, 
instructional designers had to harness critical tasks and objects related to essential tasks of the 
circumstances while also capturing the attention to transfer information to the learner to promote 
unity and social responsibility among civilians. 
Attention on War Demanded Dramatic Changes 
During World War II, instructional design viewed the learners’ attention as essential but 
lacked a specific definition due to its roots in educational psychology and behaviorist principles 
(Sizemore, 2020). World War II represents the spark that induced a first-time adoption of the 
systematic approach fundamental to modern instructional design concerning capturing the 
attention of the learners (An, 2021). For example, in response to World War II, the instructional 
design field dramatically shifted from instruction only designed to inform a learner of 
rudimentary skills they were expected to learn to a focus on capturing the learners’ attention 
using audiovisual material (An, 2021). Capturing learners’ attention in order to educate them to 

[Page 47]
36 
be adept with military machines, vehicles, weapons, and other significant items of the period was 
preestablished and ingrained in the environment as a result of the conflict, which justified the 
need for instruction to rely on behaviorist principles (Sizemore, 2020). 
On the other hand, the emotions brought on by events such as the war added relevance to 
instructions that harnessed intrinsic motivations of the target audience (Ginsberg & Wlodkowski, 
2019). Intrinsic motivation is an internal motivation that facilitates and directs all motivation to 
the desired outcome linked to the participants’ learning process (Ginsberg & Wlodkowski, 
2019). Intrinsic motivations were applied to capture social attention, gave instructional designers 
justification to capture attention, and focus it on cognitive principles to achieve group cohesion 
among the civilian, military, business, and governmental groups. While not explicitly defined in 
the initial development of modern instructional design, the goal to harness various types of 
attention of participants across cultural groups and experiences was the foundational challenge of 
designing effective instructional material for current and future use, as articulated above. 
Attention on Space Demanded a New Direction 
Just as World War II produced focused attention that researchers in instructional design 
used to develop historic advancements in education and the technology used, The launch of 
Sputnik in 1957 induced a focused attention on improving education by getting closer to the 
learners’ cognitive attentional capabilities (An, 2021). Although Sputnik represented the first 
artificial Earth satellite and the beginning of the space race, it also represents a shift in the 
instructional design field from behaviorism to a view that knowledge is a symbolic mental 
construction where the mind orders and processes all information, i.e., cognitivism (An, 2021). 
Unlike behaviorism, where the learners are viewed as passive participants who receive 
knowledge from the instructor, cognitivism redirected the practitioners in the field of 

[Page 48]
37 
instructional design to view the learners as active participants in the learning process (Boylan-
Ashraf, 2020; Drumm, 2019). In essence, a successful outcome of instruction was no longer 
solely determined by the instructor but now required the learners’ explicit attention (individual or 
group attention), motivation, and other internal processes as part of a design. The shift to the 
learners’ internal attention and perceptions instead of a more global attentional event, as 
described in current research, reveals the depth in which instructional designers were expected to 
reflect on the learners’ mental process in the design. 
S.-Y. Lo (2018) conducted a study exploring how attention interacts with perceptual 
groupings outside the learners’ awareness. Perceptual grouping in the Lo study was defined by 
various elements, colors, contours, and movements the mind uses to make meaning. Studies that 
examine perceptual grouping can be traced back to 1923 and are supported by empirical research 
demonstrating the effects on attention (S.-Y. Lo, 2018) but escalated after the shift to 
cognitivism was complete (An, 2021). Research shows that attention is what allows perceptual 
grouping to accelerate the process of making meaning from ambiguous objects (S.-Y. Lo, 2018), 
while social attention (i.e., attention of others in society) allows learners to demystify complex 
tasks (Steinmetz & Pfattheicher, 2017). 
The Lo study represents empirical research that many instructional designers looked to as 
one of many definitions of individual attention. In contrast, studies like Rennung and Göritz 
(2015) represent the attempt to define global attention shared by a society or group, as was the 
case during World War II. Rennung and Göritz’s study established a link between shared 
attention, personal sacrifice, and group cohesion that verifies the importance of attention on 
participants’ behavior and cognitive thought processes. Rennung and Göritz’s study argued that 
crises such as war are an intense negative shared effect that increases group cohesion, reduces 

[Page 49]
38 
adverse outcomes, and synchronizes brain activity among participants. Rennung and Göritz 
added that focusing on emotional stimulus alone can bypass the need to share emotional 
experiences for group cohesion to develop actively. This recognition of the type of attention 
brought on by World War II and studies that focus on the learners’ internal individual attentional 
experiences remain in today’s cognitive and constructivist pathways to instructional design 
development (An, 2021). 
The shift from a behaviorist approach in instructional design to a cognitivist approach 
gave designers a better understanding of the importance of the learners’ attention while also 
providing more insight into the many possible definitions of attention. The composition of the 
learners’ experience and where attention sits in the order of importance was defined in 1965 by 
Robert Gagné as part of the foundation of instructional design as a systematic approach to design 
(An, 2021). 
Gagné’s Historical Guiding Framework 
Frameworks/models such as Gagné’s nine events of instruction embody the current shift 
to a learner-centered approach to instructional design. Gagné’s nine events require the following 
nine events to activate the learners’ cognitive process that allows them to store information in 
long-term memory: gaining attention, informing the learner of the objects, stimulating recall 
prior to learning, presenting the stimulus, providing learning guidance, eliciting performance, 
providing feedback, assessing performance, and enhancing preparation and transfer. Existing as a 
part of Gagné’s conditions of learning theory, the nine events of instruction provide a systematic 
approach to structuring training that is optimized for the learners (Newman, 2015).

text:
Gagné’s Historical Guiding Framework 
Frameworks/models such as Gagné’s nine events of instruction embody the current shift 
to a learner-centered approach to instructional design. Gagné’s nine events require the following 
nine events to activate the learners’ cognitive process that allows them to store information in 
long-term memory: gaining attention, informing the learner of the objects, stimulating recall 
prior to learning, presenting the stimulus, providing learning guidance, eliciting performance, 
providing feedback, assessing performance, and enhancing preparation and transfer. Existing as a 
part of Gagné’s conditions of learning theory, the nine events of instruction provide a systematic 
approach to structuring training that is optimized for the learners (Newman, 2015). Although the 
instructional design process aims to store information in the learners’ long-term memory, 
Gagné’s nine events of instruction suggest that every instruction should begin with the action 

[Page 50]
39 
that activates a learner’s cognitive ability to access the long-term memory (i.e., gathering 
attention). 
Specifically, regardless of the instructional designer’s choice of frameworks, tools, or 
environment, capturing the learner’s attention is the one event that must be achieved to activate 
the long-term storage capability of the brain (Eyal et al., 2019; Güney, 2019; Kirschner et al., 
2018; Marchetti, 2014). Therefore, it is essential to understand that Gagné’s nine events of 
instructions, as described by Reiser (2001), are considered the cornerstones of instructional 
design practices. Furthermore, Gagné’s nine events of instruction were structured to give 
designers a systematic way of intentionally promoting the internal learning process (Jaiswal, 
2019). 
Although there is a large and diverse library of methodologies and frameworks for 
instructional designers to use, many of them, if not all, provide some form of Gagné’s theoretical 
structure (Jaiswal, 2019). Gagné’s nine events of instruction have been tested over many years 
and have proven to be the key to activating long-term memory (Jaiswal, 2019). Gagné’s nine 
events is a process-oriented model representing a complete shift of instructional design to a 
learner-centered instructional design approach (Jaiswal, 2019). By nature, and as suggested by 
Gagné’s nine events, the focus on the learners means initially capturing their attention. 
Furthermore, the historical iterations of instructional design have culminated much of its 
advancements to succeed in an attention economy and a learner-centered environment. 
Capturing Attention 
As instructional designers made the shift to a learner-centered approach, the notion of 
capturing the learners’ attention in the context of education has largely been relegated to a few 
basic presentation concepts (Jaiswal, 2019). Instructional design literature tacitly defines 

[Page 51]
40 
capturing attention as using prompts, body gestures, repetition, displaying relevant information, 
showing imagery, or using humor as strategies to stimulate the learners’ attention (Das, 2017; 
Demiral-Uzan, 2017; Ullah et al., 2015; Wong, 2018; Woo, 2016). However, research has 
suggested that a deeper investigation of how instructional design defines attention on a 
theoretical scale while also prescribing concrete methods of capturing attention requires 
understanding the brain’s learning process (Kuehn & Pleger, 2018; Leppink & Pérez-Fuster, 
2019; Nasrollahi & Daneshfar, 2018; Rasim et al., 2018; Szpiro & Carrasco, 2015; Wright, 
2014). 
When viewed theoretically, multiple studies investigating concepts such as behavioral 
science, constructionism, neuroscience, evolutional education psychology, and others that 
address attention and its relationship to learning represent the many ways instructional designers 
must research to get a complete picture of what attention means (Anderson & Kim, 2019; Becker 
& Rohleder, 2020; Burnik et al., 2018; Kirschner et al., 2018; Theeuwes, 2018). For example, a 
study on goal-oriented attention capture by Anderson and Kim (2019) argues that understanding 
multiple distinct learning mechanisms could create a bias. On a fundamental level, understanding 
how this bias may occur requires an instructional designer to understand the risks and benefits of 
value-driven attentional capture much better. 
Defining Capturing Attention for Instructional Design 
While the Anderson and Kim (2019) study may give designers an understanding of 
value-driven attentional capture and the biases that may occur when performing such capturing, 
it is not a complete picture of what attention means in the fullness of the instructional design 
process. To achieve a complete picture of what they may need as a guide to methods of capturing 
attention, an instructional designer may have to look at research that describes the concept of 

[Page 52]
41 
“selective attention” (Theeuwes, 2018, p.1), “uniform attention” (Leong et al., 2017, p.460), 
“gaze cueing” (R. F. Lo et al., 2021, p.3), “cognitive load” (Leppink & Pérez-Fuster, 2019, 
p.422), and or “intrinsic motivation” (Ginsberg & Wlodkowski, 2019, p.58). The preceding 
research represents a few studies addressing the definition of attention in various contexts, which 
can create a web of confusion for an instructional designer seeking practical solutions to 
capturing attention. 
Well-known cognitive concepts, such as split attention, cognitive load, or even 
Theeuwes’s research on attention selection and properties of top-down and bottom-up attention, 
merely give a designer a general idea of types of attention as opposed to methods of using the 
understanding of types of attention within the context of the instructional design process. This 
generalized position leaves the designer with the task of bridging the gap between learner-
focused instructional design frameworks that acknowledge the critical importance of attention, 
such as Keller’s ARCS model or Gagné’s conditions of learning and specific use cases present in 
various studies (Adnan & Ritzhaupt, 2018; Grincewicz, 2017; Leong et al., 2017; Lim, 2016; 
Sizemore, 2020; Yang et al., 2020).  
If a designer successfully develops a systematic approach to gaining the learners’ 
attention based on their composite understanding, they are then tasked with managing two 
concepts in defining attention. The first concept of attention is defined as stimuli, eye-focus, or 
emotional response (Risko & Kingstone, 2017). The second concept of attention afforded to 
instructional designers is articulated as a purely internal process that activates the brain’s 
capacity to learn and store information (Eyal et al., 2019; Güney, 2019; Kirschner et al., 2018). 
Each of the attentional concepts represents a vast amount of literature, research, and frameworks. 

[Page 53]
42 
A study by Bichler et al. (2020) on working memory capacity revealed that a learner’s 
working memory capacity manages both internal cognitive attention and external physical 
attentional cues. Working memory capacity is the primary explanation under Sweller’s (1988) 
cognitive load theory of why a particular instruction is effective (Bichler et al., 2020; Jeroen & 
Kirschner, 2020). Working memory is primary because the capacity it maintains determines what 
will be stored in the long-term memory (Bichler et al., 2020). The research by Sweller, Bichler et 
al, and Jeroen and Kirschner could provide a path for instructional designers to understand what 
attention means for instructional design and lead them to concepts of attention capacity.

text:
Each of the attentional concepts represents a vast amount of literature, research, and frameworks. 

[Page 53]
42 
A study by Bichler et al. (2020) on working memory capacity revealed that a learner’s 
working memory capacity manages both internal cognitive attention and external physical 
attentional cues. Working memory capacity is the primary explanation under Sweller’s (1988) 
cognitive load theory of why a particular instruction is effective (Bichler et al., 2020; Jeroen & 
Kirschner, 2020). Working memory is primary because the capacity it maintains determines what 
will be stored in the long-term memory (Bichler et al., 2020). The research by Sweller, Bichler et 
al, and Jeroen and Kirschner could provide a path for instructional designers to understand what 
attention means for instructional design and lead them to concepts of attention capacity. 
Cognitive Load 
Cognitive load theory was realized after the instructional design field had transformed 
from science that viewed the learners’ attention as behavioral responses to a field that 
understands attention as an activator of the learning process (Say et al., 2019). However, as 
previously explained, during World War II, the requirement to gain attention was inherent in the 
environment; therefore, the only requirement was a more behaviorist approach to instruction 
(Schubert, 2019; Sharif & Cho, 2015). Thus, as the attention on war and survival faded, 
researchers in instructional design included a broader lens to view the learners’ attention and the 
learning process. This more expansive view led to the understanding that attention exists in many 
forms and is the key to long-term memory. This realization eventually became recognized as 
cognitive load theory (Say et al., 2019). 
Cognitive load theory recognizes two types of knowledge: biologically primary 
knowledge and biologically secondary knowledge. Biologically primary skills are acquired 
through the evolutionary process, that is, general problem solving, face recognition, listening and 
speaking a local language, imitation, and socializing (Jeroen & Kirschner, 2020; Kirschner et al., 

[Page 54]
43 
2018). Biologically secondary skills are those skills that are not acquired through the 
evolutionary process, that is, computer skills, reading, mathematics, and internet functionality 
(Kirschner et al., 2018). The distinction between biologically primary and biologically secondary 
skills is crucial to identifying knowledge by which a learner can naturally learn with little to no 
effort and skills requiring maximum effort (Jeroen & Kirschner, 2020). 
The majority of the research concerning cognitive load theory in the past 30 years has 
focused on domains such as technology and mathematics (Sentz, 2018). The research produced 
in those 30 years contributed to discovering intrinsic, extraneous, and germane cognitive load 
(Sentz, 2018). It is possible to use educational approaches to manage extraneous load in some 
situations. However, some strategies have been demonstrated to exert a more significant strain 
on the learners’ workload; discovery and inquiry learning tasks place a greater wasteful strain on 
the working memory load than other tasks and need more time and mental effort to assess, 
process, and complete. (Jeroen & Kirschner, 2020). 
The effects and remedies were also discovered during the discovery of the three types of 
load mentioned above (Sentz, 2018). Excluding germane load, the clear binary separation of 
skills that cognitive load theory provides is further expanded on through its task categorization. 
Cognitive load theory recognizes the strain certain types of tasks apply to an individual’s 
cognitive load, i.e., intrinsic load and extraneous load (Sweller, 2019). Sweller believed that 
intrinsic load is required and that extraneous load should be avoided. 
A study by Kirschner et al. (2018) that investigated cognitive load in a collaborative 
context concluded that the effects of cognitive load are not based on attention, but attention is 
based on a learner’s cognitive load capacity. The study points out that instruction can naturally 
produce intrinsic load as part of learning a new skill while redirecting learners’ attention away 

[Page 55]
44 
from vital discussion content. In other words, even when a learner’s attention has been captured 
on the pertinent information, cognitive load can still be drained on those things that have no 
attentional focus. Instructional designers define this separation of attention regarding competing 
information as split attention. 
Split Attention 
Cognitive load theory draws on cognitive architecture models to define memory and its 
limits; cognitive load theory also explains what happens when memory is overloaded, that is, 
split attention (Ginns & Leppink, 2019). However, while the working memory can be affected by 
split attention in such a way that it does not allow the learner to focus without acquiring the 
learner’s attention, a complete attention transfer of knowledge to the working memory cannot 
take place (Wong, 2018). In effect, split attention blocks the cognitive ability of the learner to 
learn (Sweller, 2019). In the context of instructional design, this could mean that any instruction 
developed without considering split attention presents a greater risk of developing an 
environment or instructions that split the learner’s attention between vital information and long-
term memory (Sentz et al., 2019; Sweller et al., 2019). 
An example of developing instruction without considering the environment could be 
understood when outside speakers or events are included in the design. If the event or speaker is 
introduced close to important test dates, the classroom environment may be more distracted by a 
looming test than the presented information. Although much of the literature on attention 
observes the mind’s external and internal processes, little is known about designers’ specific 
strategies and experiences for specific events such as gaining attention. Studies have shown that 
there is a need to acquire the learner’s attention through aggregated methodologies by way of the 
instructional design practitioners’ implementation and design choices (Brown & Stefaniak, 2016; 

[Page 56]
45 
Chasanidou, 2018; Ciampaglia et al., 2015; Irons & Leber, 2018; Roque et al., 2016; Zhang & 
Goh, 2018). 
The relevance of attention spans from the inception of instructional design through all its 
iterations over time. Although the subject of attention as a universal idea is beyond the scope of 
this research, the general understanding of what attention means to instructional designers and 
how they achieve it is at the core of what instructional designers are trained to do (Mills & 
Harris, 2019). 
Synthesis of the Research Findings 
Unrecognized differences in which psychologists and philosophers miscommunicate a 
clear definition of attention, and ways to understand attention have been a critical problem for 
nearly as long as the subject of attention has been researched (Fortney, 2017). Collectively, the 
research presented in the literature review suggests that (a) the instructional design field was 
developed with external and internal attention as part of the environment, (b) historical and 
critical decisions based on types of attention available to designers guided the development and 
growth of instructional design and instructional technology, (c) clear definitions of capturing 
attention within the context of instructional design have not been adequately formulated but have 
been acknowledged as a critical component to learning and the instructional design process, and 
(d) methods instructional designers use to merge the research, the frameworks, and contextual 
data to develop instruction based on capturing attention have not been widely explored. 
The literature review provides a perspective of instructional design guided by the 
accepted understanding of a general idea of attention related to the environment. For example, 
the externally focused attention of World War II provided the cognitive motivation that propelled 
designers to develop instruction that controlled and could predict behavior (Sizemore, 2020). 

[Page 57]
46 
Thus a behaviorist approach was justified and dominated the instructional design field, as 
dictated by external environmental attentional factors.

However, there is a need to understand how designers define and capture attention through their design.

text:
The literature review provides a perspective of instructional design guided by the 
accepted understanding of a general idea of attention related to the environment. For example, 
the externally focused attention of World War II provided the cognitive motivation that propelled 
designers to develop instruction that controlled and could predict behavior (Sizemore, 2020). 

[Page 57]
46 
Thus a behaviorist approach was justified and dominated the instructional design field, as 
dictated by external environmental attentional factors. 
The attention to the 1957 space race and the launch of Sputnik ignited a shift in 
instructional design from behaviorist methodologies to a more cognitivist mentality that 
addressed the need for critical thinking (An, 2021). Past research and an acknowledgment of the 
need to approach instruction systematically, led by capturing the learners’ attention, paved the 
way for Glaser, in 1962, to introduce the concept of instructional design and also open a path for 
Gagné to publish his conditions of learning and the nine events of instruction (An, 2021). 
Constructivist methods encouraged learners to create their knowledge and meaning of reality and 
experiences in the 1990s, thanks to the attentional impact of the technology revolution, the 
collective attentional focus on events, and the internet’s growth (An, 2021; Sharif & Cho, 2015). 
The literature explored how, as the discipline of instructional design shifted toward a 
more constructivist approach, the significance of designer decisions increased. Additionally, 
when the designer’s involvement in the design process became the topic of study and their 
judgments became essential, designers’ methods of capturing attention were not fully addressed 
throughout the history of instructional design but instead were delegated to other sciences. 
Demiral-Uzan (2017) conducted a qualitative multicase study that explored instructional designs’ 
judgment when working on design projects and argued that instructional designers do not follow 
instructional design models but rely on their ability to design based on their core values and 
professional knowledge. In essence, the literature shows that to understand attention through the 
lens of instructional design successfully, one must primarily look to the designers, not the 
frameworks. 

[Page 58]
47 
Defining attention, capturing attention, and the role of instructional designers has been 
the critical ingredient guiding instructional design, as highlighted in the literature review. 
Without capturing the learner’s attention, the design has the potential to cause the negative 
consequences of split attention and prevent the cognitive process of learning from reaching an 
optimum conclusion (Sweller, 2019). If deprived of a consistent blueprint of what capturing 
attention means through the lens of the instructional design process, instructional designers must 
pull from the influence of psychology, communication, neuroscience, and other fields that define 
attention outside the systematic nature of the instructional design field. 
A study by Basdogan et al. (2020) shows that instructional designers naturally have 
interdisciplinary skills and must become experts in near-unlimited and overlapping resolutions. 
Furthermore, Basdogan et al. maintained that instructional designers must consider the learners’ 
mental state, physical state, intellectual state, and cultural background while also bridging 
traditional instruction and online learning. The research highlighted the idea that each 
instructional designer can address the same problem in an unlimited number of ways and runs 
the risk of reinventing solutions because they rarely construct solutions based on theory or 
frameworks but mainly on past experience and knowledge. Additionally, the literature illustrates 
the need for instructional designers to understand attention on levels ranging in the multitudes to 
interface with learners in various industries, governments, societies, cultures, and so on. 
The literature examined the importance of attention to instructional design and the 
process of learning. Specifically, capturing attention enables the human brain to learn (Bonicalzi 
& Gallotti, 2018). The literature suggests that research on how instructional designers define 
attention within the context of their field or a framework that guides designers through a 

[Page 59]
48 
systematic process of capturing the learners’ attention is needed to continue advancing a learner-
centered approach to instruction. 
Critique of Previous Research Methods 
The literature review presented studies examining instructional design, attention, 
instructional design methods, and cognition. The variation in the studies throughout the literature 
review highlights the limitations of researching instructional design. Specifically, instructional 
design is a field that is influenced by many other fields and adopts concepts from other fields as 
needed (Basdogan et al., 2020). In other words, there is no single source one can point to 
throughout the literature when investigating instructional designers and capturing attention 
through design. Research defining various types of attention and attention capture is readily 
available throughout the literature (i.e., Lin & Lu, 2016; S.-Y. Lo, 2018; Nani et al., 2019; Rasim 
et al., 2018; Yang et al., 2020). 
Similarly, research examining instructional designers, methods they use in the design 
process, and instructional design frameworks are also available throughout the literature (Adnan 
& Ritzhaupt, 2018; Basdogan et al., 2020; C.-T. Chen & Gu, 2020; Hartikainen et al., 2019; 
Hoard et al., 2019; Honebein, 2017; Waluyo, 2020). However, linking the mention of attention 
throughout the studies exploring instructional design concepts, the suggestion by instructional 
design frameworks (e.g., Gagné’s nine events of instruction and Keller’s ARCS model) that 
attracting the learner’s attention must occur before learning can begin, and research that 
exclusively examines attention and attention capture is left up to each designer. When asked to 
define gaining attention, Gagné himself could only explain it in terms of startling the learner, 
which, as the literature illustrates, is not an adequate definition for capturing attention regarding 
the learning process (Gibbons et al., 2008). Gagné also proposed that the learners’ internal and 

[Page 60]
49 
external conditions and the learners’ mental processes are critical to learning (Dimou & Kameas, 
2016; Osler & Wright, 2015), which does not match his definition of attention as simply an act 
of startling the learner. 
The literature suggests that no clear bridge connects a systematic approach to capturing 
attention to instructional design, even though it is acknowledged as a critical component of the 
instructional design process and learning. The research throughout the literature review includes 
qualitative and quantitative studies, which provided guidance when investigating how 
instructional designers design to capture learners’ attention. However, the challenge of 
equivocating capturing attention as it is defined outside of instructional design, how the 
designers develop instruction, and frameworks that mention attention capture as a requirement 
with a systematic approach to capturing attention demanded an examination of research spanning 
each subject. 
Summary 
Chapter 2 discussed source search methods, relevant theoretical orientations, a literature 
review of capturing attention, a synthesis of the review findings, and a critique of methods and 
procedures presented in the review. The outline of the search methods used in the research 
described the array of search methods used to find the literature provided in this document. The 
theoretical orientation section presented two theories for the foundation for this study while also 
describing each (i.e., conditions of learning and cognitive load theory). The theoretical 
orientation section described the importance of learning theories, behaviorism, cognitivism, 
constructivism, nine events of instruction, and cognitive load theory concerning the current 
research and the literature. 

[Page 61]
50 
Chapter 2 included a literature review that discussed the importance of capturing 
attention concerning the dynamic nature of instructional design on a global or local scale. 
Chapter 2 also described the versatile nature of instructional designers within the same context. 
The literature review outlined how capturing attention has been implicitly and explicitly 
addressed through instructional design development and growth. The literature review also 
discussed attention capturing, cognitive load, and split attention through the lens of the learning 
process and the implications placed on instructional designers and the field of instructional 
design.

CHAPTER 3. METHODOLOGY
This research explores instructional designers’ opinions, experiences, and methods to 
capture attention through the design process. Chapter 3 details an outline of the methodology 
used in this study, starting with the purpose of the study. This chapter will also discuss research 
questions, the research design, the target population and sample, procedures, instruments, and 
ethical considerations. 
Purpose of the Study 
The purpose of this study was to evaluate the processes, decisions, successes, and failures 
of professional instructional designers when combining notions of capturing learners’ attention 
as outlined in Gagné’s first event of instruction and the prevailing research on attention capture. 
Gagné’s nine events of instruction comprise a systematic framework that assists in achieving the 
desired learning outcomes beginning with capturing attention (Woo, 2016). Attention represents 
the entry point to optimized human cognitive learning and interactions (Güney, 2019; Irons & 
Leber, 2018; Jeroen & Kirschner, 2020). Therefore instructional designers must manage an 
unknowable number of human interactions while also capturing the attention of many diverse 
stakeholders to maintain the possibility of a successful project (Demiral-Uzan, 2015; Kirschner 
et al., 2018). 
The transferability of this research is related to the idea that instructional designers 
primarily learn from the works of others in the field, case studies, and their own experiences (De 
Brito Neto, 2017). In essence, by collecting data regarding a better understanding of attention 

[Page 63]
52 
through the lens of instructional designers, this research connects an explicit working definition 
and analysis of attention as articulated by designers to the reading public. 
Research Questions 
This study asked the following research question: What design process do instructional 
designers use to gain attention identified as the first event of Gagné’s nine events of instruction? 
This study also investigated the following subquestions: 
RQ1a: How do instructional designers describe their understanding of gathering attention 
related to the design process? 
RQ1b: How do instructional designers describe their decision-making processes when 
addressing Gagné’s first event of gathering attention? 
RQ1c: What approaches and resources do instructional designers use when addressing 
gathering attention? 
Research Design 
This study was conducted using a basic qualitative design to answer the research 
question. Although there are many more specialized qualitative alternatives (i.e., ethnography, 
case study, grounded theory, and phenomenology), they were not suitable for this research. 
Because generic qualitative research is used to get a comprehensive understanding of a subject 
from the perspectives of its participants, it was particularly well suited for capturing the 
experiences of instructional designers as they design to capture their audience’s attention 
(Josilowski, 2019). Furthermore, a qualitative research methodology was suited for this study 
because it provides for a more inductive approach while allowing for a theory-driven or 
descriptive approach that can unveil cause, effect, the how, and the why concerning experiences 
or phenomena (Aspers & Corte, 2019; Cleland, 2017; Rocco & Plakhotnik, 2009). 
The qualitative data collection process mirrored Mishra ( 2015) and Romero-Hall et al. 
(2018) by utilizing semistructured interviews, conducting qualitative analysis, and collecting 

[Page 64]
53 
artifacts. This study used NVivo 12, a qualitative data analysis application, to manage and 
evaluate the collected data. In essence, NVivo 12 was utilized to code, organize, and analyze all 
data and information acquired. Follow-up questions were asked and answered via a secure 
messaging system where they were saved and recorded. The resulting data revealed potential 
roadblocks, solutions, and novel ideas, which aided in identifying relevant themes throughout the 
research. 
For example, the concept of inattentional blindness by instructional designers 
unexpectedly surfaced as a theme resulting from follow-up questions from the researchers and 
the analytical capabilities of NVivo 12. When completing an attention-demanding task, 
inattentional blindness is defined as the inability of an instructional designer to notice the 
relevant unexpected stimuli in their visual field that are salient to the individual (Gao & Jia, 
2017). The research data collection and interviews were conducted during the COVID-19 
pandemic. Therefore all research operations had to be completed using network-attached 
communication technologies (i.e., online collaboration technologies, cloud drives, email, and 
online survey applications). 
Before collecting any data, eligibility questions and research questions were reviewed by 
experts in the field. Before the data collection could begin, an eligibility questionnaire was 
provided to ensure that the participants met the inclusion criteria. All interviews were audio-
recorded using Zoom and Windows Media Recorder, transcribed, and input into the NVivo 12 
application for further analysis. The basic qualitative design paved the way to analyze the 
transcriptions to highlight the interesting and pertinent parts of the participants’ experiences 
when capturing attention through their design processes. This study implemented a basic 

[Page 65]
54 
qualitative design to answer the research question by utilizing online collaborative technologies, 
backup systems, and qualitative analysis software. 
Target Population and Sample 
Population 
The target group comprised instructional designers with various competencies, career 
stages, and backgrounds who met the inclusion requirements. This study did not collect any 
organizational policy information on company practices or other confidential information that is 
not already available publicly. The participants were instructional designers from the United 
States, Canada, and the United Kingdom. The participants consisted of full-time faculty, part-
time adjuncts, working professionals, and casual instructional designers who self-described as 
instructional designers as an activity related to their current work. 
Sample 
This study implemented a purposeful sampling strategy to recruit participants according 
to predefined criteria. The sample size of this study was 13 instructional designers with skill 
levels ranging from novice to professional. The sample size of 13 instructional designers was the 
original target of the study. The sample size was inspired by a study by Josilowski (2019) on 
teachers’ perceptions. Similarly, a study by Boddy (2016) on qualitative sample size described 
examples that this research could use as a reference regarding the sample size. The following 
inclusion criteria were used to select the participants for this study: individuals who have 
designed instructional materials as a professional lead or novice, self-described instructional 
designers, developers of instructional materials in an instructional design capacity, and those 
who have met the first two criteria (i.e., experienced lead instructional designers and self-

[Page 66]
55 
described instructional designers) with 2-plus years in a professional work setting charged with 
duties mirroring instructional design.

levels ranging from novice to professional. The sample size of 13 instructional designers was the

described instructional designers) with 2-plus years in a professional work setting charged with

Procedures 
Participant Selection 
The study was able to achieve an initial sample size of 13 participants. The participants 
were selected using an online service specifically designed to connect qualitative researchers to 
qualified participants securely. The online service provided access to qualified potential 
participants and supplied a communication system through a digital dashboard that protected the 
identity and personal information of all involved. The digital dashboard allowed potential 
participants to review the recruitment information before contacting the researcher for possible 
consideration. Once potential participants agreed to be considered, they answered a few 
prescreening questions that mirrored the inclusion criteria to ensure they understood the required 
qualifications before making any commitments. 
When a potential participant was qualified and agreed to participate in the study, the 
individual was presented with an informed consent form. The information in the form explained 
what was being studied, how the information would be used, why the participant may or may not 
want to participate; what, if any, risks were involved; and other details regarding the study’s 
procedures and confidentiality. After reading the informed consent form, the participants in this 
study provided their consent by digitally signing the document using a unique systems 
identification number provided by the online service. The participants were then provided with 
the option to print out the consent form for their records, a link to a secure discussion area with 
the researcher, and a calendar for scheduling.

56

experience as instructional designers. Table 1 details the industries in which the participants were 
employed at the time of the interviews and the types of projects the instructional designers would 
often develop. Table 1 categorizes the project types as in-person, hybrid, and online project 
creation types. Online projects are instructional design projects where learners receive a fully 
online or virtual experience, in-person is a traditional in-person experience as the project’s goal, 
and hybrid is a project that implements both types as needed.

The researcher intended to recruit participants from various industries to better 
understand unique approaches to attracting attention through design, identify possible parallels in 
the practices employed, and understand how designers define attention in various work 
environments. Table 1 lists three participants from the educational industry, three in the 
engineering industry, three from the computer and technology industries, one from the food 
research industry, one from the business security industry, one from the entertainment industry, 
and one from the professional training industry. Basdogan et al. (2020) described a great 
instructional designer as becoming an expert in crafting solutions that have no limit in the 
possible overlapping variations of a workable solution. Accordingly, it was also important to rate 
the participants’ instructional design experience as a combination of skills they acquired as they 
advanced in their industries and their work as instructional designers. 
In most cases, the participants first gained experience in their respective industries and 
became instructional designers a few years later. Therefore Table 1 lists the participants’ years of 
experience, including the years of developing their skills to become instructional designers in 
their related industries. Table 1 shows the participants’ project experience related to developing 
online, hybrid, or in-person projects. Although Basdogan et al. (2020) concluded that 
instructional designers must be familiar with many solutions, the researcher only listed the 
participants’ most common project development types in Table 1 (i.e., online, hybrid, or in-
person). 
Protection of Participants 
The web interface that provided the initial contact with the participants inherently 
enforces an alphanumeric username for participants. The use of an alphanumeric number means 
that when the researcher communicates with participants in the secure discussion room, the 

[Page 69]
58 
participants are identified only by their unique identification numbers. After a meeting was 
scheduled, participants were provided a unique password-protected link to access the virtual 
meeting platform during a prescheduled meeting time. The meeting schedule, the virtual meeting 
platform, and the online dashboard all used the unique identification number for the participants. 
All communications and file sharing passed through the online dashboard for security and 
anonymity. When collecting any data from the participants, no confidential information was 
requested (e.g., age, location, gender). At every stage of the process, the participants were given 
the option to withdraw from the study. 
Data Collection 
Before any communication between the researcher and potential participants could occur, 
each possible participant was assigned a randomly generated alphanumeric identification number 
to maintain the confidentiality of those chosen to participate and those not chosen but who were 
part of the selection process. Among a pool of instructional designers who indicated an interest 
in participating, only those who passed the screening and agreed to an audio-recorded interview 
were contacted through a secure web interface. The web interface allowed the potential 
participants to receive messages and documents without revealing personal data or direct contact 
information (e.g., email addresses). 
After a participant had been verified with regard to their qualifications and had digitally 
signed an informed consent form, the participant was then contacted using the online dashboard 
to schedule a date and time that best suited their schedule. Participants could text the researcher 
their preferences or use a calendar provided by the online dashboard to select a particular date 
and time. Before each interview, the researcher prepared a PowerPoint presentation that the 
participant could view through screen share functionality. The PowerPoint presentation had 

[Page 70]
59 
images and other relevant contextual information related to the questions and made it easier for 
the researcher and the participant to refer to the same elements if needed. The researcher then 
prepared a blank document containing the participant’s identification number and the research 
questions. The prepared document was used to take notes during the interview. 
All interviews were conducted and recorded via Zoom with the camera disabled and 
screen share enabled for the researcher’s computer. The participants were not allowed to share 
their camera or screen at any time. To ensure the integrity of the interview recording, the 
researcher also recorded the interview using a Windows-based recording software that also 
captured the PowerPoint presentation presented to the participants. 
The semistructured interviews lasted approximately 45–60 minutes, depending on the 
answers given by the participants and follow-up questions asked. When ending the interviews, 
the researcher asked the participants’ permission to contact them through the secure discussion 
interface for follow-up questions, deliver transcripts for their review, or as a way for them to 
obtain any work examples they may have wanted to provide as finalization questions. The audio 
data collected through the collaboration software (i.e., Zoom) was immediately transcribed and 
stored in two places: on a secure, encrypted, and private drive accessible only to the researcher 
and on a cloud backup.

their camera or screen at any time. To ensure the integrity of the interview recording, the 
researcher also recorded the interview using a Windows-based recording software that also

The semistructured interviews lasted approximately 45–60 minutes, depending on the 
answers given by the participants and follow-up questions asked. When ending the interviews, 
the researcher asked the participants’ permission to contact them through the secure discussion 
interface for follow-up questions, deliver transcripts for their review, or as a way for them to 
obtain any work examples they may have wanted to provide as finalization questions. The audio 
data collected through the collaboration software (i.e., Zoom) was immediately transcribed and

After each audio transcription was completed, reviewed for accuracy by the participant 
involved, and marked as a final version, it was stored on a portable encrypted drive, secure cloud 
drive, and local working computer. The audio files, notes, transcriptions, and work examples 
were imported into NVivo 12 for coding, organization, triangulation, and analysis. 

[Page 71]
60 
Data Analysis 
The purpose of this study was to examine the approaches employed by instructional 
designers to address Gagné’s initial event of education, namely, attention capture. Qualitative 
data arrived in various formats (i.e., documents, audio recordings, transcripts, field notes, 
computer technology), and each format was archived meticulously (Nowell et al., 2017). 
Thematic analysis served as the foundation for this study’s data analysis (Nowell et al., 2017). 
Nowell et al.’s analysis process served as the framework for this study’s analyses. Nowell et al. 
defined a six-phase thematic analysis process that incorporates establishing trustworthiness. 
After entering the data, then inserting/updating the necessary codes, both changes and 
enhancements were considered. Codes were used both as tools for organizing the data and for 
identifying topics that could be helpful in other areas of the analysis. For example, the term 
preattention came up during separate interviews a few times and was coded because it provided 
some insight into an idea that could assist the researcher in explaining other relevant concepts 
identified in the data. Additionally, coding was used to produce a list of codes that could have 
raised concerns about a particular topic. For instance, concerns regarding a negative attitude or 
possible inconsistencies would be coded for further review. 
All interviews were audio-recorded, transcribed, and updated following the procedure 
outlined earlier and advanced using constant comparative analysis as data arrived. Constant 
comparative analysis entails comparing new data with previously collected data for coding, 
categorization, and naming (Lemon & Hayes, 2020). The procedures for data collection, 
interview transcription, and data analysis using software like NVivo 12 are not discrete but are 
interrelated and can be applied in any sequence necessary (N. Liu, 2018). 

[Page 72]
61 
A thematic structure was developed by converting codes into themes directly related to 
the research questions using NVivo functionality. To be precise, themes were created using 
NVivo 12, which generates a report and a visual map based on the transcripts and categories of 
codes created by the researcher and those automatically discovered by the software. The strategy 
of manually creating codes based on direct analysis of the research data, automatic codes 
generated by the software, and NVivo 12’s feature that could visualize the data and code 
categories in contrast to the literature assisted in searching for alternative explanations of some 
of the findings. The color-coded visual maps produced by NVivo 12 made developing themes 
from code categories a simple task. 
Instruments 
Prequalification screening questions, interview questions, online collaboration 
applications, and online qualitative research dashboards were the instruments used to find 
participants and collect data. The semistructured interviews and the screening questions were 
both developed by the researcher and reviewed by experts. The expert review resulted in a 
suggested change in the sequence of some of the questions. The researcher used a PC-based 
screen capture application to present his screen and record the audio. The researcher used C# 
code and visual studio to develop a unique word search algorithm to find words through stored 
Microsoft Word and PDF documents and save the results in a unique folder for review. 
The Role of the Researcher 
When a researcher conducts qualitative research, their transferability, the findings’ 
reliability, and credibility revolve around the researcher (Rahmi et al., 2017). The researcher’s 
role in this study was to conduct interviews as an instrument, collect the research data, and 
conduct the ethical functions of the qualitative process in the study. As a result, reflexivity, 

[Page 73]
62 
reasoning, and self-awareness remained central features throughout the qualitative process. 
When a qualitative methodology is used, preunderstanding, honesty, openness, and a lack of bias 
are prioritized (Rahmi et al., 2017). 
Basdogan et al. (2020) defined instructional designers as those who must possess many 
skills to solve a given problem. As such, the researcher’s experiences as a computer science 
professor (i.e., online and in-person), martial arts instructor, tennis instructor, inventor, artist, 
musician, actor, and film director align with the diverse nature of instructional designers. Hence 
not only did the researcher fit the attributes of many instructional designers, but the researcher’s 
breadth of expertise across several professional fields allowed him insight into the participants’ 
experiences. 
A study that combines behavioral and neurological models demonstrated that having a 
high degree of certainty about a decision for any process results in confirmation bias (Max et al., 
2020). The researcher’s responsibility is to constantly analyze the covert nature of confirmation 
bias to ensure that it does not result in research errors. According to Max et al. (2020), biases are 
formed during the process of achieving certainty. Thus the researcher overcame bias by 
concentrating on subjects participants identified concerning the research question while 
maintaining trustworthy documentation that adhered to the research’s methodology and 
philosophy (Gonot-Schoupinsky & Garip, 2019; Rahmi et al., 2017). 
Guiding Interview Questions 
The interviews were in a conversational style (Percy et al., 2015) and lasted 45–60 
minutes, depending on the responses given by the participants and follow-up questions. The 
interviews were audio-recorded, and as the participants felt more comfortable and supplied more 
information, the interviews became more open-ended. Interviews were transcribed immediately 

[Page 74]
63 
after being recorded. By reducing the time between the interview and the transcription, the 
researcher extracted codes while transcribing based on tone and other interpretations during the 
interview. The primary research question was, What design process do instructional designers 
use to gain attention identified as the first event of Gagné’s nine events of instruction? The 
following guiding research questions were used to elicit responses from the participants related 
to the research question: 
1. Please explain how you incorporate your understanding of capturing attention into 
your design. 
2. Why do you believe attracting attention is essential at the start of instruction? 
3. To what extent does attracting attention inform your design processes? 
a. For example, does it inform you as to what resources you will use throughout the 
development process? 
4. Please describe your reasoning for choosing an approach over another when 
addressing gathering attention. 
5. How would you describe your decision-making processes when you are thinking 
about capturing attention? 
6. In your own words and with as much detail as you can, please explain how effective 
you feel your process is? 
7. What resources would you recommend using or not using to other instructional 
designers who want to design instruction that addresses gathering attention? 
8. What advantages or disadvantages can you describe when designing instructional 
material with gathering the learner’s attention as the focus?

Ethical Considerations 
Ethical considerations in this study centered around protecting the participants and 
maintaining strict compliance with institutional review board (IRB) guidelines. Protecting the 
privacy and anonymity of participants while ensuring trustworthiness was among the top 
priorities in this study. Privacy protection and anonymity ensured a legitimate and trustworthy 
process would be maintained throughout the study. The participants were provided with a 
thorough overview of how their data would be used. The participants were also informed how 

[Page 77]
66 
they might withdraw from the program without penalty. The nature of this study precluded 
individuals from suffering psychological or physical injury; hence this research posed minimal 
risk to the participants. 
NVivo 12 software was used to organize, analyze, and code the interviews using an 
alphanumeric number as identification for participants throughout the process to maintain 
participants’ anonymity. The alphanumeric number provided the participants with protection that 
obfuscated their personal contact information behind the randomly generated number. The 
researcher followed all protocols as required by Capella University’s IRB. 
NVivo 12 aided in aggregating and classifying interview questions to correlate responses 
with documentation to detect patterns (Stanley, 2015) and associate codes with participants’ 
identification numbers. Furthermore, NVivo 12 ensured the study would maintain a professional 
collection of organized documents, data storage (i.e., audio, documents, and work examples), 
and data recovery and assisted in removing any identifying information from data designed to go 
into the final documentation. All data connected to this study were backed up on a secure local 
drive, an encrypted cloud drive, and a detached drive stored separately. All collected data and 
transcripts will be saved for 7 years and destroyed afterward. 
Dependability 
Dependability is defined as repeatable processes that are adequately documented 
(Johnson et al., 2020; Nowell et al., 2017). Dependability ensures a rational, traceable, and 
unambiguously recorded research process (Nowell et al., 2017). The research retained extensive 
records that enable the reader to identify proper research techniques and future researchers to 
replicate the study and ensure dependability (Johnson et al., 2020). 

[Page 78]
67 
Transferability 
Transferability is described as generalizability, which assists readers in determining 
whether the findings apply to their particular circumstances or others (Johnson et al., 2020; 
Nowell et al., 2017). The research clarified terminology and tactics presented in a broader 
discussion of the subject. Transferability also was maintained by periodically assessing the 
process, keeping all processes and data elements relevant to current patterns, and critically 
examining the strategy utilized to drive the research. As outlined in Munthe-Kaas et al.’s (2020) 
research, the transferability strategy is dependable by maintaining direct communication with 
stakeholders, mapping activities, and reflecting on results. 
Study Alignment With Standards 
The research adheres to the principles of a basic qualitative study by developing initial 
codes and modifying them as data are analyzed and events occur. Maintaining essential 
information in memos and codes based on a profusion of data points ensures that the study will 
adhere to the fundamental principles of a qualitative design. While the research data are 
analyzed, every decision is guided by identified themes. Merriam and Tisdell (2015) defined 
themes as a component of research that develops into the study’s findings once a technique for 
producing themes is implemented. 
Validity, Reliability, and Ethical Dimensions 
The study’s strength is dependent on its dependability and reputation. Without credible 
and ethical findings, the study is invalid. Qualitative methods of analysis, reliable technology, 
and all triangulation opportunities were used to strengthen the trustworthiness and rigor of the 
findings to ensure that this study adhered to the criteria for what constitutes a valid, ethical, and 
sound study (Lemon & Hayes, 2020). Triangulation was used, as were member checks, 

[Page 79]
68 
respondent validation, artifacts (shared documents), and proper engagement in the data-gathering 
process. The methodologies discussed previously are instruments that facilitate developing a 
valid, reliable, and ethical study. Any doubt about a study’s trustworthiness undermines the 
researcher’s primary objective and must be treated as seriously as the research itself (Merriam & 
Tisdell, 2015). 
To ensure ethical protections were built into all acquired data, the database was encrypted 
and restricted from collecting any personally identifiable information about the participants, who 
had not expressly given consent to disclose. As was the case with the Merriam and Tisdell 
(2015) study, it is critical to preserve individuals’ personal information while providing them 
with a secure setting. 
Summary 
A basic qualitative inquiry is fitting when investigating instructional designers’ 
experiences and their methods when designing to capture attention. This research consisted of 13 
instructional designers of various competency levels answering the research question using a 
web-based meeting technology (i.e., Zoom).

CHAPTER 4. PRESENTATION OF THE DATA
Introduction: The Study and the Researcher 
Honebein (2017) maintained that instructional designers are encouraged to assess 
conditions concerning content, assessments, learning, context, and constraints before choosing 
any instructional design method. Furthermore, Basdogan et al. (2020) explained that designers 
must consider emotional, intellectual, and cultural learning experiences when participating in the 
instructional design process. This research contains 13 participant interviews to explore the 
fundamental element of the instructional design process and learners’ ability to learn, that is, 
capturing attention. How instructional designers capture attention embodies the task instructional 
designers must complete for a successful result for a given project. This research was needed to 
understand attention-driven design and the process of how instructional designers design to 
capture attention. This chapter begins with a description of the researcher’s background, 
followed by a description of the sample, the process of basic qualitative inquiry as applied to the 
data analysis process, a presentation of the data, the analysis results, and a summary of the 
findings. 
The researcher spent over 15 years dedicated to the synergy between computer science, 
modern technology, and skills related to how learning is achieved. Over many years, the 
researcher would develop strategies and devices designed to connect knowledge and tools used 
to enhance learning. He implemented his techniques and tools to help learners develop skills as a 
martial arts instructor, computer science professional, information technology specialist,

The sample consisted of 13 instructional designers from different professional 
backgrounds with experiences ranging from novice to expert instructional designers. The 
participants were selected from various regions, that is, the United States, Mexico, Canada, and 
the United Kingdom. Each participant worked in an instructional design capacity for a minimum

designers and in different positions within their respective industries. For example, P03

The participants comprised five entry-level, three intermediate-level, two experienced, 
one advanced, and two expert-level instructional designers. Although the participants self-
described their experience levels, the critical difference between an entry-level and an advanced 
level centered around the amount of training and projects they perceived as having been 
successfully completed. Of the 13 participants’ job titles, there were three teachers, three 
engineers, two programmers, one manager, one information technology professional, one 
instructional design manager, one institutional instructor, and one media producer. Two teachers 
specialized in childhood education; all designers had experience working with adults, and two 
designers specialized in childhood education with some experience with adults. 
Of the participants who qualified, those who were selected agreed to participate by 
completing the consent form for the study. Out of 175 applicants to the study, 50 did not consent 
to take part in an audio-recorded interview, six were members of a vulnerable population, and 
100 either met the exclusion criteria or did not meet the inclusion criteria for this study. Of the 
19 participants who did qualify, one participant withdrew the consent to be audio-recorded. After 
the screening and receiving more documentation on the study, five applicants withdrew after 
concerns surrounding confidence in their experience of what they believed task related to an 
instructional designer meant. All potential participants were informed that their anonymity and 
confidentiality were of the highest priority and would be maintained throughout the process. 
The remaining 13 participants met the qualification criteria for instructional design 
experience, consented to the study, and agreed to be audio-recorded. Acquiring the 13 

[Page 84]
73 
participants for this study took several iterations of a consistent selection process that maintained 
high security, anonymity, and confidentiality. 
Research Methodology Applied to the Data Analysis 
This study was a basic qualitative design that used semistructured interviews to grasp the 
participants’ experiences when capturing attention through their design processes (i.e., attention-
driven design). The data analysis consisted of the researcher’s notes, work examples, and 
interview transcriptions. The data were analyzed inductively to uncover themes to address the 
study topic. The questions were organized to give the participants a chance to provide an 
overview of defining events in their instructional design work history and thoughts and strategies 
on attention-driven design. 
In addition, the questions in this study were designed to encourage the participants to 
give personal and professional insight into how the processes of attention-driven design were 
achieved in their experience and how these processes could be improved to avoid adverse 
outcomes. Furthermore, the semistructured interview questions allowed the researcher to clarify 
questions that helped reveal how each participant conceptualized their definition of attention by 
providing examples of particular situations. The researcher used notes to contextualize the 
conversation during each interview when transcribing the audio-recorded interviews. For 
instance, as the interview took place, codes were typed into a Microsoft Excel spreadsheet. 
Attitude, tools used, environment, and self-confidence are examples of some codes identified 
during the interview due to the data analysis. 
The interviews were audio-recorded only. The responses were entered into a note-taking 
application, which, in some cases, assisted in generating new codes. The process of collecting 
data and analyzing the data as they were being collected is accepted as an appropriate strategy 

[Page 85]
74 
when conducting thematic analysis, as done in this study (Nowell et al., 2017). Additional codes 
were generated during and after the audio-recorded interviews were transcribed using NVivo 12 
to create more generalized themes. 
The transcripts were provided to the participants for a final interview review to identify 
any possible discrepancies or clarifications. However, no corrections or clarifications were 
requested.

Presentation of Data and Results of the Analysis 
This study focused on examining how instructional designers capture attention 
throughout their design. Understanding attention through the lens of instructional designers 
benefits instructional design and education by providing insight into creating an attention-driven 
design. This study included interviews with 13 instructional designers of various experience 
levels to understand their design strategies and processes when capturing attention. This section 
discusses the evolution of emergent codes and themes as well as the relationship between themes 
and participant replies. 
This section further presents the findings concerning the guided questions posed to 
participants throughout the interview process. The top codes generated by the data analysis using 
NVivo 12 were arranged into generalized themes, as shown in Table 3. 
 
 

[Page 86]

Theme name Theme sources 
Utilizing and capturing preattention and attention is critical at the start of instruction 26 
Analyzing obstacles and dealing with mistakes 26
