In Table 3, each interview represents one source, which means a theme present in all 13 
interviews would have a theme source number of 13. For example, the theme confronting split 
attention during the design process in Table 3 was present in all 13 interviews, whereas 
analyzing obstacles and dealing with mistakes represents a composite of two themes found in all 
13 interviews combined. Some themes were grouped because of their similarities, resulting in 
theme source counts above 13. The theme conducting a multifaceted attention approach to 
design strategy is another way of similarly grouping findings. The multifaceted attention 
approach represents the many different methods, tools, and essential features the participants in 
this study deployed when conducting an attention-driven design. Cassol et al. (2018) described 
themes as patterns across data sets that are critical to a better description of a phenomenon. 
 

[Page 87]
76 
The Interview Setup 
Before the interview could begin, a few technical and practical elements were set up to 
ensure no unforeseen issues occurred during the interview process. Before the interview began, 
the researcher activated a backup audio recorder, a digital note-taking method, and an analog 
note-taking process. All techniques of capturing the full context of each interview were designed 
to maintain a level of professionalism and keep the participant as relaxed and open to dialogue as 
possible. All digital methods were tested 30 minutes before each interview, with analog copies of 
references and notes nearby. All resources were marked with the alphanumeric number 
representing the participant currently being interviewed. All analog records were immediately 
converted to digital versions and securely saved. 
Questions and Response Protocol 
This section lists the interview questions and summarizes the responses related to the 
research question. While the questions were being asked, the researcher shared his computer 
screen to show images, quotes, definitions, or anything related to the question. Each participant 
was asked the questions and any follow-up questions as the interview required. 
The questions were woven into the conversation as naturally as possible. Seamlessly 
incorporating the questions into the flow of the conversation appeared to allow the participants to 
express their experiences naturally. As a result, a natural flow occurred to the conversation, 
removing any perception of rigidity or constraints when questioned about their experiences. A 
definition, image, or quote was provided if the researcher referred to anything perceived as an 
idiom. 
For instance, the researcher provided a short review of Gagné’s nine events of instruction 
and information related to capturing attention before the interview started. The short review was 

[Page 88]
77 
paired with images and onscreen text to capture the participants’ attention to what was being 
said. Eight out of 13 participants stated that the photos and quotes made it easier to refer to 
comments communicated in the interview. Of the 13 participants, 5 had explicitly used Gagné’s 
nine events of instruction, 6 had a general understanding of the events before the interview, and 2 
mentioned they did not know them before the interview. The interviews were initiated by asking 
the participants about their respective industries’ history as instructional designers and their 
understanding of capturing attention. 
Question 1 
All 13 participants were sure that capturing attention was crucial for effective instruction. 
However, the participants also acknowledged removing idioms from educational material, 
understanding rapid prototyping concepts, and being aware of preattention were part of what 
constituted attention. Preattention is defined in this study as a form of attention that is not 
necessarily connected to the learners’ prior knowledge but is associated with their perceptions of 
where their attention should be directed during and after instruction. 
Participants stated that preattention superseded the purpose of the instruction presented to 
the learner because they perceived the preattentional item or idea as having greater importance. 
For example, P06, when talking about learners of software systems, stated, “They’re often quite 
keen already to use the software because they have other people in the business that have been 
using it.” In essence, the idea that others used the technology motivated the learners to do so, 
rather than any attention the instructional designer incorporated into the instruction. 
When discussing the idea of preattention, two participants mentioned that they did not 
need to address attention at the start of instruction because preattention (i.e., a learner’s 
perception of where their attention should be directed during and after instruction) had 

[Page 89]
78 
previously been activated. The participants’ answers revealed that they viewed attention as a 
composite of previous experiences and the current context of the lesson. All of the participants 
agreed that attention was essential, in some form, at the beginning of instruction. 
When the participants were asked why capturing attention was critical at the beginning of 
instruction, 11 of 13 responded that learners would not get the whole experience of the learning 
material without first having their attention captured. The participants acknowledged that 
preattention is advantageous in most cases because the learners begin the instruction with their 
attention in focus, as prescribed by the first of Gagné’s nine events of instruction. The 
participants also noted that preattention coupled with prior knowledge of the subject was 
favorable when developing an attention-driven design because prior knowledge helps the 
learners recognize the gaps in their ability to solve problems and manage challenges (Fries et al., 
2021; Likourezos & Kalyuga, 2017). 
Although P05 acknowledged the importance of attracting attention at the start of 
instruction,
 P05 elaborated that removing idioms from education designed for novice learners is 
a way of capturing attention. For example, when talking about technology to a learner who may 
not be familiar with the new technology, P05 explained idiomatic words such as target audience, 
MOOs (multiuser object-oriented programs), prototyping, or any technical term that may be 
outside the bounds of the learner’s understanding.

P01 expressed that when safety and security are the primary concerns in a stressful

Question 2 
All the participants defined attention as a composite of actions, attitudes, objects, events, 
and instructors’ confidence in the subject. Question 2 was designed to have the participants 
compare their assessment of the importance of attention in Question 1 with defining capturing 
attention or attention in general. The question elicited a long pause or an exclamation of surprise 
in many cases. Following the initial response to a request for a definition of attention, 4 of 13 
participants acknowledged that the question was something they did not initially think about as a 
detailed definition. The shift in some of the participants’ tones indicated that although they 
understood attention, it was not something in their minds that needed to be explained. For 
instance, P08 recalled a presentation for a large, diverse audience. However, according to P08, 
the audience was not absorbing the information. When asked how it was possible to gauge the 
attention of a large audience, P08 stated that by looking at the expressions on the learners’ faces, 
it was clear that they were lost. P08 explained how a sound in the background pulled the 
learners’ focus away from the lesson, and no matter how hard the learners tried to maintain 
attention, it could not be done. P08 mentioned a possible issue with his design not considering 
the environment when implementing an attention-driven design. 
Twenty-three percent of the participants mentioned that most people intuitively 
understand attention. When the participants described attention as a group of elements working 
together, the researcher coded it as composite attention. P09 mentioned that attention is a 

[Page 91]
80 
process. According to P09 and P08, attention is a process that is established via collaboration and 
dialogue with the learners. 
P08 recognized that attention is more than the interaction with the learners but is a 
combination of P08’s knowledge as a designer. P08 recalled a project that failed to consider 
elements associated with the environment when developing an attention-driven design. Although 
the design accomplished the initial objectives of capturing the learners’ attention, unexpected 
background noises broke the learners’ focus, created split attention, and neutralized any effort to 
complete a successful event. P08 stated that missing a fundamental concept of identifying 
possible split-attention events within context can invalidate any action to execute an attention-
driven design.  
P11 defined attention as a mental state where the mind is ready to receive. In other words, 
P11 defined attention as a composite of the designers’ perceptions, the learners’ moods, and the 
learners’ engagement. Furthermore, the other participants did not view attention or capturing 
attention as a single defined idea but as a combination. This definition of attention that is, 
composite attention, was a pattern that constantly appeared throughout the interviews in various 
forms. Although the participants gave no unified definition of attention, there was a unified idea 
of attention being a combination of elements (i.e., composite attention). The varieties of what 
constituted attention varied greatly. For example, five participants explicitly talked about how 
well they were versed in the content as part of their definition of attention. 
P04 viewed confidence differently as a part of attention by stating, “You need to use a 
different methodology with the children. . . . You need to gain their confidence first so they can 
trust you.” In essence, the designers’ confidence and the confidence of others in the designer 

[Page 92]
81 
were essential to their complete definition of attention. All participants described attention as 
many elements that required a well-planned collaboration between many aspects of the process. 
For example, P03 extended the definition in a teaching-learning context to emphasize 
working relationships in the aftermath of the global pandemic. This subject, however, is beyond 
the scope of the research. P03 explained how some predesigned information could work when 
developing material to maintain consistency. Predesigned material includes media templates, 
documentation, or methods to capture attention carried over from a previous project and 
repurposed for a current project. To many of the participants, the idea of focusing on attention 
represented the fundamental reason why they made a particular decision related to their design. 
For example, P04 described how an initial design changed from presenting educational material 
on a slide to sharing physical objects with the learner due to focusing on capturing attention 
through the instructional design. The idea of capturing attention as a primary component was in 
the design and informed the participant of what strategies would achieve the desired attention-
capturing results. 
Question 3 
According to participants, factors that attract attention include learners’ physical and 
mental states, ages, and prior exposure to technology, all of which impact the chosen pace of 
instruction. The participants’ strategies of capturing attention support their definition of 
attention. The descriptions of the elements that contribute to attention include learners, 
stakeholders, personal growth, and selecting technology and resources. P04, P08, P09, and P12 
mentioned that it is essential to know the learners whose attention needs to be captured. In other 
words, to capture the learners’ attention, it is crucial to know the learners’ physical and mental 
states. For example, P09 stated, “If they are tired, then it’s a bit hard to get their attention.” P09 

[Page 93]
82 
agreed that the process is like a scenario where the designer must learn the learners’ language as 
a part of the procedure to capture their attention. P04 stated, “Most of the time . . . if they are 
young or they are older, the technology is always important because it’s something that they live 
with on a daily basis.” In essence, P04 referred to how the attention of different learning groups 
has distinct priorities or starting points. 
When discussing a project that spanned many departments and stakeholders, P13 
explained that attracting attention requires an analysis of those involved to inform the design as a 
process. For example, P13 mentioned that getting various stakeholders related to the project to 
collaborate was the design’s strategy to capture attention. P13 stated, “I’d say the most 
challenging aspect is to get all these departments to feel sympathetic for the other department.” 
P11 articulated how capturing attention informs the initial introduction of a particular 
process. P11 referred to a mock test that was not a prerequisite test of the learners’ current 
knowledge but an “ego booster” designed to capture the learners’ attention by ensuring the 
learners began the course successfully. P11 would use the learners’ higher focus to test the 
higher-level learning of learners’ knowledge on the particular subject when the learners’ 
confidence was high.

metadata.core_insight_ko: 이 논문은 교육 설계에서 주의 집중 기반 설계 개념을 탐구하며, 학습 설계자들이 학습 과정에서 주의 집중을 핵심 요소로 인식하고 이를 통해 학습자가 정보를 장기 기억으로 전환할 수 있음을 보여줍니다. 그러나 설계자들이 주의를 어떻게 정의하고 포착하는지에 대한 이해는 아직 부족합니다.

text:
When discussing a project that spanned many departments and stakeholders, P13 
explained that attracting attention requires an analysis of those involved to inform the design as a 
process. For example, P13 mentioned that getting various stakeholders related to the project to 
collaborate was the design’s strategy to capture attention. P13 stated, “I’d say the most 
challenging aspect is to get all these departments to feel sympathetic for the other department.” 
P11 articulated how capturing attention informs the initial introduction of a particular 
process. P11 referred to a mock test that was not a prerequisite test of the learners’ current 
knowledge but an “ego booster” designed to capture the learners’ attention by ensuring the 
learners began the course successfully. P11 would use the learners’ higher focus to test the 
higher-level learning of learners’ knowledge on the particular subject when the learners’ 
confidence was high. 
P02 explained how attracting attention informs the designer on the difference between a 
good asset (i.e., an image, an audio file, or video), an effective one, and the length or size of the 
asset. P02 further explained how designing to capture attention is the primary factor determining 
the length of media or presentation. Speaking in an elevated level of excitement, P02 stated, “If 
you get their attention in 7 to 10 seconds, they can watch the rest of the 5- or 10-minute video.” 
P02 further added that capturing attention informs how much a designer can guide the learner as 
the learning process continues. P02 gave the analogy of a commercial that grabs the viewers’ 

[Page 94]
83 
attention at the start of the commercial, allowing them to add in “jump-cuts” to speed up the ad 
without the viewer realizing what has happened. 
Four participants mentioned that capturing attention informs their decision to select 
technologies, the depth of the information, and the length of the media or presentations. In the 
context of attention informing the design, P10 said, “Definitely, I would add more visuals in the 
course. I would add videos along with something that can explain it, and people can just at least 
look at the screen to see what’s happening.” P10 believed that an idea could potentially 
communicate the main point using visuals more than words. 
P02 explained how a method that uses an attention-driven design (i.e., strategies of 
capturing attention through their design process) makes familiar things appear interesting to the 
learner. Part of what makes things seem familiar to the learner is the predictability of the 
fundamentals of a course design. On the other hand, the unpredictable nature of grabbing 
attention through design can make things seem new and fun. However, P02 added that designing 
the predictable elements to work with the unexpected components of a plan “has to start with the 
attention”: “If you don’t have their attention, they’re not going to watch the rest.” P07 explained 
that capturing attention informs the process of preparing the learner to experience the technology 
they may need to finish the lesson. In essence, P07 thought that the learners have a limit to what 
they would grasp at the beginning of a task, and any technology required should be the first 
concept introduced. 
Question 4 
Consistency and predictability are two crucial reasons many participants chose a 
particular path. However, ten participants agreed that the learners’ competency level supersedes 
any plan to capture attention in a mixed class with various skill levels. P07 stated, 

[Page 95]
84 
I definitely understand familiarity because maybe I don’t want to get thrown out of my 
comfort zone internally, so I don’t want to be in a situation where I don’t know what’s 
happening and I can do things my way. 
P03 pointed out that it is essential to be consistent when dealing with learners who are used to 
procedural work “because we’ve got engineers in the food business, and engineers are 
engineers.” In other words, engineers’ preattention is an expectation of procedural work. The 
engineers’ anticipation of a procedural structure was the preattention in P03’s example and was 
included in the design to capture the learners’ attention. 
P13 explained how the participant’s decisions were based on the lowest attention capacity 
of a group. P13 stated, “When you’ve got people that don’t want a lot of information and 
somebody that wants a lot of information, you’d always have to go with the first group.” To 
solidify why a particular method was chosen over another, P13 explained, “I needed to get 
everybody on board . . . and work off the same manual, to have the same mindset, the same 
targets, the same way of working and the same understanding.” 
The participants all mentioned their own familiarity with a process as the reason for 
choosing a particular method. However, 10 out of 13 participants added that the decision was 
contingent on the education level of the learner. For example, P05 stated, “If I’m trying to teach 
a novice how to do the same piece of work, you fall back to the layman’s terms.” P05 elaborated 
on choosing an attention-driven design by stating, “Sometimes it’s just better to have the group 
of novices and the group of experts separate.” 
P09 said pictures remained the key to capturing the attention of about 60% of the learners 
in-person or online. P09 addressed the possibility of a blind person by stating, “Get them to 

[Page 96]
85 
touch things, I suppose. Like Play-Doh or something like that.” P09 further added that spoken 
words could be considered pictures if the learner could visualize them. 
Subquestion 4 
Seven out of 13 participants who worked with learners regarding access to machines or 
the production of something physical or who were required to use personality and humor with 
the learners were adamant that attention-driven design could not work 100% online compared to 
face-to-face. However, they all agreed that it could work as a design that incorporated partial 
online and in-person classes (i.e., a hybrid design or blended approach) to capture the learners’ 
attention and enhance their experience. 
The answer to Subquestion 4 is predicated on the context surrounding the lesson. The key 
to an attention-driven design is consistency, predictability, and reliability for online, in-person, or 
hybrid classes. Hybrid classes represent in-person and online classes as needed for the course. In 
essence, if a lesson plan requires the learner to train on operating real-world objects, a hybrid 
approach could achieve the lesson’s goal using attention-driven design. However, attention-
driven design can be accomplished entirely online if the subject matter is not predicated on 
working with a physical object. 
Four out of 13 participants suggested a difference between a course that uses an attention-
driven design developed without considering the human interaction between the instructor and 
the learner. The participants indicated that the actual implementation of capturing attention in 
such a course would not be as described on paper due to differences in how the learners interpret 
the content. The distinction was that a course could present information for the learner to read 
and study entirely online, but capturing attention in such a course would depend on the human 
connection. The prospect of substituting the human connection with something else regarding 

[Page 97]
86 
courses entirely online was not possible, according to P09. “I don’t think that’s going to work,” 
P09 responded when referring to the idea of compensating for the human interaction gap for 
online courses. P09 mentioned that a course entirely online is possible if the course is on a 
simple, single concept but would not work for anything more complex
. It should be noted that 2 
out of 13 participants who did not have experience developing instruction online were hesitant to 
recommend that their attention-driven design could work entirely online because of their lack of 
understanding of how it would be done.

. It should be noted that 2 
out of 13 participants who did not have experience developing instruction online were hesitant to

Question 5 
The decision-making process when developing an attention-driven design involves the 
following: an account of the technology that will be used in the design, an understanding of the 
learners on a physical and mental level, the effect on the learners of the technology or media 
used in the design, and a sense of where the learners are going after the course is complete (e.g., 
moving on to another class, job, business). Although all 13 participants mentioned that selecting 
resources based on an analysis of the learners could describe their process when implementing an 
attention-driven design, 5 out of 13 participants distinguished between starting with the needed 
resources and starting with the promise that the resources required would be available. Five out 
of 13 mentioned how decision-making begins with knowing the available resources on hand. 
Two participants expressed how technology would be the first part of the decision-making 
process and how the technology mapped to the learners.  
P12 explained that there is a “gadget” for everything and that the most challenging part of 
the decision-making process is choosing the suitable “gadget” for the group. P02 gave an 
example of using an iPad as a gadget or prop for a class where the structure was not specific. P02 
described the decision-making process when using attention-driven design as a procedure that 

[Page 98]
87 
starts by assessing how the learner or end-user may respond to the imagery or gadget used in the 
design. 
However, P02 described the learners’ “pain-point” as effective when deciding on 
attention capture. By “pain-point,” P02 referred to issues that may physically irritate the learner 
in such a way that will prevent any attention capture from taking place. In essence, if the target 
audience agrees that you understand their “pain-point,” the design has successfully utilized a 
working attentional design strategy. 
P01 and P09 explained how attention to where the learner is going next, how the learner 
will eventually apply the knowledge, and the nature of the project become essential factors when 
making decisions on attention capture. P01 described situations where the learner will be going 
to a fragile and dangerous environment immediately after the training has been completed. P01 
added, “On the other hand, some learners need to be motivated because they are just beginning a 
long process and will require a different strategy of attention capture.” P01 referred to situations 
where the learners needed to be prepared to maintain their focus on completing something 
similar to a certificate that may take months or years to complete. 
P05 and P08 mentioned that involving the learners in the instruction-creation process was 
necessary after knowing more about the target audience. P05 explained that attention-driven 
design could create a shift in the focus of the decision-making process from evaluating what 
resources are needed to analyzing how much the learners’ participation will be included in the 
design’s operation. The participants’ decision-making process for attention-driven design was 
structured around a personal understanding of the learners by establishing a connection with the 
learners. P08 stated, “As an instructor and as a person who is going to design a package, I would 
want to start off with where the students are . . . because I need to build off of that background.” 

[Page 99]
88 
Question 6 
Twelve out of 13 participants were able to explain why they felt their process of 
designing to gain and maintain attention was effective. With two overlapping opinions, 3 out of 
13 participants noted that their approach was effective because the learners were always new to 
the process. They spoke about the process being connected to learning about the learners 
themselves. P01 stated, “Because there are always fresh faces who are new.” Five out of 13 
mentioned that their methods were effective because of their positive attitudes and because the 
teaching methods were encouraging to the learners. In essence, regardless of the technique used 
to implement the attention-driven design, P03 commented that the “can-do-attitude” (i.e., self-
assured and eager to take on new challenges or duties) of the instructor would capture attention 
and respect from the learners as needed. 
P12 stated, 
You won’t necessarily always win everyone over with your methods. But when you are 
able to teach someone else, and then they get satisfaction when they realize that what 
you’ve taught them helps them achieve their end result. 
P12 continued by describing a situation where a learner from prior classes would return to 
acknowledge the success of the design by stating, “I was skeptical at first, but this actually 
works.” P04 declared that the process was effective but hard to calculate. 
P07 spoke of introducing the best parts of the instruction over time while providing the 
learner with descriptions of the exciting tasks ahead. P07 thought that creating a preview of 
future exciting elements while omitting the boring concepts was the reason the process was 
effective. P10, P12, and P08 mentioned that context, experience, and confidence in the subject 
made their processes effective. 

[Page 100]
89 
P06 provided examples of instructional design project documents intended to instruct 
learners on using a proprietary data-driven application. The example documents mirrored the 
ideas P06 espoused during the interview and were referred to when P06 answered Question 6. 
P06 was unsure if the methods used were the most effective or the least effective. 
Subquestion 6 
All 13 participants applied the question to advance their personal lives. Although many 
found the question interesting, all the participants mentioned that they would improve some 
elements regarding their attitudes and respect for resources they may not have previously 
deemed necessary. For example, P03 stated, “Maybe to have done some leadership training 
earlier.” 
P03 mentioned that personal growth through understanding oneself would have been a 
great resource. P02 said that being too cautious could cause stagnation was something the 
participant would give as advice. P02 commented that having the support of others would have 
helped the participant achieve attention-driven design sooner. P05 mentioned, “Do not be afraid 
to try and learn new things. Just pick a new thing. Right. Pick something.” P13 mentioned that 
patience was the key when thinking about the time machine question. P07 responded by noting a 
desire to be more of a “catalyst” for change. Eleven of the participants wanted to think about this 
time machine idea with their colleagues outside of the interview. Many of them believed that it 
was an excellent tool to reflect on their progress up to the present day. 
Subquestion 6b 
This question received the same level of intrigue as the previous question by the 
participants and similar responses. All participants mentioned avoiding their personal habits and 
attitudes, avoiding micromanaging, and being more collaborative. The participants’ reflection on 

[Page 101]
90 
what to be cautious of provided responses that included strategies to include others in their 
processes rather than doing everything alone. For example, P03 wished to avoid micromanaging 
because it stifles attention. P02 simply said, “Don’t be too cautious, I guess.

metadata.core_insight_ko: 이 논문은 교육 설계에서 주의 집중 기반 설계 개념을 탐구하며, 설계자들이 학습 과정에서 주의 집중을 핵심 요소로 인식하고 정보를 장기 기억으로 전달하도록 한다는 점을 밝혔다. 그러나 설계자들이 주의를 어떻게 정의하고 포착하는지에 대한 이해는 아직 부족하다.

text:
P07 responded by noting a 
desire to be more of a “catalyst” for change. Eleven of the participants wanted to think about this 
time machine idea with their colleagues outside of the interview. Many of them believed that it 
was an excellent tool to reflect on their progress up to the present day. 
Subquestion 6b 
This question received the same level of intrigue as the previous question by the 
participants and similar responses. All participants mentioned avoiding their personal habits and 
attitudes, avoiding micromanaging, and being more collaborative. The participants’ reflection on 

[Page 101]
90 
what to be cautious of provided responses that included strategies to include others in their 
processes rather than doing everything alone. For example, P03 wished to avoid micromanaging 
because it stifles attention. P02 simply said, “Don’t be too cautious, I guess. Fail faster, I would 
say.” P13 said, “Take my time, not waste too much time.” P13 continued by describing how 
attention-driven design must come from a collaborative standpoint: “It’s so easy to get wrapped 
up in a certain department and to favor them over another one. Now I have to pull myself back 
from that and not be over sympathetic.” 
P11 wanted to avoid being too friendly, whereas P05 wanted to tell a past version of the 
participant’s self to be nicer to learners and avoid thinking of the project before the learners. P05 
said, “It doesn’t matter what your personal thoughts are about the people you’re working for, 
what you’re teaching, maybe. Put a positive spin on it for the learner.” P11 rationalized the 
statement about being too friendly by stating, “Don’t be too friendly. Because that line between 
the teacher and friend, if it gets too thin, you lose everything.” P09 wanted to avoid a habit of 
relying solely on textbooks when designing for attention, stating, “Not to follow everything that 
is in the textbook.” 
Question 7 
The researcher gave the participants the opportunity to answer the advantages of 
attention-driven design before answering the question related to the disadvantages of such a 
method. The participants’ replies to the advantages and disadvantages of attention-driven design 
are given in the following sections. 
Advantages of Attention-Driven Design. The participants provided a range of opinions 
about the benefits of catching attention through design. For instance, participants stated that it 
aids in the maintenance of optimism, increases credibility, and aids in the prevention of 

[Page 102]
91 
boredom. P04 commented that a class should be designed so that the designer themselves would 
want to attend the course because it captures the designer’s attention and provides motivation. 
P04 commented that instructional designers needed to stay current with technologies and 
maintain learners’ interest. P04 argued that writing on the board and reciting what others have 
said was not effective in capturing attention. Four out of 13 participants mentioned that 
delegating time and providing an opportunity to isolate tasks were significant advantages of 
attention-driven design. 
P11 mentioned that adaptability is an advantage of attention-driven design. The example 
P11 gave was focused more on adapting to the quality of the learners’ output. The participant 
further added, “I need to learn how they will learn.” P13 stated, “It’s getting everybody to be on 
the same page . . . all work together as a team . . . as opposed to all different departments fighting 
to be the best.” 
Disadvantages of Attention-Driven Design. The participants believed attention-driven 
design has disadvantages that could counteract the learning process. For example, the act of 
promising a reward can distract from other information beyond the focus of the reward. 
Furthermore, the participants believed that an attention-driven design must be coupled with a 
finished product; otherwise, the captured attention would mutate into a negative understanding of 
the experience by the learners. The participants suggested that capturing attention without a 
strategy for utilizing the attention throughout the project could falsely raise the learners’ 
expectations or increase the complexity of the lesson. P05 mentioned that an attention-driven 
design should account for learners’ attention focused on a previous event. For example, if the 
earlier subject was dynamic, exciting, and fun, the design should recognize that the next topic 
may need to consider the context when transitioning to another section or changing pace, 

[Page 103]
92 
depending on how focused a learner’s attention is on a previous subject. In essence, while the 
course has moved on, the learner’s attention may still be on the last lesson that was more 
engaging. 
P05 believed that one could not separate the organic nature of the conversation between 
the learners and the instructor from the learning environment. While you may capture the 
learners’ attention, the conversation can create split attention if not properly managed. P05 
mentioned that if you do not return to the topic to ensure learners understand in a learning 
environment, you may cause split attention among the learners. Participants viewed the inherent 
uncertainty of some settings and potential learner behavior as possible drawbacks of attention-
driven design. For example, an otherwise effective method of deploying an attention-driven 
design could be ineffective if a designer failed to consider possible interruptions from the noise 
surrounding the area. Attention-driven design tends to focus on the required tools to fit a specific 
domain and is directed to a particular audience, so any disruption in the equation may become a 
disadvantage. Simply stated, an attention-capturing design that works for one group could be 
different from what will capture the attention of another group. 
Question 8 
The participants mentioned behavioral, technical, circumstantial, time management, 
miscommunication, and self-confidence obstacles. Two participants described behavioral 
obstacles, one mentioned circumstantial, one mentioned time management, six mentioned 
miscommunication, and two self-confidence. One participant believed that obstacles are the 
nature of attention-driven design 
Behavioral Obstacles. P05 mentioned that the only logical solution to the issue was to 
separate those not interested from those using some tasks or monetary rewards. P05 admitted that 

[Page 104]
93 
it is still an issue the participant finds challenging to resolve any other way without affecting the 
learners who want to be present. For example, dealing with bad behavior from learners who do 
not desire the learning experience distracts other learners. The participants mentioned that 
focusing on the learners who want to be involved can help capture the attention of those who are 
not interested. The participants believed that capturing the attention of those who do not want to 
be present is vastly different from designing a course to capture the attention of those who do. 
Circumstantial Obstacles. Participants who experienced health issues revolving around 
the unexpected circumstances of COVID-19 mentioned this as an obstacle. The learning was 
designed to be on-location with face-to-face interactions, but people had to work virtually during 
the pandemic. The change in setting made the previous attention getters ineffective in a virtual 
environment. 
Time Management Obstacles. The novice participants who were also instructors 
described an issue with time management. As the designers and instructors, participants who 
encountered this obstacle mentioned the difficulties of a design that is mandated to have topics 
that require a certain amount of time coupled with a scheduled lesson for less time than is 
needed. The resolution to this obstacle was to segment the subject and the attention-driven 
design techniques in chunks of 10–15 minutes. 
Miscommunication Obstacles. Although 6 out of 13 participants exclusively mentioned 
miscommunication as an obstacle, all 13 participants described some form of barriers 
surrounding miscommunication as a subset of their primary obstacle. For example, P11 
described the obstacle related to stakeholders who were not updated on the project, suggesting 
changes to the fundamental nature of the class design. Although suggestions were welcome, 
suggestions not routed in the structure of the design framework wasted time and resources. 

[Page 105]
94 
Miscommunication between team members, executives, and managers related to a given 
project was the source of the obstacles related to miscommunication. The resolution of the 
miscommunication issues required participants to design protocol-related levels of interaction.

text:
The resolution to this obstacle was to segment the subject and the attention-driven 
design techniques in chunks of 10–15 minutes. 
Miscommunication Obstacles. Although 6 out of 13 participants exclusively mentioned 
miscommunication as an obstacle, all 13 participants described some form of barriers 
surrounding miscommunication as a subset of their primary obstacle. For example, P11 
described the obstacle related to stakeholders who were not updated on the project, suggesting 
changes to the fundamental nature of the class design. Although suggestions were welcome, 
suggestions not routed in the structure of the design framework wasted time and resources. 

[Page 105]
94 
Miscommunication between team members, executives, and managers related to a given 
project was the source of the obstacles related to miscommunication. The resolution of the 
miscommunication issues required participants to design protocol-related levels of interaction. In 
essence, the participants documented who needed critical information about the project, general 
information, and those not part of the required communication chain. By segregating the 
communication protocol into a need-to-know list of stakeholders, the obstacles surrounding 
communication were transferable to other projects. 
Self-Confidence Obstacles. Two out of 13 participants described their obstacles as self-
doubt or lacking self-confidence that the learner would not respond to the attention-capturing 
techniques used. Self-confidence obstacles were resolved using two methods. The first method 
used to overcome self-confidence was for the participant to create predesigned templates for 
most occasions and document information about the learners’ reactions to previous attempts. The 
participants mentioned that a sense of control and confidence allowed the attention-driven design 
to succeed better than planned through documentation. 
Subquestion 8
 
Eight out of 13 participants believed that the solution they ultimately chose was the best 
to resolve the obstacles described. However, they all admitted that they may have taken a more 
effective path, but the overall plan was correct. P02 stated, “I didn’t take the risks I could have 
taken.” P02 thought that the participant’s solution could have been refined by taking a few more 
risks in trying new techniques and technologies. “Could possibly have to change the way it’s 
structured,” P03 said in reference to the attention-driven design process. 
P10 pointed out that it was more important to know where to find solutions instead of 
memorizing them when confronting obstacles. 

[Page 106]
95 
Question 9 
All the participants agreed that knowing the content and audience was essential for other 
designers to understand when implementing an attention-driven design. The participants 
mentioned that a healthy skepticism mixed with an optimistic attitude would assist in the success 
of a design structured to utilize an attention-driven design. Three out of 13 participants 
emphasized the need for the instructional designer to have sufficient confidence in existing 
abilities to construct a strategy for developing learners’ self-assurance. 
Four out of 13 participants mentioned that along with advice and mentorships, providing 
other instructional designers with examples and personal notes would help them capture attention 
more efficiently. The participants explained that designers must have passion for what they do, 
learn from examples, be inspired by other designers, and keep up with new methods and 
technologies. 
Summary of Findings 
The outcomes of this study are critical for comprehending the techniques, decisions, 
successes, and failures experienced by practicing instructional designers while adopting 
attention-driven design methodologies. The primary research question for this study asked, What 
design process do instructional designers use to gain attention identified as the first event of 
Gagné’s nine events of instruction? Attention-driven design represents the answer to the research 
question—th e conceptual abilities, definitions, practical tactics, and theoretical frameworks that 
instructional designers employ systematically to ensure that their designs capture learners’ 
attention as a critical component of a successful project from start to finish. 
The researcher categorized this study’s findings under attention-driven design as a 
culmination of themes generated by the research questions. Each interview question was 

[Page 107]
96 
designed to clearly understand instructional designers’ external and internal methodologies when 
implementing an attention-driven design. The participants in this study all had duties as 
instructional designers and instructors within their respected organizations. Figure 2 shows the 
themes resulting from the data analysis. 
Figure 2 
Primary Research Question and Generated Themes 
 
Understanding how instructional designers design to capture attention is a cognitive and 
practical process that can be systematic and dynamic. The research questions were designed to 
address the different elements of attention-driven design. The findings reveal that instructional 
designers design to capture attention within the seven themes shown in Figure 2. 
The results of this study reveal that instructional designers describe an attention-driven 
design as a collection of components related to the design to capture attention that, in most cases, 


[Page 108]
97 
must be integrated into the project’s core development from start to finish. The data analysis 
produced three categories by which the generated themes were organized. Table 4 lists the 
descriptions for the three main categories that summarize the findings.

objectives, and goals helps to identify types of attention designers need to capture

The themes of this research were categorized under the three categories and descriptions 
listed in Table 4. The first category listed in Table 4 is that instructional designers create a 
working definition of attention that includes the context of a situation and defined objectives and 
goals. The definition developed by a particular designer is used to select tools, references, 
technologies, and methods needed to begin and complete the design. The second category listed 
in Table 4 relates to strategies designers use to address the previously defined type of attention. 
The third category listed in Table 4 is that instructional designers must know the learners’ 
motivations, goals, and learning environment to achieve a positive result when developing an 
attention-driven design. Figure 3 illustrates how the researcher grouped the themes and the 
categories identified in this study. 

[Page 109]
98 
After establishing the themes, the researcher categorized them based on how designers 
described the design process to capture attention and not to represent a sequential order. The 
outcome of this study demonstrates that instructional designers have a sophisticated knowledge 
of attention and employ attention-driven design strategies to capture it.

Summary 
This research aimed to understand the details of how instructional designers capture 
attention when implementing an attention-driven design. This study’s findings provide insight 
into attention-driven design from 13 instructional designers of various competencies, locations, 
and industries. The data for this study were gathered through semistructured interviews. The 
interviews were audio-recorded and gradually grew more open-ended as participants gained 
confidence and gave further information. 
The interview structure enabled the researcher to probe and clarify while allowing 
participants to react based on their experiences. This chapter included a list of the research

[Page 110]
99 
interview questions, subquestions, and responses from 13 participants. This research was 
necessary to better understand how instructional designers design to capture attention. This 
chapter included a discussion of the researcher’s background, followed by a description of the 
sample, a description of the data analysis process, a presentation of the data, the analysis results, 
and a summary of the findings. Chapter 5 focuses on discussing the results of, implications of, 
and recommendations for this research. 

[Page 111]
100 
CHAPTER 5. DISCUSSION, IMPLICATIONS, RECOMMENDATIONS
This basic qualitative study was conducted to explore how instructional designers of 
various competency levels design to capture learners’ attention. Thirteen instructional designers 
with various experience levels were interviewed in this study to answer the central research 
question, What design process do instructional designers use to gain attention identified as the 
first event of Gagné’s nine events of instruction? The interview questions were structured so that 
participants could offer an overview of pivotal events in their instructional design careers related 
to capturing learners’ attention, their views, methods of attention-driven design, and potential 
solutions to challenges they had previously desired to tackle. This chapter contains a discussion 
of the results, interpretations, limits, and practical consequences. This chapter ends with the 
conclusion. 
Summary of the Results 
This study’s findings were essential to understanding the methods, decisions, successes, 
and possible failures encountered by practicing instructional designers when implementing 
attention-driven design methods. Thirteen consenting participants were recruited using a 
purposeful approach to address the study’s question. The participants were interviewed via 
Zoom, an online meeting technology. Although Zoom enables users to capture audio and video, 
the semistructured interviews were conducted entirely via audio. The 13 participants of this study 
were self-reported as working instructional designers of six different industries (see Table 1). 

[Page 112]
101 
The designers reported experience from 2 to 10 or more years with online, in-person, and hybrid 
instructional development. 
NVivo 12 was used to transcribe, store, and analyze the recordings. Additionally, 
research notes were stored in NVivo 12 for data triangulation. The interviews were analyzed 
using a continuous comparative technique, as Lemon and Hayes (2020) explained in their 
research on increasing the credibility of qualitative findings. The research data analysis produced 
the generalized themes of how instructional designers design to capture attention (i.e., attention-
driven design) and provided the answer to the research question. 
Discussion of the Results 
Seven themes grouped in three categories emerged based on the answers provided by the 
participants to answer the research question, What design process do instructional designers use 
to gain attention identified as the first event of Gagné’s nine events of instruction? The term 
attention-driven design refers to the response to the research question, the conceptual abilities, 
definitions, practical tactics, and theoretical frameworks that instructional designers use 
consistently to ensure that their designs capture learners’ attention as a critical component of a 
project’s success from start to finish. The interview questions were organized to allow the 
participants to review their professional backgrounds. The interview questions further presented 
the participants the opportunity to give detailed explanations of their beliefs and experience 
related to the subject of attention capture, their methods; any decisions and mistakes they may 
have made when attempting to capture attention, subsequent solutions for any errors, and any 
issue related to capturing attention deemed relevant. 
The participants’ responses differed substantially beyond what Gagné thought of as 
gaining attention and how it could be achieved. Gagné defined gaining attention in terms of 

[Page 113]
102 
asking questions, startling the learner with possible statements, or using imagery. According to 
the findings of this study, participants held a variety of attention definitions that were relevant to 
their diverse work contexts. The results demonstrate that the participants’ definition of attention 
was rarely a textbook description of attention but rather was tied to the consequences a 
contextual action had on the purpose of a project. The findings of this study indicate that 
instructional designers generally describe attention as an inseparable conditional element based 
on the stated objectives, goals, and context (i.e., the working environment). Figure 4 illustrates 
that the themes generated from the data analysis fit into the following three categories: defining 
attention, attentional design methods, and knowing the learners. 
Figure 4 
Categories and Themes

text:
[Page 114]
103 
Figure 4 illustrates each category and associated themes identified in this study. Once a 
definition of attention was identified, the participants of all experience levels implemented 
attentional design methods and strategies for capturing attention based on their preestablished 
definitions. Regardless of the strategy deployed, all the participants believed that attention 
needed to be maintained throughout instruction. Furthermore, as the interview process continued, 
the participants mentioned that their definition of attention was revisited for possible 
inconsistencies during instruction. The participants described capturing attention as a 
collaborative process from beginning to end. In essence, the participants viewed knowing the 
learners and their goals, gathering information, collaborating with the learners, the learning 
environment, and communicating with stakeholders as part of capturing attention. A critical part 
of the participants’ strategy was to use their knowledge of the learners and the identified type of 
attention as a reference when managing possible areas of split attention. Split attention 
minimization requires that the instructional designer and teacher consider what can trigger split 
attention and how to mitigate it prior to the class (Pouw et al., 2019). Furthermore, designers in 
this study leveraged their definition of attention and the learners’ knowledge to determine the 
tools, references, technologies, and procedures required to begin and complete a well-created 
attention-driven design. 
The overall process of how designers utilized their definition of attention and developed 
strategies related to cognitive and practical methods when implementing an attention-driven 
design was thematically listed as a multifaceted attentional approach. 
For example, P03 described a learning environment where the learners’ attention had to 
be tuned to the look of certain foods rather than the taste. P03 altered the environment with 
lighting and sound to capture the learners’ attention and direct it to how the appearance of food 

[Page 115]
104 
products can change depending on the lighting and sound in the background. Although the 
lighting and sound were not part of the original instruction, P03’s definition of attention 
presented an opportunity to use tools and equipment that could adhere to the attention P03 had 
defined and was attempting to capture. The example of how P03 defined attention based on the 
context of the working environment, adding elements such as light and sound, and the goal of the 
instruction highlight the theme incorporating the working environment in the design. 
Instructional designers in this study described how it was critical to understand the 
learners’ motivations, goals, and learning environment to create an effective attention-driven 
design. This study distinguished the participants’ definitions of attention, the cognitive methods 
derived from their definitions, and the practical methods used by the designers when 
implementing an attention-driven design. When the participants referred to practical methods, it 
centered around methods that were designed to be hands-on to assist the learners in physically 
achieving something from the first step to the last. However, cognitive methods represented 
strategies utilized by the participants in this study to help the learners think or remember a 
certain way, from simple to complex. For example, P04 described how creating simple, practical 
tasks designed to make it easy for learners to succeed early in the instruction helped to induce the 
idea that they could successfully complete the requirements as the course progressed to more 
complex tasks. Structuring a process from easy to difficult aligns with Gagné’s (1984) belief that 
procedural and intellectual knowledge should range from simple to complex. Furthermore, P04 
demonstrated how cognitive load theory could help mitigate a task’s impact on the learners’ 
available mental resources, which helps prevent possible split attention during instruction. 
Knowing the learners and their goals allowed the participants to forecast possible areas that may 
cause split attention and adjust to designs that need it. 

[Page 116]
105 
In all cases, the participants started with either an explicitly defined understanding of the 
attention they were designed to capture or an implicit definition of attention based on personal 
knowledge related to the contextual goals of the project. In other words, designers in this study 
began the attention-driven design by defining attention based on some understanding of the 
working environment of a given project. The context or working environment is where the 
learning is taking place. In essence, regardless of the context, designers in this study extracted 
their definition of attention from the start of the design process. The three categories (i.e., 
defining attention, attention design methods, and knowing the learners) were used to categorize 
the study themes based on the designers’ descriptions of their activities when developing an 
attention-driven design. Overall, seven themes emerged that describe how instructional designers 
capture attention and were organized under the category that best represented the methods and 
goals when defining attention. 
Defining Attention 
Figure 5 illustrates a generalized version of the categories used to group the themes in 
this study. 

[Page 117]
106 
Figure 5 
Highlighting Defining Attention Categories and Themes 
 
Defining attention is the first of three categories that group the themes utilizing and 
capturing preattention, and attention is critical at the start of instruction. As shown in Figure 5, 
the essential first step to understanding how instructional designers in this study designed to 
capture attention was to note a definition of attention from the participants’ point of view. 
Participants were asked to define attention to provide a general explanation of attention as it is 
understood by the participants and not a textbook description of capturing attention. Asking the 
participants to define attention before they described their methods was a piece of the puzzle 
related to the inner workings of the participants’ cognitive methods. In other words, the 
researcher wanted to understand the participants’ definitions of attention, how they were thinking 
about their processes mentally, and how their thoughts coincided with their physical actions. 
Questions concerning the participants’ definition of attention allowed the researcher an 
opportunity to match their definitions of attention with their descriptions of how they captured 


[Page 118]
107 
attention. Participants were allowed to clarify or redefine their definitions if they felt that they 
did not align with their methods of capturing attention through design. 
Participants in this study maintained various definitions of attention related to their 
different work environments. Figure 6 shows how the participants in this study formulated their 
definitions of attention. 
Figure 6 
How Participants Define Attention 
 
The outcomes of this study suggest that instructional designers describe attention as 
dependent on the stated goals and the working context, as shown in Figure 6. Working context is 
the environment in which the instruction will take place. For example, the goal of a particular 
project is to provide general instruction that could later be used by learners who are interested in 
operating a large industrial packing machine. The context may be that the device is too large to 
fit in the room where learning occurs. Therefore, the cognitive and practical strategies of the 
instructor would be centered on the closest technology or concept that can provide the learners 
with an experience that closely resembles the realities of working with the machine itself. Using 
the preceding scenario, the instructional designer may choose to capture the learners’ attention

text:
[Page 119]
108 
by incorporating tools like virtual reality, augmented reality, computer games, miniature 
robotics, or a field trip or may simply provide the learners with a video tour of the machine as a 
tool to capture their attention. In essence, the goal (i.e., cognitive and practical strategies of the 
instructor) and context (i.e., the learning environment is too small to house the actual device) 
defined the types of tools the designer needed to capture the learners’ attention. 
The results of this study reveal that attention could not be generally defined without 
knowing the goal and the context in which the goal must be completed. Furthermore, the 
participants described how additional design methods to grab attention were equally important as 
defining attention. 
Attentional Design Methods 
Figure 7 illustrates a generalized version of the categories used to group the themes in 
this study with the category attentional design methods highlighted. 

[Page 120]
109 
Figure 7 
Highlighting Attentional Design Methods Categories and Themes 
 
Figure 7 illustrates the category of themes that define how instructional designers 
perceive capturing attention and their methods to capture various types of attention across 
multiple learning environments. The following themes were categorized under attentional design 
methods: (a) conducting a multifaceted attention approach to design strategy, (b) conducting an 
instructor attitude–dependent design, (c) analyzing obstacles and dealing with mistakes, and (d) 
incorporating the working environment into the design. 
Conducting a Multifaceted Attention Approach to Design Strategy 
The theme conducting a multifaceted attention approach to design strategy represents the 
many diverse methods, various tools, and frameworks the participants in this study used and is 
supported by the literature that describes instructional designers as those who must become 
experts in a nearly limitless set of overlapping decisions when designing (Basdogan et al., 2020). 
Instructional designers in this study use their knowledge about the learners (i.e., knowing the 


[Page 121]
110 
learners) to inform their design decisions, methods, and accompanying media (Honebein, 2017) 
when conducting a multifaceted approach to their design, as Figure 7 illustrates. For example, 
P08 discussed how the presentations he used to create designs that clearly present the data, 
incorporate original audio and illustrations and require a technical understanding of combining 
them to capture the learners’ attention used overlapping abilities. Although using original 
artwork and sound was not a requirement for P08’s process, P08 thought it was needed to 
capture the learners’ attention and keep the design unique and exciting. 
Conducting an Instructor Attitude–Dependent Design 
The result of this research identifies that designers would maintain an underlying 
awareness of their level of confidence in a particular approach. The level of confidence played an 
essential part in how each designer would approach a given task or problem. If the designers 
were also the instructors, their self-confidence would be high. The participants in this study 
centered their design decisions around their personal preferences and confidence in the subject 
matter. The designers in this study were confident that increasing the interactivity between the 
learners, their peers, and the instructor would increase their confidence in a given approach’s 
success (Bickle & Rucker, 2018). Although the designers in this study described their confidence 
in a given approach as an essential element in their design process, confidence level had to be 
followed up by an analysis of possible obstacles and mistakes that may arise. 
Analyzing Obstacles and Dealing With Mistakes 
The theme analyzing obstacles and dealing with mistakes describes the methods used by 
the participants in this study when dealing with obstacles and errors when developing an 
attention-driven design. When analyzing obstacles, the participants in this study would use 
software like Microsoft PowerPoint to visualize their design process, reflect on design decisions 

[Page 122]
111 
and outcomes, and collaborate with other designers who may have encountered similar obstacles. 
During the participants’ analysis, they would identify possible mistakes and try to find a way to 
remodel a portion of the design to remedy them. The designers in this study agreed that dealing 
with obstacles and analyzing mistakes were expected and viewed as inherent feedback of every 
iterative design process. Participants explored their past errors and the mistakes of other 
instructional designers as an opportunity to grow, learn, and deal with obstacles. 
Incorporating the Working Environment Into the Design 
The theme incorporating the working environment into the design describes methods 
used by the participants in this study when integrating their work and learning environments into 
the attention-driven design. The participants in this study uniformly integrated elements of the 
learning environment (i.e., work environment) into their design. For example, P04 would use the 
structural layout and seating arrangements of where the learning was meant to occur to determine 
which hands-on and interactive event could be integrated into the design of the instruction. 
The first two categories, defining attention and attentional design methods, represent how 
the researcher organized the study’s themes based on the context in which they were used by the 
designers when developing an attention-driven design. However, it should be noted that the order 
of the categories is not meant to present a sequence of events but an illustration of their grouping 
and how instructional designers may go from one category to the next. The category-defining 
attention groups the theme related to how designers defined the type of attention they needed to 
capture. The next category, attentional design methods, groups the themes pertaining to 
instructional designers’ strategies to identify various types of attention in a given environment or 
circumstance. The next category of discussion, knowing the learners, groups the themes (i.e., 
confronting split attention during the design process and acquiring assistance and personal 

[Page 123]
112 
confidence in the design) related to how designers incorporate information about the learner into 
their plans. 
Knowing the Learners 
Figure 8 illustrates the categories used to group the themes in this study, with the third 
category (i.e., knowing the learner) highlighted. 
Figure 8 
Highlighting Knowing the Learners Categories and Themes 
 
Figure 8 illustrates the third category of themes (i.e., knowing the learner) that define 
how instructional designers perceive capturing attention and their methods to capture various 
types of attention across multiple learning environments. Knowing the learners represents the 
third category that groups two of the seven themes identified in this study. The category knowing 
the learner concerns how designers incorporate information about the learner into their designs. 
Knowing the learner includes the themes confronting split attention during the design process 
and acquiring assistance and personal confidence in the design. 


[Page 124]
113 
Confronting Split Attention During the Design Process 
Designers in this study believed that identifying areas where learners must process and 
integrate various sources of information during the design process could exhaust the learners’ 
mental resources (Seedwell, 2017). Addressing any potential area that could produce split 
attention was a continuous theme throughout the participants’ process of capturing attention. In 
accordance with the literature on attention, the participants believed that the limited capabilities 
of the working memory required extraneous stress when learning new tasks to be minimized 
(Salzman et al., 2021). The designers viewed the idea of managing split attention as important as 
capturing attention throughout the process. To manage split attention, the participants would 
identify and compartmentalize types of attention as a guide to their attention-driven design. 
Knowing the learners’ interests, motivations, objectives, and goals related to the learning context 
was essential when confronting split attention and capturing their attention. In other words, if the 
content is helpful to the learners’ jobs or careers, they would most likely be motivated to learn 
the content, which could help to mitigate the effects of split attention. For example, when the 
participants required the learner to view a presentation while also reading a document related to 
the presentation, they would separate the information in such a way that would give the learner 
time to process the information presented first, then provide direction and time to review any 
related documentation. Furthermore, the participants consistently used their knowledge about the 
learners’ lives as a resource to incorporate into the design whenever possible. 
Acquiring Assistance and Personal Confidence in the Design 
Instructional designers must consider all stakeholders, that is, subject matter experts, 
managers, administrators, and others vested in the project.

text:
Knowing the learners’ interests, motivations, objectives, and goals related to the learning context 
was essential when confronting split attention and capturing their attention. In other words, if the 
content is helpful to the learners’ jobs or careers, they would most likely be motivated to learn 
the content, which could help to mitigate the effects of split attention. For example, when the 
participants required the learner to view a presentation while also reading a document related to 
the presentation, they would separate the information in such a way that would give the learner 
time to process the information presented first, then provide direction and time to review any 
related documentation. Furthermore, the participants consistently used their knowledge about the 
learners’ lives as a resource to incorporate into the design whenever possible. 
Acquiring Assistance and Personal Confidence in the Design 
Instructional designers must consider all stakeholders, that is, subject matter experts, 
managers, administrators, and others vested in the project. Acquiring assistance represents the 
effort others, including learners, are willing to invest in a task or series of tasks. The participants 

[Page 125]
114 
in this study linked their use of learners’ and stakeholders’ support with their personal 
confidence in directing the assistance provided to a desirable completion. In essence, novice 
designers who were not confident in their ability to utilize the support of others, such as learners, 
administrators, or specialists, found themselves overworked and attempting to complete complex 
group tasks as an individual. On the other hand, experienced designers who leveraged their 
personal confidence in their ability to harness the assistance of others by delegating tasks to 
those who showed interest found the process of developing complex, attention-driven designs 
enjoyable and effective. 
For example, P03 described how years of doing things alone left her constantly searching 
for satisfactory results in her company’s design methods. After utilizing the support provided by 
managers, local universities, artists, and learners, P03 was able to redesign the attention-driven 
design that eventually expanded beyond her expectations. P13 described how his programming 
skills did not include designing user interfaces. P13’s lack of skills in creating user interfaces 
rarely seemed to affect instructional material design. However, after requesting that learners with 
artistic skills help design a few interface designs, P13 found that the course was more desirable 
to learners and himself. Furthermore, 7 of 13 participants acknowledged the importance of 
motivational frameworks, such as Keller’s (2010) ARCS model. However, Keller’s ARCS model 
is not an attention framework. 
Although attention and motivation complement each other, the literature has clearly 
distinguished between the two concepts. Motivation is related to engagement, learning, and 
educational achievements (Ginsberg & Wlodkowski, 2019). In contrast, attention is associated 
with learners’ perceptions (i.e., intellectual or perceptual) but could also exist as a component of 
motivation or learners’ ability to perceive objects using their senses (Fortney, 2017). 

[Page 126]
115 
Furthermore, Keller’s ARCS model clearly and purposely distinguishes arousing attention as the 
first essential step to triggering motivation (Drobisz, 2017). The participants viewed attention-
driven design as an added layer to their traditional duties as instructional designers, starting with 
defining attention. 
Conclusions Based on the Results 
This section presents two segments related to the study’s findings with the following 
subheadings: “Comparison of Findings With the Theoretical Framework and Previous 
Literature” and “Interpretation of the Findings.” The first section addresses the connection of the 
findings to previous literature and theoretical frameworks; the second provides an explanation of 
the findings. 
Comparison of Findings With the Theoretical Framework and Previous Literature 
The results of this study directly align with previous literature and the theoretical 
frameworks supporting this study: the conditions of learning theory (Gagné, 1985) and cognitive 
load theory (Sweller, 2019). Gagné’s conditions of learning theory define internal and external 
conditions of learning as those that affect either the type of learning or the environment (Rose, 
2019). Cognitive load theory outlines how the complexity of a task influences the brain’s 
available resources (Brachten et al., 2020). This study reveals that instructional designers agree 
that gathering attention is critical. 
However, the results of this research show that instructional designers do not view 
attention as a single event. Instructional designers in this study viewed attention as a combination 
of stated goals and the context of a given project. The idea that attention is more complex than a 
single event matches the previous literature on attention as the primary entry point to learning. 
For instance, Güney (2019) explained that attention is the gateway to the working memory; 

[Page 127]
116 
Anderson and Kim (2019) described how the effects of attention could augment learners’ 
perception of size, sound, and color; and Aleksandrov and Knyazeva (2017) spoke of attention as 
a two-way link (i.e., voluntary and involuntary) with the central processes of muscle fatigue. 
In essence, attention can affect every aspect of a learner’s physical, mental, and learning 
experience. Therefore, as found in this study and the previous literature, attention capture must 
be addressed with each unique context and obtained as part of a design to achieve the desired 
goals. For example, P04 used coloring books to encourage adults to relax their minds and bodies 
before conducting a specific unrelated task. Providing coloring books for adults was unexpected 
and unorthodox; however, it captured the learners’ attention while relaxing their minds and 
bodies to achieve the goal. The results of this study further found that the participants linked 
their ability to utilize the support of others (i.e., learners and stakeholders) with their personal 
confidence in directing the assistance provided to a desirable completion. Collaboration and 
acquiring assistance align with the literature that describes both activities as a hallmark of the 
instructional design field (Bawa & Watson, 2017). 
The literature has reinforced the concept that designers must maintain overlapping layers 
of solutions to produce informed results and make tactical decisions when designing (Basdogan 
et al., 2020). For example, the instructional designers in this study utilized the experiences of 
other designers, personal experiences, and instructional design frameworks such as the ADDIE 
(Analyze, Design, Develop, Implement, and Evaluate model) model, Bloom’s taxonomy, and 
Gagné’s nine events of instruction, as tools to solve a given problem. Furthermore, instructional 
designers in this research segregated several forms of attention capture to help mitigate split 
attention. The participants segregated types of attention for identifying situations and the method 
of attention-driven design needed to capture, maintain, and predict. 

[Page 128]
117 
The literature validates the idea of various types of attention and the need to structure a 
plan around it (Clark & Paunovic, 2018). Clark and Paunovic described attention as the primary 
factor in a learner’s imagination and self-efficacy. Additionally, S.-Y. Lo (2018) described 
attention as a condition for understanding mental and visual objects. Lai and Chang (2020) 
described an attention training model with types of attention indicators and five dimensions of 
attention for children. Furthermore, the literature has identified various types of attention and 
their distinct tasks (Chaire et al., 2020; Chanon & Hopfinger, 2011; Nani et al., 2019; Nguyen et 
al., 2020; Tonelli et al., 2020). This study’s results mimic the overwhelming research pointing to 
the types of attention, such as split attention, and the need to harness attention as a prerequisite to 
an effective attention-driven design. 
The sensory components necessary to activate working memory for encoding long-term 
memory can never be accessed if a learner’s attention is not sufficiently gained (Kirschner et al., 
2018). This research indicates that instructional designers believe designing to capture attention 
helps address most cognitive load issues that may appear otherwise. For instance, according to 
the participants, maintaining the learners’ engagement was crucial for preventing split attention 
and mind wandering.

The study reveals that instructional designers consider capturing attention as a critical component of the learning process, which enables learners to transfer information to their long-term memory. However, there is a need to understand how designers define and capture attention through their design.
