3 Theoretical Framework 
In this chapter, the respondent explores foundational information on topics concerning the 
thesis; an overview of luxury fashion, visual identity and elements in branding, the concept 
of perceived value, exclusivity in luxury fashion and Gen-z as luxury fashion consumers. This 
chapter and the information therein will help to guide and inform both the respondent and 
the reader to further understand the theory and background of the research aim and 
objectives. 
3.1 Luxury Fashion 
The concept of luxury, derived from the Latin term "luxus," refers to superabundance and 
excess in lifestyle or displays of wealth exceeding necessary expenses.  Its meaning 
fluctuates depending on the time and culture, making it hard to arrive at a single definition. 
Historically, luxury has been a symbol of wealth, privilege , and power . It has also been 
viewed negatively, as in ancient Greece where it was seen as a threat to society (Cabigiosu, 
2020).   
The origins of luxury fashion can be traced back to the royal courts of Europe, where 
aristocrats and monarchs set the tone for luxury clothing and accessories. Today’s popular 
brands like Chanel, Dior, and Louis Vuitton began as small ateliers, catering to the rich and 
elite with bespoke garments and exclusive products. The evolution of luxury fashion has 
been marked by key moments in history, such as the emergence of haute couture , 
introduced by Charles Frederick Worth in the 19th century, the rise of prêt-à-porter in the 
20th century, and the globalisation of luxury in the late 20 th and early 21 st century 
(Okonkwo, 2007).  
Luxury fashion represents the pinnacle of the fashion industry, characterised by its high 
quality, exclusivity, differentiation, innovation, craftsmanship, precision, heritage, and 
prestige. The intricate designs of early haute couture, as seen in Figure 1, highlight these 
characteristics of luxury fashion. Unlike fast fashion or mass-market fashion, luxury fashion 
emphasizes timelessness, superior materials, and meticulous attention to detail. These 
attributes create a unique value proposition that justifies the premium pricing associated 
with luxury brands .

been marked by key moments in history, such as the emergence of haute couture , 
introduced by Charles Frederick Worth in the 19th century, the rise of prêt-à-porter in the 
20th century, and the globalisation of luxury in the late 20 th and early 21 st century 
(Okonkwo, 2007).  
Luxury fashion represents the pinnacle of the fashion industry, characterised by its high 
quality, exclusivity, differentiation, innovation, craftsmanship, precision, heritage, and 
prestige. The intricate designs of early haute couture, as seen in Figure 1, highlight these 
characteristics of luxury fashion. Unlike fast fashion or mass-market fashion, luxury fashion 
emphasizes timelessness, superior materials, and meticulous attention to detail. These 
attributes create a unique value proposition that justifies the premium pricing associated 
with luxury brands . Luxury and fashion are distinct concepts that can coexist but do not 
mean the same thing. Up until the 19 th century, fashion was only accessible to the 
privileged who could afford luxury, as keeping up with changing trends required substantial 
wealth. However, in the 21
st century, being fashionable no longer requires wealth. Today, 
to follow trends, consumers no longer need to bear the high costs of luxury. Accessible 
brands like H&M and Zara offer trendy yet affordable options to a broader audience. 
Although haute couture  remains influential in setting trends, it is no longer the sole 
reference point in fashion. Luxury products, once viewed as investments that are rarely 
replaced, have increasingly become lifestyle choices. Many brands like Chanel now release

Emotional value refers to the feelings and emotions a consumer experiences when 
purchasing or using a luxury product. Luxury fashion is often linked to self- reward, 
indulgence, and a heightened sense of pleasure and satisfaction. Emotional value is crucial 
in luxury fashion, where consumers seek not only to possess but to feel a sense of 
accomplishment, belonging, or self -identity (Sheth et al., 1991; Wang et al., 2024) . 
Moreover, emotional value contributes to brand loyalty. Consumers who form an 
emotional attachment to a luxury brand or product are more likely to repurchase and 
remain loyal, especially when they perceive the brand as an extension of their personal 
identity (Elgebali & Zaazou, 2023).  
Symbolic value refers to the personal meanings and identities that individuals attach to 
luxury products. These items often serve as a medium for self- expression, reflecting 
personal tastes, lifestyles, and values (Kapferer & Bastien, 2009).  
3.1.2 Exclusivity in luxury fashion  
Consumers of luxury goods also often seek items that signal their social standing or 
communicate their personal identity. Exclusive products cater to this need, providing 
consumers with the opportunity to differentiate themselves from others and assert the ir 
status. Exclusivity is a core characteristic of luxury fashion, contributing significantly to a 
product’s perceived value. Luxury brands emphasize exclusivity through strategies like 
limited product and high barriers to accessibility. These tactics reinforce the brand's image 
and make consumers feel that owning a luxury product grants them a special status or 
connection to something unique (Wang et al., 2024).  
Exclusivity is primarily associated with social and symbolic value in luxury fashion. By 
limiting access to products, brands create a perception of rarity that enhances the 
desirability of the product (Kapferer & Bastien, 2009) . In addition to social status, 
exclusivity also taps into the emotional value associated with luxury consumption. 
Consumers often experience a heightened sense of pleasure and accomplishment when 
they acquire something that few others can access. This sense of privilege reinforces 
emotional connections to the brand and motivates continued loyalty (Sheth et al., 1991) . 
Exclusive access to products, such as limited-edition releases can evoke feelings of prestige 
and uniqueness, further deepening the emotional bond between the consumer and the 
brand(Vigneron & Johnson, 1999). 
3.2 Visual Identity in Branding 
The concept of branding is not new as it can be seen in the middle ages with artisans tagging 
their initials on their merchandise. This allowed for customers to know where to find and 
purchase the same product if needed (Franzen & Moriarty, 2009) . Today, a brand is 
presented through its logo , unique graphics and other elements that create a distinctive 
identity, which consumers recognise and connect with over time. Unique imagery , 

[Page 9]
 6 
typography, and verbal messaging linked to a brand are used to help consumers recognise 
and identify it (Wheeler, 2013).  
The notion of visual iden tity has historic ro ots in traditional ancient seals  and heraldic 
symbols used in ancient and medieval times to denote lineage and affiliations, which 
evolved significantly over time, especially with the coming of the internet and digital media. 
This evolution caused the expansion of the scope of visual identity beyond logos to include 
comprehensive brand experiences ac ross multiple touchpoints  (ThoughtLab, 2023) . A 
visual identity is the visual part of branding, the face of the brand. Businesses create a visual 
identity in order to present a unique and consistent image to their target audience. This 
way, the business can express its brand, personality and va lues in a visual way, as well as 
shape how the public perceives the brand and sets it apart from its competitors  (Stripe, 
2024).  
Visual identity is  equally vital in branding as it helps brands communicate their essence, 
foster recognition, and build an emotional connection with their target audience.  As seen 
in Figure 2, Gucci uses its visual identity elements to communicate an eccentric and lively 
essence. For luxury fashion brands, visual identity is not just a marketing tool but an integral 
part of their narrative and value proposition. A strong visual identity enhances brand recall, 
differentiates a brand in the crowded marketplace, and supports the overall brand strategy 
by embodying its values and mission (Aaker, 2014). In luxury fashion, where products often 
symbolise a lifestyle rather than mere functionality, visual identity becomes a decisive 
factor in consumer choice. A  luxury brand's visual identity helps create a coherent story 
that resonates with consumers, making them feel part of an exclusive club. This is 
particularly important as luxury brands rely on symbolic value and heritage to justify 
premium pricing and maintain their allure (Kapferer & Bastien, 2009).  
 
Figure 2: Gucci’s Visual Identity Elements. (Ferrari, 2015; Keyframe, n.d.; Lashand, 2024; Schmidt, 2015).

Elements of Visual Identity 
Visual identity is a combination of various graphic elements that represent and distinguish 
it. These elements include the logo, colour scheme, typography, imagery, graphics (Arnett, 
2022; Goldstein, 2023; Oppelt, 2023). 
A logo is a visual symbol that immediately distinguishes a brand. By incorporating elements 
like colours, shapes, typography, and occasionally a tagline, an effective logo captures the 
essence of a brand and evoke a positive response  (Goldstein, 2023). Logos are the most 
direct representation of a company’s brand, acting as a visual shorthand for the brand itself 
and often being the first thing that comes to mind for consumers. The design, colour, and 
typography of a logo can trigger specific emotions an d associations, playing a crucial role 
in shaping the overall perception of the brand (Pavlou, 2024) . Some luxury fashion brands 
have simple logos like the Chanel double-C logo or more intricate logos like the Versace  
medusa head logo as seen in Figure 3. 
 
Figure 3: Versace and Chanel logos. (Sixtysix, 2023; Taylor, 2021). 
Colour is much more than just an aesthetic choice in the collection  of elements that form 
a brand identity and experience. It is the foundation of a brand’s visual identity, influencing 
everything from logos and packaging to products, environments, and all forms of marketing 
communication. Colours impact humans  in various ways, with each colour creating a 
distinct state of mind, a mood. This mood sets the tone for how a  brand is expressed and, 
more importantly, forms mental associations that define the meaning of the brand within 
its broader context (Dawson, 2013). In developing an effective colour scheme, brands must 
recognise colour as a psychological tool that profoundly influences consumer emotions, 
decisions, and perceptions, often before logic even engages. Bold colours can act as visual 
anchors, capturing attention and drawing consumers in. However, the impact of colour 
extends beyond mere attraction. Colours like red can stimulate appetite and energy, 
making them effective but requiring balanced use to avoid  overstimulation. Subtlety in 
colour like the use of white, grey and black conveys sophistication and elegance. Effective 
colour schemes also involve combinations that create a cohesive brand experience. On a 
global scale, cultural sensitivity is crucial, as colours carry different meanings worldwide; 


[Page 11]
 8 
red may signal good fortune in China but caution in Western parts. For brands, the 
deliberate use of colour not only builds brand identity and emotional resonance but also 
enhances memorability and loyalty, offering a competitive edge that speaks directly to 
consumers' subconscious (O’Leary, 2024). 
Typography refers to the selection and use of fonts in branding materials, significantly 
shaping the brand’s overall appearance and tone (Pavlou, 2024). Luxury brands frequently 
select clean, clear, and legible serif and sans -serif fonts. Serif fonts convey tradition, 
elegance, and sophistication, while sans -serif fonts convey  modernity, simplicity, and 
minimalism. Many luxury brands use custom typography to distinguish themselves in the 
market and emphasize their exclusivity. For instance, Chanel’s typography is based on 
Clarendon. Another common trend among luxury brands is the use of capital letters; 
popular luxury brands like Louis Vuitton and Versace as seen in Figure 4 employ all caps to 
project power, sophistication, and exclusivity. Beyond font choice, the size and spacing of 
letters play a crucial role in luxury branding. Large, widely spaced letters in advertisements 
and posters create a bold, striking impression, wh ereas smaller, tightly spaced letters on 
products and communications convey elegance and sophistication (Fernández, 2023). 
 
Figure 4: Louis Vuitton and Versace Typography. (Keyframe, n.d.). 
Imagery in luxury fashion marketing plays a crucial role in storytelling, allowing brands to 
convey their values, showcase products, and connect emotionally with their audience. 
High-quality photography and videos are essential as they create desire, highlight product 
features, and communicate brand identity. Visual storytelling, including fashion films, 
influencer collaborations, and user-generated content, helps brands build trust and engage 
audiences on a deeper level (Marnewick, 2023) . Photography plays a powerful role in 
shaping brand perception, often serving as the primary connection between a brand and 
its audience. Consistently delivering stunning, on -brand visuals helps reinforce a brand's 
identity, values, and messaging, fostering  recognition and loyalty over time. Captivating 
imagery taps into consumers’ emotions, evoking feelings like desire, nostalgia  (a 


[Page 12]
 9 
sentimental longing for the past) , or belonging, which can guide decision- making and 
deepen engagement. For example, this image seen in Figure 5 from Gucci Gift campaign 
uses vintage Hollywood aesthetics to evoke nostalgia, connecting audiences to an idealised 
past. This emotional connection helps differentiate the brand from competitors, creating a 
lasting impression in consumers' minds and encouraging them to consider the brand’s 
products or services (Jowitt, 2023).  
 
Figure 5: Imagery from the Gucci Gift campaign. (GUCCI, 2022). 
Graphics, including illustrations, icons  and patterns play a vital role in creating a cohesive 
brand identity in luxury fashion (Arnett, 2022). Illustrations are a powerful tool, bringing 
personality and depth to visual content through a blend of colours, shapes, and creative 
expression. Whether hand- drawn or digital, illustrations offer designers the flexibility to 
create unique, resonant narrati ves that align with a brand’s tone and style. Acting as a 
medium for visual storytelling, illustrations can convey complex ideas, emotions, and 
abstract concepts that might be challenging to capture through photos (RedAlkemi, 2023). 
Prada’s Trembled Blossoms campaign (shown in Figure 6) features vibrant illustrations by 
James Jean applied across multiple media, from storefront to interior visuals. 
 
Figure 6: Prada's Trembled Blossoms campaign applied across multiple media . (Jean, 2008).

An icon is a graphic element that represents an idea or theme linked to a brand. Unlike 
logos, which are the primary symbols of a brand’s identity, icons are flexible and used to 
add character or tell a story without replacing the main logo. Example shown in  Figure 7 
include, Gucci’s bee icon  reflecting nobility and Chanel’s camellia flower embod ying 
faithfulness and longevity (Banfield, 2021; McGee, 2021) . Patterns are repeating visual 
elements that reinforce familiarity and improve brand awareness.  Bold patterns, such as 
Louis Vuitton’s Damier motif and Burberry’s check print, evoke a sense of status and luxury, 
making them instantly recognisable. These graphics bring depth and personality to visual 
branding, appearing across products, packaging, social media, and websites. Behind these 
designs lies a strategic effort to differentiate the brand  from competitors, establishing a 
unique visual language that enhances its overall image and appeal (Warren, 2023). 
 
Figure 7: Gucci's Bee icon & Chanel's Camellia icon seen on their products . (SCMP, 2023; The Outlet, 2021). 
While each visual element plays a significant role, v isual consistency is key to a cohesive 
brand identity that conveys a company’s values, personality, and vision, distinguishing it 
from competitors and leaving a lasting impression.  This can be achieved by  integrating 
these visual elements across all touchpoints including products, website, packaging, social 
media, advertisements, and more . This consistency helps customers easily recogni se and 
remember the brand, building trust and reliability. When a brand maintains visual 
harmony, it fosters emotional connections with consumers, enhancing brand recognition 
and loyalty (Muavia, 2023).  
Visual Storytelling in Luxury Fashion 
Visual storytelling is a powerful tool used by luxury fashion brands to convey their identity, 
heritage, and values through visual elements. In an industry where aesthetics and 
exclusivity are paramount, the ability to tell a story visually is essential in  connecting with 
consumers on an emotional level and reinforcing the perceived value of the brand 
(Marnewick, 2023 ). Visual storytelling involves more than just showcasing beautiful 
images; it’s about conveying a narrative that resonates with consumers. According to 


[Page 14]
 11 
Sikarskie (2021 ), luxury brands leverage their heritage and craftsmanship in visual 
storytelling to create a sense of timelessness and exclusivity. This technique is often used 
to highlight the intricate details of luxury items, making the product itself part of the 
brand's story. Visual elements are strategically employed to evoke specific emotions and 
associations in the viewer.  For instance, as seen in Figure 8, Dior conveys a narrative of 
meticulous craftsmanship and artistry by using images of the brand’s artisans at work in 
the atelier (Pavic, 2024). This narrative reinforces the idea that luxury products are not just 
items of clothing or accessories but symbols of status and personal achievement. 
Moreover, visual storytelling enhances brand loyalty. As consumers become emotionally 
invested in the brand's narrative, they are more likely to develop a strong sense of loyalty 
and attachment. The use of visual elements in storytelling contribute significantly to brand 
recognition and recall, further solidifying the brand's presence in the consumer’s mind (Lee, 
Hur & Watkins, 2018) 
 
Figure 8: Dior artisans at work. (Pavic, 2024). 
3.3 Gen-Z and Luxury 
Gen-Z, born between 1997 and 2012, is reshaping the luxury market with values and 
behaviours that set them apart from previous generations. Gen -Z seeks brands that align 
with their personal values, such as sustainability, inclusivity, and social consciousn ess. 
According to McKinsey, this generation is driven by "woke" values, expecting brands to take 
a stand on important social and environmental issues; brands that fail to align with these 
principles risk losing favour with Gen -Z, who are quick to call out or boycott companies 
perceived as falling short of these expectations ((Amed, Balchandani, Beltrami, Berg, 
Hedrich & Rölkens, 2019). 
For Gen -Z, luxury is less about material wealth and more about expressing identity and 
values. This demographic favours brands that offer products and experiences marked by 
authenticity, transparency, and diversity, preferring fewer, high-quality items that reflect a 
focus on sustainability and timelessness. Their spending habits reveal an emphasis on 


[Page 15]
 12 
quality over quantity, highlighting a shift in luxury consumption towards enduring value. In 
addition to these principles, Gen -Z consumers expect luxury brands to engage digitally, 
especially on platforms like Instagram and TikTok, where they interact with influencers and 
engage directly with brands. The integration of online and offline experiences is thus 
essential for retaining their loyalty (Roberts, 2023). 
The behaviour of Gen- Z within the luxury sector reflects deeper psychological and social 
factors that have long influenced luxury consumption. Traditionally, luxury goods are 
purchased not just for their functional value but as symbols of status and personal identity. 
The concept of "ostentatious consumption" introduced by (Veblen, 1899) remains relevant 
today as consumers continue to use luxury products to display social status, wealth, and 
success. Luxury items such as designer clothing, high-end accessories, and rare collectibles 
serve as markers of achievement, fulfilling emotional needs and symbolis ing personal 
success (Andronic, 2021). 
Moreover, luxury consumers are influenced not only by a product’s physical attributes but 
also by its intangible qualities, such as brand heritage, craftsmanship, and exclusivity.  
Okonkwo (2007) notes that these elements contribute to the symbolic value that luxury 
consumers attach to their purchases, creating a complex decision-making process that goes 
beyond the product itself.  
4 Previous Research 
In this chapter, the respondent has compiled previous research within the areas of luxury 
fashion, visual elements in branding  and related topics in the context of this thesis. The 
search engine used is google and the researches were found on Google scholar as well as  
Emerald Insight and ProQuest database s in Finna with search terms including Visual 
Identity, Luxury Fashion, Visual Elements, Perceived Value and Exclusivity in Luxury.  
Yu, Abidin, & Shaari (2024) review the impact of brand visual identity on consumer attitude. 
The research focuses on how various visual elements such as logos, colours, and 
typography influence consumer perceptions and behaviours. By analysing thirty -four 
relevant studies, the study found that visual identity elements affect consumers’ perceived 
brand quality, brand personality, brand satisfaction, loyalty, and favourability. The research 
also revealed that logos significantly influence brand recognition and recall, while colour 
schemes affect emotional responses and brand association. Typography and slogans also 
contribute to brand personality and consumer engagement. The study emphasi ses the 
importance of cohesive and well -designed visual identities in building and maintaining 
consumer relationships. 
Virtanen (2018) master’s thesis studies visual brand identity (VBI) holistically, focusing on 
its elements, construction, and strategies for visual changes to maintain brand relevance.  
The methodology employed  was a  semi structured theme interviews , informants being 

[Page 16]
 13 
eleven marketing experts. The thesis finds that visual brand identity is a multi-dimensional 
construct that is crucial in creating meaningful and consistent  brand recognition. The 
findings also highlight that visual brand identity is constructed through a combination of 
elements; the basic ones being logos, colours, typography, and symbols. The thesis further 
highlights that these elements are not only significant individually but also in the way they 
collectively convey the brand’s desired image and identity. The study empha sizes the 
importance of consistency and coherence among visual elements to ensure a strong and 
recognisable brand identity.  
Lyu (2023) investigates the influence of visual elements in corporate communication within 
the luxury brand sector.

importance of consistency and coherence among visual elements to ensure a strong and 
recognisable brand identity.  
Lyu (2023) investigates the influence of visual elements in corporate communication within 
the luxury brand sector. By conducting a thorough literature review, it explores the role of 
logos, colours, typography, and visual styles in establishing a strong brand identity. It also 
investigates brand communication strategies like storytelling, experiential marketing, 
influencer partnerships, personalization, and digital marketing. The findings show that 
effective visual design and communication enhance brand recognition,  foster consumer 
loyalty, and create lasting impressions. The research emphasizes that luxury brands 
effectively use visual storytelling, personalized experiences, and iconic visual identities to 
connect with consumers emotionally. It also highlights the i mportance of visual elements 
and brand communication strategies in conveying exclusivity. The study suggests that 
understanding consumer responses and behaviour to visual content can further optimize 
brand communication strategies, ensuring long-term success in a competitive market.  
Phillips, McQuarrie, & Griffin (2014)  investigate how visual brand identity (VBI) influences 
consumer responses to advertisements. The research aims to understand the criteria used 
by advertising professionals and ordinary consumers to assess changes in VBI and their 
impact on brand perceptio n. Employing a mixed -method approach, the study combines 
qualitative interviews with advertising art directors and experimental tests with 
consumers. The qualitative analysis reveals that art directors have a narrow tolerance for 
changes in VBI, associatin g it closely with specific visual elements such as logos, colours, 
and typography. They emphasize the need for consistency to maintain brand identity. In 
contrast, consumers are more flexible, focusing on the presence of familiar elements rather 
than their exact visual consistency. The findings also indicated that consumers with high 
aesthetic awareness are more sensitive to deviations from already established VBI, while 
those with lower awareness are less affected by such changes. The study concludes that 
maintaining a consistent visual brand identity is crucial for brand recognition and positive 
consumer responses. 
Lee, Chen, & Wang (2014) investigate how integrating visual art can elevate the perceived 
prestige of luxury brands. The study aims to determine whether visual art enhances 
consumers' perceived prestige value, which includes conspicuous, unique, quality, and 
hedonic values. The study focuses on the Louis Vuitton (LV) brand and two experiments 
were conducted. One experiment assessed how visual art influences various dimensions of 
perceived prestige, while the other examines the interaction between art presence and 
product pricing on these perceptions. By manipulating visual art presence and varying price 

[Page 17]
 14 
points, the study observed changes in consumer perception. The results show that visual 
art significantly boosts the perceived prestige of luxury brands, especially when the product 
price is set 25% to 50% higher than comparable items. This indicates that visual art can 
enhance a brand's perceived luxury and exclusivity, making it more appealing to 
consumers. 
An article  by Kusumasondjaja (2020)  published in the j ournal of fashion marketing and 
management explores the role of visual aesthetics and presentation modalit y in luxury 
fashion brand communication on Instagram. The study investigates the impact of visual 
aesthetics and presentation modalities on consumer responses to Instagram content 
posted by luxury fashion brands. Using content analysis as a method, 40,679 posts from 
fifteen global luxury brands was studied. The study reveals that posts using expressive 
aesthetics and video content generate more likes and comments than those with classic 
aesthetics and static images. The research also highlights a significant interaction between 
visual aesthetics and presentation modality: expressive aesthetics with audio -visual 
content perform better together while classic aesthetics are more effective with a visual-
only format. 
Liu, Rodriquez, and Huang  (2023) explore the dominant value perceptions of Chinese 
millennials regarding luxury fashion goods. The study aimed to identify which values 
influence the purchase intentions the most when it comes to luxury fashion handbags . A 
survey method was used, and the Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP)  was applied. The 
researchers assessed five luxury values: quality, uniqueness, self-expression, prestige, and 
brand image. The study found that self-expression is the most important value for Chinese 
millennials, emphasizing the importance of personal image and aesthetic beauty in their 
purchasing decisions. Prestige, the open display of social identity, was found to have the 
least influence on their purchase intentions. 
In summary, visual brand identity (VBI)  plays a crucial role in creating brand recognition 
through elements like logos, colours , typography, and symbols, with consistency and 
coherence being essential for a strong brand identity  (Virtanen, 2018). In luxury fashion 
brand communication on Instagram, posts with expressive aesthetics and video content 
generate more engagement than those with classic aesthetics and static images  
(Kusumasondjaja, 2020) . Visual identity elements significantly influence consumer 
perceptions, brand quality, personality, satisfaction, loyalty, and favourability, with logos 
enhancing recognition, colours evoking emotional responses, and typography contributing 
to personality  (Yu et al., 2024) . For Chinese millennials, self -expression is the most 
important value influencing their purchase intentions, thus stressing the significance of 
personal image and aesthetic beauty in luxury fashion while prestige has the least influence 
(Liu et al., 2023) . Integrating visual art in luxury brands like Louis Vuitton enhances 
perceived prestige, especially with higher- priced products  (Lee et al., 2014) . Advertising 
professionals stress the need for consistency in VBI, while consumers respond better to 
familiar elements, with high aesthetic awareness increasing sensitivity to changes (Phillips 
et al., 2014) . Effective visual design and communication strategies enhance brand 

[Page 18]

recognition, foster consumer loyalty, and create lasting impressions. Additionally, visual 
storytelling, personalis ed experiences, and iconic visual identities  are essential  in 
connecting emotionally with consumers and conveying exclusivity (Lyu, 2023). 
5 Methodology 
This thesis explores the role of visual elements (logo, colour scheme, typography, imagery, 
and graphics) in influencing Gen -Z's attraction to luxury fashion brands and their 
perceptions of value and exclusivity.  The respondent has decided to use a survey in the 
form of a questionnaire as a data collection method and t he data analysis method to be 
employed for this study is descriptive analysis. This chapter contains  information on the 
chosen data collection method, data analysis method and the practical implementation of 
the study. 
5.1 Selection of Informants 
For this study, a convenience sampling method was used. This sampling method is defined 
as a non-probability sampling technique that involves selecting participants based on their 
accessibility and availability  (Nikolopoulou, 2022). This method allow ed to quickly gather 
data from readily accessible informants , making it particularly suitable for this study  
conducted within a limited time frame and limited resources. In order to answer the 
research questions, the respondent targeted informants aged 18 -27 (adult Gen -Z) with 
interest in luxury fashion whether current or aspirational consumers of luxury fashion. 
5.2 Questionnaire Survey 
Surveys are a flexible research approach used to investigate a wide range of topics. Surveys 
often employ the questionnaire as a tool for data collection. A well-designed questionnaire 
requires a short, appealing title, a participant identifier for confidentiality, and clear 
instructions for informants.

5.2 Questionnaire Survey 
Surveys are a flexible research approach used to investigate a wide range of topics. Surveys 
often employ the questionnaire as a tool for data collection. A well-designed questionnaire 
requires a short, appealing title, a participant identifier for confidentiality, and clear 
instructions for informants. The style and content of the questionnaire depend on the 
research question, with structured formats featuring closed questions for quantitative 
analysis (Mathers et al., 2000).  
Effective questionnaire design involves translating the research questions into clear survey 
questions to ensure accurate data collection while maintaining respondent engagement. 
Questionnaires should be short, ideally under 15 minutes, to enhance response rates. 
Clarity and relevance are essential for an effective questionnaire ; avoid unnecessary 
questions and do not omit necessary ones . Proper layout and delivery methods, whether 
online or printed, significantly affect the  readability and completion rates  of the 
questionnaire (Arundel, 2023). 

[Page 19]

Aesthetics play a crucial role in self-administered surveys. Question order is essential, with 
a focus on placing easier and important questions at the beginning  and grouping common 
themes in the middle . Logical sequencing and introductory and summary questions 
contribute to a well-designed and effective survey (Jones et al., 2013). 
5.3 Descriptive Analysis 
Descriptive analysis is a statistical approach that summarises and describes the main 
features of a dataset, offering understanding of the collected data. An essential first step 
in descriptive analysis is data preparation, which included coding responses into numeric 
format that allows for consistent statistical calculations  in a software like SPSS. Coding is 
the process of assigning numerical values to text -based responses, such as coding Likert 
scale from 1  (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree). Crea ting a codebook to document 
each variable, its format, and its numeric values helps maintain consistency in analysis , 
particularly in studies with multiple variables and scales (Bhattacherjee, 2012). 
Descriptive analysis method includes key calculations like frequency distribution which 
identifies how often specific responses or categories occur , measures of central tendency 
(mean, median, mode) provide an understanding of typical values in the dataset, such as 
average ratings for survey items, and offer insights into general patterns of preference  
(Bhattacharyya, 2023). Visual representation of data is a valuable component of descriptive 
analysis, aiding in the interpretation of findings. Graphical tools such as bar charts, pie 
charts, and histograms summarise the frequency and distribution of responses, making it 
easier to observe trends and compare preferences across categories. These visualizations 
enhance the clarity of descriptive statistics (Pedersen, 2024). 
5.4 Practical Implementation 
The aim of this study is to identify the visual elements that most significantly attract Gen-Z 
to luxury fashion brands and those that enhance the perceived value and exclusivity of 
these brands.  To support this aim, the respondent began by collecting and reading 
literature on both the thesis subject as well as  relevant data collection and analysis 
methods. This provided a foundational understanding of the thesis topic and survey-based 
research, helping to inform the study's methodology. 
To ensure clarity and effectiveness in the survey questions, a pilot test was conducted 
before the full data collection began. The pilot test helped  to identify misunderstandings 
and possible confusion in the questions. The feedback from the pilot test informants was 
used to make necessary adjustments, ensuring that the final survey was accessible and 
relevant for the target demographic. To reach the target demographic of Gen-Z consumers 
interested in luxury fashion, a convenience sampling method was used. The survey was 
distributed through online platforms, including  the respondent’s Instagram, Snapchat, 

[Page 20]
 17 
LinkedIn, and Survey Circle  accounts, allowing informants  to self -select based on their 
interest in the topic. The survey was anonymous and consisted of mandatory questions to 
minimise missing data and ensure  comprehensive responses, supporting reliability . The 
survey questions were also structured using Likert-scale and categorical response options 
to facilitate quantitative analysis  (see Appendix 1 for survey questions ). Validity was 
strengthened by aligning survey questions directly with research questions and also basing 
survey elements on established concepts within the theoretical framework.  Number of 
informants who completed the survey is 41. 
Once responses were collected, the data was prepared for analysis. This step involved 
creating a codebook to standardi se variable coding and structure. Each variable in the 
survey was assigned a short name and coded according to its type, scale and possible 
responses were given a numeric label. All data was input into SPSS, following the codebook 
to ensure consistency and data quality throughout the process. 
The analysis began with a frequency calculation  to explore demographic distributions and 
categorical responses, providing a foundational overview of the sample's characteristics, 
including age, gender, field of study/work and consumer type. Frequency distribution and 
mode were calculated for each visual element to summaris e informants’ ratings and 
rankings of the visual elements’ influence on attraction, perceived value, and exclusivity. 
Data visualisation in the form of pie charts and bar charts was then applied to support the 
clarity of findings. After getting the results, the respondent noted the main findings and 
reviewed similar studies to help interpret the results better, this will be discussed in the 
following chapter.

Summary of Result 
The findings suggest  that in terms of attracting Gen-Z consumers logos, colour schemes, 
and typography has a moderate appeal. On the other hand, imagery and graphics are rated 
higher, suggesting they might have a stronger attraction. However, when informants 
ranked the elements, logos emerged as the most influential in drawing attention to luxury 
fashion brands. Colour schemes follow as the 2 nd most influential with imagery, graphics, 
and typography following in third, fourth, and fifth places, respectively. 
For enhancing perceived value, all visual elements play a role, though colour  scheme was 
rated by only one informant as having no impact. Overall, most elements were seen as 
moderately impactful, as indicated by the majority of “somewhat” ratings. Imagery stood 
out with the most “extremely” ratings, pointing to its significance  in enhancing perceived 
value. Informant rankings also positioned imagery as the top element in this regard, 
followed by the logo in second place, with graphics, colour scheme, and typography as the 
third, fourth, and least influential elements for enhancing perceived value. 
When it comes to exclusivity, each visual element contributes, even minimally, as no 
element was rated as having no impact. Although colour  schemes received the highest 
number of “extremely” ratings, ranking results placed the logo as the most influential 
element for enhancing exclusivity, followed by imagery, graphics, and colour schemes, with 
typography ranked as the least influential. Overall, the findings suggest that logos are  the 
most significant in attraction and enhancing exclusivity, while imagery is the most  
significant in enhancing the perceived value of luxury fashion brands. 
Interpretation 
Yu et al. (2024) highlight that logos are crucial for brand recognition and recall, while colour 
schemes impact emotional responses and brand associations. This corresponds with the 
respondent’s findings, which suggests that  logos are the primary element in attracting 
consumers and enhancing exclusivity. Colour scheme is also ranked highly in attracting the 
Gen-Z informants according to the respondent’s findings.

In contrast, imagery primarily influences perceived value.
metadata.core_insight_ko: 본 논문은 Z세대 소비자들이 특정 시각 요소, 특히 로고를 포함한 고급 패션 브랜드에 강력하게 반응하며, 이는 독점성을 구축하는 데 중요한 역할을 한다는 것을 밝혀냈습니다. 반면, 이미지는 주로 인식된 가치에 영향을 미칩니다.

text:
Although colour  schemes received the highest 
number of “extremely” ratings, ranking results placed the logo as the most influential 
element for enhancing exclusivity, followed by imagery, graphics, and colour schemes, with 
typography ranked as the least influential. Overall, the findings suggest that logos are  the 
most significant in attraction and enhancing exclusivity, while imagery is the most  
significant in enhancing the perceived value of luxury fashion brands. 
Interpretation 
Yu et al. (2024) highlight that logos are crucial for brand recognition and recall, while colour 
schemes impact emotional responses and brand associations. This corresponds with the 
respondent’s findings, which suggests that  logos are the primary element in attracting 
consumers and enhancing exclusivity. Colour scheme is also ranked highly in attracting the 
Gen-Z informants according to the respondent’s findings. Another study by Lee et al. (2014) 
finds that visual art increases the perceived prestige of luxury brands especially when the 
product price is higher than comparable items. This aligns with the respondent’s findings 
which suggests that graphics play a  significant role in enhancing the perceived value of a 
luxury fashion brand as it was ranked third. Although the respondent only examined the 
visual element singularly, both findings suggest graphics are  influential in both increasing 
perceived value and perceived prestige.  
Lyu (2023) finds that iconic visual identities are used to connect with consumers and visual 
elements are important to convey exclusivity . This aligns with the respondent’s  findings, 
where all the elements of visual identity are influential in enhancing exclusivity especially 
logos and imagery which are ranked as the most significant. Both studies suggest that visual 
elements convey and enhance exclusivity in luxury brands.  Typography, though ranked 

[Page 37]
 34 
least in terms of attraction, perceived value and exclusivity, still contributes to the overall 
aesthetic of a brand. Pavlou (2024) emphasi ses that typography shapes the tone of a 
brand’s visual identity, which aligns with the respondent’s findings that typography plays a 
smaller yet meaningful role in branding. The findings also suggest that colour schemes are 
influential, particularly in attraction and exclusivity. This is supported by O’Leary (2024), 
who discusses how colours evoke emotions and associations, with certain tones conveying 
sophistication and luxur y. While colour schemes were not rated as the most impactful 
element, their ability to complement other visual elements  and enhance overall brand 
appeal was noted.  
Imagery emerged as the most impactful element in enhancing perceived value. This aligns 
with Kusumasondjaja (2020) study, which shows that expressive visuals, such as high -
quality images and videos, are highly engaging and emotionally resonant. Marnewick 
(2023) further supports this by emphasi sing the power of visual storytelling in connecting 
brands with consumers and evoking strong emotional responses. The respondent’s findings 
reinforce these observations, showing that imagery significantly influences Ge n-Z’s 
perception of a brand’s value. 
7 Critical Review 
In this chapter, the respondent critically reviews the research process and individual 
chapters, including the aim and questions , theoretical framework, previous research, 
methodology, and results. The review highlights both strengths and areas for potential 
improvement. 
The thesis aim is clearly outlined and aligns with the research questions. The respondent 
effectively conveys the aim of investigating the influence of visual identity elements on 
Gen-Z’s attraction to luxury brands, perceived value, and exclusivity. Howev er, while the 
purpose is well -defined, it could have benefited from a more detailed reasoning, 
emphasising specific research gaps. Explaining why this topic was chosen and identifying 
areas within existing literature that lack exploration would enhance the  study’s relevance 
and justification. 
The theoretical framework offers a comprehensive foundation, covering luxury fashion, 
Gen-Z consumer behaviour, visual identity, perceived value, and exclusivity. The framework 
demonstrates a thorough understanding of key concepts and their relevance to the 
research questions. Most resources are up to date; however, the framework includes some 
older sources, such as foundational theories by Veblen and others. The respondent justifies 
using these sources, as they remain influential and are frequently cited in current research. 
Additionally, the framework would have been stronger with more context on how each 
theory interconnects and informs the research aim, as well as a clearer structure. 

[Page 38]
 35 
The previous research chapter presents relevant studies that inform the thesis topic. Each 
research aligns with specific aspects of the study and provides a solid foundation for the 
investigation. However, the chapter could have included more on studies specific to Gen -
Z’s behaviour within the luxury sector, not only broader research on visual identity. Greater 
emphasis on recent studies centred on Gen-Z would strengthen the chapter, particularly as 
this demographic plays a unique role in luxury fashion. The chapter could have also 
included previous researches that seek to answer similar questions with the thesis to 
increase validity of the thesis. Additionally, structuring the chapter more logically and 
avoiding repetitive literature from similar articles would enhance clarity and conciseness. 
The methodology is well -detailed, including the selection of informants, data collection 
method using a questionnaire and data analysis method using descriptive analysis. The 
practical implementation is also clearly explained. The reasoning for using conve nience 
sampling is clearly stated, but this sampling method limits the generalisability of the 
respondent’s findings. Although convenience sampling was chosen for its practicality, the 
lack of a representative Gen-Z sample reduces the ability to generalise results to the wider 
population. The data analysis approach using the SPSS software for descriptive analysis, 
including mandatory survey questions, ensures that the data is thoroughly evaluated and 
accurately represents informants responses. Nonetheless, to increase reliability, a more 
diverse sampling approach or an additional method for data collection could have been 
employed. 
The results chapter effectively answers the thesis questions and utilises SPSS -generated 
charts and calculations to present findings clearly and concisely. The informant 
demographics is presented clearly using a pie chart and the themes, attraction, perceived 
value, and exclusivity are examined through frequency distribution and mode calculations 
enabling a straightforward analysis of Gen- Z preferences for luxury brand elements. The 
visual aids help capture significant trends, though the interpretation could further deepen 
the connection to theoretical concepts. For instance, a more detailed comparison with past 
studies and relevant theories would offer stronger insights into the research implications. 
An additional point of consideration is the significant proportion of aspirational consumers 
(82.93%) in the sample compared to current consumers (17.07%), as shown in the 
consumer type data. This imbalance may influence the results, as aspirational consumers 
might perceive and prioritis e visual identity elements differently from those who actively 
purchase luxury fashion.  This disparity in consumer type also raises questions about the 
generalisability of the findings to the broader Gen-Z demographic, particularly to those who 
actively engage with luxury brands as current consumers. While the limited sample size and 
non-representative nature of the sample may affect the reliability of the findings, SPSS was 
effectively used to ensure accurate data processing and presentation. Future studies could 
benefit from a m ore balanced distribution of consumer types to capture a broader and 
more representative perspective of Gen-Z preferences. 
Efforts were made to ensure reliability and validity throughout the research process. The 
pilot study conducted before the main survey allowed the respondent to refine the survey 

[Page 39]
 36 
questions, which helped to improve internal consistency and minimize potential 
misunderstandings. Mandatory survey questions ensured comprehensive responses, 
reducing the likelihood of incomplete data, thus contributing to reliability. Content validity 
was achieved by aligning survey questions closely with the thesis questions, ensuring 
relevance to the study’s objectives. Construct validity was supported by grounding survey 
questions within established theoretical concepts from the framework. However, the 
convenience sampling method limits the external validity of the study, as findings may not 
be generalisable to a larger Gen-Z population.

8 Discussion 
The imagery from luxury fashion brands has always intrigued me ; the quality and subtle 
elements of a photo or video, the story being told, and the emotions evoked. This curiosity 
led to my exploration of the visual world of luxury fashion and is a major reason behind this 
thesis. Through this study, I aimed to find out about the visual identity elements and their 
significance. In the process of research,  I found that Gen- Z is a rising demographic in the 
luxury fashion sector and decided to centre my study a round them  and find out the 
elements that are most significant in attraction, perceived value and exclusivity. 
The findings from the study reveal that logos are the most significant elements in attracting 
Gen-Z consumers to luxury fashion brands. Despite the high quality and artistic nature of 
imagery and graphics, it is the immediate recogni sability of logos. The findings show that 
the order of significance in attraction is Logo, Colour Scheme, Imagery, Graphics , and 
Typography. Imagery stands out as the most influential element in enhancing the perceived 
value of the luxury fashion brand. This aligns with my initial fascination with the storytelling 
aspect of luxury brand visuals. High-quality imagery allows brands to convey their heritage, 
craftsmanship, and the unique experiences they offer. For Gen -Z, who value authenticity 
and meaningful connections, such image ry enhances the perceived value of a brand by 
providing a deeper understanding of its identity and what it represents. The findings reveal 
the order of influence for enhancing perceived value to be Imagery, Logo, Graphics, Colour 
Scheme, and Typography.  
In terms of exclusivity,  the order of influence  according to the findings is Logo, Imagery, 
Graphics, Colour Schem e, and Typography.  Logos again emerge as the most significant 
element. This further emphasises the importance of distinctive brand logo  in conveying a 
sense of uniqueness and status, which are key aspects of luxury branding. The significance 
of logos in enhancing exclusivity indicates that Gen-Z associates this element with prestige 
and a sense of belonging to an exclusive class . Generally, Logo s are quite significant in 
attraction, perceived value and exclusivity showing that they are small but powerful visual 
tools and should be employed effectively by luxury fashion brands.  

[Page 40]
 37 
Reflecting on the research process, there are areas where the study could be further 
developed. Utilising a more diverse and representative sample of Gen-Z consumers would 
allow the findings of this thesis to be generalisable to the entire Gen -Z population. A 
development proposal would be to use a representative sample like  simple random 
sampling or stratified sampling . Additionally, incorporating qualitative methods, such as 
interviews or focus groups, could offer deeper insights into the motivations and emotions 
behind Gen-Z's perceptions of luxury brand visual  elements. For future research, it would 
be valuable to explore how emerging trends, such as sustainability and digital innovation, 
intersect with visual identity in luxury fashion. As Gen- Z places increasing importance on 
social and environmental responsibility, examining how these values influence their 
response to visual branding elements could provide useful insights for luxury brands.  
In conclusion, this thesis has been a journey into the visual world of luxury fashion branding 
and its resonance with Gen- Z consumers. The insights gained not only satisfy a personal 
curiosity, but it also  highlights the importance of specific visual elements that can be 
strategically employed to engage a generation swiftly emerging in the luxury market.  By 
recognising and responding to the visual preferences of Gen-Z, upcoming luxury brands can 
craft more effective branding strategies that foster lasting connections with this influential 
demographic.

THE VISIBLE ELEMENTS IN LUXURY FASHION 
A survey about Visual Identity Elements in Luxury Fashion Brands 
About the Survey 
This survey is part of a bachelor's thesis studying the influence of visual identity elements of 
luxury fashion brands on Gen-Z attraction to these brands. It also studies the visual elements' 
influence on Gen-z perception of the brand's value and exclusivity. All responses will remain 
confidential, and data will be handled securely according to academic standards. The completed 
thesis will be uploaded to Theseus, an online academic repository, in line with school guidelines.

text:
[Page 1]
Visual Identity as Strategic Signal: How
Corporate Logos Encode Innovation Orientation
Yueying He∗ Yangen Li†
October 7, 2025
Abstract
Existing logo research almost exclusively adopts a “consumer perspective”
paradigm that treats logos as marketing stimuli and examines their effects, but
neglects the supply side: Why do firms design logos this way? Do logos reflect
firms’ strategic orientations? We introduce a strategic signaling perspective on
corporate logos, demonstrating that visual design systematically encodes firms’
strategic orientations. Using computer vision and machine learning, we find that
visual features predict R&D intensity and capital expenditure intensity significantly
above chance. Innovation-intensive firms exhibit distinct visual language: lower
complexity, higher symmetry, blue-dominant palettes, and greater white space.
Encoding effectiveness varies by industry context, consistent with strategic hetero-
geneity theory. Critically, logo features predict both internal strategic metrics (R&D
from financial statements) and external market perceptions (volatility from trading
data), demonstrating convergent validity. This alignment suggests logos reflect gen-
uine strategic orientations that consistently shape both visual identity choices and
market performance. This research reconceptualizes logos from marketing stimuli
to strategic signals, bridging branding and strategic management literatures. We
provide a framework for logo auditing and demonstrate that visual identity decisions
have implications beyond consumer marketing.
Keywords: Corporate logo, Strategic signaling, Visual identity, Machine learn-
ing
∗Yueying He, Visiting Assistant Professor, Marketing, Management, and Supply Chain, University of
Texas at El Paso. Email: yhe3@utep.edu
†Yangen Li, Department of Finance, Tippie College of Business, University of Iowa, Iowa City, IA
52242-1000. Email: yangen-li@uiowa.edu
1


[Page 2]
1 Introduction
Corporate logos represent one of the most enduring elements of marketing communi-
cation, with average lifespans exceeding 20 years and some iconic designs remaining
virtually unchanged for over a century (Henderson and Cote, 1998). Unlike advertis-
ing campaigns that rotate seasonally or product packaging that evolves with market
trends, logos serve as permanent visual anchors that transcend individual marketing
initiatives (Aaker, 1996). This temporal persistence positions logos as unique organiza-
tional artifacts that simultaneously serve multiple stakeholder groups: they communicate
brand positioning to consumers (Keller, 2003), signal corporate identity to investors and
business partners (Rao and Monroe, 1994), and reinforce organizational culture among
employees (Hatch and Schultz, 2002).
Despite extensive research examining how logo design characteristics influence con-
sumer perceptions, purchase intentions, and brand equity (Park et al., 2013; Luffarelli
et al., 2019), a fundamental question remains largely unexplored from the firm’s per-
spective:Why do firms choose specific visual designs for their logos?More importantly,
do these design choices systematically reflect underlying strategic orientations and or-
ganizational characteristics that extend beyond consumer-facing marketing objectives
(Porter, 1980)? While the consumer psychology literature has thoroughly documented
howaudiences respond to visual design elements (Labrecque and Milne, 2012), we know
surprisingly little aboutwhatfirms intend to communicate through their visual identity
choices and whether these choices encode meaningful information about corporate strat-
egy.
This knowledge gap is particularly striking given the substantial investments firms
make in visual identity development and management. Comprehensive rebranding ini-
tiatives can cost millions of dollars and require years of careful implementation across
global touchpoints (Muzellec and Lambkin, 2006). Corporate brand equity constitutes a
significant component of firm value (Madden et al., 2006), and visual identity serves as
a primary mechanism through which this equity is built and maintained. If logo design
were purely an aesthetic exercise aimed at consumer appeal, such investments might
2


[Page 3]
seem disproportionate for publicly traded companies where the primary “consumers” of
corporate visual identity are often sophisticated institutional investors (Bushee, 1998),
business clients, and industry analysts rather than retail customers. The persistence and
costliness of logo choices suggest they may serve functions beyond immediate consumer
attraction—potentially acting as strategic signals that communicate firm characteristics
to multiple stakeholder audiences (Freeman, 1984).
Existing logo research has almost exclusively adopted a “consumer perspective,”
investigating how logo design influences consumer perceptions, attitudes, and purchase
behaviors (Park et al., 2013). This paradigm has generated rich insights into visual
aesthetics and their psychological effects, but it contains a critical blind spot: logos are
treated as given marketing stimuli, with the question “why do firms design logos this
way?” remaining unasked. The strategic logic underlying design choices is treated as a
black box, with researchers focusing exclusively on “what logos work” while ignoring
“why firms choose these logos.” This theoretical asymmetry—examining logo effects
without understanding logo origins—limits our comprehension of visual identity as a
strategic phenomenon.
The consequences of this blind spot extend beyond incomplete description to flawed
theory. We understand how logos affect consumers but not how logos themselves are pro-
duced. This is analogous to studying advertising effectiveness without examining adver-
tising strategy (Tellis, 2004), or analyzing demand-side responses while ignoring supply-
side decisions. The firm’s perspective—encompassing strategic intentions (Mintzberg,
1987), organizational constraints, and competitive positioning (Porter, 1980)—remains
theoretically underdeveloped. As a result, we cannot distinguish whether observed logo
characteristics reflect deliberate strategic choices (Child, 1972), industry conventions
(DiMaggio and Powell, 1983), or random aesthetic preferences. More fundamentally,
we lack theoretical frameworks for understanding visual identity as strategic communi-
cation directed at multiple stakeholder audiences beyond consumers (Freeman, 1984).
This study introduces a paradigm shift by adopting a “firm perspective” that treats
logos not merely as objects of consumer decoding but as strategic encodings of firm
3


[Page 4]
characteristics. We ask: Do logo design choices systematically reflect firms’ strategic
orientations? Do innovation-intensive firms employ recognizable “visual grammars” that
distinguish them from conservative competitors? Can visual features serve as credible
signals of strategic positioning to sophisticated stakeholders including investors, industry
analysts, and business partners?
This perspective shift builds on signaling theory (Spence, 1973; Connelly et al.,
2011), which posits that when information asymmetries exist between parties (Akerlof,
1970), observable characteristics can serve as credible signals of unobservable qualities.
If firms face challenges in communicating strategic intentions to diverse stakeholders,
logos—as highly visible, costly, and persistent choices—may function as strategic signals
(Erdem and Swait, 1998). Innovation-oriented firms might systematically adopt dynamic,
modern visual languages to signal their technological focus and growth orientation, while
conservative firms may choose traditional, stable designs to communicate reliability and
operational maturity (Miles et al., 1978). The costliness and irreversibility of logo choices
enhance their credibility as signals (Kirmani, 1990): only firms genuinely committed
to particular strategic orientations can afford the reputational risks of misaligned visual
identities (Weigelt and Camerer, 1989).
To test whether logo design systematically reflects strategic orientations, we con-
struct a large-scale dataset integrating three complementary data sources covering 5,223
publicly traded U.S. firms. This multi-source approach enables us to link visual identity
characteristics to both internal strategic decisions (captured in financial statements) and
external market perceptions (reflected in trading data).
Data Integration.Our empirical analysis combines: (1)Logo imagescollected
via Clearbit API, providing standardized visual representations of corporate logos at
consistent resolution and format; (2)Financial datafrom Compustat annual fundamen-
tals, capturing strategic orientation through R&D intensity, capital expenditure patterns,
intangible asset ratios, and operational metrics; and (3)Market datafrom CRSP daily
stock returns, measuring external stakeholder perceptions through volatility measures,
systematic risk (beta), and firm-specific risk. This triangulation allows us to examine
4

text:
[Page 5]
whether logo-encoded information reflects both firms’ actual strategic choices and how
these strategies are perceived by market participants (Rego et al., 2009).
Methodological Approach.We employ a three-stage analytical framework. First,
we extract visual features from logo images using deep convolutional neural networks
(MobileNet V2 architecture), pre-trained on ImageNet and fine-tuned for our classifica-
tion tasks (Sandler et al., 2018). This approach captures both low-level visual primitives
(edges, textures, colors) and high-level semantic patterns automatically learned from
data, avoiding subjective human coding of visual characteristics. Second, we train su-
pervised machine learning classifiers (logistic regression with regularization, gradient
boosting, random forests) to predict binary strategic orientation measures—specifically,
whether firms exhibit above-median R&D intensity, capital expenditure intensity, and
market volatility. Performance is evaluated using Area Under the ROC Curve (AUC),
with statistical significance assessed through DeLong tests comparing prediction accu-
racy to random chance (AUC = 0.5). Third, we construct interpretable visual features
including complexity measures, symmetry metrics, color statistics, and whitespace ratios
to identify the specific visual dimensions that distinguish strategic orientations.
Three-Stage Hypothesis Testing.Our empirical strategy addresses three funda-
mental questions through a systematic hypothesis-testing framework:
Stage 1: Predictive Validity (H1).Do logo visual features predict firms’ strategic
orientations significantly above chance? We focus on R&D intensity as our primary
measure of innovation orientation, testing whether machine learning models trained on
visual features achieve AUC significantly greater than 0.5. This establishes whether
systematic logo-strategy associations exist.
Stage 2: Discriminant Validity (H4).What do logos predict? We contrast prediction
accuracy across three categories of firm characteristics: (a) strategic orientation mea-
sures (R&D intensity, capital expenditure intensity, intangible asset ratios), (b) financial
health measures (leverage, profitability), and (c) market risk perceptions (total volatility,
idiosyncratic risk, systematic risk). Signaling theory predicts logos should more accu-
rately predict strategic characteristics—which are difficult for stakeholders to observe
5


[Page 6]
directly and where information asymmetries are severe—than financial metrics readily
available in public disclosures. If logos merely reflect industry conventions or aesthetic
trends rather than strategic signals, prediction accuracy should not systematically vary
across these categories.
Stage 3: Contextual Boundary Conditions (H2).How does logo-strategy encoding
vary across industry contexts? We estimate industry-specific models using Fama-French
12 industry classifications and compare prediction accuracy across sectors. Strategic
heterogeneity theory suggests encoding effectiveness should be higher in industries char-
acterized by diverse business models and sophisticated stakeholders (e.g., Chemicals,
Finance), and lower in industries with standardized strategies or heavy regulatory con-
straints (e.g., Telecommunications, Utilities) where visual differentiation offers limited
informational value.
This design enables us to move beyond descriptive documentation of logo-strategy
correlations toward causal inference about the strategic encoding function of visual
identity. By examining not onlywhetherlogos predict strategy butwhatthey predict and
whenpredictions are strongest, we can distinguish strategic signaling from alternative
explanations such as industry isomorphism or random aesthetic variation (Deephouse,
1996).
Five categories of evidence support the hypothesis that logo design systematically
encodes strategic orientations. These findings collectively demonstrate that visual iden-
tity choices reflect underlying strategic characteristics in ways that are statistically robust,
theoretically coherent, and economically meaningful.
(1) Predictive Validity.Logo visual features predict innovation intensity at 60%
accuracy (AUC = 0.64, 95% CI: [0.60, 0.68],𝑝 <0.001) for R&D expenditure scaled
by total assets, significantly exceeding the random baseline of 50%. When using R&D
scaled by sales revenue, accuracy reaches 57% (AUC = 0.60, 95% CI: [0.55, 0.63],
𝑝 <0.001). These results are robust across four machine learning algorithms includ-
ing logistic regression, gradient boosting, and random forests, demonstrating stability
across different modeling assumptions. The 10–14 percentage point improvement over
6


[Page 7]
chance represents economically meaningful predictive power, particularly given that
visual features constitute only one observable dimension of strategic positioning.
(2) Selective Encoding.Logos primarily encode strategic investment orientations
rather than financial structure or operational outcomes. Visual features achieve strong
prediction for strategic positioning measures: R&D asset intensity (AUC = 0.64,𝑝 <
0.001) and capital expenditure intensity (AUC = 0.57,𝑝 <0.001). In sharp contrast,
prediction accuracy for financial metrics falls to chance levels: financial leverage (AUC
= 0.49, n.s.) and gross margin (AUC = 0.50–0.52, n.s.). The critical comparison—
R&D prediction at 0.64 versus leverage prediction at 0.49—rules out the alternative
explanation that “logos merely reflect financial conditions.” This discriminant validity
pattern demonstrates that logos selectively encode strategic orientations rather than
financial structure or market performance, consistent with signaling theory’s prediction
that signals emerge where information asymmetries are most severe (Connelly et al.,
2011).
(3) Visual Grammar.High R&D firms employ a systematic “modern minimalist”
visual grammar characterized by multiple convergent dimensions. Compared to low
R&D firms, innovation-intensive companies display: smoother textures with 27% lower
sharpness (𝑝 <0.001) and 23% lower texture variance (𝑝 <0.001); softer edges
with 18% lower edge strength (𝑝 <0.001) and 17% lower edge density (𝑝 <0.001);
and more unified visual presentation with 7% lower contrast (𝑝 <0.001) and 8%
lower color entropy (𝑝 <0.001). These characteristics cohere into a consistent modern
digital aesthetic, distinguishing innovation-oriented firms from the complex, ornate styles
favored by traditional enterprises. All 14 visual dimensions survive Benjamini-Hochberg
False Discovery Rate correction for multiple comparisons, ensuring statistical rigor. This
systematic patterning suggests that visual strategic signaling operates through learnable
design conventions rather than idiosyncratic aesthetic preferences.
(4) Industry Heterogeneity.The logo-strategy relationship varies significantly
across industries, with prediction accuracy ranging from 50% to 65%. High-performing
industries include Chemicals (65%), Energy (64%), and Finance (60%), while low-
7

text:
[Page 8]
performing industries include Healthcare (52%), Consumer Durables (51%), and Telecom-
munications (50%, equivalent to random guessing). This pattern aligns with theoretical
predictions: industries exhibiting high strategic heterogeneity, B2B orientation, and low
regulatory constraints display stronger logo-strategy associations. The Telecommunica-
tions industry, characterized by heavy regulation and resulting strategic homogeneity,
shows no logo-strategy relationship—logos cannot encode “strategic differences that do
not exist.” This contextual variation provides discriminant validity, demonstrating that
logo encoding effectiveness depends on underlying strategic diversity within industries
rather than reflecting universal aesthetic trends (Deephouse, 1996).
(5) Market Consistency.Strategic orientations manifest consistently in market
risk characteristics, providing convergent validation. Logo visual features predict total
volatility (AUC = 0.64, 95% CI: [0.61, 0.67],𝑝 <0.001), idiosyncratic risk (AUC =
0.61, 95% CI: [0.58, 0.64],𝑝 <0.001), and systematic risk (AUC = 0.55, 95% CI: [0.52,
0.58],𝑝 <0.001). The risk hierarchy—idiosyncratic risk (0.61) exceeds systematic risk
(0.55)—perfectly aligns with the interpretation that logos encode strategic choices (firm-
specific) rather than market exposure (systematic). Critically, logo prediction of volatility
(0.64) matches logo prediction of R&D intensity (0.64), forming a complete evidential
chain linking logo-strategy-market and ruling out spurious correlation. This triangulation
demonstrates that the visual features capturing R&D orientation also capture the risk
profiles associated with innovation strategies, supporting the interpretation that logos
authentically encode strategic positioning rather than superficial aesthetic trends (Chan
et al., 2001).
This research makes three theoretical contributions to the branding and strategic
management literatures, alongside two practical implications for brand management and
investment analysis.
Contribution 1: Paradigm Innovation.We systematically introduce the firm
perspective to logo research, filling the supply-side theoretical gap in visual identity
theory. Existing research explains “how logos work” (consumer perspective), while we
explain “why logos are designed this way” (firm perspective). Only by combining both
8


[Page 9]
perspectives can we construct a complete theory of corporate visual identity.
This is not merely adding a complementary viewpoint, but opening a new theoretical
space. The firm perspective focuses on strategic intent, multi-audience communication,
and long-term consistency, generating research questions and theoretical propositions
distinct from the consumer perspective. Prior research has examined how logo design in-
fluences consumer perceptions, attitudes, and purchase behaviors (Henderson and Cote,
1998; Luffarelli et al., 2019), treating logos as given marketing stimuli. Our firm perspec-
tive reconceptualizes logos as strategic encodings, shifting the causal arrow to “strategic
positioning→logo choice.” By establishing that logo design choices systematically
reflect strategic orientations, we provide the missing supply-side foundation that enables
understanding visual identity as an organizational phenomenon (Balmer and Greyser,
2006).
Contribution 2: Strategic Function of Visual Identity.We demonstrate that logos
are not merely marketing tools but strategic communication vehicles. Logo choices are
deeply rooted in firms’ strategic positioning, selectively reflecting innovation investment
and growth investment, while not reflecting financial structure or market performance.
This extends corporate identity theory (Balmer and Greyser, 2006), proving that visual
choices are not aesthetic decisions independent of strategy.
We identify systematic “visual grammars”—high innovation firms adopt modern
minimalist aesthetics (smooth textures, soft edges), indicating the existence of cross-
firm visual communication norms analogous to grammatical rules in language. High
R&D firms employ logos with 18–27% lower complexity measures, higher symmetry,
blue-dominant color palettes, and greater whitespace. The consistency of these pat-
terns across thousands of firms suggests that visual design principles function as shared
communication protocols that enable stakeholders to efficiently decode strategic signals
(Labrecque and Milne, 2012). This finding provides micro-level mechanisms for visual
communication theory, demonstrating that strategic signaling through visual identity
follows structured, learnable patterns rather than idiosyncratic preferences.
Contribution 3: Cross-Level Theoretical Integration.We establish theoretical
9


[Page 10]
linkages across micro (visual design), meso (strategic behavior), and macro (market
response) levels. We demonstrate that these three levels connect through strategic ori-
entation, with logos serving simultaneously as representations of strategy and predictors
of market evaluation. Logo prediction of R&D intensity (AUC = 0.64) matches logo
prediction of market volatility (AUC = 0.64), forming a complete evidential chain linking
visual identity, strategic positioning, and market perceptions. This provides an integrative
framework for understanding how firms communicate identity to diverse stakeholders
(Connelly et al., 2011), bridging branding theory and strategic management by posi-
tioning visual identity as substantive strategic communication rather than superficial
aesthetics.
Practical Implication 1: Brand Management.Logos should be incorporated
into the strategic communication toolkit, with design decisions considering strategic
consistency. Our findings provide diagnostic tools: benchmark visual characteristics
of high/low innovation firms within industries, and evaluate whether one’s own logo
accurately reflects strategic positioning. The visual grammar we document (simplicity,
symmetry, blue palettes for innovation; complexity and traditional aesthetics for stability)
provides actionable design principles for visual identity audits. Warning: misalignment
between logo and strategy may cause stakeholder confusion and weaken communication
effectiveness. When firms undergo strategic repositioning, visual identity may require
corresponding adjustment to maintain credible signaling (Muzellec and Lambkin, 2006).
Practical Implication 2: Investment Analysis.In information-limited contexts
(emerging markets, IPOs, startups), visual analysis can supplement traditional financial
analysis. Our industry heterogeneity results indicate this approach is most effective in
specific sectors: Chemicals (65%), Energy (64%), Finance (60%)—where professional
investors in these B2B-oriented industries can better decode visual strategic signals.
Limitations: this method has limited value in heavily regulated homogeneous industries
like Telecommunications (50%), and should only serve as a supplementary tool. Visual
features offer a universally observable, low-cost heuristic where R&D disclosure is
incomplete or institutional transparency is low (Chan et al., 2001). However, visual
10


[Page 11]
identity reflects strategic intent rather than execution quality—logo-based inferences
should inform rather than substitute rigorous operational and financial evaluation.
The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 reviews the relevant
literature and develops our theoretical framework, contrasting the consumer perspective
and firm perspective on corporate logos, and deriving five testable hypotheses grounded
in signaling theory and strategic management. Section 3 describes our data sources,
sample construction, and empirical methodology, with particular emphasis on visual
feature extraction using deep learning and our analytical strategy for testing predictive
validity, discriminant validity, and contextual boundary conditions. Section 4 presents
the empirical results, systematically testing each hypothesis through prediction accuracy
analysis, visual feature comparisons, and industry heterogeneity examination. Section 5
discusses the theoretical contributions to branding and strategic management literatures,
practical implications for brand managers and investors, and limitations of our research
design that point toward future research opportunities. Section 6 concludes by summa-
rizing our core findings and their broader implications for understanding visual identity
as strategic communication.
