2 Literature Review and Hypothesis Development
2.1 Corporate Visual Identity: Consumer Perspective vs. Firm
Perspective
2.1.1 The Dominant Paradigm: Consumer Perspective
Logo research has traditionally adopted a consumer perspective, focusing on how visual
identity elements influence consumer cognition, affect, and behavior. This paradigm’s
core assumption posits that logos are tools through which firms influence markets;
consequently, research should prioritize understanding “influence mechanisms” and “ef-
fectiveness evaluation.” Under this framework, logos are conceptualized as marketing
stimuli whose primary function is to facilitate brand recognition, evoke positive associ-
ations, and ultimately drive purchase intentions and brand loyalty (Keller, 1993). The
consumer perspective has generated a rich body of knowledge documenting system-
atic relationships between specific design features and consumer responses, providing
actionable insights for brand identity development.
Representative research within this paradigm has examined how discrete logo design
characteristics shape consumer perceptions and preferences. Henderson and Cote (1998)
conducted seminal work demonstrating that structural features such as symmetry, com-
plexity, and natural representativeness systematically predict consumer liking and brand
recognition. Their findings established that balanced, moderately complex designs gener-
ate more favorable consumer responses than asymmetric or overly intricate alternatives.
Subsequent research extended these insights across multiple dimensions: Park et al.
(2013) documented that logo recognizability correlates with firm financial performance,
suggesting that distinctive visual identities create measurable economic value. Luffarelli
et al. (2019) uncovered an interaction between logo design and brand personality, show-
ing that symmetrical logos enhance perceptions of brand sincerity while asymmetrical
designs signal excitement and innovation. Machado et al. (2015) explored how incor-
porating natural elements (organic shapes, nature-inspired imagery) into logo designs
12


[Page 15]
it provides an essential complement that completes the theoretical picture. The relation-
ship between firm and consumer perspectives parallels the structure of advertising re-
search: consumer-oriented studies examine advertising effectiveness (how ads influence
purchase behavior), while strategy-oriented research analyzes advertising decisions (why
firms allocate budgets to particular media channels, messages, or creative approaches).
Both perspectives are necessary for comprehensive understanding. Similarly, logo re-
search requires both reception analysis (consumer perspective: how visual features affect
brand perceptions) and production analysis (firm perspective: why firms choose partic-
ular visual configurations). A complete theory of corporate visual identity must address
both sides of the communication process—encoding by firms and decoding by audi-
ences. The firm perspective fills the production-side gap that has remained theoretically
underdeveloped despite decades of reception-side research.
The firm perspective draws theoretical grounding from corporate identity theory,
which conceptualizes organizational identity as a multifaceted construct encompass-
ing what organizations are, what they communicate, and what they aspire to become
(Balmer and Greyser, 2006). Balmer and Greyser (2006) distinguish three identity di-
mensions: actual identity (“what you are”—the organization’s current characteristics,
capabilities, and strategic orientation), communicated identity (“what you say”—the
messages and symbols through which the organization presents itself), and ideal identity
(“what you want to be”—aspirational goals and desired positioning). Corporate visual
identity, including logos, constitutes the most visible component of communicated iden-
tity. However, corporate identity theory posits that sustainable organizational legitimacy
and stakeholder trust require alignment across these three dimensions. Visual choices
that misrepresent actual characteristics or contradict strategic realities create credibility
gaps that undermine organizational reputation (Van den Bosch et al., 2005).
Empirical research provides preliminary evidence supporting the premise that visual
identity reflects and reinforces organizational realities. Van den Bosch et al. (2005)
demonstrate through longitudinal case studies that corporate visual identity systems
contribute to reputation building, but only when visual choices authentically represent
15


[Page 16]
organizational values, capabilities, and strategic priorities. When visual identity diverges
from organizational reality—projecting innovation without corresponding R&D invest-
ments, or signaling tradition while pursuing aggressive change—stakeholders perceive
inconsistency that damages credibility. Melewar and Karaosmanoglu (2006) develop
a comprehensive framework identifying seven dimensions of corporate visual identity
(name, logo, typography, color, slogan, architecture, product design) and emphasize that
effectiveness across these elements requires strategic consistency and alignment with
corporate strategy. Hatch and Schultz (2002) analyze the dynamic interplay between
organizational culture, visual identity, and external image, arguing that visual symbols
both express and shape organizational identity through iterative processes of internal
alignment and external interpretation.
These theoretical and empirical foundations suggest that logo design choices are not
arbitrary aesthetic decisions but strategic expressions embedded within broader corpo-
rate identity systems. However, existing research has primarily relied on qualitative case
studies and small-sample analyses focusing on specific organizations or industries. While
these studies establish the conceptual premise that visual identity should align with orga-
nizational strategy, they lack large-scale empirical validation of whether logos actually
do systematically reflect firm characteristics across diverse competitive contexts. The
critical empirical question remains unaddressed: Do observable visual features contain
systematic information about firms’ strategic orientations? Can visual identity choices
serve as credible signals that differentiate innovation-intensive firms from operationally
conservative competitors? Does the hypothesized alignment between visual identity and
corporate strategy manifest as statistically detectable patterns in cross-sectional data?
Our research addresses this gap by conducting the first large-scale empirical investiga-
tion of whether and how corporate logos encode strategic information, moving beyond
conceptual frameworks and case-based illustrations to systematic quantitative evidence.
16


[Page 17]
2.1.3 Integrating the Two Perspectives
It is crucial to emphasize that the consumer perspective and firm perspective are com-
plementary rather than competing paradigms. These viewpoints address different but
equally important aspects of corporate visual identity: the consumer perspective opti-
mizes logos’ market effectiveness by identifying visual features that enhance recognition,
evoke positive affect, and strengthen brand equity, while the firm perspective ensures lo-
gos’ strategic authenticity by examining whether visual choices accurately represent
organizational characteristics and competitive positioning. Optimal logo design requires
balancing both dimensions—visual identity must simultaneously communicate strategic
intentions accurately (firm perspective requirement) and influence stakeholder percep-
tions effectively (consumer perspective requirement).
This dual requirement creates potential tensions in visual identity management. A
logo that maximizes consumer appeal through familiar, symmetric, simple designs may
fail to differentiate the firm’s unique strategic orientation. Conversely, a logo that
authentically signals innovation-intensive positioning through unconventional visual vo-
cabulary may sacrifice processing fluency and immediate consumer liking. Navigating
this tension requires understanding both what visual features resonate with target au-
diences (consumer perspective insight) and what visual patterns credibly represent the
firm’s actual strategic commitments (firm perspective insight). Table 2 summarizes the
key dimensions distinguishing these complementary perspectives

The present research focuses primarily on establishing the firm perspective through
systematic empirical investigation. By demonstrating that logos systematically encode
strategic orientations, we provide the foundational evidence necessary for future re-
search integrating both perspectives. Subsequent studies might examine how firms bal-
ance strategic authenticity against consumer preferences when these objectives conflict,
identify visual features that simultaneously satisfy both firm-level signaling needs and
consumer-level aesthetic preferences, or investigate how the relative importance of each
17


[Page 18]
perspective varies across industries, firm life stages, or stakeholder compositions. Under-
standing corporate visual identity as both a strategic signal (firm view) and a marketing
stimulus (consumer view) opens rich avenues for developing comprehensive theories of
visual communication that bridge strategic management, marketing, and organizational
studies.

2.2 Signaling Theory and Visual Communication
Signaling theory provides the theoretical foundation for understanding how corporate
logos can credibly communicate strategic information under conditions of information
asymmetry (Spence, 1973). Originally developed to explain labor market dynamics, sig-
naling theory addresses a fundamental economic problem: how can parties possessing
superior information about unobservable qualities credibly communicate these attributes
to information-disadvantaged counterparts? The theory’s core logic posits that when
direct verification of characteristics is costly or impossible, observable and costly sig-
nals can serve as credible indicators of underlying quality (Connelly et al., 2011). In
the original formulation, job applicants signal unobservable productivity through educa-
tional credentials, which are costly to acquire and systematically correlated with actual
ability. This mechanism achieves separation between high-quality and low-quality types
because the cost of signal acquisition differs systematically across quality levels, making
it unprofitable for low-quality actors to mimic high-quality signals.
For a signal to effectively communicate information and achieve equilibrium separa-
tion, it must satisfy three critical conditions (Connelly et al., 2011). First,observability
requires that the signal be readily perceivable by the intended audience. Signals that
are difficult to detect or interpret cannot influence receivers’ beliefs and behaviors, ren-
dering them ineffective as communication mechanisms. Second,costlinessdemands
that signal production and maintenance impose differential costs on signalers based on
their true quality. This cost structure creates the separation necessary for credible sig-
naling: high-quality actors find it relatively inexpensive to produce authentic signals,
while low-quality actors face prohibitively high costs when attempting to send false sig-
nals. This differential ensures that only those genuinely possessing the signaled attribute
will find it economically rational to invest in the signal, thereby establishing credibility.
Third,consistencyrequires systematic alignment between the signal and the underlying
characteristic it purports to represent. Without consistent correlation, signals become
uninformative noise rather than credible indicators of quality. These three conditions
collectively determine whether a potential signal can function as an effective information
19


[Page 20]
transmission mechanism in markets characterized by asymmetric information.
Corporate logos satisfy all three conditions for effective signaling, positioning them
as potentially powerful vehicles for communicating strategic orientations to multiple
stakeholder audiences. Regardingobservability, logos represent the most visible and
ubiquitous element of corporate visual identity. Unlike internal organizational character-
istics or detailed strategic plans that remain opaque to external stakeholders, logos appear
prominently across all corporate touchpoints—product packaging, websites, advertising
campaigns, annual reports, investor presentations, retail environments, and corporate
communications. This omnipresence ensures that logos reach diverse audiences includ-
ing consumers, investors, employees, suppliers, and regulators. The high visibility of
logos makes them ideal candidates for strategic signaling: stakeholders encounter cor-
porate visual identity frequently and can easily observe design characteristics without
specialized knowledge or costly information acquisition.
Logos also exhibit substantialcostliness, both in initial design and in subsequent
changes, creating the commitment value essential for credible signaling (Kirmani, 1990).
The upfront investment in professional logo design involves significant creative fees,
market research to ensure appropriateness, legal expenses for trademark registration and
protection, and implementation costs across physical and digital platforms. More im-
portantly, changing an established logo imposes enormous switching costs: firms forfeit
accumulated brand recognition, confuse existing customers, and must invest heavily in
communicating the change across all touchpoints (Muzellec and Lambkin, 2006). These
costs create commitment value—once a firm adopts a particular visual identity, the sub-
stantial expense of reversal means the logo represents a durable strategic choice rather
than a easily reversible tactical decision. This irreversibility enhances logos’ credibility
as strategic signals: firms cannot cheaply alter their visual identity to opportunistically
exploit short-term market conditions, ensuring that logo choices reflect genuine long-
term strategic commitments.
The critical question for empirical investigation concerns the third condition:con-
sistency. Do logo design characteristics systematically align with firms’ actual strategic
20


[Page 22]
atic correlations provides direct evidence that firms use visual identity strategically to
encode and communicate information about their competitive positioning, transforming
logos from passive aesthetic choices into active strategic communication tools. Our
empirical investigation tests this fundamental prediction by examining whether visual
features contain systematic information about innovation intensity, thereby validating the
theoretical premise that corporate logos serve signaling functions beyond their traditional
role as consumer-facing marketing stimuli.
22


[Page 23]
2.3 Strategic Orientation and Visual Encoding
Strategic orientation refers to the directional thrust of a firm’s competitive strategy, re-
flecting fundamental choices about how the organization positions itself in competitive
space and allocates scarce resources across alternative activities (Miles et al., 1978).
Innovation strategic orientation, in particular, describes firms that emphasize technolog-
ical advancement, new product development, and market pioneering as primary sources
of competitive advantage (Miller, 1986). This strategic posture manifests in observable
behaviors and resource commitments: high R&D expenditure as a percentage of sales rev-
enue, substantial capital investments in cutting-edge production capabilities, active patent
portfolios protecting intellectual property, and organizational structures that reward ex-
perimentation and tolerate calculated risk-taking (Dosi, 1988). Innovation-oriented firms
pursue growth through creating new markets, disrupting established categories, and main-
taining technological leadership, accepting higher operational uncertainty and earnings
volatility in exchange for potential market dominance and superior long-term returns.
However, innovation-oriented strategies create significant communication challenges
when firms must convey their positioning to external stakeholders who lack access to
internal strategic deliberations. Innovation outcomes exhibit extreme temporal delay
and fundamental uncertainty (Kothari et al., 2002): R&D investments made today may
not yield marketable products for years, and even successful development projects face
uncertain commercial reception. During this gestation period, innovation-intensive firms
often display weaker short-term financial performance than operationally conservative
peers—lower profit margins due to heavy R&D expenses, volatile earnings driven by
lumpy project success, and negative free cash flows resulting from capital-intensive in-
vestments in unproven technologies (Chan et al., 2001). These characteristics can trigger
stakeholder concern unless firms effectively communicate that current financial sacrifices
represent strategic investments in future growth rather than operational inefficiency or
competitive weakness.
Absent credible communication mechanisms, stakeholders may misinterpret innova-
tion investments as value destruction rather than value creation, leading to suboptimal
23


[Page 24]
outcomes. Impatient investors may divest, depressing stock prices and increasing cost
of capital. Risk-averse employees may exit, draining critical talent. Conservative sup-
pliers may tighten credit terms, constraining operational flexibility. To forestall these
responses, innovation-oriented firms require channels through which they can credibly
signal their strategic commitments, helping stakeholders distinguish genuine innovation
strategies from poor operational performance. This communication imperative creates
strong incentives for firms to encode strategic orientations in highly visible, costly, and
persistent signals—precisely the characteristics exhibited by corporate logos.
The mechanism through which logos encode strategic information operates through
systematic alignment between visual design features and strategic positioning. Design
professionals and brand managers—whether through conscious strategic planning or
intuitive pattern matching—select visual elements that resonate with and reinforce the
firm’s competitive positioning (Henderson and Cote, 1998). For innovation-oriented
firms pursuing technological leadership and market disruption, this encoding process
favors dynamic visual vocabularies that connote forward momentum, creative energy,
and transformative potential. These visual languages employ specific design character-
istics that psychological research has linked to perceptions of modernity, vitality, and
innovation (Labrecque and Milne, 2012).
Innovation orientation manifests in logos through several systematic visual patterns.
First,high color saturation—the intensity or purity of hues—serves as a primary mech-
anism for conveying energy and dynamism. Highly saturated colors (vivid reds, bright
blues, intense greens) attract attention, stimulate arousal, and activate associations with
excitement and forward motion. Color psychology research demonstrates that saturated
hues evoke perceptions of youthfulness, vitality, and modernity, while desaturated or
muted colors communicate maturity, restraint, and tradition. Innovation-oriented firms
leveraging saturated color palettes thus send visual signals aligned with their strategic
emphasis on change, disruption, and technological advancement.
Second,modern typography and geometric forms—characterized by clean lines,
sans-serif fonts, angular shapes, and minimalist aesthetics—communicate technologi-

from movements emphasizing functionality, innovation, and rejection of traditional or-

and proven track records over innovation and growth potential.
Importantly, the effectiveness of visual encoding relies on shared cultural codes and
learned associations between visual features and conceptual meanings. Stakeholders
interpret logo characteristics through frameworks shaped by exposure to design conven-
tions, advertising norms, and historical associations between visual styles and organiza-
tional attributes. When design choices align with these culturally embedded interpretive

Edge Features and Perceived Precision.Edge characteristics influence perceptions
of precision and dynamism. Sharp edges convey accuracy, professionalism, and technical
competence, while soft edges convey friendliness, flexibility, and human-centeredness.
High edge strength/density communicates precise control and technical sophistication—
appropriate for industries emphasizing accuracy such as industrial manufacturing, ma-
chinery, and finance. Sharp lines increase visual tension and attention. Low edge
strength/density (softness) communicates flexibility and user-friendliness—appropriate
for services, creative industries, and consumer products emphasizing approachability.
Rounded shapes reduce perceived visual threat. Innovation firms may select soft edges
to balance technical competence with approachability, avoiding excessively “cold” in-
dustrial impressions. This design choice reflects the dual positioning challenge faced by
innovation-intensive firms: signaling technical sophistication while maintaining acces-
sibility to diverse stakeholder audiences including consumers, investors, and business
partners.
Visual Unity and Brand Consistency.Color and brightness uniformity (low entropy,
low standard deviation) signals brand control and consistency. High variability suggests
diversity but may be interpreted as lacking focus. High visual unity conveys clear
positioning and strategic focus—single dominant colors strengthen memorability and
are appropriate for emerging brands needing strong recognition. Low visual unity
conveys diversification and inclusiveness—multiple colors may dilute recognition but
are appropriate for established mature firms with proven brand equity. Innovation firms
in their establishment phase require strong recognition and therefore tend toward unified
visual presentations to rapidly occupy mental space among stakeholders. This aligns with
organizational life-cycle theory: young firms face legitimacy challenges and information
asymmetries that necessitate clear, consistent identity signals, while mature firms possess
reputational capital that permits more complex visual expressions (Hannan and Freeman,
1984).
28


[Page 29]
2.5 Moderating Role of Industry Context
Signal effectiveness depends on context (Taj, 2016; Connelly et al., 2011). We identify
three industry characteristics that should moderate the strength of the logo-strategy
relationship, determining when visual identity encoding provides greatest informational
value.
(1) Strategic Heterogeneity.The greater the strategic diversity among firms within
an industry, the higher the value of logos as differentiating signals. In industries charac-
terized by diverse business models, competitive strategies, and innovation approaches,
visual identity serves a critical discriminatory function—enabling stakeholders to quickly
categorize firms into strategic archetypes. For example, the chemicals industry en-
compasses traditional commodity chemicals, specialty chemicals, pharmaceuticals, and
biotechnology, each requiring fundamentally different strategic orientations (asset inten-
sity, R&D focus, regulatory navigation). In such contexts, logos can encode meaningful
strategic distinctions. Conversely, highly homogeneous industries offer limited differen-
tiation opportunities. The telecommunications industry, characterized by infrastructure-
intensive business models, regulatory standardization, and convergent service offerings,
provides little strategic diversity for logos to encode. When “strategic differences do not
exist,” visual identity cannot function as a discriminating signal (Deephouse, 1996).
(2) Audience Sophistication.Professional buyers and investors in B2B industries
possess greater capability to decode complex strategic signals compared to mass con-
sumers in B2C contexts. Institutional stakeholders—industry analysts, procurement
managers, venture capitalists—are trained to interpret multidimensional information
and integrate visual cues with financial, operational, and competitive data. These audi-
ences actively search for strategic positioning signals when making high-stakes decisions
(supplier selection, investment allocation, partnership formation). In contrast, mass con-
sumers in B2C industries primarily engage with brands through emotional associations
and product-level attributes rather than corporate-level strategic orientations (Keller,
1993). While B2C logos certainly convey brand personality and emotional benefits, they
carry less corporate strategic information because the audience lacks both the motivation
29


[Page 30]
and analytical tools to decode such signals. Therefore, logo-strategy encoding should be
strongest in B2B-oriented industries where sophisticated stakeholders demand and can
interpret strategic positioning information.
(3) Regulatory Constraints.Heavy regulation restricts strategic degrees of freedom,
pushing firms toward homogenization and thereby reducing the informational content
of visual identity (DiMaggio and Powell, 1983). In industries subject to rate regula-
tion, service standardization, infrastructure mandates, or licensing restrictions—such
as utilities, telecommunications, and healthcare—strategic choices narrow to execution
efficiency within regulated parameters. When regulatory frameworks dictate technol-
ogy standards, pricing mechanisms, and service territories, firms converge on similar
strategic profiles regardless of managerial preferences. Under these conditions, logos
cannot credibly signal strategic differentiation because underlying strategic diversity is
constrained. Conversely, industries with lighter regulatory touch and greater competitive
freedom enable wider strategic variation, creating opportunities for visual identity to
encode meaningful strategic distinctions (Porter, 1980).
Integrating these three dimensions, we predict that the logo-strategy relationship
should be strongest in industries exhibiting high strategic heterogeneity, B2B orientation,
and low regulatory constraints. Industries combining innovation intensity (necessitat-
ing strategic differentiation), sophisticated stakeholder audiences (capable of decoding
signals), and competitive freedom (permitting strategic diversity) provide optimal con-
ditions for visual identity to function as effective strategic communication. Conversely,
industries characterized by strategic homogeneity, consumer orientation, or heavy reg-
ulation should exhibit weak or non-existent logo-strategy associations, as the structural
conditions for meaningful visual encoding are absent.
2.6 Research Hypotheses
Building on the theoretical framework developed above, we propose five hypotheses that
systematically test whether, how, and when logos encode strategic orientations.
H1: Core Hypothesis—Logo Encodes Strategy.

H3: Specific Visual Features.

H3a: Smoother textures (low complexity, modern flat design)

H3b: Softer edges (low edge strength and density)
H3c: More unified visual presentation (low color/brightness variance)
Theoretical rationale:These features form a coherent modern digital aesthetic that
communicates innovation and forward orientation through visual psychology mecha-
nisms (modernity perception, approachability, brand focus), distinguishing innovation
firms from the complex, ornate styles favored by traditional enterprises (Labrecque and
Milne, 2012). The technology giants’ logo simplification trend in the early 21st century
established “smooth = innovative” as a visual convention.

comparing high/low R&D firm groups, with Benjamini-Hochberg correction for multiple

H4: Mechanism—Strategy vs. Finance.
H4: Logos primarily encode strategic investments (R&D, CapEx) rather than fi-
nancial structure (leverage) or market outcomes (gross margin), indicating that visual
identity reflects strategic orientation rather than financial condition or performance.
Theoretical rationale:If logos are strategic signals, they should strongly correlate
with strategic behaviors but weakly or not at all with non-strategic financial choices or
market outcomes. This discriminant validity test rules out two alternative explanations:
(1) “logos merely reflect financial risk/capability,” and (2) “logos merely reflect market
success.” Strategic investments represent deliberate resource allocation choices where
information asymmetries are severe, while financial metrics are publicly disclosed and
market outcomes reflect multiple factors beyond strategic intent (Kothari et al., 2002).

and compare prediction performance. Expected pattern: AUC for R&D and CapEx
significantly exceeds 0.5; AUC for leverage and gross margin approximately equals 0.5
(non-significant). This pattern would demonstrate selective encoding consistent with
strategic signaling theory.

R&D) should exhibit consistency with market risk characteristics (stock price volatil-

firm-specific risk.
Theoretical rationale:Innovation strategy inherently entails higher uncertainty. Ex-

volatility, particularly idiosyncratic risk (firm-specific non-diversifiable risk), while
showing weaker effects on systematic risk (market-correlated variation) (Chan et al.,

strategy-market relationship should also manifest in the logo-market relationship, form-
ing triangular validation. This convergence between accounting-based strategic measures
and market-based risk perceptions would support the interpretation that logos encode
genuine strategic information that stakeholders decode and incorporate into valuations.
Critical clarification:This hypothesis does not claim logos causally influence mar-

indirect evidence that logos encode strategic information. Both logos and volatility are
manifestations of underlying strategic orientations.

systematic risk AUC (hierarchical evidence). Alignment across these tests would demon-

3 Methodology
3.1 Research Design Overview
This research employs a large-scale cross-sectional design integrating three types of data:
visual identity (logo images), financial fundamentals (strategic investments and financial
structure), and market-based measures (risk perceptions reflected in trading data). The
core design logic follows from our theoretical framework: if logos systematically reflect
strategic orientations, we should observe statistical associations between logo character-
istics and strategic behaviors (R&D investment), and these associations should exhibit
theoretically predicted patterns in terms of mechanisms (encoding strategy rather than
finance) and contexts (industry moderation).
Three-Stage Analytical Strategy.Our empirical investigation proceeds through
three complementary analyses that collectively test the five hypotheses developed in
Section 2:
Stage 1 (H1, H4): Predictive validity and discriminant validity.We use logo visual
features to predict both strategic variables (R&D intensity, capital expenditure intensity,
intangible asset ratios) and non-strategic variables (financial leverage, gross margin). By
comparing prediction performance across these different categories of firm characteris-
tics, we test whether logos selectively encode strategic orientations—the core discrim-
inant validity requirement of signaling theory (Connelly et al., 2011). If logos merely
reflected general firm characteristics, industry conventions, or firm size, prediction ac-
curacy should be comparable across all variables. Instead, signaling theory predicts
systematically higher accuracy for strategic measures where information asymmetries
are most severe.
Stage 2 (H3): Visual feature identification.We identify systematic differences in
interpretable visual dimensions between high and low innovation firms. While Stage
1 establishesthatlogos predict strategy using automatically extracted deep learning
features, Stage 2 revealshowthey do so by examining human-interpretable visual char-
acteristics including texture complexity, edge sharpness, symmetry, color distributions,

Rationale for Data and Method Choices.Four design decisions ensure our tests
provide valid inferences about logo-strategy associations:
Large sample size (N = 5,223).Statistical power and generalizability require substan-
tial sample sizes, particularly for machine learning approaches where training-test splits
and cross-validation reduce effective sample sizes for any single model. Our sample en-
compasses diverse industries, firm sizes, and strategic orientations, enabling both overall
tests and industry-specific subgroup analyses. This scale distinguishes our study from
prior logo research typically examining dozens or hundreds of logos through laboratory
experiments or manual coding (Henderson and Cote, 1998).
Machine learning for feature extraction.We employ deep convolutional neural net-
works pre-trained on large-scale image datasets to extract visual features automatically,
avoiding subjective human judgments about logo characteristics. Human coders exhibit
inconsistent reliability when evaluating abstract visual qualities (“modernity,” “com-
plexity”), introduce experimenter demand effects, and cannot feasibly process thousands
of logos. Deep learning models learn hierarchical visual representations—from low-
35


[Page 36]
level edges and textures to high-level semantic patterns—optimized for discriminating
strategic orientations through supervised learning (Sandler et al., 2018). This approach
maximizes predictive accuracy while minimizing subjective bias.
Multiple algorithms for robustness.We compare four machine learning architectures:
logistic regression with L1 and L2 regularization (interpretable linear models), gradient
boosting (ensemble method capturing non-linear interactions), and random forests (robust
to overfitting). Consistency across algorithms with different inductive biases strengthens
confidence that results reflect genuine logo-strategy associations rather than model-
specific artifacts. Algorithm diversity also enables sensitivity analysis of key modeling
choices (regularization strength, tree depth, feature selection).
Interpretable feature analysis for mechanisms.While deep learning features optimize
prediction, they lack transparency regardingwhichvisual characteristics drive associ-
ations. We therefore construct 14 interpretable visual features measuring complexity,
symmetry, color statistics, and spatial organization. This dual approach—predictive
deep learning plus interpretable features—balances accuracy and insight, enabling both
strong hypothesis tests (Stage 1) and mechanistic understanding (Stage 2). Interpretable
features also facilitate practical application, as brand managers can operationalize design
guidelines based on concrete metrics rather than black-box model outputs.
This research design balances internal validity (through careful control of confounds
and multiple hypothesis tests) with external validity (through large diverse samples and
real-world logos rather than synthetic stimuli), providing a rigorous test of whether
corporate visual identity systematically encodes strategic orientation.
3.2 Data Sources and Sample Construction
Our empirical analysis integrates three complementary data sources, each providing dis-
tinct dimensions of firm characteristics necessary for testing logo-strategy associations.
This multi-source triangulation enables us to link visual identity (observable to all stake-
holders) with internal strategic decisions (from financial statements) and external market
perceptions (from trading data).
36


[Page 37]
(1) Financial Data: Compustat Database.We obtain standardized accounting
metrics from Compustat annual fundamentals, covering the universe of publicly traded
U.S. firms with available financial statements. Key variables include R&D expenditure,
sales revenue, capital expenditure, total assets, leverage ratios, and gross margin. All
data derive from audited annual financial reports, ensuring accuracy and comparability
across firms and time periods. We employ Fama-French 12 industry classifications to
capture broad sectoral differences in business models and strategic contexts (Fama and
French, 1997). These financial measures constitute our primary dependent variables
representing strategic orientation—specifically, resource allocation decisions reflecting
innovation intensity (R&D/assets, R&D/sales) and growth investment (CapEx/assets).
Complete variable definitions appear in Table 1.
(2) Market Data: CRSP Database.We extract daily stock returns, prices, and
trading volumes from the Center for Research in Security Prices (CRSP) database, cov-
ering all common stocks traded on NYSE, NASDAQ, and AMEX exchanges. These
market data enable construction of volatility measures capturing external stakeholder
perceptions of firm risk profiles. Following standard finance methodology, we calculate
annualized return volatility (standard deviation of daily returns), systematic risk (beta
from market model regression), and idiosyncratic risk (residual volatility from market
model) (Fama and French, 1992). These market-based measures serve as validation
variables in H5, testing whether logo-encoded strategic orientations align with risk per-
ceptions reflected in trading data. Critically, market measures derive from decentralized
decisions of thousands of investors and traders, providing independent validation that is
not mechanically related to accounting-based strategic metrics or visual design choices.
(3) Logo Images: Clearbit API.We collect corporate logo images using the Clear-
bit Logo API, a commercial service providing high-resolution visual identity assets
for publicly traded companies. Logos are delivered in PNG format with transparent
backgrounds, standardized to consistent resolution (400×400 pixels minimum) to ensure
adequate detail for visual feature extraction. We match logos to financial and market data
using stock ticker symbols as unique identifiers. The Clearbit API retrieves logos cur-
37


[Page 38]
rently displayed on corporate websites, representing firms’ active visual identity choices
rather than historical or deprecated designs. This contemporaneous matching ensures
that visual features correspond to the same time period as financial and market data.
Sample Construction Process.We construct our final analytical sample through
systematic filtering designed to ensure data quality and completeness across all three
data sources:
Step 1: Initial universe.We begin with the intersection of CRSP and Compustat
databases, identifying all U.S. publicly traded firms with both market data (trading
history) and financial fundamentals (accounting statements). This intersection represents
the population of firms for which comprehensive financial and market analysis is feasible.
Step 2: Logo matching.We query the Clearbit API using stock ticker symbols,
successfully retrieving logo images for 5,223 firms. Match rates reflect both API coverage
(not all firms have logos indexed) and deliberate exclusions (firms without distinct visual
identity, such as special purpose vehicles or holding companies with no public-facing
brand).
Step 3: Financial data screening.We exclude firms with missing values for critical
variables including R&D expenditure, sales revenue, total assets, and industry classifica-
tion. While some firms legitimately report zero R&D (no innovation activity), missing
R&D indicates incomplete disclosure and is coded as missing rather than zero. This
conservative approach ensures our sample comprises firms with complete strategic and
financial profiles.
Step 4: Market data sufficiency.We require at least 200 trading days of return data
to reliably estimate volatility and beta coefficients. This threshold balances sample size
against estimation precision—fewer trading days yield unreliable risk metrics, while
stricter thresholds unnecessarily exclude viable firms (Fama and French, 1992).
Step 5: Image quality control.We exclude images with resolution below 200×200
pixels (insufficient detail for feature extraction), corrupted files (download errors), or non-
logo content (wrong image retrieved). Visual inspection of random samples confirms
that retained images accurately represent corporate logos rather than product images,

executive photos, or generic placeholders.
Step 6: Cross-sectional snapshot.For firms with multiple years of data, we retain
the most recent fiscal year to construct a cross-sectional dataset. This design choice
reflects our focus on contemporaneous logo-strategy associations rather than longitudinal
dynamics of logo changes. Cross-sectional analysis maximizes sample size and avoids
complications from unbalanced panels, though it precludes causal identification through
within-firm variation.
Final sample: N = 5,223 firms.
Sample Representativeness.Our final sample exhibits broad coverage of U.S. pub-
licly traded firms across multiple dimensions. Industry distribution spans all Fama-
French 12 sectors, ensuring that results are not driven by narrow sectoral patterns
(industry-specific prediction accuracy appears in Table 9). Market capitalization ranges
from small-cap to large-cap firms, although larger firms are overrepresented due to higher
logo availability and data completeness—a limitation we acknowledge but do not expect
to bias tests of logo-strategy associations. R&D intensity exhibits substantial varia-
tion from zero (firms with no reported R&D) to over 50% of sales for high-innovation
biotechnology and software firms, as documented in summary statistics (Table 3). This
heterogeneity ensures adequate variation in both dependent variables (strategic orienta-
tion) and independent variables (visual features) for detecting associations, while also
enabling subgroup analyses by industry and innovation intensity.
3.3 Variable Measurement
3.3.1 Strategic Orientation Measures (Primary Dependent Variables)
Core Indicators: R&D Intensity (Two Scaling Approaches).We measure innovation
strategic orientation using two complementary R&D intensity metrics, each capturing
distinct aspects of firms’ innovation commitment:
Metric 1: R&D/Total Assets (rd assets).
Definition:Research and development expenditure (Compustat item XRD) divided
by total assets (AT). This ratio reflects the proportion of firm resources allocated to
39


[Page 40]
innovation activities, representing resource allocation structure independent of sales
performance.
Advantages:This measure captures strategic resource commitment that is less af-
fected by short-term sales cyclicality, providing greater cross-industry comparability
than sales-scaled metrics. Asset-scaled R&D reflects management’s decision about what
percentage of the firm’s total resource base to devote to innovation, making it particularly
suitable for comparing firms with different business models and market exposures (Chan
et al., 2001).
Operationalization:We classify firms into high/low R&D groups using the sample
median as the threshold, creating a binary classification task. This dichotomization
simplifies interpretation and aligns with machine learning classification frameworks.
Metric 2: R&D/Sales Revenue (rd intensity).
Definition:Research and development expenditure (XRD) divided by net sales rev-
enue (SALE). This ratio reflects innovation investment relative to market scale, repre-
senting the percentage of revenue reinvested into R&D.
Advantages:Sales-scaled R&D is the traditional metric in innovation research,
facilitating comparison with prior literature. It captures innovation intensity relative to
current business scale, indicating how aggressively firms invest in future capabilities
relative to present operations (Kothari et al., 2002).
Limitations:This measure can exhibit high volatility due to sales fluctuations, partic-
ularly for firms experiencing rapid growth or cyclical demand. Temporary sales declines
mechanically inflate R&D intensity, potentially misclassifying operationally distressed
firms as highly innovative.
Operationalization:Similar to rd assets, we classify firms into high/low groups using
sample median split for binary classification.
Our primary analyses employ rd assets (reported in Table 4, Panel A) as the main
dependent variable, with rd intensity serving as robustness check (Table 4, Panel B).
Results that hold across both scaling approaches provide stronger evidence of genuine
logo-strategy associations rather than measurement artifacts.
40


[Page 41]
Rationale for R&D as Strategic Orientation Proxy.Four considerations justify
R&D intensity as our primary measure of innovation strategic orientation:
First, direct innovation measurement.R&D expenditure directly captures innovation
input, representing firms’ explicit commitment to developing new products, processes,
and technologies. Unlike indirect proxies such as patent counts (which depend on
patenting strategy) or new product announcements (which depend on marketing strategy),
R&D spending reflects actual resource allocation decisions (Cohen, 2010).
Second, objective verifiability.As standardized financial statement data subject to
auditing and regulatory disclosure requirements, R&D metrics avoid subjective evalu-
ation biases inherent in survey-based strategy measures or manager self-reports. This
objectivity is critical for large-scale analysis where manual coding would introduce
inconsistency.
Third, established validity.Extensive prior research validates R&D intensity as
capturing innovation strategic orientation, documenting associations with firm growth,
risk profiles, valuation multiples, and competitive positioning (Chan et al., 2001; Kothari
et al., 2002). Our use of established measures facilitates comparison with this literature.
Fourth, strategic stability.R&D investments exhibit substantial persistence, re-
flecting long-term strategic commitments rather than short-term tactical adjustments.
Innovation projects require multi-year horizons, making R&D spending relatively sta-
ble compared to discretionary expenses like advertising or hiring (Miller, 1986). This
stability aligns with logos as enduring visual identity choices.
Binary Classification Rationale.We operationalize R&D intensity as binary clas-
sifications (high vs. low innovation) rather than continuous variables for three method-
ological reasons:
First, algorithmic robustness.Machine learning classification tasks exhibit greater
robustness to outliers and distributional assumptions than regression. Classification
accuracy (AUC) provides intuitive interpretation independent of scale, while regression
coefficients require assumptions about functional form and error distributions.
Second, interpretability.Binary outcomes facilitate straightforward interpretation:
41


[Page 42]
can logo features distinguish high from low innovation firms? This question directly tests
strategic signaling theory’s prediction that visual identity encodes strategic archetypes.
Continuous predictions would require specifying the precise functional relationship be-
tween visual features and R&D percentages—a relationship we have no theoretical basis
to assume is linear.
Third, extreme value management.R&D intensity exhibits extreme right skewness,
with some biotechnology and software firms exceeding 50% R&D/sales while many
traditional manufacturers report zero. Median splits naturally handle this distributional
challenge without imposing arbitrary truncation or transformation, preserving sample
size and avoiding specification uncertainty.
Auxiliary Indicators (For H4 Mechanism Tests).To test discriminant validity
(H4), we examine logo prediction accuracy across four categories of firm characteristics,
distinguishing strategic investments from financial structure and market outcomes:
Strategic investment category (predicted to be encoded):
•capex intensity= Capital expenditures (CAPX) / Total assets (AT). Measures
physical asset expansion investment, capturing growth orientation through tangible
infrastructure (Kothari et al., 2002).
•intangible ratio= Intangible assets (INTAN) / Total assets (AT). Measures accu-
mulated knowledge assets including patents, trademarks, and goodwill, reflecting
long-term innovation outcomes.
Financial structure category (predicted not to be encoded):
•leverage= (Long-term debt + Current liabilities) / Total assets. Measures financial
risk and capital structure choice. This represents a financial decision rather than
strategic orientation, and is publicly disclosed in financial statements, reducing
information asymmetry (Myers, 1984).
Market outcome category (predicted not to be encoded):

[Page 43]
•gross margin= (Net sales - Cost of goods sold) / Net sales. Measures pricing
power and operational efficiency. This reflects market success and competitive
outcomes rather than strategic inputs or orientations, and should not be encoded
in visual identity if logos function as strategic signals.
Prediction performance comparisons across these categories provide diagnostic tests
of strategic signaling: if logos encode strategic orientations specifically, they should
predict strategic investment variables (R&D, CapEx, intangibles) significantly better
than financial structure (leverage) or market outcomes (margins). Failure to observe this
discriminant pattern would suggest logos merely reflect general firm characteristics or
industry conventions rather than deliberate strategic communication.
Data Treatment.All ratio variables are winsorized at the 1st and 99th percentiles
to mitigate the influence of extreme outliers while preserving distributional information,
as noted in Table 3. This conservative approach balances outlier management against
data loss, ensuring that results are not driven by a handful of extreme observations while
retaining genuine variation in strategic orientations.
3.3.2 Visual Feature Extraction
We employ a dual-feature approach that balances predictive power with interpretability.
High-dimensional deep learning features maximize prediction accuracy for hypothesis
testing (H1, H4, H5), while low-dimensional interpretable features enable mechanistic
understanding of visual encoding patterns (H3).
Deep Learning Features (High-Dimensional).We extract visual representations us-
ing transfer learning with MobileNet V2, a state-of-the-art convolutional neural network
architecture optimized for computational efficiency without sacrificing representational
capacity (Sandler et al., 2018).
Method: Transfer Learning with MobileNet V2.
The network is pre-trained on ImageNet, a large-scale visual recognition dataset
containing 1.4 million images across 1,000 object categories. This pre-training enables
the model to learn hierarchical visual representations applicable to diverse image domains
43


[Page 44]
beyond the original training data. We remove the final classification layer (designed for
ImageNet categories) and extract activations from the Global Average Pooling layer,
yielding a 1,280-dimensional feature vector for each logo. This vector encodes learned
visual patterns ranging from low-level primitives (edges, textures, colors) in early layers
to high-level semantic concepts (shapes, compositions, styles) in deeper layers.
Preprocessing Pipeline:
1.Resize:All logo images are resized to 256×256 pixels using bilinear interpola-
tion to ensure consistent scale while preserving aspect ratio information through
padding where necessary.
2.Center Crop:A 224×224 pixel region is extracted from the center of each resized
image, matching the standard input dimensions for MobileNet V2 architecture.
This cropping removes potential border artifacts while retaining the central visual
content where logos are typically positioned.
3.Normalization:Pixel values are converted to tensors and normalized using Ima-
geNet mean and standard deviation across RGB channels (mean = [0.485, 0.456,
0.406], std = [0.229, 0.224, 0.225]). This normalization ensures that input distri-
butions match the pre-training data, maximizing transfer learning effectiveness.
Dimensionality Reduction: PCA with 95% Variance Retention.
The raw 1,280-dimensional feature vectors are subjected to Principal Component
Analysis (PCA) to reduce dimensionality while retaining 95% of total variance. This
reduction yields approximately 100–200 dimensions (exact number depends on variance
distribution in our specific dataset), providing three benefits: (1) mitigating overfitting
risk by reducing parameter space, (2) improving computational efficiency for model
training, and (3) removing redundant or noisy dimensions while preserving principal
visual semantic information. The 95% variance threshold balances information reten-
tion against dimensionality reduction, following standard practice in computer vision
applications.
44


[Page 45]
These high-dimensional features capture complex visual patterns including shape
geometry, color distributions, compositional structure, and stylistic elements, but lack
direct human interpretability. They are optimally suited for predictive tasks testing
whether logos encode strategic information (H1, H4, H5), where maximizing classifica-
tion accuracy takes priority over mechanistic transparency.
Interpretable Features (Low-Dimensional).To understand the “black box” of
deep learning predictions and directly test mechanistic hypotheses (H3), we manually
extract 14 interpretable visual features using classical computer vision algorithms. These
features are selected based on theoretical predictions from visual psychology literature
and exploratory analysis identifying dimensions that systematically differ between high
and low innovation firms (reported in Table 8).
Texture/Complexity Features (6 measures):
1.Texture Variance:Local brightness variance computed using a 5×5 sliding win-
dow across the image. Higher values indicate rougher, more irregular textures with
greater detail variation. This measure captures the degree of visual “noisiness”
versus smoothness.
2.Gradient Variance:Variance of Sobel gradient magnitudes, reflecting the hetero-
geneity of brightness changes across the image. High gradient variance indicates
complex detail with varied edge strengths, while low variance suggests uniform
simplicity.
3.Sharpness (Laplacian):Mean absolute response to the Laplacian operator, which
detects edges and fine details. Higher values indicate sharper, more defined visual
elements, while lower values indicate softer, blurred appearances.
4.Edge Strength:Mean magnitude of Sobel operator responses across all pixels.
This measures the average intensity of detected edges, with higher values indicating
more pronounced visual boundaries.
5.Edge Density:Proportion of pixels classified as edges (Sobel magnitude above
45


[Page 46]
threshold) relative to total pixels. Higher density indicates more fragmented,
complex designs with numerous visual elements.
6.Brightness Std Dev:Standard deviation of brightness values across all pixels.
This captures overall tonal variability, with higher values indicating greater contrast
between light and dark regions.
Color Features (4 measures):
1.Contrast:Root mean square (RMS) contrast calculated as the square root of pixel
value variance. This measure quantifies the degree of visual distinction between
different regions of the logo.
2.Color Entropy:Shannon entropy of the color histogram, measuring color di-
versity. Higher entropy indicates greater variety of colors, while lower entropy
indicates more uniform or limited color palettes.
3.Blue Channel Mean:Average intensity value of the blue color channel (0–255
scale). This directly tests theoretical predictions that innovation firms favor blue-
dominant color schemes associated with technology and competence (Labrecque
and Milne, 2012).
4.Number of Unique Colors:Count of distinct colors after discretizing RGB values
into bins. This measures color palette complexity, distinguishing monochromatic
designs from multi-hued compositions.
Spatial Features (4 measures):
1.White Space Ratio:Proportion of near-white pixels (all RGB channels ¿ 240)
relative to total pixels. Higher ratios indicate greater negative space and minimalist
composition, reflecting modern design aesthetics.
2.Horizontal Symmetry:Pixel-wise correlation between the original image and its
horizontal flip. Values near 1.0 indicate perfect horizontal symmetry, while lower
values indicate asymmetric designs.
46


[Page 47]
3.Vertical Symmetry:Pixel-wise correlation between the original image and its
vertical flip. Similar interpretation to horizontal symmetry, capturing balance
along the vertical axis.
4.Number of Components:Count of connected regions in the binarized image
(using Otsu’s threshold). Higher counts indicate more fragmented designs with
multiple separate elements, while lower counts indicate unified, cohesive compo-
sitions.
These interpretable features directly correspond to the theoretical predictions in H3:
texture and edge features capture the “modern minimalist” aesthetic (smoothness and
softness), while color and spatial features measure visual unity and design coherence.
By examining systematic differences in these features between high and low R&D firms,
we can identify the specific visual dimensions through which strategic orientations are
encoded, providing mechanistic insight that complements the predictive power of deep
learning features.
3.3.3 Market Risk Measures (Validation Variables)
Market risk indicators serve as validation variables for H5 consistency tests, not as
primary dependent variables. We employ standard finance methodology to calculate
three categories of risk using daily stock returns. Stock price volatility reflects in-
vestors’ updating of expectations about future outcomes. Total risk can be decomposed
into two components: systematic risk (market-correlated variation that cannot be di-
versified away) and idiosyncratic risk (firm-specific variation that can be eliminated
through portfolio diversification). Innovation strategy primarily affects idiosyncratic
risk through company-specific uncertainties (new product success, technological break-
throughs), rather than systematic risk (macroeconomic factors, interest rates). This
pattern is well-established in the finance literature.
Specific Measures (Using Past 12 Months of Daily Returns).
(1) Total Volatility—annual return volatility

49


[Page 50]
moderately elevated beta through secondary effects: (1) valuations depend heavily on
future expectations, creating sensitivity to interest rate changes (correlated with market
cycles); (2) demand depends on economic expansion, creating sensitivity to business
cycles. However, this represents a secondary effect—the primary impact of innovation
strategy operates through idiosyncratic rather than systematic risk channels.
Operationalization.All three risk indicators are dichotomized into high/low groups
using sample median splits, creating binary classification tasks consistent with our strate-
gic orientation measures. This operationalization facilitates direct comparison of pre-
diction accuracy (AUC) across different dependent variables.
H5 Validation Logic.Our consistency validation (H5) builds on established finance
literature findings to form a triangular test:
Established finance literature conclusion:
•High R&D→High idiosyncratic risk (strong effect)
•High R&D→Modest increase in systematic risk (weak effect)
Supporting evidence includes Chan et al. (2001), who document positive correlations
between R&D intensity and idiosyncratic volatility, and Mazzucato and Tancioni (2008),
who show that innovation-intensive firms exhibit elevated firm-specific volatility but
comparable systematic risk to non-innovative peers.
Our study’s inference:If logos authentically reflect R&D (innovation strategy), we
should observe three patterns:
1.Convergence:Logo features predict risk measures significantly above chance,
demonstrating that visual identity encodes information correlated with market-
based risk perceptions.
2.Magnitude consistency:Logo prediction of risk measures exhibits similar strength
to logo prediction of R&D (AUC approximately equal), indicating that the visual
features capturing strategic orientation also capture associated risk profiles.
50


[Page 51]
3.Hierarchical consistency:Logo prediction of idiosyncratic risk exceeds logo
prediction of systematic risk (AUCidio ¿ AUCbeta), mirroring the established pattern
that innovation affects firm-specific more than market-correlated risk.
Satisfaction of all three conditions would provide convergent validation that logos
encode authentic strategic information rather than spurious correlations. The align-
ment between accounting-based strategic measures (R&D from financial statements)
and market-based risk perceptions (volatility from trading data) demonstrates that the
information encoded in visual identity is interpretable and decision-relevant to sophisti-
cated stakeholders, supporting the strategic signaling interpretation.
3.3.4 Control Variables
While machine learning models automatically capture non-linear relationships and in-
teraction effects through their flexible functional forms, certain analyses require consid-
eration of potential confounding factors that may influence both visual identity choices
and strategic orientations.
Potential Confounders.Three categories of firm characteristics may influence logo
design independently of strategic orientation:
(1) Industry (Fama-French 12 classification).Different industries may exhibit dis-
tinct visual conventions reflecting sector-specific norms, regulatory environments, or
customer expectations. For example, financial services firms may gravitate toward
traditional, conservative designs to signal stability, while technology firms may adopt
modern aesthetics to signal innovation—patterns that reflect industry conventions rather
than individual firm strategies (Deephouse, 1996).
(2) Firm size (log market capitalization).Larger firms may employ more standard-
ized, professionally designed logos reflecting greater resource availability for branding
investments and pressures toward visual conservatism to appeal to broad stakeholder
audiences. Conversely, smaller firms may exhibit greater visual diversity due to resource
constraints (limiting professional design services) or entrepreneurial flexibility.

(3) Firm age (years since IPO).Mature firms may retain legacy logo designs reflect-
ing historical branding decisions, while younger firms may adopt contemporary design
trends. Logo vintage effects could confound strategic orientation signals if design era
correlates with innovation intensity (e.g., recent IPOs disproportionately comprising
technology firms).
Treatment Approach.Our analytical strategy handles these potential confounders
differently across hypothesis tests, balancing statistical control against theoretical appro-
priateness:
Primary analyses (Machine learning prediction, Tables 4–7): No explicit controls.
We do not include explicit control variables in our machine learning prediction
models for three methodological and theoretical reasons:
First, implicit information capture.Deep learning features and interpretable visual
characteristics already encode industry-specific visual styles, firm size signals (e.g., logo
complexity may correlate with organizational resources), and design era markers (e.g.,
flat design trends). Explicitly controlling for these factors would create redundancy and
potentially induce multicollinearity that degrades prediction performance.
Second, avoiding over-control bias.Our theoretical interest centers on total associa-
tions between visual identity and strategic orientation, encompassing both direct effects
(firms deliberately choosing designs to signal strategy) and indirect effects mediated
through industry norms or firm characteristics. Over-controlling would partial out the-
oretically meaningful variation. For example, if innovation firms systematically cluster
in technology industries with modern visual conventions, this clusteringispart of the
logo-strategy encoding mechanism rather than a confound to be removed (Elwert and
Winship, 2014).
Third, focus on total effects rather than net effects.Signaling theory predicts that logos
encode strategic information through multiple pathways—including deliberate design
choices, industry positioning, and organizational characteristics. Our hypothesis tests
examine whether logospredictstrategy (total association), not whether logo features exert
causal effectsconditional on all other factors (net association). The latter would require
52


[Page 53]
different identification strategies including instrumental variables or natural experiments,
which are beyond our scope and inappropriate for establishing basic predictive validity.
Interpretable feature analysis (Two-sample t-tests, Table 8): Sensitivity checks for
group imbalance.
For hypothesis H3 testing systematic visual differences between high and low R&D
firms, we conduct two-sample t-tests comparing interpretable visual features. If high
and low R&D groups exhibit substantial imbalance on industry composition, firm size,
or firm age, the observed visual differences might reflect these compositional differences
rather than strategic orientation per se.
We address this concern through two approaches:
First, descriptive balance checks.We examine whether high and low R&D groups
differ systematically in industry distribution (using chi-square tests), mean firm size
(using t-tests), and mean firm age (using t-tests). Substantial imbalances would indicate
that visual feature differences might partly reflect compositional artifacts.
Second, robustness analyses.If meaningful imbalances exist, we conduct sensitivity
analyses including: (a) within-industry comparisons, testing visual feature differences
separately within major industries to hold industry constant; (b) size-stratified compar-
isons, testing visual differences within firm size quartiles to hold scale constant; (c)
regression-adjusted comparisons, estimating linear models predicting visual features
from R&D intensity while controlling for industry fixed effects, log size, and firm age,
then testing whether R&D coefficients remain significant.
However, we emphasize that even if visual differences partly reflect industry or
size composition, this does not invalidate our signaling interpretation. If innovation-
intensive firms systematically locate in industries or size categories with particular visual
conventions, this pattern itself constitutes strategic positioning information encoded
through industry choice and organizational scale. The critical theoretical question is
whether logos predict strategic orientation (which they do), not whether this prediction
operates exclusively through within-industry, within-size variation after partialing out all
contextual factors.
53


[Page 54]
This approach balances methodological rigor (acknowledging potential confounds)
with theoretical appropriateness (testing total associations relevant to signaling theory
rather than imposing restrictive conditional independence assumptions unsuited to our
research questions).
3.4 Statistical Analysis
3.4.1 Machine Learning Models
We employ four distinct machine learning algorithms to ensure robustness of our predic-
tive findings. These algorithms represent different learning paradigms and inductive bi-
ases, providing complementary perspectives on logo-strategy associations. Consistency
across algorithms strengthens confidence that results reflect genuine patterns rather than
model-specific artifacts.
(1) Logistic Regression with L2 Regularization (Ridge)
Parameters:𝐶=0.1 (strong regularization, equivalent to𝜆=10 in penalty formu-
lation)
Model characteristics:Logistic regression assumes a linear decision boundary, mod-
eling the relationship between features and log-odds of class membership as a linear
function. L2 regularization penalizes large coefficient magnitudes, shrinking parameters
toward zero to prevent overfitting while maintaining all features in the model (Hastie
et al., 2009).
Advantages:This model provides a simple, interpretable linear baseline. Coefficients
directly indicate the direction and relative magnitude of each feature’s contribution to
classification decisions. The strong regularization (low𝐶value) prevents overfitting to
training data, particularly important given our high-dimensional feature space.
Implementation:sklearn.linear model.LogisticRegressionwith default set-
tings exceptpenalty=’l2’andC=0.1.
(2) Logistic Regression with L1 Regularization (Lasso)
Parameters:𝐶=0.1
Model characteristics:Similar to L2 regression but employs L1 penalty, which

induces sparsity by shrinking coefficients of irrelevant features exactly to zero. This
automatic feature selection identifies the most discriminative visual dimensions while
discarding redundant or noisy features (Tibshirani, 1996).
Advantages:The sparse solution enhances interpretability by identifying key visual
features that drive strategic classification. By setting many coefficients to zero, L1 regu-
larization effectively performs embedded feature selection, reducing model complexity
and highlighting the most informative dimensions.
Implementation:sklearn.linear model.LogisticRegressionwithpenalty=’l1’,
solver=’liblinear’(required for L1), andC=0.1.
(3) Random Forest
Parameters:n estimators=50,max depth=5,min samples split=20
Model characteristics:Random Forest is an ensemble method combining multiple
decision trees trained on bootstrap samples of data with random feature subsets at each
split (bagging strategy). This approach captures non-linear relationships and interaction
effects between features that linear models cannot represent (Breiman, 2001). Each tree
votes on the final classification, with the majority vote determining the prediction.
Advantages:Random Forest exhibits strong robustness to outliers and noisy features
due to averaging across diverse trees. The algorithm provides feature importance rankings
based on how frequently features are selected for splits and how much they reduce im-
purity, offering interpretability despite model complexity. Shallow trees (maxdepth=5)
and minimum split requirements (min samples split=20) prevent overfitting to train-
ing data.
Implementation:sklearn.ensemble.RandomForestClassifierwith specified
parameters andrandom state=42.

Parameters:n estimators=50,max depth=3,learning rate=0.1
Model characteristics:Gradient Boosting builds an ensemble of decision trees se-
quentially, where each new tree corrects errors made by the previous ensemble (boosting
strategy). Trees are trained on residuals from prior predictions, gradually refining the

Hyperparameter Selection.We determine optimal hyperparameters through sys-

flexibility, ensuring we explore the bias-variance tradeoff space.
Selection criterion:We select the hyperparameter combination that maximizes mean
validation set AUC across the five folds. AUC (Area Under the ROC Curve) mea-
sures classification performance independent of threshold choice, making it ideal for
comparing models where class balance or decision costs may vary (Fawcett, 2006).
Reported parameters:The parameters specified above represent the final selected
values after hyperparameter tuning. These values balance prediction accuracy against
overfitting risk, achieving strong test set performance that generalizes beyond the training
data.
Randomness Control.To ensure complete reproducibility of our results, we control
all sources of randomness in the machine learning pipeline:
Fixed random seed:We setrandom state=42for all algorithms and data operations

Randomness sources controlled:
•Train-test split: Deterministic assignment of observations to training (70%) and
test (30%) sets using stratified sampling to preserve class balance.
•Bootstrap sampling: Random Forest’s bootstrap sample draws for each tree con-
struction.
•Feature subsampling: Random Forest’s random feature selection at each split point.
•Weight initialization: Initial values for iterative optimization algorithms.
•Tie-breaking: Deterministic resolution when multiple features yield identical split
quality.
This complete randomness control ensures that rerunning our analyses with the same
data and code produces identical results, a critical requirement for scientific reproducibil-
ity and verification.
3.4.2 Performance Evaluation Metrics
We employ multiple complementary metrics to evaluate classification performance, with
AUC serving as our primary measure for hypothesis testing due to its theoretical and
practical advantages.
Primary Metric: AUC (Area Under ROC Curve)
Definition:AUC measures the area under the Receiver Operating Characteristic
(ROC) curve, quantifying classifier performance aggregated across all possible classifi-
cation thresholds. The ROC curve plots True Positive Rate (TPR, also called Recall or
Sensitivity) on the vertical axis against False Positive Rate (FPR, equal to 1 - Specificity)
on the horizontal axis, as the decision threshold varies from 0 to 1 (Fawcett, 2006).
Calculation:

where𝑡indexes classification thresholds. AUC ranges from 0 to 1, with values
computed using the trapezoidal rule for numerical integration.
57


[Page 58]
Interpretation:
•AUC = 0.5:Random guessing baseline, indicating no discriminative ability. The
classifier performs no better than flipping a coin.
•AUC = 0.6:Weak but statistically significant prediction, indicating the classifier
correctly ranks a randomly selected positive example above a randomly selected
negative example 60% of the time.
•AUC = 0.7:Moderate prediction strength, commonly considered the threshold for
acceptable classification performance in social science applications.
•AUC = 1.0:Perfect classification, where positive and negative classes are com-
pletely separable.
Importantly, AUC admits an intuitive probabilistic interpretation: it equals the prob-
ability that the classifier assigns a higher predicted probability to a randomly chosen
positive instance than to a randomly chosen negative instance (Hanley and McNeil,
1982). This interpretation directly aligns with our theoretical question—can logo fea-
tures distinguish high from low innovation firms better than chance?
Advantages for our context:
First, robustness to class imbalance.Although our high/low R&D groups are ap-
proximately balanced (near 50:50 due to median splits), AUC remains valid even with
imbalanced classes, unlike accuracy-based metrics that can be misleading when one class
dominates.
Second, threshold independence.AUC evaluates performance across all possible
decision thresholds rather than requiring arbitrary threshold selection. This is critical
because we have no principled basis for choosing a specific threshold—our theoretical
interest concerns whether visual features encode strategic information, not optimizing
operational classification decisions.
Third, direct hypothesis test.The null hypothesis AUC = 0.5 directly corresponds
to our theoretical null of “no predictive relationship.” Rejecting this null provides
straightforward evidence for logo-strategy associations.
58


[Page 59]
Confidence intervals:We compute 95% confidence intervals for AUC using the
DeLong method (DeLong et al., 1988), a non-parametric approach based on the theory
of generalized U-statistics. These confidence intervals quantify estimation uncertainty
and enable formal hypothesis tests.
Auxiliary Metrics
While AUC serves as our primary evaluation metric, we report two additional mea-
sures to provide comprehensive performance assessment:
(1) Test Accuracy
Definition:

negatives.
Interpretation:Accuracy measures the overall proportion of correct classifications
in the test set, providing an intuitive performance summary. However, accuracy depends
on the chosen classification threshold (we use 0.5 by default) and can be misleading with

(2) Test Precision
Definition:
Precision= TP

Interpretation:Precision measures the proportion of positive predictions that are
correct, diagnosing whether the model exhibits systematic bias toward over-predicting
the positive class. Low precision indicates many false alarms, while high precision
indicates that positive predictions are reliable.
These auxiliary metrics complement AUC by providing threshold-specific perfor-
mance diagnostics, helping readers assess model behavior at typical operating points.
Statistical Significance Testing
We conduct formal hypothesis tests to determine whether observed AUC values
significantly exceed the random baseline:

[Page 60]
Null hypothesis:𝐻 0 : AUC=0.5 (no predictive ability; classifier performs at chance
level)
Alternative hypothesis:𝐻 𝐴 : AUC>0.5 (classifier exhibits genuine predictive
ability)
Test procedure:DeLong test, a non-parametric method that compares the empirical
AUC against the null value of 0.5 using the asymptotic normal distribution of the AUC
estimator (DeLong et al., 1988). This test accounts for the correlation structure in classi-
fication errors and provides valid inference without requiring distributional assumptions.
Significance levels:
•*** indicates𝑝 <0.01 (highly significant)
•** indicates𝑝 <0.05 (significant)
•* indicates𝑝 <0.10 (marginally significant)
•No asterisk indicates𝑝≥0.10 (not significant)
Tables 4–7 report these significance markers alongside point estimates and confidence
intervals, enabling readers to assess both statistical and practical significance.
Data Splitting and Validation Strategy
To ensure unbiased performance evaluation, we employ rigorous train-test splitting
with stratified sampling:
Split ratio:70% training, 30% testing. This standard split balances the competing
demands of sufficient training data (for stable model estimation) and sufficient test data
(for reliable performance evaluation). With𝑁=5,223 firms, this yields approximately
3,656 training observations and 1,567 test observations.
Stratified sampling:We employ stratified splitting that maintains identical class
proportions (high/low R&D ratios) in training and test sets. This ensures that test set
performance estimates are not confounded by different base rates, and that models are
trained on representative class distributions (Kohavi, 1995).
Strict separation:The test set remains completely independent—models never ob-
serve test set data during training, hyperparameter tuning, or feature selection. All model

Single split vs. cross-validation:We use a single train-test split rather than repeated
