text:
[Page 1]
 
 
 
From Oven to Online- Enhancing Social Media Marketing for Lintskun Bakery 
Niraj KC & Kiran Neupane 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Year of publication Laurea 
 
 

[Page 3]
   
 
 
Laurea University of Applied Sciences  Abstract 
Hospitality Management and Service Design 
Bachelor’s degree thesis 
 
Niraj KC, Kiran Neupane 
From Oven to Online- Enhancing Social Media Marketing for Lintskun Bakery 
Year 2025  Number of pages 27  
 
The aim of this thesis is to develop marketing in social media for Lintskun Leipomo oy, a small 
bakery located in Helsinki, Finland. The purpose of this thesis is to examine how social media 
marketing influences sales growth. The bakery commissioned the thesis to address challenges 
related to inconsistent visual communication, low frequency of postings, and very little digital 
interaction with the customers. The development task focuses on creating a service-design-
driven social media improvement plan. 
 
The theoretical framework includes social media marketing, consumer behavior, relationship 
marketing, the AIDA model, and service design. These concepts provide the foundation for 
analyzing how bakeries can attract attention, build relationships, and deliver coherent 
customer experiences across digital and physical touchpoints. 
 
Benchmarking was the only research method used for this study. Bakery B and Bakery C were 
chosen as benchmarking cases due to the strength of their brands and their effective digital 
practices. Qualitative and quantitative observations on social media and websites provided 
data on publicly available content. Benchmarking criteria included posting frequency, visual 
identity, recipe information, content strategy, audience engagement rate and feedback. 
 
It follows that benchmark bakeries maintain clear visual identities, post rhythms, and strong 
storytelling, while Lintskun Bakery lacks coherence and engagement. Based on this analysis, it 
is suggested that Lintskun Bakery could include the creation of a unified visual identity, an 
increase in posting frequency, and integration of more narrative and back staging content. The 
recommendations also range from creating brand guidelines and using service design tools to 
implementing a structured content strategy. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Keywords: AIDA model, Benchmarking, Social media marketing

[Page 5]
  5 
 
 
1 Introduction 
In this modern age, digital tools are growing rapidly. This enables creation of a huge marketing 
place into a multidimensional process centered around engagement, experience, and value 
creation. Digital technologies and social media have been playing a crucial role for a business 
institution to interact with its customers in real time. Traditional marketing theories, such as 
Kotler and Keller’s (2016) marketing management principles, have evolved to accommodate 
digital and relational perspectives, where consumer behavior, emotional connection, and 
brand authenticity play a vital role in achieving long-term success. Social media has become 
a powerful marketing tool that influences every stage of the consumer decision journey (Court 
et al. 2009). Social media platforms such as Facebook, Instagram, and TikTok help businesses 
to reach their current and future customers. 
The aim of this thesis is to develop marketing in social media for Lintskun leipomo oy, a Finnish 
bakery. The purpose of this thesis is to examine how social media marketing influences sales 
growth. Furthermore, this thesis provides ideas to understand how Lintskun Bakery can 
enhance its online visibility through strategic improvements in posting frequency, visual 
identity, content themes, and customer engagement. The study focuses on developing a 
practical and realistic improvement plan grounded in service design principles, ensuring that 
the digital experience aligns with the bakery’s physical customer experience. 
Competitive benchmarking is therefore the only research method used in this thesis to reach 
the above-mentioned aim. Benchmarking will allow us to compare Lintskun Bakery's current 
performance with that of two relevant competitors operating in Helsinki: Bakery A and Bakery 
B. For this study, these bakeries have been selected based on their strong brand positioning, 
distinctive visual identities, and active social media practices. By examining aspects such as 
posting rhythm, recipe information, branding, engagement rate, feedback practices, and 
content style, the study identifies best practices that can be adapted to Lintskun Bakery’s 
context. 
The background, motivation, and relevance of the topic are shown in the introduction of this 
thesis. It identifies the importance of social media marketing for small bakery businesses and 
provides the key challenges faced by Lintskun Bakery. The following chapters present the 
theoretical framework, the methodological approach, the results of benchmarking, and 
recommendations for development. Finally, this thesis should develop actionable insights and 
a structured improvement plan that enables Lintskun Bakery to achieve its long-term goals 
within digital communication and brand development. 

[Page 6]
  6 
 
 
2 Company Introduction 
Lintskun bakery is in Riihipellonkuja 3, 00390 Helsinki. Lintuskun Bakery, established in 2022, 
is a family-owned business, which is famous for hand-baked meat pies, doughnuts, curd buns, 
and yeast-free country bread baked to perfection in their bakery through fresh products.  
Furthermore, as it is in Konala, so product is directly sold in its location as a delivery and k-
market Derby, Iso Omena, Ruoholathi & Jumbo are retail partners of this bakery.  
It provides an example of a single-location business: maintaining close contact with its 
customers, it can respond quickly to changes in consumer preferences. Similarly, its physical 
environment is informal and inviting-which befits a local and community-focused bakery. While 
these core factors of product quality and customer service lie at the heart of the business, 
Lintskun Bakery operates amidst the highly competitive environment of large bakery chains 
and modern artisanal bakeries in the Helsinki region. 
From the marketing point of view, Lintskun Bakery currently relies on Instagram and Facebook 
as its digital communication channel with very limited followers. The bakery's social media 
presence remains very limited. It posts irregularly, and visual identity is inconsistent. As 
consumer expectations evolve toward attractive, experiential and practical digital content, 
the bakery feels an urgent need to enhance brand identity, engagement, and bring 
communication in line with the latest developments. 
This thesis was commissioned by Lintskun Bakery to support the development of a more 
effective and cohesive social media marketing strategy.  
3 Theoretical Framework 
This chapter introduces the theoretical basis for the thesis by exploring main concepts 
required for understanding and analyzing the social media practices of Lintskun Bakery. This 
chapter reviews the main theories at the heart of the development work: social media 
marketing, consumer behavior, relationship marketing, the AIDA model, service design, and 
visual identity. Each theoretical section adds to explaining how customers interact with 
bakery brands, how digital engagement is created, and how firms can better their online 
presence with coherent branding and customer-oriented communication. The theoretical 
framework provides a knowledge base against which the benchmarking results will be 
interpreted, thereby securing an analytical approach that is not merely descriptive but 
grounded in wider academic and professional perspectives. Theoretical insights proceed from 
the general to more specific themes, providing a structured basis for empirical benchmarking 
and the development plan presented later in this thesis. 

[Page 7]
  7 
 
 
3.1 Social Media Marketing 
Social media marketing is becoming an integral part of communication and brand-building 
strategies within the hospitality sector. Social media marketing is a modern way, active and 
two-way communication. Social media marketing is the use of social networking sites to create, 
share, and exchange content that meets marketing and relationship objectives (Kaplan & 
Haenlein 2010). Social media presents a cost-effective, influential medium for small businesses 
like bakeries, which maintain high reliance on community support and repeat business, to 
acquire exposure, incite loyalty, and deepen client connections.  
3.1.1 Evolution and Role of Social Media Marketing 
The growth of social media has greatly changed how marketing works today.

metadata.core_insight_en: This thesis analyzed the social media marketing strategy of Lintskun Bakery, highlighting the importance of consistent visual communication, regular posting, and customer interaction. Benchmarking with two successful bakeries revealed areas for improvement, including a unified visual identity, increased posting frequency, and narrative content. Recommendations focus on service design and structured content strategy.

Theoretical insights proceed from 
the general to more specific themes, providing a structured basis for empirical benchmarking 
and the development plan presented later in this thesis. 

[Page 7]
  7 
 
 
3.1 Social Media Marketing 
Social media marketing is becoming an integral part of communication and brand-building 
strategies within the hospitality sector. Social media marketing is a modern way, active and 
two-way communication. Social media marketing is the use of social networking sites to create, 
share, and exchange content that meets marketing and relationship objectives (Kaplan & 
Haenlein 2010). Social media presents a cost-effective, influential medium for small businesses 
like bakeries, which maintain high reliance on community support and repeat business, to 
acquire exposure, incite loyalty, and deepen client connections.  
3.1.1 Evolution and Role of Social Media Marketing 
The growth of social media has greatly changed how marketing works today. Unlike the older 
ways of reaching out with mass communication and a top-down approach, modern digital 
spaces encourage open conversation and teamwork (Mangold & Faulds 2009). In this fresh 
setup, people are not limited to taking information only. Instead, they play an active role in 
shaping brand images through what they say online like reviews and posts. This change gives 
small businesses like neighborhood bakeries a chance to be seen and stand alongside big 
companies without the need of huge advertising funds as marketing communication is now 
more accessible to everyone. 
Social media marketing pulls together various elements like digital tracking tools, relationship 
building, communicating about products or services, and how consumers think into one 
strategy. It highlights that getting people involved with a brand matter even more than just 
being known (Brodie et al. 2013). Within this idea, customers join in on community talks, take 
ideas about the brands and connect with content emotionally as well as mentally and 
behaviorally. 
In the hotel and restaurant world, using social media for marketing serves practical needs too. 
It tells customers about things like what's available or any deals happening. In addition, it also 
shows the reality of the brand's character and vibe which are important in crafting memorable 
moments. For example, every post from places like Lintskun Bakery can share their views on 
little taste of what enjoying a pastry feels like even if it's just online. 
3.1.2 Platforms, Content, and Visual Storytelling 
Different social media platforms serve different roles in a marketing strategy. Instagram is 
design and story-oriented and thus most suitable for bakeries that can utilize the sensory 
nature of their products. Facebook facilitates community engagement and local visibility, and 
TikTok provides the opportunities of viral, personality-driven content (Ashley & Tuten 2015). 

[Page 8]
  8 
 
 
Choice of platform must therefore be determined by the media habits of the target segment 
and the brand's visual identity. 
Visual storytelling has become the strongest tool in social media marketing. Quality pictures 
and video don't merely showcase products but also transmit values and feelings toward the 
brand (Hudson et al. 2015). The setting of a just-baked loaf, dawn light, or a sneak glimpse of 
artisans making it can evoke a sense of warmth and authenticity. Such images serve a dual 
role: they raise awareness within competitive feeds as well as develop symbolic associations 
that sustain brand meaning. 
In Finland, visual culture is particularly linked with ideals of simplicity, craftsmanship, and 
authenticity. Brands who integrate these values into their digital identity are likely to resonate 
with local audiences. For Lintskun Bakery, highlighting Finnish ingredients, sustainable 
practices, or local affiliations can evoke emotional connection as well as national identity. 
Past literature suggests that authenticity and openness are significant predictors of consumer 
trust in social media contexts (Morhart et al. 2015). So, consistency of narrative and images 
between offline experience and online presence is crucial for performance and credibility. 
3.1.3 Engagement and Interaction 
Successful social media marketing is built around engagement. Engagement is the depth of 
individuals' involvement and affection with organizational activity, as defined by Brodie et al. 
(2013). In contrast to the more conventional reach and impressions measures employed in 
traditional marketing, engagement measures of likes, comments, shares, and mentions are 
measures of relational depth. Interactions establish brand equity through heightened perceived 
familiarity and affective attachment (Hollebeek et al. 2014). 
It also encourages electronic word-of-mouth (eWOM), which is quite possibly the strongest 
digital influence. Research shows that consumers rate peer-generated content higher than 
company communication (Cheung & Thadani 2012). Small bakeries encourage customers to 
take images of what they've purchased, name the brand, or participate in a challenge to 
maximize reach without showing it. The exercise makes customers fans of the brand and co-
create value by extending the brand narrative through their respective networks. Here, Service 
design methods can be applied to arrange these interactions by ascertain where and why they 
occur. Journey mapping, for example, may reveal the emotional sparks that lead users to 
comment, share, or follow a page. By marrying content to this insight, marketers can craft 
more pertinent and compelling opportunities for engagement. Moreover, the combination of 
qualitative social listening intelligence with quantitative analytics makes it possible to leverage 
evidence-based knowledge on audience behavior to maximize message resonance and 
conversion (Chaffey & Ellis-Chadwick 2019). 

[Page 9]
  9 
 
 
3.1.4 Social Media Strategy and Customer Journey Integration 
For effective social media marketing, it requires a strategic plan from where content, timing, 
and target audience are all aligned with business objectives. This framework in hospitality 
must align with the customer process steps: awareness, consideration, purchase, consumption, 
and post-purchase word-of-mouth (Lemon & Verhoef 2016). To establish or reinforce brand 
experiences opportunity, it comes with each step. For instance, during the awareness phase, 
it uses exciting posts; consideration uses reviews and user reviews to provide endorsement; 
while after purchase, follow-up behavior maintains retention and advocacy. Service design 
bridges the gap by considering the end-to-end customer experience and demanding consistency 
across touch points. In online scenarios, this entails integrating online and offline such that 
what the customer experiences on social media comes to life in the store. Lack of consistency, 
i.e., excess on social media but a low-key in-store experience can deplete trust and annihilate 
brand equity. Therefore, using service design principles for social media strategy helps deliver 
experiential coherence and builds brand/customer emotional connections (Patricio et al. 
2018). 
3.1.5 Metrics and Performance Evaluation 
The success of social media marketing depends upon the measurement of performance. Key 
performance metrics (KPIs) are engagement rate, reach, conversion, customer acquisition cost, 
and lifetime value (Tuten & Solomon 2018). However, it is challenging to measure the 
performance of social media in hospitality because most of its effects are intangible such as 
brand sentiment, emotional connection, or influencing a community. marketers increasingly 
employ quantitative measures augmented by qualitative data based on customer feedback and 
sentiment analysis (Sigala 2018). The balanced scorecard approach to social media 
performance is to monitor financial, customer, internal process, and learning perspectives 
simultaneously (Kaplan & Norton 1996). For example, a bakery would not only track increases 
in sales because of social campaigns but also increases in brand awareness, social activity, and 
customer satisfaction. All these interrelated metrics provide assurance that social media is 
leading to long-term performance and not short-term promotion spikes 
3.1.6 Ethical and Cultural Dimensions 
Ethically responsible communication and cultural sensitivity are becoming increasingly 
valuable for social media marketing. The transparency of digital media requires companies to 
be authentic, responsible, and sensitive towards cultural practices in every corner of world.

3.1.6 Ethical and Cultural Dimensions 
Ethically responsible communication and cultural sensitivity are becoming increasingly 
valuable for social media marketing. The transparency of digital media requires companies to 
be authentic, responsible, and sensitive towards cultural practices in every corner of world. 
In Finland, respect for privacy and honesty being paramount, explicitly hostile or sensationalist 
advertising can be received negatively. Responsiveness towards such cultural presuppositions 
builds trust and social legitimacy (Tuomi & Tanskanen 2020). Also, ethical marketing is applied 
to the collection and use of data. Compliance with data protection regulations such as the EU 

[Page 10]
  10 
 
 
General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) ensures compliance and has consumers continuing 
to trust. Data use transparency can even be a marketing strength, hardening a brand's 
credibility and trustworthiness. 
3.2 The AIDA Model and Its Applicability to Social Media Marketing 
The AIDA model is arguably the most enduring model of marketing communication that explains 
the thinking and affective processes a customer undertakes from the point of exposure to a 
product to the moment of purchase decision. The letters are an acronym for Attention, 
Interest, Desire, and Action, which together depict a linear process of persuasion that advises 
marketers on how to structure messages and customer experience (Strong 1925). Despite 
having been developed over a century ago, the model remains highly relevant in contemporary 
digital marketing, where consumer attention is fragmented and decision processes are 
increasingly fraught. 
In hospitality and baking, understanding and application of the AIDA model allow businesses to 
develop communication strategies that capture attention, maintain interest, and compel 
purchase. For the Lintskun Bakery, applying this model in social media can ensure that every 
digital touchpoint a post or story, for example, or an online review contributes to an integrated 
and engaging customer journey. By mapping AIDA onto service design principles, the bakery 
can systematically map and optimize how each stage of the model unfolds across its customer 
experience ecosystem. 
3.2.1 Attention: Winning Awareness in a Space Full of Competitive Stimuli 
The first step, attention, is the act of a marketer catching the eye of the target consumer in 
a marketplace filled with multiple “attractions.” On social media, attention is a fast-declining 
resource. In return, marketers from competing brands need to find ways to stand out in the 
market and attract consumer attention (Pieters & Wedel 2004). Note that a small hospitality 
business needs to strive for visibility.  
The way a product looks and feels has the final focus in this phase. According to earlier 
research, visual social media platforms like Instagram and TikTok can improve recall of content 
with movement and imagery (Ashley & Tuten 2015). This could entail sharing behind-the-
scenes videos that showcase the baking process or advertise freshly baked goods and seasonal 
treats for Lintskun Bakery. Good photography, natural lighting and narrative storytelling appeal 
to our senses and stop us in our tracks for just a moment of awareness and that’s when the 
brand gets its moment.  
Design thinking, which emphasizes service and customer touchpoints, can also help to increase 
attention. Postings ought to be scheduled, for instance, to coincide with customers' weekend 

[Page 12]
  12 
 
 
Hospitality marketing achieves its best results through the presentation of sensory. Consumers 
at this point understand product features and develop a strong desire to acquire the product. 
The stage and experiential advantages to customers. The bakery uses three key selling points 
to attract customers: fresh narrative elements such as "handcrafted daily" and "made with 
local butter and love" create emotional products, skilled preparation and premium quality and 
traditional methods. Research indicates that using evocative images and connections boost 
customer willingness to buy (Hudson et al. 2015). 
Social media platforms enable users to express their preferences through interactive features 
and personalized content. Interactive product displays, geotagged promotions, and 
personalized recommendations all combine to create an immediate connection with the brand. 
By fostering human connections, the use of emotional storytelling in brand communication aids 
consumers in strengthening their brand attachment. The introduction of Lintskun Bakery bakers 
and local partnership stories creates emotional connections with customers through shared 
experiences. 
Service design adds value to this point by making sure all communication maintains an 
emotional tone which matches the complete brand experience. The online presentation of 
sensory elements including typefaces and colors and photographs should duplicate the actual 
sensory experience found in the physical store. The combination of offline and digital 
experiences that match each other creates authentic feelings which drive people to act 
(Morhart et al. 2015). The process of co-creation through consumer participation in seasonal 
flavor selection and new pastry naming transforms passive longing into active involvement 
which strengthens the emotional connection between brands and their audience. 
3.2.4 Action: Turning Intention into Behaviors 
The last stage of the AIDA model requires consumers to execute their intentions by making 
purchases or visiting locations or subscribing to services or sharing content. The digital stage 
of this process requires users to experience minimal obstacles while progressing toward their 
target goal. Service design abilities that create availability and simplify understanding and 
enhance convenience work together with persuasive elements to achieve action (Bitner et al. 
2008). 
Social media marketing uses call-to-action (CTA) elements to connect user desires with actual 
behavioral responses. The use of direct behavioral signals such as "Order now" and "Visit us 
today" and "Try our new croissant" helps users save mental work. The success rate of CTAs 
depends on three essential factors which include timing and context and perceived value 
according to Tuten and Solomon (2018). The combination of time-sensitive promotions with 
customer feedback and simple one-click purchasing options leads to higher conversion rates. 

[Page 14]
  14 
 
 
especially when ideally it can be bridges to more recent models like the consumer decision 
journey or service-dominant logic (Vargo & Lusch 2008). 
In social media environments, it is possible for a customer to move back and forth between 
stages of finding a brand, encountering content (for example delaying), returning later in time 
as result of having been exposed by retargeting or through an individual’s social referral. So, 
AIDA works best for marketers as a sketchy guide, rather than an immutable step-by-step 
process. Both feedback and data analysis enable incremental optimization of each phase. 
Service design also overcomes these constraints by providing methods for prototyping and 
testing the customer experience in real rather than abstract assumptions. 
Lastly, the AIDA model endures because it boils down fundamental principles of attention 
economics, emotional connection, and behavioral motivation, all of which remain at the core 
of effective marketing. For smaller businesses like Lintskun Bakery, it provides an intuitive but 
useful structure for social media strategy to ensure that every piece of content serves a 
particular purpose in moving consumers further toward meaningful action. 
3.3 Consumer Behavior and Relationship Marketing in Hospitality and Bakery industry 
This section explores the concepts of consumer behavior and relationship marketing in the 
context of the hospitality and bakery industry. The aim is to explain how customers form 
expectations, make purchase decisions, and develop loyalty for bakery businesses. The 
discussion centers around psychological, emotional, and experience-based factors of customer 
preference, including product quality, authenticity, sensory appeal, and brand trust.

3.3 Consumer Behavior and Relationship Marketing in Hospitality and Bakery industry 
This section explores the concepts of consumer behavior and relationship marketing in the 
context of the hospitality and bakery industry. The aim is to explain how customers form 
expectations, make purchase decisions, and develop loyalty for bakery businesses. The 
discussion centers around psychological, emotional, and experience-based factors of customer 
preference, including product quality, authenticity, sensory appeal, and brand trust. The 
section also highlights how important relationship marketing is in maintaining long-term 
customer engagement through personalized communication, consistent service, and 
meaningful interactions. Such behavioral and relational understanding allows bakery 
businesses to design more appropriate social media practices that will result in a positive 
relationship with their customers and help them sustain their loyalty. This section introduces 
concepts that will later be used in the interpretation of the benchmarking findings and in 
guiding the development plan for Lintskun Bakery. 
3.3.1 Consumer Behavior 
Consumer behavior is the study of how individuals or groups select, purchase, use, and evaluate 
products or services to satisfy their needs and desires (Solomon et al. 2020). In the field of 
Hospitality and Baking industry, knowing about customer behavior on purchasing of product 
always determined by emotions, experience and social influences of customers. Hospitality 
consumption is inherently experiential, meaning that customers evaluate value through the 
totality of their sensory, effective, and symbolic experiences rather than only through price 
or functionality (Kotler et al. 2019). 

[Page 15]
  15 
 
 
The decision making of customers seeks products that fulfill physical needs such as hunger but 
in addition to this customer decision involves emotional satisfaction including taste, aroma, 
visual appearance, and atmosphere. Studies show that food purchases in artisanal bakeries are 
often associated with pleasure, nostalgia, and social belonging (Holbrook & Hirschman 1982). 
These dimensions play a key role in shaping brand perception and loyalty towards its 
customers. 
Digitalization in modern era has fundamentally transformed customer behavior in food and 
hospitality industry. Social media platforms such as Facebook, Instagram, TikTok have become 
critical sources of inspiration, information, and peer influence (Hudson & Thal 2013). Visual 
platforms particularly affect how consumers recognize food quality and its authenticity. In 
social media, visualization of artisanal craftsmanship, sustainable ingredients, or local identity 
stimulate positive emotional responses and drive intention to visit or purchase. This reflects 
the concept of social proof, where consumers rely on others’ visible experiences to validate 
their own choices (Cialdini 2009). 
Here in Finland, the customer preferences in bakery sector are greatly shaped by values 
related with sustainability, authenticity, local production. Finnish Consumer favor small 
producers as it depicts about transparency, environmental awareness and ethical sourcing 
(Autio et al. 2013). This values orientation is aligned with social identity theory, which holds 
that consumers gain self-expression through the brands they consume. Thus, bakeries like 
Lintskun Bakery can position themselves well by projecting a brand narrative that resonates 
with consumers' cultural and personal values. 
Service encounters in hospitality are not only judged by product quality, but it includes 
emotional engagement and service atmosphere. As Parasuraman, Zeithaml, and Berry (1988) 
demonstrated, perceived service quality depends on the alignment between expectations and 
actual experiences across multiple touchpoints. In digitally, social media interactions have 
become wide extensions of these touchpoints, influencing pre-purchase perceptions and post-
purchase satisfaction. A customer who experiences positive engagement online through 
personalized responses or appealing visuals is more likely to form favorable expectations 
before visiting the bakery, illustrating the growing interdependence of digital and physical 
service experiences. 
Looking out on consumer behavior from a service design perspective means mapping how 
consumers interact with both physical and digital touchpoints and identifying their emotions, 
motivations, and pain points along that journey. Customer journey mapping thus becomes a 
valuable analytical tool to visualize and improve these interactions (Zomerdijk & Voss 2010). 
This perspective of social media can be understood as an experiential phase of the service 
process, influencing not only awareness but also loyalty and advocacy. 

[Page 16]
  16 
 
 
3.3.2 Relationship Marketing 
Relationship marketing means the way of creating long term relationships with an organization 
and its customers and to create understanding about customer behavior. This helps institutions 
to bond with customers, and this is more about higher profitability than constant acquisition. 
Gronroos (1994) defines relationship marketing as establishing, maintaining, and enhancing 
relationships with customers and other stakeholders at a profit, so that the objectives of all 
parties are met through mutual exchange and fulfilment of promises. 
In hospitality, there's an important role of repeat business and word-of-mouth referrals and 
relationship marketing has become a foundation for strategic management. The emotional 
component of service encounters means that customer satisfaction alone is insufficient; loyalty 
depends on the development of trust, commitment, and shared values (Morgan & Hunt 1994). 
According to their commitment–trust theory, successful relationships are built when both 
parties demonstrate reliability and emotional investment. For a bakery, consistent product 
quality, friendly interactions, and responsiveness to feedback, both in-store and online are 
required. 
Social media platforms have modified relationship marketing as it makes the two-way 
communication between customers and businesses two-way. They serve as relationship spaces 
where bakeries can promote their brand, express gratitude, share contents, and customer 
participation. Research shows that when businesses interact authentically and respond to 
customer comments or reviews, perceived relational quality and trust significantly increase 
(Sashi 2012). Online communication has also become a vital precursor for loyalty and positive 
word-of-mouth. 
From the perspective of service-dominant logic, relationship marketing and service design 
converge on the principle of value co-creation (Vargo & Lusch 2008). Customers are active 
participants, and they contribute to the knowledge, creativity, and feedback. In social media 
contexts, brands can be promoted and spread to the greater area through likes, comments, 
shares, and user-generated content that praise the brands. Service design provides the tools 
to structure these co-creative processes systematically, ensuring that customer participation 
enhances rather than fragments the brand experience (Patrício et al. 2018). 
 
Consistency and emotional resonance are the key factors in digital channels for building and 
sustaining relationships. Studies show that social media interactions evoke feelings of 
belonging and connectedness when brands communicate in a personal and transparent tone 
(Hudson et al. 2016). For a small bakery, strengthening of relational bonds and transforming 

[Page 17]
  17 
 
 
of transactional exchanges into emotional affiliations is more done through regularly sharing 
authentic stories about staff, ingredients, and community events 
Relationship marketing can benefit from customer experience management, which involves 
designing holistic experiences that integrate all touchpoints; digital and physical, into a 
coherent narrative (Lemon & Verhoef 2016). Service design facilitates this integration by 
visualizing customer journeys and identifying critical moments that influence loyalty. A bakery 
can deliver the consistent value proposal through the alignment between marketing 
communication and these moments, a bakery and it can reinforce trust and satisfaction. 
3.3.3  Integrating Consumer Behavior and Relationship Marketing 
The integration of consumer behavior and relationship marketing provides a comprehensive 
understanding of how social media marketing can enhance customer engagement for Lintskun 
Bakery. Consumer behavior explains why customers are attracted to certain visual and 
emotional prompts whereas relationship marketing explains how these interactions can evolve 
into loyalty and advocacy.

3.3.3  Integrating Consumer Behavior and Relationship Marketing 
The integration of consumer behavior and relationship marketing provides a comprehensive 
understanding of how social media marketing can enhance customer engagement for Lintskun 
Bakery. Consumer behavior explains why customers are attracted to certain visual and 
emotional prompts whereas relationship marketing explains how these interactions can evolve 
into loyalty and advocacy. When interpreted through service design, both concepts form a 
repeated cycle of observing consumer responses, redesigning touchpoints, testing new 
engagement methods, and refining experiences based on feedback. 
This integration also supports the transition from transactional marketing to experiential 
branding. Social media interactions like likes, comments, and shares are important components 
of the customer journey that contribute to perceived value. The use of service design methods 
such as journey mapping, personas, and prototyping helps translate behavioral insights into 
actionable marketing strategies which help to maintain a long-term relationship. 
3.4  Business Performance and sales growth 
Business performance and sales growth are an important part of organizational viability and 
success, especially in small hospitality enterprises such as bakeries. Long-term performance in 
competitive urban markets in cities such as Helsinki depends on the ability to achieve value 
by means of differentiation, customer engagement, and innovation. In recent years, 
measurements of business performance and the attainment of sales growth have been 
transformed dramatically due to the digitalization and the rising dominance of social media of 
sales growth dramatically (Chaffey & Ellis-Chadwick 2019). For service companies, such 
transformation means shifting from efficiency in operations alone to customer experience-
based growth. 

[Page 18]
  18 
 
 
3.4.1 The Concept of Sales Growth 
Growth in sales means that an organization can increase revenue within a specified time 
through expanding customer base, purchase frequency, and transaction value (Kotler & Keller 
2016). It is a function of both external market forces and internal responses to them such as 
marketing effectiveness, service quality, and loyalty of customers. Sales expansion in the 
hospitality sector is not limited to product quality but has a broad spectrum of experiential 
value, positioning, and reputation. Bakeries and cafes are highly influenced by repeat business 
and word-of-mouth, meaning growth is highly associated with relational and perceptual 
variables as opposed to promotional spending (Zeithaml et al. 2020). Expansion through sales 
can follow three main paths: acquiring new buyers, repeat sales from repeat buyers, and 
expansion of product or service lines. For small bakeries, social media marketing provides a 
ascendable way for all three. Social media visibility attracts new audiences, engaging content 
promotes loyalty among repeat buyers, and feedback obtained online can influence new 
product ideas. Literature in hospitality management shows that businesses employing digital 
engagement have more conversions and stable revenues than those employing traditional 
marketing alone (Leung et al. 2015). 
3.4.2 Digital Marketing as a Driver of Sales Growth 
The digital environment has converted the sales pipeline from a linear one; awareness , 
interest, desire, action to a cyclical process with emphasis on continuous engagement and 
advocacy (Court et al. 2009). Along these lines, social networks are significant platforms where 
customers flow smoothly between discovery, consideration, and purchase. Literature has 
affirmed that visual content, authenticity, and interactive online experience are driving 
factors influencing purchasing intent for hospitality and retail sectors (Hudson et al. 2015), 
the degree to which the brand communicates its unique value proposition and emotional 
connection will decide whether social interaction is translated into tangible purchases. Service 
design delivers sales growth through optimizing digital touchpoints within customer 
experience. By aligning friction points and redesigning the purchasing experience i.e., 
optimizing web ordering, simplifying communication, or enhancing visual presentation of 
products, service design has a direct influence on conversion rates. Bitner et al. (2008) point 
out that physical and virtual service environments both impact behavioral intentions through 
convenience and emotional perceptions. To this end, a good social media presence is a “virtual 
servicescape” wherein visual aspects, tone, and interactivity create expectations that are 
translated into purchasing behavior. 

[Page 19]
  19 
 
 
3.4.3 Business Performance in the Hospitality Sector 
Business performance for hotel business is a multi-dimensional construct that includes financial 
performance, customer satisfaction, operational effectiveness, innovation, and brand equity 
(Mattila 2010). While financial measures such as revenue growth, profitability, and return on 
assets remain basic, other non-financial measures like customer satisfaction, employee 
attitude, and reputation have also become equally significant indicators of long-run 
performance (Kaplan & Norton 1996). The balanced measured approach brings together these 
multiple dimensions, with a focus on interdependence between customer perspectives, 
internal processes, learning and growth, and financial measures. Performance in bakery 
companies is also affected by seasonal variation, consumer preference, and quality 
consistency. Strategic flexibility responding quickly to feedback and changing trends, therefore 
represents a key ingredient for competitiveness. Small companies can use data analysis and 
digital technologies to monitor such dynamics in real time, making evidence-based decisions 
on pricing, product range, and promotion tactics. Evidence shows that smaller hospitality 
businesses adopting evidence-based marketing practices outperform businesses relying on 
intuition or tradition only (Sigala 2018).  
4 Report and Methodology  
This chapter presents the methodological choices made for the empirical part of this thesis 
and how the research was conducted. It gives a critical account of why benchmarking was 
chosen as the only research method for this study and how competitive benchmarking can 
provide relevant and reliable data to compare Lintskun Bakery with other bakeries in Helsinki. 
This chapter describes issues such as how the benchmark bakeries were selected, how the 
data were collected, and what precisely was considered in the comparison: posting 
frequency, information on the recipe, visual identity, engagement rate, content strategy, and 
practices related to feedback. Reliability, validity, and ethical issues are also discussed to 
ensure the transparency of the research. The chapter clarifies how the empirical data were 
gathered and analyzed, thereby providing the methodological basis for the results of 
benchmarking and the development plan presented in the following chapters. 
4.1 Benchmarking 
Benchmarking is a systematic and continuous process of evaluating an organization’s 
performance, practices, or strategies against industry leaders or best performers with the goal 
of improving its own performance (Camp 1989). It is essentially a learning process that 
identifies what others do better, why they do it better, and how those practices can be 
adapted to achieve superior results. 

[Page 20]
  20 
 
 
According to Spendolini (1992), benchmarking is not imitation but adaptation — understanding 
successful practices and applying the insights to one’s own organizational context. In business 
management, benchmarking has evolved from simple performance comparison to a strategic 
management tool used to drive innovation, efficiency, and competitiveness. The purpose of 
this benchmarking analysis is to compare Lintskun Leipomo’ s social media with other similar 
bakeries in Helsinki.  
Out of five benchmarking: Internal benchmarking, Competitive benchmarking, Shadow 
benchmarking, Industrial benchmarking, Universal benchmarking (Mears 1995), this thesis has 
applied competitive benchmarking of social media for its report.  The elements that assist 
benchmarking consists of Posting frequency, Recipe information on websites, visual identity 
(brand logo, colors, fronts), engagement rate, content strategy.

4.2 Benchmarking anyalsis 
The benchmarking results reveal important differences between Lintskun Leipomo and two 
comparable bakeries. First, in terms of posting frequency, there is considerably less frequency 
that can be noticed in Lintskun bakery compared to B and C bakeries. Bakery B has been 
showcasing outstanding performance and portraying themselves as actively posting about their 
products. A consistent scheduled posting helps a business to create brand awareness and helps 
in visibility and customer engagement 
Secondly, there is no actual recipe information in the three bakeries. Although there are fewer 
pictures in social media where they showed manufacturing pictures in all three bakeries, there 
is no valid recipe of any products in websites nor in social media. If there are descriptions of 
any one or more recipes available in websites or social media, there will be a chance that 
customers might get curious or interested in more products. 
Thirdly, visual identity builds brand recognition and differentiates from competitors.  While 
comparing visual identity each bakery has its own features of visual identity and makes them 
unique. According to visual identity, Bakery A has used flavours from the family in the logo 
which makes it more traditional than B and C. 
Fourth, the engagement rate of audiences has made each bakery significant up and down. In 
terms of Facebook B has the highest number of audiences which is 8K following A and B 
afterwards respectively. Similarly, on Instagram B has secured the highest position following B 
and A. 
Furthermore, Comparison of content strategy all bakeries have showcased their products, but   
bakery A has depicted remarkable posts featuring Finnish artists showcasing a new music video 
about the curd burn which makes a unique strategy for updating content online to its 
audiences. Meanwhile B and C have always used their products and occasionally mention 
business partners.  
Lastly, Feedback from customers, A has been actively using Facebook and Instagram as a source 
of feedback and responding timely to its customers. But B has been a game changer as it has 
used websites to receive feedback from social media and managed its websites in such a way 
that they can receive anonymous feedback too. Meanwhile C has been using social media 
platforms for its feedback from its customers. 
 

[Page 23]
  23 
 
 
4.3 Development plan from Benchmarking anyalsis 
Benchmarking shows bakery A post less frequent than competitors. According to Kotler & Keller 
(2016), consistent communication strengthens brand recall and helps customers move through 
the awareness and interest stages of the customer journey. Additionally, Mangold & Faulds 
(2009) emphasise that regular social media activity enhances visibility in crowded markets. 
There should increase of posting frequency at least 1-2 times per week on social media for 
consistent visibility among audiences and helps to expand growth furthermore for B2B 
customers too.  In addition to this, use of content calendar might be beneficial to stay 
consistent. For increasement of positing frequency and consistency, sharing of mix product 
highlights, behind-the-scenes content and seasonal updates which eventually improves brand 
visibility, customer engagement and algorithm reach.

4.3 Development plan from Benchmarking anyalsis 
Benchmarking shows bakery A post less frequent than competitors. According to Kotler & Keller 
(2016), consistent communication strengthens brand recall and helps customers move through 
the awareness and interest stages of the customer journey. Additionally, Mangold & Faulds 
(2009) emphasise that regular social media activity enhances visibility in crowded markets. 
There should increase of posting frequency at least 1-2 times per week on social media for 
consistent visibility among audiences and helps to expand growth furthermore for B2B 
customers too.  In addition to this, use of content calendar might be beneficial to stay 
consistent. For increasement of positing frequency and consistency, sharing of mix product 
highlights, behind-the-scenes content and seasonal updates which eventually improves brand 
visibility, customer engagement and algorithm reach.  
To introduce Ingredient-Focused and Recipe-Related Content, Research by Kaplan & Haenlein 
(2010) shows that educational content increases engagement and builds trust. Consumers 
respond positively to “value-adding content” rather than pure promotion. Offering short recipe 
reels, or behind the scenes baking process can be beneficial for advertising and channels to 
get customer engagement.  
Although Bakery A has a traditional logo with family symbolism, the visual identity must remain 
consistent across all social media platform for example while posting any posts or reels. 
Keller’s Brand Equity Model (2008) states that consistent visual cues (colours, typography, 
imagery) help customers build stronger associations with the brand. 
Competitors B has used anonymous website feedback, which is strong advantage. Timely 
responses and easy feedback channels eventually boost trust and service quality towards 
customers. Bakery A can use simple feedback form on its websites too. For content strategy 
and beyond products posts, there is certain applicable that can be introduced here. Seasonal 
promotions, baking tips, customers story are the significant for highlights for content. Probably 
Instagram reels and Facebook story has strong influence to increase visibility.  
5 Conclusion 
This thesis depicts how social media marketing influences business performance of the bakery 
with a particular focus on Lintskun leipomo. Through a theoretical overview and a competitive 
bench marking analysis with two comparable bakeries, the study shows role of digital social 
media platforms in enhancing visibility, customer engagement and sales growth.  
The results show that all the reviewed bakeries are present on social media actively, however, 
the strategies and methods of posting and visual identity, as well as the level of engagement 

[Page 24]
  24 
 
 
and feedback management differ significantly. Competitor B had better performance due to a 
regular posting schedule, a significant number of followers, and appropriate feedback systems, 
but Bakery A stood out due to the cultural partnerships and maintaining the traditional 
branding. Comparatively, Lintskun Leipomo demonstrated a sense of response and authenticity 
but showed deficiencies clearly as far as consistency, content variety and strategic visual use 
was concerned. 
The results of benchmarking indicate the need to improve the posting frequency, enhance 
visual identity, offer value-based content like behind-the-scenes pictures or ingredient stories, 
and optimize feedback mechanisms, which may significantly increase competitiveness. These 
suggestions are supported by the available literature on social media marketing that has 
determined consistency, engagement, and content quality as the key factors in determining 
online success. 
Overall, the paper finds that working social media strategy is not just a promotion tool but a 
vital part of modern customer-relationship management. The proposed steps can be followed 
to ensure that Lintskun Leipomo can increase its online presence, appeal to a wider audience, 
and achieve sustainable business development. As a result, this study contributes to the 
existing knowledge on how to use digital marketing strategically by small bakery businesses in 
an ever-competitive environment.

MANAGING CORPORATE IMAGE AND STAKEHOLDER PERCEPTION IN A
CHANGING WORLD: A CRITICAL EVALUATION OF THE ROLE OF
CORPORATE VISUAL IDENTITY ASSET
Nnachi Okafor
Abstract
This study evaluates the role of Corporate Visual Identity Assets (CVIA) in managing
corporate image and the perception of organisational stakeholders. It examines the
interrelationships among corporate image, identity management, and corporate visual elements
and their impact on stakeholder perceptions and corporate image management. The study
applied the mixed methods of quantitative and qualitative data collection and analysis research,
surveys, and inferential statistical analysis techniques. They were complemented with
interviews, descriptive, content and critical discourse analysis techniques to provide a clear and
comprehensive understanding of the research problem and objectives. The study reviewed
relevant empirical literature, identifying critical CVI elements – logo designs, typography,
colour palettes – and how they interact with other corporate artefacts and key stakeholders to
shape their perceptions, organisational image, and overall corporate and marketing
communications. Findings show that 70 per cent of an organisation’s corporate communication
goals are better achieved if brand builders, corporate communications and reputation managers
adopt more effective harmonisation and integration strategies in utilising CVI elements and
digital assets to shape their stakeholders’ perceptions and corporate image. The study
repudiates the misconception that well-polished CVI and consistent branding strategies
automatically translate to positive stakeholder perception and a favourable image. The study
proffers sustainable solutions including the need for PR and marketing communications
managers to adopt a more innovative, harmonious, consistent and strategic approach to CVI
management andChanging world, application that resonate with the organisation’s publics and
contribute to effective stakeholder perception and sustainable corporate image management.
Introduction
Scholars and practitioners in public relations (PR), advertising, marketing, and
corporate communications, have long recognised the importance of corporate visual identity
Assets (CVIA) as an indispensable component of an organisation’s corporate heritage,
strategic communication and overall corporate image promotions in commercial and non-
commercial organisations. In today’s fast-changing competitive business environment, the
application of an effective and creative CVIA can significantly contribute to managing an
organisation’s corporate image, stakeholder perception and public sentiment to impact its
reputation, progress and prosperity. Marziliano (1997), Fiol and Kovoor-Misra (1997), and
Whetten and Godfrey (1998)reinforce this view by observing that:
Neither the importance of examining the relationship among these concepts has
received much attention from researchers or practitioners, nor has its urgency been adequately
felt. Although the need to pay more and immediate attention to these has been strongly
advocated (e.g. Whetten 1997) as a way of enhancing a firm’s competitive position (Dowling

[Page 2]
Uniuyo Journal Of Communication Studies, UJCS Vol. 6, No. 1, November 2025
176
2001), exploiting the significance of the relationships among these concepts from the
standpoint of stakeholder groups has often been neglected (Rufaidah, 2004, p.1).
Therefore, for effective management of an organisation’s corporate image and
stakeholders’ perception, it is critical to understand the complex interrelationships among
corporate image, stakeholder perception, and corporate visual identity assets, and their
significant contributions to promoting a company’s reputation and prosperity. According to
Bernstein (1984), “The image does not exist in the organisation but in those that perceive the
organisation”, while Fill (2009) argues that “an organisation cannot change its image in a
directly managed way, but it can change its identity. It is through the management of its
identity that an organisation can influence the image held of it” (Fill, 2009, p.399). Fill further
notes: “The image stakeholders hold of an organisation is a result of a particular combination
of many different elements, but is essentially a distillation of the values, beliefs and attitudes
that an individual has of the focused organisation” (ibid). Since corporate images are shaped
by stakeholders’ interpretation of the identity cues they perceive about an organisation, for an
image to be sustainable, the identity cues around which the image is fashioned must be based
on reality, reflect the values and culture of the organisation.
Imagine the fascinating swoosh of NIKE, the memorable and iconic golden arches of
McDonald’s; the three parallel black-and-white stripes of Adidas, (symbolising a sense of
movement and the herculean mountains that athletes have to climb); and the sleek logo design
of the leaping Puma sportswear company. One can also visualise the three overlapping ovals
of Toyota automobile company cast in shades of blue and silver (conveying a sense of trust,
ruggedness, reliability, technological innovation), and the Hewlett-Packard ‘HP’ monogram
logo, reflecting the company’s focus on personal computers, and the ICT innovation. These
designs are not mere logos, but symbolic corporate assets, representing their brand experience
that spark emotional responses, positive associations, a deep sense of fraternity, concord and
consistency.
The study argues that well-designed CVIA create brand personality, recognition,
awareness, acceptance, brand loyalty, positive image, and stakeholder perception, which
translates into brand patronage and loyalty, favourable purchasing decisions, and increased
investment. They serve as an integral and indispensable component of a company’s overall
identity and reputation. In this regard, the growing importance of corporate image and identity
management can be attributed to the increasing recognition of tangible and intangible
corporate assets as key drivers of an organisation’s value. Thus, an effective corporate image

[Page 3]
Uniuyo Journal Of Communication Studies, UJCS Vol. 6, No. 1, November 2025
177
and identity management can distinguish an organisation from its competitors, foster brand
loyalty, and bolster stakeholder engagement.
Given the preceding analysis, the study critically evaluates the role of corporate visual
identity assets, in managing stakeholder perceptions and corporate image. Copious research
evidence from extensive literature reviews show that so much research effort has been
expended in the field of semiology and corporate identity studies (CIS), centering on
marketing and organisational behaviour. However, theresearcher found that little or no study
seems to have been done on the role of CVIA in managing stakeholder perception and
corporate image within the context of stakeholder relations and a changing corporate world
order. He and Balmer (2005) affirm this view by noting that “Within the disciplines of
marketing and organisational behaviour, identity studies have attained considerable
prominence over the last decade. However, little has been done to synthesise both bodies of
literature and to discover in-depth implications for corporate-level marketing” (He and
Balmer, 2005, p.1).
2. Statement of the Problem
With the upsurge of business activities and brand competition, the need for
entrepreneurs, marketers and PR managers to communicate with consumers about the
availability of certain products and the unique quality of their brands, has become imperative.
As the global economy becomes more volatile, complex and competitive, the need for
business organisations to seek more effective and efficient strategies not only to maximise
profit, but also to achieve competitive advantage and manage their corporate reputation and
stakeholders’ perception, is even more compelling. As the tempo of production increases,
stocks and inventories pile up, and business organisations, ad agencies and PR managers need
to adopt more creative and sustainable strategies to boost their sales volume. They can
achieve this significant objective by identifying their brands’ CVIA) and unique selling point
(USP), and communicating them to their customers.
Flowing from the preceding analysis, and extensive empirical literature reviews in the
field of PR, advertising and marketing communications, the researcher uncovered a critical
research problem that impelled him to investigate the role of CVIA in managing corporate
image and organisational stakeholders’ perception.

text:
As the global economy becomes more volatile, complex and competitive, the need for
business organisations to seek more effective and efficient strategies not only to maximise
profit, but also to achieve competitive advantage and manage their corporate reputation and
stakeholders’ perception, is even more compelling. As the tempo of production increases,
stocks and inventories pile up, and business organisations, ad agencies and PR managers need
to adopt more creative and sustainable strategies to boost their sales volume. They can
achieve this significant objective by identifying their brands’ CVIA) and unique selling point
(USP), and communicating them to their customers.
Flowing from the preceding analysis, and extensive empirical literature reviews in the
field of PR, advertising and marketing communications, the researcher uncovered a critical
research problem that impelled him to investigate the role of CVIA in managing corporate
image and organisational stakeholders’ perception. Within the context of effective stakeholder
relations and corporate image management in a new world corporate order, the study
identifies the research problem by answering the following critical questions: What roles can
CVIA play in enhancing organisational image and stakeholder perception? How can PR and

[Page 4]
Uniuyo Journal Of Communication Studies, UJCS Vol. 6, No. 1, November 2025
178
brand practitioners leverage CVIA to manage their corporate image and stakeholders’
perception of their policies and programmes?
4. Research Questions
Consistent with the study's research problem and objectives, four research questions
were formulated and analysed, while providing appropriate answers to them with empirical
data. The research questions are as follows:
1. What roles can corporate visual identity (CVI) tools play in managing organisation’s
corporate image and stakeholders’ perception in response to changing global market
conditions?
2. How can stakeholders’ perception help companies to develop effective image
management strategies in a changing world?
3. What are the effective CVIA management strategies that can be used to
managecorporate image and stakeholder perception?
5. Research Hypotheses
Three research hypotheses were formulated for further investigation in line with the
preceding research questions, the research problem, and the study's objectives. This helped
the researcher to proffer practical solutions to the research problem according to the
recommendations of Asika (1991, p. 75) and Dominick & Wilmer (2006, p. 26).
Hypothesis 1
Ho: Corporate visual identity assets cannot play any role in managing organisation’s corporate
image and stakeholders’ perception in response to changing global market conditions.
H1:Corporate visual identity assets can play some roles in managing organisation’s corporate
image and stakeholders’ perception in response to changing global market conditions.
Hypothesis 2
Ho: Stakeholders’ perception cannot help organisations to develop effective image
management strategies in a changing world.
H1: Stakeholders’ perception can help organisations to develop effective image management
strategies in a changing world.
Hypothesis 3

[Page 5]
Uniuyo Journal Of Communication Studies, UJCS Vol. 6, No. 1, November 2025
179
Ho: There are no specific CVI strategies that can be used to manage corporate image and
stakeholder perception.
H1: There are specific IMC strategies that can be used to penetrate the table water market and
gain a market share for Aquifer brand in the FCT?
5. Review of Related Literature
5.1 Conceptual Review
The following concepts were reviewed: Corporate Image/Reputation, Identity,
Stakeholder Perception, and Corporate Visual Identity Assets.
Corporate Image versus Corporate Reputation
The concept of image refers to the set of beliefs, impressions, notions, sentiments, and
perceptions that individuals, groups, audiences, or members of the public hold about a person,
persons, institutions or organisations arising from their understanding or interpretation of the
cues presented by the organisation.
Conversely, reputation is “the collective representation of an organisation’s past
performance that describes the firm’s ability to deliver valued outcomes to multiple
stakeholders” (Wilcox and Cameron, 2009, p. 267). It consists of the track records,
achievements and virtues that distinguish an individual or organisation in the minds of its
stakeholders. While image deals with how an organisation’s publics see it, reputation, on the
other hand, refers to what the organisation really is, including its past accomplishments.
According to Wilcox and Cameron, 2009, “Reputation isn’t formed by packaging and slogans.
A good reputation is created and destroyed by everything an organisation does, from the way
it manages employees to the way it handles conflicts with outside constituents” (Wilcox and
Cameron, 2009, p. 268).
Corporate image is the impression, perceptions or opinions an organisation’s internal
and external publics and other stakeholders have about the organisation. It is a complex
construct shaped by various factors, including communication, experiences, reputation and
visual cues. It is a dynamic entity influenced by internal and external forces – corporate visual
identity heritage, corporate objectives, vision and mission, corporate culture and values, as
well as management style, quality of human resources, product quality, research and
development and innovation. Other factors influencing corporate image include company
history, purpose, corporate social responsibility (CSR) programmes, staff attitudes and
accomplishments.

[Page 6]
Uniuyo Journal Of Communication Studies, UJCS Vol. 6, No. 1, November 2025
180
Stakeholder Perception
Stakeholders refer to individuals, groups, institutions, organisations, including key
shareholders existing within an organisation’s internal and external environments, and who
have direct or indirect relationships or contacts with the organisation. Organisational
stakeholders are known for having vested socioeconomic, political and environmental interest
in their organisation’s operations, performance and success, influencing their management’s
policies and actions.
Generally speaking, perception deals with the cognitive process of selecting,
organising and interpreting meaning, messages, information, action and behaviour to create a
meaningful picture of the real world. Schiffman and Kanuk, (2003) describe perception as
“the process by which an individual selects, organises, and interprets stimuli into a
meaningful and coherent picture of the world" (Schiffman and Kanuk, 2003, p. 158).
Contextually, stakeholder perception deals with how an organisation’s publics including
individuals, groups, institutions, customers, employees, contractors, investors, the media, and
other forces in its internal and external operational environment see, perceive, interpret,
understand the organisation, its image, products and services, corporate identity and
philosophy, messages, behaviours, actions and inactions. Stakeholders’ perception plays a
critical role in shaping their opinions about an organisation – how they think, feel, behave, act
and relate with the organisation.
Corporate Identity
Kotler and Keller (2006) define identity from the corporate level standpoint as “the
way a company aims to identify or position itself or its products”, while image is “the way the
public perceives the company or its product” (Kotler & Keller, 2006, p. 321). Fill in his view,
sees identity as a means by which an organisation differentiates itself from other organisations,
while Oliver (2010) defines identity as “a state of having unique identity or individual
characteristics by which a person or thing recognizes or defines him/her/itself” (Oliver, 2010, p.
71). He and Balmer (2005) notes that “The concept of identity provides the platform by which
many corporate-level concepts can be understood such as corporate branding, corporate
communications, corporate image and corporate reputation. As such, it can be viewed as
providing the foundation to the nascent field of corporate marketing” (He and Balmer, 2005, p.
1).

[Page 7]
Uniuyo Journal Of Communication Studies, UJCS Vol. 6, No. 1, November 2025
181
Corporate identity, on the other hand, deals with a series of visual cues by which the
publics or stakeholders of an organisation can recognise a company or firm or differentiate an
organisation from another.

many corporate-level concepts can be understood such as corporate branding, corporate
communications, corporate image and corporate reputation. As such, it can be viewed as
providing the foundation to the nascent field of corporate marketing” (He and Balmer, 2005, p.
1).

[Page 7]
Uniuyo Journal Of Communication Studies, UJCS Vol. 6, No. 1, November 2025
181
Corporate identity, on the other hand, deals with a series of visual cues by which the
publics or stakeholders of an organisation can recognise a company or firm or differentiate an
organisation from another. Fill (2009) describes corporate identity as “the promotion of the
cues by which stakeholders can recognise and identify the organisation” and “a means by
which an organisation differentiates itself from other organisations”(Fill, 2009, p.394).
However, some contemporary writers feel that corporate identity is increasingly
becoming an obsolete term that needs to be replaced with brand identity or corporate branding.
According to scholars like Balmer (1988), “Corporate identity was the accepted terminology
in the 1980s and early 1990s, and this gave way to corporate branding at the turn of the
century”. Nevertheless, organisations need to address identity-related issues that provide
answers to three critical questions: ‘Who are we?’, ‘What business are we in?’, and ‘What do
we want to be?’
5.2 Empirical Review
Corporate Visual Identity Assets (CVIA)
Corporate Visual Identity (CVI) is a branch of semiology that deals with the study and
analysis of how sign systems work. Also known as semiotics, CVI deals with the language of
signs, symbols, signifiers and the signified. According to O’Shaughnessy and Stadler, (2008),
semiology “explores the logic and methodology behind communication, and shows how we
can understand systemically, through the semiotic method, what communications mean. It is
also concerned with the meaning and with how meanings are produced and transmitted”
(O’Shaughnessy and Stadler, 2008, p.133). Semiotics is also the science or study of signs, and
signs systems, e.g. logos, insignia, trademarks, nameplates, traffic lights, road signs, colour
and other symbolic representations that can be interpreted and analysed with meaning.
Therefore, Corporate Visual Identity Assets (CVIA), refers to the various physical,
concrete or abstractive signs, symbols and optical representations that communicate meaning
by representing a thing or an idea, philosophy, culture, belief system or values to which it
refers. Such communication artefacts like the Nigerian Coat of Arms, the National Flag, First
Bank’s “White Horse”, the Shell of Shell Development Company, and the bitten Apple Mac
logo of Apple Computers, are all visual and abstractive signs and symbolic corporate
resources and heritages that speak the language of reputation management.
However, Bernstein (1984) avers that “All organisations have an identity whether they
like it or not”. But, some organisations may choose to manage their CVIA, just as some
individuals decide on some specific lifestyles. Other organisations may be careless about their

[Page 8]
Uniuyo Journal Of Communication Studies, UJCS Vol. 6, No. 1, November 2025
182
identity and end up confusing and misleading their publics and other stakeholders.
Nevertheless, there is little evidence to show that PR and corporate managers are consistent in
their approach to managing CVI resources as they often claim.
Corporate Visual Identity and Image Management
Corporate visual identity and image management deal with “the way in which
organizations or companies are presented and perceived, and how they interact with their
various stakeholder audiences. It is also concerned with the images that people form as a result
of interpreting the various identity signals that organizations transmit and any interaction that
may ensue” (Fill, 2009, p. 388). Melewar (2003) observes that corporate identity is concerned
with the set of meanings by which an organization allows itself to be known and through
which it enables people to describe, remember and relate to it” (Cited in Fill, 2009, p. 388).
Hatch and Schultz (2000) identify two schools of thought about strategic identity
management – the ‘visual school’, and a ‘strategic school’. According to them, the visual
school deals with operational aspect of strategic identity management, while the strategic
school is concerned with an organization’s aims and how it positions and distinguishes itself.
Chris Hill underscores the importance of the differentiation or ‘demarcation’ as it facilitates
the identification of the evolution of identity management and reputation management.
An example is Shell Development Company’s logo. Created over a century ago, Shell
logo seems to have remained unchanged, while in reality “it has undergone many changes and
what we see today is nothing like the original. This has occurred through careful continuity of
the idea of the seashell and adaption of it to various contexts through tine” (Fill, ibid). He and
Balmer (2007) identity some identity-related topics, which include “visual identity, strategic
identity, social identity and organizational identity”. Fill suggests that “The social and
organizational forms of identity are part of the organizational behaviour school of thought.
Forms of Corporate Visual Identity Assets (CVIA)
1. Corporate Logo
A logo is a unique symbol, signature, icon or word mark that represents a company’s
identity and its stakeholders. It is one of the popular virtual or graphic elements of a brand’s
visual identity (VI) that harmoniously provide a system for identifying and representing a
corporate brand. Examples are the iconic Spenserian script spelling out CocaCola in a
distinctive flowing elegant and timeless typeface with red colour lettering and white
background, conveying a sense of tradition and corporate global heritage. Google’s logo
presents a 5-letter word mark with each letter elegantly illuminated in various bright, vibrant

[Page 9]
Uniuyo Journal Of Communication Studies, UJCS Vol. 6, No. 1, November 2025
183
and attractive colours in a playful, slightly rounded sans-serif font, reflecting the brand’s
innovative and hi-tech global image. Though Nokia’s logo has undergone several iterations, it
is symbolised in a simple word mark with dark blue sans-serif font, conveying a profound
sense of reliability, durability and sophistication.
2. Colour Schemes
A colour scheme or palette is a combination of colours used consistently across all
brand’s visual elements or platforms. It is an organisation’s in-house corporate colour or colour
palette. In-house corporate colours are complementary visual identities of business
organisations as they support the corporate logos and names of companies to give them the
desired identity. Corporate colours evoke emotions, mood, aesthetics, elegance and prestige
about an organisation. A good combination of colour schemes can provide memorable and
sustainable impressions for organisations, e.g. Red + Blue = Purple; Red + Yellow = Orange;
Blue + Yellow = Green. Instances of corporate colours are the beautiful colours of UBA and
Zenith, and the vibrant colours of MTN, and Chelsea FC.
3. Typefaces and Typography
Typography refers to the style, arrangement and appearance of text. A consistent
corporate typography helps to create a distinct visual identity and reinforce the brand’s
message. Typefaces and typographies constitute the major elements of corporate branding and
reputation management. They include all the symbolic and textual representations of a
company such as fonts, type sizes, and typefaces used in corporate branding, and
communicating messages such as letterheads, memos, colours, layouts, special effects and
installation points. They promote maximum exposure and corporate image. Integrating
corporate elements such as names, symbols, payoffs, and typefaces, express the
distinctiveness of organisation’s CVIA.
4. Signs and Symbols
Signs and Symbols are indispensable CVI artefacts often used in strategic brand
promotion, brand-building, stakeholder relations and image management campaigns.
