information of segments of the plot, scene space, role, still 
according to the conveying of the film, by using montage 
language logic. The audience interpreted these events 
according to the associated graphics, tried to figure out the 
story content, and movie posters also rely on the words of 
these incomplete to reveal the suspense of the story, to inspire 
the watching desire of the audience.

SYMBOLIC SIGNIFICANCE 
The original graphics of our ancestors used for 
communication and thinking is a kind of specific image 
symbols. The sign and symbol in English is all meaning 
symbol. The sign has strong concentration and unity, and the 
symbol and universal concept of things are closer, with broad 
"sub-consciousness" implied in it. "Symbol uses   the image of 
the external emotional things to suggest an abstract, universal 
significance. What symbol brings to people or to make people 
realize it is not this specific and direct significance that the 
external thing has, but rather is the universal significance 
implied by certain features” 
Jerry N Uelsmann Jerry, American surrealism 
photographer used the traditional darkroom technology. In his 
work, he often overlapped and outlined the tree, river, vessels, 
character and inanimate object and other common elements, 
broke our habit of thinking “Fig. 2 ”. The turning is from 
photos to "image narrative" to create a dream-like montage, to 
bring us wonderful visual enjoyment and psychological 
experience.

Processing Fluency, Processing Style and Aesthetic Response to Artistic Photographs 
Nathalie Vissers and Johan Wagemans 
KU Leuven, Belgium 
 
Correspondence to: 
Nathalie Vissers, Laboratory of Experimental Psychology, KU Leuven (University of Leuven), 
Tiensestraat 102 - box 3711, BE-3000 Leuven, Belgium. Phone: +3216376275 E-mail: 
nathalie.vissers@kuleuven.be 
  

[Page 2]
2 
 
Processing Fluency, Processing Style and Aesthetic Response to Artistic Photographs 
Abstract 
We are processing many photographs on a daily basis, but our understanding of perceptual 
and aesthetic processing of photography is limited. The relationship between processing fluency and 
aesthetic evaluations was studied in a varied set of high-quality artistic photographs. Interactions 
between subject matter (e.g., portrait), medium (e.g., sharpness, colour, portrait orientation) and 
form (e.g., filling of the frame, uniform background, vertical symmetry) appeared to be relevant for 
evaluated fluency of processing. The Pleasure-Interest Model of Aesthetic Liking (Graf & Landwehr, 
2015) was tested on a selection of low, medium and high fluency photographs. Results were partly in 
line with the model, showing two routes to aesthetic liking with different relationships to fluency. In 
the automatic condition, high fluency photographs were found most pleasant, but in the controlled 
condition, low fluency photographs were found most pleasant. Regarding interest, however, all 
conditions showed the highest interest for the low fluency photographs, irrespective of processing 
style. We therefore explored the relationship between fluency and interest for larger sets of 
photographs (heterogeneous and homogeneous in subject matter), finding similar low interest 
percentages for the highest fluency photographs, but here the highest interest ratings were found for 
medium levels of fluency. In general, the studies show that investigating how processing fluency 
relates to aesthetic impressions of photographs can be a promising but complex avenue. Data and 
analyses code can be found at: https://osf.io/b3z2y/ 
Keywords: photography, empirical aesthetics, processing fluency, pleasure, interest 
  

[Page 4]
4 
 
This aesthetic result of processing fluency has been brought back to the link between 
processing fluency and positive affect, referred to as the hedonic marking of processing fluency 
(Winkielman et al., 2003). High processing fluency is supposed to trigger positive affect, because it 
indicates a positive state in the world or within the cognitive system, whereas low fluency indicates a 
negative state of affairs in the world or in the cognitive system. Furthermore, this affective response 
is considered the crucial link between fluency and positive aesthetic evaluations. Within this 
framework, certain findings within the aesthetic literature can be explained in terms of processing 
fluency, such as preferences related to symmetry, contrast and clarity, figural goodness, amount of 
information (objective features of stimuli), as well as findings related to repeated exposure, implicit 
learning, exposure duration and priming (related to viewers’ previous experience with stimuli).  
Other theoretical accounts have also proposed a relationship between processing dynamics 
and aesthetic preferences, however, proposing different mechanisms and predicted outcomes. For 
example, Van de Cruys and Wagemans (2011) state that the processing fluency account cannot 
explain why many great, and aesthetically appreciated, works of art violate characteristics that lead 
to high processing fluency. Often these artworks introduce incongruities, processing difficulties and 
unpredictable patterns. However, the reward of looking at such works of art lies in transitioning from 
this state of violated expectations (prediction error), towards more predictability. Thus, it is not 
processing fluency in itself, but a dynamic increase in being able to process an artwork that leads to 
aesthetic reactions to great works of art. Similarly, Muth and colleagues (e.g., Muth, Hesslinger, & 
Carbon, 2015) showed that perceptual challenge and ambiguity can indeed be preferred by viewers. 
Participants were more interested and affected by the artworks with a higher subjective degree of 
ambiguity. Moreover, the strength of insights also related to aesthetic appreciation.  
Pleasure-Interest Model of Aesthetic Liking 

[Page 5]
5 
 
With their Pleasure-Interest model of Aesthetic experience (PIA), Graf and Landwehr (2015) 
aim to account for the potential paradoxical aesthetic effects of processing fluency in one model. The 
PIA model is a hierarchical model that combines the hedonic marking theory of processing fluency 
with a dual-process perspective (see Gawronski & Creighton, 2013 for an overview chapter of dual-
process theories). Graf and Landwehr (2015) add two modes of processing (automatic vs. controlled 
processing) to the fluency-based models of aesthetic liking, which results in a more nuanced model 
that can explain both the attraction to easy-to-process, as well as the fascination for difficult-to-
process stimuli. Specifically, the PIA model focuses on two main outcomes: aesthetic pleasure and 
aesthetic interest, that could be two pathways to aesthetic liking. Stimulus-driven automatic 
processing and the perceived fluency of this processing will result in either pleasure (when 
experiencing higher fluency than expected) or displeasure (lower fluency than expected). However, 
more elaborate or controlled perceiver-driven processing – because of the need of cognitive 
enrichment – could give rise to interest (when disfluency is reduced), confusion (when disfluency is 
not reduced) or boredom (when there was no disfluency to account for). 
More recently, researchers from the same research group have also quantified four low-level 
visual properties that can be seen as fluency-based antecedents of aesthetic preference: visual 
simplicity, visual symmetry, visual contrast and visual self-similarity (Mayer & Landwehr, 2018). 
Visual simplicity refers to the amount of visual information in an image, and is calculated as “one 
minus the ratio between compressed and uncompressed image file size” (p. 402). Visual symmetry is 
measured by calculating the correlation of pixel values to the left and right of an image axis (e.g. 
vertical for vertical symmetry). The authors also take into account colour information by calculating a 
weighted mean of the values for the different colour channels. Furthermore, they do not only 
examine the most central axis, but also calculate the symmetry for axes that are off-center and use 
the maximum of 11 calculated symmetry values. Visual contrast is calculated using a weighted mean 

[Page 6]
6 
 
of the root-mean-squared contrast of an image (the standard deviation of pixel intensities) for each 
colour channel. Finally, visual self-similarity is also calculated as a weighted mean for the different 
colour channels of self-similarity calculated as a function of the slope of the power spectrum (see pp. 
402-403 in the article for more details on these calculations).  
Photography and Processing Fluency 
Photography takes up a unique position between reality and other images.  On the one hand, 
photography is inherently tied to reality: A photograph is (almost1) always a trace of something that 
happened in reality in front of a lens.

metadata.core_insight_en: This study explored the relationship between processing fluency and aesthetic responses to artistic photographs. The researchers found that high fluency photographs were initially found most pleasant in an automatic condition, but in a controlled condition, low fluency photographs were found more pleasant. Interest showed the highest ratings for low fluency photographs across all conditions, and exploring further, medium levels of fluency showed the highest interest ratings. The studies indicate that investigating processing fluency's relationship to aesthetic impressions can be a promising but complex avenue.

Photography and Processing Fluency 
Photography takes up a unique position between reality and other images.  On the one hand, 
photography is inherently tied to reality: A photograph is (almost1) always a trace of something that 
happened in reality in front of a lens. As a result, researchers often use photographs as a convenient 
stand-in for reality. In these cases, photography is seen as a window onto the world and viewers are 
expected to look through this window in the same way as they are looking at the world itself. 
However, a photograph is also always a construct: camera and photographer are transforming a 
temporal, dynamic event in our visual reality into a 2D image that is cut out of its context and 
translated into a flat and framed surface which renders new relationships between visual elements. 
Therefore, even the most straightforward natural images of people, objects and scenes are still 
transforming reality. Every photographic decision, even when the photographer (or the researcher) is 
not conscious of them, will impact the final photograph and how it is processed. On the other hand, 
researchers in empirical aesthetics should be careful not to equate the processing of (artistic) 
photography fully to the processing of other created 2D images, such as paintings or digital art, 
precisely because of the intimate connection between photography and reality which sets boundary 
                                                            
1 Some exceptions include cameraless photographs – using light and photographic paper, etc. 
 

[Page 7]
7 
 
conditions for the photographer (e.g., he/she cannot bring together visual elements that are 
separate in space/time to construct a symbolic narrative).  
It is high time that we study a photograph for what it is: a photograph; neither a convenient 
stand-in for reality, nor a fully created 2D picture, such as a painting. In order to tease apart, and 
bring back together, the different layers of a photograph, it is useful to consider the following 
equation from art educator Terry Barrett’s Principles for Interpreting Photographs: “subject matter + 
medium + form + context = content” (Barrett, 2010, p. 155). Figure 1 combines the idea about the 
unique position of photography, with these different elements that play a role in forming the final 
content of the photograph. Below, we consider how each of these layers affects the (processing) 
fluency of photography.

 Subject matter can be described as “the people, places and things depicted in a work of art” 
(Barrett, 2010, p. 155). Photography’s subject matter is (a trace of) reality itself. When comparing 


[Page 8]
8 
 
how viewers process different types of images (magazine photographs, stock photographs, 
abstract/surreal graphics), researchers found that photographs were mainly categorized based on 
their semantic content (thus: subject matter), whereas abstract/surrealist graphics were categorized 
relatively more based on visual attributes (Laine-Hernandez & Westman, 2010).  
It is therefore very likely that the perceived fluency of processing a photograph will depend, 
at least partly, on how fluent we are in perceiving the depicted subject matter. This could, in turn, 
relate to people’s aesthetic experiences. For example, a potential explanation for people’s aesthetic 
preference for photographs with natural scenes, compared to man-made (or combined) scenes 
(Biederman & Vessel, 2006; Smith et al., 2018; Tinio et al., 2011) and the finding that natural 
photographs elicit more positive and less arousing emotions compared to urban photographs 
(Kuzinas et al., 2016) is that our visual system is more efficient in processing these natural scenes. 
Other aspects that relate to processing fluency, such as prototypicality or familiarity with the subject 
matter, could also play a role. Thömmes and Hübner (2020) found that their aesthetic measure 
(based on Instagram data), for the category of dance photographs, was higher for photographs of 
female dancers (as compared with mixed gender groups or male gender). They explain this by 
suggesting that females are more prototypical of a ballet dancer, as well as wearing more colourful 
and flamboyant dresses. The difference in semantic content also predicted more of the variance in 
aesthetic liking than their calculations for image features such as balance and curvature.  
 Medium can be described as “the materials and processes with which artworks are made: for 
example, clay, acrylic paint, bronze, silver gelatin, dye, and so forth. Considerations of the 
characteristics of media and how the image maker has used them is important to understanding the 
work being interpreted.” (Barrett, 2010, p. 155). The photographer can make many medium-specific 
decisions, such as which camera, lenses, sensor/film emulsion to use; as well as the settings each of 
these allows, such as ISO, aperture, shutter speed, focus point, etc. These will affect different image 

[Page 9]
9 
 
features, such as sharpness/blur, contrast, grain/noise, colour, resolution, distortions, etc. Recently, 
researchers are more aware that these medium-specific aspects interact with the subject matter to 
produce certain aesthetic preferences. Tinio and colleagues (2011) found that natural scenes were 
preferred over human-made scenes, but that image quality mattered, with degraded images less 
preferred than their high-quality variations. Moreover, the degradations (in contrast, sharpness, 
grain) had additive effects, so that the more degradations, the less preferred the images were. 
Similarly, Smith and colleagues (2018) found that manipulations of colour influenced the pattern of 
preference for natural, human-made or combined photographs. For example, a preference for 
human-made over combined (natural + human-made) photographs was only significant in colour 
photographs, but not in black-and-white versions of the photographs.  
Form can be described as “how an image has been put together by its maker (or altered by 
its editor). Form is a combination of how subject matter, materials, and elements of art are put 
together according to some organizational principle. Form is synonymous with composition.” 
(Barrett, 2010, p. 156). General principles of visual organization or composition that are supposed to 
influence processing fluency and aesthetic preference over different image types might play a similar 
role in photography.

text:
Similarly, Smith and colleagues (2018) found that manipulations of colour influenced the pattern of 
preference for natural, human-made or combined photographs. For example, a preference for 
human-made over combined (natural + human-made) photographs was only significant in colour 
photographs, but not in black-and-white versions of the photographs.  
Form can be described as “how an image has been put together by its maker (or altered by 
its editor). Form is a combination of how subject matter, materials, and elements of art are put 
together according to some organizational principle. Form is synonymous with composition.” 
(Barrett, 2010, p. 156). General principles of visual organization or composition that are supposed to 
influence processing fluency and aesthetic preference over different image types might play a similar 
role in photography. For example, Reber and colleagues (2004) propose that features such as 
symmetry, figural goodness and amount of information are related to aesthetic preference, due to 
their impact on processing fluency. Relatively small changes in the visual organization of a 
photograph, such as changing the direction in which visual elements are facing, can also change 
processing fluency and preference. For example, Leonhardt, Caitlin and Pirouz (2015) found that 
product photographs where the product is facing inward toward the center are easier to process and 
result in more positive evaluations, in comparison to facing outward to the edge. Similarly, 
Chahboun, Flumini, Pérez González, McManus, and Santiago (2017) found that, when people focus 
on the lateral spatial dimension of photographs (compare left-to-right versus right-to-left directional 

[Page 10]
10 
 
variants of the same photograph), they prefer photographs that are more in line with their reading 
and writing directions. The authors suggest scanning fluency as a potential cause for this finding.  
Finally, the context in which the photograph is made and seen should also be taken into 
account. Researchers should keep in mind that the presentation context (size, aspects of the 
screen/print, presentation time, instructions, other photographs or context information) will 
influence processing fluency and (sometimes in interaction with other photograph features) 
influence aesthetic impressions. For example, Landwehr and Eckmann (2020) reduced the 
presentation size of the photograph (full-size versus reduced size) as a manipulation of fluency. 
Unexpectedly, they found that reducing the size (and thus decreasing fluency) resulted in more 
positive evaluations than for the original-size. One explanation they offer is that, in the reduced-size 
pictures, participants focused mainly on  the gist of the picture, but could focus more on details and 
image quality in the original-size photographs. They mention that their stimuli do not necessarily 
reflect “up-to-date content or a high standard of picture quality” (p. 11), which might have been 
more evident in the full-size versions (see also Goetschalckx, Moors, Vanmarcke, & Wagemans, 2019 
for another study using shrinked variants of images to examine the relationship between goodness of 
image organization and memorability).  
A few observations stand out from the studies above. First, these scattered studies, even 
when they were not directly assessing the role of processing fluency, suggest that processing fluency 
can play a role in the aesthetic experience of photography. Second, it becomes clear that processing 
fluency for a photograph will depend on the complex interplay of different layers. The fact that these 
interactions already show up for relatively easy image manipulations with natural images (e.g., 
contrast degradations) only promises much more intricate interactions for high-quality photographs, 
made by photographers with full control over their medium. McManus and Stöver (2014) sum it up 
nicely as follows: “What distinguishes a bad photo, from a good photo, from a great photo, from a 

[Page 11]
11 
 
masterpiece, is in part content, part a different angle or view on an otherwise familiar scene, part the 
subtleties of composition and part technical manipulations to enhance the content. All can be chosen 
well or badly or done well or badly” (p. 244).  
A few general studies focusing on photography and aesthetics also show promise for a 
further exploration of processing fluency. Axelsson (2007) started from a wide range of 564 
photographs and found that three dimensions were underlying participants’ judgments of aesthetic 
quality: Hedonic Tone-Familiarity, Absence of color and Expressiveness-Dynamics. The first 
dimension is of particular relevance here. It contrasted more conventional with less conventional 
photographs and related to participants’ labels of hedonic tone and familiarity. The finding suggests 
that people hedonically prefer more familiar photographs (because of familiar subject matter, but 
also familiarity in terms of photographic construction). Similarly, Mullennix and colleagues (Mullennix 
et al., 2013), using artistic black-and-white photographs that varied in subject matter and aesthetic 
attributes, conclude that participants preferred photographs that were “pleasant, clear, interesting 
and easy to process and understand” (p. 145), again indicating a potential relationship between 
processing fluency and aesthetic evaluation of photography. 
The Current Studies 
In this project, we explore the following research questions, starting from a broad set of high-
quality contemporary artistic photographs :  
Study 1: Which artistic photographs are difficult (low fluency) or easy (high fluency) to process? 
Which image features relate to this perceived fluency?  
Study 2: How do photograph fluency and processing style (automatic vs. controlled) interact to 
predict pleasure, interest and attractiveness?  

[Page 12]
12 
 
Based on the results from the first two studies, we added a third post-hoc exploration of the main 
findings with a different group of participants. 
Study 3: How does photograph fluency relate to interest with a larger set of photographs (selected 
for their heterogeneous vs. homogeneous subject matter)?  
Additional information about the project design, photographs, data and analyses code in R 
(RStudio Team, 2018) can be found at: https://osf.io/b3z2y/. 
Artistic Photography from the Life Framer Competition 
We believe it is worthwhile to explore the topic of interest with a set of high-quality artistic 
photographs. The skilled photographer will have intimate knowledge about his/her medium and will 
be a master of playing with subject matter, form, medium and context to reach optimal levels of 
(dis)fluency for his/her purposes in a way that goes above and beyond simple researcher-based 
assumptions and manipulations. In fact, this skilled photographer might be the true master of fluency 
(compared to other artists), because she/he needs to combine the messy ongoing and boundless 
nature of reality and the “mechanical and mindless process” of photography to “produce pictures 
meaningful in human terms – pictures with clarity and coherence and a point of view” (Szarkowski, 
1966, p. 6).  
The selected photographs were all nominated and winning photographs from edition 2017-
2018 of an online photography competition that celebrates creative photography: Life Framer 
(www.life-framer.com). Each month, a call was launched to submit photographs on a specific theme.

In fact, this skilled photographer might be the true master of fluency 
(compared to other artists), because she/he needs to combine the messy ongoing and boundless 
nature of reality and the “mechanical and mindless process” of photography to “produce pictures 
meaningful in human terms – pictures with clarity and coherence and a point of view” (Szarkowski, 
1966, p. 6).  
The selected photographs were all nominated and winning photographs from edition 2017-
2018 of an online photography competition that celebrates creative photography: Life Framer 
(www.life-framer.com). Each month, a call was launched to submit photographs on a specific theme. 
Photographers had to pay for entry in the competition, and each theme was judged by a different 
expert in the photography field (curator, art photographer, museum expert, editor, gallery owner, 
etc.) resulting in very high-quality contemporary artistic photographs. There were 10 content-related 
themes - Civilization, Street Life, World Travelers, The Human Body, An Instant, Colors, After Dark, 

[Page 13]
13 
 
Urban Life, Youthhood, Faces of Life – as well as 2 open calls. Each month, 20 photographs were 
nominated and there were two prize winners (first and second prize). This summed up to a varied set 
of 239 artistic photographs (as one photograph was nominated two times). In the current project, we 
start from a varied subset of 154 photographs from this set2.  
Study 1 
This study examines  perceived fluency ratings for our broad set of artistic photographs.  
Method 
Participants 
72 psychology students between 17 and 26 years (59 women, 13 men, Mage = 18.58 years, 
SDage = 1.22 years) participated in the task. The group can be described as interested novices in the 
field of artistic photography. Most of them did not receive any art education (n = 56, 77.78%), owns 
none (43.06%) or one (44.44%) photography book. The majority rarely visit a photography 
gallery/exhibition/museum (9.72% never, 41.67% less than once a year; 20.83% once a year; 25% two 
or three times a year; 2.78% often). They are somewhat interested in photography (M = 3.65, SD = 
0.87) on a scale from 1 (not at all) to 5 (definitely). 
Measures and Procedure 
Participants were tested in February 2019 in collective testing sessions in a reserved 
computer class of the University of Leuven. The experiment was run on Windows computers (Dell 
                                                            
2 These were photographs, which were left after removing photographs for which photographers had 
actively refused consent before the start of the project, as well as photographs used for other tasks 
in the data collection session. Note that, accidentally, one photograph did end up in two different 
tasks. This means that 17 participants in Study 1 had already seen one photograph before in another 
task. This photograph was not part of the lowest or highest ratings and was not selected among the 
nine photographs for the second stage, and therefore did not influence our results in any way. 

[Page 14]
14 
 
Optiplex 7050) with TFT screens of 21.5”. Brightness and contrast of all screens was put at the same 
level (75%) before testing occurred and where necessary curtains were closed to avoid sun glare on 
the screens. Participants were instructed to take the tasks at their own tempo, that there were no 
right or wrong answers, and we were interested in their personal experience with the photographs. 
Participants took part in the fluency rating task, and another photography-related task with another 
set of photographs (not discussed here). The order of the two tasks was counterbalanced. In the end, 
participants received a short demographics questionnaire and answered a few open-ended questions 
regarding interactions with photographs.  
Stimulus Material. 154 artistic photographs from the Life Framer competition (described 
earlier).  
Fluency Rating. Participants were shown a random subset of 80 photographs (out of the 
larger set of 154) and rated the fluency of each photograph using one item “The process of studying 
this photograph is…” on a visual analog scale, ranging from 0 (difficult) to 100 (easy). Each 
photograph was rated by between 28 and 49 participants (M = 37.40; SD = 4.30).  
Results 
Difficult (Low Fluency) and Easy (High Fluency) to Process Artistic Photographs  
Participants varied in their average response time for making the fluency rating (range = 
1.66–11.01 seconds, M = 4.15 seconds, SD = 1.41 seconds). The full rating scale was used, with 
participants’ ratings varying between 0 (difficult to process) and 100 (easy to process). The average 
fluency rating (over participants and photographs) was 56.12 (SD = 21.54). Average fluency scores 
per photograph ranged between 30.66 and 79.35. Figure 2 shows the distribution of average fluency 
ratings for the set of 154 photographs.

First, in terms of subject matter, the majority of photographs in the high-fluency group 
showed one person, often photographed from the mid-waist upwards. Some of them are looking 
straight at the viewer (photographs 11,13,14,19,20) and some have an expressive face, but look 
somewhere to the side of the viewer (photographs 12,17,18). In the low-fluency group, most 
photographs also contain people, but they are not as prominent within the frame and are often 
combined with other visual elements. For example, photographs 3 and 8 are interior scenes which 
also contain many other objects; photographs 1, 2, 7 and 10 show exterior scenes where multiple 
dynamic events seem to be taking place; photographs 4 and 5 show an interaction between a human 
within a larger landscape setting; and photographs 6 and 9 are photographs of natural scenes 
without humans. 
Second, regarding medium-specific aspects, the photographs in the high-fluency group are all 
in portrait or square format, whereas there are more landscape-orientation photographs in the low-
fluency group. More photographs are made in studio settings with a uniform background and even 
lighting in the high-fluency group (photographs 11,12,13,16,17,18,20), compared to the low-fluency 
group. These photographs also show a higher contrast between the sharp main subject and the 
background. In the low-fluency group, we find more black-and-white photographs and more 
photographs where it is difficult to see everything clearly, because of blur (photograph 2) or darker 
and/or less contrasting scenes in terms of  luminance or colour (photographs 1,6,9). Furthermore, 
there are more peculiar light effects in the low-fluency group (e.g., the contrasting light stripe in 
photograph 10; the light blurred area in photograph 2; the shades of light in the upper left corner of 
photograph 3).  

[Page 17]

Third, in terms of form, the low-fluency group shows photographs with higher complexity, 
because there are more visual elements within the frame. There are also photographs that play with 
frames within frames (e.g., photographs 4,7); with figure-ground ambiguity, because the person 
seems to disappear within the interior (photograph 8) or exterior (photograph 5) scene. In general, 
photographs in the low-fluency group seem to make the eye wander around, because of different 
lines, angles, frames, planes and visual elements. Photographs in the high-fluency group are much 
more focused on one specific main subject (the person or owl) who fills up most of the frame and 
where the head of the person is often positioned somewhere central in the upper half of the frame.

Discussion 
We examined perceived fluency ratings for a set of 154 high-quality artistic photographs and 
visually observed the differences between low- and high-fluent photographs, as well as the 
relationship between perceived fluency and the proposed fluency-based image features (simplicity, 
contrast, self-similarity, symmetry).  
Overall, our visual observations show that there is not one particular photographic 
characteristic that determines processing fluency, but rather a combination of different aspects. For 
example, many of the highest rated photographs for fluency showed one person from the waist-up 
with a rather expressive face (subject matter), photographed in colour, portrait orientation, sharp 
and with even lighting against a uniform background (medium) with little other visual information 
and with the face somewhere rather central, but above the mid-line of the frame (form). Many of the 

[Page 20]
20 
 
lowest rated photographs also included people, but surrounded by many other visual objects in an 
interior or exterior scene (subject matter), photographed relatively more in black-and-white in 
unique lighting conditions and less visual clarity because of these conditions or because of blur 
(medium) and introduce more complexity, because of more ambiguous foreground/background 
separation, frames within frames, many visual elements, or angles and shapes guiding the eye 
towards different aspects in the photograph (form).  
The idea that all these elements are working together to create a fluent or disfluent content 
of the photograph explains why it is difficult to find clear predictors of fluency in terms of overall 
calculated low-level visual properties. In fact, only vertical symmetry (out of the four proposed 
fluency-based visual antecedents; Mayer & Landwehr, 2018) showed a (positive) correlation to the 
perceived fluency ratings. This finding can be related to the fact that many of the high fluent 
photographs were portraits against a uniform background. 
Generally, the fact that our set of photographs, explicitly selected by experts for their artistic 
and aesthetic quality, show a variation in perceived fluency also gives an indication that a 
straightforward linear relationship between fluency and aesthetic preference will probably not be 
able to fully explain our aesthetic experiences. In the next study, we further examine the relationship 
between fluency and aesthetic experience with the more nuanced PIA model.  
Study 2 
This study examines how processing fluency (low-medium-high) and processing style 
(automatic vs. controlled) predicted pleasure, interest and attractiveness ratings of the artistic 
photographs. The study builds upon the theoretical PIA model and empirical set-up by Graf and 
Landwehr (2015, 2017).  
Method 

[Page 21]
21 
 
Participants 
187 psychology students between 17 and 24 years (162 women, 25 men, Mage = 18.46 years, 
SDage = 0.96 years) participated in this experiment. Participants had not taken part in Study 1.They 
can be described as interested novices in the field of artistic photography. Most of them did not 
receive any art education (n = 172, 91.98%), owns none (50.27%) or one (42.25%) photography book. 
The majority rarely visit a photography gallery/exhibition/museum (20.32% never; 42.25% less than 
once a year; 21.39% once a year; 14.44% two or three times a year; 1.60% often). They are somewhat 
interested in photography (M = 3.66, SD = 1.02) on a scale from 1 (not at all) to 5 (definitely).  
Measures and Procedure 
Participants were tested in similar conditions as in Study 1, but performed a different set of 
tasks. They took part in the current fluency experiment, followed by three other tasks with different 
sets of photographs (not discussed here). Finally, they filled out a demographics questionnaire and 
answered a few additional questions regarding interactions with photographs.  
Stimulus Material. Based on the fluency ratings (average and spread)4, nine photographs 
were selected for the experimental procedure. Three photographs with low average fluency ratings 
(M = 33.39; SD = 0.65), three photographs with medium average fluency ratings (M = 57.90; SD = 
0.20) and three photographs with high average fluency ratings (M = 78.03; SD = 1.51) (Figure 4)5.

metadata.core_insight_en: This study explored the relationship between processing fluency and aesthetic responses to artistic photographs. The researchers found that high fluency photographs were initially found most pleasant in an automatic condition, but in a controlled condition, low fluency photographs were found more pleasant. Interest showed the highest ratings for low fluency photographs across all conditions, and exploring further, medium levels of fluency showed the highest interest ratings. text:
Fluency experiment. A 3 (fluency level: low/medium/high) by 2 (processing style: 
automatic/controlled processing) by 2 (aesthetic rating: pleasure/interest) mixed design was used 
(similar to Graf & Landwehr, 2017, Study 1). Fluency level serves as a within-subject factor and the 
processing style and aesthetic rating as between-subject factors. Participants were semi-randomly 
allocated to the four between-subject conditions based on the computer they decided to sit at during 
the session. There were 46 (controlled-interest) or 47 participants each (automatic-interest, 
automatic-pleasure and controlled-pleasure respectively) per condition. Participants went through 
the following phases in the experiment. Photographs were always presented in a random order. 
1) Subjective baseline fluency: Participants rated the fluency for each photograph on a visual 
analog scale with the item “The process of studying this photograph is…” ranging from 0 (difficult) to 
100 (easy).  
2) Processing style manipulation and aesthetic rating: Participants in the automatic 
processing condition were asked to give their aesthetic ratings of either pleasure on a visual analog 
scale ranging from 0 (displeasing) to 100 (pleasing) or interest on a scale ranging from 0 
(uninteresting) to 100 (interesting). Participants in the controlled processing condition were first 
asked to focus on the photograph intently and to write down an appropriate title, followed by the 
aesthetic rating (pleasure or interest).  

[Page 24]
24 
 
3) Manipulation check: Participants answered the following three items to examine how 
much cognitive elaboration they engaged in: “How thoroughly and intensively did you 
contemplate/think about the photos/engage yourself with the pictures before you evaluated them?’. 
All were rated on a 7-point scale ranging from  1 (not at all thoroughly and intensively) to 7 (very 
thoroughly and intensively).  
4) Post-processing fluency: Participants rated the photograph fluency again, based on their 
current gut feeling of fluency, using the same scale as in phase 1.  
5) Attractiveness rating: In the last phase, participants saw all photographs a final time and 
gave a general evaluation of the pictures, taking into account their general feelings, thoughts and 
impressions of the photograph, on a scale from 0 (unattractive) to 100 (attractive).  
Adaptations to the Design by Graf and Landwehr (2017). In line with the results of a recent 
factor analysis by the same authors (Graf et al., 2018), we use only one item of fluency (as opposed 
to three). Second, we also use only one item for pleasure, and one for interest. This was done 
because the Dutch translations of original items were very similar, and it simplified the procedure for 
participants. Third, and in line with the second experiment by Graf and Landwehr (2017, Study 2), we 
added a final overall attractiveness rating. Fourth, our visual analog scales ranged from 0-100, 
whereas closer reading of Graf and Landwehr (2017) showed that their endpoints were 0-101. 
Results 
Pleasure 
Automatic vs. Controlled Processing. An average elaboration score was calculated per 
participant by averaging over the three elaboration items that served as a manipulation check. 
Participants in the controlled processing condition showed a higher average elaboration score (M = 
5.50, SD = 0.77) than participants in the automatic processing condition (M = 4.72, SD = 0.99) 

[Page 25]
25 
 
(Welch’s Two-Samples t-test: t(86.51) = -4.30, p < 0.01), indicating that the instruction to give an       
appropriate title did induce more cognitive elaboration, as planned.  
Fluency Ratings for Different Fluency Levels. After averaging over photographs per fluency 
level, a repeated-measures ANOVA on the baseline fluency ratings showed that they differed 
significantly between the different fluency levels (F(1.79, 166.37) = 319.68, p < .001; Greenhouse-
Geisser Ɛ = 0.89, ηp2 = .77). LSD post-hoc contrasts revealed that all three levels differed significantly 
from each other in the expected directions, with low-fluency set (M = 31.51, SD = 13.18) rated lower 
than the medium-fluency photographs (M = 58.14, SD = 14.76; t(186) = -15.10, p < .001), which in 
turn were rated lower than the high-fluency set (M = 75.78, SD = 15.64; t(186) = -10.01, p < .001) (see 
Figure 5A), indicating that the subjective baseline fluency is robust between groups of participants 
(this group of participants vs. those in the first procedure to select the photographs).  
Processing Fluency, Processing Style and Pleasure. After averaging over photographs per 
fluency level, a mixed-ANOVA on the pleasure ratings with fluency level as a within-subject factor 
and processing style as between-subject factor showed a significant interaction effect (F(1.69, 
155.32) = 3.95, p < .05, Greenhouse-Geisser Ɛ = 0.84, ηp2 = .03). Figure 5B visualizes this interaction: 
In the automatic condition, average pleasure rating was highest for the high-fluency images, whereas 
participants in the controlled condition assigned the highest average pleasure ratings to the low-
fluency photographs. 
It was expected that this influence of stimulus fluency on pleasure is mediated through a 
subjective experience of fluency in the viewer and moderated by the type of processing. Therefore, a 
moderated mediation analyses was performed using Linear Mixed Models (LMM) with the lme() 
function of the nlme library in R (Pinheiro et al., 2019). To prepare for these analyses, fluency and 
pleasure ratings were standardized and processing style (automatic = 0, controlled = 1) and fluency 
level (low = -1, medium = 0, high = 1) were dummy-coded. Ratings for all nine photographs separately 

[Page 26]
26 
 
were used for these analyses (so no averaging over photographs per fluency level as in the previous 
analyses). Figure 5C shows the results of this analysis. The same visualization is used as in Graf and 
Landwehr (2017) with only significant paths shown, and paths that are not of primary conceptual 
interest shown as dashed lines.6 However, we did not find the expected moderated mediation effect. 
When taking into account subjective baseline fluency, the relation between fluency and pleasure 
became non-significant (indicative of a possible mediation), but subjective baseline fluency in itself 
did not significantly predict pleasure, thus strictly there was no mediation effect. Moreover, 
processing style did not show any moderating effect after taking into account subjective baseline 
fluency.

Automatic vs. Controlled Processing. Similar to the results for pleasure, participants in the

automatic condition (M = 4.67, SD = 0.95) (Welch’s Two-Samples t-test: t(89.804) = -5.16, p <.001).  
Fluency Ratings for Different Fluency Levels. Again, the subjective baseline fluency scores for 
the three selected fluency levels (averaged over photographs per fluency level) were compared using 
a repeated measures ANOVA. The general difference was significant (F(1.67,153.88) = 267.84, p < 
.001, Greenhouse-Geisser Ɛ = 0.84 , ηp2 = .74) as were the post-hoc LSD comparisons between 
specific levels. This was in the predicted directions, with low-fluency set (M = 31.56, SD = 14.71) rated 
lower than the medium-fluency photographs (M = 57.28, SD = 15.22; t(184) = -13.56, p < .001), which 
in turn were rated lower than the high-fluency set (M = 75.24, SD = 14.32; t(184) = -9.47, p < .001). 
Disfluency Reduction. Next, we explored whether there was a difference in average fluency 
change scores (change between post-processing fluency and subjective baseline fluency, thus 
disfluency reduction) using the averages over photographs per fluency level in a mixed-ANOVA with 
fluency level as within-subject factor and processing style as between-subject factor. Results showed 
a significant main effect of processing style (F(1, 91) = 6.36, p < .05, ηp2 = .07) and a significant main 
effect of fluency level (F(1.80, 164.03) = 17.48, p < .001; Greenhouse-Geisser Ɛ = 0.90, ηp2 = .16). 
Figure 6A shows that there is more disfluency reduction for photographs with lower fluency levels. 
Moreover, participants in the controlled condition showed higher levels of disfluency reduction (low-

controlled: M = 15.19, SD = 17.39; low-automatic: M = 8.50, SD = 14.99; medium-controlled: M = 
8.28, SD = 16.14; medium-automatic: M =  1.09, SD = 10.65; high-controlled: M = 3.74, SD = 12.47; 
high-automatic: M = 1.40, SD = 9.52).  
Processing Fluency, Processing Style and Interest. After averaging over photographs per 
fluency level, a mixed-ANOVA on the interest ratings with fluency level and processing style as 
predictors shows a significant main effect of fluency level (F(1.57, 142.48) = 112.74, p < .001, 
Greenhouse-Geisser Ɛ = .78, ηp2 = .55). Figure 6B visualizes that the highest interest levels are found 
for the low-fluency images, irrespective of processing style. This is what would be expected based on 
the PIA model for the controlled condition, but not for the automatic condition. It was hypothesized 
that this negative relation between stimulus fluency and interest would be based on an increase in 
fluency as people spent their time deliberately processing the photograph.  
However, the moderated mediation analysis (using the same LMM approach as outlined 
above, using data for all nine photographs) with fluency change as the mediator between stimulus 
fluency and interest, and processing style as moderator, is not in line with these predictions.7 In fact, 
Figure 6C shows that the relationship between fluency and interest stays similar when including 
fluency change into the model (so no mediation), and the relationship between fluency change and 
interest goes in a different direction than expected (more fluency change is less interest). However, 
processing style does seem to relate to more fluency change (as expected) and it seems to affect the 
relationship between fluency change and interest, so that the negative effect gets cancelled out 
(meaning fluency change does not negatively affect interest anymore, but instead shows a very 
minimal positive effect).

Title Type, Fluency Change and Interest. Previous studies have examined how adding a 
descriptive versus elaborate title to a painting/photograph for the aesthetic experience  influenced 
elaboration, meaning-making and aesthetic appreciation (Leder et al., 2006; Millis, 2001). Here, we 
report a short follow-up of the controlled processing condition to examine whether the type of title 
(descriptive vs. elaborate) gives insight in the amount of cognitive effort participants put into 
processing the photograph, and whether this relates to disfluency reduction and interest ratings. 
Inspired by definitions from previous studies (Leder et al., 2006; Millis, 2001) and adapted for our set 
of photographs, we used the following definitions: Descriptive titles are those titles where a viewer 
has tried to – partly or fully – describe the subject matter that is seen in the photograph, or where 
he/she made a very obvious association to the photo (e.g., an obvious broader theme); or where 
he/she is referring to the colour, style or another visual characteristic of the photograph. Elaborate 
titles are those titles where the viewer is using a metaphor, interpretation, explanation or evaluation 
of (the meaning of) the photograph; or where he/she used creativity to come up with an original title 
that goes beyond solely describing the photograph (e.g., a less obvious association or a more abstract 
theme that could have been depicted in a very different way too).  
414 titles (46 participants; 9 photographs) were categorized by the two main researchers into 
descriptive versus elaborate, resulting in interrater agreement of 82.37%. In order to solve the 

[Page 32]
32 
 
disagreement for the remaining titles, a third independent observer (familiar with photography) was 
asked to categorize the titles, and the remaining titles were organized based on the majority of two 
out of the three raters. The translated titles and their categorization can be found in Supplementary 
Table S3. There were differences in the amount of descriptive versus elaborate titles for the three 
fluency levels. Participants were more likely to give elaborate titles for the low fluency (elaborate: n = 
88; descriptive: n = 50) and medium fluency (elaborate: n = 80; descriptive: n = 58) photographs; but 
more likely to give a descriptive title for the high fluency photographs (elaborate: n = 51; descriptive: 
n = 87).  
Figure 7 shows the average fluency change (Fig 7A) and interest ratings (Fig 7B) per fluency 
level and title type. An ANOVA with fluency change as dependent variable, and title type, fluency 
level and their interaction as predictors revealed a main effect of title type  (F(1,408) = 8.78, p < .01) 
and a main effect of fluency level (F(2,408) = 8.171, p < .001), but no significant interaction (F(2,408) 
= 1.44, p =.24). An ANOVA with interest as dependent variable, and title type, fluency level and their 
interaction as predictors showed a main effect of title type (F(1,408) = 19.36, p < .001) and fluency 
level (F(2,408) = 48.26, p < .001), but no significant interaction (F(2,408) = 0.30, p = .74).

Attractiveness 
Finally, a moderated mediation analysis (using the same LMM approach as above, using data 
for all nine photographs) was done on the final attractiveness score as the outcome, using aesthetic 
rating (pleasure or interest) as mediating variable and processing style as moderating variable in the 
relationship between stimulus fluency and attractiveness. Analyses were done for the two aesthetic 
ratings separately, but Figure 8 shows the results together to be able to compare them8. The results 
show that the relationship between stimulus fluency and attractiveness is mediated through the

Discussion 
This study examined Graf and Landwehr’s (2015) PIA model for the medium of artistic 
photography, using a similar empirical design as Graf and Landwehr (2017). Three low-, three 
medium- and three high-fluent photographs were selected; and processing style was manipulated by 
letting people give their aesthetic ratings based on their gut-feeling in one condition (automatic 
processing) versus first letting them focus intently on the photographs and figuring out an 
appropriate title in another condition (controlled processing).  
Generally, our results are in line with two routes between stimulus fluency and overall 
attractiveness, one mediated by pleasure, the other by interest. The mediated pathway through 
pleasure resulted in a positive relation with attractiveness, whereas the one by interest resulted in a 
negative relation with attractiveness. Furthermore, the photographs that were highly fluent showed 
the highest pleasure ratings in the automatic conditions, whereas the low fluent photographs 
showed the highest pleasure ratings in the controlled condition. These findings are in line with the 
PIA hypotheses.  
Yet, not all results were consistent with the hypothesized processes. First, against the 
expectation derived from the PIA model, the relationship between photograph fluency and pleasure 
was not mediated by subjective baseline fluency. Second, the photographs that were least fluent 
showed the highest interest ratings in both conditions. This was expected for the controlled 
condition, but not for the automatic condition. 
It is therefore worthwhile to further explore the manipulation for controlled processing in 
our design. Participants in the controlled condition showed higher levels of cognitive elaboration, 

[Page 37]
37 
 
and also more fluency change than people in the automatic condition, which is what was expected. 
Interestingly, a further exploration of the titles that participants in the controlled-interest condition 
provided resulted in a few additional insights on the cognitive process: First, the fluency level of the 
photographs seemed to trigger different ratios of descriptive versus elaborate titles, indicating that 
disfluency can spark more elaboration (or creative elaborate titles) of photographs as compared with 
very high fluent photographs. Second, when elaborate titles were given, fluency changes were also 
larger, indicating that the elaborative process helped in reducing disfluency. Third, the interest 
patterns were still mainly explained by the fluency level of the photographs, rather than the 
descriptive/elaborate titles (although there was a significant, but rather small difference between 
descriptive and elaborative titles). This is largely in line with the differences we found for the 
difference between automatic and controlled processing. Thus, there is an interesting interaction 
between fluency level of the photographs, how much cognitive effort is triggered by the photograph 
(number of descriptive vs. elaborate titles) and how much cognitive effort the participant engages, 
which determines how the photograph is processed and how much disfluency will be reduced. Yet, 
the most clear effect on interest was still the difference between fluency levels (irrespective of 
condition or title type). However, the current experiment was performed with only 9 photographs 
(similar to Graf & Landwehr, 2017), which makes it difficult to tease apart idiosyncratic photograph 
preferences from general processing fluency influences. In Study 3, we therefore examine the 
relationship between perceived fluency and interest for three larger sets of photographs (differing in 
how homogeneous/heterogeneous they are for particular subject matter themes) to examine how 
robust this relationship is.  
Study 3 
In this study, we further explore the relationship between perceived fluency and interest for 
three larger sets of artistic photographs (heterogeneous vs. homogeneous in subject matter). The 

[Page 38]
38 
 
study is a post-hoc exploration that combines previously collected fluency averages (Study 1) with 
interest percentages calculated from data collected as part of another project. 
Method 
Participants 
309 undergraduate students enrolled in an introductory psychology course participated in 
exchange for course credit. Date from 18 participants were removed because they did not complete 
the survey or because Dutch was not their native language. Among the 291 remaining participants 63 
identified as male (21.65%), 227 as female (78.01%), and 1 did not identify as male or female (.34%). 
Their age ranged between 17 and 49 years with a mean of 18.83 (SD = 2.11).  
Measures and Procedure 
Stimulus Material. In total, data was available for ten sets of photographs, from which three 
sets are relevant for the current purposes, because they consist of Life Framer photographs for which 
we had fluency ratings available (from Study 1). There were two sets that were selected to be more 
homogeneous in subject matter, because they were based on specific themes: Urban Life and Faces 
of Life. Of the two, the Faces of Life category is the most homogeneous in terms of subject matter. 
For the current purposes, we select only the 15 photographs per set for which we have average 
fluency ratings available. Furthermore, there was a heterogeneous set that includes two photographs 
per theme that varied in fluency (by choosing, where possible, a low and a high fluent photograph9). 
For the present purposes, we removed the photographs from the Faces of Life and Urban Life 
                                                            
9 This depended on copyright permissions, the available fluency averages and excluding the selected 
photographs from Study 2. 

[Page 39]
39 
 
themes, to avoid overlap between the three sets, resulting in 18 photographs in total (8 content 
themes + 1 open call).  
Procedure. The survey was implemented in Qualtrics (www.qualtrics.com) and participants 
accessed it through an anonymous survey link on their home computer. After providing informed 
consent, participants answered some questions regarding demographics, art expertise and a 
personality inventory. After completing this, participants were randomly assigned to one of two 
alternative versions of the survey, each consisting of five out of the ten available photography sets. 
Half of the participants (n = 145) were randomly assigned the first version (among which the Faces of 
Life set); the other half (n = 146) was assigned the second version (among which both the Urban Life 
set and the heterogeneous set). The presentation order of photographs within sets was randomized 
for every participant. Photographs were presented individually in the center of the screen against a 
white background with the question and answer alternatives positioned beneath them. Participants 
were presented with the respective five sets of photographs twice. On the first presentation of the 
photographs, participants were requested to indicate whether they found the photographs beautiful 
or not (yes/no). Once they had judged the photographs from all sets in terms of beauty, the 
participants were presented with the photographs once more and requested to indicate whether 
they found the photographs interesting or not (yes/no). In this study, we focus only on the interest 
data. 
Results  
Relationship Average Fluency and Percentage Interesting in Three Subsets 
For each photograph, the interest score was defined as the percentage of participants that 
indicated they found the photograph interesting.

Fluency and Interest in Artistic Portrait Photography 
In this section, we explore photographs from the Faces of Life set (Fig. 10), where 
photographers were asked to show us faces – individuals or groups, the iconic or the unknown – that

Discussion 
This study examined the relationship between fluency and interest in three sets of 
photographs: a heterogeneous set of photographs with different themes; a (medium) homogeneous 
set from the Urban Life theme and a homogeneous set from the Faces of Life theme. Whereas Study 
2 showed a negative relation between fluency and interest with the highest interest ratings for the 
most disfluent photographs (averages between 32.64 and 33.80), the present findings are in line with 
an inverted U-shape pattern, with the highest interest percentages for medium fluency photographs, 
lying slightly on the easy to process side of the scale, but still relatively close to the mid-point 
(somewhere between 50-60 on a scale from 0 to 100). This inverted U-shaped pattern was a better 
fit for the data than the linear model for all three photography sets. 
We examined the Faces of Life photographs in further detail, as they are the most 
homogeneous in terms of subject matter and are all relatively fluent to perceive. The largest drop in 

[Page 45]
45 
 
interest scores is seen for the three photographs with the highest perceived fluency. Interestingly, 
these photographs were all studio type portraits with a clear background, and are similar to two out 
of the three selected high fluency photographs for Study 2, where we also found the largest drop in 
interest ratings for these high fluency photographs. Thus, there might be something in this specific 
combination of subject matter (portrait with human face and shoulders against uniform background), 
medium-related visual aspects (sharpness, clearness, contrast) and form (person taking up most of 
the frame, and head relatively central  in the upper half of the photograph) that makes these 
photographs less interesting than others. When examining photographs with similar characteristics 
within the set, we indeed also find relatively lower interest ratings than for other photographs within 
the subset, irrespective of fluency ratings. It might be a combination between perceived fluency and 
familiarity with this type of photographic set-up that explains (low) interest percentages.   
General Discussion 
Photography is an omnipresent and unavoidable medium in our current society, yet we still 
know relatively little about how we process photographs and aesthetically respond to them. Within 
empirical aesthetics, processing fluency has been put forward as an important predictor of aesthetic 
response. However, there are different theoretical accounts on the nature of this relationship (e.g. 
positive relationship, Reber et al., 2004 vs. depending on processing style, Graf & Landwehr, 2015, 
2017). Furthermore, there is little in-depth research on this relationship for the medium of 
photography. In this study, we explored the relationship between processing fluency and aesthetic 
preferences of high-quality artistic contemporary photographs.  
Fluency of Artistic Photographs 
First, we examined which visual features related to the photographs’ perceived fluency 
ratings (Study 1). Visual comparison of the lowest- versus highest-rated photographs in terms of 
perceived fluency revealed differences in subject matter (e.g., portraits of one person that filled up 

[Page 46]
46 
 
most of the frame in the high-fluency group versus scenes with or without people in the low-fluency 
group), medium-related characteristics (e.g., more black-and-white and landscape format 
photographs in the low-fluency group) and form (e.g., more complexity and frames within frames in 
the low-fluency group). The combination of these characteristics made for a particular type of 
photograph that dominated the high-fluency group: colour photographs in portrait orientation of 
one person, often photographed from the mid-waist upwards, filling up most of the frame and with 
uniform lighting and a uniform background. In Study 3, we further explored whether these high 
fluency ratings were mainly related to the subject matter (human portraits) or to those other specific 
image characteristics, by visually examining the photographs for the Faces of Life theme. The subject 
matter might indeed partly explain why these photographs received high fluency ratings, with almost 
all of the Faces of Life photographs having medium to high fluency averages. Yet, there were still 
differences within this group in terms of processing fluency and observation showed similar trends to 
what we had noticed in the larger set (more black-and-white and landscape orientation in the lower-
fluency group). However, it also showed that very similar photographic constructions (portrait 
against uniform background) did not always result in similar fluency ratings, potentially because of 
added disfluency by other visual features (very high contrast, blur, emotional connotation).  
The fact that all the different layers of the photograph (subject matter, medium, form and 
certain connotations) interact with each other to produce a fluent or disfluent image might explain 
why perceived fluency was not easily captured by the four fluency-based image calculations (visual 
simplicity, symmetry, contrast and self-similarity) proposed by Mayer and Landwehr (2018). These 
authors already showed that there were differences in which proposed fluency-based image features 
predicted (indirect) aesthetic ratings for abstract images versus landscape photographs. In a set of 
abstract art images, all of these visual properties contributed independently to aesthetic liking (in 
descending order: self-similarity, contrast, symmetry and complexity). In a second study, with a more 

[Page 47]
47 
 
controlled set of abstract art stimuli, they replicated the positive effect of contrast and self-similarity, 
and the positive effect of complexity (thus negative effect of simplicity). However, in their set of 500 
landscape photographs from the Flickr.com website, they found that only self-similarity and 
simplicity significantly predicted the number of views (as an indirect measure of aesthetic 
preference), but including all four measures significantly improved the explained variance. It is not 
clear however, whether these features also related to perceived fluency (as this was not directly 
measured for that set of photographs). For our set of artistic photographs, only vertical symmetry 
related to perceived fluency ratings, which might be related to the predominance of portraits 
receiving higher fluency ratings.  
Interestingly, we observed a parallel between our findings and cutting-edge research on 
image memorability with Generative Adversarial Networks (GAN; Goodfellow et al., 2014). GANs 
have been used to generate natural-looking images with fine-grained details in their visual attributes, 
in order to manipulate and understand what features make an image more or less memorable 
(Goetschalckx, Andonian, Oliva, & Isola, 2019).

measured for that set of photographs). For our set of artistic photographs, only vertical symmetry 
related to perceived fluency ratings, which might be related to the predominance of portraits

have been used to generate natural-looking images with fine-grained details in their visual attributes, 
in order to manipulate and understand what features make an image more or less memorable 
(Goetschalckx, Andonian, Oliva, & Isola, 2019). The GANs seemed to manipulate memorability 
through a combination of features such as making the size of the object (or animal) larger within the 
frame, centering, simplifying (e.g., by reducing clutter and/or the number of objects or making the 
background more homogeneous) brighter and more colourful images (as well as striving for more 
circular or square shapes where appropriate; Goetschalckx et al., 2019). Moreover, visual 
examination of the images seemed to indicate a trend towards more pronounced and expressive 
eyes (of animals, as the GAN was not optimized for human features). These features seem to be 
similar to what we observed in the high-fluency photographs. As memory-based fluency is also 
considered as one of the instantiations of fluency that contributes to the general subjective 
experience of fluency (Alter & Oppenheimer, 2009), these findings can also be interpreted in terms 
of fluency. Future research could gain from combining knowledge based on ecologically valid 

[Page 48]
48 
 
explorations for a wide range of artistic photographs (the present study) with controlled experiments 
focused on specific image features that might be relevant (e.g., the role of colour in the aesthetic 
processing of photographs; Mullennix et al., 2016), machine learning studies with large sets of 
photograph, and GANS trained to generate images optimized for certain features (such as 
memorability or aesthetic qualities).  
Processing Fluency, Processing Style and Aesthetic Ratings (PIA model) 
We explored whether the relationship between fluency and aesthetics in our set could be 
described by Graf and Landwehr’s two routes to aesthetic liking in their PIA mode (Graf & Landwehr, 
2015). A first route relates high-fluent (easy-to-process) images/designs to aesthetic liking, because 
they induce pleasure when processed automatically. A second route shows that low-fluent (difficult-
to-process) images/designs can also lead to aesthetic liking, but through a process of disfluency 
reduction when they are cognitively elaborated upon (processed in a controlled fashion). 
Three low-, three medium- and three high-fluency photographs were selected to empirically 
examine how processing fluency and processing style (automatic vs. controlled) related to aesthetic 
preferences of pleasure, interest and attractiveness. Generally, we did find that pleasure and interest 
mediated two different routes between fluency and aesthetic attractiveness. Yet, we did not find all 
proposed mediations and processes of the PIA model. We found the expected interaction between 
fluency and processing style for pleasure ratings, specifically, highest pleasure for high fluency in 
automatic conditions, but for low fluency in controlled conditions (albeit rather small differences). 
However, we found no evidence for the proposed mediation through baseline fluency. Furthermore, 
there was no interaction between processing style and fluency for the interest ratings, even though 
participants in the controlled condition showed more disfluency reduction (especially when they had 
put in additional cognitive effort to come up with an elaborate title) than participants in the 
automatic condition.  

[Page 49]
49 
 
It is quite likely that the distinction between automatic and controlled processing was more a 
matter of amount of cognitive effort rather than a qualitatively different process, because in the 
automatic condition, participants had also already rated the photographs for fluency and were free 
to look at the photographs as long as they wanted. Yet, we would still expect that the quantitative 
differences in cognitive effort might have resulted in more pronounced changes in terms of interest 
(if the findings would follow the PIA model), but our findings showed that these cognitive processes 
were not particularly differentiating when it came to interest ratings. Interest ratings were similarly 
determined by fluency level in both processing style conditions and there were some interactions 
between fluency, disfluency reduction and processing style, but they did not mediate the strong 
negative relationship between fluency and interest. Another explanation might be that participants 
were not relying on cognitive processes to do the aesthetic rating task. This is in line with studies 
with artistic photographs that showed that cognitive load did not affect an aesthetic preference 
scaling task, suggesting that aesthetic processing of artistic photography is an automatic process 
(Mullennix et al., 2013, 2016).  
Interestingly, the negative relationship between fluency and interest (irrespective of 
processing style) was one of the most pronounced findings in our study, and is in contrast with the 
findings by Graf and Landwehr (2017) with abstract digital images. They found that there was not 
much variation in the total effect of stimulus fluency on interest, which was explained by two 
opposing processes that cancelled each other out (fluency change suppressed the relationship 
between stimulus fluency and interest). One reason for this difference could be the difference in 
images we used. Potentially, disfluency might be more aesthetically interesting for our set of (more 
representational) photography, compared to abstract digital artworks, because it is a type of 
disfluency that we can cope with better. Silvia (2010) proposes that interest is triggered by the most 
ideal combination between high novelty and high potential to understand, and our set of 

[Page 50]
50 
 
representational photographs might have a high potential to understand, which might increase our 
interest for more novel types of photographs. However, even in a set of semi-abstract artistic 
photographs with little recognizable subject matter, we found that there was a positive relationship 
between perceived complexity and interest (especially pronounced for a cluster of around  1/3th of 
the participants; Vissers, Moors, Genin, & Wagemans, 2020). In this study too, perceived complexity 
seemed to show a more interpretable relationship with interest ratings than pleasure or beauty 
ratings, indicating the importance of seeing aesthetic reactions as more than just beauty and 
pleasure, and taking into account that complexity or fluency related measures or manipulations in 
photographs might mainly affect interest in viewers. 
Fluency and Interest 
 The experimental paradigm that showed the highest interest ratings for the most disfluent 
photographs was based on only nine photographs (Study 2), so we also examined the fluency-
interest relationship in larger sets of photographs (Study 3). Here, we found that the relationship was 
best captured by an inverted U-shape pattern, with the highest interest percentages for photographs 
with a medium level of fluency.

The studies indicate that investigating processing fluency's relationship to aesthetic impressions can be a promising but complex avenue.
