1 Introduction
Interactive products help users in completing tasks. The interaction between the 
user and such products is through a user interface (UI) that allows users to touch 
pads, press buttons, or turn knobs on a control panel to cause various actions to 
transpire. In turn, the products indicate their status, inform users about possible 
actions, and ask for further input, usually through displays. Common examples of 
these products are household appliances, TVs, and smart phone applications.
Marketing research has identified the role of packaging design at the point of 
purchase as the most important vehicle of communication of product quality to 
potential consumers (e.g., Garaus and Halkias 
2019). However, because the core 
of interactive products is often software-based, the packaging of these products 
may not serve users in their evaluations. Instead, the visual design of the prod -
ucts, especially their UI, may serve as the vehicle to communicate product qual -
ity (Eytam et al. 
2017). Similar to how aspects of package design such as color, 
shape, and texture influence consumer preferences (Garaus and Halkias 2019), 
product UIs help users to determine the quality of the technology embedded in a 
product and how to use it (Norman 
2004). The design of the UI communicates, or 
“signifies” (Norman 2008), pre-purchase information about the product to poten -
tial users.
The number of elements included in a product’s UI is an important signifier 
of its complexity (e.g., Mollerup 2007, 2015), which we propose has a major 
influence on how users perceive that product (e.g., Eytam et al. 2017; Tuch et al. 
2012; Reinecke et al. 2013). This is the reason that experts often advocate sim -
plicity in interactive product designs. They suggest that visual simplicity eases 
cognitive load and improves processing fluency due to our limited information 
processing resources (Zhao and Meyer 
2007). Complex designs, on the other 
hand, confront the customer with excessive information, decreasing processing 
efficiency (Fukuda and Vogel 
2009; Mazzoni et  al. 2014). However, anecdo -
tal evidence suggests that people may, in fact, prefer designs that appear more 
complex (e.g., Norman 
2007). For example, in the online marketplace, since the 
results list in search engine advertising shows product pictures, many marketers 
actually include additional information, adding complexity to appeal to potential 
consumers (Wu et al. 
2016).
This discrepancy between experts’ views on simplicity and people’s actual 
choices in the market place is referred to as the paradox of simplicity  (Eytam 
et al. 2017). Resolving this paradox is important to control for what appears to 
be a complexity crisis  (Mariotti 2007), that causes feature fatigue and decreases 
consumer satisfaction over time (Thompson et al. 2005). In this paper, we sug -
gest that the consideration of individual differences may help resolve the para -
dox of simplicity because while some individuals look for simple product designs 
that are easy to use, others may prefer complex ones because they are more 
stimulating.
McFadden (
1974, 2001) suggests that expressed preferences of people are 
functions of their taste, experience, and personal characteristics. Friedmann and

1 3

Lowengart (
2013) explain that including personal characteristics in the analy -
sis of purchase considerations allows marketers to tailor their efforts to better 
address different consumers’ needs. For example, gender differences influence the 
weight of acquisition utility and identity consumption in forming purchase inten -
tions (Friedmann and Lowengart 
2013) and preferences of visual design (Cyr and 
Bonanni 2005). Chen and Chan ( 2011) suggest that including age differences in 
the analysis of interactive product acceptance provides a powerful explanation of 
the perception and usage of such products. Similarly, perceptions of complexity 
(or simplicity) are affected by personal characteristics (e.g., Reinecke et al. 
2013).
While researchers acknowledge the important effect of individual differences on 
post-adoption belief behaviors (e.g., Tams et al. 2017), less attention has been ded -
icated to these differences in pre-use product evaluations. Pre-use evaluations are 
often a necessity as the rapid technological pace of producing novel products contin-
ues. Consumers browse a product on the internet or see it in a shop, but they rarely 
have a chance to test it before deciding whether to purchase it. Consequently, the UI 
becomes a major source of information about a product. Perceptions of complexity 
(or simplicity) may be used as a cue for product evaluation in situations where there 
is no direct interaction with a product before it is purchased.

Similarly, perceptions of complexity 
(or simplicity) are affected by personal characteristics (e.g., Reinecke et al. 
2013).
While researchers acknowledge the important effect of individual differences on 
post-adoption belief behaviors (e.g., Tams et al. 2017), less attention has been ded -
icated to these differences in pre-use product evaluations. Pre-use evaluations are 
often a necessity as the rapid technological pace of producing novel products contin-
ues. Consumers browse a product on the internet or see it in a shop, but they rarely 
have a chance to test it before deciding whether to purchase it. Consequently, the UI 
becomes a major source of information about a product. Perceptions of complexity 
(or simplicity) may be used as a cue for product evaluation in situations where there 
is no direct interaction with a product before it is purchased.
In individual differences, we include demographic variables that are reported to 
influence design perception (e.g., Reinecke and Gajos 
2014), differences related to 
technological orientation and social-related factors (e.g., Thompson et al. 2006), and 
differences that influence decision making in general, such the maximization per -
sonality trait (Schwartz et al. 2002). We suggest that individuals form preferences 
(McFadden 1986) regarding the acquisition of interactive products by evaluating 
their visual design. Given the inability to experience interactive products before pur-
chase, product evaluation is based largely on how the user perceives various aspects 
of the product’s visual design.
We organize this work as follows: First, we explore the theoretical background of 
the concepts used in this research and suggest how individual differences influence 
preference formation. We then propose a model to explain how these differences 
influence the evaluation process of interactive products. Next, we describe the study 
methodology. Section 
5 reports the results of the study, and Sect.  6 its findings. Sec-
tion  7 discusses its managerial implications, and Sect.  8 details research limitations 
and suggests directions for future research.
2  Theoretical background
Visual Simplicity Level (VSL) is a potent design element. It refers to the visual 
complexity or simplicity of a design and is often measured by a simple count of 
the number of design elements. VSL may be depicted as a continuum with design 
simplicity at one end and complexity at the other end. It was found to influence first 
impressions, emotions, and aesthetic preferences (see Jang et  al. 
2018). Although 
researchers have not reached consensus on how to measure the VSL of an interactive 
product (Wu et al. 
2016), it is generally defined not only by the number of elements 
presented, but also by the visual diversity or information rate of the visual stimuli 

[Page 4]
1350 E. Eytam et al.
1 3
(Deng and Poole 2010). Nadkarni and Gupta ( 2007) argue that VSL is an example 
of a design element individuals analyze based on personal perspective, and they dif-
ferentiate between objective and perceived VSL. Thus, in order to understand how 
this perception is formed, there is a need to go beyond an objective analysis and con-
sider the subjective impression products make on potential consumers.
In addition to pragmatic usage (Hassenzahl 
2004), the subjective perception of a 
design is especially important when goods such as interactive products (e.g., Mahlke 
et al. 
2007; Tractinsky and Zmiri 2006) are intended to fulfill hedonic motivations 
(McFadden 1974, 2001). This differentiation between objective complexity and its 
subjective interpretation corresponds to Norman’s ( 2010) differentiation between 
the terms complex and complicated. Norman suggests that whereas the term “com -
plex” describes a state of the world, the term “complicated” describes a state of 
mind. This approach hints at the importance of the perspective beholders have when 
evaluating VSL.
Some studies have explored the effect of VSL on consumer response to virtual 
store designs (Jang et al. 
2018). From such studies, we can draw similarities to the 
potential effect of simplicity or complexity on response to interactive products. In 
both cases, consumers rely on visual design to infer about the store (e.g., Jang et al. 
2018; Porat and Tractinsky 2012) or product (e.g., Eytam et  al. 2017; Thompson 
et al. 2005). Jang et al. ( 2018) suggest that consumers’ involvement with the type 
of products should be considered when studying VSL effects. Eytam et al. ( 2017) 
explain that perceived VSL is concluded from analyzing the design from either a 
structural or behavioral perspective. Both perspectives rely on analyzing the number 
of controls—components that allow a user to interact with the products (e.g., push 
buttons, keyboard keys, and sliders)—included in the product’s design. Relying on a 
structural perspective, perceived VSL is concluded from a simple count of the num -
ber of these features in the design. From a behavioral perspective, it is judged by 
mapping actions to the controls. Because the form of analysis depends on a personal 
perspective, different individuals may conclude different qualities from similar prod-
uct designs.
Therefore, a possible resolution to the paradox of simplicity lies in individual dif-
ferences (heterogeneity). For example, while some individuals are attracted by tech-
nological products, especially when these products are innovative, others may be 
reticent about using them (Thompson et al. 
2006). Thus, although a complex prod -
uct design can be perceived as difficult to use by some individuals because there are 
too many controls, others, who are more technology-oriented, may perceive it differ-
ently because, according to their perspective, the many controls are mapped to many 
actions, and the product is thus easier to use, as suggested by Norman (
1988). The 
next section discusses this issue in more detail.
Dillon and Watson ( 1996) argue that individual differences are stable character -
istics that influence interaction with technology. These differences affect the percep-
tion of product qualities and personal tastes. Some individuals are motivated to learn 
new skills and may not appreciate instructions that are too explicit because they 
prefer to figure things out themselves, and can even become annoyed if given help 
(Mun et al. 
2006). Others, who tend to seek support in task completion, may appre -
ciate a “Help” feature (Nurkka 2008). While some individuals pay more attention to

pragmatic uses, others stress hedonic considerations (e.g., Ahmad 
2012). Some indi-
viduals appreciate ease of use, whereas others choose greater functionality even at 
the cost of more complicated use (e.g., Thompson et al. 
2006). Below, we elaborate 
on individual differences and their effects on the evaluation process of interactive 
products.
3  Establishing the research model
VSL affects the perception of major product qualities (i.e., ease of use, functionality, 
and aesthetics) (Eytam et al. 
2017). Our model suggests that individual differences 
play a major role in evaluating product design in two manners. First, these differ -
ences influence subjective judgments of product qualities concluded from a design’s 
VSL.  Second, the differences influence the  weight  assigned to each  of the major 
product qualities when forming preference to a product.

Some indi-
viduals appreciate ease of use, whereas others choose greater functionality even at 
the cost of more complicated use (e.g., Thompson et al. 
2006). Below, we elaborate 
on individual differences and their effects on the evaluation process of interactive 
products.
3  Establishing the research model
VSL affects the perception of major product qualities (i.e., ease of use, functionality, 
and aesthetics) (Eytam et al. 
2017). Our model suggests that individual differences 
play a major role in evaluating product design in two manners. First, these differ -
ences influence subjective judgments of product qualities concluded from a design’s 
VSL.  Second, the differences influence the  weight  assigned to each  of the major 
product qualities when forming preference to a product.
In order to identify potential traits that may influence the evaluation of interac -
tive products, we reviewed the literature for relevant trait-related and demographic 
variables. We conducted a preliminary pilot experiment interviewing 16 respondents 
(median age: 35 years old; age range: 5–70; 56% female) who volunteered to take 
part in the study. In semi-structured interviews, respondents were asked to rate seven 
general control panels and to explain what they liked and disliked about each. Then 
they were asked about their general evaluation strategy for interactive products and 
about their attitudes towards technology. Following these two phases, we selected 
two demographic variables (age and gender) and five personality traits as measures 
in the study, detailed in the following subsections.
3.1  Age
Age was widely studied in relation to the technology acceptance model (TAM; see 
Chen and Chan 
2011). The literature generally reports that older respondents com -
pared to younger ones are more concerned about ease of use because they often find 
technology confusing (McCloskey 
2006). Thus, older consumers are likely to accept 
easy-to-use technologies with simple interfaces (Mitzner et  al. 2010) because of 
their lower technological self-efficacy and higher degree of anxiety about technol -
ogy (Laguna and Babcock 2000; see Chen and Chan 2011). Age is often used as 
a proxy for consumers’ level of perceived behavioral control and habits. Because 
habits usually become more ingrained with age, and routines are difficult to change 
(Burton-Jones and Hubona 
2006), older adults are reported to have positive attitudes 
towards technology mainly when it supports activities and enhances convenience 
(Conci et al. 
2009). Another explanation for the differences in perceptions of tech -
nology could be the mediating effect of efficacy that varies with age (Tams et al. 
2017).
Morris and Venkatesh (2000) explain that while young consumers have grown up 
with technology and learned to rely on it, older adults have had less experience with 
it, which makes them often look for traditional, easy-to-use solutions. Ahmad (
2012)

1 3

ease of use (Venkatesh and Morris 
2000). These pre-dispositions could hint at 
their tendency to favor simple designs (Hsiu-Feng 2013). Still, empirically, the 
effect of gender on VSL preferences is inconsistent. While Reinecke et al. ( 2013) 
reported no significant interaction effect between gender and VSL, Reinecke and 
Gajos (
2014) found that females compared to males dislike websites with low 
VSL.
Because of the above tendencies, we expect women to prefer simpler designs 
that are considered easier to use (Thompson et al. 2005), and to consider all qual -
ities as important. On the other hand, men, who are reported to be more strongly 
influenced by perceptions of functionality (Venkatesh and Morris 
2000; Eytam 
et al. 2017), are expected to emphasize these considerations.
H2a: The proportion of respondents preferring simple designs is significantly 
higher among women than among men.
H2b: Women evaluate product design through three main  qualities (namely, 
ease of use, functionality, and aesthetics).
H2c: Men evaluate product design only through functionality considerations.
3.3  Personal innovativeness in the domain of information technology (PIIT)
The diﬀusion of innovation theory  (Rogers 
2003) differentiates innovators from 
laggards. Innovators are individuals who are enthusiastic about new technologies 
even when these are complicated to use (Wu et al. 
2011), and usually score high 
on the innovativeness in information technology (PIIT) measure compared to oth -
ers (Agarwal and Prasad 1998). In contrast, laggards see a high risk in adopting 
new products, they are more skeptical of them, and usually score low on the PIIT 
measure. Innovators find the exploration of a system rewarding in itself (Lee et al. 
2007; Limayem et  al. 2000); however, laggards dislike change and accept new 
products only when forced to do so.
Venkatesh and Davis ( 1996) explain that the more people use technology, the 
easier they perceive it to use. The enthusiasm innovators have for technology 
causes them to seek out new forms of it, and allows them to increase their profi -
ciency with it (Thompson et al. 
2006). The more they use interactive products, the 
more user friendly these products seem to them. This can explain why previous 
research reports that high PIIT scores correlate with higher perceived ease-of-use 
judgments (Lewis et al. 
2003; Wu et al. 2011). Thompson et al. ( 2006) report that 
respondents who scored high on the PIIT scale had more positive judgments of 
ease of use, and explain that the more that people actively experiment with new 
technologies, the simpler they become to use because controls and functions tend 
to be similar across technological domains. We, therefore, expect high-PIIT indi -
viduals to rate product ease of use higher than low-PIIT individuals. Because they 
are more skeptical and cautious (Rogers 
2003), we expect low-PIIT individuals 
to employ more comprehensive evaluation strategies and to consider all product 
qualities important.

(both simple and complex) as high is higher among those with high-PIIT scores 
compared to those with low-PIIT scores.
H3b: Respondents low in PIIT evaluate product design through its three 
main qualities (namely, ease of use, functionality, and aesthetics).
H3c: Respondents high in PIIT consider fewer qualities in their evaluations com-
pared to their counterparts.
3.4  Internal computer self-efficacy (ICSE)
Self-efficacy influences behavior; it influences what individuals choose to perform, 
the amount of effort they are ready to exert, and the period they will endeavor to 
overcome obstacles (Bandura 
1986). Computer self-efficacy (CSE) is the belief one 
has in their ability to independently accomplish a task using computers (Compeau 
and Higgins 
1995), and this is expected to influence pragmatic judgments of interac-
tive products (e.g., Hasan 2007; Thompson et al. 2006).
Thus, self-efficacy has a key role in analyzing the perception of simplicity or 
complexity of interactive products.

3.4  Internal computer self-efficacy (ICSE)
Self-efficacy influences behavior; it influences what individuals choose to perform, 
the amount of effort they are ready to exert, and the period they will endeavor to 
overcome obstacles (Bandura 
1986). Computer self-efficacy (CSE) is the belief one 
has in their ability to independently accomplish a task using computers (Compeau 
and Higgins 
1995), and this is expected to influence pragmatic judgments of interac-
tive products (e.g., Hasan 2007; Thompson et al. 2006).
Thus, self-efficacy has a key role in analyzing the perception of simplicity or 
complexity of interactive products. Complex tasks can easily be achieved when sup-
ported by interactive products. Still, task completion can only happen if the con -
sumer understands how to operate the product. Individuals who doubt their ability to 
perform a task with the product at hand perceive the task as complex, whereas indi -
viduals with high confidence in their capabilities may view the same task as simple 
(Campbell 
1986; Hasan 2007).
Hasan ( 2006) distinguishes general from application CSE. While general CSE 
is trait-oriented, application CSE is a state-oriented efficacy applicable to specific 
tasks. Thatcher et al. (
2008) further suggest that general CSE has two dimensions: 
internal and external. While the external dimension focuses on how individuals per -
ceive their ability to use technology with assistance, the internal dimension (ICSE) 
focuses on how individuals perceive their own self-capacity to use technology inde -
pendently. Thatcher et al. (
2008) further explain that while individuals high in exter-
nal CSE feel less anxious because they trust that external support is available, a high 
level of ICSE lowers anxiety about using the computer because it implies that one 
has personal control over it. ICSE taps into individuals’ beliefs about their ability to 
independently accomplish computer-related tasks.
In general, CSE acts as a precursor to perceived ease of use because individuals 
who are confident in their ability to use specific technologies are likely to view them 
as easier to use compared to those who are less confident in that ability (Venkatesh 
and Davis 
1996). Thatcher et  al. ( 2008) specify that ICSE, but not external CSE, 
exerts this positive effect on perceived ease of use (see also Thompson et al. 2006) 
because individuals who perceive themselves as controlling their own lives have 
positive beliefs about their abilities to operate even complicated products. Tams 
et al. (
2017) found that internal compared to external CSE is associated with more 
control over factors such as effectively using technology.
Consequently, we expect that those who are confident about their technological 
skills (high on the ICSE scale) will generally perceive interactive products as easier 

[Page 9]
1355
1 3

to use compared to those who doubt their technological skills (low on the ICSE 
scale). We further expect these latter respondents to emphasize ease-of-use consid -
erations to ensure that their encounters with a product will not be too challenging.
H4a: The proportion of respondents who rate ease of use of interactive products 
(both simple and complex) as high is higher among those with high ICSE com -
pared to those with low ICSE scores.
H4b: Respondents low in ICSE evaluate product design mainly through ease-of-
use considerations.
3.5  Social comparison orientation (SCO)
The effect of social influence on the decision to use a system is defined as “the 
degree to which an individual perceives that important others believe that he or she 
should use the new system” (Venkatesh et al. 
2003, p. 451). We rely on the social 
comparison orientation (SCO) measure to operationalize the effect of social factors 
on the drive to gain accurate self-evaluations by comparing oneself to others (Buunk 
and Gibbons 
2006; Gibbons and Buunk 1999). Because this tendency varies from 
one person to another, it is expected to influence the perception of product qualities 
and their relative importance in the evaluation process of interactive products.
Research has shown that participants high in SCO have poorer self-perceptions, 
lower self-esteem, and more negative affect balance compared to their low-SCO 
counterparts after engaging in brief social comparisons (Vogel et al. 
2015). These 
negative effects may drive people high in SCO to conform to common perceptions 
(Buunk and Gibbons 
2006). Thompson et al. ( 2006) found that social factors influ -
ence perceived functionality (i.e., perceived usefulness) judgments, while these have 
either a negative or no effect on ease-of-use perceptions. Because high-SCO indi -
viduals are more influenced by what others may think, and because market trends 
favor complexity (e.g., Mariotti 
2007; Norman 2007), we posit that this group will 
prefer complexity because it allows them to conform to what others may think of 
their choices.
In general, individuals high in SCO tend to make their judgments according to 
acceptable standards (Buunk and Gibbons 
2006). Because both ease of use and func-
tionality are considered to be standard norms for effective interaction with products 
(as reflected by the TAM model, see Davis 
1989), these two qualities are expected to 
be important in the evaluation process of individuals high in SCO. Because aesthet -
ics is an attribute that is easily observable by others, we expect it to serve as a major 
consideration for them, in addition to instrumental qualities.
H5a: The proportion of respondents preferring complex designs is significantly 
higher among those with high compared to those with low SCO scores.
H5b: Respondents high in SCO evaluate product design through its three 
main qualities (namely, ease of use, functionality, and aesthetics).
H5c: Respondents low in SCO have fewer considerations in their evaluations.

[Page 10]
1356 E. Eytam et al.
1 3
3.6  Maximizers versus satisficers (MAX)
Maximizers are people who are interested in achieving the best outcomes; there -
fore, they feel compelled to examine all the alternatives because they constantly feel 
they may have done better had they chosen otherwise. Satisficers, on the other hand, 
consider something that crosses the threshold of acceptability as satisfactory (Nen -
kov et al. 
2008; Schwartz et al. 2002). Adding more options to a maximizers’ set of 
alternatives reduces their overall satisfaction because they decrease the likelihood of 
achieving the goal of maximization (Schwartz et al. 
2002). Potential regret is ever-
present for them, as they are preoccupied with the question, “Is this the best out -
come I can get?”
Because they are constantly trying to optimize their choice, we expect maximiz -
ers to favor complex design. They see feature-laden designs as providing all the 
functionality that they may need (Porter 
2007). Because they are compelled to exam-
ine all the alternatives (Schwartz et al. 2002), maximizers overlook hedonic aspects 
of a product in order to make sure they are not distracted by considerations that are 
irrelevant to its actual use. Satisficers, on the other hand, settle for simpler designs, 
and find aesthetic considerations equally important when evaluating products.
H6a: The proportion of respondents preferring complex designs is significantly 
higher among those with high compared to those with low maximization scores.
H6b: Respondents with high maximization scores evaluate product design 
through instrumental qualities.

3.7  Centrality of visual product aesthetics (CVPA)
Centrality of visual product aesthetics (CVPA) is a construct that assesses the 
importance of visual aesthetics for a particular individual in his or her product rela -
tionship (Bloch et al. 
2003). Individuals who measure high on the CVPA scale have 
greater concern for visual aesthetics. Simplicity and complexity also relate to aes -
thetic notions; therefore, individuals high in CVPA may prefer simplicity or com -
plexity, not for the product’s instrumental value, but rather for its aesthetic value.
Because simplicity is considered beautiful (Karvonen 2000; Mollerup 2007, 
2015), and following Reinecke and Gajos (2014), who report that in most countries, 
simplicity is rated as having high visual appeal, individuals with high CVPA scores 
are expected to prefer simpler designs. In addition, because individuals with high 
CVPA scores have greater than average concern for visual aesthetics (Bloch et al. 
2003), they are expected to emphasize aesthetic considerations in their evaluation 
process.
H7a: The proportion of respondents preferring simple designs is higher among 
those with high compared to those with low CVPA scores.

H7b: Individuals with high CVPA scores evaluate interactive products mainly 
through aesthetic considerations, while their counterparts, low in CVPA, give 
less weight to these considerations.
4  Method
4.1  Research approach
In studying the effect of individual differences on interactive product preferences, 
possible confounding design aspects may influence product evaluations that are 
based on self-reports. For example, familiarity with the study stimuli may influence 
evaluative judgments (Huber and Holbrook 
1981). Specifically, previous experi -
ence with a product may influence perceptions of how easy it is to use that product 
(Thompson et  al. 
2006). Similarly, Sylcott et  al. ( 2016) note that detailed stimuli 
representations allow accidental details to play into participants’ decisions. To con -
trol for such confounding effects that result from respondents’ experience rather than 
from their personal characteristics, we used general illustrations as research stimuli. 
Thus, in designing the stimuli, although the designs were inspired by control panels 
of interactive products, they could not be identified as specific familiar products. 
The use of an illustration of a generic product, as opposed to realistically depict -
ing a specific product, was intended to capture the essence of the qualities under 
study (i.e., ease of use, aesthetics, and functionality), while controlling for various 
potential confounders that could be present in a specific and realistic depiction (for 
example, previous experience with specific products or brands, preference for spe -
cific design styles and colors, and so on).
Previous research (e.g., Eytam et  al. 
2017; Mahlke et  al. 2007; Tractinsky and 
Zmiri 2006) has reported that the qualities under study are correlated, and that they 
may be related to a smaller set of latent factors. In order to eliminate potential con -
founding and multi-collinearity effects, and because exploratory methods are used to 
uncover the underlying structure and relationship of and between large numbers of 
variables (Fabrigar et al. 
1999; Osborne 2015), we chose to use exploratory factor 
analysis (EFA) for further analyses.
Sample. Three hundred respondents took part in the study (age: M = 29.86; 
SD = 8.09, age range: 14–66; 49% female). Respondents were recruited using a 
convenience sample via undergraduate students taking a Data Analysis course at an 
engineering college. All students volunteered to complete a questionnaire and had 
additional surveys completed by their friends and family to collect data that served 
in their completing a project that was a course requirement. As this task was done 
simultaneously and involved other respondents who were not part of the course, we 
believe that interaction between respondents was very limited.
Stimuli As a broad rule, more parts or elements in a design mean less simplicity 
(Colborne 
2017; Thomas and Richards 2009). Thus, an acceptable qualitative meas-
ure of VSL relies on the number of elements included in a design (e.g., the number 
of controls) to determine how simple or complex the design is (e.g., Mollerup 
2007, 
2015; Reinecke et  al. 2013). This rule guided the design of the different research 

[Page 12]
1358 E. Eytam et al.
1 3
stimuli. Two stimulus sets were used, each including a simple and a complex illus -
tration of a UI of a general interactive product. These sets were judged as the most 
simple and the most complex examples from among 27 illustrations tested for VSL 
in a preliminary pilot experiment. The choice of stimuli was intended to ensure a 
pre-use evaluation of the stimuli and to control for previous experience with similar 
products that could influence attribute judgments. One hundred and five respondents 
participated in the pilot study (age: M = 24.36, SD = 2.98, age range: 18–30; gender: 
46% female). They rated each illustration on a Likert scale of 1 to 10, where 1 repre-
sented a simple design and 10 represented a complex one. The descriptive statistics 
for the two most simple and two most complex illustrations are detailed in “Appen -
dix 
1”.
Measures The product evaluation measure included nine items, three for each 
evaluated attribute (i.e., ease of use, functionality, and aesthetics; see Eytam et al. 
2017). A single item asking the respondent to rate their preference for each stimu -
lus on a Likert scale of 1 to 7 measured preference towards each model. The five 
individual differences scales were re-validated in a series of pilot studies, and their 
reliability was adequate. “Appendix 
2” lists the scale items, and Table  1 details their 
reliabilities.
Procedure Respondents received an email message asking them to complete 
two questionnaires that were accessed through two links included in the message: 
a Google Docs questionnaire regarding individual differences scales and a Qualtrics 
one regarding design qualities in order to evaluate one of the two design sets. The 
order of these links was counterbalanced in the emails sent to respondents. Half 
of the messages first introduced the Google Docs link in the first line and then the 
Qualtrics link. The other half presented these links in the opposite order. Respond -
ents were given a one-week period in which to complete the two questionnaires, and 
responses were automatically sent back.

5  Results
5.1  Properties of individual differences measures
EFA with maximum likelihood estimation were applied to all individual differences 
measures. We specified an extraction criterion of eigenvalue > 1, and the solution 
was rotated using an oblique method (direct oblimin with Kaiser Normalization). 
Items matching ICSE and CVPA were each loaded on a distinct factor as initially 
expected. Maximization scale items were loaded on three distinct factors. These fac-
tors matched three dimensions of the maximization trait reported in the literature 
(alternative search, decision difficulty, and high standards) (Schwartz et al. 
2002). 
Five reversed items were not loaded on their hypothesized factor: one PIIT, two 
SCO, and two MAX items. Hinkin (
1998) suggests that although reverse-scored 
items may reduce response set bias, they may impair scale reliability. Because the 
remaining four PIIT items, 13 MAX items, and four SCO items were loaded on their 
main distinct factor, respectively, all reversed-scored items were removed from fur -
ther analysis.
Responses to the individual differences questionnaire were averaged for each 
scale (excluding responses to recoded items). Correlations between the scales were 
relatively low, indicating discriminant validity. ICSE and PIIT had a slightly higher 
correlation (r = .39). These two traits are reported in the literature as correlated (e.g., 
Agarwal et al. 
2000), perhaps because personal innovativeness is an antecedent of 
CSE (e.g., Thompson et al. 2006). All computed scale scores, reliabilities, descrip -
tive statistics, and correlations are presented in Table  1.
EFAs with maximum likelihood estimation were applied to the responses of 
the nine items in each VSL tested. Three factors were specified for retention, 
and the solution was rotated using an oblique method (direct oblimin with Kai -
ser Normalization) for the analysis of each. Items were loaded on three distinct 

[Page 14]
1360 E. Eytam et al.
1 3
factors matching their original categorization: ease of use, functionality, and aes -
thetics. These factors explained between 66% and 70% of the variance in the sim -
ple design analysis and between 68% and 71% of the variance in the complex 
design. All item loadings on each factor exceeded .50, and there were no cross-
loadings (see “Appendix 
4”).
Correlations between aesthetics and the instrumental qualities were high 
(Table  2). These correlations are theoretically important because they suggest 
that aesthetics appraisals are perhaps used as a cue for instrumental judgments 
(Eytam et al. 
2017; Tractinsky 2012). We further discuss these correlations in the 
discussion section, and the correlations in Sect.  6.
In order to control for a possible effect of a stimulus set, a one-way ANOVA 
was conducted with respondent groups (evaluating Set 1 vs. Set 2) as a between-
groups factor and qualities (ease of use, functionality, and aesthetics), and pref -
erence of VSLs (simple vs. complex) as a within-subjects factor. Assigning 
respondents to groups based on the experimental stimulus set they evaluated had 
no significant effect on qualities or preference ratings [F (df1, df2) = 1.36, p > .05] 
across the two VSLs tested. Therefore, further analysis relates to the pooled 
responses of 300 respondents evaluating a simple versus complex design of gen -
eral interactive products.
A Chi square analysis of the demographic variables was conducted with each 
of the individual differences (i.e., PIIT, ICSE, SCO, MAX, and CVPA) sepa -
rately to test for possible interaction effects between these variables and individ -
ual differences. No association was observed between age and any of the indi -
vidual variables tested. An association was observed between gender and PIIT 
(χ 2 (3) = 14.61, p = .002). Gender differences interacted with PIIT scores.

The relations between VSL and all measured attribute ratings were tested in a 
previous study reported in Eytam et al. ( 2017); this part of the current study con -
stituted a replication attempt of that study. We conducted a series of mixed-design 
ANOVAs with VSL as a between-groups factor, and ease of use, functionality, aes -
thetics, and preference as within-subjects factors. Tables 
3 and 4 present the descrip-
tive statistics of the design attribute evaluation broken down by VSL and respondent 
groups (groups were assigned according to demographic variables and individual 
differences) and the ANOVA results. All pairwise comparisons used the Bonferroni 
correction for multiple tests. Results reveal that the VSL had a significant effect on 
all measured attribute ratings and design preferences. Respondents rated the simple 
designs as significantly easier to use and more aesthetic compared to the complex 
designs. The complex designs were rated as more functional compared to the simple 
ones. Additionally, respondents rated their preference of the simple designs as sig -
nificantly higher compared to their preference for the complex designs. These results 
replicate the results reported by Eytam et al. (
2017), and are in line with the associa-
tion between simplicity and ease of use and complexity with functionality reported 
by Thompson et al. (
2005), as well as with the association between simplicity and 
beauty suggested by Karvonen (2000).
Assigning respondents to experimental groups based on age had no effect on any of 
the attribute ratings. Still, the interaction effect between VSL and functionality ratings 
was significant (p = .049). While younger respondents (Q1) rated functionality of the 
simple design higher than their older counterparts (Q4), this trend shifted when evaluat-
ing the complex design in which younger respondents rated the complex design as less 
functional (see Table 
3 for descriptive statistics of the different respondent groups).
5.2  Effects of individual differences on perceived design qualities
In order to examine the influence of individual differences on attribute judgments and 
preference formation, the sample was divided by quartiles according to individual dif-
ferences ranks (PIIT, ICSE, SCO, MAX, and CVPA). Comparisons were performed 
using a series of separate mixed-design ANOVAs for each attribute rating as a depend-
ent variable with VSL as the within-subjects factor, and with respondent groups 
assigned according to demographic variables or individual differences as a between-
groups factor. Table 
4 presents the descriptive statistics of the design attribute ratings 
and effects of respondent group and VSL over attribute evaluation for individual dif-
ferences recorded as having a significant effect on at least one attribute measured.
Assigning respondents to experimental groups based on their ICSE score affected 
ease-of-use ratings. Those who scored high on the ICSE scale (Q4) rated ease-of-use 
of the simple design higher than their lower scoring counterparts (Q1). The effect of 
ICSE on ease-of-use ratings was significant ( p = .05). Post hoc Tukey tests revealed 
that respondents high in ICSE (Q4) rated both designs as easier to use than the low 
ICSE participants (Q1). There was no interaction effect. A Z-Ratio for proportions of 
ease-of-use ratings and ICSE group (low vs. high) was significant for both simple and 
complex design judgments. Thirty-six of 77 respondents high in ICSE (belonging to 
Q3 or Q4) (47%) compared to 22 of 75 respondents (29%) who were low in ICSE

the Likert scale) ( Z = 2.21, p = .027). Fifteen of 77 respondents high in ICSE (19%) 
compared to 6 of 75 respondents (8%) who were high in ICSE rated ease of use for 
the complex design as high (6 or 7 on the Likert scale) (Z = 2.05, p = .040), supporting 
H4a (see “Appendix 
6” for ICSE vs. ease-of-use rating frequencies).
Assigning respondents to experimental groups based on their SCO and MAX 
scores affected the ratings of all perceived product qualities. Post hoc Tukey tests 
conducted on all possible pairwise contrasts (4 quartiles of SCO/MAX scores) 
revealed that respondents high in the measured traits (categorized as belonging to 
the fourth quartile, Q4) rated functionality, aesthetics, and preference significantly 
higher than their lower counterparts (belonging to the first quartile, Q1) in the two 
VSLs tested. The interaction effect of VSL and SCO was significant. Although com-
plexity was not their most favored option, respondents high in SCO rated their pref -
erence for the complex design significantly higher than those low in SCO. There was 
no interaction effect of VSL and the MAX group.
5.3  Preference formation
A regression analysis was conducted separately for each VSL (simple or complex), 
with preference as the dependent variable and product qualities as the predictors. 
Table 
5 presents the preference model’s standardized coefficients and collinearity 
diagnostics. Tests to see if the data met the assumption of collinearity indicated that 
multicollinearity was not a concern (tolerance > .2; Montgomery et  al. 
2001). All 
three qualities served as significant predictors of preference variance for the simple 
stimuli, and ease of use and aesthetics served as significant predictors of preference 
variance for the complex stimuli. The results agree with the preference model sug -
gested by Eytam et al. (
2017) for consumers (but not for users).
In order to test the percentage of respondents preferring  simple versus com -
plex designs, we used a Z-ratio test. 1 To achieve the maximal difference  between

6  Discussion
The objective of this study was to test whether the paradox of simplicity for inter -
active products could be explained, at least in part, by considering the effects of 
individual differences in perceptions of the VSL of product UIs. Previous research 
has argued that the subjective perception of VSL (Nadkarni and Gupta 
2007) 
translates into a perceived quality of product qualities (e.g., Eytam et al. 2017; 
Thompson et al. 2005). Therefore, we expected that individual potential hetero -
geneity in individual characteristics would lead to differences in the evaluation

scales) in order to examine their influence on perceived product qualities and on 
preference formation. Below, we discuss the general evaluation of VSL, and then 
elaborate on the effects of individual differences on product attribute judgments 
and preference formation.
Our aggregate analysis of the data with the simple stimuli revealed that 
respondents paid attention to all product qualities. Functionality was never an 
important attribute per se, but rather it was evaluated as a part of a comprehen -
sive strategy. When analyzing the complex stimuli, respondents paid attention to 
ease of use and aesthetics, overlooking functionality considerations. Eytam et al. 
(
2017) report a similar pattern of evaluation for respondents with purchase, but 
not with use intentions. Overlooking functionality considerations in complex 
stimuli evaluations could hint at how the paradox of simplicity is formed. Good -
man and Irmak (
2013) argue that consumers often fail to estimate their feature 
usage rate before purchasing multifunctional (i.e., complex) products. Thus, sim -
ple products are meticulously scrutinized for all their qualities. Complex prod -
ucts, in comparison, are assumed to have good functionality because complexity 
is associated with high product capability (e.g., Thompson et al. 
2005); therefore, 
these items are evaluated less rigorously.
As suggested by a previous extensive body of research (e.g., Creusen and Schoo -
rmans 2005; Tractinsky and Lavie 2002; Tractinsky and Zmiri 2006), ease-of-use 
and aesthetic considerations were relatively important throughout the analysis of 
both the simple and complex stimuli. Ratings of both qualities were highly cor -
related (e.g., Eytam et  al. 
2017; Tractinsky et  al. 2000). We argue that these cor -
relations hint at the informative role of aesthetics, and they suggest that aesthetic 
appraisals may serve as a cue for instrumental judgments (Tractinsky 
2012). Espe-
cially high were the correlations between ease of use and aesthetics in the evaluation 
of the complex stimuli (Table 
2). Not trusting the ease of use of the complex designs 
that are often associated with difficult use (e.g., Thompson et al. 2005), our respond-
ents may have relied on their aesthetic judgments to reaffirm their impression of the 
ease of use of these stimuli.
As already noted by Eytam et  al. (
2017), respondents generally did not favor 
complex over simple stimuli. Still, when individual differences were included in the 
analysis, attribute judgments, the relative importance of qualities in the evaluation 
process, and preference for the different VSLs were affected. Assigning respond -

6.1  Age differences
While age differences had no effect on perceived ease of use or on the perceived 
aesthetics of the designs evaluated, there was an interaction effect between age 
group and design VSL. While generally the simple design was rated as less func -
tional compared to the complex one, in agreement with previous research (e.g., 
Eytam et  al. 
2017; Thompson et  al. 2005), younger respondents rated it as more 
functional compared to their older counterparts. This trend shifted for evaluations 
of the complex design, which older respondents thought was more functional. These 
differences may have resulted from the fact that each group encountered technology 
for the first time at different stages in its evolution (Morris and Venkatesh 
2000). 
Younger respondents met technology when it had evolved to a stage where it had 
already become automated (Tannen 
2009) in contrast to older respondents, who may 
recall interactive products in the early stages when control-laden products were a 
guarantee for technological capability.
Still, as was initially hypothesized, a greater number of older respondents pre -
ferred simple deigns compared to younger ones. Examining the evaluation models 
of the two groups may explain these different preferences. While for the younger 
age group, aesthetics was considered the most important attribute in both VSLs, the 
older group regarded ease-of-use considerations as important, especially for com -
plex stimuli, a tendency that has long been noticed. McCloskey (
2006) reported 
that older users often find it difficult to use technology. They are described as hav -
ing lower computer self-efficacy and a higher degree of anxiety regarding technol -
ogy (e.g., Chen and Chan 2011; Laguna and Babcock 2000; Mitzner et al. 2010). 
Another issue worth noting is that while younger respondents had considerations 
that could be identified as strictly hedonic, older respondents emphasized utilitarian 
considerations across the VSLs tested, perhaps because they encountered it at a later 
life stage (Morris and Venkatesh 
2000; Ahmad 2012).
6.2  Technology-related traits
PIIT has been noted in the literature as an antecedent of CSE (Agarwal et al. 2000), 
and it is reasonable to assume that this is also an antecedent of its ICSE deriva -
tive (Thatcher et al. 2008). Following Thompson et al. ( 2006), we hypothesized that 
these technology-related traits would act as a precursor of ease-of-use perceptions 
because being technologically oriented (reflected as high on either the ICSE or PIIT 
scales) leads to proficiency with technology. This proficiency, in turn, enables these 
people to perceive products as easier to use relative to people who are not as tech -
nologically savvy. Although both traits were mildly correlated, their recorded effects 
on perceived ease of use were different.
Assigning respondents to experimental groups based on high versus low ICSE 
scores affected the relative importance of considerations in the evaluation process. 
Thatcher et al. (
2008) explained that the ICSE dimension of CSE focuses on how 
individuals perceive their capacity to use computers independently (i.e., without

evaluating simple stimuli, low-ICSE respondents were consistent in emphasizing

evaluating simple stimuli, low-ICSE respondents were consistent in emphasizing 
these considerations across the VSLs tested. Not trusting their proficiency with tech-
nology, low-ICSE respondents looked for reassurance and wanted to make sure that

logical efficacy, could overlook this concern when evaluating the simple stimuli, and 
concentrated more on their hedonic aspects, as reflected by the relative importance 
of aesthetics in their considerations. Another explanation may be rooted in the level 
of involvement with technology. Jang et al. (
2018) report that the level of involve -
ment with certain products influences different consumers in different ways. Con -
sumers with higher levels of involvement with a certain line of products were able 
to accept and comprehend the design more easily than their counterparts. They sug -
gest that more experience of a given stimulus tends to increase preference for higher 
complexity.
The gender variable interacted with the PIIT score. The majority of female 
respondents reported that they were low in PIIT compared to male respondents, in 
line with Beckwith et al. (
2006), who reported that gender differences are manifested 
in the early exploration of software qualities. They suggest that females have lower 
self-efficacy compared to males, which hinders their ability to cope with unfamiliar 
new qualities. They further suggest that because females are more risk averse, they 
may be less willing to explore and adopt new qualities. Initially, we hypothesized 
that respondents low in PIIT would consider all qualities important in their evalu -
ation, as do laggards in Rogers’ (
2003) model. Rogers suggests that laggards see a 
high risk in adopting new products, and thus tend to adopt a traditional, more skepti-
cal view towards product evaluation. We assumed that this view would encourage 
respondents low in PIIT to be more meticulous in their evaluation, and to consider 
all product qualities as important when evaluating all stimuli. In fact, considerations 
of respondents low in PIIT differed by gender. While low-PIIT male-respondents 
considered only ease of use as an important product attribute, their female counter -
parts considered aesthetics equally important. Still, while males high in PIIT con -
sidered only aesthetics important, their female counterparts related to ease of use 
as important. Generally, our respondents overlooked functionality considerations 
when evaluating the complex stimuli. Complexity of stimuli may have made func -
tionality judgments redundant for them because, as reported by Thompson et  al. 
(
2005), in pre-use situations, complexity is often associated with good functionality. 
Respondents high in PIIT, however, consistently overlooked functionality considera-
tions, regardless of gender. Their deep acquaintance with technological innovations 
may have brought them to conclude that VSL cannot serve as a cue for functionality 
because while complex designs have good functionality, simple ones can be just as 
effective due to automated features (Tannen 
2009).
6.3  Traits that are non-technology related
As initially hypothesized, more respondents high in SCO and MAX scores rated 
their preference to the complex design higher than their lower-scoring counterparts. 

[Page 30]
1376 E. Eytam et al.
1 3
Although they preferred similar designs, their motivations could be different. In the 
following subsection, we elaborate on the possible motivations of each group.
Respondents high on the maximization scale rated functionality, aesthetics, and 
their preference to the different stimuli significantly higher than satisficers (i.e., 
respondents low on the maximization scale). When evaluating the simple stimuli, 
they related to both instrumental qualities (i.e., ease of use and functionality) as 
important. This finding sheds light on the decision-making process of maximizers 
and on how individual differences play an unexpected role in evaluating design qual-
ities. Schwartz et al. (
2002) explain that maximizers engage in more active coping 
strategies (i.e., problem solving in order to optimize their decisions). Perhaps over -
looking aesthetic considerations reflected these coping strategies. Many cultures, 
acknowledging the effect of aesthetics over preference formation (e.g., Bloch et al. 
2003; Creusen and Schoormans 2005; Tractinsky and Lavie 2002), advise people 
“not to judge a book by its cover.” Maximizers may have actively followed this rule, 
trying to judge stimuli by instrumental merits, deliberately overlooking aesthetics 
that could be misleading.
Schwartz (
2004) provides another explanation for the attempt of maximizers to 
rely on instrumental rather than non-instrumental product qualities in the evalua -
tion process. He suggests that, by definition, a maximizer has high standards and 
high expectations. While Hassenzahl (
2003, 2004) emphasizes the psychological 
well-being value of a product when defining its hedonic value, Schwartz defines the 
hedonic assessment as deriving from the relation between the objective qualities and 
expectations of the beholder about the experience to be gained from these quali -
ties. He argues that the same experience that is considered positive by a satisficer 
may be viewed as negative by a maximizer. Because they are more susceptible to 
disappointment, and to play it safe, maximizers rely only on instrumental pragmatic 
qualities that are expected to support task completion.
Similarly, respondents high in SCO rated functionality, aesthetics, and preference 
of all evaluated stimuli significantly higher than their lower-scoring counterparts. 
Previous research reports that maximizers are more affected by social comparison, 
and that one of their coping strategies is to seek social support (Parker et al. 
2007; 
Schwartz et al. 2002), which perhaps explains this similarity in attribute judgments. 
Thompson et al. ( 2006) also report that social factors positively affected perceived 
usefulness (i.e., functionality). Klein and Sorra ( 1996) explain that social influ -
ence operates through processes of compliance and internalization. Compliance is 
defined as acting as others expect, and internalization relates to adopting the views 
of others for oneself. Individuals, who feel persuaded to use a product by their refer-
ence group, attribute this persuasion to a rational judgment on the part of the group 
that the product at hand is useful. Our high-SCO respondents rated their preference 
for the complex design significantly higher compared to their lower-scoring counter-
parts. Being more affected by what others think, they may have been more attentive 
to market trends. By internalizing the positive perception of complexity reflected in 
these trends (Mariotti 
2007; Norman 2007), they may have complied with them.
Finally, respondents high in CVPA were expected to favor simple designs 
because these are considered to have high visual appeal (e.g., Karvonen 2000; Mol-
lerup 2007, 2015). Yet, assigning respondents to experimental groups based on their

plex stimuli. Still, the effect of CVPA was present in the relative importance of aes -

to market trends. By internalizing the positive perception of complexity reflected in 
these trends (Mariotti 
2007; Norman 2007), they may have complied with them.
Finally, respondents high in CVPA were expected to favor simple designs 
because these are considered to have high visual appeal (e.g., Karvonen 2000; Mol-
lerup 2007, 2015). Yet, assigning respondents to experimental groups based on their

Effects of visual simplicity in product design and individual…
CVPA did not have any effect on aesthetics ratings of either the simple or the com -
plex stimuli. Still, the effect of CVPA was present in the relative importance of aes -
thetic considerations in the evaluation process. Respondents high in CVPA empha -
sized aesthetic considerations to a greater degree than the pragmatic qualities across 
the two VSLs tested. These consistent important considerations echo the central role 
of aesthetics in the lifestyle of high-CVPA individuals. Bloch et al. (
2003) explained 
that for these individuals, aesthetics can be the sole attribute differentiating between 
products, and our findings provide strong support for this claim.
7  Managerial implications
Immediate marketing implications that can be drawn from this research pertain to 
the more detailed specification of developing a visual design strategy for interac -
tive products. The utilized manipulation of the degree of VSL indicates that when 
marketers design a new interactive product, they must pay attention to the number 
of controls in the design to convey the desired image of the product to appeal to dif-
ferent consumer groups. While some consumers prefer a more detailed product with 
many controls, others prefer a more “lean” number. Thus, accounting for consumer 
heterogeneity is a major factor to consider in using design VSL effectively.
In order to handle this heterogeneity, marketers should first find ways to know 
their audience. For instance, age is a major precursor for design preferences. While 
younger users may see some advantages to a simple design, such as automation, 
they judge a design by its aesthetics. Older users are more concerned with ease-of-
use considerations. Being able to evaluate consumers’ tendency towards technology 
can also be advantageous for marketers. For example, when products are designed 
for consumers proficient with technology (e.g., gamers, programmers), in general, 
“more is more.” That is, a greater number of controls may enhance product accept -
ability and preference. Conversely, for consumers who are not technologically savvy 
or for novices, “more” becomes “less” in the sense that more controls are perceived 
as complicated to use, intimidating, and, as a result, less useful.
Understanding differences between consumer groups with different personal 
characteristics becomes even more challenging when the target market is charac -
terized by limited technological orientation. Variables that typify this problem are 
consumers who behave as maximizers or those who are more influenced by others. 
As this tendency can be identified by direct measures and not prior to purchase, it is 
difficult to effectively use such a variable. Even so, its importance requires marketers 
to address this type of difference to prevent loss of potential sales. One way to han -
dle this type of heterogeneity is to introduce two product models in such a market: 
a simple and a complex design for the same product, probably with different brand 
serial identification, to appeal to different consumer needs and wants. Many compa-
nies already offer similar types of products with different qualities and degrees of 
complexity. Norman (
2007) noted this in the traditional “white goods” sold in South 
Korean markets, where toasters, refrigerators, and coffee makers all have multiple 
control dials although all could be operated with a single knob. In order to decrease 

[Page 32]
1378 E. Eytam et al.
1 3
uncertainty about what proportion to produce from each design, a preliminary study 
could be conducted to measure consumer differences.
Finally, there are also instances where complexity is a necessity since the func -
tionality of a product requires a minimum number of controls that increases its VSL. 
While consumers may choose complexity at first, it may potentially decrease cus -
tomer lifetime value (Thompson et al. 
2005). Thus, it is wise to consider the layout 
of the controls to make them clearer, for example, by grouping together those des -
ignated for similar actions (e.g., Deng and Poole 2010) so that complexity is less 
confusing (Norman 2010).
8  Limitations and future research
This research studied the effect of individual differences on the evaluation process of 
interactive products, but it is clearly subject to some limitations. First, although some 
respondents were more positive in evaluating the complex designs than others, the 
general preference ratings did not support a sweeping claim of users’ preference for 
complex designs (e.g., Mariotti 
2007). When differences in personal characteristics 
were significant, respondents rated their preference of the simple stimuli differently 
than the complex stimuli. Reinecke and Gajos (
2014) reported that their respondents, 
sampled in various countries, favored mid-level complexity over extremely complex 
designs. Perhaps the paradox of simplicity can be more explicit when mid-level com-
plexity designs are evaluated rather than the extremely complex stimuli used in our 
study. Thus, future research should include mid-level complexity stimuli to repli -
cate the paradox of simplicity that is reported to be important in market trends (e.g., 
Eytam et al. 
2017; Norman 2007). In addition, the present study focused on the num-
ber of elements as a manipulation of the product’s control panel design VSL. Future 
research might consider examining different styles, colors, or interaction effects with 
the number of elements to manipulate the simplicity or complexity of a product’s UI.
Furthermore, the records of individual differences relied on self-report meas -
ures. While such questionnaires are a common method of collecting data, they are 
subject to several biases that may influence the data. Choi and Pak (
2005) remind 
us that questionnaires that are lengthy can induce fatigue among respondents and 
result in uniform and inaccurate responses. In addition, because of social desirabil -
ity, respondents may systematically alter their responses in the direction they per -
ceive to be desired (e.g., they may want to be perceived as being high or low in spe -
cific traits). Ben-Bassat et al. (
2006) suggested overcoming these flaws by including 
economic measures. Therefore, future research can rely on additional measures to 
reaffirm self-reports of individual differences. For example, recording the amount 
of time respondents spend in scrutinizing product illustrations and the number of 
actions they perform during the evaluation (such as mouse hovers over an evalu -
ated product illustration when the stimuli are presented on a computer screen) can 
help in separating maximizers from satisficers. By allowing respondents to consult 
with other respondents about a product’s use, respondents low in ICSE can be bet -
ter sorted. Future research should also encourage older respondents to express their 
opinion about technology for a more balanced sample.

Finally, the stimuli used in this study were general and artificial, and did not indicate 
the tasks they were intended to support or the qualities that the product at hand could 
provide. By using general illustrations, we intended to control for variables that could 
have confounded VSL manipulation (e.g., color, style, familiarity, etc.). Generally speak-
ing, choice of stimuli boils down to the tension between internal and external validity 
of a study.

Finally, the stimuli used in this study were general and artificial, and did not indicate 
the tasks they were intended to support or the qualities that the product at hand could 
provide. By using general illustrations, we intended to control for variables that could 
have confounded VSL manipulation (e.g., color, style, familiarity, etc.). Generally speak-
ing, choice of stimuli boils down to the tension between internal and external validity 
of a study. While internal validity is about the relations between the research variables, 
external validity concerns generalizing aspects of it (to other stimuli, populations, prod-
ucts, etc.). Because it is impossible to achieve control of both types of validity within a 
single study, future research should apply the same methodology to real-world interac-
tive products. However, such stimuli may impose further challenges to understanding 
the effect of individual differences on preference of interactive products’ VSL because 
familiarity and previous experience with similar products on preference may confound 
the results. Indeed, further understanding the issues discussed in this paper hinges on 
conducting additional studies using a multiplicity of methods, designs, contexts, and 
consumer populations.

 1. When I watch TV, I channel surf, even when I watch an interesting program.

Architectural Wayfinding Design as a Means of 
Communication in Environmental Perception 
Georgia Cheirchanteri 
     University of West Attica, 13 Valtetsiou St., 15231, Chalandri Athens, Greece 
geoxeirr@gmail.com 
Abstract. From prehistoric times, Signage was a means of visual communication helping 
people reaching out different environments (internal or external). Long before paper’s 
invention, humans made marks on objects, such as cave walls, in the surrounding environment, 
for their communication.  As cities grew and mobility increased, making the built environment 
more complex, people requirements for better information concerning spatial perception and 
navigation, also grew. Thus, the necessity of proactive, systematically planned, visual unified 
signage and wayfinding programs have been emerged. Wayfinding is how people get from one 
location to another, including their information -gathering and decision -making processes for 
orientation and movement through space.  Wayfinding design builds on resea rch in cognition 
and environmental psychology to design built spaces and products that facilitate the movement 
of people through urban settings and individual buildings.  Despite its demonstrated importance 
to building use, costs, and safety, wayfinding rec eives less than its due in planning, research 
and building evaluation. The aim of this study is to provide a “clear” reading of the 
environmental space and city’s routes to the users, through architectural wayfindig design. 
Also, architectural wayfinding d esign addresses built components, including spatial planning, 
articulation of form-giving features, circulation systems and environmental communication.    
1.  Introduction 
The external environmental space includes a total of natural and anthropogenic factors and elements 
that interact and affect the quality of life, historical and cultural tradition as well as aesthetic values.  
The outer environment is considered the built environment of every city, where tableboards with word 
signs, special colors and symbols give information, defining routes and directions within the city itself.  
 
  
Figure 1. Wayfinding System in a smart city.  
As it is known, at least every major city on planet  earth is inhabited by people of different racial, 
ethnic, cultural origins, who speak different languages.  In order the difficulties concerning the

seamless communication and movement of users in internal or external environments to be solved, it is 
investigated whether the creation of a communicative language based on visual communication is an 
important factor of operation (Figure 1).[1]-[2] 
 
The ultimate goal is to help all users of indoor and / or outdoor environments through design 
innovations in the study of spatial signage both in architectural and visual communication so that 
accessibility and movement within them are easy. In general, the intended subject of the presentation 
is the "pure" reading of the space and directions of both the city and the publi c buildings, by their 
users, through the marking of space.  According to current theories, the human mind organizes human 
perception to capture first the "essential form" and secondarily the exact copy. Thus a schematic arrow 
is more effective as a directio n indicator than a realistically painted hand with outstretched finger 
(Figure 2). As visual  communication scientist Rudolf Arnheim claims, "The human mind may be 
forced to make exact copies of things, but it is not by  its nature to be inclined to this" – which means 
that he can learn it, but it does not come by itself.  As a result, it is easier to communicate with signals 
that convey the general characteristics, rather than the specific and detailed ones.[3] 
 
 
 
Figure 2. Direction’s indication by a realistic hand drawing. 
2.  Histo                           2. Historical Data of Signage and Wayfinding 
Spatial marking is a means of visual communication of people in general, helping them to approach 
different environments (internally or externally). Long before the paper invention, people created 
images of symbols on objects surfaces, as well as in the inner surroundings of the caves, in order to 
exchange information through visual communication. Therefore, environmental graphic design, which 
can also be defined as visual communication of information in the structured environment, is one of 
the world's oldest professions.  From the invention of paper and electronic television or computer 
screen, most people think that graphic communication takes place mainly in these two media. But, just 
as the people of the caves created important images, object symbols of communication, as well as, in 
the surrounding space, huge quantities of information are being transmitted today through the signage 
of other objects in the struc tured environment. The modern reincarnation of Environmental Graphic 
Design (EGD) is a relatively new, multidisciplinary field that has been recognized over the last 30 
years. Sure, there were signs before, but it was revealed in an unplanned, almost reactionary way - in 
other words, as a second thought. [4] 
As cities became larger , in the course of time , their mobility was also increased, making the 
structured environment more complicated. At the same time, people's need for information has been 
upsized, in order to understand better the structured environment and navigate through it. This created 
the necessity to design dynamic and u nified visual signage and guidance ( wayfinding) systems. If 
anybody thinks that Environmental Graphic Design (EGD) is not important, must ask himself: Could 
he understand how to use a major international airport or an urban rail system if there were no clues or 
if the spatial marking was just a mass of messages, graphics and natural forms? The answer is 
definitely not! Consequently, modern signage and guidance systems (wayfinding) give a unique, 
unified voice in an environmental space. [1]-[5]

metadata.core_insight_en: This study aims to provide a clear reading of the environmental space and city routes to users through architectural wayfinding design, which involves proactive, systematically planned, and visual unified signage and wayfinding programs to facilitate movement through urban settings and individual buildings.

Spatial semi otics and orientation (wayfinding) are more often expressed in uniform signage 
systems, which both in terms of information and visualization are linked together in a space. 
Environments that support this successful orientation behaviour can also be of spat ial interest, 
sophisticated and complex. In fact, "the challenge of designing wayfinding is to create interesting 
signs that allow satisfactory space experiences and are safe, accessible and cost effective, despite  the 
complexity they may have." Although signage and orientation search are often used interchangeably, it 
is very important to make this special distinction: usually the primary objective of a signage system is 
to help people find their way through an environment, and often effective orientation solutions are 
required from a simple signal or symbol. Clear, well -defined paths and other visual signs, such as 
landmarks that stand out in the environment, help to find one's orientation, like printed maps, people 
guides, and more recently portable GPS systems.[6] 
 
As a matter of fact, the good architectural design of wayfinding is important for global planning, 
because it facilitates user s access, increases their satisfaction, while reducing the users isolation with 
disabilities. It also reduces visitor confusion and employee mistakes, saving time and money, 
preventing accidents while reducing stress, enhancing health and productivity. Moreover, according to 
the designer Jerry Weisman in 1981 , "the ability to fin d a destination inside and outside a building is 
clearly a prerequisite for achieving higher goals". [7] 
 
Weisman, also, claimed , that "the readability of an environ mental space - the extent to which the 
wayfinding detection is facilitated" has serious consequences for behaviour, referring to the following 
example: the readability results of the surrounding space to the happiness of some elderly people, who 
were housed in groups. Lynch also says that the readability of an environment al space means the 
convenience with which it can be perceived, while the offered choice degree depends on how readable 
it is. The main features that affect the readability are the paths, edges, nodes, milestones and areas. [8] 
 
In 1990, Arthur and Passini introduced the term "environmental communication", ie the orientation 
transfer, direction ( wayfimding), and other information within the structured environment through 
signage a nd other means of communication  or architectural features that allow people re aching 
different destinations (Figures 3,4). [9] 
 
            
 
   Figure 3. Floor wayfinding signage, USA.        Figure 4. Wayfinding System in Seattle roads, USA.  
For example, in the city of Dublin in 211, an elaborate, bilingual search system was installed in the 
town, including more than 100 individual elements, which made the city readable to its numerous 
cultural tourists. The first integrated public space signa ge system with over 100 bilingual panels and 
information poles was installed, creating signal chains for pedestrians seeking to reap the cultural 
benefits of the Irish capital (Figure 5). [9]

In 2001, CIDEA (Center for Inclusive Design and Environmental Access) states in New York that 
"spatial semiotics is the organization and communication of people's dynamic relationship with 
environmental space. Lynch (1960), the author of the book: The Image of the City , is the founder of 
spatial semiotics research about people’s orientation in the surrounding area (the term "wayfinding" 
was devised in the 1970s). Lynch, therefore, in this book defines that spatial semiotics is based on a 
consistent use and planning of specific sensory indications from the outside environment. [11]-[12] 
 
Also, Lynch, in his own book, refers to maps, stre et numbers, directional signals  and other  
elements as "spatial devices". This terminology, of course, has evolved into the five following main 
architectural elements: 
1. Directions and traffic (paths).  Recording of roads that are near or crossing an area, classifying 
them according to their importance in the area. 
2. Landmarks. Recording any separate elements that differentiate into shape, meaning or location. 
3. Nodes.  Recording of central points such as squares, junctions and crossroads, as well as 
buildings that attract people like cinemas and shopping centres. 
4. Edges. Recording any intense linear barriers and distinct boundaries in areas with different using 
modes or visual character. 
5. Zones or districts. List of areas that differ in character and identify the factors describing these 
differences, such as material and form. [12] 
 
It should be noted tha t landmarks, points of interest , as Lynch calls them, to the contrary to the 
nodes that can be introduced, are individual characteristics that behave as reference points. 
Additionally, milestones vary according to each person's personal experience. They are usually static 
(or they can also be movable objects such as the sun) and unique objects (physical structures or 
geographic features), which can be distinguished from a number of different objects. Landmarks are 
very important signs in the orientation process when they are distinct and not too many. [12]-[13]  
 
Many people with different types of cognitive abilities, as well as those who cannot read at all or 
who cannot read their mother tongue are based on milestones to mark and remember a path. The 
landmarks are distinguished by the dominance and peculiarity of shape, colour, size, height, position 
and visibility, and ultimately intense contrast to the surrounding area. Still, milestones must be  in 
harmony with their surroundings and not too many, 'as already mentioned, like many milestones may
