Therefore, we propose H3: Emotional responses (pleasure and arousal) will mediate 
the relationship between visual design condition and food intake. 
2.4 Immersive VR as a Method for Evaluating Design — Research Question 1 (RQ1) 
2.4.1 Evaluating Architectural Design before Construction 
The evidence regarding the detrimental impacts of built environments on the health of 
occupants, as well as insights into how to design for health, often stems from studies known as 
Post Occupancy Evaluations (POEs). POE can be defined as the “examination of the 
effectiveness for human users of occupied designed environments” (Zimring and Rosenheck, 
2001). Various methods, such as observation studies, ethnographic research, surveys, and 
interviews, are employed in POE studies (Zeisel, 2006). However, despite their potential, POE 
studies are not widely adopted in industry practice as they are considered expensive. They tend to 
be context-specific, making it challenging to generalize their findings to all design scenarios (Li 
et al., 2018). Moreover, the findings from POE are often not linked back to the design intention 
which makes it difficult to generate meaningful knowledge for designers (Li et al., 2018). 
Additionally, the recommendations arising from POEs to improve design and indirectly enhance 
user well-being can be costly and may necessitate significant building renovations, rendering 
them impractical in some cases. Given these limitations, there is merit in suggesting the 
incorporation of a Pre-Occupancy Evaluation (PreOE) stage into the design process. 
A PreOE would aim to predict the effectiveness of proposed building designs before they 
are constructed and occupied. While POE provides valuable feedback, it occurs too late to 
influence the evaluated building and cannot test unbuilt alternatives. Traditional pre-occupancy 
methods—physical models, 3D renderings, CAD visualizations, flythroughs—struggle to convey 

[Page 23]
14 
 
experiential qualities of full-scale space (Meagher, 2015). These tools often emphasize and 
convey technical or design details over perceptual experience, potentially causing designers to 
overlook spatial quality and human-centered outcomes. Integrating a health-oriented design 
approach using VR into the design process can yield numerous benefits, including providing an 
immersive experience of space before it is built, and saving time and resources by proactively 
addressing potential issues upfront. Moreover, interdisciplinary collaboration between architects, 
urban planners, public health experts, and other stakeholders can enrich the design process by 
integrating diverse perspectives and expertise and can allow educated design decisions. 
Simulation tools can also facilitate the evaluation of design alternatives and their potential impact 
on health outcomes.  
2.4.2 Virtual Reality Technology 
Unlike these traditional visualizations viewed on a flat screen, immersive virtual reality 
simulates architectural spaces in an immersive format by wrapping one’s field of view with a 
head-mounted display (HMD), thus altering the reality people experience. Unlike viewing static 
images on screens, VR provides stereoscopic vision and natural body-based interaction, creating a 
sense of “presence”—the psychological experience of being physically located in the virtual 
space. Mixed Reality (MR) blends virtual and physical elements: users can see real objects (like 
actual food) integrated into virtual environments through pass-through cameras on headsets 
(Milgram and Kishino, 1994). 
Two concepts prove critical for VR research validity. Immersion refers to technological 
capabilities: display quality, field of view, tracking precision, and rendering speed. Presence 
refers to psychological experience: the subjective sense of “being there” in the virtual space, 
including perceived ability to act within that environment (Slater, 2002). When VR systems 

[Page 24]
15 
 
achieve high immersion, users report strong presence and behave naturally despite wearing 
equipment. For presence to occur, technology must track movements precisely and render updates 
without perceptible lag. 
2.4.3 VR for Eating Behavior Research 
Eating behavior research faces inherent tension: laboratory settings provide experimental 
control but lack ecological validity, while real restaurants provide authenticity but prevent 
systematic manipulation of variables. VR offers potential resolution by combining control with 
realism. 
Long et al. (2023) developed a mixed-reality system where participants ate actual meals 
while immersed in virtual restaurant environments. Pass-through cameras allowed users to see 
their real hands and food integrated seamlessly into virtual dining spaces, creating experiences 
that felt authentic rather than artificial. Expert evaluators rated the refined virtual restaurant as 
more acceptable than traditional sensory lab booths for conducting research, though slightly 
lower than real restaurants. Critically, participants reported high presence and natural interaction, 
and behavioral research shows that eating responses in VR—such as portion size effects—mirror 
real-world patterns. 
This technology enables researchers to test multiple design variations cost-effectively, 
manipulate specific environmental variables systematically, and reach diverse populations 
through mobile deployment. However, questions remain about generalizability: not all users may 
respond identically, and system usability could moderate behavioral responses. 
Markowitz and Bailenson (2019) emphasize that VR’s research value depends on 
usability and perceived realism. If users find the system intuitive and the environment lifelike, 
their behaviors likely reflect genuine tendencies. If technology feels awkward or artificial, 

[Page 25]
16 
 
behaviors may not generalize to real settings. Factors including simulator sickness, interface 
complexity, and individual differences can all influence whether virtual experiences produce 
valid behavioral data. 
RQ 1: Can immersive VR mixed reality environment using pass-through technology 
be used as a valid method to evaluate how visual design in restaurant environments 
influences food-related behaviors and emotions? More specifically, how does mixed-reality 
VR system usability influence behavioral responses (food consumption) in immersive eating 
environments? 
2.5 Research Gaps and Conceptual Model 
Existing literature reveals several critical gaps that this study addresses: 
1. Gap 1: Causal Evidence. Most restaurant atmospherics research is correlational or 
uses self-report rather than observed behavior. Experimental studies establishing 
causal links between specific design features and eating outcomes remain rare. 
2. Gap 2: Visual Design Elements. While sensory factors like lighting and music 
receive attention, geometric form and visual complexity is less explored in eating 
contexts. Existing geometry research focuses on aesthetic preference rather than 
behavioral outcomes, particularly eating behavior. 
3. Gap 3: Mediation Mechanisms. Although theory suggests emotion mediates 
environmental effects on behavior, few studies test this pathway empirically, 
especially regarding food consumption.

More specifically, how does mixed-reality 
VR system usability influence behavioral responses (food consumption) in immersive eating 
environments? 
2.5 Research Gaps and Conceptual Model 
Existing literature reveals several critical gaps that this study addresses: 
1. Gap 1: Causal Evidence. Most restaurant atmospherics research is correlational or 
uses self-report rather than observed behavior. Experimental studies establishing 
causal links between specific design features and eating outcomes remain rare. 
2. Gap 2: Visual Design Elements. While sensory factors like lighting and music 
receive attention, geometric form and visual complexity is less explored in eating 
contexts. Existing geometry research focuses on aesthetic preference rather than 
behavioral outcomes, particularly eating behavior. 
3. Gap 3: Mediation Mechanisms. Although theory suggests emotion mediates 
environmental effects on behavior, few studies test this pathway empirically, 
especially regarding food consumption. 
4. Gap 4: VR Validation for Eating. While VR shows promise for architectural 
evaluation and in eating behavior research, its validity for behavioral research 

[Page 26]
17 
 
involving actual food consumption requires further investigation, particularly 
regarding how usability affects response patterns. 
This study addresses these gaps through a within-subjects experimental design testing 
how contrasting visual schemes (Curved Green vs. Angular Red) influence emotional responses 
and eating behavior in immersive VR dining environments. By measuring emotion before and 
after meals and assessing actual food consumption, the research provides causal evidence for 
environmental effects and tests emotional mediation. Examining usability as a moderator 
contributes methodological insights for VR pre-occupancy evaluation. 
Based on reviewed literature, we test three hypotheses and one research question as 
shown in the conceptual model (Figure 1). 
 
Figure 1 Conceptual Model summarizing the relationship between variables to be tested. 
  


[Page 27]
18 
 
Chapter 3 
3. Method 
This research employed a two-phase approach to investigate how visual environmental 
design influences emotional responses and eating behavior in an indoor restaurant setting. Phase 1 
consisted of an online study to develop and validate café environment stimuli through 
manipulation checks. Phase 2 involved a within-subjects laboratory experiment. Twenty 
participants (N = 20) were recruited from a university community to take part in a three-visit, 
within-subjects experiment. Each participant completed the study across three different sessions, 
corresponding to exposure to three distinct restaurant environments. After excluding incomplete, 
the final dataset included 57 valid observations. All procedures received approval from the 
Institutional Review Board (IRB) and informed consent was obtained from all participants prior 
to data collection. 
3.2 Phase 1: Online Pilot Study for Stimuli Development 
3.2.1 Participants 
An initial sample of 100 participants was recruited through MTurk. Due to poor data 
quality and failure to find significantly different restaurant environments, a second online study 
was conducted on Cloud Research Connect with a sample of 100 participants. Following data 
quality screening, the final sample consisted of 83 participants. Participants’ ages ranged from 18 
to 58 years (M = 33.02, SD = 9.43). The sample comprised approximately 53% individuals 
identifying as female, 46% as male, and about 1% identifying as another gender. Participants 
received monetary compensation ($1) for their participation through the platform. 

[Page 28]
19 
 
3.2.2 Design and Procedure 
The online study employed a within-subjects design with randomized presentation order. 
Participants viewed two restaurant environment designs presented as static images from four 
different angles and completed questionnaires assessing the visual differences between the 
environment and their aesthetic responses to each environment. The order of environment 
presentation was counterbalanced, with 47 participants (56.6%) viewing the Curved Green 
restaurant first followed by the Angular Red one, and 36 participants (43.4%) viewing the 
environments in reverse order. 
Participants accessed the study through an online platform and completed all materials 
remotely. After providing informed consent, participants viewed the first café environment 
image, completed response measures, then viewed the second environment and completed the 
same measures. The study concluded with demographic questions.  
3.2.3 Initial Restaurant Designs 
The initial stimulus set was developed to create two contrasting virtual restaurant 
environments that differed systematically in architectural form, and color palette. Both 
environments were designed as dining spaces with seating arrangements, tables, and windows 
providing exterior views. 
Curved Green Restaurant: This environment incorporated curved architectural elements 
in the ceiling and furniture, complemented by a warm color palette dominated by wood tones and 
green accents. A prominent green living wall and smooth, flowing lines contributed to an overall 
sense of organic movement and visual harmony (See Figure 2). 
 

[Page 29]
20 
 
Angular Red Restaurant (Version 1): This environment emphasized angular, geometric 
forms and sharp-edged striping patterns. The design employed a high-contrast black-and-white 
color scheme, excluded natural green elements, and conveyed a more industrial, stark aesthetic 
(See Figure 3). 
 
Figure 2 Curved Green restaurant with curved roof and furniture and warm green color tones. 
 


[Page 30]
21 
 
 
Figure 3 Angular Black restaurant (version 1) with angular roof and black and white contrast color tones. 
 
Statistical analysis revealed that the initial two restaurant designs were not perceived 
significantly differently showing that the visual manipulation did not work. A second online study 
was conducted to test the final stimuli. 
3.2.4 Stimuli Modification 
Based on these findings and guided by Mehrabian and Russell’s (1974) framework on 
information rate and arousal, the author of this MS thesis redesigned the stimulus environments to 
increase differentiation along key design dimensions. 
Design Modifications: The curved green restaurant was retained without any 
modification. The angular black restaurant underwent substantial redesign to create a high-
arousal, visually complex environment (see Figure 4). Specific modifications included: 


[Page 31]
22 
 
• Elimination of the black and white color palette in favor of a stark red color scheme to 
increase arousal and reduce warmth. 
• Introduction of dramatic diagonal striping patterns across ceiling and wall surfaces to 
increase visual complexity and reduce visual harmony. Enhanced visual complexity 
through asymmetrical arrangements 
These modifications aligned with theoretical predictions that higher information rate 
correlates with higher arousal responses, while the color shift to red was expected to reduce 
pleasure and increase stress responses. 
 
Figure 4 Final Angular Red restaurant. The color was changed from black to red and the visual complexity 
of the environment was increased. 
3.2.5 Measures of Environmental Perception 
To check whether the participants perceived the visual differences between the two 
environments two measures were used, the. Aesthetic and Stress Response (ASR) and the 


[Page 32]
23 
 
Affective and Spatial Experience (ASE). Participants’ perceptions of the aesthetic quality and 
stress response elicited by each restaurant environment were assessed using a modified version of 
the scale developed by Tawil et al., (2021) and Tawil et al. (2022). This scale consisted of 16 
bipolar adjective pairs presented on visual analog sliders (0-10). The adjective pairs assessed 
multiple dimensions of environmental perception including spatial qualities (e.g., “narrow-
spacious,” “closed-open”), aesthetic qualities (e.g., “ugly-beautiful,” “depressing-cheerful”), 
stress and affective responses (e.g., “stressful-calming,” “cold-warm”), and organizational 
properties (e.g., “chaotic-ordered,” “asymmetrical-symmetrical”). Higher scores indicated more 
positive ratings (e.g., more curved, more spacious, more calming).

Participants’ perceptions of the aesthetic quality and 
stress response elicited by each restaurant environment were assessed using a modified version of 
the scale developed by Tawil et al., (2021) and Tawil et al. (2022). This scale consisted of 16 
bipolar adjective pairs presented on visual analog sliders (0-10). The adjective pairs assessed 
multiple dimensions of environmental perception including spatial qualities (e.g., “narrow-
spacious,” “closed-open”), aesthetic qualities (e.g., “ugly-beautiful,” “depressing-cheerful”), 
stress and affective responses (e.g., “stressful-calming,” “cold-warm”), and organizational 
properties (e.g., “chaotic-ordered,” “asymmetrical-symmetrical”). Higher scores indicated more 
positive ratings (e.g., more curved, more spacious, more calming).  
Information Rate. Perceived visual complexity and information density of each 
environment were measured using a 14-item adaptation of Mehrabian and Russell’s (1974) 
information rate scale. Participants rated each environment on bipolar adjective pairs using visual 
analog sliders (0-10). Items assessed dimensions including variety (“varied-redundant”), 
complexity (“simple-complex”), novelty (“novel-familiar”), density (“dense-sparse”), 
organization (“patterned-random”), and other perceptual qualities relevant to environmental 
information load. This measure was included to verify that the Angular Red restaurant was 
perceived as having higher information rate (more complex, varied, and stimulating) compared to 
the Curved Green restaurant, consistent with theoretical predictions. 
3.2.6 Manipulation Check Results 
To verify the effectiveness of the visual design manipulations, independent samples t-
tests compared ratings between the Curved Green and Angular Red restaurant environments on 
key dimensions (Table 1). As intended, the Curved Green restaurant was rated significantly 
higher on having a curved (vs. angular) roof form, t(82) = –20.37, p < .001. The Curved Green 

[Page 33]
24 
 
environment was also perceived as significantly more spacious, t(82) = –5.11, p < .001, more 
familiar, t(82) = –3.32, p = .001, simpler, t(82) = –3.82, p < .001, more ordered, t(82) = –4.46, p < 
.001, more harmonious, t(82) = –5.16, p < .001, and more symmetrical, t(82) = –4.11, p < .001, 
than the Angular Red restaurant. These results confirmed that the two environments were 
perceived as intended, with the Curved Green restaurant characterized by curved roof and lower 
visual complexity and information rate, and the Angular Red restaurant characterized by angular 
roof and higher information rate.

3.3 Phase 2: Laboratory VR Pilot Study 
3.3.1 Participants 
Twenty participants were recruited from a large university in the North East USA 
through announcements on Viva Engage, the university’s internal community platform. A power 
analysis was conducted using GPower 3.1.9.4 and determined that a sample size of 20 has 80% 
power to detect a significant main effect of environment with an α=.05 and effect size of 0.28.  A 
total of 20 participants (9 men and 11 women) completed the study. Participants ranged in age 
from 18 to 65 years (M = 35.8). Most identified as right-handed (80%), with a small number 
reporting left-handedness (15%) or no preference (5%). 70% wore corrective glasses or contact 
lenses. Most participants identified as non-Hispanic (90%), and the sample included individuals 
identifying as White/Caucasian, Asian, and Mixed/Other ethnicities. Reported annual income 
levels varied widely, ranging from below $10,000 to above $90,000, indicating a 
socioeconomically diverse group. Participants received $10 compensation per session, totaling 
$30 for completing all three visits. Since one participant could not complete their visit 3 due to 
health issues, they were excluded from the analysis, leaving a total sample of N=19. Participants 
were eligible if they: 
• Were between ages 18-65 
• Were fluent in English 
• Were free of self-reported food allergies or sensitivities to study foods 
• Had no diagnosis of cognitive or physical disabilities that might affect appetite or eating 
behaviors 
• Had no diagnosis of disabilities affecting sensory proprioception related to virtual reality 
(e.g., severe motion sickness, vestibular disorders) 

[Page 35]
26 
 
• Were willing to fast for 3 hours prior to each study visit 
• Were able to attend three in-person laboratory sessions scheduled one week apart 
• Were willing to eat the food provided during the study as advertised in the recruitment 
flyer. 
3.3.2 Study Design 
This study employed a within-subjects, crossover design with repeated measures. Each 
participant experienced all three environmental conditions across three separate laboratory visits, 
each scheduled exactly one week apart. Visits occurred at participants’ typical meal times, 
between 11:00 AM - 2:00 PM for lunch sessions or 4:00 PM - 7:00 PM for dinner sessions, to 
ensure participants were appropriately hungry. The environmental conditions were 
counterbalanced across the three visits: 
• E1 (Control): A virtual reproduction of the physical lab’s actual physical environment, 
providing a neutral baseline condition 
• E2 (Curved Green): The restaurant featuring curved forms, green color palette, and low 
information rate 
• E3 (Angular Red): The restaurant featuring angular forms, red color palette, and high 
information rate 
Participants were randomly assigned to one of six possible condition orders using a 
random number generator to control for order effects: E1-E2-E3, E1-E3-E2, E2-E1-E3, E2-E3-
E1, E3-E1-E2, or E3-E2-E1. 

[Page 36]
27 
 
3.3.3 Mixed Reality System and other materials 
VR Hardware: The study utilized the Meta Quest Pro head-mounted display (HMD), 
which features high-resolution color pass-through cameras enabling mixed reality experiences.

3.3.3 Mixed Reality System and other materials 
VR Hardware: The study utilized the Meta Quest Pro head-mounted display (HMD), 
which features high-resolution color pass-through cameras enabling mixed reality experiences. 
This technology allows users to see real-world objects (including their hands and food) integrated 
seamlessly into virtual environments, preserving ecological validity while maintaining 
experimental control over the visual environment. 
Environment Rendering: All three virtual restaurant environments were developed using 
Unity Engine and optimized for the Meta Quest Pro’s specifications. Environments featured 
realistic lighting and rendering to enhance immersion and presence. The virtual spaces were 
designed to accommodate seated dining from a first-person perspective, matching the 
participant’s actual seated position in the laboratory (see Figure 5). 
 
Figure 5 E1, E2 and E3 environments as seen during the mixed-reality experiment. 
 
Food used during the study: To facilitate eating while wearing the VR headset and to 
standardize consumption measurement, foods were selected based on several criteria: ease of 
consumption with minimal messiness, and common foods consumed by the US population. The 
standardized meal included (see Figure 6 for food plating and Table 2 for the amount of food 
served): 
• Chicken nuggets 
• French fries 
• Corn 


[Page 37]
28 
 
• Grapes 
• Bread 
• Chocolate chip cookies 
• Condiments: Buffalo/BBQ sauce and ketchup 
• Water 
All food items were prepared fresh in the Health, Ingestive Behavior, and Technology 
(HIT) Laboratory kitchen immediately before each session. Portion sizes were standardized 
across all sessions and participants. Foods were served at warm on identical dishware for all 
conditions.

3.3.5 Measures 
Appetite and Satiety. Fullness Rating Questionnaire. Participants rated their current 
hunger, thirst, fullness, nausea, and prospective food consumption using a visual analog scale 
(VAS) anchored at 0 = not at all and 100 = extremely (Flint et al., 2000). Example items included 
“How hungry do you feel right now?” and “How full are you right now?” Ratings were recorded 
both before VR exposure and after meal completion to assess changes in appetite and satiety 
states. 
Emotional and Affective States. Positive and Negative Affect Schedule (PANAS; 
Watson et al., 1988). Twenty emotion adjectives (10 positive, 10 negative) were rated on a 5-
point scale from 1 = very slightly or not at all to 5 = extremely. Example items included 
interested, excited (positive affect), and distressed, upset (negative affect). Ten items were 
averaged to form each subscale. 
Pleasure–Arousal–Dominance (PAD; Mehrabian & Russell, 1974). Eighteen bipolar 
adjective pairs captured participants’ emotional responses to the VR environments on 9-point 
semantic differentials (–4 to +4). Example pairs included unhappy–happy (pleasure), excited–
calm (arousal), and controlled–in-control (dominance). Six items per dimension were averaged to 
yield pleasure, arousal, and dominance scores. The dominance score was measured for 
exploratory analysis and was not included in the main study analysis. 

[Page 39]
30 
 
State Anxiety Inventory (STAI-State; Spielberger et al., 1983). Twenty items (e.g., “I feel 
calm,” “I feel tense”) assessed current anxiety on a 4-point scale from 1 = not at all to 4 = very 
much so. Negatively worded items were reverse-coded, and all were averaged to form a total 
state-anxiety score. 
Environmental Perception and Experience. Aesthetic and Stress Response (ASR) and  
Affective and Spatial Experience (ASE) which were used in the online study was also used here. 
Presence. VR Presence was measured using a scale adapted from standard presence 
questionnaires (Slater et al., 1994; Hartman et al., 2015). 10 items assessed spatial presence (“I 
felt like I was actually in the café”). Participants rated items on 7-point scales (1 = strongly 
disagree to 7 = strongly agree). 
 
Perceived Realism, Natural Interaction, and Natural Eating (Visit 3). Three measures 
assessed participants’ subjective experience of the virtual reality setup after each session (Long et 
al., 2023). Natural Interaction (Natural_Interaction) included eight items evaluating how natural 
and intuitive participants found using their hands and interacting with food in the VR 
environment, as well as the responsiveness and comfort of the system (e.g., “How natural was 
your experience in the virtual environment using your hands and interacting with your food?”, 
“Did the virtual hands cause problems with reaching for or grabbing food?”, “Were there any 
observable delays between manipulating foods in the real world and the virtual interface?”, “How 
restrictive was the headset to your eating and drinking?”). Natural Eating (Natural_Eating) 
consisted of three items assessing how natural and comparable eating felt in VR compared to 
real-world dining (e.g., “How natural was eating in virtual reality compared to eating in the real 
world?”, “How comparable was eating in the immersive restaurant compared to a real-world 
restaurant?”). Perceived Realism (Real) was measured using two items assessing the visual 
realism of the environment and food (e.g., “The food looked realistic,” “The shape of the food in 

[Page 40]
31 
 
the virtual interface matched the shape of the food in the real world.”). All items were rated on 7-
point scales tailored to each question (e.g., 1 = not at all to 7 = extremely). 
Engagement (Visit 3). Engagement Questionnaire (Long et al., 2023).

text:
Natural Eating (Natural_Eating) 
consisted of three items assessing how natural and comparable eating felt in VR compared to 
real-world dining (e.g., “How natural was eating in virtual reality compared to eating in the real 
world?”, “How comparable was eating in the immersive restaurant compared to a real-world 
restaurant?”). Perceived Realism (Real) was measured using two items assessing the visual 
realism of the environment and food (e.g., “The food looked realistic,” “The shape of the food in 

[Page 40]
31 
 
the virtual interface matched the shape of the food in the real world.”). All items were rated on 7-
point scales tailored to each question (e.g., 1 = not at all to 7 = extremely). 
Engagement (Visit 3). Engagement Questionnaire (Long et al., 2023). Seven items 
measured attentional and motivational engagement during the VR tasks (e.g., “I found the tasks 
meaningful,” “I wanted to devote my full attention to the tasks”). Responses ranged from 1 = 
strongly disagree to 7 = strongly agree. Items were averaged to create an overall engagement 
score. 
Food Consumption. Each food item and water was weighed (in grams) before and after 
the meal using a digital scale. The difference determined the amount consumed. 
Eating-Behavior Measures (Visit 3). Reasons Individuals Stop Eating Questionnaire 
(RISE-Q; Cunningham et al., 2021). Assessed internal and external cues for meal termination on 
a 7-point scale (1 = not at all to 7 = very much). Example items included “I stopped eating 
because I felt physically full” and “The food was no longer appealing.” Subscales captured 
decreased food appeal, physical satisfaction, and planned amount. 
Adult Eating Behavior Questionnaire (AEBQ; Hunot et al., 2016). Thirty-five items 
measured stable appetitive traits across eight subscales such as food responsiveness (“When I see 
or smell food that I like, it makes me want to eat”), emotional overeating (EOE; “I eat more when 
I’m upset”), emotional undereating (EUE), and satiety responsiveness (“I get full up easily”). 
Items were rated on 5-point scales (1 = strongly disagree to 5 = strongly agree) and averaged by 
subscale. 
Three-Factor Eating Questionnaire (TFEQ-R18; Karlsson et al., 2000). Eighteen items 
assessed cognitive restraint, uncontrolled eating, and emotional eating (e.g., “I deliberately take 
small helpings to control my weight,” “Sometimes when I start eating, I just can’t seem to stop”). 
Responses were on 4-point scales (1 = definitely false to 4 = definitely true). Items were averages 
to create the subscale. 

[Page 41]
32 
 
External Food Cue Reactivity (EFCR; Finlayson et al., 2011). Nine items measured 
sensitivity to external food cues on 4-point scales (1 = rarely to 4 = a lot). Example items 
included “I want foods or drinks that I see others eating” and “I notice restaurant signs or logos.” 
Items were averaged to create a reactivity score. 
Comparative Evaluation (Visit 3 Only). After participants had experienced all three 
environments (pleasant, unpleasant, and control), they completed a comparative evaluation 
questionnaire. Items asked participants to directly compare the three environments on several 
dimensions of preference, comfort, and perceived healthiness of the eating atmosphere. 
Example items included: 
“Which environment did you prefer the most?” 
“In which environment did you feel the most relaxed while eating?” 
“Which restaurant design made the food seem healthier?” 
Responses were provided on 7-point Likert scales (1 = not at all to 7 = very much), and 
participants also ranked the environments from most to least preferred. Ratings were averaged to 
form indices of environmental preference, relaxation, and perceived healthiness. 
Internal Consistency. Internal consistency for all self-report scales was assessed using 
Cronbach’s alpha (α) for each visit and timepoint (see Table 3). Reliability for the Pleasure–
Arousal–Dominance (PAD) scale ranged from acceptable to excellent across sessions (α = .65–
.96). Specifically, the pleasure subscale demonstrated high internal consistency across all visits (α 
= .88–.96), while arousal showed moderate reliability (α = .59–.83), and dominance ranged from 
acceptable to good (α = .70–.83). The Positive and Negative Affect Schedule (PANAS) exhibited 
excellent reliability across visits and timepoints, with α values ranging from .89 to .95 for positive 
affect and .79 to .92 for negative affect. 
For environmental appraisal, the Aesthetic and Stress Response (ASR) scale 
demonstrated consistently high internal consistency across all visits (α = .84–.93). Among the VR 

[Page 42]
33 
 
experience measures, the Spatial Presence subscale demonstrated adequate reliability (α = .72–
.74), Involvement was acceptable (α = .61–.81), and Realism showed lower reliability at early 
sessions but improved by Visit 3 (α = .20–.65). 
Overall, the reliability values indicate that most self-report measures exhibited 
satisfactory internal consistency, with variability in subscales assessing physiological arousal and 
perceived realism.

Pre-Visit Preparation. Prior to Visit 1, participants completed online consent forms and 
demographic questionnaires via REDCap, a secure web-based data collection platform. 
Participants were instructed to refrain from eating or drinking anything except water for at 
least 3 hours prior to each visit to ensure comparable hunger levels across sessions. 
Visit 1 (Day 1). The procedure for the experiment is given below. 
1. Arrival and Verification (5 minutes): Upon arrival at the lab, the participant 
was greeted and verified adherence to the 3-hour fasting requirement.  
2. Baseline Assessment (10 minutes): Participants completed baseline 
questionnaires via a tablet using REDCap, assessing current hunger, thirst, fullness, 
nausea, state anxiety, and emotional state (PANAS, PAD). 
3. VR Orientation (5 minutes): The research assistant fitted the participant with 
the Meta Quest Pro headset and provided brief orientation to the device controls and 
pass-through functionality. This familiarization period ensured participant comfort with 
the technology. 
4. Environmental Exposure (2 minutes): The first environmental condition (as 
determined by random assignment) was presented. Participants spent 2 minutes freely 
exploring the virtual environment visually, becoming acclimated to the space. 
5. Post-Exposure Assessment (5 minutes): Participants removed the headset 
temporarily and completed questionnaires assessing emotional responses to the 
environment (state anxiety, PANAS, PAD). 
6. Eating Session (30 minutes): Participants donned the VR headset again and 
remained immersed in the virtual environment. The standardized meal was served, and 
participants were instructed to eat until comfortably full at their natural pace. A GoPro 
camera positioned in front of the participant recorded the eating session to enable future 
analysis of eating behaviors (bite count, chewing duration). Participants could see their 

[Page 44]
35 
 
hands and food through the headset’s pass-through cameras while perceiving the virtual 
restaurant environment surrounding them. The eating session lasted up to 30 minutes or 
however long they needed until the participant indicated fullness. 
7. Post-Meal Assessment (10 minutes): After completing the meal and removing 
the headset, participants completed final questionnaires including fullness ratings, ASR, 
ASE, presence and engagement measures. Remaining food was weighed to calculate 
consumption.  
Visit 2 (Day 8). The second visit occurred 7 days after Visit 1. The procedure was 
identical to Visit 1. The participant experienced the second environmental condition according to 
their assigned order The same standardized meal was served. 
Visit 3 (Day 15). The third visit occurred 7 days after Visit 2. The procedure 
matched Visit 2, with the participant experiencing the third and final environmental condition. 
Following the post-meal questionnaires, participants completed the RISE-Q, AEBQ, EFCR, 
TEFQ. Additionally, they also completed the comparative questions asking them to directly 
compare their experiences across the three environments they had encountered. The participant’s 
height and weight without shoes for body composition assessment was measured in the end.

All questionnaire data were collected electronically via REDCap and stored on secure, 
password-protected servers. Food intake data (pre- and post-meal food weights) were recorded 
manually and entered into a REDCap form. Video recordings were stored on onedrive with

4. Results 
4.1 Emotional Response Outcomes – H1 Partially Supported 
To assess the effect of the virtual restaurant environment on emotional responses, four 
linear mixed models were conducted with environment as a fixed effect and visit as a repeated 
measure, controlling for familiarity of the environment. The outcomes examined changes in 
pleasure, arousal, positive affect, and negative affect from pre- to post-exposure. 
4.1.1. Pleasure Change 
The effect of environment on change in pleasure was not statistically significant, F(2, 
38.64) = 1.32, p = .280. Familiarity also did not significantly predict pleasure change, F(1, 35.30) 
= 2.63, p = .114. 
4.1.2. Arousal Change 
Environment did not significantly affect change in arousal, F(2, 45.03) = 0.05, p = .954. 
Familiarity was not a significant predictor either, F(1, 43.17) = 2.47, p = .123. 
4.1.3. Positive Affect Change 
The effect of environment on change in positive affect was not significant, F(2, 35.90) = 
0.97, p = .391. However, familiarity significantly predicted increases in positive affect, F(1, 

[Page 47]
38 
 
43.69) = 6.17, p = .017, suggesting that environments that felt familiar to participants were 
associated with more positive emotional responses. 
4.1.4. Negative Affect Change 
The effect of environment on change in negative affect was statistically significant, F(2, 
44.48) = 3.91, p = .027. Specifically, participants in the Angular Red environment experienced 
greater increases in negative affect compared to the control environment, B = 0.519, SE = 0.199, 
p = .012. Familiarity did not significantly predict negative affect change, F(1, 44.10) = 2.22, p = 
.143. 
4.1.5. Summary of Emotional Findings 
Participants’ emotional responses to the VR restaurant environments revealed distinct 
patterns for positive and negative affect. While the environment itself did not significantly 
influence changes in positive affect, participants who reported higher familiarity with the 
environment experienced significantly greater increases in positive affect. This suggests that 
feelings of recognition or comfort within a space may enhance positive emotional reactions, 
regardless of the visual condition. 
In contrast, negative affect was significantly influenced by the environment, with the 
Angular Red environment leading to a greater increase in negative affect compared to the control. 
Importantly, this effect was independent of familiarity, which was not a significant predictor of 
negative affect change. These results imply that positive emotions may be shaped more by 
personal associations or comfort (familiarity), whereas negative emotions are more sensitive to 
the visual design features of the environment itself, such as angular geometry and red color 

[Page 48]
39 
 
palette. Thus, H1 was partially supported: while the Curved Green and Angular Red 
environments did not differ significantly on pleasure or arousal, the Angular Red environment did 
significantly increase negative affect. 
4.2 Effect of Environment on Food Consumption – H2 Not Supported 
A linear mixed-effects model was conducted to examine the effect of environment on 
food intake while controlling for pre-exposure nausea levels and individual differences, including 
BMI and eating behavior traits measured through the Adult Eating Behavior Questionnaire 
(AEBQ). The effect of environment on food intake was not statistically significant, F(2, 46.02) = 
0.322, p = .727.

environments did not differ significantly on pleasure or arousal, the Angular Red environment did

4.2 Effect of Environment on Food Consumption – H2 Not Supported 
A linear mixed-effects model was conducted to examine the effect of environment on 
food intake while controlling for pre-exposure nausea levels and individual differences, including 
BMI and eating behavior traits measured through the Adult Eating Behavior Questionnaire 
(AEBQ). The effect of environment on food intake was not statistically significant, F(2, 46.02) = 
0.322, p = .727. 
Estimated marginal means showed a nonsignificant trend in which participants consumed 
slightly more in the Angular Red environment (M = 440.84, SE = 23.34) than in the Curved 
Green (M = 420.18, SE = 21.86) or control (M = 416.60, SE = 22.22) conditions. These findings 
suggest that the virtual restaurant environment alone does not significantly influence food intake 
in this pilot study. Thus, H2 was not supported. 
However, emotional overeating (EOE)—a stable trait assessed via the AEBQ that 
captures individuals’ tendency to eat more in response to negative emotions—was a significant 
positive predictor of food intake, B = 68.75, SE = 30.31, p = .028. This indicates that individuals 
with higher trait-level tendencies toward emotional overeating consumed more food across all 
environments, regardless of the specific visual design condition. Emotional undereating (EUE), 
enjoyment of food (EF), BMI, and nausea levels did not significantly predict food consumption. 
Notably, although the Angular Red environment significantly increased negative affect 
(as reported in section 4.1), this emotional change did not translate into increased food 
consumption. This pattern contrasts with previous research showing correlations between 

[Page 49]
40 
 
negative emotional states and increased food intake (Macht, 2008; Newman et al., 2007). This 
discrepancy may reflect several factors: the relatively brief exposure duration (30 minutes), the 
counterbalancing of state-level emotional changes by stable individual traits (such as EOE), or the 
possibility that visual design features alone require accompanying multisensory cues (e.g., 
ambient sound, temperature, or olfactory stimuli) to produce measurable behavioral effects on 
eating. 
4.3 Mediation Analysis – H3 Not Supported 
A mediation analysis was conducted to examine whether negative affect change 
(mediator, M) mediates the relationship between the environment (independent variable, X) and 
food intake (dependent variable, Y). The environment variable was coded such that the Angular 
Red condition was compared to the Control condition, as this comparison showed the significant 
emotional effect. 
First, the total effect of the environment on food intake was assessed. The regression of 
food intake on the environment (Control vs. Angular Red) indicated that the total effect (c) was 
not statistically significant, B = −20.90, SE = 34.998, p = .553. 
Next, the effect of the environment on negative affect change (path a) was examined. The 
regression of negative affect change on the environment (Control vs. Angular Red) showed a 
statistically significant positive effect, B = 0.490, SE = 0.200, p = .014. This indicates that 
participants in the Angular Red environment experienced a significantly greater increase in 
negative affect compared to those in the Control environment, replicating the finding reported in 
section 4.1.4. 
Then, the effect of negative affect change on food intake, while controlling for the 
environment (path b), was assessed. The regression of food intake on both the environment and 

[Page 50]
41 
 
negative affect change revealed that negative affect change did not have a statistically significant 
effect on food intake, B = 13.524, SE = 20.519, p = .510. The direct effect of the environment on 
food intake (c′) remained non-significant, B = −25.691, SE = 35.908, p = .478. 
Finally, the indirect effect of the environment on food intake through negative affect 
change was calculated using the product of coefficients (a × b). The indirect effect was 6.627. 
Sobel’s test was performed to assess the statistical significance of this indirect effect. The Sobel 
test statistic was Z = 0.636, p = .524 (see Table 4 for all the regression coefficients). 
Given that the indirect effect was not statistically significant (p = .524), there is no 
evidence to support that negative affect change mediates the relationship between the 
environment (Control vs. Angular Red) and food intake. Neither the total effect nor the direct 
effect of the environment on food intake were statistically significant. Thus, H3 was not 
supported. Although the Angular Red environment successfully induced greater negative affect 
(path a), this emotional response did not translate into changes in eating behavior (path b), 
resulting in no significant mediation effect.

fairly consistent for most participants, but the underlying technical factors enabling that

[Page 53]

4.4.1. Effect of System Usability on Food Intake 
To assess whether usability factors influenced food intake, a linear mixed-effects model 
was conducted with environment (control, Curved Green, Angular Red) and Natural Interaction 
scores as predictors. Natural Interaction was selected as the predictor because it most 
comprehensively captures the technical factors that could facilitate or impede natural eating 
behavior (hand visibility, system lag, headset comfort). 
The analysis revealed that food intake was significantly influenced by Natural Interaction 
ratings (B = 1.301, p = .038). Participants who experienced smooth hand-tracking, minimal lag, 
and comfortable headset wear consumed more food, while those who struggled with technical 
difficulties consumed less. In contrast, the design of the environment (Curved Green, Angular 
Red, control) did not significantly affect food intake (p = .757), consistent with findings in 
section 4.2. 
This finding indicates that technical usability could potentially directly influence eating 
behavior. When participants experienced poor Natural Interaction—difficulty seeing their hands, 
noticeable delays, or discomfort from the headset—they likely ate less because the technical 
problems may have disrupted their ability to eat normally. Conversely, when the system worked 
smoothly, participants could engage in more natural eating patterns.

Chapter 5 
5. Discussion 
5.1 Overview of Findings 
This pilot study investigated whether visual design features of restaurant environments—
specifically curvilinear versus angular geometry combined with green versus red color palettes—
influence emotional responses and eating behavior in an immersive mixed reality setting. The 
research tested three hypotheses and one research question regarding environmental effects on 
emotion (H1), eating behavior (H2), emotional mediation (H3), and the validity of VR as a pre-
occupancy evaluation tool (RQ1). 
Results revealed a complex pattern of findings. Visual design significantly affected 
negative affect, with the Angular Red restaurant eliciting greater increases in negative emotions 
compared to the control environment, providing partial support for H1. However, environmental 
design did not significantly influence food consumption (H2), and emotional responses did not 
mediate the relationship between environment and eating behavior (H3). Notably, the technical 
usability of the VR system—particularly participants’ ratings of natural interaction—emerged as 
a significant predictor of food intake, while the environmental design conditions did not. These 
findings suggest that while mixed reality can effectively capture emotional responses to 
architectural features, achieving behavioral validity requires addressing technical challenges 
related to system usability. 
 

[Page 55]
46 
 
5.2 Environmental Design and Emotional Responses (H1) 
The finding that the Angular Red environment significantly increased negative affect 
aligns with established principles in environmental psychology and neuroaesthetics. Previous 
research has consistently shown that angular forms activate threat-detection neural pathways and 
elicit discomfort (Vartanian et al., 2019; Bar & Neta, 2006), while red coloring increases 
physiological arousal and can evoke stress responses (Elliot & Maier, 2014). The current study 
extends this work by demonstrating that these effects persist even in virtual environments and 
occur during a two-minute exposure to the VR environment. 
The specificity of this effect is noteworthy. The Angular Red environment increased 
negative affect but did not significantly alter pleasure, arousal, or positive affect compared to the 
Curved Green environment. This dissociation suggests that unpleasant design features may 
operate through a distinct emotional pathway—one that elevates feelings of discomfort, tension, 
or unease without necessarily reducing positive feelings or dramatically increasing physiological 
activation. The lack of significant differences in pleasure and arousal between conditions was 
unexpected given the theoretical basis for H1. Several factors may explain this pattern. First, the 
short duration of exposure could not given the time for development of positive feelings and 
activation of physiological arousal. Second, individual differences in aesthetic preferences—
which prior research shows can be substantial (Cotter et al., 2017)—may have introduced noise 
that obscured average treatment effects. Some participants may have found the Angular Red 
design exciting or interesting rather than aversive, particularly if they had personal or cultural 
associations with angular modernist architecture. 
An unexpected but important finding emerged regarding familiarity. While familiarity 
did not predict changes in negative affect, it significantly predicted increases in positive affect 
across all environments. This suggests that emotional comfort and recognition—feeling that a 

[Page 56]
47 
 
space is known or safe—may enhance positive emotional responses independent of the specific 
design features present. This finding has practical implications for architectural design: even 
spaces with less conventionally “pleasant” aesthetics may support positive emotional experiences 
if they feel familiar or culturally resonant to occupants. Future research should systematically 
manipulate both design features and familiarity to disentangle these effects. 
5.3 Environmental Design and Eating Behavior (H2 and H3) 
5.3.1 Why Visual Design Did Not Affect Food Intake 
The absence of significant environmental effects on food consumption is an interesting 
finding. Despite successfully manipulating negative affect, the Angular Red environment did not 
lead to increased food intake compared to the Curved Green or control conditions. Several factors 
may explain this null finding. 
Duration and Intensity of Emotional Experience. The eating sessions lasted 
approximately 30 minutes, which may have been insufficient for state-level emotional changes to 
translate into behavioral effects.

The results suggest that visual design can shape emotional experience, but may not directly impact eating behavior. Additionally, VR usability is found to be a critical factor in determining behavioral outcomes.

This finding has practical implications for architectural design: even 
spaces with less conventionally “pleasant” aesthetics may support positive emotional experiences 
if they feel familiar or culturally resonant to occupants. Future research should systematically 
manipulate both design features and familiarity to disentangle these effects. 
5.3 Environmental Design and Eating Behavior (H2 and H3) 
5.3.1 Why Visual Design Did Not Affect Food Intake 
The absence of significant environmental effects on food consumption is an interesting 
finding. Despite successfully manipulating negative affect, the Angular Red environment did not 
lead to increased food intake compared to the Curved Green or control conditions. Several factors 
may explain this null finding. 
Duration and Intensity of Emotional Experience. The eating sessions lasted 
approximately 30 minutes, which may have been insufficient for state-level emotional changes to 
translate into behavioral effects. Much of the research linking negative emotion to increased food 
intake involves chronic stress or sustained negative mood states (Macht, 2008; Wallis & 
Hetherington, 2009), whereas the current study induced relatively brief emotional responses 
during a single meal. Participants’ negative affect increased in the Angular Red environment, but 
this temporary emotional shift may not have reached the threshold needed to trigger emotional 
eating responses. 
Individual Differences Override Situational Effects. The finding that trait emotional 
overeating (EOE) significantly predicted food intake while environment did not suggests that 
stable individual characteristics may be more powerful determinants of eating behavior than 

[Page 57]
48 
 
situational environmental cues. Participants high in EOE consumed more food across all 
conditions, indicating that their dispositional tendency to eat in response to negative emotions 
outweighed any environment-induced emotional states. This pattern aligns with psychology 
research showing that traits often predict behavior more strongly than situational factors, 
particularly when situational manipulations are relatively subtle (Mischel & Shoda, 1995). 
Visual Cues Alone May Be Insufficient. The most theoretically important implication is 
that visual design features—geometry and color—may require accompanying multisensory cues 
to influence eating behavior. Real restaurant environments engage multiple sensory channels 
simultaneously: ambient sound levels, temperature, scent, lighting intensity (not just color), social 
presence, and tactile qualities of furniture and dishware. Previous research on restaurant 
atmospherics has shown that music tempo, lighting brightness, and ambient noise all 
independently influence eating pace and consumption (Milliman, 1986; Stroebele & De Castro, 
2004). Vision may be necessary but insufficient for shaping eating behavior when these other 
sensory channels are completely absent. 
Moreover, eating is a complex motivated behavior involving hunger signals, satiation 
mechanisms, food palatability, and learned associations—factors that may be less sensitive to 
ambient environmental aesthetics than behaviors like lingering, exploring, or purchasing. The 
environmental design may have needed to be far more extreme, or paired with other sensory 
manipulations, to overcome the homeostatic (appetite-based eating) and hedonic (reward-based 
eating) systems regulating food intake (Campos et al., 2022). 
5.3.2 Absence of Emotional Mediation 
The mediation analysis revealed that although environment affected negative affect, 
negative affect in turn did not predict food intake. This breaks the causal chain proposed by the 

[Page 58]
49 
 
Mehrabian-Russell model and suggests that emotion may not be the mechanism linking 
environment to eating behavior—at least not in the way hypothesized. 
This finding challenges the assumption that environmental effects on behavior 
necessarily operate through conscious emotional experience. Alternative pathways may exist. For 
example, environmental features could influence eating through cognitive mechanisms (attention, 
distraction, cognitive load) rather than emotional ones. The visual complexity and asymmetry of 
the Angular Red environment may have created cognitive interference without necessarily being 
processed as emotional distress. Participants may have eaten less efficiently or paused more 
frequently to orient to the unusual visual stimuli, but if asked, would not report feeling 
particularly distressed. 
Alternatively, the PAD and PANAS measures may not have captured the specific 
emotional dimensions relevant to eating behavior. These general affect scales assess global 
positive and negative mood but may miss discrete emotions like disgust, anxiety, or comfort that 
have more direct links to appetite and consumption. Future research should employ eating-
specific emotional measures or physiological indicators (heart rate variability, cortisol) that may 
better capture the stress responses theorized to link environment to eating. 
The absence of mediation also raises questions about temporal dynamics. Emotional 
responses were measured before and after the VR exposure, and before the VR eating experience 
but not continuously during eating or after. The environment may have influenced momentary 
emotional fluctuations during the meal that affected bite-by-bite consumption patterns, but these 
transient effects would not be captured by pre-post self-report scores. Experience sampling 
methods or continuous physiological monitoring could reveal dynamic emotional processes 
obscured by the current measurement approach. 

[Page 59]
50 
 
5.4 Implications for VR as an Evaluation Tool (RQ1) 
These findings provide a nuanced answer to RQ1 regarding the validity of immersive 
mixed reality for pre-occupancy evaluation. The results suggest that VR effectively captures 
emotional responses to architectural design features—the Angular Red environment significantly 
increased negative affect regardless of usability issues. However, behavioral validity depends 
critically on technical system performance. 
The substantial variability in Natural Interaction (SD = 22.21, range = 11-96.5) represents 
a significant methodological challenge. The fact that Natural Interaction significantly predicted 
food intake (p = .038) while environment did not (p = .757) suggests that technical factors 
overshadowed environmental design effects on behavior. Participants struggling with hand-
tracking problems, system lag, or headset discomfort likely had their eating behavior shaped more 
by these technical frustrations than by whether the restaurant had curved green forms or angular 
red geometry. 
The tight clustering of Natural Eating scores for most participants (despite the technical 
variability in Natural Interaction) suggests that many participants were able to adapt to eating 
with the headset on, achieving a moderately consistent experience. However, the outliers indicate 
this adaptation was not universal. More importantly, even when participants subjectively felt 
eating was “natural enough,” the underlying technical difficulties captured by Natural Interaction 
still influenced how much food they consumed. 
Therefore, while mixed reality shows promise for evaluating emotional and perceptual 
responses to architectural design, achieving behavioral validity requires ensuring consistently 
high technical performance across participants. The current system achieved moderate usability 
on average, but the wide variability—particularly in Natural Interaction—likely masked the 
effects of environmental design on eating behavior. Future VR eating studies should prioritize 

[Page 60]
51 
 
technical optimization, possibly implement minimum usability thresholds for participant 
inclusion, or a more time/one session to simply get used to the system when testing 
environmental effects on behavior. 
5.4.1 When VR Works and When It Doesn’t 
The divergent findings for emotional versus behavioral outcomes illuminate an important 
boundary condition for VR validity. VR appears well-suited for studying perceptual and 
emotional responses to architectural features because these responses depend primarily on visual 
information processing, which VR can effectively simulate. The visual cortex and limbic system 
respond to virtual stimuli similarly to real ones when immersion is sufficient (Slater, 2002), 
explaining why the Angular Red environment successfully triggered negative affect despite 
moderate realism ratings. 
Behavioral outcomes requiring fine motor control and proprioceptive feedback present 
greater challenges. Eating involves precise hand-eye coordination, tactile feedback from food 
textures, and unconscious adjustments based on visual and haptic information.

text:
5.4.1 When VR Works and When It Doesn’t 
The divergent findings for emotional versus behavioral outcomes illuminate an important 
boundary condition for VR validity. VR appears well-suited for studying perceptual and 
emotional responses to architectural features because these responses depend primarily on visual 
information processing, which VR can effectively simulate. The visual cortex and limbic system 
respond to virtual stimuli similarly to real ones when immersion is sufficient (Slater, 2002), 
explaining why the Angular Red environment successfully triggered negative affect despite 
moderate realism ratings. 
Behavioral outcomes requiring fine motor control and proprioceptive feedback present 
greater challenges. Eating involves precise hand-eye coordination, tactile feedback from food 
textures, and unconscious adjustments based on visual and haptic information. Even small 
technical imperfections—slight lag, hand-tracking drift, or limited peripheral vision—can disrupt 
these motor sequences. The current passthrough system, while innovative, could potentially not 
fully replicate the seamless sensorimotor integration of natural eating. This distinction has 
important implications for architectural research. VR may be valid for pre-occupancy evaluations 
focused on: 
• Aesthetic preferences and emotional responses 
• Wayfinding and spatial cognition 
• Perceived spaciousness, brightness, or visual complexity 
• Approach-avoidance intentions and attitudes 

[Page 61]
52 
 
But may require substantial technical refinement before reliably capturing: 
• Fine motor behaviors (typing, manipulating objects, eating) 
• Behaviors sensitive to thermal comfort, acoustic or other multisensory properties 
• Long-duration activities where headset discomfort accumulates 
5.4.2 Recommendations for Future VR Research 
Based on these findings, researchers using VR for behavioral research should: Report and 
control for usability variance. System usability should be measured and included as a covariate or 
moderator in analyses, not assumed to be constant across participants. Establish minimum 
usability criteria. Consider excluding participants who report very poor usability (e.g., Natural 
Interaction scores below 40) or analyzing subgroups who achieved adequate usability separately. 
Match methodology to research question. Use VR confidently for perceptual and emotional 
outcomes but exercise caution when behavioral fidelity is critical. For behaviors requiring fine 
motor control, pilot testing with behavioral validation is essential. 
Prioritize technical optimization. Invest in high-quality hand tracking, minimize system 
lag, ensure comfortable headsets, and conduct extensive pilot testing focused on usability rather 
than assuming the technology works uniformly well.  
5.5 Limitations 
Several limitations constrain the interpretation and generalizability of these findings. 
Sample Size and Statistical Power. With 20 participants providing 57 valid 
observations across conditions, this pilot study had limited statistical power to detect small or 
moderate effect sizes. The nonsignificant trends observed (e.g., slightly higher consumption in the 

[Page 62]
53 
 
Angular Red environment) may represent real effects that would reach significance with larger 
samples. The null findings for H2 and H3 should therefore be interpreted cautiously—they 
indicate absence of evidence rather than evidence of absence. Future research should conduct 
power analyses based on these effect size estimates to determine adequate sample sizes. 
Technical Limitations of VR System. As discussed extensively, the substantial 
variability in system usability represents a major limitation. The moderate mean usability scores 
and wide individual differences suggest the technology had not yet reached the maturity needed 
for seamless behavioral research. Future studies will benefit from rapidly improving VR 
hardware, including higher-resolution displays, better hand tracking, lighter headsets, and more 
sophisticated passthrough systems. The findings regarding VR validity are necessarily time-
bound and may not apply to next-generation systems. 
Measurement Limitations. The study relied on self-report measures of emotion 
collected pre- and post-meal rather than continuous assessment. This approach may have missed 
dynamic emotional fluctuations during eating. Physiological measures (heart rate variability, skin 
conductance, cortisol) would provide objective emotional indicators less subject to demand 
characteristics. Additionally, the PAD and PANAS scales assess general affect rather than eating-
specific emotions (food-related anxiety, disgust, comfort), which may have obscured relevant 
emotional pathways. 
Ecological Validity Constraints. Despite efforts to create realistic eating scenarios, 
several factors limited ecological validity beyond the VR system itself. Participants ate alone in a 
laboratory setting rather than with social companions in a real restaurant. The standardized meal, 
while common foods, may not have matched participants’ preferences. The 30-minute duration 
and scheduled timing, while controlling for hunger levels, constrained natural meal pacing. The 
novelty of eating in VR may have created demand characteristics or distraction effects. All these 
factors likely suppressed the sensitivity of eating behavior to environmental manipulations. 

[Page 63]
54 
 
Design Feature Confounding. The Curved Green and Angular Red environments 
differed on multiple dimensions simultaneously—geometry (curved vs. angular), color (green vs. 
red), visual complexity, and overall pleasantness. While this multivariate approach creates 
maximally differentiated environments, it prevents attribution of effects to specific features. The 
significant effect on negative affect could be driven by angularity, redness, high visual 
complexity, or their interaction. Factorial designs systematically varying individual features 
would clarify which specific design elements drive emotional and behavioral responses. 
5.6 Future Directions 
This pilot study opens several promising research directions for environmental psychology, 
public health, and architectural practice. 
5.6.1 Multimodal Sensory Environments 
Future research should test whether adding non-visual sensory cues enhances 
environmental effects on eating behavior. Studies could systematically add: 
• Acoustic environments: Ambient nature sounds in the Curved Green restaurant versus 
harsh industrial sounds in the Angular Red environment 
• Olfactory cues: Pleasant scents (lavender, vanilla) versus neutral or unpleasant odors 
• Thermal variation: Comfortable warmth versus cooler temperatures 
• Tactile elements: Soft, curved furniture versus hard, angular seating 
This multimodal approach would better approximate real restaurant experiences and test 
whether visual design effects emerge when supported by congruent sensory information across 
modalities. Based on research showing that multisensory congruence enhances flavor perception 

[Page 64]
55 
 
and eating enjoyment (Spence, 2020a), combining visual, auditory, and olfactory cues may be 
necessary to shift consumption behavior. 
5.6.2 Non-architectural Cues and Marketing Ecology 
Beyond architectural geometry and color, real dining settings layer numerous commercial 
and marketing cues that shape consumption: food advertising and signage, menu board salience 
with pictures of food, open/visible food counters, and promotional prompts at tables or checkout. 
Future studies should embed these elements into the immersive environments to test how 
marketing cues interact with architectural features. For instance, visible counters and dynamic 
food displays may amplify approach tendencies even in visually “unpleasant” rooms. A factorial 
VR study design that crosses form/color with marketing visibility/intensity (e.g., ad presence, 
counter sightlines, motion/display frequency) would reveal whether commercial affordances 
moderate or outweigh architectural effects on eating behavior. This would move the work from 
testing isolated design variables to modeling the full decision ecology that real diners encounter. 
5.6.3 Extended Exposure Studies 
The 30-minute exposure duration may have been insufficient for environmental effects to 
accumulate. Longitudinal studies examining repeated exposures over days or weeks would reveal 
whether environmental features influence eating behavior when people adapt to and become 
familiar with a space. Research on environmental habituation suggests that initial emotional 
responses often diminish with repeated exposure (Ulrich, 1984), but behavioral habits may 
develop over longer timescales.

5.6.3 Extended Exposure Studies 
The 30-minute exposure duration may have been insufficient for environmental effects to 
accumulate. Longitudinal studies examining repeated exposures over days or weeks would reveal 
whether environmental features influence eating behavior when people adapt to and become 
familiar with a space. Research on environmental habituation suggests that initial emotional 
responses often diminish with repeated exposure (Ulrich, 1984), but behavioral habits may 
develop over longer timescales. Studies could compare: 
• Single-meal exposures (current study) versus week-long exposures 

[Page 65]
56 
 
• Cumulative effects across multiple visits to the same environment 
• Whether habituation to the emotional effects occurs but behavioral effects persist 
This approach would better model real-world scenarios where people eat repeatedly in 
the same environment (workplace cafeterias, home dining rooms) rather than experiencing novel 
restaurant designs. 
5.6.4 Individual Difference Moderators 
The finding that trait emotional overeating predicted consumption while environment did 
not suggests that environmental effects may vary substantially across individuals. Future research 
should examine moderators including: 
• Eating behavior types: Restrained eaters, emotional eaters, external eaters may show 
different sensitivity to environmental cues 
• Aesthetic sensitivity: Individuals with high aesthetic responsiveness may be more 
affected by design features 
• Interoceptive awareness: People more attuned to internal hunger and satiety signals may 
be less influenced by external environmental cues 
• Cultural background: Aesthetic preferences and eating norms vary across cultures, 
potentially moderating environmental effects. This could also affect taste/diet preference 
as well. 
Person × environment interaction designs could identify which individuals benefit most from 
health-promoting environmental design and which are relatively insensitive to these features. 

[Page 66]
57 
 
5.6.5 Real-World Implementation Studies 
While VR enables experimental control, field studies testing environmental interventions 
in actual restaurants, cafeterias, or dining halls are needed to establish ecological validity and 
practical impact. Quasi-experimental designs could: 
• Compare consumption before versus after environmental renovations 
• Test different design features across multiple locations 
• Examine long-term behavior change and habituation 
These studies would bridge the gap between laboratory findings and real-world implementation, 
identifying whether environmental design represents a scalable public health intervention. 
5.6.6 Mechanism Studies 
Understanding how environmental features influence emotion and behavior requires 
process-focused research examining: 
 
• Attention patterns: Eye-tracking studies measuring where people look in different 
environments and whether visual attention mediates emotional or behavioral responses 
• Cognitive load: Testing whether complex or unpleasant environments create cognitive 
interference that disrupts eating self-regulation 
• Physiological pathways: Measuring heart rate, cortisol, and other stress biomarkers to 
identify physiological mechanisms linking environment to eating 
• Temporal dynamics: Experience sampling methods capturing moment-to-moment 
fluctuations in emotion and eating across the meal 

[Page 67]
58 
 
These mechanism studies would refine theoretical models and identify intervention 
targets more precisely. 
5.6.7 VR Technology Validation 
Given the critical importance of system usability, dedicated validation studies should:  
• Compare eating behavior in VR versus matched physical environments to establish 
criterion validity 
• Test next-generation VR systems with improved hand tracking and display technology 
• Test other VR systems that are not completely immersive, such as CAVE (Cave 
Automatic Virtual Environment) systems, which allow users to experience virtual 
environments without wearing a headset, thereby reducing physical discomfort and 
improving natural interaction during eating tasks 
• Develop standardized usability benchmarks for VR eating research 
• Examine whether familiarization training reduces usability variance across participants 
This methodological work would establish best practices for VR behavioral research and 
identify when VR has achieved sufficient fidelity for behavioral applications.  

[Page 68]
59 
 
Chapter 6 
6. Conclusions 
This pilot study found that visual design features—specifically angular geometry and red 
color versus curvilinear forms and green tones—significantly influenced emotional responses but 
not eating behavior in a mixed reality restaurant environment. The Angular Red environment 
increased negative affect, supporting theories from environmental psychology and 
neuroaesthetics regarding human responses to architectural form and color. However, these 
emotional changes did not translate into altered food consumption, and individual differences in 
emotional eating tendencies were stronger predictors of intake than environmental conditions. 
The findings suggest that environmental design effects on complex behaviors like eating 
may require multisensory integration, extended exposure, or particular individual characteristics 
to manifest. Visual features alone, experienced for a single meal, produced reliable emotional 
differentiation but insufficient behavioral impact to overcome homeostatic regulation and stable 
individual differences in eating style. 
Importantly, the usability of the VR system emerged as a critical factor, with technical 
performance predicting eating behavior more strongly than environmental design. This highlights 
both the promise and the current limitations of VR for behavioral research: while effective for 
capturing emotional and perceptual responses, behavioral validity depends on achieving 
consistently high technical quality across participants. 
Future research should extend these findings by testing multimodal sensory 
environments, examining extended exposures, identifying individual difference moderators, and 
validating VR methods against real-world outcomes. As VR technology continues to improve, it 
holds significant promise as a tool for evidence-based architectural design—enabling researchers 

[Page 69]
60 
 
and practitioners to test how built environments influence human health and well-being before 
committing resources to construction. 
Despite its limitations and null findings for the primary behavioral hypothesis, this pilot 
study makes three important contributions to environmental psychology, public health, and 
architectural research. 
6.1 Empirical Contributions 
Causal Evidence for Environmental Effects on Emotion. The finding that the Angular 
Red environment significantly increased negative affect provides experimental evidence that 
architectural features causally influence emotional experience. Most prior research has been 
correlational or based on preference ratings rather than emotional responses during actual 
activities. This study demonstrates that geometric form and color influence emotion even during a 
goal-directed behavior (eating), not just during passive observation. 
Null Findings Inform Theory. The absence of effects on eating behavior, while 
unexpected, provides important theoretical information. It suggests that environmental effects on 
complex motivated behaviors may be smaller, more conditional, or operate through different 
pathways than effects on simpler outcomes like approach-avoidance or aesthetic preference. This 
challenges overly simplistic interpretations of the Mehrabian-Russell framework and points 
toward more nuanced models incorporating individual differences, multisensory integration, and 
behavioral specificity. 
Usability as a Critical Moderator. The finding that VR system usability significantly 
predicted eating behavior while environmental design did not represent a methodological 
contribution for the growing field of VR research. It demonstrates that technical factors can 

[Page 70]
61 
 
overwhelm or obscure the substantive variables researchers intend to study. This highlights the 
need for VR validation studies and usability reporting in behavioral research. 
6.2 Practical Contributions 
Evidence-Based Design Guidance. While the study did not find effects on eating 
quantity, the emotional findings have practical relevance for restaurant and dining hall design. 
Environments featuring angular geometry and red color schemes may create discomfort or 
negative affect even if they do not directly alter consumption. For settings where positive 
emotional experience is valued (fine dining, healthcare facilities, residential dining), curvilinear 
forms and calmer color palettes may enhance user experience.
