text:
When browsing the web, user interaction with a website 
is more important for the user experience than only viewing [50]. 
Nevertheless, frst impressions are formed while initially visiting a 
website by passive viewing, which is close to our screenshot assess-
ment. By viewing screenshots rather than interacting with websites, 
participants would use less cognitive capacities [10] and thus there 
was less interference with measuring processing fuency. Still, to 
enhance the ecological validity of the fndings, future studies need 
to go beyond viewing screenshots to include actual interactions 
CHI EA ’23, April 23–28, 2023, Hamburg, Germany Jan Pre�ler et al. 
and performance measures of usability. The latter would also be 
desirable to avoid common-method bias. 
Third, the participants were university students, and, in our 
case, the sample was biased towards young, computer-savvy and 
predominantly female participants. As this is not representative 
of the general website user population, further research should 
include broader samples. 
6 CONCLUSIONS AND FUTURE WORK 
The present work was the frst to investigate the role of processing 
fuency in explaining the aesthetic-usability efect. A set of fuent 
and disfuent city websites was selected from a larger pool of web-
sites in a pre-study to manipulate fuency. This set was shown to 
participants who rated these on perceived aesthetics, perceived 
usability and processing fuency. We not only found that perceived 
fuency, perceived aesthetics, and perceived usability were highly in-
terrelated, but that controlling for processing fuency considerably 
diminished the aesthetic-usability efect. In addition, the fuency 
manipulation led to a distinction between aesthetic and unaesthetic 
as well as usable and unusable websites, thereby showing a causal 
relationship between fuency and aesthetics/usability. Although 
further research is necessary to address the limitations of this study, 
it seems that the repeatedly found aesthetic-usability efect can be 
explained by processing fuency as a third factor underlying both 
aesthetics and usability judgements. Instead of "what is beautiful is 
usable" [49], we should better say, "mind at ease makes beautiful 
and usable" (cf. [55]). 
This change in perspective on what lies behind the aesthetic-
usability efect has immediate practical implications. As it is not 
aesthetics that drives perceived usability, designers should not try 
to manipulate aesthetics to make things appear more usable. Rather, 
they should enhance the processing fuency of an interface to shape 
both aesthetics and usability. Fluency research has found several 
parameters that infuence the processing fuency of a design, e.g., 
visual complexity, visual contrast or typographical legibility [1]. 
The feld of fuency research ofers a range of correlates of pro-
cessing fuency that are relevant to HCI. Among these are credi-
bility and trust, preference and liking, the perception of risk and 
customer loyalty [1, 12, 42]. Without fuency as the explaining vari-
able, we might fall for other apparent but spurious correlations 
among these factors. We would propose, for example, an aesthetic-
trust efect, a usability-risk efect, or a preference-loyalty efect, 
but behind all these, processing fuency would be the third explain-
ing factor. While these efects are mainly speculative at present, 
it shows that HCI can possibly gain more than an explanation of 
the aesthetic-usability efect by intensifying the investigation of 
processing fuency in the future.

metadata.core_insight_en: This text explores the interplay between aesthetic perception and usability judgment, drawing from studies that highlight how cognitive fluency, design aesthetics, and metacognitive experiences influence user perceptions of both the attractiveness and functionality of products or interfaces. Notably, research underscores that ease of processing and aesthetic appeal significantly affect perceived usability and overall user satisfaction.

text:
Mediation analysis. This paper uses the Preacher and
Hayes' (2004) Bootstrap method to test for moderated mediation
effects. We set a bootstrap sample size of 5000 and selected 95%
confidence intervals using model 8 (color = 0, BW = 1; utilitarian
appeal = 0, hedonic appeal = 1). The results indicated that the moder-
ated mediation effect was statistically significant (index = 0.51, 95%
CI = 0.2076, 0.9202; see detail in Figure 4). In addition, the mediation
effect of luxuriousness was significant for ad appeals focusing on
hedonic content (indirect effect = 0.55, 95% CI = 0.3136, 0.8287)
but not for those focusing on functional content (indirect effect = 0.04,
95% CI = /C00.2133, 0.2771). This result showed that luxuriousness
plays a mediator in the relationship between color design and ad eval-
uation when ad appeals focus on hedonic content, supporting H4.
4.4 | Discussion
Study 2 provides evidence for the hypothesis that color designs that
interact with ad appeal influence ad evaluations. We prove that the
effect of BW on ad evaluation is significant when ad appeal focuses
on hedonics, and luxuriousness mediates this relationship. However,
some limitations remain with Study 2. Next, we further examine the
robustness of the relationship using different manipulated scenarios
and investigate whether special color can improve consumers' evalua-
tions toward luxury ads.
5 | STUDY 3
In the luxury industry, many major brands have a signature color code
that is often expressed in their products. For instance, Fendi applies a
design code of yellow to all aspects of its products, from bags and
watches to perfumes. Dior prefers gray, believing it suits everything
and looks stylish in any situation. Beige is a classic and leading color
for the Burberry brand. Consumers associate specific colors with
brands, and when they see, hear or think of a brand, memories associ-
ated with particular colors are activated in their brains (Quillian, 1967;
Tavassoli, 2012). More importantly, these iconic colors, in turn,
become important identifiers for the brand and can greatly enhance
brand authenticity, as they are often rooted in the essence of the
brand, stemming from the brand's historical heritage (Clerc, (2018,
November 20)). Therefore, the purpose of Study 3 was to investigate
the differences in the impact of iconic colors, noniconic colors and
BW on ad evaluations. In this study, Tiffany was chosen as the target
FIGURE 3 The interaction of color design and ad appeal on ad
evaluation (Study 2)
WANG ET AL . 7

[Page 8]
brand since it is associated with blue and ignites countless women's
dreams with this signature color.
5.1 | Design and participants
This study employed a three-level one-factor between-subjects
design (color design: BW vs. iconic color vs. noniconic color). Color
design was the independent variable, and ad evaluation was the
dependent variable. Similar to Study 2, 170 adult participants across
mainland China were recruited from Sojump in exchange for a minor
monetary compensation. In addition, as the stimulus of this study was
specific to women, we selected only female participants. Fifteen par-
ticipants were excluded for failing the attention test. Overall, we
obtained 155 valid samples. Among them, 72.3% were 18 –25 years
old; participants with college degrees accounted for 92.3%, and par-
ticipants with monthly income in the CNY 3000 –8000 range
accounted for 79.4%. The value of G*Power was 0.99 (>0.80) after
setting group number of the ANOVA as 3, sample size as 155, and the
effect size ( f ) as 0.4 within the 95% confidence interval.
At the beginning of the study, participants were asked to imagine
that they were planning to purchase a watch for themselves and were
browsing an online magazine for the new Tiffany watches soon to be
available. Following the method of previous studies, each ad is designed
as BW, noniconic color or iconic color. For all three conditions, we only
used the hedonic appeal because the effect of BW is only manifest with
the hedonic appeal. Specifically, hedonic appeals highlight the sensory-
social benefits of the product (i.e., a watch with a classic style makes
you feel luxurious and prestigious; see detail in AppendixC). After that,
participants were asked to assess the luxuriousness ( α = .90;
Hagtvedt & Patrick, 2008), uniqueness ( α = .81; Park et al., 2020),
authenticity (α = .94; Napoli et al., 2014) and ad evaluations ( α = .92;
Park & Hadi, 2020) adopted by Study 1. Finally, to successfully manipu-
late ad appeals, color iconicity and ad colors, participants reported the
focus of advertising appeals (two items like Study2), to what extent they
viewed the color as iconic to the brand (1 = n o ta ta l l ,7= very much),
and the color of the advertisement (1 = definitely color, 7 = definitely
black-and-white; Wang et al., 2020). In addition, participants answered
the level of brand familiarity (1 = “extremely unfamiliar, ” and
7 = “extremely familiar”), fondness (1= “dislike extremely,” and 7 = “like
very much”) and demographic variables.
5.2 | Results
Manipulation check. The result of manipulation checking shows that
the mean score of hedonic rating is higher than the mean score of util-
itarian rating ( Mhedonic rating = 5.12, SD = 1.42; Mutilitarian rating = 2.74,
SD = 1.20; t [154] = 15.41, p < .001). The mean color scores in the
BW condition were significantly higher than those in the color condi-
tion ( MBW = 5.41, SD = 1.32; Mcolor = 2.62, SD = 1.22; F
(1,153) = 162.82; p < .001, η2
p = 0.52). In addition, the mean score for
the perception of color iconicity was higher in the iconic color condi-
tion than in the other conditions ( Miconic color = 5.20, SD = 1.21; Mnon-
iconic color = 2.87, SD = 1.64; F(1,153) = 80.12, p < .001, η2
p = 0.34).
Ad evaluations. The results show that the main effect of color
design (BW vs. iconic color vs. noniconic color) on the ad evaluations
is significant ( F(2, 150) = 18.63; p < .001, η2
p = 0.19) after controlling
for brand familiarity and likeability.

5.3 | Mediation analysis
Using the Bootstrap method of Preacher and Hayes' (2004), we con-
ducted a serial mediation model (model6, bootstrap sample size of
5000 and 95% bias-corrected confidence intervals) to investigate the
relationship between color design (non-iconic color = 0, BW = 1),
unique/authenticity (M1), luxuriousness (M2) and ad evaluations. The
results showed that the direct effect of BW (vs. color) on ad evalua-
tions was no longer significant after adding authenticity and luxurious-
ness ( β = .06, SE = 0.09, p > .05), while the indirect mediation of
color design ! authenticity ! luxuriousness ! ad evaluations was
significant (indirect effect = 0.23, 95% CI = 0.1349, 0.4017). Similarly,
when entering the uniqueness and luxuriousness, the direct effect of
BW (vs. color) on ad evaluations was not significant ( β = .12,
SE = 0.08, p > .05), while the indirect mediation of color des-
ign ! uniqueness ! luxuriousness ! ad evaluations was significant
(indirect effect = 0.14, 95% CI = 0.0610, 0.2696; see detail in
Figure 6). It follows that authenticity/uniqueness and luxuriousness
play a multi-chain mediating role in the effect of BW on evaluations
of luxury brand ads.
5.4 | Discussion
By introducing iconic color conditions, Study3 provides a deeper
understanding for the color effect of luxury ads. The results show that
BW is optimally effective for luxury brand ads, followed by iconic
colors and noniconic colors. Furthermore, the analysis of luxurious-
ness, uniqueness and authenticity shows that BW induces consumers
to perceive both authenticity and uniqueness, increasing their percep-
tion of the luxuriousness of products. However, iconic color can only
enhance consumers' perceptions of authenticity, and thus, its effect
on ad evaluations is relatively weak compared with BW.
6 | GENERAL DISCUSSION
Through theoretical and empirical analysis, we investigated the effect
of color design on a product's luxury brand ad evaluation and the
moderating role of ad appeals on this relationship.
Our findings are as follows: first, color designs (BW vs. color) can
influence consumers' perception of products' luxuriousness and luxury
brand ad evaluations. Compared to color design, BW designs can
induce consumers' perception of luxuriousness of products, increasing
their evaluations of luxury ads (Study 1). Second, color designs inter-
act with ad appeals to influence consumers' evaluation of luxury
brands, such that the effect of BW inducing luxuriousness and posi-
tive ad evaluations is manifest for ad appeals that highlight hedonic
brands (Study 2). Third, BW designs are most effective in enhancing
the advertising of luxury brands, followed by iconic colors and non-
iconic colors (Study 3). To robustly test the results, we used different
samples (e.g., student and nonstudent samples) and stimuli (e.g., men's
and women's wear, bags and watch) in the three studies. The results
show that the effect of BW is consistent across different manipulated
scenarios.

manship. In addition, for brands that are associated with a specific
color, a more subtle way to achieve successful communication is to
infuse their iconic colors in hedonistic ad appeals. Taken together,
color is one of the most flexible, versatile and creative elements in
ads, and how to use it to shape brand impressions is an important
issue for luxury brands.
6.3 | Limitations and future research
The current paper has a number of limitations that require further
improvement and exploration. First, personal consumer traits
(e.g., independent vs. interdependent self) are likely to influence the
effect of BW on consumers' evaluations of luxury brand ads. Previous
research has shown that interdependent individuals value relation-
ships and social connections with others (Bettman & Escalas, 2005;
Torelli, 2006), and thus, the impact of BW on perceived luxuriousness
and ad evaluations may be diminished for them. Therefore, a possible
research direction in the future is to investigate how self-construal
affects the impact of BW (vs. color) on consumers' perceptions.
Second, the luxury products in all three studies emphasize self-
presentation or self-improvement, such as clothing, leather goods or
watches. We note whether our results apply to other luxury catego-
ries used for relationship construction (e.g., wedding rings). In addi-
tion, the effects of BW on luxuriousness may not apply to high-class
vegetables and fruits, which require vivid color to enhance perceived
attractiveness (Schifferstein et al., 2017). Although our three studies
examined different types of products and provided a more practical
application scenario for our findings, they still neglected other types
of luxury goods. Therefore, more studies involving different product
types and manipulated scenarios may be needed in the future to
explore the boundary conditions of our findings.
Third, the current study does not provide additional evidence that
would rule out alternative explanations for the interaction between ad
appeals and color design. Although our study has confirmed that per-
ceived luxuriousness mediates the interactions of color design
(BW vs. color) and ad appeals (hedonic vs. utilitarian) on ad evaluation,
there may be other theoretical perspectives that could explain our
findings. For example, according to previous research, BW evokes
high-level construal, while color evokes low-level construal (Lee
et al., 2014, 2017; Stillman et al., 2020). Thus, under a BW (vs. color)
design, consumers are more likely to choose hedonic (vs. functional)
appeals because high (vs. low) levels of interpretation lead individuals
to prefer abstract (vs. concrete) information (Liberman et al., 2007;
Trope & Liberman, 2010). As such, construal level theory may poten-
tially be a theoretical mechanism to explain the interactive role of
color cues and ad appeals on consumers' ad evaluations and should
not be excluded from future research. Furthermore, the choice of the
particular color (especially in Study 3, the color pink) may have
influenced the experiment results. For example, colors (e.g., gold or
brown for a watch) that match the product or that have previously
appeared frequently in product ads may produce an effect similar to
iconic colors. Therefore, future studies could choose more other
colors to explore the color effect of luxury ad.

Considering the impact of medicine label design
characteristics on patient safety
E. HELLIER*, J. EDWORTHY, N. DERBYSHIRE and A. COSTELLO
Centre for Thinking and Language, School of Psychology, University of Plymouth,
Plymouth, Devon PL4 8AA, UK
Medication errors involving patients receiving the wrong medicines, the
wrong dosages or failure to take medicines according to the prescribed
schedule are a substantial threat to patient safety. In the medical domain,
research evidence on the beneﬁts of improved labelling are piecemeal and
often single-product or single-manufacturer driven and often do not inform
the more general process of label design. Government and other guidelines on
this topic are often low level and non-speciﬁc, often failing to give evidence-
based guidance. However, there is a wealth of evidence-based research
ﬁndings in related areas such as food labelling, chemical labelling and more
general warnings research, which can provide systematic evidence on the
eﬀects of design characteristics such as font size, colour, signal words and
linguistic usage on crucial performance variables such as compliance,
understandability and discriminability. This research is reviewed and its
relevance to medicine labelling is presented.
Keywords: Patient safety; Label design; ‘Warning’ labels
1. Introduction
Medication errors, in which patients receive the wrong medicine, the wrong dosage of
medicine or do not take medicines according to the prescribed schedule, represent an
important threat to patient safety. They are a common form of medical error with one
estimate suggesting that they accounted for 7000 deaths in the USA during 1993 alone
(e.g. Kohn et al . 1999). Medication errors can arise through the preparation or
administration of drugs, at the point of pharmacy dispensing, or from the use of medicines
by patients in the home. While the causes of medication errors are numerous, the
characteristics of medicine labelling and packaging are increasingly being implicated as
one causal factor. For example, Berman (2004) estimates that 33% of medication errors
can be attributed to packaging or labelling confusions. Similarly, Orser (2000) reports that
confusing, inaccurate or incomplete labelling contributed to 21% of drug errors reported
through the US Pharmacopoeia Practitioners’ Reporting Network in 1999. Orser et al .

metadata.core_insight_en: Medication errors occur due to various reasons including wrong medication, dosage, or failure to take medication as prescribed. Research suggests that improved labelling can reduce these errors. The study reviews evidence-based research findings from areas such as food labelling, chemical labelling, and warnings research to inform the design of medicine labelling. The analysis highlights the importance of design characteristics such as font size, colour, signal words, and linguistic usage in improving compliance, understandability, and discriminability.

text:
[Page 3]
(2001) surveyed the medication errors experienced by Canadian anaesthesiologists. They
found that ‘syringe swaps’ were the most common type of medication error and that label
misidentiﬁcation was a likely causal factor in 46% of these cases. Ashcroft et al . (2005)
reported that 9% of pharmacy dispensing errors could be attributed to similarity in
packaging. In short, labels and packaging have been implicated as a causal factor in
medication errors from across the medical context; for example, in drug swaps during
anaesthesia (e.g. Jensen et al . 2004), in incorrect dose administration in hospitals
(e.g. Guchelaar et al. 2004), in dispensing errors in the pharmacy (e.g. Peterson et al. 1999)
and non-compliance with drug schedules in the home (e.g. Brass and Weintraub 2003).
There have been many calls to use variations in package and label design as a means of
reducing medication errors (e.g. Orser and Oxorn 1994) but to date the research that has
looked at the eﬀects of package design characteristics on drug handling has been sparse
and piecemeal, often focusing on single drugs and subjective measures of eﬀectiveness.
In other areas, such as food labelling, pesticide labelling and warning labelling, research
into the eﬀects of labelling and packaging is more developed and clear links have been
established between the design features of labels and packaging and the behaviour
associated with those products. This paper reviews this research and will consider the
extent to which the relationships that have been revealed between design features and
behaviour might improve patient safety if they were generalized to the labelling and
packaging of medicines.
2. Label design features that have been shown to inﬂuence behaviour
The general area of label and packaging research is one in which there is a great deal of
interest, testimony to which is the large amount of new research evidence being published
on a regular basis. From a small pool of studies around the mid-1980s, there now exists a
huge body of empirical data mapping out the relationship between the design of labels
(especially warning labels) and packages and behaviour with regard to those products.
The relationship between labels and behaviour is a complex one because it requires
understanding of psychological processes, design issues, knowledge of speciﬁc risk
domains, standardization and government regulation issues and, increasingly, legal and
litigious aﬀairs.
Initially, the research ﬁeld appears complicated, reporting seemingly haphazard and
unpredictable eﬀects. This is because studies are often not comparable, using diﬀerent
groups of participants (with diﬀerent levels of skill and familiarity), hazards with dif-
ferent levels of associated danger, diﬀerent levels of independent variable and so on.
Furthermore, research is carried out using a range of methodologies, from questionnaire
studies, through subjective ratings studies, focus groups, discourse analysis, policy-
capturing methodologies to direct observation of compliance using empirical methods
and ﬁeld studies. However, when experimental ﬁndings are analysed systematically and in
detail (e.g. Edworthy and Adams 1996, Wogalter et al . 1999a) it has been found that
some variables, in fact, have strikingly consistent eﬀects both within and across studies.
There is a large body of evidence, for example, showing very clear and consistent eﬀects
for those kinds of variables that attract attention to labels (such as colour, shape, font
size, use of signal words such as ‘danger’ or ‘warning’). Somewhat less clear are areas of
linguistic usage, although again there have been studies of the role of explicitness and
severity in warning label information, as well as other studies looking at passive/active
modes of expression, message length and the use of the personal pronoun. The label and
package design characteristics that have been shown to have consistent eﬀects on

text:
[Page 4]
the behaviours and variables associated with label eﬀectiveness (measures such as
compliance, understanding, noticeability, distinctiveness and perceived hazard) are high-
lighted below. The potential for these ﬁndings to generalize to medicine labelling and to
improve patient safety is considered later.
2.1. Signal word
Signal words are single terms (e.g. ‘danger’, ‘warning’, ‘caution’) that are used on warning
labels to denote the overall level of hazard implied. Their function is to provide the
recipient with a hazard overview of the situation being indicated, in terms of its severity
and probability (Leonard et al. 1999). The idea of a signal word summarizing the level of
hazard implied by a warning is an appealing one, whereby the signal word alerts the
recipient to the warning and helps to calibrate the response to it. This issue of how much
hazard is implied by a label is important, since research has revealed positive correlations
between the hazard implied by a label and reading, remembering and complying with its
contents (e.g. Friedmann 1988). In principle, any words could be used as warning signal
words, but for them to operate as hazard indicators in this way, the words chosen must
exhibit speciﬁc properties when used in a warnings context. First, there must be a clear
relationship between the potential signal word and the level of hazard understood by
that term and, second, this relationship must be consistently interpreted by the target
population. In addition, just as dangers exist on a continuum from not very threatening
to life threatening, so too must the terms used to summarize those dangers.
The research to date has generally revealed a strong and consistent relationship
between diﬀerent warning signal words and perceptions of hazard. Bresnahan and Bryk
(1975) found that ‘danger’ was associated with the highest hazard values, followed by
‘caution’, ‘think’ and ‘notice’. In addition, they found that the presence of any signal
word increased the perceived hazard associated with a warning sign as compared to signs
without signal words (this ﬁnding was replicated by Wogalter et al . 1992). Dunlap et al .
(1986) also asked participants to rate the hazard implied by potential signal words and
found that ‘danger’ was perceived as implying the most hazard, followed by ‘warning’,
‘caution’, ‘beware’, ‘attention’, ‘notice’ and ‘think’. Similar ﬁndings have been made by
Leonard et al . (1988), who found participants could distinguish a descending order
of perceived hazard between ‘deadly’, ‘danger’, ‘warning’, ‘caution’, ‘be careful’ and
‘attention’. Similarly, Leonard et al . (1989) found that when participants were asked to
assign signal words to hazard situations, they used ‘danger’ to denote the most serious
situation and ‘caution’ to denote the least. Findings such as these support the use of
signal words as recommended by standardization bodies such as the American National
Standards Institute (ANSI), who suggest the terms ‘danger’, ‘warning’, and ‘caution’ to
denote decreasing levels of hazard (e.g. American National Standards Institute 2002).
The picture is not as simple as this research suggests, however, for there is also evidence
to suggest ambiguity in people’s interpretation of the level of hazard implied by speciﬁc
words. Wogalter et al . (1992), for example, found that the terms ‘lethal’, ‘danger’,
‘warning’, ‘caution’ and ‘note’ were ordered in a decreasing order of perceived hazard
but, importantly, they did not ﬁnd signiﬁcant diﬀerences in the hazard associations
between the terms ‘danger’, ‘warning’ and ‘caution’. Similarly, Kline et al . (1993) found
that the term ‘danger’ attracted the highest hazard association values, followed by
‘caution’ and then ‘warning’, with signiﬁcant diﬀerences only between ‘danger’ and the
other two terms. Chapanis’ (1994) research also cast doubt on the hazard associations of
signal words recommended by ANSI. They found that while the majority of their

text:
[Page 5]
participants did rank the terms ‘danger’, ‘warning’ and ‘caution’ as predicted, there was
some confusion in meaning and perceived suitable usage between ‘warning’ and ‘caution’.
So, as can be seen from the research cited, while there are terms that denote levels of
hazard on a continuum, there is some doubt over the levels of hazard implied by some of
the speciﬁc terms. In particular, it is not clear whether the terms ‘warning’ and ‘caution’
are as clearly distinguishable from one another in the hazard they imply as the ANSI
recommendations suggest. Wogalter and Silver (1990) conducted one of the most
comprehensive investigations into the eﬀects of warning signal words and argued that the
signal words usually recommended to convey hazard associations were too limited in
number and so were likely to be overused, resulting in desensitization to them and
habituation. They attempted to create a broader list of warning signal words, which,
because they would be more novel, could be used to indicate ﬁner degrees of hazard
while remaining more resistant to habituation eﬀects. They asked participants to rate
84 potential signal words on six dimensions and from these dimensions they derived a
scale of ‘arousal strength’. Again, they found that the terms ‘warning’ and ‘caution’ were
not rated as being signiﬁcantly diﬀerent from one another. Wogalter and Silver (1990)
selected a subset of 20 signal words on the basis of understandability and conciseness,
which represented a wide range of arousal strengths. The signal words, in descending
order of hazard, were: ‘deadly’; ‘fatal’; ‘poison’; ‘danger’; ‘hazard’; ‘vital’; ‘severe’;
‘serious’; ‘urgent’; ‘beware’; ‘warning’; ‘harmful’; ‘caution’; ‘alarm’; ‘alert’; ‘careful’;
‘prevent’; ‘needed’; ‘notice’; ‘note’. This set of 20 words was then, and has since been
(Edworthy and Adams 1996), recommended as a set of alternative signal words that
denote a wide range of hazards and are diﬀerentiable from one another in known ways.
Warning signal words do then have clear potential to indicate the overall level of
hazard implied by a warning and to help individuals to calibrate their response to it.
Although there may be some debate as to the relative order of the terms ‘warning’ and
‘caution’ in terms of the hazard they imply, cross-cultural work generally has suggested
that the hazard associations of signal words do generalize, with terms such as ‘deadly’
and ‘danger’ consistently interpreted as implying high levels of hazard, and terms such as
‘notice’ and ‘important’ consistently interpreted as implying less (e.g. Dunlap et al. 1986,
Wogalter and Silver 1995, Wogalter et al . 1997, Leung and Hellier 1998).
2.2. Colour
While colour has obvious potential to aid the discriminability and categorization of
labels and packages, as with signal words, the majority of labelling research that has
investigated colour has considered its potential as a means of coding the level of hazard
implied. In general, this research on warning labels, food labels and general visual
displays has been consistent in revealing that, in Western culture at least, the colour red is
perceived as implying a high level of hazard, followed by colours such as orange and
yellow, then blue and green, with white implying the least hazard (e.g. Dunlap et al. 1986,
Chapanis 1994, Adams and Edworthy 1995, Braun and Silver 1995, Costello et al. 2002).
In addition to indicating the level of hazard implied by a label, the use of colour
(as opposed to monochrome) has also been associated with increasing the noticeability of
a label (e.g. Young 1991), with increases in label identiﬁcation speed and accuracy
(e.g. Ellis et al. 1980, Young 1991) and with increases in perceived readability (Kline et al.
1993). Some authors (e.g. Braun and Silver 1995) have even been able to demonstrate that
label colour inﬂuences compliance levels – they found higher levels of compliance to red
labels than to either black or green ones.

text:
[Page 6]
Within the medical domain, there have been speciﬁc calls for investigations into the use
of colour as an identiﬁcation and classiﬁcation aid to reduce medication errors (e.g. Stuth
2002, Frush et al. 2004, McCoy 2005). Indeed, The Medicines Control Agency’s own Best
Practice Guidelines on the Labelling and Packaging of Medicines is encouraging about the
use of colour to improve drug handling but is vague about how this might be achieved,
encouraging nothing more speciﬁc than the ‘judicious use of colour’ (Medicines Control
Agency 2002).
One area in which colour coding has received particular attention is with reference to
syringe labels for anaesthetic medications, where colour coding is used and recommended
to aid drug identiﬁcation. In USA, Australia, New Zealand and Canada a standardized
colour code exists, whereby anaesthetic drugs are colour coded by substance class (with,
for example, muscle relaxants carrying orange labels and induction agents coloured
yellow). In the UK 96% of anaesthesia departments use colour coding, but not according
to any standardized scheme, despite the fact that there is widespread support for
standardization among college tutors of the Royal College of Anaesthetists (Christie and
Hill 2002). Direct evidence for the utility of colour coding of syringe labels in anaesthesia
is limited and mixed. Stuth (2002) reports that such coding has led to a reduction in
medication error, but other authors (e.g. Fasting and Gisvold 2000) compared drug
errors in anaesthesia with and without colour-coded syringe labels and found that colour
coding did not reduce syringe swaps – which appeared to occur primarily between
syringes of a similar size.
Some speciﬁc evidence relating to colour coding of medical information in the home is
encouraging. Frush et al . (2004) compared two methods of dosing over-the-counter
medications for children in a home setting, a colour-coded method and conventional
package labelling. They found a marked improvement in caregiver ability to correctly
dose the medicine, both for measures of dose determination and dose measuring, using
the colour-coded method. The average deviation in dose determination was 25% for the
conventional packaging group compared to 1.7% for the colour coded group. For dose
measuring the average deviation ﬁgures were 29% and 0.5% respectively.
3. Interactions between colour and signal words
A factor that moderates the eﬀect of both colour and signal word on the hazard
association of labels is the way in which the two variables interact when they are
presented together. Braun and Silver (1995) considered the interaction between colour
and signal word in determining hazard association values in the US. They required
participants to rate the perceived hazard of 21 diﬀerent potential signal words each
presented in ﬁve diﬀerent colours. The resulting ‘isoperformance curves’ that they derived
speciﬁed how a particular hazard level could be achieved by means of various colour and
signal word combinations. In general, the interactions showed that printing words in
blue, green or black reduced their hazard association values compared to printing them
in red or orange. More speciﬁcally, printing high hazard words, such as ‘danger’, in blue
resulted in them communicating less overall hazard than moderate hazard words
presented in red.
3.1. Label format
There have been a range of speciﬁc investigations looking at how features of the general
formatting of a label or package inﬂuence the way in which the user is able to interact

text:
[Page 7]
with it. The shape of a label is a variable that can potentially communicate a level of
hazard and can be used to increase the attention-getting of the label. Riley et al . (1982)
compared preferences for 19 diﬀerent shapes of warning label. They concluded that, in
general, people saw more ‘unstable’ shapes such as inverted triangles, diamonds and
octagons as the most appropriate warning indicators. They suggested that shape could be
used to code the priority of warning labels in the ways that road signs in the UK are
categorized by shape. Rodriguez (1991) also investigated label shape and found that a
written label surrounded by a shape (either an octagon or a triangle) resulted in higher
levels of compliance and improved retention scores in a chemistry task compared to
labels with no surrounding shapes.
Adams and Edworthy (1995) also considered the impact of label formatting variables
on the perceived hazard of the label. They manipulated font size, border width and
colour. Increases in font size and border width both increased perceived hazard and they
discussed how trade-oﬀs between the three variables could be used to communicate the
same level of hazard by diﬀerent means. For example, a signal word would have to be
presented twice as big in black as in red to convey the same overall impression of hazard.
Studies on label format in the medical domain have focused primarily on the factors
likely to inﬂuence label readability and information acquisition. Sansgiry et al . (1997)
surveyed a range of non-prescription drugs and reported various factors that they felt
would degrade the readability of the drugs’ packaging. Font size on warnings and
indications averaged 6 point, 63% of packages used no boldface, 30% used all uppercase
font and 19% lacked paragraph breaks. The Medicines Control Agency Best Practice
Guide warns against these practices in its recommendation that important information
should be presented in ‘as large a font as possible’ and that white space should be used to
improve legibility, although it is not speciﬁc about what might be a minimum acceptable
font size (Medicines Control Agency 2002). Wogalter et al. (1999b) and Bernardini et al.
(2001) also warn against the use of the small type typically found on over-the-counter
medicines, particularly for older adults.
Also broadly considering readability, Filik et al . (2004) looked at design interventions
to prevent medication errors that arise from confusion between drug names that look
alike. They printed sections of the drug names in ‘TALLman’ (capital) lettering
to emphasize diﬀerences between otherwise similar words. Eye tracking studies of
participants searching for target drugs from among distractors revealed that the use of
tall man lettering made participants less likely to incorrectly identify a distractor, that is,
the tall man lettering improved the accuracy of their drug identiﬁcation performance.
Wogalter et al . (1999b) used experimental studies to compare medicines with con-
ventional labels to those with additional cap-top labels that repeated the most important
information in large print. The medicines with the cap-top labels were rated more
favourably in terms of noticeability and readability and scored higher on objective
measures of information acquisition. In a similar vein, Wogalter and Vigilante (2003)
compared younger and older participants’ information acquisition and readability ratings
of over-the-counter medicine bottles that varied in the print size, white space between text
and standard vs. pull-out label type. Older adults’ information acquisition scores were
improved in the medium and larger print conditions, and both younger and older adults
rated the larger print conditions with more white space as being the most readable.
The pull-out label type improved the performance of older adults.
In warnings research, these label and package design modiﬁcations that interfere with
the use of the product and either specify some important information or direct the user
to read information elsewhere on the product are termed ‘supplemental directives’ or

text:
[Page 8]
‘interactive warnings’ and have been found to be a very successful means of improving
compliance. For example, Wogalter et al . (1994) found that the introduction of a
supplemental directive (a strip of paper over the seal of a container suggesting that
participants read the safety instructions prior to using the product) improved compliance
for professional users. Edworthy et al . (2004) also found that the presence of a supple-
mental directive improved professional pesticide users’ compliance with on-product
instructions and Duﬀy et al . (1995) along with Frantz and Rhoades (1993) also report
that interactive labels are read, recalled and complied with more than non-interactive
ones.
3.2. Message wording
There have been a few studies from a variety of domains that have considered how the
way in which a label or package is worded inﬂuences various outcome measures.
For example, Laughery et al . (1993) looked at the relationship between the explicitness
and severity of information on warning labels. They found that expressing a hazard
explicitly (for example, ‘If you drink while you are pregnant, your child may be born with
Foetal Alcohol Syndrome and need institutionalization’) rather than non-explicitly
(for example, ‘Mixing alcohol and medicine can be life-threatening’) led to higher ratings
of the seriousness of the risk. Heaps and Henley (1999) also tested explicitness vs.
implicitness and found that explicitness improved a label’s believability and increased
perceived product danger. In a study measuring actual compliance rates rather than
measuring subjective responses, Frantz (1994) showed that procedural explicitness also
increased compliance rates.
Heaps and Henley (1999) also compared what they called ‘probabilistic’ statements
of risk (such as ‘Avoid contact with eyes or skin’) with ‘deﬁnite’ instructions (such as
‘Do not get into eyes or skin’) and showed that deﬁnite expressions scored signiﬁcantly
higher on believability. In a similar vein, Costello et al . (2002) found that deﬁnitive
(rather than probabilistic) statements increased the hazard associated with genetically
modiﬁed food labelling.
Another avenue of research has considered in what form information is pre-
sented, whether as a statement of hazard (such as ‘contains tar’), as a statement of
consequences (harmful to lungs) or as an instruction (do not smoke). A study by
Wogalter et al . (1987) showed that when judging the eﬀectiveness of a warning label,
instruction and hazard statements were considered to be more important than
consequence statements. This was supported by Edworthy et al . (2001), who also
showed that instruction statements were ranked as the most appropriate way of
expressing pesticide warning information. Taylor and Bower (2004) reported that in the
case of consumer products, compliance with instruction statements can be further
improved by making explicit how compliance will lead to the desired outcome
(by including the process-cause information).
Edworthy et al. (2001) went on to investigate the eﬀects of a range of linguistic
variables on measures of appropriateness and compliance to pesticide labels. They found
that in terms of appropriateness ranking, active (rather than passive) modes of
expression, explicit (rather than non-explicit) statements and statements that included
the use of a personal pronoun were all rated as being more appropriate than their
alternatives. Probabilistic statements, where the level of the risk was expressed as ‘may’,
‘might’ or ‘could’ rather than deﬁnitively, were ranked as the least appropriate
descriptors of risk by a considerable margin. In terms of actual compliance measures,

text:
[Page 9]
Edworthy et al . (2004) revealed that presenting information as an instruction with a
personal pronoun (for example, ‘You must wear gloves and a respirator mask’) resulted
in higher levels of compliance than presenting it as a probabilistic hazard (May be
harmful to people not wearing gloves and a respirator mask).
Within the medical domain, the majority of research on wording has been done within
the context of patient information leaﬂets (PIL) and has focused on measures of reading
complexity and diﬀerent ways of organizing the material. Research on PIL is generally
beyond the scope of the current review but one particular area of focus in PIL research
has been on numerical vs. verbal presentation of information, as this clearly has
implications for label and packaging design. Berry et al. (2002) investigated the extent to
which users of the contraceptive pill understood the risks of thrombosis as expressed
according to the Committee on the Safety of Medicines’ recommended wording in the
PIL. They revealed that less than 12% of users properly understood the absolute levels of
risk and less than 40% properly understood the relative risks. Berry et al . (2004)
examined patients’ understanding of the European Commission-recommended verbal
descriptors for side-eﬀect risks on over-the-counter medicines. The risks of side eﬀects
were presented either verbally (common) or numerically (6%) and, in line with their
earlier work on prescription medicines (Knapp et al . 2004), they found that the verbal
descriptors led to large overestimations in the side-eﬀect risk. A similar theme is picked
up by Wheeler et al . (2004), who report that the labelling of drug solutions variously as
ratios or percentages caused confusion among doctors as to how to calculate the correct
percentages to administer.
3.3. Summary
It is evident from the research presented that some clear eﬀects have been demonstrated
for the relationship between label and package design characteristics and users’
interactions with those products. Research suggests that signal words can be used in
predictable ways to communicate the level of hazard implied by a label, as can colour and
shape. The importance of perceived hazard as an outcome variable lies in the positive
correlations that have been demonstrated between perceived hazard and the tendency to
read, recall and comply with label directives. In addition to communicating perceived
hazard, colour has also been shown to increase measures of noticeability, identiﬁcation
speed and accuracy, perceived readability and compliance, and label shape to increase
measures of noticeability, compliance and retention. Increases in font size have been
shown to increase perceived hazard and also noticeability and readability and measures
to improve the distinctiveness of lettering, such as the use of the ‘TALLman’ format, have
also been shown to be eﬀective. The language used to express information has also been
shown to inﬂuence measures of hazard, believability and compliance with explicit and
deﬁnitive phrases, instructions and the use of the personal pronoun all having positive
eﬀects. The following section considers these design characteristics and evaluates
their utility for application to the labelling and packaging of medicines for improving
patient safety. There are other label features that are known to inﬂuence per-
ceptions and behaviour, variables such as the source to which information is
attributed. Some variables like this have been excluded from this review because they
are less applicable to medicine labelling. It is unlikely that legislation would permit
information on dosing, for example, to be attributed to a consumer organization, which
has been shown to be the most trusted and complied with information source
(e.g. Costello et al . 2002).

text:
[Page 10]
4. Can label design improve patient safety?
In order to consider the extent to which label design features might improve patient safety
it is necessary to consider which outcome variables these design features have been shown
to inﬂuence and to evaluate how they relate to the causes of medication error. As can be
seen from the summary above, label and package design features have been related
primarily to changes in noticeability, discriminability, understandability, compliance and
perceived hazard. Measures of noticeability and discriminability are relevant to errors
that involve confusing whole drugs containers with each other or to confusing or not
noticing speciﬁed pieces of information on a package or bottle, such as warning or dosage
information. These measures obviously have relevance to all forms of medication error
that arise from confusions between drugs or drug dosages in the hospital, pharmacy and
home. Noticeability, understandability and compliance as measures also relate to
medication errors resulting from failures of compliance. Compliance can be (and is)
measured directly or indirectly through noticeability and understandability, which are
both necessary (but not suﬃcient) conditions for compliance. For example, if an
instruction or warning is not noticed (or understood) then it cannot be complied with.
Perceived hazard is the outcome measure used in many studies of label design, and its
utility as a measure derives from the positive correlations that are shown to exist between
increases in perceived hazard and outcomes such as compliance, reading or recall of
labels (e.g. Friedmann 1988). It is tempting to conclude that increasing the perceived
hazard of all labels would increase their eﬀectiveness. This would not, however, be a
desirable design policy, as people would soon habituate to being presented with labels
that were perceived as implying a lot of hazard and would cease to respond appropriately
to them (e.g. Wogalter et al . 1987, Thorley et al . 2002). The success of designs that
inﬂuence perceived hazard may depend on appropriate matching between the hazard
implied by the label and that inherent in the situation, on ‘hazard matching’, so that by
perceiving hazard, the user is able to calibrate their response to the warning
(e.g. Edworthy 1998). Responding to warnings and other safety information will depend
not just on the information itself, but also the perceived costs and beneﬁts of compliance,
which can be modelled (e.g. Edworthy 1998). If the safety information eﬀectively
represents the risk, then the degree to which the various design parameters represent the
risk will determine how useful the information is in informing the cost beneﬁt analysis.
The relationship between perceived hazard and outcomes such as noticeability, recall and
compliance has not been clearly delineated, although it is likely that perceptions of
hazard are arousing and trigger the recipient to increase attendance thus increasing recall,
noticeability and, ultimately, compliance.
In traditional warning research the ultimate indicator of eﬀectiveness is compliance,
and measures of noticeability, understandability and so on are precursors to that.
When one considers the labelling and packaging of medicines, however, it can be seen
that there are two important eﬀectiveness indicators, discriminability (as in avoiding drug
confusions) and compliance (with warnings and other directions). The ways in which
understanding can be developed of the relationship between design characteristics and
measures of discriminability and compliance are outlined below.
4.1. Signal words in the labelling and packaging of medicines
Signal words have clear potential for use on medicine labelling and packaging to draw
attention to features such as dosage instructions and warning information. They provide

text:
[Page 11]
what is described by Edworthy and Adams (1996) as an iconic representation of the
hazard implied by a message. This might be particularly useful in home settings, as
medical jargon and verbal descriptors of risk are generally poorly understood, yet signal
words provide a means of presenting complex hazard information in an understandable
form. If signal words are appropriately matched to the hazard inherent in a situation, as
recommended by the many calls for ‘hazard matching’ as a warnings implementation
strategy (e.g. Wogalter et al. 1987), then they help recipients to calibrate their response to
the information and this includes increasing the tendency for recipients to attend to, recall
and comply with directions preceded by higher hazard signal words.
The other area in which signal words have potential beneﬁts is in reducing habituation
to messages. Wogalter and Silver (1990) suggest that, over time, habituation reduces the
attention paid to warning and other information and this has been supported by other
authors (e.g. Thorley et al . 2002). In addition, product familiarity reduces the likelihood
of perceived hazard and consequently of reading warning information (e.g. Godfrey et al.
1983, Wogalter and Young 1991, Hyde and Hellier 1997). Many of the prescription and
over-the-counter medicines found in the home are used regularly and are familiar to the
user, both factors that increase likelihood of warning messages not being attended to.
It has been suggested (e.g. Wogalter and Silver 1990) that label designers could alternate
the use of diﬀerent signal words that imply the same level of hazard so as to reduce
habituation to the messages they precede.
For signal words to be used in the ways suggested, it is important that a set of words
with clearly understood and stable hazard associations in the medical context is
established. While authors have recommended lists of words, and have begun to establish
the stability of hazard associations across culture and age group, the terms recommended
by standardization bodies such as ANSI are not supported by research.
4.2. Colour in the labelling and packaging of medicines
Colour is the design feature that has been most researched in the medical setting, as an
identiﬁcation aid, and package and dosage identiﬁcation and discrimination is a critical
means of reducing drug confusions. There is little doubt that colour has utility when used
in this way, particularly for the discrimination of medicine dose-strength information.
Picking errors in pharmacies, whereby a pharmacist selects the wrong strength of a
medicine from the shelves, are a common cause of medication error. While medicine dose
strength is necessarily speciﬁed on the side of a package it is not necessarily highlighted or
coded in any way. If this dosage information was coded so that, for example, 100 mg was
presented on an orange dosage panel and 10 mg was presented on a yellow dosage panel,
it would be more diﬃcult to misperceive the colours orange and yellow than the text
‘100 mg’ and ‘10 mg’. What remains to be seen is how the use of colour can be
standardized and which diﬀerent colours are best to use for indicating what features. It is
already known that colour has clear associations with communicating diﬀerent levels of
hazard and it is likely that there are other aﬀective responses that diﬀerent colours elicit
that will make diﬀerent colours more or less appropriate for communicating diﬀerent
things. Indeed, Bernardini (2001) found clear colour preferences for diﬀerent parts of
PIL – side eﬀects, therapeutic indications and contraindications. These things should be
determined empirically and questions that might be considered include which colours are
most suited to indicate high and low dosages of a medicine so that the colour coding of
dosage panels can be standardized, and which colours are most appropriate to use for
representing diﬀerent classes of medicine.

text:
[Page 12]
It should be noted that the existence of colour blind users does not rule out the use of
colour as a package design and coding aid. The use of colour has enormous potential
beneﬁts for the majority of the colour-sighted population and it would always be
recommended that redundancy is built into the use of colour. Furthermore, some
medicine producers are already beginning to use colour on their packaging without the
beneﬁt of systematic research into its eﬀects.
4.3. Format variables in the labelling and packaging of medicines
The format variables that appear to have most utility are shape, font size, font charac-
teristics and the use of supplemental directives. Shape can be used as a coding aid
(perhaps in conjunction with colour) and has potential for use in coding the drug
dosage strength information as described above. With regard to colour and shape, it is
possible to consider these variables not only for coding packages and information; it
could be carried through to the colour and shape of the medicines themselves in some
cases. Font characteristics such as TALLman lettering have obvious beneﬁts for
increasing the discriminability of text, and size is also an important determinant of the
readability and noticeability of information and is obviously an important consideration
for older users. The problem with increasing font size on labelling and packaging is
usually the space considerations but developments in the use of innovative package
design and the use of supplemental directives have enormous potential to overcome some
of these issues.
Innovative pack designs are explicitly encouraged by the Medicines Control Agency
(2002), particularly for medicines in small containers, as they oﬀer the opportunity
to provide more information than would otherwise be possible. While the Medicines
Control Agency (now the Medicines and Healthcare Regulatory Agency) is not explicit
about what these innovative designs might be, here it can be seen that the use of cap-
top additions and supplemental directives that interfere with product usage not only
enable more information to be displayed but are also successful in attracting users’
attention to information that might otherwise be missed, improving its noticeability
and ultimately compliance. There is some additional evidence that supplemental
directives are most eﬀective for professional product users (e.g. Edworthy et al . 2004),
this is likely to be because professional users are more familiar with products and it is
already known that increased product familiarity makes users less likely to attend to
aspects of packaging and labelling. The supplemental directive may either dishabituate
users to familiar packaging or just demand attention by interfering with product usage.
In either case, this avenue has great potential for reducing medication errors by medical
staﬀ and the more useful forms of supplemental directive would be a fruitful area of
investigation.
4.4. Wording for the labelling and packaging of medicines
For medicines, the content of the information that must be included in labelling and
packaging is set out in article 54 of the Council Directive 2001/83/EEC and is further
recommended to include the name of the medicine, an expression of strength, the route of
administration, dosage and warnings (Medicines Control Agency 2002). Whilst the
content of some of the information on medicine packaging and labelling is thus pre-
speciﬁed, there is still scope to manipulate the way in which content is expressed to
increase compliance with it.

text:
[Page 13]
In general the eﬀects of diﬀerent styles of wording, whilst promising, require further
research development. Whilst increased explicitness in messages appears to be associated
with increases in perceived hazard and compliance, increased explicitness necessarily
increases the amount of wording on a sometimes already cluttered label and so it is
important to explore the robustness of this eﬀect. Similar eﬀects may be achieved by more
economic means, such as the introduction of the personal pronoun or deﬁnitive rather
than probabilistic wording.
5. Conclusion
This paper has considered some of the ways in which the wealth of general research on
labelling might be applied to the labelling and packaging of medicines in order to
reduce medication errors and improve patient safety. While the eﬀects of the design
variables, which have been outlined, on medication errors largely remain to be quantiﬁed,
here an organizing framework has been provided that can be used to focus future
research eﬀorts in this direction. Research in other ﬁelds has suggested that signal words,
colour, format and wording are the design variables that have the most consistent eﬀects
on user outcomes, and the outcomes that are likely to be most relevant to reducing
medication errors are those that relate to product noticeability and discriminability
and those that relate to compliance. It is here that future research eﬀorts should be
directed.

text:
[Page 1]
Int. J. Human-Computer Studies 64 (2006) 670–682
Computational modeling and experimental investigation of effects of
compositional elements on interface and design aesthetics
Michael Bauerly /C3, Yili Liu
Department of Industrial and Operations Engineering, The University of Michigan, 1205 Beal Avenue, Ann Arbor, MI 48109-2117, USA
Received 17 May 2005; received in revised form 15 December 2005; accepted 24 January 2006
Available online 7 March 2006
Communicated by J. Scholtz
Abstract
This article describes computational modeling and two corresponding experimental investigations of the effects of symmetry, balance
and quantity of construction elements on interface aesthetic judgments. In the ﬁrst experiment, 30 black and white geometric images were
developed by systematically varying these three attributes in order to validate computational aesthetic quantiﬁcation algorithms with
subject ratings. The second experiment employed the same image layout as Experiment 1 but with realistic looking web pages as stimuli.
The images were rated by 16 subjects in each experiment using the ratio-scale magnitude estimation method against a benchmark image
with average balance and symmetry values and a standard number of elements. Subjects also established an ordered list of the images
according to their aesthetic appeal using the Balanced-Incomplete-Block (BIB) ranking method.
Results from both experiments show that subjects are adept at judging symmetry and balance in both the horizontal and vertical
directions and thus the quantiﬁcation of those attributes is justiﬁed. The ﬁrst experiment establishes a relationship between a higher
symmetry value and aesthetic appeal for the basic imagery showing that subjects preferred symmetric over non-symmetric images. The
second experiment illustrates that increasing the number of groups in a web page causes a decrease in the aesthetic appeal rating.

Keywords: Aesthetics; Engineering aesthetics; Balance; Symmetry; Display evaluation
1. Introduction
Research on visual displays has traditionally deﬁned
display effectiveness with criteria such as legibility or
difﬁculty of target search and information access. Most
of this research focuses on qualitative description
and summarization and does not utilize a quantitative
mathematical modeling approach. Because the majority
of human factors design guidelines are qualitative, the
effectiveness of many design techniques is left to debate
because there are no methods to provide numerical analysis
or direct comparison between different design proposals.
Tullis (1988b) , for example, gives many well-deﬁned but
qualitative guidelines for text-based screen design. Most of
these principles can be transferred to many types of visual
bitmapped displays, which prove to be extremely helpful in
many design situations. One major drawback, however, is
that they do not provide a way for the designer to assign
quantiﬁed values to the speciﬁc components of screen
design.
There are some past attempts to adopt a quantitative
and computational approach to interface design. For
example,
Tullis (1983) developed metrics for quantifying
the effects of item grouping, density and complexity on the
usability of text-based displays and later tested those
attributes against measures of search time and preference
(
Tullis, 1984, 1988a ). Streveler and Wasserman (1984)
propose creating several classes of screen measures for
alphanumeric displays including the aesthetic measures of
balance and symmetry. One of the overlapping attributes in
these two lines of research is the use of characteristics such
as size or number of groups as a descriptive metric.
Liu and
Wickens (1992) use cluster analysis to achieve visual
grouping and encoding of data in a two-dimensional

[Page 2]
(2-D) grid according to quantitative similarity values.
Subjects were then asked to complete various judgment
tasks with the display grids and their judgment perfor-
mance showed signiﬁcant improvement with the use of the
display grids.
Sears (1993) developed a metric for develop-
ing and comparing user interface widget layout based on a
simple description of the stages required to complete a task
within the interface.
In addition to the research challenge of developing
quantitative metrics for interface evaluation and analysis,
there is an issue of integrating aesthetic factors in interface
evaluation. Consideration of aesthetics has largely been
ignored in human factors analysis of displays until some
recent work that has emerged on the increasing importance
of aesthetics in various domains of contemporary society.
Liu (2003a, b) provided a comprehensive review of the
major schools of aesthetic theory and their relationship to
aesthetic design and human factors engineering.
Jordan
(1997) calls for the design of products that provide
particular aesthetic pleasure beyond simple usability and
the associated positive feelings of security, conﬁdence,
pride and satisfaction.
Hallnas and Redstrom (2002)
declare that increasing the aesthetics of the computational
interface will only aid in the widespread acceptance and
‘presence’ of ubiquitous computing devices. A recent
survey by
Kim et al. (2003) analyzes several web pages
to determine the common aesthetic design factors
and the corresponding emotional responses of users.
Another study by
Healey and Enns (2002) manipulates
visualization techniques in order to provide guidelines for
designing effective visual displays by encoding weather
data in a map of the US. This process optimized aesthetic
appeal and information retrieval through the creation of
different presentation techniques to ﬁnd an optimal
strategy. The relation of aesthetics to system effectiveness
cannot be ignored.
Tractinsky et al. (2000) concluded
that users of an automated teller machine (ATM)
found the system to be more usable based solely on
aesthetic alterations to the interface without any changes in
functionality.
In addition to this recent interest from many areas,
artists and designers have long treated aesthetics as a
primary aspect of their work; however, they mainly
describe aesthetic terms in qualitative or subjective
languages that do not easily allow for engineering
implementation. Recently, several artists have started to
include themes of a computationally generated superior
aesthetic. One of the earliest groups to utilize computation
was Group de Recherche d’Art Visuel (GRAV) of the
1960s.
Prince (2000) notes that this group was ‘‘dedicated
to understanding mathematical simulation and aesthetics’’
and served as pioneers in this artistic ﬁeld. The use of an
exploratory approach that utilized the most appropriate
solution in future iterations is one that would appear here
for the ﬁrst time computationally. Another contemporary
artist making similar efforts is Steven Rooke. His art
utilizes a genetic process of aesthetic selection such that
aesthetically interesting features emerge in subsequent
iterations of the design process as recorded by
World
(1996). At each iteration, certain generations are given
higher aesthetic ﬁtness scores which are passed on to future
generations, creating an aesthetically superior set of
offspring. The aesthetic ﬁtness, however, relies on the
judgment of the artist to assign a score and thus the process
remains highly subjective.
Reiser and Reiser (1995) create a list of aesthetic
considerations speciﬁc to multimedia; but the end result
is one that only extends the qualitative human factors
checklist to include more items to consider without
knowing quantitatively where an optimal design space
exists.
This paper describes our computational modeling and
experimental research work that attempts to bridge the
scientiﬁc methods of human performance and display
analysis with aesthetic design principles.

text:
At each iteration, certain generations are given
higher aesthetic ﬁtness scores which are passed on to future
generations, creating an aesthetically superior set of
offspring. The aesthetic ﬁtness, however, relies on the
judgment of the artist to assign a score and thus the process
remains highly subjective.
Reiser and Reiser (1995) create a list of aesthetic
considerations speciﬁc to multimedia; but the end result
is one that only extends the qualitative human factors
checklist to include more items to consider without
knowing quantitatively where an optimal design space
exists.
This paper describes our computational modeling and
experimental research work that attempts to bridge the
scientiﬁc methods of human performance and display
analysis with aesthetic design principles. This is executed in
a quantitative manner through the development and
validation of numerical quantiﬁcations of the effects of
three compositional elements on aesthetic judgments. The
three elements—symmetry, balance and compositional
blocking—are present in 2-D medium.
Inspiration is taken from the development of methods
for quantifying the grouping, density and complexity of
text-based displays by
Tullis (1983) . Relatively similar
attempts have been made using many more attributes than
what are presented here (
Ngo, 2001; Ngo et al., 2003 ; Lavie
and Tractinsky, 2004 ). These earlier studies, however, have
not been validated with any experimental investigation of
user judgment of the proposed quantiﬁcation methods. It is
important that we develop quantitative methods that
match the perceptual and mental processes
of system users, which creates the necessity of human
experimental veriﬁcation.
While the objective of the present study is to develop
quantitative indexes for interface aesthetic evaluation, not
for constructing or assessing a theoretical model, the
present study is inspired by the psychophysical school of
aesthetic theories. As discussed in detail in
Liu (2003a) ,
several major schools of aesthetic theories exist, including
philosophical theories, cognitive and social theories,
natural and sexual selection theories and psychophysical
theories. Among these schools of theories, psychophysical
theories emphasize investigations of quantitative relation-
ships between aesthetic response and basic pictorial
elements, which is an approach adopted by the present
study. The results of the present study, in return, provide
an evaluation of the role of this school of theories in
aesthetic interface design and evaluation.
The compositional elements chosen in this study
represent three basic pictorial elements and design concepts
that follow from previous research. The element of balance
is well understood by experts and non-experts alike and the
preference for balance in visual displays is well documented
(
Wilson and Chatterjee, 2005 ). Existing theories suggest
that visual balance is necessary because it uniﬁes the
ARTICLE IN PRESS
M. Bauerly, Y. Liu / Int. J. Human-Computer Studies 64 (2006) 670–682 671

[Page 3]
elements of a display into a cohesive whole thus creating
integrity and meaning (
Locher et al., 1998 ). Pre-attentive
visual processing of balance can be accomplished within
100 ms (
Ognjenovic, 1991 ; Locher and Nagy, 1996 ) and
thus can quickly help to structure and guide the viewer’s
gaze through an image (
Locher, 1996 ).
Subject preferences for symmetry also exist for the same
reason as those for balance. Any composition with perfect
symmetry is by deﬁnition perfectly balanced and thus it
serves as an element that can be pre-attentively processed
and serves as a guide for the viewer. The preference for
symmetry is also grounded in sexual selection theories. For
example, cross-cultural preferences for symmetrical faces
may be explained by evolutionary processes that favor
symmetrical facial features, among other things (
Langlois
and Roggman, 1990 ). Additionally, symmetric faces may
reveal a higher level of ability to resist parasites and may
have indicated a stronger hunter in males. In females, many
symmetrical body and facial features that are considered
attractive may be indicators of higher fertility levels (
Buss
and Barnes, 1986 ).
The number of design elements or visual groups is also
related to aesthetic appraisal. Depending on the number
and size of the ‘compositional building blocks,’ a display
can appear empty and sparse or dense and overcrowded. A
high information density may cause perceptual channels to
become overloaded (
Cropper and Evans, 1968 ). Tullis
(1983) summarizes the recommendations for an appro-
priate level of density for alphanumeric displays but he
points out that it is not always possible to convert from one
density measure to another. This is particularly true when
using density as a measurement in modern bitmapped
displays.
The role of symmetry, grouping and balance in visual
perception has long been recognized by the Gestalt
theory of perceptual organization. ‘‘Gestalt’’ means
form or shape and, particularly, ‘‘good form’’ or ‘‘good
shape’’ that emerges when the parts of a perceived
object are grouped to form the perceptual whole (
Boring,
1950). Symmetry, grouping and balance are among the
numerous Gestalt principles that have been proposed to
describe how the perceptual elements are grouped
into recognizable whole objects or ‘‘good forms.’’ Accord-
ing to the Gestalt principles, the more symmetrical a
region’s shape, the more likely it is seen as a ﬁgure in
contrast to its background. Similarly, visual patterns
grouped together by similarity or proximity tend to be
seen as a whole ﬁgure and visual arrangements that are
more uniform and homogeneous tend to be perceived as
‘‘good forms.’’
These existing theories and research illustrate the
importance of balance, symmetry and grouping on
perception and preference. However, none of these
previous studies has adopted a mathematical approach
to quantify the joint effects of these variables on
user’s aesthetic judgment, which is the focus of the
present study.
1.1. Introduction to the experimental procedure
Two experiments are reported in this paper whose
purpose is twofold: to determine whether the metrics of
three interface compositional elements (symmetry, balance
and the number of compositional groups) reﬂect subject
ratings of those attributes and to determine whether there
is a relationship between the compositional elements and
subject ratings of aesthetic appeal. Numerical values
representing the three compositional elements are calcu-
lated for two different types of stimuli in the two
experiments. In Experiment 1, basic black and white
geometric images were used and in Experiment 2, web
pages following the exact same compositions as the images
from Experiment 1 were used to represent a real-world
interface situation.
The three visual elements of balance, symmetry and the
number of groups were chosen because they represent
simple, intuitive concepts in design and they are related
to the measures described or utilized earlier in the analysis
of alphanumeric displays. For example,
Streveler and
Wasserman (1984) proposed several types of screen
measures including the aesthetic measures of balance
and symmetry. The work by
Tullis (1984) on interface
usability metrics included the number of the groups.
In the current study, balance is derived from summing
the visual moments in the horizontal and vertical direc-
tions to zero about the balance point. Symmetry is
analyzed with a pixel-by-pixel comparison about a central
axis of reﬂection giving more inﬂuence to comparisons
closer to the axis because of the increased visual inﬂuence
in that area. The number of groups is a simple count of the
distinct visual groups that exist in an image. Because
rectangles or pictures are used as compositional elements
the number of groups is trivial to compute in both
experiments.

Streveler and
Wasserman (1984) proposed several types of screen
measures including the aesthetic measures of balance
and symmetry. The work by
Tullis (1984) on interface
usability metrics included the number of the groups.
In the current study, balance is derived from summing
the visual moments in the horizontal and vertical direc-
tions to zero about the balance point. Symmetry is
analyzed with a pixel-by-pixel comparison about a central
axis of reﬂection giving more inﬂuence to comparisons
closer to the axis because of the increased visual inﬂuence
in that area. The number of groups is a simple count of the
distinct visual groups that exist in an image. Because
rectangles or pictures are used as compositional elements
the number of groups is trivial to compute in both
experiments.
The validity of the quantitative analysis for symmetry
and balance was tested through subject ratings of
various images with the ratio-scale magnitude estima-
tion method. The experimental stimuli were created
according to target parameters for symmetry, balance
and composition elements and all were compared to a
benchmark image. Three experimental sessions were
completed where: (1) the subjects rated the aesthetic
appeal of the images compared to the benchmark;
(2) subjects ordered images from least appealing to most
appealing in a Balanced-Incomplete-Block (BIB) metho-
dology to establish an overall preference of the images;
and (3) subjects rated their impression of the image
balance and symmetry in both the horizontal and
vertical directions as well as rated the aesthetic appeal for
a second time.
The results show that subject responses validated the
methods for determining symmetry and balance. Addi-
tionally, aesthetic appeal was highly dependent on sym-
metry for the basic images in Experiment 1 and on the
number of groups for the web pages in Experiment 2.

2. Image quantiﬁcation methods
Three basic compositional attributes were each quanti-
ﬁed on individual scales. Simple algorithms were created in
an attempt to mimic the human cognitive representation of
the attributes of symmetry and balance, with the third
attribute being the number of compositional building
blocks used in the image.
2.1. Symmetry
Symmetry, s, is an analysis of the similarity of pixels on
opposite sides of an axis of reﬂection. This particular type
of symmetry is referred to as ‘bilateral symmetry’. This
algorithm takes a microscopic approach and compares
each half of an image pixel by pixel, as opposed to a
macroscopic view that might compare higher level elements
such as speciﬁc shapes or lines. It should also be noted that
this algorithm only considers symmetry about a vertical or
horizontal axis, but the general strategy can be utilized
about any axis of reﬂection.
It was hypothesized that those pixel comparisons that
are close to the axis of reﬂection have a higher inﬂuence on
the overall impression of symmetry than do comparisons
which are further away from the reﬂection axis. Take
Figs. 1 and 2 as illustrations of this assumption. Each
image is 5 /C2 6 pixels and has only one non-matching pixel
pair. Fig. 1 has a non-matching pixel pair closer to the
vertical axis of symmetry (at coordinates C3 and D3) than
does
Fig. 2 (at coordinates A3 and F3). According to the
algorithm discussed below, Fig. 1 is less symmetric than
Fig. 2 because as the pixel comparisons move farther away
from the axis of reﬂection, their inﬂuence on the overall
symmetry values are decreased.

The variable n is the number of comparisons required
in each row or column of pixels. Taking the case where
the axis of reﬂection is again vertical, the number of
comparisons is the image width in pixels divided by 2 when
the width is an even number of pixels, or it is the image
width less 1 divided by 2 when the width is odd. The
